episodes.title: The Last Layer of Light
episodes.opening:
The architecture studio smells like spray adhesive and cold coffee. Near the north windows, a tall graduate student taps the northwest corner of a large sketch with a mechanical pencil, patient as a metronome. Stacks of paper models crowd his desk, and one small house sits apart, its edges warped and stained.

He notices you and straightens up.

"I'm Yanzhou, architecture grad. The drawings just need the final layer of lighting. Would you sit closer and take a look at this part for me?"
episodes.dialogue:
He pulls a second stool over with his foot, then slides a lamp down the desk edge.

"This corner. The client review is tomorrow morning, and I can't tell anymore whether the evening light actually reaches the reading nook. I've been staring so long my eyes have stopped being honest. Sit there—no, one chair over. There. Now tell me what you see when I angle it."

He tilts the lamp in slow increments, watching your face instead of the paper.

"Good. Stop. There—that gray band along the floor. That's what I wanted. A person reading there at six in the evening gets exactly that much sun before it goes."

He writes a measurement on the margin, then catches you looking at the stained little house and doesn't rush to hide it.

"That one took a month. Two nights ago a storm came through and a pipe in the ceiling let go right over my desk. I stayed up all night trying to save it—hair dryer, tweezers, the whole absurd ritual. The walls dried crooked."

He turns the model a few degrees, so the warped facade catches the window light.

"Everyone keeps saying, rebuild it, you have time. But the review is about whether the house feels like somewhere you'd want to wait out the rain. And right now I look at it and I can't tell if it does. That's the part I can't fix with tweezers."

He laughs quietly at himself, and begins collecting the paper scraps around the lamp into a neat pile, one by one, like counting breaths.

"Sorry. You came in for a quiet corner and got a confession. The truth is I think better when my hands are tidying something."

He holds up a scrap—a curl of pale blue card stock.

"Actually. If you're around tomorrow evening, I'll be free at seven. There's a bench by the lotus pond where the light does something worth watching at that hour. I owe you one honest opinion about whether this corner works. I'd rather return it in better light than this lamp."

choices.text: Then I'll hold you to it—seven o'clock, the lotus pond bench. Bring the crooked house if it survives the review.
choices.response: He blinks, then something in his shoulders loosens. "Seven. I'll bring it, crookedness and all. A building that's been through a flood deserves to be seen by someone who heard the whole sorry story and still asked to see it." He writes the time on the corner of the sketch, small and exact, as if the paper itself might forget.

choices.text: (You pick up the nearest handful of paper scraps and sort them onto his pile, matching colors without a word.)
choices.response: He watches your hands work for a moment, then joins in without comment, and the desk clears faster than it would have alone. When the last scrap lands, he says, "See, that's the thing. Spaces are just this—someone quietly helping with the small stuff." He taps the bench appointment into his phone himself.

episodes.ending: The review goes the way reviews go—half praise, half surgery. But at seven, a message arrives with a single photo: the crooked house on the lotus pond bench, evening light lying along its warped roof like an apology. Beneath it: "It survived. The corner works. Same bench, if you're still coming." The studio has one more person in it who knows your name.

episodes.title: Water Under Old Roofs
episodes.opening:
A week of passing hellos has turned into a habit: he saves the window seat, you bring the coffee, and he moves your cup three centimeters to the left so the light falls perfectly on whatever he's explaining. Today the studio is emptier than usual—most of the program is away on a trip to Hongcun.

He slides a thick report across the table instead of a sketch.
episodes.dialogue:
"Everyone else is at Moon Pond right now, photographing the same reflection from the same three angles." He taps the report's cover. "I went two years ago and spent the whole trip looking down instead of out."

He opens it to a hand-drawn section of an old Huizhou house.

"See this channel? It runs under the whole courtyard. Rain hits the roof, the roof hands it to the eaves, the eaves hand it to the stone, the stone carries it to a cistern under the kitchen. Nothing is wasted, and none of it is hidden. The builders made drainage beautiful on purpose. Water moving through a house was considered good fortune—literally. They built the luck in."

He slows down, the way he does when he's in his own territory.

"When I came back I gave a talk on it. Just our department, one evening. I expected six people and a lot of yawning. Instead the old craftsmen the department keeps on retainer showed up—one of them had built channels like these with his own hands. He corrected two of my drawings on the spot, gently, like fixing a child's homework. The discussion afterward ran two weeks. People were arguing about water in the stairwells."

He turns a page to a printed citation and doesn't point at it, just lets it sit there.

"That talk got written up eventually. It's cited now, in the proper boring way. Some paper on the aesthetics of traditional water systems. My name is in the footnotes, which is exactly where I like it."

He closes the report and looks out the window at the empty campus.

"I'm telling you this because of the house that got flooded, I think. The one on my desk. Everyone said rebuild it, and I did, and it's fine now. But the reason I stayed up all night with the hair dryer wasn't the deadline. When I was in Hongcun, an old woman saw me sketching her courtyard and brought me tea, and I sat under her eaves while rain came off the roof in a curtain, a full sheet of falling water, and I thought—this is what I've been trying to draw my whole life and I keep missing it."

He straightens the report's corner against the table edge.

"Anyway. That's the story behind the footnotes. You're the first person here who's heard it."

choices.text: The curtain of rain off her eaves—did it ever make it into a drawing, or is it still just yours?
choices.response: He's quiet a moment. "Still mine. Every version I draw of it turns into a diagram and the diagram kills it." He taps the report. "Maybe that's the real project, then. The curtain. Ask me again someday whether I've managed it. I'd like having someone who asks."

choices.text: (You turn the report back to the section drawing and trace the channel under the courtyard with one finger, slowly, all the way to the cistern.)
choices.response: He watches your finger travel the water's whole route. "You read it correctly," he says softly. "End to end, no shortcuts. Most people stop at the pretty part." He refills your cup without being asked, and the afternoon settles into the kind of silence that doesn't need filling.

episodes.ending: The department returns from Hongcun with four hundred near-identical photos, and he never does get around to seeing them. Instead, the report stays on the window seat as a shared reference, and he starts leaving small questions in its margins—about light, about water, about whether a house can hold luck. The footnotes have become a conversation between the two of you.

episodes.title: The Material Room at Midnight
episodes.opening:
The material room in the basement of the department building holds twenty years of discarded competition models, and tonight Yanzhou has claimed it. Shelves of acrylic offcuts, bent balsa, orphaned foam core. His thesis model is due in nine days, and his budget for materials is effectively zero.

He hands you a dust mask and a box labeled in his careful handwriting: ACRYLIC — BY TRANSPARENCY, 1–12.
episodes.dialogue:
"I found this room by accident last month. Decades of models, thrown in whole. There's usable acrylic in here worth thousands." He lifts a sheet to the overhead light, checking its clarity against his fingers. "The thesis model needs a glass facade I can't afford. So. Twelve boxes, sorted by transparency, and somewhere in box nine or ten there's my facade."

The work is slow and quiet and oddly calming. He sorts the way he tidies scraps—completely.

"Here's the honest problem," he says after a while, not looking up. "My advisor wants the facade in clear acrylic with visible seams. Structural, legible, safe. But the whole point of the design is that the wall should disappear at dusk, and seams are exactly what doesn't disappear. If I cut the panels to hide the seams, the joints get weaker. If the joints get weaker, the review committee asks why my building falls down in a strong wind."

He sets the sheet down and finally looks at you.

"Nine days. I can have strong, or I can have gone-at-dusk, and I've been walking past both options for a week pretending I hadn't noticed them. My fear has always been the same one— that what I build comes out clever but cold. Compromise on the core structure and I'll feel it every time I look at it."

He picks up the sheet again and holds it toward the light at an angle, and something shifts in his face.

"Wait. Look. If I orient the seams along the light's path instead of against it—at dusk they'd read as part of the light, not a break in it. The seam becomes the design instead of the failure."

He laughs, short and real.

"I've been staring at this for a week and it took two hours of sorting garbage with someone to see it. Not solved—box ten might not have enough clear sheet, and the joints still need testing, and nine days is nine days. But it's a direction instead of a wall."

He starts writing on the box in pencil: SEAM ALONG LIGHT PATH — TEST AT DUSK.

"The younger students have started stealing from my boxes, by the way. I caught one yesterday. So I'm labeling everything." He holds up a scrap with a tiny hand-drawn instruction on it, almost fond. "The room's becoming something. I don't know what yet."

choices.text: Test at dusk—then box ten, my hands, and your dusk. Nine days is enough if we stop pretending it isn't.
choices.response: He looks at you over the mask, and the tiredness in his eyes turns into something steadier. "All right. Dusk tests, both of us, starting tomorrow." He writes your initials next to his on the box, then adds, quietly, "That helps more than the acrylic would."

choices.text: (You pick up the next unsorted tray and begin matching sheets to the transparency scale, box by box, working until the tray is empty.)
choices.response: He works alongside you in the same rhythm, and an hour passes before he speaks. "You sort like you trust the system," he says. "That's rarer than you'd think." He slides the finished box onto the shelf himself, then adds two more empty boxes beside it—one of them, you notice, labeled with a blank space where a second name could go.

episodes.ending: Over the following days the basement fills with evening light tests, pencil notes, and younger students who come for scraps and leave with hand-drawn instructions. The thesis model gets built—seams running with the light, joints tested twice. It's a direction that held. On the shelf, the twelve boxes acquire a second set of handwriting.

episodes.title: An Invitation, Measured Twice
episodes.opening:
The thesis is defended, the model survived, and the material room's twelve boxes are now officially the department's recycling library. To mark it, Yanzhou has mounted a small evening exhibit in the studio: the rebuilt flooded house, the thesis model, and—new since the defense—a paper shelter with a transparent south wall, sized exactly for a cat.

He's waiting by it, hands in his pockets, more nervous than he's been at any review.
episodes.dialogue:
"You've seen everything else I've made," he says. "But not this one. I built it in secret, which is a stupid thing to do with a cat shelter, since cats keep no confidentiality agreements."

He tilts the shelter so the interior catches the lamp.

"The campus strays sleep badly in winter—wind comes off the lake and there's nowhere warm that isn't under an engine. So. Raised floor, south wall in that acrylic from box ten, angled to hold the afternoon sun. I tested it with a hot water bottle and a borrowed cat. The cat approved. Eventually."

He straightens the shelter a millimeter, then makes himself stop.

"Here's the thing. The facilities office approved one trial placement by the lake—starting this weekend, and they want a person present for the first evening. To see whether the cats actually use it, and to be a known face if anyone has questions. I asked for that job. It's mine if I show up."

He finally looks at you directly.

"And I realized I didn't want to do the first evening alone. That's the invitation. This. Sitting by a lake at dusk, waiting to see if a cat trusts something I built, with you."

He rubs the back of his neck.

"I've thought about how to say this for two weeks, which is embarrassing, so I'll say it plainly and then give you room. Some people I'd want there as my closest friend—the person who sorted acrylic with me at midnight and never once made it feel like a favor. And with some people, honestly, I'd want it to be more than that. With you, I've been hoping for the second and I'd be glad of the first. Both are true. You don't owe me an answer tonight, and whichever it is, the shelter, the boxes, and the lotus pond bench all stay exactly as they are."

choices.text: Then let it be more. I'll be there at dusk—as the person who's been hoping for this too.
choices.response: He exhales like he's been holding that breath for two weeks. "More," he repeats, testing the word the way he tests a material. "Then it's settled, and I'll bring tea, and I won't move your cup three centimeters this time—I'll leave it exactly where you put it." The shelter between you seems, absurdly, to warm the room.

choices.text: "Closest friend, then—gladly. I'll bring the thermos and we'll name the first cat to claim it together."
choices.response: His smile arrives slowly and lands fully. "Closest friend. Good. That word has never once disappointed me." He taps the shelter's roof. "Thermos, dusk, naming rights shared. Some partnerships are better than romances at holding a building up. I intend to keep this one for a long time."

episodes.ending: The weekend comes, and the shelter stands by the lake with its transparent south wall aimed at the setting sun. At dusk the first cat appears, inspects the seams, and steps inside. Yanzhou writes the time in his notebook, then writes a second line, and doesn't read either aloud.

episodes.title: The Long Maintenance
episodes.opening:
A year on, the shelter by the lake is on its third roof, the recycling library has forty boxes and a laminated sign, and the lotus pond bench has a small brass plate neither of you ever mentions directly. Graduation came and went; Yanzhou stayed on as a researcher and, unofficially, as the department's keeper of discarded materials.

Today he's repainting the shelter's raised floor and has saved the second brush for you.
episodes.dialogue:
"Third roof," he says, dipping his brush. "The first two were education. Wind off the lake is a client with strong opinions."

The work settles into its old rhythm—him precise, you steady, the lake doing its light thing in the background.

"I've been offered a studio position in another city. Real salary, real buildings, the kind of facade I'd never get to touch here." He says it evenly, the way he reads a drawing aloud. "I'm taking it. In the fall."

He watches the paint go on, then adds, "The hard part is that the shelter, the library, and the bench don't move. So I've spent a month drafting something, and I'd rather hand it to you than to a committee."

He pulls a folded sheet from his jacket: a hand-drawn maintenance charter, absurdly thorough. Roof inspection every season. Box inventory twice a year. One evening at the bench, whenever either of you is in town, with tea.

"You sorted the first twelve boxes. You tested the seams at dusk. The younger students already call the library yours half the time. I'm asking you to hold these three things with me, across whatever distance the city puts between us. Co-signers. Equal, boring, permanent."

He holds out a pencil.

"I signed already. Mine's there, under the roof clause, because I'm claiming the roof and you get the boxes, and we split the bench. If you sign, I'll frame the original and leave a copy in box one, where the thieves started."

The lake flickers. A cat—descendant, plausibly, of the first tenant—supervises from the south wall.

"And the other thing I wanted to say," he adds, quieter, "is that the curtain of rain from Hongcun finally made it into a drawing last month. It took a year, and a friend who kept asking about water in the margins of that old report until I stopped drawing it alone. You should see it before I ship it off. It's yours first."

choices.text: Co-signer, gladly. Roof, boxes, bench—and I'm holding you to the tea clause every single visit.
choices.response: He passes the pencil like it weighs something. When your signature lands beside his, he studies the pair of names for a long moment. "There," he says. "Structurally sound." He rolls the charter with the care he gives a model, and the first visit's tea is scheduled before the paint dries.

choices.text: (You take the pencil, sign under the roof clause without ceremony, then hand the charter back and pick up your brush to finish the floor.)
choices.response: He accepts the signature the way he accepts a correct measurement—no speech, just a nod and a small exhale. Then he kneels and finishes the far side of the floor beside you, brush in rhythm with yours, and says only, "Good. Now it's real," and the two of you work until the coat is even.

episodes.ending: The framed charter hangs in the recycling library, and a copy lives in box one where the thieves started. In the fall he leaves for the new city, and the three small holdings carry on: seasonal roofs, counted boxes, tea at the bench. Some friendships are built the way he builds—slowly, load-bearing, meant to be maintained rather than admired. The maintenance schedule, like the friendship, has no end date.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Seams Along the Light
romance.opening:
A year on, the shelter by the lake has its third roof, the recycling library has forty boxes, and the lotus pond bench has a small brass plate with no words on it, which was his idea and still makes him pleased every time he walks past. Graduation came and went; Yanzhou stayed on as a researcher, and the two of you have kept the dusk tests, the tea, and the naming of every cat who ever moved in.

Tonight he's waiting at the shelter with a drawing tube and two cups of tea already poured.
romance.dialogue:
"Sit," he says. "The light does its best work in about four minutes, and I timed the tea to it."

You sit. The south wall glows amber, and inside, a cat who answers to Box Ten is pretending not to care.

"I'm leaving in the fall," he says, without ceremony. "A studio position. Another city. Real buildings, the kind of facade I'd never get to touch here. I said yes last week."

He lets that sit, then opens the drawing tube.

"Before you say anything—this first. You remember the rain curtain in Hongcun. The old woman's eaves, the sheet of falling water I could never draw without turning it into a diagram." He unrolls the sheet across both your knees, weighted at the corners with the tea cups.

It's the eaves, the falling water, and—drawn into the transparent sheet of rain, in the same line weight as everything else, easy to miss until you don't—two small figures on a bench, one of them holding a cup.

"It took a year," he says. "And it took every question you left in the margins of that water report, and every dusk since. I stopped trying to draw the rain alone. That was the whole problem. The rain needed someone in it."

He looks at the drawing rather than at you, which is how he says the difficult things.

"So here's my proposal, stated plainly, because every plan we've ever set together—the bench, the boxes, the dusk tests—has been kept, and I've decided to keep setting them. Different cities, same water system. I'll design buildings there that make people pause and breathe. Here, we keep the roof, the boxes, the bench, and every visit gets tea and the four best minutes of light. Two full lives, deliberately running through the same channel. Like the old builders. Nothing wasted, nothing hidden."

He finally turns from the drawing.

"I'm not asking you to answer tonight. But if the answer is yes, I'd like to move your cup three centimeters to the left. The light will fall perfectly on the figures. I checked."

choices.text: Yes—two lives, one channel. Move the cup. I want to see us in the rain properly.
choices.response: He moves the cup three centimeters, and the light settles exactly where he said it would, on the two small figures in the falling water. "There," he says softly. "That's the drawing finished." He reaches over and, briefly, covers your hand with his—one touch, measured and sure, then back to his own cup, as if the point was made and didn't need repeating.

choices.text: (You reach over and move his cup three centimeters to the left instead, then look at him.)
choices.response: He stares at the relocated cup, then laughs—short, real, the material-room laugh. "Outmaneuvered by my own system," he says. "The light's on you now, and honestly, that's the better placement." He covers your hand with his, brief and warm, and neither of you moves the cups again.

romance.ending: In the fall he leaves, and the city gets an architect who designs for pausing and breathing, and the campus keeps its shelter, its library, and its brass plate with no words. The drawing ships to a competition, then comes home to hang above his desk there. Every visit: tea, the bench, four minutes of light, a roof inspected together. The rain curtain finally has people in it, and the water runs end to end.

episodes.title: 最后一层光影
episodes.opening:
建筑系工作室里弥漫着喷胶和冷咖啡的气味。北窗边，一个高个子的研究生正用机械铅笔轻点大幅草图的西北角，耐心得像节拍器。桌上堆着一摞摞纸模型，只有一座小房子单独放在一旁，边缘翘曲，还带着水渍。

他注意到你，直起身来。

“我叫宋砚舟，建筑系的。图纸还差最后一层光影。你愿意坐近一点，替我看看这里吗？”
episodes.dialogue:
他用脚勾过另一张凳子，又把台灯沿桌沿推了过来。

“就是这个角。明天早上客户评审，可我已经看不出傍晚的光到底照不照得到那个读书角了。盯得太久，眼睛都开始说谎了。坐那儿——不对，过去一张椅子。对。我调角度的时候，你告诉我看到了什么。”

他一点点缓缓倾斜台灯，看的却是你的脸，不是图纸。

“好。停。就是那里——地板上那条灰色的光带。这就是我想要的。傍晚六点坐在那儿看书的人，在天黑前正好能晒到这么多太阳。”

他在页边写下一个尺寸，然后发现你在看那座带水渍的小房子，也没有急着把它藏起来。

“那座做了一个月。两天前夜里来了场暴雨，天花板上一根水管正好爆在我桌子正上方。我熬了一整夜想救它——吹风机、镊子，整套荒唐的抢救流程。墙干是干了，全歪了。”

他把模型转了几度，让翘曲的立面迎着窗光。

“所有人都说，重做一个吧，你有时间。可评审真正要看的是这座房子让人觉得，愿不愿意在这里躲一场雨。而现在我看着它，连自己也说不上来。这才是镊子修不好的部分。”

他低声笑了笑，然后开始把台灯周围的纸屑一片片收拢成一小堆，像在数呼吸。

“抱歉。你只是想找个安静的角落，结果听了一场忏悔。说实话，我手上一边整理东西，脑子才转得清楚。”

他举起一片纸屑——一卷淡蓝色的卡纸。

“对了。如果你明晚有空，我七点没事。莲花池边有条长椅，那个钟点的光值得一看。我还欠你一句关于这个角落行不行的实话。与其用这盏灯还，不如换个更好的光线还。”

choices.text: 那我就不客气了——七点，莲花池长椅。要是那座歪房子能挺过评审，就把它带来。
choices.response: 他眨了眨眼，肩膀上有什么东西松了下来。“七点。我把它带来，歪着也带。一座经历过水灾的房子，值得被一个听完整段狼狈故事、还主动想见它的人看到。”他把时间写在草图一角，小小的，一笔一画，好像怕纸自己会忘记。

choices.text: （你拿起手边的一把纸屑，默默按颜色分好，归到他那一小堆上。）
choices.response: 他看了一会儿你手上的动作，然后什么也没说，跟着一起整理，桌子清得比一个人干快多了。最后一片纸屑落定时，他说：“你看，就是这样。空间说到底就是这个——有人安安静静地帮你收拾小事。”他自己在手机里敲下了长椅之约。

episodes.ending: 评审就是评审那副样子——一半是夸奖，一半是动刀。但七点整，一条消息来了，只有一张照片：那座歪房子摆在莲花池的长椅上，傍晚的光沿着它翘曲的屋顶铺开，像一句道歉。照片下面写着：“它挺过来了。那个角落没问题。还是那条长椅，如果你还来的话。”工作室里，从此多了一个知道你名字的人。

episodes.title: 老屋檐下的水
episodes.opening:
一周以来，见面打声招呼渐渐成了习惯：他占靠窗的位子，你带咖啡来，他把你的杯子往左挪三公分，让光线刚好落在他要讲解的地方。今天的工作室比平时空得多——系里大部分人都去宏村考察了。

他推过桌面的不是草图，而是一份厚厚的报告。
episodes.dialogue:
“现在所有人都在月沼，从同样三个角度拍同一片倒影。”他轻点报告封面。“我两年前去过，整个行程都在低头看，而不是抬头看外面。”

他翻开报告，是一栋老徽州民居的手绘剖面图。

“看到这条水道了吗？它从整个院子底下穿过。雨落在屋顶，屋顶交给屋檐，屋檐交给石头，石头把水引到厨房下面的蓄水池里。没有一滴被浪费，也没有一处被藏起来。造房子的人是有意把排水做美的。水从屋里流过被视为福气——是字面意思的福气。他们把好运直接砌进了房子里。”

他放慢了语速，就像谈到自己领地时那样。

“回来之后，我做了一次关于这个的讲演。就我们系的人，某个晚上。我以为会有六个人来，加上呵欠连天。结果系里长期聘着的那几位老工匠都来了——其中一位亲手砌过这样的水道。他当场改了我的两张图，手法很温和，像批改小孩子的作业。之后的讨论持续了两个星期。大家连在楼梯间里都在争水的事。”

他翻到一页印出来的引用文献，没有指给你看，就让它那样摆着。

“那次讲演后来被写进了论文。现在被引用了，用那种正经又无聊的方式。有篇关于传统水系统美学的论文。我的名字在脚注里——那正是我喜欢待的位置。”

他合上报告，望向窗外空荡荡的校园。

“我跟你说这些，我想是因为那栋被水淹的房子。桌上那栋。所有人都说重建，我照做了，现在它没问题了。但我熬夜守着吹风机，不是为了赶截止日期。当年在宏村，一位老奶奶看见我在画她家院子，给我端来了茶。我在她屋檐下坐着，雨水从屋顶垂下来，像一整幅水帘，一整面往下落的水。我那时候想——这就是我这辈子一直想画的东西，可我总是一再错过。”

他把报告的边角在桌沿上对齐。

“总之，这就是脚注背后的故事。你是这里第一个听我讲的人。”

choices.text: 她屋檐下那道水帘——后来有没有画进图里？还是说，它至今仍只属于你？
choices.response: 他安静了片刻。“仍然只属于我。每次我把它画出来，它都变成一张示意图，而示意图会杀死它。”他轻敲那份报告。“那也许这才是真正要做的项目。是那道水帘。改天再问问我是不是做到了。我希望有个人会这么问。”

choices.text: （你把报告翻回那张剖面图，用一根手指沿着院子底下的水道缓缓描画，一直描到蓄水池。）
choices.response: 他看着你的手指走完水的整条路线。“你看懂了，”他轻声说。“从头到尾，没有走捷径。大多数人只停在漂亮的那一段。”他没等你开口就替你续了杯，午后便沉进一种不需要填补的安静里。

episodes.ending: 系里的人从宏村带回了四百张几乎一模一样的照片，他却始终没去看。那份报告留在靠窗的座位上，成了你们共用的参考资料，他开始在页边留下一些小小的提问——关于光，关于水，关于一栋房子能不能盛住福气。脚注，变成了你们两个人之间的对话。

episodes.title: 午夜的材料间
episodes.opening:
系馆地下室的材料间堆着二十年来的落选竞赛模型，今晚被宋砚舟征用了。架子上有亚克力边角料、弯折的轻木、无主的泡沫板。他的毕业设计模型九天后就要交，而他的材料预算实际上等于零。

他递给你一只防尘口罩，还有一个纸箱，上面是他工整的字迹：亚克力——按透光度，1—12。
episodes.dialogue:
“上个月我误打误撞发现了这间屋子。几十年的模型，整个整个地被扔进来。里面能用的亚克力值好几千。”他举起一块板材对着头顶的灯，用手指检查它的通透度。“毕设模型需要一面玻璃幕墙，我买不起。所以。十二个箱子，按透明度分好，第九或第十个箱子里，会有我的幕墙。”

工作又慢又安静，却出奇地让人心定。他分拣的样子和他整理模型碎屑时一样——彻底。

“说个实在的问题，”过了一会儿他开口，头也没抬。“导师要幕墙用透明亚克力，接缝可见。结构清晰、可读、安全。可这个设计的全部意义，就在于那面墙在黄昏时会消失，而接缝恰恰是最不会消失的东西。如果我把板材切开藏起接缝，节点强度就会变弱。节点一弱，评审委员会就会问，为什么我的房子一阵大风就塌。”

他放下板材，终于抬眼看你。

“九天。我要么选结实，要么选黄昏时消失，而这两个选项我绕着走了一个星期，装作没看见。我的恐惧一直只有一个——我做出来的东西，聪明，但冷。要是在核心结构上妥协，那之后我每次看到它都会心里发堵。”

他又拿起那块板材，斜着举向灯光，脸上的神情忽然变了。

“等等。你看。如果我把接缝顺着光线的走向排，而不是逆着它——黄昏时，接缝就会像光的一部分，而不是光里的一道断口。接缝就成了设计本身。”

他笑了一声，短促，却是真的。

“我对着这个问题盯了一个星期，结果跟人一起分了两个小时的垃圾才看见答案。还没解决——第十个箱子未必有足够的透明板，节点也还得测试，九天就是九天。但这至少是一个方向。”

他开始用铅笔在箱子上写字：接缝顺光——黄昏测试。

“对了，低年级的学生已经开始偷我箱子里的东西了。昨天抓到一个。所以我现在什么都贴标签。”他举起一块碎料，上面画着一条小小的手写说明，语气几乎带着点宠溺。“这间屋子正在变成一个什么东西。我还不知道是什么。”

choices.text: 黄昏测试——那第十个箱子、我的双手、还有你的黄昏，都算上。只要别再装看不见，九天够了。
choices.response: 他从口罩上方看着你，眼里的疲惫变成了某种更沉稳的东西。“好。黄昏测试，我们两个一起，从明天开始。”他在箱子上自己名字旁边写下你的名字缩写，然后轻声补了一句，“这比那堆亚克力管用多了。”

choices.text: （你拿起下一格还没分拣的托盘，开始把板材对照透光度分档，一格一格地做，直到托盘见空。）
choices.response: 他和你用同样的节奏一起干起来，一个小时过去他才开口。“你分拣的样子，像是真的信任这套方法，”他说。“这比你想象的少见。”他亲手把分好的箱子推上架子，又在旁边多摆了两个空箱——你注意到，其中一个上面留了一块空白，正好够写第二个名字。

episodes.ending: 接下来的几天，地下室里满是傍晚的光线测试、铅笔笔记，还有来捡边角料、带着手绘说明离开的低年级学生。毕设模型建成了——接缝顺着光走，节点测了两遍。这是一个撑住了的方向。架子上，那十二个箱子上多出了一手新的字迹。

episodes.title: 量了两次的邀请
episodes.opening:
毕业答辩结束，模型完好存活，材料间那十二个纸箱也正式成了系里的回收图书馆。为了纪念这件事，宋砚舟在工作室里布置了一场小小的晚间展览：重新修好的被水淹的房子、毕业设计模型，还有——答辩之后新做的——一个纸制猫窝，南墙是透明的，尺寸刚好够一只猫住。

他站在猫窝旁边等着，双手插在口袋里，比任何一次评审都紧张。
episodes.dialogue:
“我做的其他东西你都看过了，”他说，“唯独这个没有。它是偷偷做的——给猫窝保密其实是件蠢事，猫又不签保密协议。”

他把猫窝倾斜过来，让内部接住灯光。

“校里的流浪猫冬天睡不好——湖边风大，暖和的地方只有发动机底下。所以。架空的地板，南墙用的是第十箱里的那块亚克力，斜一个角度，好接住午后的太阳。我用热水袋和一只借来的猫测过。猫最终批准了。”

他把猫窝摆正了一毫米，然后强迫自己停下。

“事情是这样的。后勤处批准了一个试摆位置，在湖边——这个周末开始，而且第一天晚上他们要求有人在现场。看看猫到底用不用它，万一有人有疑问，也好有个熟脸。那个差事是我主动要的。只要我到场，就是我的。”

他终于直接看向你。

“然后我发现，我不想一个人度过第一晚。这才是邀请。是这件事。黄昏时分坐在湖边，等一只猫决定要不要信任我造的东西——和你一起。”

他揉了揉后颈。

“这句话我想了两个星期该怎么开口，挺丢人的，所以我就直说，说完给你留出余地。有些人，我会希望他们以挚友的身份在场——就是那个半夜陪我分拣亚克力、从来没让这件事显得像帮忙的人。而对有些人，说实话，我会希望不止如此。对你是哪一种，我一直盼着是后者，但前者我也求之不得。两句话都是真的。你不用今晚给我答案，不管答案是什么，猫窝、纸箱、还有莲花池长椅，都原样留着。”

choices.text: 那就让它不止如此吧。黄昏的时候我会在场——作为同样盼着这一天的人。
choices.response: 他长长吐出一口气，像是憋了两个星期。“不止如此。”他重复了一遍，像检验材料一样检验着这个词。“那就说定了，我会带茶来，这次也不会把你的杯子挪三公分——你放在哪儿，就让它待在哪儿。”你之间的那个猫窝，仿佛荒谬地让整个房间都暖了起来。

choices.text: 那就做你最亲近的挚友——我很乐意。我会带上保温壶，第一只入住的猫，我们俩一起给它起名字。
choices.response: 他的笑容来得缓慢，落得踏实。“挚友，好。这个词从来没让我失望过。”他轻敲猫窝的屋顶。“保温壶，黄昏，起名权共享。有些伙伴关系，撑起一栋建筑比恋爱还稳。我打算把这一份维持很久很久。”

episodes.ending: 周末到了，猫窝立在湖边，透明的南墙朝着落日。黄昏时分，第一只猫出现了，查看接缝，然后走了进去。宋砚舟在本子上写下时间，又写下一行，两行都没有念出声。

episodes.title: 长期维护
episodes.opening:
一年过去，湖边的猫窝已经换了第三版屋顶，回收图书馆有了四十个箱子，还挂了块塑封的牌子，而莲花池长椅上有块小小的铜牌，你们俩谁都没正面提起过。毕业季来了又走；宋砚舟留校做了研究员，还有一个不成文的身份——系里废弃材料的看管人。

今天他在给猫窝的架空地板刷漆，特意给你留了第二把刷子。
episodes.dialogue:
“第三版屋顶，”他蘸了蘸漆说，“前两版都是学费。湖面上的风，是个很有主见的甲方。”

活儿又回到了从前的节奏——他精细，你稳当，湖在背景里自顾自地玩着光影。

“另一个城市给了我一个工作室的职位。真正的薪水，真正的建筑，还有那种在这儿根本摸不到机会的幕墙。”他说得很平静，像在念一张图纸，“我打算去。秋天走。”

他看着漆一点点刷上去，又补了一句：“难的是猫窝、图书馆和长椅，它们搬不走。所以我画了一个月图，这份东西，我宁愿交给你，也不想交给什么委员会。”

他从外套里抽出一张折好的纸：一份手绘的维护章程，细致得近乎夸张。每季度检查屋顶。每半年盘点箱子。只要两个人里有谁在这个城市，就找个晚上去长椅坐坐，配茶。

“头十二个箱子是你整理的。黄昏测试接缝也是你做的。学弟学妹们早就一半时间把那图书馆叫成你的了。我要你和我一起守着这三样东西，不管那座城市在我们之间隔多远。共同签署人。平等的、无聊的、永久的。”

他递出一支铅笔。

“我已经签了。我的名字在那儿，屋顶条款下面——因为我认领了屋顶，箱子归你，长椅我们平分。你要是签了，我就把原件装框，在第一个箱子里放一份复印件，就是当初小偷动手的那个箱子。”

湖面闪着光。一只猫——多半是第一任房客的后代——在南墙边上监工。

“还有件事想说，”他放轻了声音，“宏村那场雨帘，上个月终于画进一张图里了。花了整整一年，还有一个朋友，一直在旧报告的页边空白处问我水的事，直到我不再一个人画为止。我寄走之前，你应该先看看。它是你的，第一个看。”

choices.text: 共同签署人，我很乐意。屋顶、箱子、长椅——还有，每次见面我都可要让你兑现喝茶那条。
choices.response: 他把铅笔递过来，像递一件有分量的东西。当你的签名落在他名字旁边时，他盯着并排的两个名字看了很久。“好了，”他说，“结构上没问题。”他像对待模型一样仔细地把章程卷起来，而第一次喝茶的约定，在漆干之前就定好了。

choices.text: （你接过铅笔，不由分说地在屋顶条款下面签了名，然后把章程递回去，拿起刷子继续刷地板。）
choices.response: 他接过签名，就像接受一个精确的测量数据——没有长篇大论，只是点了点头，轻轻呼出一口气。然后他蹲下来，在你旁边把地板另一侧刷完，刷子的节奏和你的一致，只说了一句：“好。现在它成真了。”你们俩一直干到漆面均匀为止。

episodes.ending: 装框的章程挂在回收图书馆里，复印件放在当初小偷动手的那个箱子里。秋天他去了那座新的城市，而三份小小的产业继续运转：按季换的屋顶，清点的箱子，长椅上的茶。有些友情，就像他造房子一样——慢慢建，承重，是要长期维护的。这份维护日程，就像这份友情，没有截止日期。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 光影里的接缝
romance.opening:
一年过去，湖边的猫窝已经换了第三任屋顶，回收图书馆攒到了四十个箱子，莲花池长椅上多了一块小小的铜牌，上面什么字也没有——这是他的主意，每次路过他还是暗自得意。毕业季来了又走；宋砚舟留校做了研究员，你们俩把黄昏测试、那杯茶、还有给每只搬进来的猫起名字的习惯，都留了下来。

今晚，他带着一筒图纸在猫窝等你，两杯茶已经倒好。
romance.dialogue:
“坐。”他说，“光线最好的时候只有大概四分钟，我掐着表泡的茶。”

你坐下。南墙被照成琥珀色，里面一只应名儿叫“十号箱”的猫，装作毫不在意的样子。

“我秋天要走。”他毫不铺垫地说，“一个工作室的职位。另一座城市。真正的建筑，那种在这里永远碰不到的幕墙。上周我答应了。”

他停了停，让这句话落地，然后打开图纸筒。

“你先别急着说话——先看这个。你还记得宏村的那道雨帘。老太太家的屋檐，那片往下落的水，我怎么画都会画成一张示意图。”他把图纸在你们两人的膝盖上摊开，四个角用茶杯压住。

那是屋檐，是落下的水，还有——画在那层透明的雨幕里，线重和其他部分一模一样，不留神根本发现不了——长椅上的两个小小的人影，其中一个手里端着杯子。

“画了一年。”他说，“也用了你写在那份水报告页边上的每一个问题，还有从那以后的每一个黄昏。我不再试着只画雨了。问题原来在这儿。雨里得有人。”

他看着图纸，而不是看着你——他就是用这种方式说那些难开口的话的。

“所以我的提议是，明明白白地说出来：我们立下的每一个计划——长椅、箱子、黄昏测试——全都守住了，所以我决定继续立下去。不同的城市，同一条水系。我在那边设计让人驻足呼吸的建筑。这边，屋顶、箱子、长椅照旧，每次回来都有茶，有光线最好的那四分钟。是两段完整的人生，有意识地流进同一条水道。像那些老匠人一样。一点不浪费，一点不隐瞒。”

他终于从图纸上抬起头。

“不用今晚回答我。但如果答案是愿意，我想把你的杯子往左移三公分。光会正好落在那两个人影上。我核对过了。”

choices.text: 愿意——两段人生，同一条水道。移杯子吧。我想好好看清雨里的我们。
choices.response: 他把杯子移了三公分，光落下的位置和他说的分毫不差，正好在那片落水里两个小小的人影上。“好了。”他轻声说，“这张图，画完了。”他伸过手来，短暂地覆住你的手——一次触碰，克制而笃定，然后收回自己的杯子，仿佛该说的已经说了，不必再重复。

choices.text: （你伸过手去，把他的杯子往左移了三公分，然后看着他。）
choices.response: 他盯着那个被挪了位的杯子，然后笑了——短促的、真实的、材料间里的那种笑。“被自己的系统反将一军。”他说，“现在光落在你身上了，说实话，这个位置更好。”他覆住你的手，短暂而温暖，之后你们俩谁也没再动那两只杯子。

romance.ending: 秋天他离开，那座城市多了一位懂得为驻足和呼吸而设计的建筑师，校园里留下猫窝、图书馆，和那块无字的铜牌。那张图纸寄去参加比赛，然后回到他那边，挂在书桌上方。每次回来：一杯茶，那张长椅，四分钟最好的光线，一起检查一遍屋顶。雨帘里终于有人了，水从头到尾，一直流着。

episodes.title: One Patch of Shade
episodes.opening:
The field is loud with afternoon practice, and the only shade on it belongs to a bench gone pale from sun.

A club booth flutters nearby, its tent rope slapping in the breeze.

A young man in a light campus jacket sets a frisbee down on the table, notices you hesitating at the edge of the grass, and turns around with the kind of smile that doesn't demand anything back.
episodes.dialogue:
I'm Leo Luo, new to the frisbee club.

You've found the one shady patch on this field — that bench is prime real estate after two o'clock.

Want to watch a round first?

No need to play; I can save you a shady spot.

He picks up the frisbee and spins it once on his finger, not showing off, just keeping his hands busy.

Honestly, half the people who stop here never touch a disc, and that's fine.

Watching counts.

Sitting counts.

Leaving counts too — I mean that.

He glances at the field, where someone makes a diving catch and immediately loses the disc over a fence.

Okay, that guy's showing off.

You don't have to be him.

He digs through his canvas bag and pulls out a club flyer, already covered in pencil lines — little arrows, a sketch of the bench, a dotted path along the fence.

Sorry, my maps get everywhere.

I draw routes on everything.

Anyway.

You can sit, you can stand, you can tell me the shade math is wrong.

All options are live.

He steps back half a pace, giving the bench and the whole field back to you.

So — what sounds good?

choices.text: Your shade math is wrong — that tree moves by three, not two.
choices.response:
Leo's whole face lights up like you've handed him a present.

Three!

He flips the flyer over and redraws the shadow line right there on the grass, tongue between his teeth.

You're the first person to argue with the map instead of the mapmaker.

Sit anywhere, chief critic — the bench is yours, and the argument is mine to lose.

choices.text: (Walk to the bench and sit down without a word.)
choices.response:
He reads it instantly and doesn't make it a moment.

Good call, he says, dropping his voice like the field is a library.

He drags the booth's spare folding stool over with his foot, parks it in the shade at a polite distance, and sits too — facing the field, not you, so the quiet has somewhere to go.

After a minute he points out a good catch without expecting a reply.

episodes.ending:
The round ends and players drift toward the booth for water.

Leo stands, brushes off his jacket, and tears a clean corner off a flyer.

He sketches a small arrow pointing from the bench toward the booth and holds it up so you can see.

Practice runs again Thursday, same field, same migrating shade.

If you're passing by, the spot keeps.

If not, the bench will hold its own.

episodes.title: Half an Hour on the Sideline
episodes.opening:
Thursday, and the shade has migrated exactly where a certain pencil map said it would.

Leo is already at the bench, two bottles of water sweating on the wood beside him, sketching the field's edge lines on the back of another flyer.

He spots you before you're halfway across the grass and scoots his bag off the good end of the bench.
episodes.dialogue:
You came back — the map works.

He caps his pen and hands over one of the waters without ceremony.

Today's mostly drills, which is honestly the boring part.

The interesting part is watching who drifts to the edge and why.

He follows your glance to a cluster of first-years hovering at the fence, holding discs like they're live animals.

See?

Half of them want in and don't know how to say so.

I know the feeling.

He turns the flyer over and draws a small stick figure under a drawn tree.

First club event I ever went to, back home in Xiamen, I stood on the sideline for half an hour.

Full half hour.

Watched, held my disc, told myself I was scouting.

My mom still thinks I joined that day.

I didn't.

I went home and practiced throws against a laundry rack for a week first.

He laughs at himself, easy, no wince in it.

So when I see someone at the fence now, I don't drag them in.

I just make sure the shade's decent and the exit's obvious.

That's the whole trick.

My family's nothing special — ordinary Xiamen, my dad fixed awnings for shops, which is why I notice every bad canopy on this campus.

That man could diagnose a rain awning from a moving bus.

He flips the pen in his fingers and looks over, direct but unhurried.

You don't have to tell me your whole story in exchange.

I just figured you'd rather know why the bench is always saved.

choices.text: Half an hour of scouting, then a laundry rack? That's the most stubborn thing I've heard.
choices.response:
Stubborn is fair.

He grins and adds a tiny laundry rack to the stick figure's sideline, then dates it like a historical record.

My sister called it the rack era.

She still brings it up at dinner.

He taps the drawing.

But here's the thing — the rack worked.

Slow entry, real entry.

So I figure anyone's timeline is legitimate, including a fence-hugger's, including mine, including yours.

He slides the finished flyer to your side of the bench, a small archive of one ordinary afternoon.

choices.text: (Pick up the water and turn it slowly in your hands, looking out at the fence-huggers.)
choices.response:
He watches where you're watching and doesn't fill the silence with noise.

Instead he draws the fence-huggers onto the flyer's margin, one stick figure each, mid-hover.

Then, quietly: They'll sort it out.

Or they'll sit here.

Both fine.

He leaves the sketch facing you and drinks his own water, and the two of you watch the drills in a silence that feels kept rather than empty.

Before you leave, he tears off the corner with the figures and pockets it.

episodes.ending:
Drills wrap and the first-years finally drift onto the field, one of them throwing a wobbly but genuine disc.

Leo watches them go with visible satisfaction, then gathers his flyers into a neat stack.

Same time Thursday, he says, standing and shouldering his bag.

The bench keeps.

And if you ever want the laundry rack's full history, that's also on the menu.

episodes.title: The Wind Route
episodes.opening:
The club is hosting an open showcase Saturday, and the field is chaos in a good way — nets going up, first-years everywhere, a banner being wrestled by two people and losing.

Leo flags you over from the bench, and today he doesn't look entirely sunny.

There's a clipboard under his arm with a list that keeps growing.
episodes.dialogue:
Okay, real talk.

He drops onto the bench beside his bag, clipboard on his knees.

I volunteered to design the layout for Saturday — shade stations, water, the flow of people.

Environmental design student finally does something relevant, very exciting.

Except.

He shows you the list.

Every new person who signed up also asked where to rest, where to watch without joining, where to leave without it being a whole thing.

Forty-one questions, all the same question.

And here's my problem: I keep wanting to answer all forty-one myself, personally, at full speed.

He rubs the back of his neck.

That's how I overwhelm people.

I know this about me.

So the actual risk is me talking Saturday into the ground.

What I need is the thing done before I can ruin it.

He pulls out a fresh flyer and flattens it on the bench: the field, drawn properly this time, with real scale.

Wind comes off the harbor side, so shade shifts fast.

I've got the wind route half-mapped.

If you walk it with me and mark where the shadow actually lands hour by hour, we finish the map, and Saturday I can just... point.

Instead of performing.

He holds out the pen, handle first.

No obligation to show up Saturday itself.

This is just the walk.

And if you'd rather sit, honestly, sitting here and telling me when I'm overdesigning is also a real job.

choices.text: Give me the pen. You've drawn the fence twice; it only exists once.
choices.response:
He looks at the flyer, finds the doubled fence, and laughs loud enough to turn a first-year's head.

Two fences.

Incredible.

He hands over the pen like it's a formal transfer of power.

Okay.

You hold the truth, I hold the clipboard.

That's the division of labor and I will not override it, even when I'm excited.

Especially when I'm excited.

You walk the field's edge together at an easy pace, and the map comes back with one fence, honest shadows, and three rest spots Leo hadn't thought of.

choices.text: (Pick up his clipboard and hold it flat against the bench so the wind stops flipping pages.)
choices.response:
The pages settle.

Leo looks at the clipboard, then at your hand on it, and something in his shoulders comes down an inch.

“Right,” he says.

One problem at a time.

He works through the list out loud while you hold it steady, crossing out every item that was really him wanting to be useful louder.

By the end the list is half its size and the plan is better for it.

You didn't say a word, and he noticed, and he says so plainly: You just saved me from myself.

That's a real assist.

episodes.ending:
Saturday's showcase runs without a single lost newcomer.

The wind-route map hangs laminated at the booth — finished the night before — shadows marked hour by hour, arrows for the moving shade.

Leo points people to it instead of narrating, and only talks too fast twice, catching himself both times.

Afterward he sits on the pale bench and admits the map did more work than he did, and that this is his favorite outcome so far.

episodes.title: Under the Awning
episodes.opening:
Rain arrives sideways, the kind that makes umbrellas dishonest, and the showcase cleanup scatters indoors.

Leo corrals you under the shop-style awning by the equipment shed — a good one, sloped right, water running off clean at the edge.

He watches the runoff with professional approval, then turns, and there's something more careful in his face than usual.
episodes.dialogue:
Good awning, right?

My dad would approve.

Water goes where it's told.

He shakes rain off his jacket sleeve, then hesitates — actually hesitates, which you've never seen him do.

Okay, two things, and they're separate, and you can take either, both, or neither.

He holds up one finger.

Thing one: the design department's winter showcase is in a few weeks, and I want to submit the shade-and-wind project.

Extended — every bench on campus, rated for shade, wind, and escape routes.

It's a bigger job than one person sketching on flyers.

I'd like a partner on it.

A real one.

Your name on the board next to mine.

He holds up the second finger, slower.

Thing two is different.

There's a teahouse two streets off campus, dry roof, corner table, best view of rain I know.

I'd like to take you there.

Just as — he gestures loosely between you — us.

Whatever that is.

I like you.

I've liked you for a while, and I'd rather say it plainly than circle it.

He steps back half a pace, the same half pace as the first day, giving the whole moment back to you.

No wrong answer.

The project stands either way.

The rain doesn't care.

Take whichever door is yours.

choices.text: Then let's start with the teahouse — the benches can wait for a dry day.
choices.response:
The careful look breaks into something bright and a little stunned, like he'd prepared for every answer except an easy yes.

Yeah?

Okay.

Yes.

He laughs at himself, rain drumming the awning above you.

Corner table, I promised you the best rain on this street and it delivers.

He doesn't reach for your hand or close the half pace; he just tilts his head toward the dry path beyond the awning and walks with you at exactly the pace you set, talking about the teahouse's crooked roof tiles like they're the most important design on campus.

Before the corner, he says quietly, plainly: I'm really glad you picked this door.

choices.text: (Nod toward the campus map on the shed wall — the winter project first.)
choices.response:
He follows your nod and his smile settles into something warm and steady rather than diminished.

Partner it is.

He means it; you can hear that he means it.

Then the teahouse stays what it is — a good story about a crooked roof, told another day, no debt attached.

He pulls out a flyer, right there in the rain-noise, and writes both names at the top of the bench survey, then shows you the page.

There.

On the record.

He talks route plans until the rain quits, easy company, and walks the dry edge of the quad with you when it ends.

episodes.ending:
The rain stops before evening.

The winter project stands — that was the promise under the awning, and Leo keeps it. The work is shared from the first page.

The walk home from the field passes shaded benches that both of you look at with the same professional suspicion.

Leo's pace is unchanged — easy, exit always visible — but the direction is no longer random.

episodes.title: The Question That Needs No Answer
episodes.opening:
A term has turned since the rain.

The bench survey is real now — laminated cards on a dozen benches across campus, each rated for shade, wind, and a clean exit, two names at the top of every one.

Leo waits at the original bench with his canvas bag and a thermos, older in the way of someone whose maps finally got built.

He pours a second cup without asking, then remembers himself and holds it out as a question.
episodes.dialogue:
Bench nine is a scandal, by the way.

He nods toward the far quad.

Shade rating excellent, wind rating a lie.

Someone trusted our card and got a face full of harbor gust.

We're fixing it Thursday.

He settles back, cup steaming in both hands.

My dad visited last month.

Walked the whole route with me, said nothing for an hour, then pointed at one awning and said, that one leaks at the seam.

He was right.

It was the best review I've ever gotten.

He laughs, then turns quieter, turning his cup.

Can I tell you the thing I figured out?

For a long time I thought my job was to make sure nobody stood on a sideline feeling like I did.

Half an hour, holding a disc, scouting.

So I'd swoop in with shade and options.

Good instinct, wrong scale.

What actually helps is the bench being there, mapped, honest, with the exit drawn — so they can choose anything, including nothing, and it counts.

He looks over, direct as ever.

You taught me that, mostly by sitting.

So here's what I want to ask, and it doesn't need an answer today: the survey keeps growing.

Next term, the fields across the river.

I want the standing arrangement — you and me, every season, mapping whatever campus hands us, for as long as it stays good.

That's the whole proposal.

No deadline.

The question can just sit there, like the bench.

choices.text: Bench nine's wind rating isn't a lie — the card just needs a second arrow for gusts.
choices.response:
Leo goes still, then starts laughing into his thermos steam.

A second arrow.

We reprint the whole card for one arrow.

He pulls out a flyer on reflex, draws bench nine with two arrows, and holds it up like a verdict.

And notice what you did there — fixed the map before the question even got an answer.

The question can keep sitting, like the bench. No deadline.

But anyone who repairs the card first is exactly who I want doing this every season, whenever the answer comes.

He writes the date small in the corner, the way people do with things they intend to keep, and clinks his cup against yours without ceremony.

choices.text: (Take the poured cup and tap it once against his before drinking.)
choices.response:
The small tap says it, and Leo receives it without needing it translated.

He drinks, looks out at the field where new first-years are hovering at the fence, and doesn't rush them or you.

Standing arrangement, he says at last, tasting the words.

Yeah.

That holds.

He tears the bench-nine corner off his flyer, adds a second gust arrow from memory, and pins it inside his bag flap where the other kept maps live.

The river fields can wait for Thursday.

The arrangement doesn't need a start date; it was already running.

episodes.ending:
Thursday you and Leo fix bench nine, and the card comes back with two arrows and a note in the corner: wind shifts after three, sit closer to the wall.

The survey grows one field at a time after that, across the river and beyond, two names at the top of every card.

Some afternoons you two talk the whole walk; some afternoons nobody says anything, and the maps do the talking.

Both kinds count.

Both were always going to count.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Corner Table
romance.opening:
The teahouse finally gets its day.

Rain again — Leo claims the weather conspired, and the crooked roof tiles do send the water off in satisfying ropes.

The corner table is exactly as advertised: dry, quiet, the whole street running with silver.

He hangs his jacket, sits, and for once doesn't fill the first minute with anything at all.
romance.dialogue:
Okay, I've been composing a speech for two weeks and it's bad, so I'm skipping it.

He turns his cup a quarter turn on the table, a small nervous ritual you've never seen.

Here's the plain version instead.

Since the awning, we've built a bench survey, argued about wind arrows, and I've learned your silence from your thinking-silence, which are different, and I notice both.

I like my life more with you in it.

I'd keep the project partnership too.

I choose you, on purpose, where it counts.

He looks up, direct even now.

I know my pace.

I go too fast when I'm excited, I turn everything into a map, I will absolutely sketch on our restaurant receipts.

You'd be getting the whole flawed set.

And I don't need you to match my speed.

I need you to tell me when to slow down, and I'll do it — I've gotten better, ask the first-years I no longer swoop at.

He slides a folded paper across the table: a flyer, sketched with the corner table, the crooked roof, two cups, and a small arrow labeled us, current position.

No deadline on it.

No exit drawn, either — first time for that.

He waits, rain loud and unhurried around you, entirely willing to wait longer.

choices.text: The arrow's wrong — current position should be both of us, facing the rain.
choices.response:
He looks at the sketch, then at you, and something unguarded crosses his face before the grin arrives.

He borrows your pen — a first, borrowing your pen — and adds a second small figure beside the first, both facing the drawn window.

Better, he says, quieter than usual.

That's accurate.

Then, plainly, the way he says everything that matters: I'm choosing you too.

On purpose.

He doesn't reach across the table; he lets the drawing carry it, and his foot finds yours under the table for one brief, deliberate tap — the only touch, and he pulls back smiling like it cost him real discipline.

The rain keeps its schedule.

Nobody's going anywhere.

choices.text: (Turn the flyer around and add the rain-ropes running off the crooked roof before sliding it back.)
choices.response:
Leo watches the pen move, sees the rain-ropes appear off the drawn roof, and goes very still — then laughs, low and delighted, the sound of a map being read correctly for the first time.

“You drew the weather,” he says.

That's a whole sentence in your language and I speak it fluently.

He folds the flyer with exaggerated care and puts it in the inside pocket, not the bag.

For the record, he says, steady now, I choose this too — slowly, at your pace, with excellent rain.

The talk that follows is easy and long: roof tiles, bench nine, the river fields, nothing urgent.

When the rain thins, he walks you back along the dry side of the street, matching your step exactly.

romance.ending:
The flyer from the corner table migrates, eventually, to the first page of the survey binder, labeled in his handwriting: origin point.

The bench work continues — new fields, new seasons, two names at the top of every card — because the project was never the thing that changed.

What changed is that the maps now carry two names — and the exits are still drawn on every one, for both of you, because Leo never stopped believing a good map leaves every door open.

Leo still sketches on receipts.

You still tell him when to slow down.

He still does, mostly.

The corner table becomes a standing reservation neither of you ever cancels.

episodes.title: 一片树荫
episodes.opening:
操场上下午训练喧闹一片，全场唯一的荫凉落在一张被太阳晒得发白的长椅上。

旁边的社团摊位被风吹得帐篷绳啪啪作响。

一个穿浅色校园夹克的年轻男生把飞盘放到桌上，注意到你在草地边缘犹豫，转过头来，露出那种不求任何回应的笑容。
episodes.dialogue:
我叫罗阳，飞盘社新来的。

你站的这块是全场唯一的树荫——两点以后，这张长椅就是黄金地段了。

要不要先看一轮？

不想上场也没事，我给你留个阴凉位置。

他拿起飞盘，在指尖转了一圈，不是耍帅，只是让手别闲着。

说实话，停在这儿的人有一半碰都不碰飞盘，这完全没问题。

看着算参与。

坐着也算。

走了也算——我是认真的。

他朝场地瞥了一眼，那边有人一个鱼跃接盘，飞盘随即飞出了围栏。

好吧，那家伙在耍帅。

你不用学他。

他在帆布包里翻找，掏出一张社团传单，上面已经画满了铅笔线条——小箭头、长椅的草图、沿着围栏的虚线路径。

抱歉，我的地图到处都是。

我什么都拿来画路线。

总之。

你可以坐着，可以站着，也可以告诉我我的树荫计算是错的。

所有选项都有效。

他往后退了半步，把长椅和整个场地都还给了你。

那么——你觉得怎么样好？

choices.text: 你的树荫算错了——那棵树的影子到三点会挪三米，不是两米。
choices.response:
罗阳整张脸都亮了，像你送了他一件礼物。

三米！

他把传单翻过来，当场在草地上重画阴影线，咬着舌尖认真得很。

你是第一个跟地图抬杠、而不是跟画图的人抬杠的。

随便坐，首席批评家——长椅归你，这场辩论归我，输定了也归我。

choices.text: （你一言不发地走到长椅前坐下。）
choices.response:
他立刻读懂了，没有把这变成一个大场面。

好选择，他说，压低了声音，好像这片操场是图书馆。

他用脚把摊位旁边的备用折叠凳勾过来，摆在荫凉里一个有礼貌的距离，自己也坐下——面朝场地，不看你，让安静有处可去。

过了一会儿，他指给你看一个精彩的接盘，并不指望你回应。

episodes.ending:
这一轮结束，队员们三三两两朝摊位走过来喝水。

罗阳站起身，拍了拍夹克上的灰，从传单上撕下一个干净的角。

他画了个小箭头，从长椅指向摊位，举起来给你看。

周四还有训练，同一块场地，同一片会挪动的树荫。

要是你路过，这个位置一直给你留着。

要是不来，长椅也会自己好好待着。

episodes.title: 场边的半小时
episodes.opening:
星期四，树荫正好挪到某张铅笔画地图预测的位置。

罗阳已经在长椅上了，两瓶水放在木头上冒着汗珠，他在又一张社团传单背面画着场地的边线。

你才走到草坪一半，他就看见了你，把自己的帆布包从长椅好的那一头挪开。
episodes.dialogue:
你真的回来了——地图管用。

他扣上笔帽，顺手递给你一瓶水，一点不客气。

今天主要是训练，说实话是最无聊的部分。

有意思的是看谁会往场边漂，以及为什么。

他顺着你的目光看过去，一群大一新生在围栏边徘徊，抱着飞盘像抱着什么活物。

看见没？

一半人想上场，又不知道怎么开口。

我懂那种感觉。

他把传单翻过来，在画的树下添了个小火柴人。

我第一次参加社团活动，还是在家乡厦门那会儿，在场边站了整整半小时。

整整半小时。

一边看，一边攥着飞盘，跟自己说这是在考察。

我妈到现在还以为我那天就入社了。

并没有。

我先回家对着晾衣架练了一周传接，才去的。

他说到这儿自己笑了，很轻松，没有一点难为情。

所以现在看到围栏边有人，我不会硬拉他们进来。

我只要保证阴凉够好、出口够明显就行。

全部窍门就这些。

我家没什么特别的——厦门普通人家，我爸以前给店铺修雨棚，所以这校园里每个破遮阳棚都逃不过我的眼。

我爸能坐在行驶的公交车上诊断出一顶雨棚的问题。

他手指间转着笔，抬眼看你，直接但不急。

你不用非得拿你的故事来换。

我只是想，你大概会想知道这张长椅为什么总给你留着。

choices.text: 考察半小时，然后对着晾衣架练一周？这是我听过最犟的事。
choices.response:
犟这个评价，我收下。

他咧嘴一笑，在火柴人的场边添了个小小的晾衣架，还标上日期，像做历史记录一样。

我妹管那阵子叫晾衣架纪元。

她到现在吃饭还爱拿出来讲。

他敲了敲那幅画。

但重点是——晾衣架管用了。

慢慢进来，也是真的进来。

所以我觉得每个人的节奏都成立，抱围栏的人的节奏成立，我的成立，你的也成立。

他把画好的传单推到你那半边长椅上，一个普通午后的小小档案。

choices.text: （你拿起那瓶水，在手里慢慢转着，望向围栏边那些徘徊的新生。）
choices.response:
他看着你在看的地方，没有用声音去填满安静。

只是把那些围栏边的人一个个画上传单的页边，一人一个小火柴人，都停在半空中欲上未上的样子。

然后，他轻声说：他们会想明白的。

或者过来坐这儿。

都挺好。

他让那张画朝着你，自己喝起水来，你们俩就这样看着训练，那份安静像是被好好保存着的。

你离开前，他撕下画着火柴人的那一角，塞进了口袋。

episodes.ending:
训练结束，大一新生们终于飘上了场，其中一个扔出一记歪歪扭扭却真心实意的飞盘。

罗阳看着他们跑动，一脸藏不住的满足，然后把传单整整齐齐摞成一叠。

“周四，还是这个点。”他说着站起身，把帆布包甩上肩。

这张长椅一直留着。

你要是哪天想听晾衣架的完整历史，菜单上也有这一项。

episodes.title: 风的路线
episodes.opening:
社团周六要办开放展示日，操场上乱得让人高兴——球网正往上挂，大一新生到处都是，一条横幅被两个人扯来扯去，眼看要输。

罗阳从长椅那边朝你招手，今天他看起来不全是晴天。

他胳膊底下夹着一块写字板，上面的单子越来越长。
episodes.dialogue:
好，说实话。

他在帆布包旁边的长椅上坐下，写字板搁在膝盖上。

我自告奋勇负责周六的场地布置——阴凉点、饮水处、人流走向。

环境设计学生总算干了件对口的事，特别激动。

但是。

他把单子给你看。

每个报名的新人都问了同一个问题：在哪儿休息，在哪儿只看不玩，在哪儿能不引人注意地悄悄走掉。

四十一个提问，全都是同一个问题。

而我的毛病是：我总想一个人、亲自、全速把四十一个全答完。

他揉了揉后颈。

我就是这么把人压垮的。

我了解我自己这点。

所以真正的风险是我在周六把大家说得耳朵起茧。

我得在做完的事还没被我搞砸之前，先把事做完。

他抽出一张新的社团传单，在长椅上摊平：这次是正经画的操场图，比例也对。

港口那边的风一吹过来，阴影就变得很快。

风的路线我已经画了一半。

如果你陪我走一遍，把每小时影子实际落在哪儿都标出来，这张图就完成了，到时候周六我只要……指一指就行。

不用表演。

他把笔递过来，笔杆朝前。

周六当天来不来都没有义务。

今天就只是走一走。

要是你更想坐着，说实话，坐在这儿提醒我哪儿又过度设计了，也是正经活儿。

choices.text: 笔给我。你把围栏画了两遍，围栏可只有一道。
choices.response:
他看着图，找到那道重复的围栏，笑得旁边一个大一新生都回了头。

两道围栏。

绝了。

他像正式交接权力一样把笔递给你。

行。

你掌管事实，我掌管写字板。

就这么分工，我不会越权的——兴奋的时候也不会。

尤其是兴奋的时候。

你们沿着场地边缘慢慢走，最后图上只剩一道围栏，影子标得实实在在，还有三处罗阳没想到的休息点。

choices.text: （你拿起他的写字板，平按在长椅上，风再也翻不动纸页。）
choices.response:
纸页安静下来。

罗阳看看写字板，再看看你按着它的手，肩膀往下松了一寸。

“好。”他说。

一次只解决一个问题。

他一边念一边过那张单子，你替他按稳，划掉了每一项其实只是他想显得更有用的条目。

到最后，单子短了一半，方案反倒更好了。

你一个字都没说，他注意到了，而且直说：你把我从我自己手里救下来了。

这算是真正的助攻。

episodes.ending:
周六的展示日顺利结束，没有一个新生迷路。

那张风的路线图过塑后挂在社团摊位上——前一晚刚完成——每小时投下的阴影都标了出来，还有箭头指示阴影移动的方向。

罗阳只是给大家指指图，不再从头讲到尾，只有两次说话太快，两次都自己察觉了。

结束后他坐在浅色的长椅上，承认那张图比他干的活还多，还说这是他目前为止最喜欢的结果。

episodes.title: 雨棚下
episodes.opening:
雨是横着下的，那种打了伞也白打的雨，作品展的收尾只好散进屋里。

罗阳把你拦进器材房旁边那个店铺式的雨棚下——这棚不错，坡度刚好，雨水顺着边缘干净利落地淌下去。

他带着一种专业的欣赏盯着水流看了一会儿，然后转过身来，脸上比平时多了几分小心。
episodes.dialogue:
这棚子不错吧？

我爸看了都得点头。

水往哪儿流，听指挥。

他甩了甩夹克袖子上的雨，然后犹豫了——是真的犹豫了，这你可从来没见过。

好，两件事，两件分开的事，你可以选一件、两件都要，或者都不要。

他竖起一根手指。

第一件：设计系的冬季作品展再过几周就要到了，我想投那个遮阴避风方案。

就是扩展版——全校每条长椅，遮阴、挡风、退路都打分。

这活儿比一个人在传单背面画图大得多。

我想找个搭档。

真正的搭档。

展板上，你的名字写在我旁边。

他竖起第二根手指，慢了一些。

第二件是另一回事。

校外两条街有家茶馆，屋顶不漏，角落有张桌子，是我知道的最适合看雨的地方。

我想带你去那儿。

只是——他在你和他之间随手指了指——我们。

不管那算什么。

我喜欢你。

喜欢有一阵子了，与其绕来绕去，不如直说。

他后退半步，和第一天一样的半步，把整个瞬间还给你。

怎么答都不会错。

不管怎样，项目都在。

雨才不管这些。

选属于你的那扇门就行。

choices.text: 那就先去茶馆吧——长椅的事等天晴再说。
choices.response:
那副小心的神情一下子亮了起来，还带着点被惊到的样子，像是他把每种回答都预演过了，唯独没料到你会这么爽快地答应。

真的？

好。

好！

他笑了，笑自己，雨点在你们头顶的雨棚上敲得咚咚响。

角落那张桌子，我跟你保证过这条街的雨最好看，它还真没让我食言。

他没有伸手牵你，也没有跨过那半步的距离；只是朝雨棚外那条不淋雨的路偏了偏头，用你定的步速陪你走，一路讲着茶馆那片歪歪扭扭的屋瓦，好像那是全校最重要的设计。

拐角之前，他轻声、清清楚楚地说：你选了这扇门，我真的特别高兴。

choices.text: （你朝器材房墙上的校园地图点点头——先聊冬季项目。）
choices.response:
他顺着你的目光看过去，笑容落成一种温暖而稳当的样子。

那就说定了，搭档。

他是认真的；你听得出来他是认真的。

那家茶馆就还是茶馆——一个关于歪屋瓦的好故事，改天再讲，不欠谁什么。

他抽出一张社团传单，就在这一片雨声里，在长椅调查表的顶端写下你们两个的名字，然后把那一页拿给你看。

喏。

白纸黑字。

他一直聊着路线规划，聊到雨停，是个轻松的伴儿，雨停后又陪你沿着操场边上干燥的那一侧走。

episodes.ending:
雨在傍晚前停了。

冬季项目照常进行——这是雨棚下的约定，罗阳做到了。工作从第一页起就是两个人分担的。

从操场走回去的路上，你们经过一条条有遮阴的长椅，都用一模一样的专业审视眼神打量着它们。

罗阳的步子还是老样子——轻松，随时看得见出口——但方向不再是随机的了。

episodes.title: 不需要回答的问题
episodes.opening:
那场雨之后，一个学期过去了。

长椅调查真的落地了——校园里十几张长椅上都贴着塑封卡片，每张都标好了树荫、风向和干净的退路，落款是两个名字。

罗阳在最早那张长椅等你，帆布包和保温杯都在手边，整个人有种终于把图纸变成现实之后的沉稳。

他没问就倒好了第二杯，随即回过神来，把杯子递出，当成一个问题。
episodes.dialogue:
顺便说一句，九号长椅简直是丑闻。

他朝远处的草坪扬了扬下巴。

树荫评分优秀，风向评分是个谎言。

有人信了我们的卡片，结果被港口方向灌来的风糊了一脸。

我们周四就去改。

他靠回椅背，杯子在两只手里冒着热气。

我爸上个月来了。

陪我走完了整条路线，一个小时没说话，然后指着一处雨棚说，那个，接缝会漏水。

他说对了。

那是我收到过的最好的评审。

他笑了，随后安静下来，转着手里的杯子。

我能跟你说说我想明白的那件事吗？

有很长一段时间，我以为我的任务是别让任何人站在场边时，体会到我当时的感受。

半个小时，手里攥着飞盘，观察试探。

所以我总是带着阴凉和选项冲过去。

直觉是对的，尺度错了。

真正有用的，是那张长椅就在那里，画好了图，写得诚实，退路也标出来了——这样他们选什么都行，包括什么都不选，而且怎么选都算数。

他看过来，一如既往地直接。

这件事多半是你教我的，就靠坐在那儿。

所以我想问的其实是这个，今天不用回答：调查还在扩大。

下个学期，轮到河对岸的操场。

我要的是长期的约定——你和我，每个季节都一起，校园给我们什么就画什么，只要这件事还让人觉得好。

提议就这些。

没有期限。

这个问题可以就这么放着，像那张长椅一样。

choices.text: 九号长椅的风向评分不是谎言——卡片只是需要第二支箭头，标阵风。
choices.response:
罗阳愣了一下，然后对着保温杯冒出的热气笑出了声。

第二支箭头。

为了一支箭头，我们把整张卡片重印一遍。

他条件反射地抽出一张传单，画下九号长椅和两支箭头，举起来像宣读判决。

你注意到自己干了什么了吗——问题还没得到回答，你先把地图修好了。

问题可以继续放着，像那张长椅一样。没有期限。

但谁会先把卡片修好，谁就是我想要的、每个季节一起做这件事的人，什么时候想回答都行。

他在角落里小小地写下日期，像人们对待打算珍藏的东西那样，然后不经意地拿杯子和你碰了一下。

choices.text: （你端起倒好的那杯，喝之前先和他轻轻碰了一下杯。）
choices.response:
轻轻一下碰杯把话说了，罗阳接住了，不需要翻译。

他喝了口，望向操场，栅栏边有几个大一新生正在探头探脑，他不催他们，也不催你。

长期的约定，他终于开口，把这几个字在嘴里咂了咂。

嗯。

成立。

他把传单上九号长椅那一角撕下来，凭记忆补上第二支阵风箭头，夹进帆布包翻盖内侧，那里收着他舍不得扔的旧地图。

河对岸的操场可以等周四。

约定不需要开始日期；它早就跑起来了。

episodes.ending:
周四你和罗阳修好了九号长椅，卡片换回来时多了两支箭头，角落里写着一行小字：三点以后风向会变，往墙那边坐。

之后调查一张操场一张地扩大，过了河，又更远，每张卡片的顶端都是那两个名字。

有些下午你们一路都在聊；有些下午谁也不说话，让地图替你们开口。

两种都算数。

两种从来都算数。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 角落那张桌子
romance.opening:
茶馆终于等来了它的好日子。

又下雨了——罗阳非说这天气是串通好的，而那几片歪歪的屋顶瓦，也确实把雨水甩成一道道好看的银线。

角落那张桌子跟传说中一模一样：干燥，安静，整条街都在哗哗淌着银光。

他挂好外套，坐下，头一回没急着把第一分钟填满，就那么安静地待着。
romance.dialogue:
好吧，我这两周一直在打腹稿，写出来很烂，所以那段我跳过了。

他在桌上把杯子转了四分之一圈——一个小小的、紧张的小动作，你从没见过。

那我直接说大白话。

从雨棚那次开始，我们一起做了长椅调查，为阵风箭头吵过架，我学会了分辨你的沉默和思考时的沉默——这不一样，两种我都留意到了。

有你在，我的日子变得更好过了。

搭档我也想继续当。

你是我选的人，认真的、在最要紧的地方选的那个人。

他抬起头，就算这种时候也依然坦率。

我知道自己的节奏。

一兴奋就走太快，什么都要画成地图，还绝对会在餐厅小票上涂涂画画。

你得接住的是这样一套缺点齐全的我。

而且我不需要你跟上我的速度。

我只要你在我该慢下来的时候提醒我，我会照做——我真的有进步，不信可以去问那几个我不再猛冲过去的一年级新生。

他把一张折好的纸推过桌面，没什么惊天动地的架势：就是一张社团传单，上面画着角落那张桌子、歪歪的屋顶、两只杯子，还有一个小箭头，标着“我们，当前位置”。

上面没写期限。

也没画出口——这可是头一回。

他等着，雨声在四周又响又不急，他也完全愿意等得更久。

choices.text: 箭头画错了——当前位置应该是我们俩，一起看着这场雨。
choices.response:
他看了看那张画，又看看你，脸上先闪过一丝毫无防备的神情，然后才咧嘴笑起来。

他借走了你的笔——头一回借你的笔——在原来那个小人旁边添了第二个小人，两个都朝着画上的窗户。

这样好多了，他说，比平时轻。

这下准确了。

然后，用他平时说正经话的方式，平平实实地：我也在选你。

认真的，自己选的。

他没伸手过桌；他让那张画替他传话，只在桌子底下用脚轻轻碰了一下你的脚——一下，很郑重的一下——就收了回去，笑得像是费了好大劲才忍住。

雨照着自己的时刻表下。

谁也不急着去哪儿。

choices.text: （你把传单转了个方向，在歪屋顶上添了几道甩下来的雨线，再推回去。）
choices.response:
罗阳看着笔尖移动，看见画上的屋顶甩出雨线，整个人静了一瞬——然后低低地笑出声，又开心又惊喜，像是有人头一次把他那张地图读对了。

“你把天气画上去了。”他说。

这在你那儿可是一整句话，而我听得懂，很流利的那种懂。

他小心翼翼地、甚至有点夸张地把传单折好，放进衣服内侧口袋，不是帆布包。

声明一下，他说，这回声音很稳：我也选这个——慢慢来，按你的节奏，配上这么好的雨。

接下来的闲聊又轻松又长：屋顶瓦、九号长椅、河对岸的操场，没有一件是急事。

雨小了，他沿着街上干燥的那侧送你回去，每一步都正好踩着你的节奏。

romance.ending:
角落那张桌子传单，最后被挪进了调查文件夹的第一页，上面是他手写的标注：起点。

长椅调查还在继续——新的操场，新的季节，每张卡片顶端都写着两个名字——因为从来不是这个项目变了。

变的是地图上如今写着两个名字——而每一张图上仍然画着出口，给你们两个人都留着，因为罗阳始终相信，一张好地图应该把每一扇门都敞开着。

罗阳还是会往小票上画画。

你也还是会提醒他慢一点。

他也大多会照做。

角落那张桌子，成了你们俩谁都不会取消的长期保留位。

episodes.title: One Question in the Margin
episodes.opening:
The corridor outside the literature wing smells of chalk and old paper.

Loose pages rest by the window, fanned by a draft, and a woman in a light cardigan is pinning one of them flat with two fingers.

A pen is tucked behind her ear like it grew there.

A notice taped to the glass reads READING CIRCLE, THURSDAYS, ALL WELCOME, in handwriting that has clearly been rewritten twice.
episodes.dialogue:
She glances up as you slow down, and does not seem surprised to be caught mid-rescue of her own handouts.

Wind, presumably.

Books escape their owners constantly in this building.

She gathers the pages, taps them square against the sill, and offers the smallest nod of thanks for your patience rather than your help, which you have not yet offered.

Then she notices where your eyes have gone.

One of the pages is dense with print, and in the margin beside a single sentence, in small careful characters, she has written a question.

A question, as if the book were expected to answer.

She catches you reading it and does not cover it up.

Instead she holds the page out, unhurried, like someone handing over a map rather than grading your map-reading.

“We can start with this sentence,” she says.

We just have not found the door.

She admits, with dry humor, that the question in the margin is her own habit, and that half her best ideas began as things she had gotten wrong on the first pass.

The reading circle, she explains, is Thursday, in the small seminar room where the radiator bangs.

People assume they need to have finished the book.

They do not.

They need to have opened it somewhere, anywhere.

She asks, without weight, which line on the page looks inviting to you.

Not which one you understand.

Which one looks inviting.

The distinction matters to her; you can see it in how she waits.

Down the hall a door slams, and she does not flinch, only keeps the page steady, as if the corridor itself were part of the seminar.

choices.text: This one. I don't know what it means, but it sounds like someone arguing with the rain.
choices.response:
She laughs, briefly and genuinely, the pen almost falling from behind her ear.

An argument with the rain, she repeats, testing it.

Good.

That sentence has defeated two classes of graduate students, and you just handed me a better door than any of them did.

She writes nothing down, but you can tell she is filing the phrase somewhere permanent.

“Thursday,” she says.

Bring that reading.

The one about rain can sit next to you and defend itself.

choices.text: (Trace the margin question with one finger, saying nothing.)
choices.response:
She watches your finger stop just short of her handwriting, and something in her posture eases, as if silence were a language she had been waiting for someone to speak.

That question took me three drafts, she says quietly.

The first two sounded like a test.

I rewrote them until they sounded like a doorway instead.

She squares the pages once more and looks at you the way a host looks at someone deciding whether to come in.

“The door stays open either way,” she says.

But you are welcome on Thursday.

episodes.ending:
She tucks the handouts into a canvas bag worn soft at the handles, and walks you a few steps toward the stairwell, pointing out the seminar room as though giving directions to a place that already expects you.

The radiator bangs, she warns, so sit near the window if you plan to hear anything after the first ten minutes.

At the corner she pauses, half-turning.

If the book fights you, she says, fight it back politely.

Then she is gone down the corridor, and the notice in the window seems, somehow, addressed specifically to you.

episodes.title: The Copied Pages
episodes.opening:
Thursday's reading circle has outgrown its radiator.

The seminar room holds a dozen people and one misbehaving window, and Dr. Lin stands at the front with a stack of freshly copied excerpts that she is distributing with the calm of someone who has not yet looked at them closely.

You have been coming for a few weeks now, long enough to have a preferred seat by the window.
episodes.dialogue:
Halfway through handing out the copies, she stops.

Frowns.

Turns one page over, then another, and you watch the exact moment she realizes the photocopier has scrambled the order, pages shuffled like a deck of cards.

A ripple of unease goes around the room.

Someone near the front asks if they should wait for corrected copies.

She considers it honestly, then does something you have not seen her do before: she tells the room a story.

A few years ago, she says, she ran a reading session for the campus journal, and she herself stapled the handouts with the pages in the wrong order.

She discovered it only when a student raised a hand and asked why the ending came before the middle.

She had stood there mortified, about to apologize, when she noticed everyone was still reading.

Intently.

So she asked them instead to pick out one clue they were certain of, anything that told them what came before what.

That session, she admits, never went according to plan, and it was one of the best she ever ran.

People found out what they actually rely on to judge a text.

Order, she says, is a courtesy.

Judgment is the muscle.

She sets the misordered copies down and tells the room they may treat today the same way, or wait, both are fine, no one will be graded on their flexibility.

Then her eyes find you by the window, and her voice drops to the register she uses when a sentence is meant for one person.

You have been sitting there for weeks, she says, and you have never once looked worried about being wrong.

She asks whether you would read your scrambled page aloud first, any line, so the room can watch someone start without a map.

choices.text: Sure. Line twelve, out of order, feels like starting a letter in the middle. I'll take it.
choices.response:
You read the line, and the room goes quiet in the good way.

Dr. Lin nods slowly, then tells everyone that this is the whole method, nothing hidden: start anywhere, notice what you can be sure of, let the rest come find you.

A student in the back actually opens their copy.

Afterward she passes your desk and says, low, that a letter started in the middle is still a letter.

She sounds like she is keeping the phrase.

choices.text: (Shake your head slightly and slide your copy toward the center of the table.)
choices.response:
She reads the gesture instantly and does not press, which is its own kind of respect.

Instead she takes the offered page herself, reads a line aloud in her even voice, and asks the room what they can be certain of.

The discussion catches.

When it winds down she stops by your chair on her way past.

“You let someone else go first,” she says.

That is also a way of opening a door.

Some of the best hosts in literature never say a word on page one.

episodes.ending:
The session ends late and nobody minds.

She collects the misordered copies without straightening them, and when you are last out the door she holds it with her foot and mentions, offhand, that next week's text is harder, and that she will probably misread it in front of everyone, and that you should come watch.

It is the closest thing to a promise she has made you, and she makes it while looking at the radiator, not at you.

episodes.title: The Open Lecture
episodes.opening:
The department has asked Dr. Lin to give an open lecture in the largest hall on campus, the one with the sloped seats and the microphone that eats first words.

She mentions it at the end of a reading circle, casually, the way people mention weather they are dreading.

Two hundred expected attendees.

Her handouts are already printed, in the correct order, checked three times.
episodes.dialogue:
After the room empties she stays at the table with her lecture notes, and you stay too, and eventually she says the true thing instead of the tidy one.

She is afraid, she says, of what the microphone does to her.

In a small room she can hear when her phrasing starts to sound like a test, and she can stop and rephrase.

In a hall with a microphone, she cannot take it back.

Her fear is specific: that some first-year in row R will hear one sentence and decide that serious literature is a gate with her standing in front of it, checking papers.

She once sat in such a row herself, she admits, and nearly walked away from the whole subject because a lecturer's joke landed like a verdict.

She does not want to be on that stage.

She sets her notes down and rubs the pen smudge off the side of her hand.

What she needs, she says, is a rehearsal with an audience of one.

Someone who will tell her, honestly, when a sentence starts to sound like a quiz.

She asks if you would sit in the empty hall tomorrow while she runs the first ten minutes, and flag the moments where her voice goes up at the end, the way it does when she is about to sound like she is grading.

It is a real request and a real cost; she is giving you a job that requires you to be honest at her expense, and she knows it.

She waits, pen in hand, ready to write your answer in the margin of her notes the way she writes questions in the margins of books.

choices.text: I'll flag every sentence that sounds like a pop quiz. You might hate me by minute nine.
choices.response:
She writes something in the margin of her notes, and you catch the words minute nine, underlined.

“Good,” she says.

If I hate it, that means the sentence needed rewriting anyway.

She tells you the hall will be open at four, and that she will bring coffee as payment, and that honesty between rehearsal partners does not require an apology afterward.

Her shoulders have come down from around her ears for the first time all evening.

The next day, you take a seat in the empty hall while she stands at the lectern with two coffees beside her notes.

At the third sentence you raise a hand.

Already? she says, then reads it back to herself and hears the question turning into a test.

She crosses out three words and tries again.

choices.text: (Nod, then tap the margin of her notes where she can write tomorrow’s rehearsal time.)
choices.response:
She understands the answer without words, and something in her face unclenches.

Tomorrow at four, then, she says, and writes it in the margin of her notes.

The next day the hall is exactly as she feared: empty, sloped, echoing. She picks up her notes, walks to the lectern, and looks down at the single person in the seats.

“A rehearsal audience of one,” she says.

Historically, the most honest kind.

She begins, and her voice does go up at the end of the third sentence, and you shift in your chair, and she sees it, and stops, and rephrases.

It works.

She knows it works.

episodes.ending:
The rehearsal runs long past the ten minutes she promised, because once she starts trusting the flagging, she wants all of it.

Nothing is cured; the microphone will still be a microphone tomorrow, and two hundred people will still be two hundred people.

But the notes now carry small honest questions in their margins, written in a hand that has learned to doubt itself usefully.

She walks you to the corridor doors and says the lecture will be better for having been wrong in front of you first.

episodes.title: An Evening Without Grades
episodes.opening:
The open lecture went well; the microphone ate only two of her first words, and row R laughed in the right places.

Now, a few weeks later, the term is bending toward its end, and Dr. Lin has proposed something new: a final reading evening, no texts assigned, no discussion questions, everyone brings one page they love and reads it aloud.

She has booked the small seminar room for the evening, after the building empties.
episodes.dialogue:
She finds you by the window seat before the circle starts, holding two paper cups and looking, for the first time since you have known her, slightly unsure of her own script.

She hands you one cup, which is already a small event; she does not usually spend the department's coffee on individuals.

The reading evening, she explains, is her way of ending the term without a grade, hers or anyone's.

But she wants to ask you something separate from the circle, before the room fills and the moment gets shared among twelve people.

After the reading evening, she says, she would like to keep seeing you, in a way that is not the reading circle.

She is precise about it, because precision is how she is brave.

There are two shapes this could take, and she genuinely wants either.

The first: she has found a secondhand bookstore across the river that stays open late, and she would like to go there with you, wander the shelves, argue about titles, let this become a friendship with its own geography, its own places, independent of the seminar room and the term calendar.

The second: the same bookstore, the same shelves, but as a beginning, a first evening of something that would not stay on the friendship side of the line, something she has been carefully not naming for weeks and is now naming.

She says she does not want an answer that is polite instead of true, and she will not treat either choice as a verdict on the term, or on you.

The room is filling behind her.

She holds her cup with both hands and waits, giving you the same unhurried space she gave you over a margin question in a corridor, once.

choices.text: Then let's make it a beginning. The bookstore, the shelves, all of it. I'd like that.
choices.response:
She exhales, a small controlled breath, and smiles in a way you have not seen before, less curated, more real.

A beginning, she repeats, as if checking the word for structural soundness and finding it solid.

Then the circle calls her to the front, and she reads her page first, a short passage she loves, and her voice is steadier than usual, and afterward she catches your eye across the room once, briefly, like sharing a joke with the rain.

choices.text: (Raise your cup slightly toward her, a quiet toast to the bookstore and the friendship.)
choices.response:
She reads the gesture exactly right and returns the toast with her own cup, and her relief is visible and unembarrassed.

“Good,” she says.

A friendship with its own geography.

I have wanted a book-arguing companion for years and kept interviewing the whole campus without telling them.

Then she says the bookstore trip is on, Saturday, late, and that she already knows which shelf she will defend first.

episodes.ending:
The reading evening runs until the building staff start turning off corridor lights out of politeness, one bank at a time.

Pages are read by people who never volunteered all term.

Nothing is graded; the radiator bangs twice and is ignored.

When you both leave, the corridor is half dark and she walks beside you to the doors, still holding her cooling cup, already halfway into an argument about which shelf the bookstore will hide its best book on.

episodes.title: The Hallway We Kept
episodes.opening:
Terms have turned over more than once since the reading evening.

The seminar room has a new radiator that does not bang, which Dr. Lin claims ruined the acoustics of honesty, and the reading circle has doubled in size.

The secondhand bookstore across the river now knows you both by name, and the owner holds disputed titles behind the counter like a referee who has stopped pretending to be neutral.
episodes.dialogue:
Tonight is the last circle of the term, and afterward the room empties slowly, the way it does when nobody wants to be the first to leave a good thing.

She sits on the table's edge rather than behind it, which she only does when something is settled in her mind.

She tells you, without preamble, what has changed.

She used to measure her teaching by whether anyone was confused, she says, and confusion frightened her, so she kept tightening her sentences until they sounded like gates.

You were there the week the copies came out of the photocopier in the wrong order, and you watched her turn an accident into a method.

That was the term she stopped tightening.

Now she writes her margin questions for the room instead of against it, and last month a student told her the circle felt like a hallway where you are allowed to sit down.

She has repeated that sentence to herself more times than she will admit.

Then she says the other thing, the specific one.

She wants to make it official, in her precise way: the bookstore, first Saturday of every month, regardless of term calendars, regardless of whether either of you is teaching or studying or simply tired.

A standing place.

The friendship as a fixed point on the map, the way the seminar room was, except this one belongs to no institution and cannot be cancelled by a schedule change.

She has even picked the disputed shelf she intends to defend first, and she pulls the folded list from her cardigan pocket to prove it, because of course she made a list.

She asks if the first Saturday works for you, permanently, and waits with her pen already uncapped, ready to write it in the margin of her planner like a question she expects the world to answer.

choices.text: First Saturday, every month. Put it in the margin. I'll bring the coffee this time.
choices.response:
She writes it in her planner margin, dates it in her small careful hand, and caps the pen with ceremony.

Coffee, she notes, reverses the debt from the reading evening; she approves of balanced ledgers between friends.

She tells you the list has four contested titles on it and that she has been saving her best argument for a worthy opponent.

The hallway, she says, now has two chairs in it that are always yours.

choices.text: (Take the folded list from her hand, unfold it, and add your initials beside the shelf she means to defend.)
choices.response:
She watches you initial the list and laughs, the unguarded version.

“Counter-signing my battle plan,” she says.

That is either friendship or an act of war against my bibliography, and I have decided it is friendship.

She takes the list back, folds it along its existing crease with the care of an archivist, and returns it to her pocket, where it will clearly live for years.

First Saturday, she confirms.

It is settled in ink now, and ink is her jurisdiction.

episodes.ending:
You walk out together through the corridor where you once rescued nothing but were welcomed anyway, past the window where loose pages once scattered, past the notice that now reads, in her hand, ALL WELCOME, STILL.

At the doors she does not make a speech; she says the bookstore opens late and the disputed shelf will not defend itself, and that she will see you on the first Saturday, and every first Saturday after that, for as long as the map holds.

Then she heads for the river bridge, list in her pocket, unhurried.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Her Favorite Page
romance.opening:
Terms have turned over more than once since the evening you chose a beginning.

The bookstore across the river has become a habit with a history: a disputed shelf, an owner who referees, a standing Saturday.

Tonight the reading circle ended early, the building is quieting around you, and Dr. Lin has asked you to stay behind in the seminar room, which she has never done before without a pretext ready.
romance.dialogue:
She has a book with her, an old paperback soft at the spine, and she holds it the way she holds things she is nervous about, with both hands.

She tells you there is a page in it she has loved for years, and that the page holds something she has never shown anyone.

She opens it near the middle.

Pressed between the pages, years ago by someone she will not name except to say it was her, is an unsigned note, written in a younger version of her own careful hand.

It is a single question about the passage, the kind she writes in margins, except this one was written at a time when she believed questions had to be answered correctly to be worth asking.

She kept the note unsigned, she says, because at the time she was not ready to sign her own doubts.

She has spent years teaching other people that misreading is an entrance, and the note is the proof that she once needed the lesson herself.

She is showing it to you now because you were there in the corridor, and the week of the scrambled copies, and the empty hall, and you have never once treated her precision as armor to be gotten past; you treated it as the way she is brave.

So, she says, the same precision, pointed the other direction: she is telling you that she does, that she has for a while, carefully, and that her life stays her own, the circle, the bookstore, the river bridge at night; she wants someone beside it.

She asks if you want this too, and says the honest answer matters more than the kind one, and then does something you have never seen: she caps her pen and sets it on the table, so that her hands are empty and there is nothing between you and the question.
