He closes the booklet and holds it against his chest. "Today we log the mystery and go home with unfinished business. That's a legitimate stopping place. I even have a slip of paper for the occasion."

episodes.ending:
Whatever you chose, Samir walks back with you as far as the archive steps, the booklet under his arm and the pencil tucked in its cloth spine.

"Page six is better than it was this morning," he says. "It has a confirmed mystery, and it has company in the margins. Both improvements."

He pauses at the door, turning the booklet over in his hands once.

"There are about forty more pages," he says. "Some are just benches. Some are the routes to the good chess table and the cafeteria seat with the right amount of noise. If you ever want to test another one — slowly, quickly, or halfway and then revise — the booklet opens flat. That's the whole design principle."

He taps the cover once, dry and warm. "Next time, I want your handwriting in it. Consider that an open invitation with no posted hours."

episodes.title: The Stopping Slip
episodes.opening:
The archive lights have gone down to the evening half-setting — amber in the stacks, the reading room almost dark. Samir is still at his desk, glasses pushed up into his curls, bent over the same photo box he was on this morning.

"One more page," he says, without looking up. Then he hears himself and laughs quietly. "I said that an hour ago. Possibly two."

He sits back. His tea isn't steaming. It isn't even pretending to be warm. He picks up the cup, considers it like evidence, and sets it down.

"Right. That's the sign." He pulls a small slip of paper from the drawer, writes in pencil — a box number, a sleeve count, a few words — and slides it into the exact place between two photographs. He closes the lid and presses the box back onto the shelf with both hands, the crutch leaning where he can reach it.

"Marked and closed. If I open it tonight, the slip will judge me." He reaches for his jacket. "I promised Nadia I'd eat something that isn't eaten standing at a desk. And you're here, so the promise has witnesses."
episodes.dialogue:
The cafeteria at this hour is half-empty and bright, which Samir seems to consider a feature. He picks a table near the window, sits with the ease of someone who has measured every seat in this building, and takes the menu even though neither of you needs it.

"The rice has two colors again," he says, studying the serving line. "I'm mapping it properly this time. Last week I lost the thread at the pickled radish and had to start over." He says it with complete seriousness, and you can't tell how much is a joke.

Halfway through the meal, he pulls an envelope from his jacket — thick, soft, already opened, his sister's handwriting on the front. "Nadia sent this Monday. She mails me puzzles. It's a system that's worked for years, and neither of us sees a reason to fix it."

He turns the box over in his hands but doesn't open it further. "She includes a clue instead of showing me the picture. This one says: 'Everything in it is either leaving or waiting to leave.'" He shakes his head. "I've been turning it over all week. Trains, I thought. Boats. An airport. She won't confirm anything — she says confirming defeats the purpose."

He sets the box on the table between you, unopened, and picks up his fork again. "I'm not spending dinner on it. I made that mistake once — turned a whole evening into an investigation and forgot to eat. She called me out on it. Older sisters keep records too."

choices.text: Everything leaving or waiting to leave... a departure board?
choices.response:
Samir stops with his fork halfway up and looks at you for a long moment.

"A departure board," he repeats. "Letters flipping over. Half showing the next thing, half showing nothing yet." He puts the fork down and stares at the puzzle box like it has just confessed something.

"That's annoyingly good. And I'm not messaging her to check. If you're right, she gets to be smug for a month; if you're wrong, we've lost nothing." He slides the box into his jacket pocket, deliberately, the way you'd close a folder. "It goes in the theory pile. Not the record pile. The record pile stays empty until I open it Sunday."

He points his fork at you, mildly. "You realize this means you're involved now. If it's a departure board, I'm telling her a friend solved it. She'll like that better than if it was me."

choices.text: (Say nothing about the clue and just keep eating with him.)
choices.response:
You don't reach for the puzzle box, and Samir notices. Something in his shoulders eases, like he'd been braced for dinner to turn into a project.

"Good," he says quietly. "Thank you for not doing that. Most people would've started guessing by now. I would've started guessing by now." He maps the rice with his fork, finds the radish landmark on the first try, and looks genuinely pleased about it.

The meal goes slow, the way he likes things slow. He tells you about the chess friend who let him call a loss conclusive evidence, and about the cat photo he's printing for the lounge shelf — the one that refuses to look at the camera. "It's the most honest photograph in the building," he says. "Everyone else in the archive is performing for the lens. That cat simply declined."

When the trays are cleared, he stands, tucks the unopened puzzle box under his arm, and pauses. "Sunday, I'll open it. If you happen to be near the common room, there's a board and an empty table and no obligation attached. The clue stays a clue until then."

episodes.ending:
He walks you as far as the doors, where the evening air comes in cool through the gap. Behind you, the archive windows are dark except for one lamp someone left on over the indexing desk.

"The slip stays in the box until morning," he says, patting his jacket pocket where the puzzle sits instead. "Two closed things, one evening. That's a personal record."

He adjusts his grip on the crutch and looks out at the path toward the dorms, the one with the benches he's drawn in his booklet. "Nadia's clue is under advisement. The rice was successfully mapped. And next week there's a box of theater photographs nobody signed — a whole new set of faces I refuse to guess about." He smiles at you, unhurried. "Same table works, if you want to hear how the departure board theory holds up. No pressure. The puzzle keeps either way."

episodes.title: A Route for Two
episodes.opening:
The bench under the trees is in the late-afternoon shade, and Samir has already set his booklet open on the slats beside him, weighted with a small stone so the pages don't turn on their own.

His graphite crutch rests against the armrest, within easy reach, and there's a paper bag of cafeteria rolls between you — he carried it himself, in the hand he didn't need for the walk.

"Fair warning," he says, easing down and stretching his leg out. "I planned this as a two-part outing. Bench first, then the north path back. But I built in a rest point halfway, and the revision option is standing and official."

He taps the booklet's blank corner. "I've walked this route twice this week. One bench has a wobbly slat, the fountain by the greenhouses works, and the gate past the labs sticks unless you lift the handle. Ordinary details. I like knowing them before I go anywhere with someone."

He takes a roll, tears it in half, and offers you the bigger piece without comment.
episodes.dialogue:
He eats slowly, in no hurry at all, and watches two students argue cheerfully about a flyer taped to the lamppost.

"So," he says finally, dusting crumbs off his fingers. "I drafted three versions of what I want to say, and they all sounded like a catalog entry. So I'm just going to say it."

He turns to face you, one arm along the back of the bench but not touching you.

"I want to meet you outside the archive. Not just walking routes, not just boxes and ledgers. I like who I am on these walks with you, and I've noticed I check my phone on slow indexing afternoons hoping you've written. That's evidence. I trust evidence."

A pause. He adjusts his glasses, which is what he does when the next sentence matters.

"So here's the question, and both answers are good ones. Would you want to go on a date with me? Somewhere you choose, at a pace you choose, with a route we can revise as many times as you like — that's just how I plan anything, so don't read extra weight into the ramp notes. Or, if that's not what this is for you, I'd honestly like to keep walking together as close friends, and that offer doesn't expire or come with a downgrade."

He picks up his tea, finds it's gone cold, and sets it back down with a small rueful sound. "That's the whole thing. Take your time. I mean that literally — the bench is good for at least an hour."

choices.text: Yes. A date — I'd like that.
choices.response:
Samir exhales, long and visible, then laughs at himself.

"Good. Okay. You'd think I'd be calmer, given I rehearsed." He opens the booklet to a fresh page and clicks his pencil. "So — a date. You pick the what, I'll handle the how of getting there. I'll walk the route beforehand, note the doors and the good seats, and leave the whole plan in pencil so we can change any line of it."

He writes a small heading — Date, options — and leaves three blank lines under it.

"No deadline on the blank lines. When you think of something, tell me, and I'll do the ordinary planning that makes it work. That's just my part of any outing, with anyone." He closes the booklet and looks at you, the corner of his mouth lifting. "For the record, this is the best thing that's happened at this bench, and this bench once had excellent shade in July."

choices.text: (Shake your head gently, and lean back beside him.)
choices.response:
Samir reads it in a second and nods, easy and unbothered, like you've just confirmed a route revision.

"Friends, then. I genuinely mean it when I say that's a good answer." He flips to a different page and adds a small mark beside the bench drawing. "I'm noting this spot as a regular stop. Just a place we come sometimes."

He hands you the other half of the roll he'd been holding in case you wanted more.

"Close friends get the full service, you know. Route notes, puzzle mail reports, conclusive chess evidence." He settles back, shoulder a comfortable hand-width from yours. "Same walks, same pace, nothing downgraded. And if that ever changes on your side or mine, we revise. That's how good plans work."

episodes.ending:
The afternoon doesn't rush off anywhere. The shade shifts slowly across the bench, and Samir tells you about the cat photo that refuses to look at the camera and has become the lounge shelf's biggest star.

Eventually he packs the booklet, checks the route north with a glance at the gate that sticks, and stands, hooking his hand back through the crutch cuff.

"North path, one rest point, sticking gate," he recites. "Same time next week? I'll bring the roll halves. I've found the bigger piece is a reliable incentive to come back."

He waits for you to fall in step before setting off, matching a pace he asks about rather than assumes — and he is clearly glad to be walking beside you.

"I'll mark today's page tonight," he adds. "Some entries deserve a date on them."

episodes.title: The Open Table
episodes.opening:
The common room smells like late afternoon — warm radiator, someone's abandoned tea. Samir has the small round table by the window, the one he always says is the right height for two people and one board.

The jigsaw between you is one his sister mailed him: five hundred pieces, a lighthouse, nothing too stubborn. You're down to the sky, which he calls 'the honest section' — you either match the shade or you don't.

He works with the box lid propped against the board and his crutch hooked on the chair edge within reach. Every so often he picks up a piece, turns it, and sets it back in the same spot, like he's filing it for later.

'Last four,' he says, sliding one toward you. 'Take your pick. I've already decided which one I want, and I'm pretending I haven't.'
episodes.dialogue:
You place yours first. It clicks in with the river, the last blue of the water before the rocks. Samir turns his over twice, finds the angle, and sets it into the sky with a small, satisfied tap.

'That's the lighthouse finished.' He leans back and looks at it the way he looks at a completed index — settled. 'I'll write to Nadia tonight. She'll want the completion time, and whether the sky was as tedious as advertised.'

He packs the pieces in loose rows and leaves the finished picture on the table a moment longer. 'Can I tell you something I've been sitting on?' he says. 'The first weeks I knew you, I kept planning around you. Checking your schedule before I suggested anything, picking routes I thought you'd handle.' He shakes his head. 'It took me embarrassingly long to figure out that's not the same as knowing you.'

He taps the finished lighthouse once. 'You showed me. You told me your pace, and I adjusted mine, and it turned out that was the better system all along. Pauses, changed plans, boring Tuesdays — all of it fits, and I'd rather have all of it than a neat schedule without you in it.'

He caps the piece box and stands, taking his crutch in one easy motion. 'Come on. The maples on the north path have started turning, and I drew that bench last spring when it had no shade at all. The booklet needs updating.'

Outside, the light is long and gold. He walks at an unhurried rhythm, and at the corner where the cracked pavement starts, he takes the gentle detour he marked months ago without comment, because it's just the way he goes.

choices.text: 'For the record — the tedious sky was worth it.'
choices.response: Samir laughs, short and genuine. 'I'll quote you in the letter. Witness testimony carries weight.' He holds the door to the stairwell lobby open with his shoulder and lets you through first. 'And when she sends the next one — and she will, there's a system in place — the table's yours too. You've earned sky rights.'

choices.text: (Walk the rest of the way beside him without saying anything.)
choices.response: He doesn't fill the quiet, and neither do you. The maples really have turned, and when you reach the bench he pulls out his pencil and shades a new line over the old drawing of bare branches. 'There,' he says, mostly to himself. 'Accurate now.' Then he glances at you, easy and content, and pats the seat beside him.

episodes.ending:
You sit on the bench while he finishes the page, the campus going soft around you. In the blank corner he always leaves, he writes a small note — date and all, like a catalog entry.

'There's a new puzzle coming, a chess rematch pending, and a cafeteria Tuesday with my name on it,' he says, putting the booklet away. 'Nothing on that list needs deciding today.'

He checks his watch, decides he has time anyway, and asks, 'Same time next week?' It's just the plan, held loosely, yours to change.

When you part near the archive steps, he lifts his hand in an unhurried wave. The path booklet has one more page in it now — a bench with shade where there used to be none, and a small note in the corner naming who was there when the page was drawn. The space beside the section on past club activities, the one he once said had room for something new, is still open. He seems in no hurry to close it. You already have a place in the routes he keeps, and next week is already a plan the two of you share.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: An Evening at Our Pace
romance.opening:
The common room is nearly empty by the time you arrive. One lamp is on over the small table by the window, and Samir is already there, setting out the pieces. His forearm crutch is hooked over the table edge where he can reach it, and two cups of tea steam beside the board — one of them on your side.

He looks up when the door clicks shut behind you. "You came. I know I asked, but asking by message and knowing are different things." He pulls out the chair opposite him — the one with the cushion he put there earlier.

Outside the window, the campus lamps have just come on, and the trees along the path you both walked last week make a dark line against the sky. "No timer tonight," he says. "I checked the room schedule. We have it until the building closes, and the person at the desk knows to knock before locking anything."
romance.dialogue:
Samir turns the board so the lighter pieces face you, then leaves his hands in his lap, waiting.

"Before we start, I want to say something plainly." He adjusts his glasses. "We chose to date. I chose it too — that part I want to be clear about. But a choice made once isn't a contract. So I'm checking, once, tonight, with my actual face visible: do you still want this? The answer can be different from last week and nothing here breaks."

He taps the edge of the board, a small nervous habit you've seen during close games. "I'd rather hear a no in a warm room with tea than find out through someone going quiet. That's the whole speech. The rest of the evening is just chess."

choices.text: Yes. I still want this — I'd have said so sooner if you'd let me.
choices.response:
Samir exhales, and the tension in his shoulders lets go all at once. "Good. Noted, dated, witnessed by thirty-two chess pieces." He smiles and reaches for his first pawn, then pauses. "For the record, I wanted to ask properly, out loud, looking at you. Some things deserve the slower route."

He moves the pawn two squares forward and settles back. "Your turn. Take all the time you want. I mean that about the board and, apparently, about everything else too."

choices.text: (Rest your hand over his and say, "Yes. I still want this.")
choices.response:
Samir goes still, then turns his hand palm-up under yours for a moment before you both draw back to your sides of the board. "I wanted to hear you say it," he says, his voice a little rougher than usual. "Yes from me, too." He clears his throat, but he's smiling as he studies the pieces.

"Nobody has ever answered a question that way mid-opening. I'm going to be distracted for at least six moves. I hope you're proud of yourself."

romance.ending:
The game runs long and neither of you minds. Samir loses a knight to an oversight he blames entirely on the tea, and by the time the desk worker's knock comes, the board is half-cleared and the window shows a sky gone fully dark.

He packs the pieces while you finish your cup. "Next week there's a small exhibition at the student gallery — photographs, which feels on brand for me. I walked the route this afternoon. Step-free entrance on the north side, a bench halfway if we want it, and the gallery has actual chairs, not those leaning stools." He taps his booklet, sitting on the table with a fresh pencil mark on one page. "That's the plan. And if you want to change it — the day, the pace, the whole destination — we change it. That's how I'd like this to work. Routes and everything else."

He holds the door for you with his shoulder, crutch in hand, and the two of you walk out together under the lamps, taking the long way that has the most shade, even though at this hour it doesn't matter. He notices you notice, and smiles. "Habit," he says. At the bench he offers his free hand. You take it, and he waits until your steps match before walking on. "And another date next week," he adds. "I am glad we both want that."

episodes.title: 没有名字的盒子
episodes.opening:
档案室里弥漫着纸张和凉空气的味道，过了第二道门之后一直是这个味道。萨米尔把盒子打开，摆在窗边那张矮桌上——整个房间里唯一一个不用弓着背就能真正坐着阅读的座位。照片是几十年前的，社团活动日拍的，全都没有署名。

“这张是原件，”他捏着照片的边缘说。“这行台账是记录。而这个——”他敲了敲托盘旁的便利贴，“——只是我的推测。在它配得上编号之前，不会得到任何来源编号。”

照片上是老科学馆台阶前的一群人，后排有个人半转过身去。你问他觉得那是谁。他小心地把照片放下。

“我不猜。至少不会凭一张脸去猜。”他朝便利贴点点头。“建筑我能证明，季节能，也许还能从横幅认出是哪个社团。但那个人在被记录点名之前，会一直保持无名。凭空猜测就是目录变简略的原因——而简略的目录会让人失去东西。我抽屉里就有一个文件夹能证明这一点。”
episodes.dialogue:
你们一起又整理了几张照片，把说明文字和台账一一核对。萨米尔故意放慢速度，每行都读两遍，还会讲出哪些是白纸黑字写着的、哪些只是他的猜测。

这时他的手机震了一下。他瞥了一眼，皱起眉头。“主电梯又坏了。维修单上写的是最早明天才能修。”

这盒照片需要送回下层书库。一位同事路过门口，爽快地提出可以帮他直接把盒子搬下去。萨米尔道了谢，却没有把盒子递过去。

“东走廊有一条有据可查的无障碍路线，”他说。“坡道没问题，那扇门有点卡，但能打开，半路还有一个休息点。我自己走过。它就记在目录里。”

同事犹豫了一下，显然是一片好意。“我搬的话就是快一点嘛。”

“对你来说是快一点，”萨米尔说，语气并不刻薄。“可这样一来，下次电梯再坏的时候，就没人去检查那条路线还能不能用了。我宁愿它一直是一件理所当然的事，而不是一种恩惠。”他用一张纸条在台账上标好停下的位置，合上盒子，看向你。

“愿意的话就跟我来。我带你看看那扇门为什么值得记住。”

choices.text: 我想看看那条路线。带我去看看那扇卡住的门吧。
choices.response:
萨米尔的肩膀松了下来，好像他一直在为一场并不想发生的争执做准备。“好。反正它也比电梯有意思。”

他自己提起盒子，前臂杖靠在顺手的位置，领你穿过东走廊。坡道很平缓。那扇门确实卡——得用胯部顶一下、找对特定的角度才行，他毫不做作地演示了一遍。

半路有一张窗下的长椅，他指着它，像在介绍一位老熟人。“休息点。它写在目录条目旁边的备注里，所以任何人都能找到，而不只是那些早就知道的人。”

到了下层书库，他把盒子上架，更新了位置那一行，并标上日期。“原件归位，记录更新，推测还留在楼上的桌上。这就是完整的一趟。”他看起来挺满意。“电梯明天会修好，但这条路线从来就没坏过。”

choices.text: （安静地待着，趁他安排路线的时候，拿起一张剩下的照片看看。）
choices.response:
萨米尔耐心地、没有提高嗓音地向同事解释他的道理，而你手里翻着那张半转身陌生人的照片。背面一片空白。没有日期，没有名字，什么都没有。

同事离开后，萨米尔注意到你拿着的东西。“是这张啊？”他回到桌边。“每个人都会问起那些半转身的。一个人背对着镜头，总会让人想替他把那句话说完。”

他轻轻接过照片，正面朝上放回托盘里。“但替他说完，就只是我一个人的声音而已。记录总会到位的——只要我不催它，它一直都会。”

他提起盒子，朝门口偏了偏头。“路线照样能走，电梯坏不坏都一样。你坐着看照片，我下去把盒子归位，回来讲给你听。”

episodes.ending:
盒子归了位，你们回到楼上。窗边的托盘里，那些没有署名的照片还在等着，那个半转身的陌生人暂时依然无名。萨米尔把已经凉了的茶放到一边。

“记录迟早会替他们命名，”他说，“这就是这份工作的全部。替他们保持耐心。”

他跟你讲起刚才那趟路——那扇要用特定角度才能推开的门，那张窗下的长椅，还有盒子如今安放的确切书架，位置那一行的日期刚刚更新过。讲起来就像那本来就是下楼的路，因为它本来就是。

他瞥了你一眼，带点自嘲。“你听完了关于恩惠和无障碍的整篇大道理。大多数人都会找个借口，从那扇卡住的门溜走。”他说这话不像抱怨，倒像一个人在记下一件值得留存的事实。

“目录里有一个关于过去社团活动的部分，”他补充道，敲了敲台账。“旁边还有空位。如果你哪天想回来帮忙把面孔和记录对上——用什么节奏都行——窗边这个座位是最好的。”

episodes.title: 地图上的长椅
episodes.opening:
档案馆的阅览室每逢星期五提前关闭。萨米尔等在门边，一手拄着石墨色前臂拐杖，一手拿着一本小方册子，四个边角都用软布包着。

“走之前等一下，”他说，“我带了证据来。这次总算是我自己的证据。”

他把册子摊在窗边的矮桌上。纸页上是铅笔画的校园路线，每张长椅都有独立的一页——树荫用排线画出，旁边写着小注：上午十点前晒得到太阳，扶手在左侧，周二离装卸货区太近。

“我画了两年了，”他说，“任何路线，我都会先自己走一遍，才推荐给别人。哪扇门卡，哪个时段人多，哪台饮水机真的出水。今天我想请你陪我实地检验一条——我想让第六页多一双眼睛。”
episodes.dialogue:
第六页画的是从档案馆到人文楼的路——标注为大部分良好，半路有一张长椅，还有一部按钮时灵时不灵的电梯。

“有个角落我留了空白，”他敲了敲那里，“我不常留空白。人文楼的侧门，我从来没碰见它开过。不知道是上了锁，是时间安排，还是闭门器坏了。我宁愿如实记下，也不愿写一个猜测。猜测拿不到来源编号，哪怕在我自己的册子里。”

午后的天气暖而不灼人。萨米尔在坡道上保持着从容的节奏，拐杖凭着熟练的小绕行找到路面的平整处。他不用人问就开始解说——那段排水沟篦子会卡住手杖尖，这一段路缘石完全没有落差。

到了人文楼侧门，门纹丝不动。他试了一次把手，检查了铰链那一侧，然后看向那块小小的黄铜牌。上面没标任何开放时间。

“就是它了，”他说，与其说恼火，不如说像账目终于对上时那种满意，“谜团被确认为谜团。”

他掏出一截短铅笔，在第六页上写道：上锁，无标示开放时间，周五下午已查验。然后看向你。

“接下来才是我真正想听你回答的部分。我们可以绕远路——平坦，经过那张好长椅，大约多花八分钟。或者今天到此为止，绕行路线改天再记。我见过太多人还没被征求意见，就先被塞了一条路线。我不会那样对你。你的节奏，你的决定。如果你说今天算了，那也是一个正经的回答。”

choices.text: 那就走远路吧。我想看看你一直夸的那张长椅。
choices.response:
萨米尔脸上浮起一种掩不住的、安静的高兴。“证据终于确凿了——原来想看第九页的不止我一个。”

他领你绕过楼角，铅笔已经握在手里，边走边改图——原来他把长椅旁那棵树画偏东了。走到那里，长椅和画上分毫不差：浓浓的树荫，有扶手，正对着小路，能看着来往的人走近。

“这是我最喜欢的一页，”他坐下时轻轻吐了口气，承认道，“因为，这是我意识到这本册子可以有同伴之后，画下的第一页。”

他把铅笔留在你们之间摊开的那页上。“发现我漏了什么，就标上去。这条路线现在也是你的了。”

choices.text: （指指第六页的空白角落，然后等待。）
choices.response:
你指了指上锁的那扇门旁留下的空白。萨米尔顺着你的手指看过去，轻轻笑出声。

“对哦。空白要如实填上才算完成。”他在那条记录下面写道：已提议备选路线，尚未走过。

“有道理，”他说，“我刚才差点就把远路硬塞给你了。这正是我得不断自我检查的地方——太喜欢一个计划，就忘了对方可能有自己的打算。”

他合上册子抱在胸前。“今天我们就记下这个谜团，然后以两个手头都有未竟之事的同事身份回家。这是一个完全正当的停点。我甚至专门为这种场合备了一小纸条。”

episodes.ending:
无论你选了哪一条，萨米尔都陪你走回档案馆的台阶前，册子夹在腋下，铅笔插在布面的书脊里。

“第六页比今天早上更完整了，”他说，“有了一个被证实的谜团，页边还有了同伴。两项都是进步。”

他在门口停了一下，把册子在手里翻了个面。

“还有大约四十多页。有些只是长椅，有些通往那张好棋桌，还有食堂里喧闹程度正合适的那个位置。哪天你想再检验一条——慢慢地、快一点，或者走一半再改——这本册子摊开来是平的。这就是它全部的设计原则。”

他在封面上轻轻敲了一下，语气干涩而温和。“下次，我要你的字迹出现在里面。就当作一份没标开放时间的公开邀请。”

episodes.title: 停下的纸条
episodes.opening:
档案室的灯光已经调到傍晚的半亮档，书架间泛着琥珀色，阅览室几乎暗了下来。你在索引桌前找到萨米尔，眼镜推上卷发，还俯身对着今天早上就在整理的那箱照片。

“再看一页。”他头也不抬地说。然后他自己听见了，轻声笑起来。“我一个小时前就是这么说的。也可能是两个小时前。”

他靠回椅背。他的茶已经不冒热气了，连假装温热都做不到。他拿起杯子，像对待证物一样端详了一下，又放回去。

“好，这就是信号了。”他从抽屉里抽出一张小纸条，用铅笔写下一个箱子编号、一个封套数量、几个词，然后把它插进两张照片之间确切的位置。接着合上盖子，双手把箱子推回书架，拐杖靠在伸手可及的地方。

“标记完毕，收工。今晚要是我再打开它，这张纸条会审判我的。”他伸手去拿外套。“我答应过娜迪亚，要吃一顿不是站在桌边匆匆解决的东西。而你正好在这儿，所以这个承诺有证人了。”
episodes.dialogue:
这个钟点的食堂半空而明亮，萨米尔似乎把这当成一个优点。他挑了靠窗的桌子，坐姿从容，像把这栋楼里的每个座位都测量过。他还拿了一份菜单，尽管你们俩都用不上。

“今晚的米饭又是两种颜色。”他研究着取餐线说，“这次我要好好画个地图。上周我在腌萝卜那儿迷了路，只好从头再来。”他说得一本正经，你分不清其中有几分是玩笑。

吃到一半，他从外套里掏出一个信封，厚实、柔软、已经拆开过，正面是娜迪亚的字迹。“周一寄到的。她给我寄拼图，这套体系运转了好几年，我们俩都觉得没必要改。”

他把盒子在手里翻了个面，但没有再打开。“她不给我看图，而是给一条线索。这次的线索是：里面的一切，要么正在离开，要么在等待离开。”他缓缓摇头。“我琢磨了一整周。我猜是火车。轮船。机场。她什么都不肯确认，说确认了就失去意义了。”

他把没打开的盒子放在你们之间的桌上，又拿起叉子。“我不打算把晚餐耗在这上面。我犯过一次这种错，把一整个晚上变成调查，忘了吃饭。她把我数落了一顿。姐姐们也是会留记录的。”

choices.text: 要么离开，要么等待离开……是出发信息牌？
choices.response:
萨米尔的叉子停在半空，看了你好一会儿。

“出发信息牌。”他重复了一遍。“字母在翻动。一半显示着下一班，一半还空着。”他放下叉子，盯着拼图盒，像它刚刚招供了什么。

“这……好得让人恼火。不过我不会发消息找她核实。你要是猜对了，她能得意一个月；你要是猜错了，我们也没损失什么。”他刻意地把盒子放回外套口袋，动作像合上一个文件夹。“它归入理论堆，不归记录堆。记录堆在我周日打开它之前保持空白。”

他重新拿起叉子，温和地朝你一指。“你意识到这意味着你被卷进来了吧。如果真是出发信息牌，我会告诉她是一个朋友解开的。这比我解开更让她高兴。”

choices.text: （不提那条线索，只是陪着他安静吃饭。）
choices.response:
你没有去碰那个拼图盒，萨米尔注意到了。他肩上有什么东西松了下来，像他原本绷着劲，准备把这场对话变成一个课题。

“好。”他轻声说，“谢谢你没那么做。大多数人这时候已经开始猜了。我自己这时候也已经开始猜了。”他用叉子在米饭上画地图，这次第一下就找到了腌萝卜地标，看起来是真心高兴。

这顿饭吃得很慢，就像他喜欢的一切都慢。他给你讲那位棋友的故事——那位棋友让他把输棋宣布为决定性证据，不许上诉；还讲了他正准备打印、放在休息室架子上的那张猫的照片，那只死活不肯看镜头的猫。“这是整栋楼里最诚实的照片。”他说，“档案室里其他所有对象都在对着镜头表演。只有那只猫干脆拒绝了。”

餐盘收走后，他站起身，把没拆的拼图盒夹在臂下，停顿了一下。“周日我会打开它。你要是碰巧在公共休息室附近，那儿有一块拼图板、一张空桌，不附带任何义务。在那之前，线索就只是线索。”

episodes.ending:
他送你到门口，晚风从门缝里透进来，带着凉意。身后的档案室窗户已经暗了，只剩索引桌上方有人留下的一盏灯还亮着。

“纸条会留在箱子里直到明早。”他说着，隔着外套口袋拍了拍，那里现在装的是拼图盒。“两件收好的东西，一个晚上。这是我的个人纪录。”

他调整了一下拐杖的握姿，望向通往宿舍的那条小路，就是他在册子里画过那些长椅的那条。“娜迪亚的线索暂缓裁定。米饭地图绘制成功。下周还有一箱没人署名的剧院照片，也就是说，又有一整批我不肯去瞎猜的面孔。”他朝你笑了笑，不慌不忙。“还是那张桌子，要是你想听听出发信息牌理论站不站得住脚的话。不勉强。反正拼图怎么都放得住。”

episodes.title: 两人的路线
episodes.opening:
树下的长椅正处在午后偏晚的阴凉里。萨米尔已经把小册子摊开在身旁的椅板上，用一块小石头压着角，免得书页自己翻动。
他的石墨色前臂拐杖靠在扶手上，一伸手就能拿到。你们两人中间放着一袋食堂的面包卷——走路时腾出来的那只手，被他坚持用来自己拎袋。
“先说清楚，”他慢慢坐下，把腿伸直，“这次出游我计划成两个部分。先在长椅上待着，然后走北边的路回去。半路我安排了一个休息点，修改方案长期有效、正式记录在案。”
他敲了敲小册子的空白角。“这条路线我这周走过两次。有一张长椅的椅板会晃，温室旁的饮水机能出水，实验室后面那道门不抬起把手就会卡住。都是些普通的细节。要和人一起出门，我喜欢先弄清楚这些。”
他拿起一个面包卷撕成两半，什么也没说，把大的那半递给你。
episodes.dialogue:
他吃得很慢，一点也不着急，看着两个学生站在路灯柱前兴致勃勃地争论一张海报。
“那么，”他拂掉指尖的面包屑，终于开口，“我打了三遍草稿，每一版读起来都像一条目录条目。所以我决定直接说。”
他转过身面向你，一只手臂搭在长椅背上，没有碰到你。
“我想在档案馆之外见你。不只是走路线，不只是箱子和台账。和你一起走这些路的时候，我喜欢那时的自己。而且我注意到，索引进展缓慢的下午，我会看手机，盼着上面有你写的消息。这是证据。我相信证据。”
他停顿了一下，扶了扶眼镜——每当下一句话重要时，他就会这么做。
“所以问题是这样的：你愿意和我约会吗？两个答案都是好答案。地点你选，节奏你定，路线想改多少次就改多少次——我做任何计划本来就是这样，所以别因此把那些无障碍备注想得太重。如果这不是你想要的，我也真心希望继续以好朋友的方式一起散步。这个邀请不会过期，也不会降级。”
他端起茶，发现已经凉了，轻轻叹了一声又放回去。“就是这样了。慢慢想。我是认真的——这张长椅至少还能坐一个小时。”

choices.text: 好。约会——我愿意。
choices.response:
萨米尔长长地、清清楚楚地呼出一口气，然后自嘲地笑了。
“好。行。你会以为排练过三遍就不该这么紧张，可我还是这样。”他翻开小册子新的一页，按下铅笔。“那么——约会。你定做什么，我来搞定怎么去。我会提前把路线走一遍，记下哪些门不好开、哪些座位好坐，整个计划都用铅笔写，这样随时可以改掉其中任何一行。”
他写下一个小标题——约会，选项——下面留了三行空白。
“空白行没有截止日期。等你想到什么，告诉我就好。让事情顺利进行的那些普通准备，是我对任何出游都会做的那部分。”他合上小册子看向你，嘴角微微扬起。“郑重声明，这是这张长椅上发生过的最好的事——而这张长椅在七月可是有过极好的树荫。”

choices.text: （轻轻摇摇头，在他身边靠回去。）
choices.response:
萨米尔一秒就看懂了。他点点头，神态轻松自如，就像你只是确认了一次路线修改。
“那就做朋友。我是真心觉得，这是个好答案。”他翻到长椅那一页，在画旁添了一个小记号。“我把这个地点记作常规停留点。只是一个我们偶尔会来的地方。”
他把一直留着以防你还想吃的另外半个面包卷递给你。
“亲密朋友可是享受全套服务的，你知道的。路线备注、拼图邮件进度报告、不容上诉的棋局证据。”他靠回去，肩膀离你正好一掌宽，不近也不远。“同样的散步，同样的节奏，什么都不降级。哪天你或我想法变了，我们就修改计划。好的计划本来就是这样运作的。”

episodes.ending:
这个下午谁都不赶时间。树影在长椅上缓缓移动，萨米尔给你讲那张死活不肯看镜头的猫的照片，讲它怎么成了休息室书架上最大的明星。
最后他收好小册子，瞥了一眼那扇会卡住的门，确认了北边的路线，然后站起身，把手套回前臂拐杖的臂箍里。
“北边的路，一个休息点，一扇会卡的门，”他念叨着，“下周同一时间？我带面包卷来，分成两半。我发现大的那半是让人回来的可靠动力。”
他等你跟上了脚步才出发，配合着一种他会开口询问而不是擅自假设的步速——他显然很高兴能与你并肩走这段路。
“今晚我会给今天这页标上日期，”他补充道，“有些条目值得写上日期。”

episodes.title: 敞开的桌面
episodes.opening:
傍晚的公共休息室里有暖气片的余温和谁忘下的茶。萨米尔占着窗边那张小圆桌——他总说这张桌子的高度刚好适合两个人加一副拼图。

桌上摆着他姐姐寄来的拼图：五百片，一座灯塔，不算难。只剩天空了，他管这部分叫“诚实区”——色调对得上就是对得上，对不上就是对不上。

他把拼图盒盖立在拼图板边，拐杖挂在椅沿上，伸手就能拿到。每隔一会儿，他会拿起一片，转一转，再放回原处，像先归档，留待以后处理。

“最后四片。”他把一片推到你面前。“随便挑。我已经想好要哪片了，只是假装没想好。”
episodes.dialogue:
你先放下了你那片。咔哒一声，嵌进河流里，是礁石前最后一块蓝色水面。萨米尔把手里的那片转了两圈，找准角度，轻轻一按嵌进天空，带着一点满足的轻响。

“灯塔完工了。”他向后靠去，用看一份编完的索引的眼神打量它——安心。“今晚我给娜迪亚写信。她会想知道完成用了多久，还有天空是不是像传闻里那么磨人。”

他把拼图片松松排成几排收进盒里，没有分类，又让完成的画面在桌上多留了一会儿。“有件事我想跟你说说，”他说，“刚认识你的那几周，我一直在替你做计划。提议任何事之前先查你的时间表，挑我以为你能应付的路线。”他摇了摇头。“我花了很久才弄明白，那不等于了解你。久得有点难为情。”

他轻轻敲了一下灯塔。“是你让我看明白的。你告诉我你的节奏，我调整我的，结果那才是更好的系统。停顿、改计划、无聊的星期二——全都装得下。与其把日程排得整整齐齐，却见不到你，我宁愿留点空白给这些日子。”

他扣上拼图盒，站起身，顺手拿起拐杖。“走吧。北路的枫树开始变色了。那张长椅我去年春天画过，那时它连一点树荫都没有。小册子该更新了。”

外面，光线又长又金。他走着不紧不慢的节奏，到了裂缝人行道开始的那个拐角，一言不发地拐进几个月前就标记好的平缓绕路——那就是他走路的方式。

choices.text: 郑重声明——磨人的天空是值得的。
choices.response: 萨米尔笑了，短促而真诚。“我会把这句话写进信里。证人证言是有分量的。”他用肩膀撑开楼梯间门厅的门，让你先走。“等她寄下一副来——她一定会寄的，这里面有一套规矩——那张桌子也有你的份。下次拼天空那一块，还得请你来。”

choices.text: （默默走完剩下的路，什么也不说。）
choices.response: 他没有打破安静，你也没有。枫树真的变色了，他在长椅前停下，掏出铅笔，在旧画的光秃枝干上添了一道新的阴影线条。“好了。”他多半是对自己说。“现在准确了。”然后他看向你，神情轻松而满足，拍了拍身边的座位。

episodes.ending:
你坐在长椅上，等他画完这一页，校园在四周渐渐柔和下来。他在一直留白的那一角写了一条小注，连日期都写上，像一条目录条目。

“有一副新拼图在路上，还有一局棋等着再下，还有下周二在食堂的约定。”他收起小册子说。“这清单上没有一样需要今天决定。”

他看了看手表，又检查了一下自己那套信号——茶凉到不冒热气就该走了，然后认定反正还有时间。“下周同一时间？”他问。这只是你们共同的计划，松松地握着，随时可以由你更改。

在档案室台阶附近道别时，他抬起手，不紧不慢地挥了挥。路径小册子又多了一页——一张有树荫的长椅，角落里写着这页画成时有谁在场。他答应过会有空位的那个角落，如今有了你的名字；而“过往社团活动”那一节旁边，他还留着空间。他一点也不急着合上这本册子，下一个星期，已经在你们两人之间排好了。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 以我们自己的节奏度过的一个晚上
romance.opening:
你到的时候，公共休息室几乎已经空了。窗边小桌上亮着一盏灯，萨米尔已经坐在那里摆棋子，不慌不忙，一枚一枚放好。他的前臂拐杖挂在桌边，伸手可及，棋盘旁放着两杯冒热气的茶——你注意到其中一杯摆在你那一侧。

门在身后咔哒一声关上，他抬起头。“你来了。我知道我邀请过你，但发一条消息，和亲眼看见你推门进来，是两回事。”他拉开对面的椅子——椅子上放着坐垫，显然是他提前摆好的。

棋盘已经为一场慢棋布好。窗外校园的路灯刚亮起来，你们上周一起走过的那条路旁的树，在天幕下勾出一道深色而柔和的线条。“今晚不定计时。”他说，“我查过这间房的日程表，闭楼之前都归我们。前台的人也说了，锁门之前会先敲门。”
romance.dialogue:
萨米尔把棋盘转过来，让浅色棋子朝着你，然后把手放回膝上，等着。

“开始之前，我想把一件事说清楚。这句话我从周二就开始在心里排练，可每排练一次，它听起来就更别扭一分。”他扶了扶眼镜。“我们在交往。这也是我的选择，这一点我想说清楚。但一次做出的选择并不是一份契约。所以今晚，我想当面问你：你还想要这份关系吗？答案可以和上周不同，这里不会有任何东西因此碎掉。”

他轻敲了一下棋盘边缘——棋局胶着时你见过他这样，紧张时的小习惯。“我宁愿在一间温暖的、有茶喝的房间里亲耳听到一句拒绝，也不愿从一个人渐渐的沉默里自己猜出来。演讲完毕。今晚剩下的时间，就只是下棋。”

choices.text: 是的。我还想要这份关系——要是你早点让我开口，我早就说了。
choices.response:
萨米尔长长呼出一口气，肩上的紧绷一下子全松开了。“好。记录在案，注明日期，三十二枚棋子作证。”他笑着伸手去拿第一个兵，中途停了一下。“郑重声明，我想好好地、出声地、看着你的眼睛问一遍。有些事值得走慢一点的路。”

他把兵向前推了两格，靠回椅背。“轮到你了。想用多久就用多久。这话对棋盘是真的——显然，对其余的一切也是。”

choices.text: （把手覆在他的手上，说：“是的。我还想要这份关系。”）
choices.response:
萨米尔怔了一下，然后把手翻转过来，掌心朝上，在你的手底下停了片刻，你们才各自收回手，回到棋盘两侧。“我想亲耳听你说出来。”他说，声音比平时略有些沙哑。“我这边，也是愿意。”他清了清嗓子，却笑着端详起棋子。

“你知道吗，下了这么多年棋，从没有人曾在开局中途用这种方式回答一个问题。接下来至少六步棋我都会心不在焉。希望你能为自己感到骄傲。”

romance.ending:
棋局下得很长，你们谁也不介意。萨米尔因为一步疏忽丢了一个马，他把这完全归咎于那杯茶。等前台的工作人员来敲门时，棋盘已经收了一半，窗外天色已完全黑透。

你喝完杯里的茶时，他正在收拾棋子。“下周，”他说，“学生画廊有个小型展览——展的是照片，这倒挺合我的喜好。我今天下午把路线走了一遍。北侧有无台阶的入口，半路有一条长椅，想歇就歇，画廊里还有真正的椅子，不是那种靠墙的高脚凳。”他敲了敲桌上的小册子，其中一页上有个新画的铅笔记号。“计划就是这样。如果你想改——改日子、改节奏、连目的地一起改——我们就改。我希望以后也是这样，有事就一起商量。”

他用肩膀替你撑住门，一手拄着拐杖，你们两人一起走进灯下，特意绕了那条树荫最多的远路——虽然在这个时辰，树荫已经无关紧要。走到长椅旁，他朝你伸出空着的手。你握住了，他等你跟上自己的步子才继续走。“下周再约会，”他说，“我很高兴我们都愿意。”

episodes.title: The Empty Frame
episodes.opening:
Club week at Riverside University, and the afternoon light slants low across the main path, making every ordinary wall look worth a second glance.

Sophie Xia is waiting for you outside the club booth, camera hanging from the washed old strap, ponytail catching the light. She holds up two fingers. 'Forty minutes till our shift. Perfect. I've been meaning to show you something.'

She leads you a few steps toward the bulletin board near the lecture halls, where a fresh club poster has been put up — upside down. The club name reads like a puzzle. She stops and lifts the camera to her eye.

'First lesson,' she says. 'Before any real shot, I take an empty frame. No subject, just the light and the timestamp. Watch.'

She photographs the blank wall beside the poster, checks the screen, nods. 'Okay. The light's good. Now we can actually take something.'
episodes.dialogue:
She turns to you and holds out the camera, strap first. 'Your turn. Empty frame. Just the wall, nothing in it.'

You take it. It's lighter than you expected, warm from being carried all afternoon. You press the shutter at the blank stretch of brick, and she leans in to check the screen with you, shoulder almost touching yours.

'See the timestamp? That's your proof of when. And the exposure tells you if the light will betray you later.' She grins. 'My roommate says I treat this thing like a lab notebook. She's not wrong.'

Then she steps back and points at the upside-down poster. 'Okay, now look at this. Seriously? Someone hung the whole club announcement upside down.'

She takes the shot, then instead of telling you what she saw, she turns the screen around so you can see for yourself. The poster, upside down, the tape corners, a corner of someone's dropped flyer on the ground below.

'I could just say trust me,' she says. 'But a photo should show you. That's my rule.'

She hesitates, camera half-lowered, and looks at you directly. 'Actually — one more thing. Can I take one of you? Just you, next to the poster, for my term-start set. I'm asking first. If you'd rather not, that's completely fine, no explanation needed.'

She waits, thumb resting light on the shutter.

choices.text: Go ahead — but fix the poster first.
choices.response:
Sophie laughs, a short bright sound. 'Deal. Poster first, dignity restored, then the photo.'

She works the tape corners loose carefully, and you steady the paper while she turns it right side up. The club name reads properly now. She smooths the last corner with the heel of her hand and steps back to check it like she's framing a shot.

'There. Now the photo is just a good poster in good light.'

She raises the camera, waits until you're ready, and takes one frame. Then she turns the screen toward you without being asked. 'You look like someone who just did a decent thing. That's worth keeping.'

She glances at her phone. 'Twenty minutes to booth shift. Come on, I'll buy you a pancake on the way — the crooked ones, the best kind.'

choices.text: (Shake your head gently and point at the empty-frame photo instead.)
choices.response:
You shake your head and tap the screen where the empty frame still sits — the blank wall, the timestamp, nothing else.

Sophie follows your finger, then smiles slowly. 'Oh. You like that one better.' She tilts her head at it. 'A wall doing nothing, in good light. Honestly? Fair.'

She lowers the camera and lets it hang from the strap. 'Thanks for telling me straight, by the way. Asking first only works if the answer can be no.'

She crouches down and photographs the dropped flyer on the ground, then stands and straightens the upside-down poster, smoothing the corners.

'Okay, new plan. No photo of you today. But that empty frame goes in my term-start set — first page, right after the strap.' She grins. 'You're in good company. Come on, booth shift soon. I'll race you to the table.'

episodes.ending:
The two of you walk toward the booth together, the poster now hanging right side up behind you, the camera swinging gently against Sophie's hip.

'So,' she says, counting on her fingers. 'You've learned the empty frame, you've seen me turn the screen around instead of saying trust me, and you know I'll ask before I point this thing at a person. That's basically the whole Sophie Xia photography philosophy in forty minutes.'

She stops at the booth table and starts setting out the sign-up sheets, then pauses. 'One more thing. I've been wanting to start a first real club project — nothing grand. Everyday campus stuff. The duck in the display window that looks like a giant bird. A blurry tree. Maybe that empty wall you shot.'

She slides a sign-up sheet toward you and taps the blank line next to her own name.

'Want in? We'd both be on booth duty anyway. Might as well build something.'

She waits, pen ready, the afternoon light still good behind her.

episodes.title: The Notice Board: Two Frames
episodes.opening:
Club week is half over, and the afternoon sun slants across the bulletin board outside the main building. Sophie is beside you, camera up, when she goes very still.

"Seriously?" she says, low, and tilts the screen toward you. In the frame, a student stands close to the club's exhibition sign-up notice, one hand raised high, fingers near the corner of the paper. "That's our sign-up sheet. They're tearing it down."

She takes a second shot, jaw set. Then a doubt crosses her face — you can see her weigh the certainty in her voice against something she once told you about angles.

"Wait," she says quietly. "Wait. That's how I got it wrong last time. The wall juts out here. I can't actually see their hand."

She glances at you, then at the path around the east side of the board. "Come with me? I need to look from the other side before I say anything to anyone."
episodes.dialogue:
You cross the courtyard and come around the board from the east. From here, the whole picture changes.

The student — a boy in a gray hoodie — is reaching above the notice, not at it. Below his hand, leaning against the wall, sits a clear trash bag half full of old tape strips. He's peeling dried tape residue off the brick above the fresh paper, one careful strip at a time.

Sophie stops walking. Her shoulders drop.

"He's cleaning," she says. "I almost — " She doesn't finish. She lifts the camera and takes a third photo from beside him at honest distance: the notice straight, the bag of tape, his hand well above the paper.

The boy notices you both and turns, a little startled. Sophie lowers the camera entirely.

"Hi. Sorry — I photographed you from over there, and the angle made it look like you were pulling the notice down. I thought it was you." She doesn't soften it or pile on excuses. "I was wrong. I shouldn't have decided so fast."

He blinks, then shrugs with a small laugh. "It happens. The old tape was gross anyway. You want the corner? It keeps curling."

She does. She waves you over, and the three of you fix the notice together — you hold the lower edge steady while Sophie presses the top corners flat and he smooths out the middle. Nobody makes it a ceremony.

"Thank you," she tells him once it's done. "For not being angry. And I'm keeping both photos — the bad angle and this one. Together. So I remember to check."

choices.text: Keeping the wrong one takes guts. Most people would delete it.
choices.response: Sophie looks at you for a second, then down at the screen where the two frames sit side by side. "Deleting it would be easier," she says. "But then I'd only remember that I checked. Not that I almost didn't." She snaps the screen shut. "Besides, you were there for both versions. It's kind of our photo now." She says it simply, like stating the weather, but her ears have gone slightly pink as she turns back toward the booth.

choices.text: (Press the last corner flat a second longer than needed.)
choices.response: Sophie notices, because she notices everything. "Good instinct," she says, smoothing the paper edge with her thumb. "Posters fail from the corners." She steps back to check the board straight-on, camera hanging loose at her side. For a moment she doesn't take a photo at all — just looks at the notice sitting square and clean in the afternoon light. "Okay," she says finally, exhaling. "Booth duty in ten. Walk back with me? I want to write the caption while I still remember how it felt to be wrong."

episodes.ending:
You walk back toward the club booth together, the notice fixed behind you and the boy gone back to his tape scraping.

Sophie reviews the two photos one more time as she walks, then pockets the camera instead of fiddling with it further. "Exhibition sign-up stays up," she says. "Nobody gets accused. Good outcome." A beat. "Almost-good. The outcome's fine because we checked."

At the booth she pulls out a folded chair for you, then sits down with her notebook and writes two lines you can half-see: album — keep both frames. caption: look at them together.

"That's the reminder," she says, snapping it shut. "Just — look twice." She glances at the clock, then at you, and something like her usual brightness comes back. "Forty minutes left on duty. Your turn to pick the unexpected thing. I need one thing today I got right."

episodes.title: The Slow Route
episodes.opening:
The shaded path behind the lecture halls is cooler than the rest of campus, dappled and uneven — the kind of light Sophie likes.
She walks half a step ahead with the map folded wrong, and admits it right away.
'I had it right-side up at the start. Then I turned it to show you and now I've lost north. Seriously?'
You retrace one checkpoint together and find marker three has been taken down for repainting, its post bare. Sophie photographs the empty post, then turns the screen toward you.
'Evidence we didn't fail. The marker failed first.'
She logs it in the map's margin with a small frowning face and declares the route officially slow. By the time you loop back to the griddle cart, both of you have earned the crooked star pancakes she promised.
She holds hers up — pancake in one hand, a stack of napkins and her camera strap in the other — and studies its lopsided edges.
'Crispy edges, soft middle, completely unbothered about being symmetrical.'
episodes.dialogue:
She sits on the clean step by the cart and spreads the map flat between you, marker three's frowning face and all.
'Okay. First club project. We actually have to pick a subject now, and I keep going back and forth.' She taps the map. 'Everyday campus things. Nothing grand. The duck in the display window that refuses to look like a duck. The tree shadows that blur when the wind picks up. Maybe even this route — the slow one nobody takes.'
She eats a corner of the pancake and watches you over it.
'So. Which one do you think has enough weight to carry a whole series? And what's your reasoning, specifically, with—'
She stops mid-sentence and laughs at herself, not you.
'That sounded like an oral exam. My parents would be proud and everyone else would run.' She sets the pancake down on its napkin and starts over, slower. 'Can I ask again, properly? I'm curious what catches your eye when you walk this campus. I just want to know what you see that I walk past.'
She waits, camera loose in her lap, not reaching for it.
'No wrong answers. Even if your answer is the pancakes. Honestly, the pancakes are strong contenders.'

choices.text: 'I keep noticing the small things nobody photographs — like this path.'
choices.response: 'Exactly that.' She points the last corner of pancake at you like a verdict. 'Nobody photographs this path because it's just a path. But the light comes through the leaves in patches, and the marker posts are all slightly different ages, and someone carved a tiny lopsided star into the third bench.' She pulls the map toward her. 'Small things nobody photographs. That could be the whole title. Ten shots, each with a reason.' She writes it in the margin next to the frowning face, then looks up. 'You realize you just did the hard part. I've been circling this for a week.'

choices.text: (Say nothing and hand her the other half of your pancake.)
choices.response: She takes it like she's been handed evidence, looks at it, then at you. 'Is this a bribe? Are you bribing me into picking the pancakes as the project subject?' She bites into it anyway, crispy edge first. 'Because it's working, and I want that on record.' She chews, thinks, and softens. 'Also — thank you. For not rushing me. I ask too hard sometimes and people go quiet, and then I learn nothing.' She smooths the map flat again. 'We'll figure out the subject together. Just walking and looking.'

episodes.ending:
The map goes back inside her book, next to the flattened orienteering one, the shoe sticker still pressed in its blank space.
Sophie stands, brushes crumbs off the step, and shoulders her camera.
'Same time next week? We'll walk the route again and see what the small things look like in different light. And we're stopping at the display window — the duck deserves an audition.'
She hesitates at the corner of the lecture hall, half-turned back toward you.
'For the record, today counts. Missed marker, crooked pancakes, one project idea. That's a real start.'
She taps the camera once against her palm like a promise — no lens pointed at you.
'See you at the club room. Bring your eyes.'

episodes.title: A Photograph You Choose
episodes.opening:
Club week is winding down. By the lecture halls, the display window hums softly in the empty corridor.

Sophie crouches in front of it, camera on one knee. The plastic duck inside has stretched into the giant-bird reflection she keeps trying to catch.

'Okay,' she says. 'Selection deadline is tomorrow. I've got the duck, the blurry tree, and the notice board after we set it straight. One place left.'

She turns the screen toward you. The last frame is the route map spread on a bench, with two empty seats beyond it. 'I had an idea for one more picture,' she says. 'You could sit there with the map. I haven't taken it. Would you want to be in the club display? If not, I use this frame as-is. No explanation needed.'
episodes.dialogue:
Sophie keeps the camera low while she waits. She asks before pointing it at a person, even when the light is good and the deadline is close.

'A no ends the photo question. A good display isn't worth making someone feel watched.' She glances at the duck in the glass. 'And I do have a very tall duck.'

She sets the camera on the bench. 'There's another question. It isn't about the club.'

'We've spent a lot of time together lately. Booth duty, that wrong turn behind the lecture halls, pancakes at the griddle. I like being with you.' She rubs the old strap between her fingers, then lets go. 'I'd like to see you outside all that. As a date, if you want one.'

'If friendship is what you want, I want to keep that too. I can hear no without turning it into a debate.' She looks at you instead of the camera. 'Answer both questions plainly. I'll listen.'

choices.text: Please use the empty seats, not me. But yes, I would like a date.
choices.response:
Sophie nods at the camera first. 'Empty seats. Done.' She checks the frame once more and leaves the strap hanging loose.

Then she looks back at you. 'And a date. I heard that part too.' Her smile arrives slowly, without the camera coming up to catch it.

'Tomorrow I submit the display. This weekend, pancakes and the shaded path? I can leave the camera at home, or bring it and keep the lens on buildings. Your call.'

choices.text: (Shake your head at the photo, then say, "I'd like us to stay close friends.")
choices.response:
Sophie slides the camera into its case. 'No photo of you. The empty seats it is.' No sales pitch, no second attempt.

'And friends,' she says. 'Good. I meant it when I said that was an answer I wanted to hear too.'

She taps the map on the screen. 'Booth duty next term, if you want it. Or pancakes with no clipboard in sight. I can ask about either one another day.'

episodes.ending:
Sophie selects the photograph of the map and the two empty seats. She checks that no one is caught in the window's reflection, then marks it for the club display.

The duck stays in the next frame, impossibly large in the glass. She shows you both images and asks which should lead — a question about pictures, and she waits for your answer.

At the corridor door she slings the camera over her shoulder. 'Thanks for saying what you wanted,' she says. 'I can work with a clear answer.'

The display goes up tomorrow. Your face will not be in it. Sophie walks beside you toward the club room, already talking about how to hang the map so the shaded path is easy to see.

episodes.title: The Album with Space
episodes.opening:
The club room smells like tape and late afternoon. The first club display is finished — Sophie's duck photo, your wind shots, the notice board series, all mounted in a row with slightly crooked captions neither of you bothered to fix.

Sophie sits back on her heels, the album open across her knees. The last page is blank. She taps it once.

'Seriously?' she says, to nobody in particular. 'We actually finished a whole project.'

Outside, the lecture hall shadows have gone long. She looks up at you, ponytail coming loose, flour dust still on her sleeve from pancakes she bought an hour ago and never ate.
episodes.dialogue:
'Okay, executive decision.' Sophie holds the album flat so you can see it. 'This last page stays empty. Because I don't want to fill it just to feel finished.'

She turns back a few pages instead. The dusty tabletop test shot comes first. Then her damp camera strap, documented before it ever did its job. The misleading notice photo and the corrected one, side by side. The orienteering map with the shoe sticker pressed flat. The blurry tree that caught the wind.

'Look at this,' she says, quieter. 'Six months ago I didn't know you. Now there's a whole album and half of it only makes sense because you were there.'

She closes it and sets it on the table, then splits the last two crooked star pancakes between you without asking — crispy edges first, obviously.

'I skipped these for the display,' she says, mouth half full. 'Happily. Sophie Xia does not skip pancakes. That's how you know it mattered.'

She wipes her hands and picks the camera up, turning it over.

'So. Future ordinary day — that's what the empty page is for. And today — I'd like one photo of the two of us finishing this. But that's your call. You know my rule.'

choices.text: 'Take it. This page earned a photo.'
choices.response:
'One photo, best behavior, no weird angles — promise.'

She checks the light, takes her empty test frame like always, then sets the timer and scrambles onto the bench beside you. The shutter clicks. On the screen: two flour-dusted people, one finished display, one crooked caption.

'Printed copy goes right behind the duck photo on my wall,' she says. 'The page stays empty. This one's just for us.'

choices.text: (Shake your head and finish your pancake instead.)
choices.response:
'Deal.' She pockets the camera without a flicker of disappointment and crunches her crispy edge. 'The album doesn't need proof of today. I'll remember it anyway.'

She leans back against the table and looks at the finished display, then at the blank last page.

'That page is my favorite part, honestly,' she says. 'An ordinary day we haven't had yet, and we both already know we'll spend it like this.'

episodes.ending:
The club room light goes amber as the sun drops. Sophie packs the album into her bag, the empty page waiting inside it, unhurried.

At the door she stops and holds out her hand for a high-five, then turns it into a handshake halfway through because she can't decide.

'First project: done. You: chosen, on purpose, over pancakes — and if you knew me, you'd know that's saying something.' She grins. 'Whenever that ordinary day comes, I'll bring the camera and ask first. Same as always.'

She shoulders her bag and heads down the shaded path beside the lecture halls, past the display window where the duck stretches into something bigger than itself.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The First Date Frame
romance.opening:
Saturday morning, the shaded path beside the lecture halls. The club display went up yesterday afternoon, and the plastic duck in the window still stretches into something that isn't a duck at all. Sophie texted you a time, a place, and one line: 'No booth, no clipboard, no hurry.'

When you arrive she's already there on a clean step, camera in her lap, the strap she once photographed hanging loose around her neck. Her ponytail is the same as always, but she's turning the lens cap over and over in her fingers, which she never does.

'Seriously?' she says when she spots you — the word that always comes before something absurd, though today her smile is more careful than usual.

She stands and looks at you straight on.

'Okay. Before anything gets cute, I want to say it plainly. I asked you on a date, and you said yes, and I've been checking the light on this path all morning like that changes anything. But a date is a two-person decision. Do you actually still want this? Not out of politeness, not because backing out feels awkward. I'd rather hear it once, clearly, than guess at it all afternoon.'

She holds the camera against her chest like she's protecting it from the question.
romance.dialogue:
'I practiced saying that in the mirror this morning,' she admits. 'My roommate heard me and asked why anyone rehearses honesty. Because people shouldn't have to read minds. That's my whole thing, right? Turn the screen around instead of saying trust me.'

She taps the camera. 'Today's plan is embarrassing in its simplicity. Pancakes from the griddle by the humanities building — the crooked star ones, crispy edges. Then the slow route behind the lecture halls, like orienteering except nobody's clocking checkpoints. And I brought the camera, but not for a project. For us.'

She counts on her fingers. 'Rules of the day. One: any photo with a person in it gets asked out loud first — including you. Always you. Two: nothing goes to the club unless we both look at it and agree. Three: no work talk after the first pancake. I gave the seniors my submission notes last night.' She holds up both hands, empty. 'See? Officially free.'

She slips one hand into her jacket pocket. 'Mostly free. I brought one blank sticker, the shoe kind, from orienteering. I've been saving it for a good ordinary day. I think today might qualify, but I'm not deciding that until it's over. Evidence first.'

The griddle guy waves from down the path. She waves back with her free hand, then laughs at herself — apparently she's decided you're walking together now, and how easy that felt caught her off guard.

choices.text: 'Yes. I still want to date you. And yes to one private photo, if we both like it.'
choices.response: Sophie exhales like she's been holding that breath since morning. 'Okay. Okay, good. Seriously — I interrogate strangers for a living and I still couldn't ask one simple thing of someone I actually like.' She grins, the full bright one. 'I'll take you up on that photo. And ask me again anytime, too. Both directions.' She shoulders the camera. 'Now come on. The griddle guy pulls the crooked ones off first and we're losing the crispy-edge window.' She sets a slow pace, like neither of you has anywhere to be.

choices.text: (Say, "Yes, I want this date. One photo for us is okay, too.")
choices.response: Sophie smiles at the words instead of searching your face for a clue. 'Thank you for saying both things clearly,' she says. 'Yes from me, too.' She pockets the lens cap at last. 'Pancakes first, then the slow route. We'll look at the photo together before we decide to keep it.' She falls in beside you, matching your steps without thinking about it.

romance.ending:
The pancakes come out crooked as promised — five uneven points, crispy edges, soft centers — and Sophie eats hers with both hands full of napkins and camera, somehow, refusing help on principle. She taps along to no music on the step while you finish yours.

When the plates are empty she lifts the camera, then lowers it without taking anything.

'One photo today — the one we agreed on,' she says. 'We decide whether to keep it once we see it.' She doesn't pose you. She sets the camera on the low wall, frames the two of you against the shaded path, and takes one empty test frame first — light check, timestamp, the old habit — then joins you in the shot with seconds to spare. The timer clicks. It comes out slightly off-center, the duck in the far window stretching into a giant bird over both your heads.

She turns the screen around so you can see it together.

'That one,' she says. 'That's the keeper. It stays between us and the memory card.'

She presses the shoe sticker onto a blank page she's keeping just for today, then tucks the camera away and falls into step beside you, unhurried. 'Would you like to do this again?' she asks, and she leaves the answer to you, walking close the whole way.

episodes.title: 空相框
episodes.opening:
社团周，午后的光线斜斜地低照在主路上，连最普通的墙面都值得多看一眼。

夏遥在社团摊位外等你，相机挂在那条洗过的旧背带上，马尾辫在光里发亮。她竖起两根手指。“离我们值班还有四十分钟。完美。我一直想给你看点东西。”

她带你朝阶梯教室附近的公告栏走了几步。一张社团海报刚贴上去，贴倒了，社团名字看着像道谜题。她停下脚步，举起相机放到眼前。

“第一课，”她说，“拍任何正式照片之前，我会先拍一个空相框。没有主体，只有光线和时间戳。看好了。”

她拍下海报旁边空白的墙，查看屏幕，点点头。“好，光线不错。现在可以真正拍点什么了。”
episodes.dialogue:
她转向你，背带朝前地把相机递过来，像递什么重要的东西。“该你了。空相框。就拍那面墙，什么都不放进去。”

你接过相机。它比想象中轻，带着被背了一下午的余温。你对准那片空白的砖墙按下快门，她凑过来和你一起看屏幕，肩膀几乎碰到你的。

“看到时间戳了吗？那是你证明拍摄时间的凭据。曝光则告诉你，光线之后会不会背叛你。”她咧嘴一笑，“我室友说我把这东西当实验记录本用。她说得没错。”

然后她退后一步，指向那张倒贴的海报。“好，现在看这个。认真的吗？有人把整张社团通知贴倒了。”

她按下快门，没有直接说她看到了什么，而是把屏幕转过来递到你面前，让你自己看。倒挂的海报，胶带的四个角，地上不知谁掉落的一角传单。

“我本可以只说一句相信我，”她说，“但一张照片应该展示给你看。这是我的原则——证据要有分量，照片里的人也要被尊重。”

她犹豫了一下，把相机半放下来，直视着你。“其实——还有一件事。我能拍你一张吗？就你一个人，站在海报旁边，放进我学期初的组照里。我先问过你。如果不愿意，完全没关系，不需要任何解释。”

她等着，拇指轻轻搭在快门上，不预设任何答案。

choices.text: 拍吧——但先把海报扶正。
choices.response:
夏遥笑了，短促而明亮。“成交。先扶正海报，恢复尊严，然后拍照。”

她小心地揭开胶带的角，你帮她扶稳纸张，她把海报转正。社团名字现在读起来正常了。她用手掌根抚平最后一个角，退后一步检查，像在给一张照片取景。

“好了。这样照片就是一张好光线里的好海报。”

她举起相机，等你准备好，拍了一张，然后不用你开口就把屏幕转向你。“你看起来像一个刚做了件像样的事的人。这值得留着。”

她瞥了一眼手机上的时间。“离值班还有二十分钟。走吧，路上我请你吃煎饼——就那种歪歪扭扭的，最好吃的那种。”

choices.text: （轻轻摇头，指向那张空相框的照片。）
choices.response:
你摇摇头，点了点屏幕上还留着的那张空相框——空白的墙，时间戳，别无其他。

夏遥顺着你的手指看过去，慢慢笑了。“哦。你更喜欢那张。”她自己又看了一遍，歪着头。“一面什么都没做的墙，光线还很好。说实话？合理。”

她没有勉强，放下相机，让它挂在背带上晃着。“谢谢你直接告诉我。先问一句，只有在答案可以是不的时候才算数。”

她蹲下身，拍下地上那张掉落的传单，然后站起来，主动把倒贴的海报扶正，抚平边角。

“好，新计划。今天不拍你。但那张空相框会进我的学期初组照——第一页，紧跟在背带那张后面。”她咧嘴一笑，“你的同伴可不差。走吧，快到值班时间了。我跟你赛跑去摊位。”

episodes.ending:
你们一起朝摊位走去，海报在你们身后端端正正地挂着，相机轻轻晃在夏遥身侧。

“所以，”她掰着手指头数，“你学会了空相框，见过我把屏幕转过来而不是让你只管相信我，也知道我会先问过才把镜头对准一个人。这基本上就是夏遥摄影哲学的全部了，四十分钟速成。”

她在摊位桌前停下，开始摆出报名表，然后顿了顿。“还有一件事。我一直想启动第一个真正的社团项目——不搞宏大的，就拍校园里的日常。展示橱窗里那只看起来像巨鸟的塑料鸭。一张模糊的树影。也许还有你拍的那面空墙。”

她把一张报名表推到你面前，敲了敲自己名字旁边那行空白。

“要加入吗？反正我们俩都要值摊位，不如一起做点什么。”

她身后，午后的光线依然很好，而小路那头的展示橱窗，正等着把一只塑料鸭变成它不是的东西。

episodes.title: 公告栏：两个画面
episodes.opening:
社团周过半，午后的阳光斜斜地照在主楼外的公告板上。夏遥举着相机站在你身边，忽然整个人静止了。

“不会吧？”她压低声音，把屏幕转向你。画面里，一个学生站在社团展览报名通知前，一只手高高抬起，手指停在纸张的边角附近。“那是我们的报名通知。他们要撕它。”

她又按了一张快门，下颌绷紧。可就在这时，一丝疑虑掠过她的脸——你能看见她在权衡，话音里的笃定，和她自己讲过的那些关于角度的话。

“等等，”她轻声说，“等等。上次我就是这么弄错的。这段墙面是凸出来的，我根本看不清那只手在干什么。”

她看了你一眼，又看了看公告板东侧的路。“陪我过去一趟好吗？我得从另一边看清楚，才能对任何人说什么。”
episodes.dialogue:
你们穿过庭院，从东面绕到公告板旁。换了个方向，整个画面都变了。

那个学生——一个穿灰色连帽衫的男生——手是伸向告示上方，而不是告示本身。他手边的墙根靠着一只透明垃圾袋，装了半袋旧胶带条。他正把新纸上方砖面上干掉的残胶一条一条小心地撕下来。

夏遥停住脚步，肩膀垂了下去。

“他在做清洁，”她说，“我差点就——”她没说完。她举起相机，从男生身边以诚实的距离拍了第三张：告示端端正正，胶带袋，他的手远在纸张上方。

男生注意到了你们，转过身，有点吃惊。夏遥把相机完全放了下来。

“你好。抱歉——我从那边拍了你的照片，那个角度看起来像你在撕告示。我还以为是你干的。”她没有轻描淡写，也没有堆一堆借口。“是我错了，我不该那么快下结论。”

他眨了眨眼，耸耸肩，轻轻一笑。“难免的。反正旧胶带也脏了。要弄那个角吗？它一直翘。”

她要了。她朝你招手，于是你们三个人一起把告示弄好——你按住下缘，夏遥把上面的两个角压平，他把中间抚平。没有人把这搞成什么仪式。

“谢谢你，”弄好之后她对他说，“谢谢你没有生气。两张照片我都会留着——拍坏角度的那张，和这一张。放在一起。这样我才会记得先核实。”

choices.text: 留着拍错的那张需要勇气。大多数人会直接删掉。
choices.response: 夏遥看了你一秒，然后低头看向相机屏幕，两张照片并排躺在那里。“删掉当然更轻松，”她说，“但那样我就只会记得我核实过了，而不是记得我差点没核实。”她合上小屏幕。“再说，两个版本你都在场。这算得上是我们的照片了。”她说得平平常常，像在报天气，可转回摊位方向时，耳朵微微红了。

choices.text: （把最后一个角多压平了一秒。）
choices.response: 夏遥注意到了，因为她什么都注意得到。“直觉不错，”她说着，用拇指抚平纸张边缘。“海报总是先从角上掉的。”她退后一步，正面检查公告板，相机松松地挂在身侧。有那么一会儿，她根本没有拍照——只是看着那张告示方方正正、干干净净地立在午后的光线里。“好了，”她最后说，长出一口气。“十分钟后轮到我们守摊。陪我走回去吧？我想趁着还记得做错时的那种感觉，赶紧把说明写下来。”

episodes.ending:
你们一起朝社团摊位走回去，告示已经修好，男生也回去继续刮他的胶带。

夏遥边走边把两张照片又看了一遍，然后把相机放进口袋，没有再摆弄。“展览报名通知贴住了，没有人被冤枉，”她说。“好结局。”顿了顿。“差点就不好了。结局还好，是因为我们核实了。”

到了摊位，她帮你拉开一把折叠椅，然后坐下打开笔记本，写下两行你能半看懂的字：相册——两张都留着。说明：要放在一起看。

“这就是提醒，”她说着合上本子，“只是——多看一遍。”她瞥了一眼时钟，又看了看你，惯有的神采重新浮上来。“还有四十分钟轮值。该你挑最出人意料的东西了。今天我需要一件我做对的事。”

episodes.title: 慢速路线
episodes.opening:
教学楼后面的林荫小路比校园别处凉爽，光斑斑驳、深深浅浅——正是夏遥喜欢的那种光线。
她走在你前面半步，地图折错了，她自己先招认。
“一开始我是拿对的。后来为了给你看，把它转了个方向，现在北都找不着了。不是吧？”
你们一起折返一个检查点，发现三号标记点被拆掉拿去重新刷漆了，只剩一根光秃秃的柱子。
夏遥还是给空柱子拍了照，然后把屏幕转向你。“证据：我们没失败，是标记点先失败的。”
她在地图边角记下来，画了个小小的皱眉脸，宣布这条路线正式进入慢速模式。
等你们绕回煎饼小推车时，两个人都挣到了她承诺的歪歪扭扭的星星煎饼。
她双手满满地举起来——一手煎饼，一手抱着一叠纸巾和相机背带——端详着歪斜的边缘，一脸赞许。
“边缘酥脆，中间柔软，根本不在乎自己长得对不对称。这就是我想要的选题标准。”
episodes.dialogue:
她坐在推车旁干净的台阶上，把地图在你们之间摊平，连三号标记点旁边那个皱眉脸也露着。
“好，第一个社团项目。现在真得选个主题了，可我一直在犹豫。”她敲敲地图。“校园里的日常小事。不要宏大的。展示窗里那只怎么都不像鸭子的鸭子。起风时糊成一片的树影。说不定还有这条路线——这条没人走的慢路。”
她咬了一角煎饼，越过煎饼看着你。
“所以，你觉得哪个有分量撑起一整个系列？理由是什么？要具体，要举例，还有——”
她说到一半停住了。
她的肩膀垮下来一点，对着自己而不是对你笑了笑。
“这话听着像口试。我爸妈会很骄傲，其他人大概会跑掉。”她把煎饼放到纸巾上，放慢语速重新开口。“我能重新问一次吗？好好问。我很好奇——走在这个校园里，什么会吸引你的目光。我只是想知道，你看见了哪些我路过时忽略的东西。”
她等着，相机松松地搁在腿上，没有伸手去拿。
“没有错误答案。就算你的答案是煎饼也行。说实话，煎饼是很有竞争力的选手。”

choices.text: 我总是注意到那些没人拍的小东西——比如这条小路。
choices.response: “就是这个。”她把最后一角煎饼指着你，像下判决一样。“没人拍这条路，因为它只是条路。可光从树叶间一块块漏下来，那些标记柱的年头都不一样，还有第三张长椅上刻着一颗歪歪的小星星。”她俯身把地图拉到自己面前。“那些没人拍的小东西，本身就能当标题。大概十张照片，每一张都得有个理由。”她把这句话写在皱眉脸旁边的空白处，抬起头。“你意识到没，你刚刚把最难的部分完成了。这个点子我已经绕了一个星期。”

choices.text: （什么也不说，把你那半块煎饼递给她。）
choices.response: 她接过来，郑重得像在接收证物，看看煎饼，再看看你。“这是贿赂吗？你是想贿赂我把煎饼选成项目主题吗？”她还是咬了下去，先咬酥脆的边缘。“因为奏效了，而且我要把这一点记录在案。”她嚼着，想了想，语气软下来。“还有——谢谢你没催我。我有时候问得太冲，别人就不说话了，然后我什么都学不到。”她重新把地图抚平。“主题我们一起定。就是走走、看看。”

episodes.ending:
地图被她夹回书里，和那张压平的定向越野地图放在一起，鞋贴还贴在空白处。
夏遥站起来，掸掉台阶上的碎屑，把相机背上肩。
“下周同一时间？我们再走一遍这条路线，看看那些小东西换一种光线是什么样子。还要在展示窗前停一下——那只鸭子值得一次试镜。”
她在教学楼转角犹豫了一下，半个身子转回来朝着你。
“郑重声明：今天算数。错过一个标记点，吃到歪煎饼，得到一个项目点子。这是个真正的开始。”
她举起相机，没有对准你，只是往掌心轻轻一磕，像一个承诺。
“社团活动室见。你来帮我看看。”

episodes.title: 你选择的那张照片
episodes.opening:
社团周接近尾声。教学楼旁的展示窗在空荡的走廊里安静地亮着。

夏遥单膝跪在窗前，相机架在膝上。窗里的塑料鸭被玻璃拉变形，成了她一直想捕捉的巨鸟倒影。

“好了，”她说，“选片截止就是明天。我有鸭子、那张模糊的树影，还有我们摆正之后的通知栏。还剩最后一个位置。”

她把屏幕转向你。最后一张是摊在长椅上的路线图，图后是两个空座位。“我有个想法，”她说，“你可以坐进那个空位，和地图一起。我还没按快门。你想出现在社团展示里吗？如果不想，我就用现在这张。不需要任何解释。”
episodes.dialogue:
夏遥把相机放得很低，安静地等着。哪怕光线正好、截止日期也近，她还是先开口问，再把镜头对准人。

“如果你说不，照片这件事就到此为止。一个好的展示，不值得让任何人觉得被盯着。”她瞥了一眼玻璃里的鸭子。“何况我还有一只特别高的鸭子。”

她把相机放到长椅上。“还有另一个问题。和社团无关。”

“最近我们在一起的时间很多。摊位值班、教学楼后面那次走错路、煎饼摊前的煎饼。我喜欢和你待在一起。”她用手指捻了捻那条旧背带，然后松开。“我想在那些之外也见到你。如果愿意的话，作为一次约会。”

“如果你想要的是朋友，我也想留住这份友谊。别人说不，我不会把它变成一场辩论。”她看着你，而不是相机。“两个问题都可以直说。我会听。”

choices.text: 请用空座位那张，别拍我。不过，我愿意和你约会。
choices.response:
夏遥先对着相机点了点头。“空座位。就这么定了。”她又检查了一遍取景框，让背带松松地垂在一边。

然后她看向你。“约会。这部分我也听到了。”她的笑容慢慢浮现，相机没有举起来捕捉它。

“明天我提交展示。这个周末，煎饼和那条林荫小路，怎么样？相机可以留在家里，或者带上但镜头只对准建筑。你说了算。”

choices.text: （对着照片摇摇头，然后说：“我希望我们还是做好朋友。”）
choices.response:
夏遥把相机收进包里。“不拍你。就用空座位这张。”她没有再劝。

“还有朋友这件事，”她说，“很好。我说过这也是我想听到的答案之一，这话是真心的。”

她指着屏幕上的地图。“下学期的摊位值班，如果你想要的话。或者不带任何记录板的煎饼。这两样，我改天都可以再约你。”

episodes.ending:
夏遥选定了那张地图和两个空座位的照片。她确认窗面倒影里没有拍到任何人，然后把它标记进社团展示。

鸭子留在下一张画面里，在玻璃中大得不可思议。她把两张照片都给你看，问哪张该放在最前面。这是一个关于照片的问题，她等着你的回答。

在走廊门口，她把相机往肩上一挎。“谢谢你说出自己想要什么，”她说，“一个清楚的答案，我很好办。”

展示明天就会挂出。你的脸不会出现在里面。夏遥走在你身边，朝社团活动室去，已经在讲怎么把地图挂得让那条林荫小路一眼就能看见。

episodes.title: 留白的相册
episodes.opening:
社团活动室里弥漫着胶带和午后斜阳的味道。社团的第一次展览终于完成了——夏遥的鸭子照片、你拍的风、公告栏系列，全都一字排开，配着几条歪歪扭扭、你们俩谁也懒得扶正的说明文字。

夏遥跪坐着往后一靠，相册摊在膝上。最后一页是空白的。她用手指轻轻敲了敲那页纸。

“不是吧？”她像是对谁随口说了一句，“我们居然真的做完了一整个项目。”

外面，阶梯教室的影子已经拉得很长。她抬头看你，马尾有些松散，袖口上还沾着面粉——来自一小时前买的那份煎饼，她一直没来得及吃。
episodes.dialogue:
“好，拍板决定了。”夏遥把相册端平，让你能看清。“这最后一页就空着。因为我不想为了凑出一种已经完成的感觉，随便塞点什么进去。”

她反而往前翻了几页。落灰的桌面测试照排在第一页，后面是那条还没正式上岗就被她拍下来的相机背带。再往后，角度误导人的公告照片和修正后的那张并排放着，她一直就是这么保存的。压平的定向越野地图上还贴着鞋贴。还有那张拍糊了的树——它拍下了风。

“你看，”她的声音低了些，“六个月前我还不认识你。现在有了一整本相册，而其中一半，只有因为你在场才说得通。”

她合上相册放到桌上，把最后两个歪歪扭扭的星星煎饼分了一半给你——当然，脆边先吃。

“为了布展我把它们搁下了，”她嘴里塞得半满地说，“心甘情愿。这就说明这次展览有多重要。夏遥可是从来不错过煎饼的。”

她擦了擦手，重新拿起相机，若有所思地把它翻过来。

“所以呢。将来那个平凡的日子——空页会一直等着。至于今天——我挺想拍一张咱们俩完成这件事的照片。但这由你决定。你知道我的规矩。”

choices.text: 拍吧。这一页配得上一张照片。
choices.response:
“就拍一张，规规矩矩，不搞奇怪的角度——我保证。”

她先检查光线，像往常一样拍了一张空框测试照，然后设好定时，手脚并用地爬上你旁边的长椅。快门响了。屏幕上：两个沾着面粉的人，一个完成的展览，一条歪歪的说明文字。

“打印出来的版本就放在我墙上鸭子照片的后面，”她说，“相册那一页还是空着。这张只属于我们。”

choices.text: （摇摇头，先把煎饼吃完。）
choices.response:
“成交。”夏遥把相机收进口袋，没有一丝失望，咔嚓咬下她的脆边。“相册不需要今天的证明。反正我会记得的。”

她靠在桌边，看看完成的展览，又看看空白的最后一页。

“说实话，那一页是我最喜欢的部分，”她说，“一个还没到来的平凡日子，而我们俩都已经知道会怎么度过它。”

episodes.ending:
太阳西沉，活动室的光线变成了琥珀色。夏遥把相册装进包里，连同那条在正式上岗之前就洗过的相机背带，空页也一起带走了——等着，不急。

在门口她停下来，伸出手要击掌，中途又变成了普通的握手，因为她拿不定主意。

“第一个项目：完成。而你，是我主动选的，排在煎饼前面——你要是了解我，就知道这有多难得。”她咧嘴一笑。“等那个平凡的日子到来时——我会带上相机，先征求同意。一如既往。”

她背起包，沿着阶梯教室旁的林荫小路走去，经过那扇展示窗——窗里的鸭子正伸展成比它自己更大的什么。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 第一次约会的取景框
romance.opening:
周六早晨，教学楼旁的林荫小路。社团展示窗昨天下午刚布置好，橱窗里的塑料鸭子依然被玻璃拉成一只完全不像鸭子的东西。夏遥发来时间、地点，还有一句话：“没有摊位，没有记录板，不赶时间。”
你到的时候，她已经坐在干净的台阶上，相机放在腿上，那条她拍过的相机带松松挂在脖子上。马尾辫和平时一样，可她在手指间反复翻弄镜头盖——她从来不这样。
“不是吧？”她看到你时说。这个词总是出现在什么荒唐事之前，只是今天她的笑比平时谨慎一些。
她站起来，直视着你。
“好。趁一切还没变得可爱，我先把话说明白。我约你出来约会，你答应了，然后我整个上午都在检查这条路的光线，好像那能改变什么似的。但约会是两个人的决定。你还真的想要这个吗？不是出于客气，也不是因为退出更麻烦。我宁愿清楚地听你说一次，也不想猜一下午。”
她把相机抱在胸前，像是要护着它不被这个问题伤到。
romance.dialogue:
“这段话我早上对着镜子练过，”她承认，“我室友听见了，问我为什么诚实还要排练。因为人不该靠猜心思过日子。这不就是我一贯的做法吗？把屏幕转过去给人看，而不是让你只管相信我。”
她敲了敲相机。“今天的计划简单得有点丢人。人文楼旁铁板摊的煎饼——歪歪的五角星那种，边缘脆脆的。然后像定向越野那次一样，走教学楼后面那条慢路线，只是这次没人打卡。相机我带了，是为了我们。”
她掰着手指头数。“今天的规矩。一：任何有人的照片，都要先开口问过——包括你，永远包括你。二：拍的东西，除非我们一起看过、都同意，否则不进社团。三：吃完第一个煎饼之后，不聊工作。投稿笔记我昨晚已经交给学长学姐了。我的手正式空了。”
她举起双手，然后把一只手插回外套口袋。“基本空了。我带了一张空白贴纸，定向越野那种鞋用贴纸。我一直留着它，等一个美好的普通日子。我觉得今天可能够格，但我要等结束了才下结论。先看证据。”
铁板摊老板从路那头朝她挥手。她用空着的那只手挥回去，然后笑了自己一下——她显然已经默认你们现在是并肩走了，这份自然让她自己都没料到。

choices.text: 嗯，我还是想和你约会。也同意拍一张只属于我们的照片，只要我们都喜欢它。
choices.response: 夏遥长长地呼出一口气，像是从早上就一直憋着。“好。好，太好了。说真的，我审问陌生人是家常便饭，结果对自己真正喜欢的人，连一件简单的事都问不出口。”她咧嘴笑了，是那种完整的、明亮的笑。“那我可要占这个便宜了。你也随时可以反过来问我，双向的。来吧——铁板摊老板最先铲出来的就是歪的那些，我们要错过脆边的时间窗口了。”她把相机往肩上一挂，把节奏放得很慢，好像你们俩都没有别的地方要去。

choices.text: （说：“嗯，我想要这次约会。拍一张属于我们的照片也没问题。”）
choices.response: 夏遥对着这句话本身笑了，没有再从你脸上找线索。“谢谢你把两件事都说得这么清楚，”她说，“那我也答一句好。”她终于把镜头盖塞进口袋。“先吃煎饼，然后走慢路线。照片我们到时候一起看，再决定要不要留下。”她走到你身边，不知不觉就和你的脚步对齐了。

romance.ending:
煎饼出锅时果然是歪的——五个角大小不一，边缘酥脆，中心柔软。夏遥一手餐巾一手相机，居然就这么吃了起来，并且本着原则拒绝帮忙。她坐在台阶上，跟着不存在的音乐用手指打拍子，等你吃完你那份。
盘子空了之后，她举起相机，又什么都没拍就放了下来。
“今天只拍一张，就是我们说好的那张。它只留在我们这里，看到了再决定要不要留着，”她说。她没有让你摆姿势。她把相机架在矮墙上，取景框对准你们两个和身后的林荫小路，先拍了一张空白测试帧——检查光线、记录时间戳，老习惯——然后在倒计时结束前几秒跑进画面。快门响了。照片稍微有点偏，远处橱窗里的鸭子在你们头顶被拉成一只巨大的鸟。
她把屏幕转过来，让你和她一起看。
“就这张，”她说，“它只属于我们和存储卡。”
之后，她把那张鞋用贴纸贴在她专门为今天留的一页的空白角落上。“你愿意再来一次吗？”她问。她不紧不慢地走在你身边，把答案留给你。

episodes.title: The Light That Wouldn't Turn On
episodes.opening:
Practice ran long and the campus field emptied out slow, the way it does when nobody has anywhere better to be.
I sent the offense in before I went, because Marcus gives me a look if I linger like the grass needs my supervision.
One problem: the big light over the north sideline jammed halfway up its pole and wouldn't shut off.
Grounds had gone home.
So there I was under the tower with a maintenance number I'd already called twice, holding my football more out of habit than use, when I saw someone cutting across the end zone.
I knew the face from campus, from the field and the club-week tables, though I hadn't put a name to it yet.
That bothered me more than the light did, honestly.
A guy who grew up around a tire shop learns that noticing people is most of the job.
My first coach used to say the quarterback who forgets a name has already thrown the ball away.
I waved before I could overthink it.
"Hey!
You're the one from club week, right?
I'm Garrett.
" I kicked at a pebble, which is not a solution to anything.
"Fair warning, I might be here a while.
The light won't quit and the guy who can fix it won't pick up.
You headed out?
I ask because walking past a stadium light at night feels different with company, and I'll admit that out loud since it's true.
" The air smelled like cut grass and cold aluminum.
Somewhere past the fence a bus sighed at its stop.
I tossed the ball up and caught it, once, twice, the old rhythm that calms me down when nothing else does.
episodes.dialogue:
The maintenance line picked up on my third try and a tired man named Hollis told me the switch housing had been acting up all season and he'd come by in the morning, no earlier.
I thanked him, and I meant it, because a guy who shows up at seven for your light deserves thanks.
I set the football down on the track and sat next to it, and after a second of deciding, you sat too.
"You know what this reminds me of?
" I said.
"My dad's garage.
Something breaks, you sit with it until you understand it, then you fix it or you wait for the part.
Sitting is the hard part.
" I stretched my legs out.
"I'm not great at sitting.
I keep notes after practice, every night, even when the guys have already showered and gone.
Some nights it's forty minutes of me writing what I did wrong.
My roommate Ben can tell from the sound of my keys whether practice went badly, which is either sweet or concerning.
" I laughed at that, and it came out easy, which surprised me because I hadn't told a stranger any of that before.
The light buzzed above us and threw our shadows long across the track.
"Anyway.
Sorry, you came out here to walk somewhere and now you're babysitting a light with a quarterback.
" I glanced over.
"Trade you a question for your time.
What brings you past the field this late?
Most people cut through the quad.
"

choices.text: Tell him the truth: you like walking past the field at night, and tonight you noticed someone stubborn sitting under a broken light.
choices.response:
"Stubborn is accurate," I said, and grinned.
"My sister would back you up on that, and she doesn't even like football.
" I picked at the turf.
"Notes every night.
It's how I keep the starting job, or how I tell myself I do.
Either way, thanks for stopping.
Most people would've waved and kept going.
"

choices.text: Say nothing much, just sit a while longer under the light with him.
choices.response:
We sat there without talking for a couple of minutes, and it wasn't awkward, which is rarer than people think.
"Okay, that's it, that's the whole show," I said finally, standing and brushing off my jeans.
"Light stays, I go, you were here for the historic occasion.
I'll see you around the field, club-week stranger.
"

episodes.ending:
The light finally clicked off on its own around nine, which figured, since it had made us sit through the whole story before it quit.
I walked you to the edge of the lot and we traded a couple more lines about the campus, nothing deep, the kind of talk that doesn't cost anything.
Before we split I did the thing I'd been putting off all evening.
"Hey, real question.
What's your name?
I've been calling you club-week person in my head and that's getting embarrassing.
" You told me.
I repeated it once, out loud, the way you lock a thing in.
"Garrett," I said, and we'd already done that part, so I just nodded like a normal human instead of introducing myself twice.
I walked back across the field to grab the football and the light pole stood there dark and ordinary, like it had never made anybody wait.
In the parking lot I texted Ben that I'd be late for dinner and he replied with a thumbs up and one word, light?
which made me laugh in the empty lot.
Small thing, a jammed light.
But I remembered the name all the way home, and the next morning I wrote it at the top of a practice page for no reason I could explain, and kept it there.

episodes.title: The Notebook Page
episodes.opening:
We'd been running into each other for a while by then, enough that a nod across the dining hall meant something and the dining hall workers knew both our orders, which is the real test of a friendship.
It was a Tuesday after a rough practice, the kind where my long arc of a throw kept sailing and the freshman receivers kept running routes they'd run wrong all week because I kept telling them it was fine when it wasn't.
Marcus called me out at the line, in front of everybody, the way he does.
"Stop eating the whole loss, Kincaid.
Some of that is mine.
" He was right, which made it worse and better at the same time.
After everyone cleared out I stayed, same as always, notebook out on the bench, going through the practice in my head play by play.
You showed up at the fence with two drinks from the stand by the gym and that easy way of arriving like it was no event.
I waved you in through the gate.
"You want to see something nobody sees?
" I said it before deciding whether I meant it, then checked, and I did.
I held up the notebook.
"Every practice since I took the starting job.
The bad ones are the most honest.
Tonight's got a whole page on me throwing before the receiver turns.
" The field lights were on but low, and the grass still had the evening shine on it.
episodes.dialogue:
I sat down on the bench and let you read a page.
It felt strange, like handing someone a mirror from a bad angle.
"Marcus handed back a page I'd torn out of my own notebook after that sophomore spring scrimmage loss," I told you.
"He wrote on it, half these mistakes are coaching, stop being a martyr.
I keep it folded in here.
I don't reread it much, I just like knowing it's in there.
" I took a breath and said the true thing, the one I rarely hand out.
"I don't sleep well after losses.
I lie there quietly rewriting the third quarter.
And I don't usually tell anyone that, because the team needs me to be steady, and I get mixed up sometimes between being reliable and being available every hour of every day.
" I looked at the notebook, not at you.
"Nia, our trainer, has a whole system for checking whether I've actually rested.
She asks me what I did that wasn't football.
Some weeks the answer is dinner with Ben and a call to my sister, and she takes it.
" I closed the book and tapped it.
"You're the first person outside the team who's seen tonight's page.
That's a big thing for me.
I want you to know that.
" The drink in my hand had gone warm and I didn't care.

choices.text: Tell him the notes read like someone who cares too much, in the good way, and ask what he'd write if he were allowed to be unfair to himself.
choices.response:
That got a real laugh out of me.
"If I was allowed to be unfair?
Page one would just say throw the ball, Garrett, it's a game.
" I got quiet for a second.
"My mom's a librarian, you know.
She'd tell me to return the worry to its rightful owner.
I'm working on it.
Thanks for reading it without flinching.
"

choices.text: Hand the notebook back gently and tell him you'll sit with him while he finishes tonight's page.
choices.response:
I nodded, not trusting my voice for a second, then finished the entry with them sitting there.
It came out shorter than usual and more honest.
"There.
Done.
" I put the pen away.
"Usually this part takes forty minutes and costs me an hour of sleep.
Took ten tonight.
Interesting.
"

episodes.ending:
We walked out through the gate together and I locked it, the clank echoing across the empty lot.
You asked what was next on my night and I told you the truth: dinner, half a chapter of a book I keep pretending to finish, bed.
Nia would've approved.
On the walk I realized something had shifted in me, small but real.
Letting someone read those pages had felt like standing on the field without pads, exposed and lighter at the same time.
"Same time next bad practice?
" I joked at the corner, and you didn't laugh, you just said sure, which was better.
That night I wrote one extra line at the bottom of the page, under the notes on my throws and the routes and the freshman who'd run everything sideways.
It said: showed someone.
Slept okay.
I've kept notebooks since I was fourteen, back when my first coach drilled us on writing what we actually did instead of what we meant to do, and in all that time I never once wrote down a thing like that.
The notebook was for football.
Maybe I'd been wrong about what it was keeping track of.

episodes.title: Rain Delay
episodes.opening:
The sky opened up forty minutes before kickoff and turned the field into a pond, so the game got pushed and half the crowd went home and the other half stood under the overhang of the covered stadium stairs getting
slowly soaked anyway.
I was down near the tunnel in my warmups, tossing a ball to nobody, when the announcement came through that we'd be restarting in an hour.
An hour of nothing is dangerous for me.
My head starts running the film of everything I could mess up.
I spotted you on the stairs and climbed up to you, ducking under the roof edge, dripping.
"You picked the worst stadium in America to stand in tonight," I said, wringing out my sleeve.
"Or the best, depends how you feel about free water.
" I sat down on the concrete step, the cold coming up through my jeans.
The truth was I'd made a mistake earlier that week and it had been sitting on me like a weighted vest.
In Wednesday's practice I'd yelled at a sophomore receiver for running a route wrong, loud, in front of the whole offense, and it turned out the route was my fault, because I'd changed the play at the line without
telling him.
I hadn't said sorry yet.
Every day I didn't, the saying of it got heavier.
episodes.dialogue:
I turned the ball over in my hands a few times before I said anything real.
"Can I tell you the thing I'm actually thinking about, since we've got an hour of rain?
" You nodded.
"Wednesday I chewed out one of my receivers for a busted route.
Loud enough that half the campus could've heard it.
Problem is the busted route was mine.
I changed the play at the line and never told him, then blamed the kid for doing exactly what I told him to do.
" I shook my head.
"My dad repairs tires for a living.
He's fixed my mistakes my whole life and never once made me feel small about one.
There's no excuse for me being worse than my dad.
" I stood, sat again, stood again.
The stairs were empty except for us and a couple of band kids arguing about sheet music below.
"So tomorrow morning, first thing, I'm finding that kid and apologizing.
Plain, no speech, no turning it into a performance about what a great guy I am for apologizing.
Marcus taught me that.
He handed me a torn notebook page after our worst loss and it rearranged my whole head.
" I finally looked at you.
"I guess I wanted to say it out loud first, to somebody who'd know if I was talking myself out of it.
Am I?
"

choices.text: Tell him it sounds like he already knows the answer, and that saying it out loud was the apology rehearsal the sophomore will never see.
choices.response:
"Rehearsal.
Yeah, that's exactly what this was.
" I exhaled, long, like I'd been holding that week in my chest.
"Okay.
Tomorrow it's just me and the kid and a real sorry.
Thanks for not letting me dress it up.
You'd be surprised how good I've gotten at dressing things up.
"

choices.text: Reach over and put a hand on his shoulder, and let the rain say the rest.
choices.response:
We sat there through a long roll of thunder and I felt something in my shoulders finally let go.
"Okay," I said, quiet.
"Okay.
" I bumped their knee with mine, which is as close to thank you as I get without writing it in a notebook.
"Game's gonna be sloppy in this mud.
Stay for it?
"

episodes.ending:
The game restarted under lights with the field steaming and it was ugly football, sliding routes, a fumbled snap, a defense that bit on everything.
We won by a little, which nobody remembers by December, and I threw one ball I'd like back and one I'll keep forever.
After, in the tunnel, my ears still ringing, I did the math on my week and realized the apology mattered more than either throw.
I found the sophomore at breakfast the next morning, sat down across from him, and said the plain version.
I'm sorry.
The route was my fault.
You ran what I told you.
He went red and shrugged and said it was fine, and I said it wasn't fine and that was the whole conversation, and then he asked me to explain the screen play, and we talked football for twenty minutes, and that was that.
Marcus passed me in the dining hall line later and said nothing, just tapped his fist on my tray, which from Marcus is a standing ovation.
That night I called June and listened to her new recording with the false starts left in, all six minutes of it, and I didn't touch my notebook until the last note.
Some weeks the win isn't the thing you write down first.

episodes.title: Past the Empty Field
episodes.opening:
After the last home game of the season the campus goes quiet in a specific way, the bleachers empty and the goalposts holding nothing up, and I've always liked that hour more than the loud ones.
You and I ended up walking the long way past the field, no plan, which is how the best evenings go.
We'd eaten at the diner after practice the way we do sometimes, and the night was cold enough to see our breath, and the field sat there under one working light like a stage after the show.
I had my football under one arm out of habit, though my arm was tired enough that I switched sides twice.
There was a thing I'd been carrying for a few weeks, and the empty field made it impossible to keep pretending I'd carry it casually forever.
Somewhere along the fence I stopped walking.
"Hey.
Hold up a sec.
" The light buzzed.
June's newest recording was in my pocket and I'd been listening to it all week, false starts and all, and something about the imperfection of it had made me brave, or stupid, one of the two.
episodes.dialogue:
I set the ball down on the track and faced you, hands in my jacket pockets because otherwise they'd be everywhere.
"So.
You know me pretty well by now.
You've read my notebook, you've survived a rain delay with me, you've watched me apologize to a sophomore over eggs.
" I laughed, short.
"What I'm trying to say is I don't do this gracefully, so I'm just going to do it plainly.
I like who I am when you're around.
The guy under a broken light.
And I don't want to guess what this is anymore, because guessing is its own kind of pressure and I've got enough of that.
" I looked at you straight on.
"So you tell me.
Friends, the way we've been, which has already been one of the better things in my life, no tricks attached.
Or something more, the real version, where I stop pretending the diner runs are just convenient.
" I swallowed.
