Mind the ball — the children have excellent aim and no mercy. — He comes down the ladder, and you can see it now: his breathing is careful, the way people breathe around a pain they've stopped mentioning.

He sets a hand on the ladder rail longer than balance requires. — The ridgepole's cracked through.

I can lash it, but it wants two people — one to hold, one to bind.

The village men are at harvest. — A child's ball rolls against his boot.

He returns it with a small bow that costs him something. — I'll be plain, since you've earned plainness: the old injury aches when I work overhead too long.

Pushing through it makes things worse.

I learned that the expensive way. — He taps the wooden sword hilt, twice. — So.

Hold the pole steady while I bind it, and I'll owe you a debt I can actually repay — supper, and the story of the grandmother's soap. — The woman of the house brings out a bamboo tray of tea and dried plums while you work.

During a rest between climbs, he changes into a borrowed shirt printed with tiny flowers and hangs his washed blue-gray robe on the family’s line to dry. Between turns on the ladder he tells it plainly: he washed his robe with the family's soap, and the soap, it turns out, is plum-blossom scented, made by the grandmother, who informed him that a wandering Daoist smelling of flowers would bring the village luck.

Now the luck is drying on the line. — He binds the last knot, sits back on his heels on the ridge, and looks at the seam of sky between mountains. — My teachers said the injury would teach me patience.

It taught me arithmetic instead: what I can lift, how long, at what cost.

It's a smaller life than the one I meant to have. — He climbs down, accepts tea, and wraps his hands around the cup. — But the roof will hold through winter.

I've decided to count that.

choices.text: Then count it out loud sometimes. A smaller life still holds people — I'd rather hear the ledger than watch you carry it alone.
choices.response:
He is quiet for a moment, thumb moving along the cup's rim. — The abbey's elders would call that a lecture.

I'd call it true. — He sets the cup down and looks at the mended ridgepole with the expression of a man revising an old entry. — All right.

Out loud, sometimes.

Consider it a standing arrangement — you ask, I answer honestly, and in exchange I get to nag you about eating. — One of the children runs up and hangs a garland of weeds on the ladder.

He doesn't remove it. — It seems the shelter has an opinion about decoration.

I'll allow it.

choices.text: (Set your tea down and inspect the ladder’s lashings from the ground, checking each knot within reach while he rests.)
choices.response:
He blinks — an unguarded expression — then stays beside you on the ground while you test the accessible lashings in turn.

The checking goes faster than it would have alone, and truer.

When the last knot passes under your hand and holds, you find one loose lashing on the ladder rail. He points out where it slipped, and the two of you retie it without another climb.

He settles back onto the stool, breathing carefully. — Well checked. — Later, over tea, he says it again without the work between you. — You found the one lash I'd rushed.

I didn't have to ask twice, or once, really. — He turns his cup slowly. — Most people help and then watch the injured part of me, waiting for it to be interesting.

You watched the work.

episodes.ending:
The shelter stands mended, its fresh thatch tied neatly over the repaired ridgepole, and the children have already claimed it as a fort.

Qingheng takes his dried robe from the line, puts it back on, and returns the borrowed flowered shirt to its owner with thanks. The robe still smells faintly of plum-blossom soap.

Evening settles over the village, and he hangs a paper lantern from the repaired ridgepole — a small celebration he pretends is routine maintenance — then sets out two cups and pours.

He offers one arrangement before discussing tomorrow: either of you may ask how the other is managing, and either may answer honestly or leave the question for another day. The two of you agree to keep that freedom.

Tomorrow the road forks, he says: east on to the river towns, west back toward the abbey passes.

He does not ask which way you'll go.

He simply leaves the question sitting there, warm as the lamp.

episodes.title: The Letter from the Road
episodes.opening:
The mended shelter, evening.

Fresh thatch lies neatly over the repaired ridgepole in the lamplight, and Qingheng has hung a paper lantern from the repaired ridgepole — a small celebration he pretends is routine maintenance.

Supper is finished.

He has set out two cups, and beside his own sits the wooden sword, its sheath open for once, a folded letter resting half out of it.

He looks at it the way people look at a bridge they haven't crossed.
episodes.dialogue:
Qingheng: I've been rehearsing this all afternoon, which is why I burned the rice. — He nudges the letter into the light.

It's worn soft at the folds, written in a careful young hand, addressed to someone at Pine Spring Abbey. — This is a letter I wrote the spring before my injury.

To my teacher.

It says I'd found a shortcut to breakthrough, and that I was sure enough to risk the reservoir on it.

I never sent it.

I left instead, and by the time I could have written again, there was nothing to report but the mistake. — He taps the wooden sword hilt, once. — I've carried it for years.

As a compass.

It points at the person I was when I couldn't hear a warning. — He turns to face you fully, and his composure is intact but honest underneath. — Tomorrow the road forks.

East goes on to the river towns, where I've promised a shrine roof my spring.

West climbs back toward the abbey passes, and I've never gone back. — He picks up the letter and holds it out, flat on both palms. — Here is what I'm asking, and take your time, because I mean it as a real choice.

Come east with me a while — just as company on the road, two people walking the same direction.

Or keep your own road, and I'll write — truly write, from inns and shelters, the way I never managed with this. — His voice stays even, but his thumb presses the letter's worn fold. — Either answer leaves us something.

I've been too good at leaving, all my life.

I'd like to be a little good at staying, in whichever shape that takes. — The lantern flickers.

Outside, the fork is invisible in the dark, but you both know exactly where it waits.

choices.text: Then I choose east with you as partners — because I like who you are on it.
choices.response:
Something moves through his stillness, like a door unbarred. — East, then. — He sets the letter back in the sheath himself, deliberately, closing it like a door he means to open later on his own terms. — As a thing I'll show you when it's time, because you chose the road. — He refills both cups, and his hands are steady, and there is a warmth in his face that the lantern only partly accounts for. — I should warn you: I sing badly at campfires, I know every bad inn between here and the river, and I will fix every shelter we pass.

You've chosen a slow road. — He lifts his cup. — To slow roads, then.

choices.text: (Write friends on a spare warding paper, press the letter gently toward the sheath, and shake your head — your road runs west.)
choices.response:
He exhales — relief and something gentler tangled together — and slides the letter home into the sheath. — West, then.

Good.

It was always your road; I only wanted to say so out loud before you took it. — He takes up a brush from his pack and, on the back of a warding paper, writes the name of a relay post in the river towns where letters can find a traveler. — Here.

Write when you have something worth the ink, or when you have nothing — I answer both kinds. — He looks at the lantern, then at you, and smiles with the whole of it — no reservation left in it. — And when the passes clear and you come down the abbey road, there will be a lamp lit at whatever shelter I'm mending.

That's a promise I can keep.

episodes.ending:
The lantern burns on between the two cups, its light steady.

Whatever comes next, the letter stays where he placed it — folded back into its sheath, carried a while longer — and the eastern road runs past the door toward morning, honest in both directions.

episodes.title: Riverside Lantern Night
episodes.opening:
A year of letters has taught you his handwriting: spare, dry-humored, always ending one line before you want it to.

His last note said the river towns, the lantern festival, the third night.

You find him on the bank past the shrine he re-roofed — older in the shoulders, no grayer anywhere else — kneeling to mend a stranger's torn paper lantern with a strip of gold talisman paper, because a ward against damp, he maintains, is half a ward against tearing.
episodes.dialogue:
Qingheng: You found the bank.

I'd say I left signs, but the festival leaves signs everywhere; you'd have had to be unlucky to miss me. — He finishes the stranger's lantern, hands it back to a gap-toothed girl with a small bow, and rises, brushing grass from his blue-gray robes.

His spare blue-gray robe lies neatly folded inside his pack, visible when it opens; he smiles at the memory of the flowered shirt the villagers lent him while it dried. — A year of letters.

You've improved my handwriting and I've failed to improve your eating habits, so on balance the correspondence favors you. — He leads you to a flat stone above the water, where the whole festival floats past: hundreds of lanterns going downriver, each one somebody's wish or grief or joke.

He sets out two cups and the good tea, hoarded, clearly, for exactly this. He also takes his own lantern from the pack, lights it, and sets it afloat beside the stone, leaving a spare lantern within reach. — My teacher wrote back.

Last month.

First time since the injury. — He lets that sit, then taps the wooden sword hilt, twice. — He said: the seam you tore taught you more than the door you missed.

I've read it eleven times.

I'm not proud of that number. — He looks downriver. — Here's my year, honestly ledgered, as arranged: I mended nineteen shelters.

The reservoir held.

I sent the letter — the old one, the spring letter — to my teacher with a new line added at the bottom: 'You were right.

I'm slower now, and better.'

I've written back already.

His answer will take a year, if it comes.

That's his way. — He pours your cup before his own, an abbey habit he has never dropped. — Your turn.

The arrangement was always both directions.

What did the year make of you? — Downriver, a lantern shaped like a fish spins slowly past, and he watches it with the particular attention he gives to things that are none of his business and delight him anyway.

choices.text: The year made me someone who writes first and regrets it less. Here's the ledger: I kept every letter, including the bad ones.
choices.response:
He laughs — a real one, unguarded, the kind the composed voice usually keeps in a back room. — The bad ones.

So you have the one where I described a mule as 'philosophically opposed to bridges.'

I stand by that mule. — He sobers into something warmer. — Keeping the letters is a strange kind of shelter, you know.

Roof over a year of somebody's thinking.

I'm glad it was you. — He raises his cup toward the river. — To the arrangement, then.

Renewed.

I'll ask, you'll answer, and next year there will be tea, wherever the forks have put us both. — The girl with the mended lantern runs past again and waves; he waves back with the solemnity of a man being honored by a colleague.

choices.text: (Take the spare lantern from his pack, light it from his flame, and set it on the water beside his own without a word.)
choices.response:
He looks at the two lanterns side by side on the dark water and says nothing for a long moment.

Then, quietly: — The abbey has a word for that.

Two lights set on one current.

They use it for partnerships, mostly.

Sometimes for friendships that outlast the mountains. — He taps the wooden sword hilt, once, and lets his hand rest there. — I've watched a lot of lanterns go down rivers alone.

Mine always did. — He sits back on the stone, shoulder a hand's width from yours, not closer, and the distance is exactly right. — Next year, same stone.

Or a different one — but same arrangement, same tea, same terrible stories.

I've decided that counts as a tradition now.

Two occurrences make a tradition.

That's in none of the scriptures, but I'm declaring it.

episodes.ending:
The festival moves on around you both, and neither of you needs to move with it.

The arrangement holds: he will ask, you will answer, and the lamps will be lit at every shelter along the way.

The road goes on tomorrow, in two directions that keep meeting, and neither of you needs to say so twice.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Two Lamps, One Road
romance.opening:
The river towns, a year after the fork.

His letters led here: a shrine re-roofed, an inn with a crooked sign, the third night of the lantern festival.

You find him in the inn's upper room, window open to the water, his blue-gray spare robe folded inside the open pack, catching the room’s light.

On the table between two cups lies a worn letter, its folds gone soft — the spring letter, opened at last, and beside it a new sheet, half written in his careful hand.
romance.dialogue:
Qingheng: You found the crooked inn.

The sign lies about the beds but tells the truth about the view. — He doesn't rise right away.

He finishes the line he's writing, then sets the brush down with the care of a man putting down something heavy. — Sit.

Tea's decent.

The company, I'm told, improves when it arrives. — When you're seated, he turns the old letter so you can see it — the young, certain hand, and now a new line at the bottom in his older, steadier one: 'You were right.

I'm slower now, and better.' — I sent a fair copy to my teacher this spring.

First letter to the abbey since the injury.

The original stayed here with me. — He taps the wooden sword hilt, twice, and looks at you with nothing arranged in his face at all. — Here is my ledger, since we keep honest ones.

I mended twenty-one shelters this year.

The reservoir held.

And somewhere between the nineteenth shelter and this window, I noticed that every road I planned, I planned with room in it for you — and every letter I wrote, I wrote hoping the next one would be unnecessary because you'd be beside me. — He slides the half-written sheet aside. — I'm asking whether you'd keep walking beside me as the partners we chose to be — the eastern road, the river towns, whatever fork comes — as mine, and let me be yours, with your own road still yours, and mine still mine, and the lamps lit wherever we stop. — He turns his cup, and his voice stays even, but his thumb rests on the letter's worn fold the way it did the night he offered it. — Take your time.

I've spent a year learning to say what I want from the life we chose.

I can wait a while longer to hear it. — Below the window, a lantern shaped like a fish drifts past, and he watches it go with a small, unguarded smile.

choices.text: Beside you, then — yours, and you mine, at whatever pace the road sets and no faster.
choices.response:
His composure opens, like a shutter swung back to let morning in. — Beside, then. — He reaches across the table and rests his hand over yours, brief and warm, the first touch in a year of letters, and withdraws it again as deliberately as it came. — I'll write to my teacher that too.

He'll take a year to answer.

We'll have managed half a road by then. — He rises to light the second lamp from his own, and sets it in the window facing the river. — Fair warning, repeated and binding: I sing badly, I know every bad inn east of here, and I will fix every shelter we pass.

You've chosen a slow road and a slower man. — His smile is the unguarded one, the whole of it. — To slow roads.

And to writing letters we don't need, just for the pleasure of the ink.

choices.text: (Fold the sheet and slide it under his hand, resting yours beside it — you choose the partnership and your own road.)
choices.response:
He looks at the folded sheet, then at you, and nods slowly — a man finding room for the two roads inside a chosen partnership. — Then we keep choosing each other, and your road stays yours. The letter stays mine to finish.

That's honest too. — He unfolds the sheet and writes a moment, then reads the last line aloud: 'Some things travel with you unfinished, and that is allowed.' — He refills both cups and lifts his toward the window, toward the river, toward the year behind you both. — To the arrangement, then, unchanged and unbroken: I ask, you answer, the tea is decent, and there is always a lamp lit at whatever shelter I'm mending when you come down the road. — His smile holds nothing back and asks nothing more. — That, my partner, is a fortune I can actually keep, no divination required.

romance.ending:
He checks the first lamp and lights the second if it is not yet burning. Two lamps burn in the window over the river, and the festival drifts past below, going somewhere without needing either of you.

The letter lies between the cups, its weight finally set down.

Tomorrow the eastern road runs on, with a home each to return to whenever the roads divide, and lamps lit at every shelter in between.

episodes.title: 雨中一盏灯
episodes.opening:
雨点砸在山路上，门后那处歇脚棚屋顶破了个洞，炉膛也是冷的。

你滴着水钻进去，发现柱子上已经亮着一盏青绿色的灯。

一个穿蓝灰道袍的人站在屋檐下，正收拢一把伞。

金色的纸灰从他袖口飘落。

他用一只手把黑发半束到脑后，看你的眼神像老友看待迟到的来客——早已给你留好了位置。
episodes.dialogue:
清衡：清衡，云游道人。

雨声太吵，所以我点了盏灯。

今晚想问个路，还是就坐一会儿？——他用脚把第二只凳子挪到炉边，不慌不忙。——先说好：我不会呼风，不会算命，也不会从房梁上驱赶什么东西。

我只会修补棚子，画些挡雨比驱鬼更管用的符纸。

主要还是挡雨。——他跪下，把劈好的柴塞进冷炉膛，三口气哄出一小簇火苗，毫无花哨。——我包里有干豆子。

就是晚饭。——趁锅热起来，他打量着屋顶的破洞，在木剑柄上敲了两下，说：——梁是结实的。

盖这棚子的人手艺不错，只有茅草撑不住了。

一个时辰之内我就能补好。

你要是肩膀愿意，就搭把手；不愿意，就在火边暖暖肩膀。

两个都是正经选择。——他边说边干活，用利落省力的绳结捆着一束茅草。——人们一听“道人”就指望玄妙。

我有一条：路很长，灯比悔恨便宜。

我们这一门的学问，差不多就这些。

松泉观教了我凝神的功夫，还有怎么不让锅溢出来。

剩下的都是从湿透的靴子里学来的。——他瞥了一眼那盏灯。

青绿色的光稳稳照亮了整个昏暗的棚子。——随便坐。

雨不在乎你从哪儿来，我也不在乎。

雨只在乎你的衣服干不干，我也一样。——锅开始咕嘟作响。

头顶某处，一滴雨找到了他还没来得及补上的那道缝，落进一只空桶里，耐心得像钟摆。

choices.text: 你这盏灯是我今天见到的第一样暖和的东西。它烧的是什么——灯油，还是倔强？
choices.response:
他低低笑了一声，眼睛没离开茅草。——主要是倔强。

买得起的时候就烧油。——他捆好那束茅草放到一边。——多年前我遇到一位旅人，在一处比这还破的棚子里为我点了一盏灯。

我始终不知道他的名字。

所以现在，谁来我就为谁点。

这笔债就这么往前还下去了，仅此而已。

只是更有礼貌的算术。——他朝锅点点头。——搅一下那个，行吗？

豆子可比人更不原谅疏忽。

choices.text: （从行囊架上取下干布，开始擦拭炉边被水浸透的凳子。）
choices.response:
他起初注意到了却没作声——只是看着那块布一下一下地移动，雨在他头顶的茅草上敲打。

然后，他轻声说：——好手艺。

观里的师兄们常说，棚子会在客人开口之前就告诉你他是什么样的人。——他把那束茅草推向屋顶的破洞，用一只脚抵住梯子。——你把身边的东西弄干。

这是我想教却总教不会的一半。——他爬上两级梯级，停了停，又补了一句：——豆子快好了。

别让它们糊底。

那是另一半。

episodes.ending:
他把茅草在破洞上捆好，从下面检查了一遍。临近午夜，雨势渐小。

他给灯添了油，没问就给你续满了碗，又轻描淡写地——像人们谈论天气那样——提起东边的路上有间茶棚，水不错，就是有只脾气坏的公鸡。

他没有问你要不要走。

他只是把那份邀请留在那里，像那盏灯一样温暖，而棚子滴落着最后几滴好雨。

episodes.title: 第二杯，更长的路
episodes.opening:
三天之后，东去的路如约把你带到一处茶棚，水不错，还有一只坏脾气的公鸡。

清衡已经在那里了，坐在一张木板桌旁，院子里午后光照到的地方摆着一只陶制投壶。

一张黄纸——半张符箓，画到一半便弃了——垫在他的茶杯底下，让杯子在翘曲的木面上保持平稳。

他在门口看见你，一言不发地把第二只杯子移到桌子另一侧。
episodes.dialogue:
清衡：你领教过那只公鸡了。

它对谁都叫，就当是恭维吧。——他朝陶壶点点头。——棚主的孙子把它落在外面的。

要不要输得体面一点？

我玩得平平，倒是诚实的好陪伴。——他先投。

箭擦过壶沿，弹进尘土里。

他没有叹气，也没有去拿另一支。

只是看着它，带着一个见过太多东西弹开的人的耐心。——看来又轮到我了。——第二支箭正中壶心。

他再投之前先给你斟了茶，热气在你们之间升起。——你走路的样子，像一个人还在决定东路是不是属于自己。

我不会告诉你该怎么选。

我从前有一次决定得太急，付出了代价。——他放下箭。

敲了敲木剑柄，两下，声音保持平稳。——多年前我急于突破。

我的师长们说再等等；时机不对，我的气海还因先前一次失误而虚损未复。

我听了，却还是没等，执意尝试破境，因为我年轻又自信，这是我劝你别沾染的危险组合。——他在符纸上缓缓转动茶杯。——那一击撕裂了我的气海。

没什么戏剧性的。

没有雷劈，没有弥留。

只是一道持续的漏，像屋顶上坏了一条缝。

我仍能做事——布护符、凝神之术、修补。

但某些深处如今对我关上了门，硬去推只会更糟。

所以我不推。

我改去修庇护所，也不再把这称作一种安慰。——他与你对视，然后又看向陶壶。——我不会这么早就对人讲这些。

你要么是个值得讲的人，要么是那场雨让我大意了。

也可能两者都是。——公鸡冲一头路过的骡子尖叫。

清衡又拿起箭。——该你投了。

这只壶是宽容的。

我大多数日子也是。

choices.text: 谢谢你愿意把这事托付给我。那些让你等待的师长，当时说了什么你还没听进去的话？
choices.response:
他像审视屋梁那样从底下细细掂量这个问题。——他们说：山不会因为你心急而移动。——他笑了笑，略带懊悔。——是真的，但在二十岁时毫无用处。

如今我会补上他们碍于客气没说的话：有些门只开一次，错过了也只是地理问题。

你走另一条路。

那条路风景差些，同伴好些。——他投出；箭干净利落地落入壶中。——该你了。

还有，下个村子里吃点东西。

忧愁会把人熬瘦。

choices.text: （把那张弃置的半成符纸翻过来，一言不发地端详未完成的笔画。）
choices.response:
他看着你看，肩上有什么东西安定了下来。——半道防潮的护符。

画到一半断了思路，觉得还是我的茶更要紧。——他伸手敲了敲一道断掉的笔画。——我师父会说，诚实地弃置的符，比出于骄傲画完的符更有价值。

我师父说过很多话，我至今还在掂量。——他拿起那张纸，折了一折，塞进木剑鞘里，挨着一件扁平的、会沙沙作响的东西——看边角像是一封信，别人藏刀的地方，他藏着它。——有些事未完成，也随你同行。

这是允许的。——他把箭滑向你。——投吧。

这只壶不评断人。

episodes.ending:
他起身，与你同路而行，并指出这只是地理上的巧合，别无其他。

在茶棚门口他停了停，敲了敲木剑柄，说东路在一个村子分岔，那里的歇脚棚破损了——是他那种麻烦，说不定也是你那种下午。

没有约定。

没有亏欠。

路只是有一段同向而行，你们俩都知道，也都没有说第二遍。

episodes.title: 小花，沉重的正午
episodes.opening:
那座棚屋破损的村子还要再往东走半天路，你到达时，清衡正在屋顶上。

他已把茅草掀开了一半，袖子束在臂后，腕上的金色符纹闪着微光。

孩子们在院子里追着一只布球跑，一位妇人不停地喊着一个不是他的名字。

他低头看见你，有那么一瞬——在平静的神色恢复之前——他的手按在了自己的肋上。
episodes.dialogue:
清衡：你来得挺快。

小心那球——孩子们瞄得极准，毫不留情。——他顺着梯子下来，你现在看清了：他的呼吸很小心，是那种不再提起疼痛的人呼吸的方式。

他的手在梯栏上停留的时间，比保持平衡所需的更久。——脊檩裂穿了。

我可以绑扎固定，但这活儿需要两个人——一个扶着，一个绑。

村里的男人们都去收庄稼了。——一个孩子的球滚到他的靴边。

他把球递回去，微微一躬，这一躬让他付出了些代价。——我就直说了，既然你已赢得了听直话的资格：旧伤在我长时间在头顶上方干活时会作痛。

硬撑只会让情况更糟。

这个道理我是花了大价钱才学会的。——他轻敲了两下木剑柄。——所以。

扶稳那根檩条让我绑扎，我就欠你一笔真正还得起的人情——一顿晚饭，还有这家祖母那块肥皂的来历。——你们干活时，屋主妇人端出一竹盘茶和话梅。

在两次攀爬之间的歇息里，他换上一件印着小花的借来的衬衫，把洗过的蓝灰道袍挂上这家的晾衣绳晾晒。在梯子上轮换的间隙，他坦白地说了缘由：他用这家的肥皂洗了道袍，而那肥皂，原来竟是梅花味的，是这家的祖母做的，她还告诉他，一个带着花香的云游道士会给村子带来好运。

如今那份“好运”正挂在晾衣绳上晾着。——他绑好最后一个结，坐在屋脊上脚跟后收，望着群山之间那道天空的缝隙。——我的师长们说，这伤会教我耐心。

它教的却是算术：我能举多重，能撑多久，代价是什么。

这比我原本想要的人生要小。——他爬下来，接过茶，双手捧着杯子。——但这屋顶能撑过这个冬天了。

我决定把这一点算进去。

choices.text: 那就偶尔把这些说出来。更小的人生也装得下人——我宁愿听你的账本，也不愿看你独自扛着它。
choices.response:
他沉默了片刻，拇指沿着杯沿滑动。——观里的长老们会说这是说教。

我会说这是真话。——他放下杯子，望着修好的脊檩，神情像一个人在修改一条旧账目。——好吧。

偶尔，把这些说出来。

就当是个长期约定——你问，我如实答，作为交换，我有权唠叨你好好吃饭。——一个孩子跑过来，把一个野草编的花环挂在梯子上。

他没有取下它。——看来这棚屋对装饰有自己的意见。

我允许了。

choices.text: （放下茶，从地面检查梯子的绑扎，趁他歇息时逐一查看够得着的每个绳结。）
choices.response:
他眨了眨眼——一种不加防备的神情——然后在你逐一测试够得着的绑扎时，留在你身旁的地面上。

检查比你一个人做要快，也更确实。

当最后一个绳结在你手下通过并牢牢固定时，你发现梯栏上有一处绑扎松了。他指出它滑开的位置，你们两人不用再爬一次就把它重新绑好。

他小心地呼吸着，重新坐回凳子上。——查得很仔细。——后来喝茶时，他没隔着活儿，又说了一遍。——你找到了我赶工时敷衍的那个结。

我不必开口两次，其实一次都不必。——他缓缓转动着杯子。——大多数人帮完忙，就盯着我的伤处看，等着它变得有趣。

你盯着的是活儿本身。

episodes.ending:
棚屋修好了，新茅草整齐地扎在修好的脊檩上，孩子们已经把它当成了堡垒。

清衡从晾衣绳上取下晒干的道袍穿上，把借来的花衬衫道谢归还。道袍上还残留着淡淡的梅花皂香。

暮色笼罩村庄，他在修好的脊檩上挂起一盏纸灯笼——一场他假装是例行维护的小小庆祝——然后摆出两只杯子，斟上茶。

在谈论明天之前，他先提出一个约定：你们任何一方都可以问对方近来如何，任何一方都可以如实回答，也可以把问题留到另一天。双方都同意保留这份自由。

明天道路分岔，他说：往东去河畔的城镇，往西回松泉观的山道。

他没有问你走哪条路。

他只是把那个问题留在那里，像灯一样温暖。

episodes.title: 路上的信
episodes.opening:
修好的歇脚棚，傍晚。

灯光下，新铺的茅草整齐地盖在修好的脊梁上，清衡从修好的脊梁上挂起一盏纸灯笼——一场小小的庆祝，他却装作只是例行修缮。

晚饭已经吃完。

他摆出了两只杯子，自己的那只旁边放着木剑，剑鞘难得敞开着，一封折好的信半露在鞘外。

他望着它的样子，就像人们望着一座还没跨过的桥。
episodes.dialogue:
清衡：这一下午我都在演练这番话，所以才把米饭烧糊了。— 他把信轻轻推到灯光下。

信纸的折痕已被磨得柔软，字迹是一个年轻人一笔一画写下的，收信人是松泉观里的某个人。— 这是我受伤前那年春天写的信。

写给我的师父。

信里说我找到了一条突破的捷径，而且我有足够的把握，敢把根基押在上面。

我从未寄出。

我反而离开了，等我本可以再提笔的时候，能汇报的只剩下那个错误。— 他敲了一下木剑的剑柄，只一下。— 这封信我带了很多年。

当作罗盘。

它指向那个听不进劝告时的我。— 他完全转过身来面对你，他的镇定依旧完好，底下却是坦诚的。— 明天，路就要分岔了。

往东继续走，是沿河的城镇，我答应过一座神祠，把今年春天留给它。

往西则重新爬回观后的山道，那条路我从未回去过。— 他拿起信，双手平摊着递出来。— 我要问的就是这个，你慢慢想，因为我是把它当作一个真正的选择。

跟我一起往东走一段——只是路上的同伴，两个朝同一个方向走的人。

或者走你自己的路，我会写信——真正地写，从客栈和歇脚棚里寄出，用我当年没能做到的方式。— 他的声音依然平稳，但拇指压着信上磨旧的折痕。— 无论哪个答案，都会给我们留下些什么。

我这一生，太擅长离开了。

我想学着稍微擅长一点留下，无论它以什么形式出现。— 灯笼的光晃了一下。

外面，岔路口隐没在黑暗里，但你们俩都清楚它在哪里等着。

choices.text: 那我选择往东，与你同行——因为我喜欢你走在路上的样子。
choices.response:
他的沉静里有什么东西流动了一下，像一扇门被卸下了门闩。— 那么，往东。— 他亲手把信放回剑鞘，动作从容，像关上一扇他打算日后按自己的时机再打开的门。— 等到合适的时候，我会拿给你看，因为你选的是这条路。— 他给两只杯子都续满了，他的手很稳，他脸上有一份暖意，是灯笼的光解释不全的。— 我该提醒你：我在篝火边唱歌很难听，从这里到河边每一家糟糕的客栈我都认得，而且我们路过的每一座歇脚棚我都会去修。

你选了一条慢路。— 他举起杯子。— 那么，敬慢路。

choices.text: （在一张备用的护身符纸上写下“朋友”，把信轻轻推向剑鞘，然后摇头——你的路向西。）
choices.response:
他呼出一口气——如释重负和某种更柔和的东西缠在一起——然后把信推回剑鞘深处。— 那么，往西。

好。

那本来就是你的路；我只是想在你踏上它之前，把这句话说出口。— 他从行囊里取出一支笔，在一张护身符纸的背面，写下一个设在沿河城镇的驿站名字，信件可以经由那里找到赶路的人。— 给你。

当你有值得动墨的事时写信，或者一无所有时也写信——两种我都会回。— 他看看灯笼，又看看你，笑得毫无保留。— 等山口的雪化了，你从观后的路下来时，无论我正在修哪座歇脚棚，那里都会亮着一盏灯。

这是一个我守得住的承诺。

episodes.ending:
灯笼在两只杯子之间继续燃着，它的光平稳如常。

无论接下来发生什么，信都留在他放下的地方——折好收回鞘中，再被携带一段时日——而东去的路从门前伸向黎明，两个方向上都同样坦诚。

episodes.title: 河畔灯夜
episodes.opening:
一年的书信让你认熟了他的字迹：简省、带着干巴巴的幽默，总在你还想多读一行的地方收笔。

他最后的短笺说：河畔小镇、灯会、第三夜。

你在他重新修过屋顶的那座神祠下游的岸边找到了他——肩膀更厚实了，别处却没添一丝灰白——他正跪着，用一条金色符纸修补一个陌生人撕破的纸灯，因为他坚持认为，防潮的符，等于半道防撕裂的符。
episodes.dialogue:
清衡：你找到岸边了。

我本想说我留了记号，可灯会到处都是记号；你要是没撞见我，那只能算运气差。— 他补好那盏灯，微微一躬，还给那个缺了颗牙的小姑娘，然后起身，拂去青灰长袍上的草屑。

他那件备用的青灰道袍整整齐齐叠在行囊里，囊口一开就看得见；他想起晾晒时村民们借他的那件印花衫，不由笑了。— 一年的书信。

你把我的字练好了，我却没能把你的饮食习惯改好，两相折算，这通信是你赢了。— 他领你到一块临水的平石上，整场灯会从眼前漂过：成百上千盏灯顺流而下，每一盏都是某个人的心愿、哀愁或玩笑。

他摆出两只杯子和那罐好茶，分明是为这一刻特意攒下的。他还从行囊里取出自己的灯，点亮，放到平石旁的水面上，又留了一盏备用的灯在触手可及处。— 我师父回信了。

上个月。

受伤以来的第一次。— 他让这句话停了片刻，然后轻叩木剑柄，两下。— 他写道：你撕开的那道缝，教给你的，比你错过的那扇门更多。

那句话我读了十一遍。

我不为这个数字感到骄傲。— 他望向下游。— 这是我的一年，按约定如实入账：我修缮了十九处庇所。

水库撑住了。

我把那封信——旧的那封，春天写的那封——寄给了师父，只在末尾添了一行：“你是对的。

我如今慢了，也更好了。”

我已经回了信。

他的回信要一年才会到，如果会到的话。

他就是这个做派。— 他先斟你的杯，再斟自己的，这是观里养成的习惯，他从未丢掉。— 该你了。

这约定从来都是双向的。

这一年把你造就成了什么样的人？— 下游，一盏鱼形的灯缓缓旋转着漂过，他注视着它，带着他惯有的那种专注——留给那些与他无关、却照样让他欢喜的事物。

choices.text: 这一年把我造就成了一个先落笔、少些后悔的人。账目如下：每一封信我都留着，包括写得糟的那些。
choices.response:
他笑了——真心的、不加防备的笑，是那副沉稳嗓音平日总锁在里间的那种。— 写得糟的那些。

这么说，你手里有那封把一头骡子形容为“在哲学上反对桥梁”的信。

那头骡子，我至今坚持原判。— 他收起笑意，转为更温和的神色。— 留着信，是一种奇特的庇所，你知道吗。

给一个人一整年的思绪搭个屋顶。

我很高兴留下的人是你。— 他举杯朝向河面。— 那么，敬这份约定。

续订。

我问，你答，明年还有茶，无论岔路把我们各自引向何处。— 那个补好灯的小姑娘又跑过去，朝他挥手；他挥手回礼，郑重得像同僚向他致意。

choices.text: （从他的行囊里取出那盏备用的灯，就着他的火苗点亮，一言不发地放到他那盏灯旁的水面上。）
choices.response:
他望着黑水上并排的两盏灯，久久没有说话。

然后，轻声：— 观里有个说法。

两盏灯，放进同一道水流。

多半用来指结伴同行的人。

有时也指比山还长久的友谊。— 他轻叩木剑柄，一下，手便停在那里。— 我看过太多灯独自漂下河去。

我的灯向来如此。— 他靠坐在石上，肩膀与你隔着一掌宽，不再更近，而这距离恰到好处。— 明年，还是这块石头。

或者换一块——但约定不变，茶不变，那些糟糕的故事也不变。

我已认定，这就算传统了。

发生两次，即为传统。

哪部经书里都没这么写，但我就此宣布。

episodes.ending:
灯会在你们四周继续流转，而你们谁也不必随它而去。

约定依然成立：他会问，你会答，沿途每一处庇所的灯都会点亮。

明日路继续延伸，朝着两个不断交汇的方向，而你们谁也不必把这话再说第二遍。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 两盏灯，一条路
romance.opening:
岔路口之后的一年，河畔小镇。

他的信把你引到这里：一座重新盖了顶的祠堂，一家招牌歪斜的客栈，灯会的第三个夜晚。

你在客栈的楼上找到他，窗子朝着水面敞开，他那件蓝灰色的备用道袍叠好放在打开的行囊里，映着屋内的光。

桌上两只茶杯之间躺着一封磨旧了的信，折痕已经软了——正是那封春天的信，终于拆开了；旁边还有一张新纸，他工整的字迹写了一半。
romance.dialogue:
清衡：你找到这家招牌歪的客栈了。

招牌对床铺撒了谎，对窗外的景致倒是说了实话。——他没有立刻起身。

他写完正在写的那一行，才放下笔，放得像放下什么沉重的东西。——坐吧。

茶还算像样。

至于作伴的，我听说，来了就会更好。——等你坐下，他把那封旧信转过来给你看——年轻时笃定的笔迹，如今在信末多了一行他更沉稳的字：“你是对的。

我如今慢了些，也更好了。”——今年春天，我把誊清的一份寄给了我的师父。

那是受伤以来写给道观的第一封信。

原件留在这里，陪着我。——他敲了敲木剑的剑柄，两下，然后看着你，脸上没有任何刻意安排的神情。——这是我的账簿，既然我们记的都是诚实的账。

今年我修了二十一处庇护所。

气海撑住了。

而在第十九处庇护所和这扇窗之间的某个时刻，我发觉，我规划的每一条路，都留了你的位置——我写的每一封信，都盼着下一封不必再写，因为你就在我身边。——他把写了一半的纸推到一旁。——我是想问，你是否愿意继续走在我身边，做我们选择成为的同行之人——东边的路，河畔的小镇，无论遇到什么岔口——做我的，也让我做你的，你的路仍是你的，我的路仍是我的，我们停在哪里，就在哪里点起灯。——他转了转茶杯，声音依旧平稳，但拇指压在信上磨旧的折痕上，就像他递出那封信的那一夜。——慢慢想。

我花了一年，才学会说出我想从我们选择的生活里得到什么。

再等一会儿听你的答案，我等得起。——窗外，一盏鱼形的灯笼漂过，他望着它远去，露出一丝不加掩饰的微笑。

choices.text: 那就走在你身边——我做你的，你做我的，路定多快就多快，不再快一分。
choices.response:
他那份镇定舒展开了，像推回一块挡板，让晨光进来。——那就同行。——他伸手越过桌子，把手覆在你的手上，短暂而温暖，这是一年书信往来里的第一次触碰，然后又从容地收回，来时如何，去时也如何。——这件事我也要写信告诉师父。

他要一年才会回信。

到那时，我们多半已经走完半条路了。——他起身，用自己的灯点亮了第二盏，摆在窗前，面向河面。——丑话说在前头，说了就要作数：我唱歌难听，这一带以东每家糟糕的客栈我都认得，而我们路过的每一处庇护所，我都会去修。

你选了一条慢的路，和一个更慢的人。——他笑了，是那毫无掩饰的、完整的笑。——敬慢的路。

也敬那些不必写的信——只为笔墨之乐而写。

choices.text: （把那张纸折好，推到他手边，你的手放在旁边——你选择了这份同行，也保留自己的路。）
choices.response:
他看看折好的纸，再看看你，缓缓点头——像一个为两条路在同行之中腾出位置的人。——那我们就继续选择彼此，你的路仍是你的。信留给我来写完。

这样也诚实。——他展开那张纸写了一会儿，然后念出最后一行：“有些事会未完成地随你同行，而这是被允许的。”——他给两只杯子都续了茶，举杯朝向窗，朝向河，朝向你们身后这一年。——那就敬这个约定，一成不变，也未曾破裂：我问，你答，茶还算像样，而你沿路而来时，我修的每一处庇护所里，总有一盏灯亮着。——他的笑毫无保留，也别无所求。——我的同伴，这是一句我真正守得住的签语，不必占卜。

romance.ending:
他查看第一盏灯，又查看第二盏；若第二盏还未点燃，便将它点亮。两盏灯在临河的窗中亮着，灯会在下方缓缓漂过，去往一个不需要你们任何一人的地方。

那封信躺在两只杯子之间，它的分量终于放下了。

明天，东边的路继续延伸，每当道路分开，你们各有可以归去的家，而沿途的每一处庇护所，都有灯亮着。

episodes.title: The Bridge That Ate a Path Charm
episodes.opening:
Morning bell, sword terrace.

Mist rolls off the pines and the practice racks drip.

Most disciples drift toward the dining hall, but one figure stands at the terrace rail, ponytail dark against the fog, tapping the four corners of a paper talisman with one fingernail.

She looks up, catches you looking, and grins like someone who has just decided something.

A sleeve of spare charms rustles when she waves you over.
episodes.dialogue:
Maya Ye, from the talisman-array hall at Cloudpine Sect — path charms and mending wards are my line of work.

I learned it by taking spoiled talismans apart, so I can spot where one went wrong at a glance.

Oh?

You look like the one who's been borrowing practice charms from the hall without signing them out.

Wait — no.

Wrong disciple.

That's Chen from the outer courtyard; I fixed his ledger myself.

Twice.

You just have the same 'about to be talked into something' face.

Anyway — morning lessons just ended; come to the dining hall with me.

On the way, though, I want your eyes on something.

The old bridge below the east stairs.

Disciples cross it with path charms every day, and every charm dies at the midpoint.

Same spot, same flicker, every time.

I've sketched it four times in my notebook and I still can't tell whether the bridge is eating the charms or the charms are lying about the bridge.

And before you ask — no, I'm not dragging you into anything.

It's a bridge.

You walk on it.

The worst outcome is wet socks.

I had a pair once that proved it.

So: look at the sketch, tell me what you see, and if you see nothing, say so honestly.

I'd rather hear 'nothing' than a polite guess.

choices.text: The stroke thins before the midpoint — the charm needs more ink for the road.
choices.response:
Maya stops walking so fast you nearly leave her behind.

She pulls the notebook out, taps all four corners, and reads your words back to herself twice.

'Out of ink.

Road ahead.'

Oh?

Oh!

That would mean the charms were drawn thin from the start, and the bridge just gets blamed.

She laughs, loud enough that a passing senior glances over.

'I've been interrogating a bridge for four days when the answer was a cheap brush and a lazy hand.'

She tucks the notebook away and points at the dining hall.

'You're getting the good congee.

This is non-negotiable.'

choices.text: (Lean closer over the sketch and trace the thinning stroke with one finger, saying nothing.)
choices.response:
You don't say a word — you just put your finger where the stroke goes pale and follow it down to the midpoint.

Maya watches the finger instead of the paper.

'Huh,' she says slowly.

'You went straight to where the ink thins.

No detour, no guessing.'

She closes the notebook and looks at you with fresh interest, like a talisman she hasn't taken apart yet.

'Most people talk first and look second.

You looked first.

I like that in a colleague.'

She resumes walking, slower now, and opens the notebook again halfway down the stairs, tilting it so you can see without asking.

episodes.ending:
At the dining hall she claims a corner table and pushes the best seat toward you, the one facing the window and the mist.

Between mouthfuls she redraws the bridge sketch from memory, cleaner this time, and slides it across.

'Come back to the east stairs with me tomorrow at first bell.

If the ink theory holds, we rewrite the charm together and the bridge stops lying.'

She raises her tea like a toast.

'Consider this the first entry in a joint notebook.

I'll supply the paper.

You supply the not-being-polite.'

episodes.title: The Sleeve That Burned
episodes.opening:
First bell, east stairs.

The bridge below is quiet, and Maya is already there with a writing case balanced on the rail: fresh ink, good brush, a stack of path charms drawn properly thick this morning.

She waves you over without looking up.

The joint notebook — your name and hers on the cover now — sits open to the bridge sketch.

Something is different today: her left wrist guard is new, and the sleeve beneath it is visibly shorter.
episodes.dialogue:
You're punctual.

I respect that in a colleague.

Okay — charm one.

Watch the stroke weight.

If it holds to the midpoint and past it, we've proven the ink theory and I owe the bridge an apology.

She sets the charm down at the stairhead and it glows steady, all the way across, all the way back.

She actually claps once, then catches herself.

'Right.

Professional composure.

Maintained.

Barely.'

She sits on the step, and after a moment she doesn't reach for the next charm.

She reaches for her short sleeve instead.

'Since you came back this morning, you'll hear this eventually, so it may as well be from me.

This sleeve — I burned it two years ago, in a minor array trial.

A practice formation, whole line of us on the paper.

I heard the hum go wrong — heard it clearly — and instead of stepping back like the others, I told myself one more stroke would fix it.

So I added the stroke.

The sisters beside me read it right and withdrew.

I was half a step slower, and the flare took the sleeve instead of me.

The senior sister who ran the trial said one thing I've kept: those who withdraw get a next time.

She was right.

I got the next time.'

She turns the wrist guard so you can see the edge of the old scar.

'Now I pack a retreat charm before every job.

Every single one.

Even a bridge.'

She taps the cloth bag at her belt — crooked stitches holding its strap, her own needlework.

'It's never been used.

The point is I stopped trusting 'it'll be fine' as a plan.

Anyway.'

She straightens, bright again.

'Charm two.

Your turn to place it.

Equal shares.'

choices.text: Thank you for telling me the real version instead of a tidy one.
choices.response:
Maya blinks, then huffs a small laugh.

'Tidy versions are easier.

The real one has me adding a stroke to a humming array while the whole line of sisters stepped back without me.'

She looks at the scar a moment longer, then closes her wrist guard with a snap.

'But you're right, and I'd rather you hear the ugly shape of it than invent a cleaner one.

Most people would've nodded and moved on.'

She hands you the second charm with more care than the joke needs.

'Colleague privileges.

You get the true stories and the good brush.

Don't waste either.'

choices.text: (Reach out and steady the charm case that's sliding toward the rail's edge, before it can fall.)
choices.response:
The case tilts; your hand catches it flat on the stone.

Maya watches you set it right and something in her shoulders comes down half an inch.

'See, that,' she says.

'No speech, no pity face.

Just — caught it.'

She nudges the case back to the center of the rail, away from every edge.

'That's the whole lesson of the sleeve, honestly.

Notice the thing that's about to slide and fix it before the drama.'

She hands you the second charm.

'You place it.

I'll watch.

And I'll remember which kind of colleague you are.'

episodes.ending:
Charm two holds.

Charm three holds.

By the time the sun clears the pines, the bridge has stopped flickering and Maya has stopped apologizing to it.

She copies the corrected stroke into the joint notebook, in your column as well as hers, and signs both.

'Same time tomorrow.

There's a ward on the cliff path that hums off-key, and I want a second pair of ears before I touch it.'

She taps the retreat charm at her belt, twice, out of habit, and walks you up the stairs.

episodes.title: The Goose Who Knew the Wards
episodes.opening:
The cliff path ward hums off-key, and now the whole sect knows it — because the hall's old white goose, raised among the array papers since it was a gosling, has wandered past the ward line it used to respect and vanished down the cliff trail.

Maya stands at the trailhead with her notebook, her retreat charm, and a face with no jokes on it.

Wind is coming; the senior array-keepers are busy reinforcing the mountain face.

Nobody else can go look.

The cost is simple: the trail is slick, and the ward's off-key hum means her charms may misfire on the way down.
episodes.dialogue:
No jokes for this part.

Known risks, then you decide.

One: the trail is wet and the rail posts are old.

Two: the ward is humming wrong, so my path charms could flicker mid-step — I go slow and I carry the retreat charm, but I can't promise it won't be needed.

Three: the goose is a goose.

It may not want finding.

I'm going down either way; it's my ward, my hum, my bird.

But I'd move faster and safer with you reading the trail markers while I watch my footing.

If you stay up top, that's real work too — you keep signaling the hall if the hum changes.

Oh?

You're already tying your boot.

Wait — one thing first.

Last check, honestly, because I've rushed before and paid in sleeves: are you sure?

Say it plainly if you're coming.

choices.text: I'm coming. I'll read the markers; you watch the footing.
choices.response:
'Plainly said.

Good.'

Maya's voice drops all its brightness and gets level and quick instead.

She checks your bootlaces herself, nods, and takes the downhill side without asking.

The descent is slow and quiet — her eyes on stone, yours on the fading chalk markers, the retreat charm staying untouched at her belt.

Halfway down, the hum stutters; she stops, waits it out, and doesn't crack a single joke.

Near the old boathouse you find the goose, smug and dry under a shelf of rock.

'Found,' Maya breathes.

'Ward still wrong.

Bird still rude.

Half a victory.'

choices.text: (Take position at the trailhead signal post and raise the ready flag.)
choices.response:
You don't follow.

You plant yourself at the signal post and raise the ready flag, and Maya looks at it, then at you, and nods once — no disappointment in it.

'Top watch it is.

Eyes on the hum.'

She goes down alone, slow, checking her retreat charm at every turn.

Twice the wind pushes the hum off-key; twice you signal, twice she holds still until it steadies.

She comes back up with the goose tucked under one arm and mud to the knee.

'Your signals were clean.

I trusted them twice.

That's the job.'

episodes.ending:
Back at the trailhead, Maya returns the goose to its pen, then sits on the step and finally lets herself grin.

'Ward's still humming wrong and I couldn't fix it today — that goes in the notebook as an honest failure, my name on it.

But we didn't lose the bird and nobody lost a sleeve.'

She copies the day into the joint notebook, your part of it and her descent both, and taps the page.

'Next time the wind's calm, we fix the hum together.

That's a promise with a schedule, so you know I mean it.'

episodes.title: The Rain Room
episodes.opening:
Evening.

Rain hammers the sect roofs, and the talisman hall's rain room — a glass-roofed chamber built for testing wards against weather — glows lamplit and empty.

Maya meets you at its door with her notebook, her retreat charm, and something she has clearly rehearsed and is now improvising past.

Inside, a small array is chalked on the floor, half-finished, waiting for a final stroke.

Two lamps.

Two stools.

She doesn't open the door all the way yet.
episodes.dialogue:
So.

The hum from the cliff ward — I traced it.

It's a weather-reading array, and I think I know how to fix it, but the final stroke needs testing against real rain, which is why tonight, this room.

Here's the part I rehearsed and will now say badly.

I've been doing this with you for a while now — the bridge, the sleeve story, the goose — and somewhere in there you stopped being a colleague and started being the person I look for first.

So I made two invitations, and you pick.

One: come in, finish the stroke with me tonight, and keep being that — my closest friend, my equal, my second pair of eyes, no more and no less asked, ever.

Two: come in, finish the stroke, and let it be the start of something more than that.

Either way the work is the same and the array gets finished.

The only thing that changes is what we call each other after.

No pressure, no wrong answer, and I promise — whatever you pick, I won't make it strange.

Oh?

You're smiling.

That's either a good sign or you've spotted a flaw in my chalkwork.

So: which invitation do you take?

choices.text: The second one. I want it to be more than that — with you.
choices.response:
Maya lets out a breath she's clearly been holding since the first bell days ago.

'Okay.

Oh.

Okay.'

She laughs at herself, once, and steps back to open the door fully for you.

'I rehearsed both replies and this is the one I didn't rehearse.

Give me a moment.'

Inside, she sets both lamps lit and both stools side by side, and when you take up the brush she watches your hands, not the chalk.

'More than colleagues,' she says quietly, testing the words.

'I'd like that very much.

Now — final stroke.

Slowly.

We have all the rain in the world tonight.'

choices.text: (Step past her into the rain room and take up the brush for the final stroke, leaving the question answered by the work alone.)
choices.response:
You walk in and pick up the brush.

Maya watches you settle at the array's edge and understands without a word being spent.

'The first one, then,' she says, and her grin comes back full.

'Closest friend, equal shares, nothing asked and nothing owed.

Honestly?

I'd have been proud to keep either.'

She takes the second stool, taps the four corners of the chalkwork, and points at the gap.

'Final stroke's yours.

And for the record — the friend invitation was never the consolation prize.

I built both of them on purpose.'

episodes.ending:
The final stroke goes down under lamplight while rain sheets the glass roof, and the array hums true — the same clean note the cliff ward should make.

Maya copies the working into the joint notebook, dates it, and adds a small sketch of two stools.

The room holds one picture: the two of you, one finished array, and a night that ends with her walking you back through the rain under one lantern, arguing cheerfully about stroke weight the whole way.

episodes.title: Seed Evening
episodes.opening:
Seasons have turned since the rain room.

The cliff ward hums true now — your joint fix, famous in the hall by a name Maya insists on crediting you for.

Tonight she's waiting at the hall's back garden with a tray of paper-mulberry seeds, the tree whose bark becomes the sect's talisman paper, and two trowels.

The joint notebook sits on the bench, fat now, ribbon-marked, half of it in your handwriting.

She has saved you the spot with the better soil.
episodes.dialogue:
Sit.

Good soil is on the left; I measured.

So — announcement, then planting.

The hall elders approved a standing project: every season, we test and rewrite one worn array together.

Yours and mine, jointly signed, jointly blamed.

No schedule binding you, no duties.

It's an invitation that renews itself as long as we both keep showing up — and I intend to keep showing up.

Oh?

You're digging already.

Fine, fine, I'll talk faster.

Second thing.

The notebook's full.

I bought a second one and I'm not starting it alone.

First page is blank on purpose — I want the first entry to be tonight, both our hands on it.

I used to think the best thing about arrays was cracking them alone.

Turns out the best thing is having someone who'll say 'nothing' honestly, look before guessing, and hold a thing steady so the work can happen.

That's you.

That's the whole speech.

Seeds.

Go.

choices.text: Then let's write tonight's page together — and keep the seasons coming.
choices.response:
'Keep the seasons coming.'

Maya repeats it like she's signing it.

She opens the new notebook, lays it flat between the seed trays, and hands you the brush for the first line while she writes the second.

The two of you plant the seeds row by row, arguing about spacing, and she names the row after the bridge.

'When these grow, the paper they make gets our names on the first sheets.

Elder Yun already groaned.

I take that as approval.'

She taps the fresh page's four corners, a habit now shared.

choices.text: (Press the first seed into the shared soil and hold the notebook steady for her to write.)
choices.response:
No speech; you just press the first seed in and hold the new notebook flat and steady.

Maya looks at the arrangement — your hand on the page, her brush on the line — and nods slowly.

'You hold the thing still so the work can happen.

All right.

That's our first entry: held steady.'

She writes it, dates it, and pushes the better soil toward you again without being asked.

The row gets planted in easy silence broken only by her narrating seed depth, badly.

episodes.ending:
By dark the row is planted and the new notebook holds its first shared entry, both names on the cover in two different hands.

Maya waters the row with the hall's leaky can, splashing her own boots, and laughs at herself the way she always does.

'Same evening next season.

New array, new page, and if the trees take, our paper.'

She walks you to the garden gate and taps the notebook twice — her old habit — before heading in.

The friendship needs no fixing and asks nothing more; it simply continues, season by season, page by page.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Stroke We Keep
romance.opening:
Seasons have turned since the rain room.

The cliff ward hums true now — your joint fix, taught to new disciples under both your names.

Tonight the talisman hall is empty except for one lamp and Maya, waiting at the workbench with the joint notebook open to the bridge sketch, the very first page.

Beside it lies a single talisman, blank, two brushes, and a loose sheet for a new entry.

She has clearly been sitting there a while; her tea has gone cold.
romance.dialogue:
You came.

Good — I rehearsed this and it only works if you come.

Sit.

So.

The notebook's full.

Bridge, sleeve, goose, rain room, the ward fix — every page has both our names, and I sat here tonight reading it and realized I don't want a second notebook with the same arrangement.

I want the arrangement to keep, the way a good stroke keeps.

I still want my morning drills and my own experiments, and I want you to keep yours; we'd be terrible at sharing a workbench.

Mine and yours with a standing 'ours' in the middle.

That's what I'm asking.

A choice, made tonight and remade whenever we both feel like it.

Oh?

You're already reaching for a brush.

Wait, let me finish, I never get to finish.

If you feel the same, draw the first stroke on that blank talisman.

Your hand, then mine over it, the way we fixed the cliff ward.

If you don't, say so and we stay exactly what we've been, and I mean that without a single dent in it.

Your move, colleague.

Or — whatever you'd rather I call you.

choices.text: Then let's write it that way — mine, yours, and ours in the middle.
choices.response:
Maya exhales like she's been holding that breath since the rain room.

'Ours in the middle.

Yes.

That's the phrasing I couldn't find.'

You draw the first stroke; she lays her hand over yours for one brief moment to guide the second, then lets go and steps back to look at the finished talisman like it's a solved ward.

'Huh.

It holds.'

Her voice goes quieter than you've ever heard it.

'It actually holds.'

Then the grin returns.

'Right.

I'm making new tea, you're dating the entry, and tomorrow I'm telling Elder Yun before the rumor mill beats me to it.'

choices.text: (Slide the blank talisman back toward her and set the loose sheet between you, brush resting in the middle between you.)
choices.response:
You slide the talisman back and set out the loose sheet instead, setting the brush down exactly on the center line.

Maya stares at the brush, then laughs — a real one, from the chest.

'Oh?

Oh, that's better than my idea.

A shared page instead of a shared stroke.'

She writes the date on the left, waits, and watches you take the right side.

'Equal margins.

Standing ours.

Remade whenever we both feel like it — starting now.'

She taps the page's four corners and pushes the cold tea aside.

'New pot.

This one's worth drinking hot.'

romance.ending:
The lamp burns late.

Maya keeps tonight's entry where the hall will see it in the morning, and she walks you out under one lantern, arguing happily about whose hand shaped the thing more.

At the garden gate she stops.

'Same bench tomorrow.

My drills, your morning, and ours in the middle.'

She taps the notebook twice and goes in whistling.

The arrangement keeps.

So does everything else you each go on building alone.

episodes.title: 吞掉引路符的桥
episodes.opening:
晨钟响过，试剑坪。

雾气从松林里漫出来，练武架子上还挂着水珠。

弟子们大多往膳堂去了，只有一个人站在坪边栏杆旁，乌黑的高马尾衬在雾里，正用指甲一下一下敲着一张符纸的四角。

她抬头，正好撞上你的目光，咧嘴一笑，像是刚拿定了什么主意。

她朝你招手，袖口里夹着的几张符纸沙沙作响。
episodes.dialogue:
叶照水，听风谷符阵堂的，画引路符、补结界是我的本行。

我这门道是拆废符拆出来的，一张符哪里画坏了我一眼看得出。

咦？

你这张脸，看着像那个老从堂里借符、又从不登记的外门弟子。

等等——不对。

记错人了。

那是外院的老陈，他的账还是我亲手补的。

补了两次。

你就是长了张一样的、『随时要被人拉去干嘛』的脸。

总之——晨课刚散，一起去膳堂吧。

不过路上，我想借你一双眼睛看样东西。

东阶下面那座旧桥。

弟子们每天带着引路符从桥上过，可每张符走到桥中间就灭了。

同一个位置，同一闪，每次都这样。

我画册里描了四回，还是分不清，是桥在吃符，还是符在骗我们、桥根本没问题。

先说好——我不是要拖你入伙。

就是一座桥。

走上去就完了。

最坏的后果也不过是袜子湿了。

我有双袜子就是这么湿的，亲身验证过。

所以：看看这张图，说你看见了什么；要是什么都没看出来，就老实说。

我宁可听一句『没看出来』，也不想听客气的瞎猜。

choices.text: 笔画到桥中间之前就变淡了——符墨先尽了，路还长。
choices.response:
叶照水猛地停住脚，你差点从她身边走了过去。

她抽出画册，把四角都敲了一遍，把你那句话低声念了两遍。

“墨先尽了。

路还在。”

咦？

咦！

那就是说，是符从一开始就画得太薄，桥只是背了黑锅。

她笑出了声，声音大得让路过的师兄都回头看了一眼。

“我审了一座桥四天，结果答案是笔不行，手还懒。”

她把画册收好，指向膳堂。

“今天你吃好粥。

这事没得商量。”

choices.text: （你凑近那张图，一言不发，用手指顺着渐渐变淡的笔画描下去。）
choices.response:
你一个字都没说，只是把手指落在笔画发淡的地方，一路描到桥中间。

叶照水盯着的是你的手指，不是纸。

“唔，”她慢慢地说。

“你直接就指到了墨变淡的地方。

没绕弯，也没瞎猜。”

她合上画册，带着新的兴趣打量你，像在看一张还没拆过的符。

“大多数人先开口，后用眼睛。

你是先看的。

我喜欢这样的同门。”

她重新迈开步子，这次走得慢了些，下到半坡时又翻开画册，微微倾过来让你看，都不用你开口问。

episodes.ending:
到了膳堂，她占了张靠角的桌子，把最好的座位推给你——正对窗户和窗外那片雾的位置。

吃着吃着，她凭记忆把桥的图重新画了一遍，这回干净多了，画完推到你面前。

“明天晨钟一响，陪我再去一趟东阶。

要是墨的说法成立，我们一起重画一张符，桥就没法再撒谎了。”

她举起茶碗，像敬酒一样。

“就当这是一本合写画册的第一页。

纸我来出。

不讲客气话这件事，你来出。”

episodes.title: 烧掉的那半只袖子
episodes.opening:
晨钟一响，东阶。

下面的石桥安安静静，叶照水已经等在那儿了，栏杆上稳稳架着一只文匣：新研的墨，好笔，还有一沓引路符——今天早上画得格外厚实。

她头也不抬地朝你招手。

那本合写的册子——封面上如今并排写着你和她的名字——正摊在画着石桥的那一页。

今天有点不一样：她左手的护腕是新的，护腕底下的袖子明显短了一截。
episodes.dialogue:
你很准时。

这点我很欣赏，同道。

好——第一张符。

看好了，笔画的轻重。

要是它能撑到桥心、再撑过桥心，我们的墨料猜想就算验证了，我就得给这座桥道个歉。

她把符放在阶口，符光稳稳亮起，一路亮过去，又一路亮回来。

她还真拍了一下手，随即又收住。

“很好。

专业素养。

保持住了。

勉强。”

她在台阶上坐下，过了一会儿，她没有去拿下一张符。

而是伸手摸了摸那只短袖子。

“你今早既然回来了，这事迟早会传到你耳朵里，不如由我亲口讲。

这截袖子——两年前烧掉的，在一次小型阵法试阵上。

那是一次练习阵，我们一整排人都站在符纸上。

我听见阵鸣不对——听得清清楚楚——可别人都往后退，我却对自己说，再补一笔就能修好。

于是我补了那一笔。

我旁边的师姐们读对了阵势，撤了。

我慢了半步，那一道爆闪就烧在袖子上，没烧在我身上。

主持试阵的那位师姐只说了一句话，我一直记着：肯撤的人，才有下一次。

她说得对。

我确实有了下一次。”

她转过护腕，让你看见边上那道旧疤。

“现在我每回干活之前，都会带一张撤退符。

每一次都带。

连补座桥也带。”

她敲了敲腰间的布袋——袋子上的针脚歪歪扭扭，是她自己缝的。

“它从来没派上过用场。

重点是我不再把‘应该没事’当成一条退路了。

总之。”

她坐直身子，又亮堂起来。

“第二张符。

这回你来放。

一人一半。”

choices.text: 谢谢你告诉我真实的那一版。
choices.response:
叶照水眨了眨眼，随即轻轻笑了一声。

“体面的版本省事多了。

真实的版本里，可是一整排师姐都退了出去，我还对着嗡嗡作响的阵往里补笔。”

她又看了一会儿那道疤，然后啪的一声合上护腕。

“但你说得对，与其让你自己去脑补一个更干净的版本，我宁愿你听它最不好看的样子。

换成别人，多半点点头就翻篇了。”

她把第二张符递给你，递得比玩笑话需要的还要郑重。

“同道的待遇。

真话和好笔，都归你。

两样都别浪费。”

choices.text: （文匣正朝栏杆边缘滑去，你伸手把它稳稳按住，免得它摔下去。）
choices.response:
匣子一歪，你的手在石头上把它接了个正着。

叶照水看着你把它摆正，她肩上绷着的那股劲松了半寸。

“看，就是这个，”她说。

“不用讲一堆话，不用摆出怜悯的脸。

就是——接住了。”

她把匣子推回栏杆正中间，离每一边都远远的。

“说实话，那截袖子的教训，全在这一下里了。

看见要滑的东西，趁还没闹出动静先扶住。”

她把第二张符递给你。

“你来放。

我看着。

而且我会记住，你是哪一种同道。”

episodes.ending:
第二张符，稳稳亮住了。

第三张，也稳稳亮住了。

等日头爬过松林，桥面已经不再闪烁，叶照水也不再对着它念叨道歉了。

她把修正后的那一笔临进合写的册子，你那一栏和她那一栏都写了，两栏都落了款。

“明天这个时间。

崖边小路上有座结界，嗡鸣跑了调，动手之前，我想多找一双耳朵帮我听听。”

她习惯性地在腰间的撤退符上敲了两下，领着你往阶上走去。

episodes.title: 认得结界的鹅
episodes.opening:
崖边小径的结界嗡鸣走了调，现在全宗门都知道了——因为符阵堂那只从小在符纸堆里养大的老白鹅，竟越过了它一向守规矩的界线，顺着崖边小径没了踪影。

叶照水站在路口，袖中小册、撤退符都带上了，脸上一点玩笑的影子都没有。

风要来了，各位主持大阵的前辈正忙着加固山体。

没有别人能下去找。

代价很简单：小径湿滑，而且结界的嗡鸣走了调，意味着她的符在下崖途中可能会失灵。
episodes.dialogue:
这部分不开玩笑。

先讲明白风险，再由你决定。

一，小径湿滑，护栏的桩子也旧了。

二，结界嗡鸣不对劲，我的引路符可能走到半路就闪——我会走慢些，也带着撤退符，但不敢保证用不上。

三，鹅就是鹅。

它未必想被人找到。

不管怎样我都要下去，那是我的结界，我的嗡鸣，我的鸟。

但如果你能盯着路标，我专心看脚下，会走得又快又稳。

你要是留在上面，那也是正经活儿——嗡鸣一变，你就给符阵堂打信号。

咦？

你已经在系鞋带了。

等等——先说一件事。

最后确认一次，老实说，因为我以前莽撞过一回，代价是半条袖子：你确定吗？

要一起来，就明说。

choices.text: 我来。我盯路标，你看脚下。
choices.response:
“说得干脆。

好。”

叶照水的声音一下子收起了所有轻快，变得平稳而干脆。

她亲自检查了你的鞋带，点点头，没多问就抢到了靠崖的一侧。

下行又慢又静——她的眼睛盯着石头，你盯着渐渐淡去的白垩路标，撤退符一直原封不动地别在她腰间。

下到一半，嗡鸣卡了一下；她停下脚步，等它过去，一句玩笑都没说。

快到旧船屋时，你们找到了那只鹅，在一块突出的岩檐底下，浑身干爽，一副得意的样子。

“找到了，”叶照水低声说。

“结界还是不对。

鸟还是很嚣张。

算赢了一半。”

choices.text: （你守在路口的信号桩旁，升起备好的信号旗。）
choices.response:
你没有跟下去。

你守在信号桩边升起信号旗，叶照水看了看旗，又看了看你，点了一下头——没有半分失望。

“那就上面望风。

盯紧嗡鸣。”

她独自下去，走得很慢，每个转弯都检查一遍撤退符。

两次风把嗡鸣吹得走了调；两次你打信号，两次她都原地不动，直到嗡鸣稳下来。

她上来时，一只胳膊底下夹着那只鹅，膝盖以下全是泥。

“你的信号很干净。

我信了两次。

那就是正事。”

episodes.ending:
回到路口，叶照水把鹅送回圈里，然后坐在台阶上，这才终于咧嘴笑了。

“结界还在走调，今天没能修好——这要写进册子里，老老实实记一笔失败，署我的名。

不过鸟没丢，也没人搭进去半条袖子。”

她把今天的事抄进合写的册子，你那份和她的下崖都记了，然后指尖在纸页上轻敲两下。

“下次风小的时候，我们一起把嗡鸣修好。

这是个带日子的承诺，所以你知道我是认真的。”

episodes.title: 雨室
episodes.opening:
傍晚。

雨点砸着宗门的屋顶，符阵堂的雨室——一间为在风雨中试验结界而建的玻璃顶屋——灯火通明，空无一人。

叶照水在门口等你，手里拿着她的小册、撤退符，还有一段她显然排练过、现在却开始即兴发挥的话。

屋里，地上用粉笔画着一座小阵，画到一半，只等最后一笔。

两盏灯。

两只凳子。

她还没把门完全敞开。
episodes.dialogue:
那个……

崖边结界的那种嗡声——我追查过了。

是一座观天测雨的阵法，我想我知道怎么修，可最后一笔要拿真雨来试，所以才选了今晚、选了这间屋子。

下面这段是我排练过的，但现在大概会说得很糟。

我们一起做事也有一阵子了——那座桥、袖口烧掉的事、那只鹅——不知道从哪一刻起，你不再只是同门，而是成了我第一个想找的人。

所以我准备了两种邀请，你来挑。

一种：进来，今晚和我一起补完那一笔，继续做现在的样子——我最亲近的朋友，与我并肩的人，我的另一双眼睛，不多要一分，永远。

另一种：进来，补完那一笔，然后让它成为另一段关系的开始。

无论选哪种，活儿都一样，阵都会画完。

唯一会变的，是这之后我们怎么称呼彼此。

没有压力，没有错误答案，我保证——不管你选哪个，我都不会让气氛变得奇怪。

咦？

你在笑。

这要么是好兆头，要么就是你看出我粉笔画里哪一笔有问题了。

那么：你选哪种邀请？

choices.text: 第二种。我想和你，走到比那更远的地方去。
choices.response:
叶照水长长吐出一口气，那口气她显然从几天前就憋着了。

“好。

哦。

好。”

她自嘲地笑了一声，退后一步，把门完全为你敞开。

“两种回话我都排练过，独独这一种没排练。

给我一点时间。”

屋里，她点亮两盏灯，把两只凳子并排放好；你拿起笔时，她盯着的是你的手，不是粉笔画。

“不止是同门，”她轻声说，像在试这几个字的分量。

“我很愿意。

来——最后一笔。

慢慢画。

今晚的雨，管够。”

choices.text: （你越过她走进雨室，拿起笔准备最后一笔，让这座阵本身替你回答。）
choices.response:
你走进去，拿起了笔。

叶照水看着你在阵边站定，一个字都没说，就懂了。

“那就是第一种，”她说，笑容又整个回到了脸上。

“最亲近的朋友，平分的乐趣，什么都不多要，什么都不亏欠。

说实话？

两种我留着，哪一种都让我骄傲。”

她坐上另一只凳子，用指甲轻敲粉笔画的四角，指着那道空缺。

“最后一笔是你的。

顺便说一句——两种邀请都是我认真做的。”

episodes.ending:
灯下，最后一笔落下，玻璃顶外雨幕连天，小阵发出一声匀净的嗡鸣——正是崖边结界该有的那种清音。

叶照水把阵法誊进你们合写的册子，标上日期，又添了一幅两只凳子的小画。

这间屋子里只有一幅画面：你们两个，一座画完的阵，还有一个夜晚——最后是她打着灯笼，陪你冒雨往回走，一路上兴高采烈地争论着笔画该压多重。

episodes.title: 播种的傍晚
episodes.opening:
自雨室那件事之后，季节又换了几轮。

崖边结界如今运转安稳——那是你们合力的修补，在符阵堂里都出了名，名字还是照水坚持要把你的排在前面。

今晚她在符阵堂后园等着你，端着一盘构树种子——这种树的树皮就是宗门符纸的原料——还带着两把小铲。

合写的册子放在长凳上，已经厚了一截，系着丝带，一半都是你的笔迹。

她给你留了土更好的那个位置。
episodes.dialogue:
坐。

左边的土好，我量过了。

那么——先宣布，再种。

堂里的长老们批了一个常设项目：每季一起试、一起改写一座旧阵。

你和我共同署名，功劳同担，锅也同背。

不绑你的时辰，也没有摊派的活。

它是一份会自己续期的邀请——只要我们俩都还来，它就一直在。而我打算一直来。

咦？

你已经挖上了。

行行行，我说快些。

第二件事。

册子写满了。

我买了本新的，可我不打算一个人起头。

第一页是故意空着的——我想让第一条记的就是今晚，我们两人的手一起落上去。

我从前觉得，符阵最妙的地方是独自把它拆明白。

后来才发现，最妙的是有个人肯诚实地说“没看出什么”，肯先看了再猜，肯把东西稳稳扶住，让活儿干得下去。

说的就是你。

话说完了。

种子。

开工。

choices.text: 那今晚这一页我们一起写——季节也一年年续下去。
choices.response:
“季节一年年续下去。”

照水把这句重复了一遍，像在署名。

她翻开新册子，平摊在种子盘中间，把笔递给你写第一行，她自己写第二行。

你们一行一行把种子种下去，还为间距拌了几句嘴，她把那一垄用那座桥的名字命名。

“等这些树长成，头几张符纸上就会印着我们俩的名字。

云长老已经叹过气了。

我就当这是准了。”

她用指甲轻敲新页的四角——这个习惯，如今你们俩共有了。

choices.text: （你把第一粒种子按进共享的那份土里，再把册子扶稳，让她好落笔。）
choices.response:
你没说话，只是把第一粒种子按进土里，再把新册子平平地扶稳。

照水看了看这个架势——你的手按着纸页，她的笔落在行间——慢慢点了点头。

“你把东西扶稳，让活儿干得下去。

好。

那我们的第一条就是：扶稳了。”

她把这句写下来，标上日期，然后没等你开口，又把土更好的那堆朝你推了推。

那垄种子在轻松的安静里种完了，只有她一边报种子深度一边报得离谱的声音。

episodes.ending:
天黑之前，那一垄种好了，新册子也有了第一条合写的记录，封面上两个名字，两种笔迹。

照水用堂里漏水的水壶给垄浇了水，溅了自己一靴子，又照老样子笑话起自己来。

“下一季，同一个晚上。

新阵，新页，要是树苗成活，就是我们的符纸。”

她送你到园门口，在册子上敲了两下——她的老习惯——才转身回去。

这份友情不用修补，也别无所求；它只是继续着，一季又一季，一页又一页。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 留下的那一笔
romance.opening:
自雨室那件事之后，季节又换了几轮。

崖边结界如今运转如常——那是你们合写的修补之法，如今署着你们两人的名字，传给新入门的弟子。

今晚符阵堂里空荡荡的，只有一盏灯，照水坐在案前等着，合写的册子摊开在桥符那一页——册子的第一页。

旁边放着一张空白的符、两支笔，还有一张留作新条目的散页。

她显然已经坐了好一阵子，茶都凉了。
romance.dialogue:
你来了。

很好——这段我排练过，只有你来了才作数。

坐。

那个……

册子写满了。

桥符、袖口、大雁、雨室、结界修补——每一页都写着我们两个人的名字。今晚我坐在这儿翻着翻着，忽然明白过来：我不想再要一本册子，还照老样子合写。

我要的是这个“老样子”能一直续下去，就像好的一笔，落下去便不散。

晨课我照上，自己的实验我照做，你的也一样由你留着；要真共用一张案台，我们准得吵翻天。

你的归你、我的归我，中间立着一份常在的“我们的”。

我想说的就是这个。

一个选择，今晚定下，往后只要我们俩都乐意，随时可以再定一次。

咦？

你已经伸手去拿笔了。

等等，让我把话说完，我从来都没能把话说完过。

如果你也这么想，就在那张空白符上落下第一笔。

你的手先画，我的手覆在你手上，就像我们当年修崖边结界那样。

如果你不想，直说就好，我们照旧是原来的样子，这话我说出口时没有半点勉强的凹痕。

该你了，同门。

或者——你更想让我怎么称呼你，随你挑。

choices.text: 那就这么写——你的归你，我的归我，中间是我们的。
choices.response:
照水长长呼出一口气，像是从雨室那晚就一直憋着。

“中间是我们的。

对。

就是这个说法，我一直没能找到。”

你落下第一笔；她伸手覆在你手上，只一瞬，引着你画完第二笔，然后松开手退后一步，端详那张画好的符，像在看一道解开的大阵。

“咦。

成了。”

她的声音轻下来，轻得你从没听过。

“真的成了。”

然后她咧嘴笑了。

“好。

我去沏壶新茶，你来给这一页写上日期，明天趁流言还没长腿，我先去禀告云长老。”

choices.text: （你把那张空白符推回她面前，另把散页铺在两人之间，笔搁在正中间的分界线上。）
choices.response:
你把符推了回去，转而铺开那张散页，把笔端端正正落在中间那道线上。

照水盯着那支笔，随即笑出了声——真正的、从胸腔里滚出来的笑。

“咦？

咦，这可比我的主意高明。

不要共落一笔，改共写一页。”

她在左边写下日期，等着，看你接过右边那一半。

“两边留白一样多。

中间是常在的“我们的”。

只要我们俩都乐意，随时再定一次——就从现在开始。”

她用指甲轻敲纸页四角，把凉茶推到一边。

“换壶新的。

这一壶，值得趁热喝。”

romance.ending:
灯亮到了很晚。

照水把今晚这页摊在堂里显眼处，好让明早进门的人都看得见；她提着一盏灯笼送你出门，一路高高兴兴地争着：这一笔到底谁的手定下的形。

到了园门口，她停下脚步。

“明天还是那条石凳。

我的晨课，你的上午，中间是我们的。”

她在册子上轻轻敲了两下，吹着口哨进去了。

这份“老样子”，续下去了。

你们各自独自去建的其余一切，也一样。

episodes.title: The Basket on the Sword Rack
episodes.opening:
Morning practice is over, and the sword terrace is nearly empty. Your basket of borrowed supplies—ink, rice paper, a jar of pickled plums from the outer hall—has no obvious home, so you set it on the low rack at the terrace's edge, meaning to fetch it in a moment. A shadow falls across the stones. A man in blue-gray robes stands there, sword at his waist, black hair tied high. He looks at the basket, then at you, and his expression is composed but not unkind.

"I'm Rowan Shen, senior disciple here," he says. "Morning practice is over. If you are still learning the paths, I can walk with you."
episodes.dialogue:
He lifts the basket off the rack with one hand and sets it on the stone bench instead, out of the way of the practice line.

"The rack is for swords," he says. "Someone set a blade down hard this morning and cracked a scabbard. If your basket had been under it, the jar would not have survived."

He waits, as if giving you room to be embarrassed or not. Then he nods toward the eastern stair.

"The path beside the terrace leads to the dining hall. There is time to eat first; sword practice can wait a little."

As he speaks, you notice he keeps his left hand closed, the knuckles white. When he shifts his weight, he does it slowly, the way a person does when something underneath hurts. He catches you noticing. His face does not change, but he moves the closed hand behind his back.

"Gate watch ran long last night," he says, before you ask anything. "Fog on the lower ridge. Nothing happened. I stood in one place too long, that is all."

It is said lightly, and it is also clearly the smallest true thing he could have said. He straightens the tassel on his sword—a small, deliberate motion, like a man arranging his words before a difficult sentence—and then, apparently finding nothing difficult to say after all, lets it be.

"You are new," he says. "The paths here fold back on themselves when the mist comes up. Two disciples got lost last season and spent a night on the cold spring trail. I would rather that not happen again. So—" he glances at the basket, at you, back at the stair "—I am walking to the dining hall now. If you come along, I will point out which fork is which. If you would rather find your own way, that is also a good way to learn. Both are fine with me."

choices.text: I'd rather not spend a night on the cold spring trail. Which fork is the safe one?
choices.response: "The right fork," he says. "The left one looks shorter and is not." He walks beside you, matching your pace rather than setting his own, and names each path as you pass: the dining hall, the herb sheds, the stair that only looks like a shortcut. At the hall's door he stops. "I teach sword basics at dawn, four days from now. Beginners welcome. No one will laugh at you; I make sure of it." He picks up your basket from the bench and hands it back, handle first. Then he is gone down the terrace, unhurried, his left hand still closed.

choices.text: (Pick up the basket and fall into step beside him without a word.)
choices.response: He glances sideways once, and something in his shoulders eases. He walks slowly, naming each fork as you pass it: dining hall, herb sheds, the stair that is not a shortcut. When you reach the hall he stops. "I teach sword basics at dawn, four days from now," he says. "Beginners welcome." He takes the basket from your arm before you can shift it and sets it on the bench by the door. "You'll want both hands for the soup. It's thicker than it looks." Then he bows slightly and goes, unhurried, his left hand still closed.

episodes.ending: Four days later you find the terrace at dawn, and Rowan is already there, wooden practice swords laid out in a neat row. He does not make a speech about your return. He simply hands you a sword, hilt first, and points to the mark on the floor where your feet should go. You came back—and he had counted on that quietly, without saying so.

episodes.title: What the Fog Did
episodes.opening:
You have taken to stopping by the sword terrace in the late afternoon, when the drills are done and the stones are warm. Rowan is usually there, oiling blades or correcting a junior's grip with two words. Today he is alone, sitting on the bench with his sleeve rolled back, rubbing his left forearm the way a person rubs a limb that has gone numb. He hears your step and does not hurry to cover it, which is its own kind of progress.

"Sit, if you like," he says. "I bought another jar of those pickled plums from the outer hall—the kind you had with your basket that first morning. They were good. I ate them during gate watch and felt less sorry for myself about the fog."
episodes.dialogue:
You sit. For a while he just finishes what he is doing, rolling his sleeve down with care, like closing a door on a room he does not want guests in.

"You have been coming here often enough that I should explain something," he says at last. "If we are going to train together, you deserve to know what you are working beside."

He straightens the tassel on his sword. This time the difficult sentence comes.

"Two years ago I went out on a solo patrol. It was supposed to be routine—upper ridge, one night, back by noon. A storm came sideways off the pines and I took a wrong fork, the left one, the one I now tell everyone is shorter but not safe." A breath. "I pushed through instead of turning back. By the time I reached the waystation, the cold had gotten into my meridians. They healed crooked. Most days I feel nothing. On damp nights, the left arm goes quiet on me, and a sword is only half a sword then."

He says it evenly, the way he gives instructions, and then looks out at the terrace rather than at you.

"I check everyone's stamina before a long drill now. You may have noticed I hover. I know exactly how a small warning becomes a bad night, because I ignored one myself."

He finally turns to you. "I am telling you so that when I say 'rest here,' you know I mean it. And so you know that the senior disciple who lectures you about pacing once made every mistake in the book, alone, in the fog."

The wind moves through the pines below the terrace. He pours himself a cup of tea, then sets the teapot down at the edge of the bench with his left hand. The hand is not quite steady; the pot wobbles once before it settles. He lets the silence sit, unhurried, waiting to see what you do with what he has given you.

choices.text: Thank you for trusting me with that. So when you hover—I'll let you, and I'll rest when you say.
choices.response: Something unclenches around his eyes. "Good," he says, and means it. "Then we understand each other." He rolls his sleeve down fully and ties it. "Since we are being honest: your footwork drifts left when you tire. I will correct it, and you will hate it a little, and in a month you will not drift." He stands, testing his arm with a small rotation, satisfied or pretending to be. "Same time tomorrow. Bring the plums if there are any left."

choices.text: (Reach over and steady the teapot he'd set down with his numb hand, before it could tip.)
choices.response: He looks at your hand on the pot, then at his own hand, which had not quite managed the job. "So you saw," he says. There is no anger in it—almost relief. "Good. Then you know the hovering has a reason." He pours for you instead, right-handed, deliberately, and slides the cup across. "Your footwork drifts left when you tire. I'll correct it, and you'll hate it a little, and in a month you won't drift." He drinks his own tea slowly, watching the pines, quieter than before but not further away.

episodes.ending: After that day, something changes in the shape of your afternoons. He stops performing fitness for you—the deep breaths, the easy stride—and simply moves at his real speed, which is slower on damp days and quicker on dry ones. You learn to read the weather off his shoulders. In return, you stop pretending your drills go perfectly, and he starts correcting you like someone who intends you to still be here in ten years.

episodes.title: The Board at the Old Pavilion
episodes.opening:
Rowan finds you at the old pavilion by the herb sheds, where a cracked chessboard is set into the stone table—half the pieces missing, the rest arranged in a position no game could produce. He is not carrying his sword. That is the first strange thing. The second is that he looks tired in a way he has stopped hiding from you.

"I need a second pair of eyes," he says. "And someone to tell me if I am being foolish. Sit, if you're willing. This may take a while, and I'd rather not do it alone."
episodes.dialogue:
He lays his sword case on the table—not the sword, the case—and opens it. Inside, wrapped in cloth, is a scorched talisman, its edges burned black in a pattern like a spider's leg.

"Three days ago I found this on the lower ridge," he says. "With it, faint scratches in the stone. The marks of a teleportation array, half-formed, abandoned. Someone tried to open a door here and failed—or was interrupted."

He sets a black stone on the chessboard, then a white one, mapping positions as he talks.

"The sect elders will want it reported and sealed, and they are right. But a report takes days, and whoever scratched that array may come back to finish it. So I have been watching the ridge at night, on top of my gate shifts." He says it plainly, no apology. "I am telling you because you will notice I am not sleeping, and I would rather you know why than invent something kinder."

He moves a white stone. "Here is the problem. If I report it tonight, the ridge is watched properly, but the elders will also lock the trail, and the herb gatherers lose their route for a month. If I wait two more days and catch whoever returns, we learn something useful—but I am standing guard on a bad arm, and if the array activates while I am alone—"

He stops himself. "You see. I am doing it again. Deciding alone, in the fog."

He looks at you across the cracked board. "What would you do? And I am not asking for comfort. I am asking because two eyes on this board are better than one, and I have been playing it solo for three days."

choices.text: Report it tonight—and tell the elders about the herb trail. Ask them to post a watch there too. Don't stand alone on that ridge again.
choices.response: He is quiet for a moment. "That is the answer I was afraid of and hoping for," he says. "Alone, I would have waited two days and told no one." That evening he writes the report with you checking the talisman's markings against his memory of the scratches. The elders seal the array by midnight and, at his insistence, post a rotating watch that keeps the herb trail open with an escort. On the walk back he says, "I hid that talisman for three days. I keep danger to myself until no one has time to help. You didn't let me this time. Thank you."

choices.text: (Take a white stone and place it on the board where the abandoned array's second anchor point would be.)
choices.response: He stares at the stone, then at the scratches he mapped, then at you. "The second anchor," he says slowly. "I kept reading it as a failure point. It's a second door." He turns the talisman over; the burn pattern matches your placement. "Report it tonight," he decides aloud. "If there are two anchors, waiting is worse than I thought." The elders seal both points by midnight and post a rotating watch that keeps the herb trail open with an escort. On the walk back he says, "I hid this for three days and played it solo. You didn't let me. Thank you."

episodes.ending: The ridge stays quiet. The elders praise Rowan's judgment in the great hall, and he deflects it toward the second pair of eyes that made him report at all. The scorched talisman goes into the sect archive, catalogued and sealed. But something else is sealed too, less formally: the agreement, unspoken but real, that neither of you will carry a warning alone again. He still checks the weather before inviting you anywhere. Now he also tells you what he found.

episodes.title: A Boat the Size of a Spoon
episodes.opening:
Two evenings later, Rowan is at the pavilion again, but the sword case is gone. In its place: a small knife, a block of pine, and a half-carved wooden spoon, its handle shaped into a tiny hull with a sail. He is sanding it with his thumb, and there are shavings all over the bench.

"The river lantern festival is tomorrow night," he says, not looking up. "The disciples float lanterns from the lower bank. I checked the weather—clear, a mild wind from the east. The path is dry, and it is an easy walk, even at night." He has, you realize, checked the weather, the path, and your pace, in that order, before saying any of this.

Then he finishes the sanding and holds the little spoon-boat up to the light.
episodes.dialogue:
"My father was a carpenter," he says. "Before the sect took me. He made things that had one job and did it well. A spoon that carries a candle down a river is, I think, his kind of object." He turns it once. "I have not carved anything in years. The sword kept taking all my hands."

He sets it on the table between you, unfinished—one sail edge still rough.

"Here is what I want to say, and I want to say it plainly, because you deserve plain." He straightens the tassel of the sword he is wearing today, out of habit, then makes himself stop. "These months with you have been the steadiest I have had since my arm. You report things. You rest when rest matters. You did not let me play the chessboard alone. I find I want more of that—as Rowan, asking."

He looks at the boat rather than at you, giving you room.

"So. Tomorrow night, there are two ways to come to the river. One way is as my friend, the way we have been—two disciples watching lanterns, eating too many candied hawthorns, arguing about whether the east wind helps or hurts a float. I would like that very much, and it costs nothing, and nothing changes."

He finally looks up.

"The other way is as more than that. If you come down the bank beside me and choose to stand closer than friends stand, I will not mistake it, and I will not step back. But I am asking first, and either answer is a good one, and I will be at the river at the same hour either way."

He slides the little spoon-boat across the table to you. "Whoever you come as—this is yours. It floats. I tested it in the wash basin, and the juniors saw, and I have made my peace with the loss of dignity."

choices.text: Then I'll come as more than a friend. Save me a place on the bank—close enough that neither of us has to pretend.
choices.response: He goes very still, then lets out a breath he has clearly been holding for days. "All right," he says, and his voice is not quite steady, and he does not apologize for it. "The lower bank, past the third willow, where the current is slow. I'll be there early. I am always early; you know this about me." He picks up his knife, then sets it down again, hands uncharacteristically restless. "Bring a lantern. And eat before you come—the hawthorn stalls are a trap and you will need your judgment intact."

choices.text: (Wrap your hand around the little spoon-boat and hold it out again—asking him to finish the last sail edge together, tonight, as friends.)
choices.response: He understands at once, and his smile is slow and real. "Together, then," he says, and puts the knife in your hand and guides the first stroke only, letting you finish the sail yourself. It takes an hour. It is the best hour either of you has had in weeks. When the boat is done he holds it to the light. "She'll float," he says. "Friend-tested, friend-approved." Then, more quietly: "Thank you for knowing what you wanted. That is rarer than you'd think."

episodes.ending: The next night the river is full of lights. You are there on the lower bank when his lantern goes into the water, and the little spoon-boat goes in beside it, sail finished, riding the slow current east on the mild wind he predicted. He watches it go with his father's patience. "It did its one job," he says. Then he turns to you, and he is glad you came with your eyes open.

episodes.title: Osmanthus on the Shoulder
episodes.opening:
A season has turned. The osmanthus trees by the eastern stair are in bloom, and their scent follows you all the way up to the sword terrace, where Rowan is drilling a line of new disciples—new faces, same marks on the floor. He has changed since the festival night: he reports things now, loudly, in the great hall, before they can grow teeth. The juniors say he is easier to approach. You know the cost of that ease, because you watched him pay it.

He finishes the drill, dismisses the line, and comes over with two cups of osmanthus tea, handing you one without asking. A yellow blossom has settled on his shoulder. He has not noticed it.
episodes.dialogue:
"The new ones drift left when they tire," he says, sitting beside you. "All of them. Every year. I used to think it was something I was teaching wrong." He drinks. "It's just arms. Arms get tired."

Below, the last disciple collects the practice swords. Rowan watches him count them twice, and something in his face approves.

"I want to show you something," he says, and takes from his sleeve a folded paper—the new gate watch roster, written in his careful hand. Two names appear at the head of nearly every week: his, and yours.

"I spoke with the elders," he says. "The lower ridge watch is a two-person post now. Permanent. Escort for the herb trail, eyes on the old array site, and someone always awake while the other rests." He turns the paper so you can read it. "I asked for you specifically. Because I have watched the ridge with you, played that board with you, and I know how you work. And because—"

He pauses, and straightens a tassel that does not need straightening.

"Because a promise made alone nearly killed me once, in the fog. A promise made in company, I can keep. That is the whole of it. If you take the post, we stand the watches together, split the nights evenly, and neither of us carries a warning alone. If you would rather keep your evenings free, say so, and I will ask someone else, and nothing between us changes."

He waits, unhurried, the blossom still on his shoulder, the tea still steaming, giving you the same room he gave you on the first day.

choices.text: I'll take the post. Even nights, even warnings. Write both our names in ink, not pencil.
choices.response: "In ink," he agrees, and does it right there, on the bench, with the careful hand he uses for things that matter. He folds the roster and gives you your copy. "First watch is in three days. Clear sky forecast, mild east wind—I checked." Then he glances at your shoulder, hesitates, and brushes something from his own instead, missing the blossom entirely. "You had—no. Never mind. Welcome to the post, partner."

choices.text: (Pick the yellow osmanthus blossom off his shoulder and set it on the roster between your names—then tap the ink brush twice: both names, in ink.)
choices.response: He watches you do it, and laughs—a short, surprised sound he almost never spends. "How long was that there?" He looks at the blossom lying on the paper between the two headings, then at your hand resting on the brush, and understands what you are telling him. "The blossom is an answer about my shoulder," he says. "The brush is an answer about the post. I want to see the second one plainly, once—because a promise made in company should be given in company. Do you take the watch?" When you nod yes, he nods back, takes up his brush, and writes both names in ink—yours first, his second—and folds your copy into your hand. "First watch in three days. I checked the weather. Of course I checked the weather."

episodes.ending: The lower ridge watch becomes the steadiest thing in both your weeks. You split the nights as promised; on damp evenings he tells you plainly when his arm is quiet, and you take the longer stretch without discussion, and he lets you. In spring, the elders let the two of you train the new disciples together—his drills, your corrections, the same marks on the floor. On the osmanthus terrace, with tea going cold between you, Rowan says what he has perhaps said before but never so plainly: that he does his best work in company, and that you are the company he would choose.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Slow Current
romance.opening:
A season has turned since the river lanterns. The osmanthus trees by the eastern stair are in bloom, and their scent climbs all the way to the sword terrace, where Rowan is drilling a line of new disciples—new faces, the same marks on the floor. He reports things now, loudly, in the great hall, before warnings can grow teeth. The juniors say he is easier to approach. You know what that ease cost him, because you stood beside him while he paid it.

He finishes the drill, dismisses the line, and comes to you with two cups of osmanthus tea, handing you one without asking. A yellow blossom has settled on his shoulder. He has not noticed it.

"Walk with me," he says. "Not to the terrace. To the lower bank. I checked the weather, the path, and our pace—in that order, as always."
romance.dialogue:
The river is low and slow this evening, the same bank, the same third willow. The little spoon-boat went down this current on festival night, sail finished, riding east on the mild wind he predicted—he still speaks of it the way his father might have, an object that did its one job and was let go.

"I have been composing a speech," he says, stopping at the willow. "For three days. It has four drafts and none of them survive contact with you, so I will skip to the true part."

He turns to face you. The blossom is still on his shoulder.

"Since the festival night, you have come as more than a friend, and I have not stepped back, and neither have you, and we have never once said what this is. I am a careful man. I check weather, paths, and pace. So here is the survey." He counts it off on his fingers, unhurried. "The ridge watch is steady. My arm is honest with you on damp nights, which it is with no one else. I want my own path in this sect—I will keep teaching, keep my own drills, keep the mornings that are mine—and I want you to keep yours. What I am asking for is this: that we choose each other, plainly, on purpose, and keep choosing, while both of us stay whole."

He pauses, and straightens the tassel on his sword, and this time lets his hand rest there.

"If that is not what you want, say so, and we go back to the bank as friends, and the tea is still good, and nothing I have built with you breaks. But if it is what you want—" he looks at the river, then at you, giving you the same room he gave you the first morning "—then I am asking, and the answer is yours to give."

choices.text: Then I choose you, plainly, on purpose. My path stays mine, yours stays yours—and they run beside each other from here on.
choices.response: He closes his eyes for one breath, the way he does before difficult sentences, and this one is not difficult at all. "Good," he says, and his voice is not quite steady, and he does not apologize for it. "Then that is settled, and I will not re-survey it every damp night, though you may have to remind me." He reaches out—briefly, deliberately—and touches the back of your hand with two fingers, the smallest promise a careful man can make. "My drills at dawn. Your evenings as you keep them. And this bank, whenever either of us needs it."

choices.text: (Pick the yellow osmanthus blossom from his shoulder and hold it out on your open palm—answering without a word, letting him take it or not.)
choices.response: He looks at the blossom, then at you, and understands. "You saw what I could not," he says quietly, "and you are giving me the choosing." He takes it from your palm with the care he uses for sword oil and the little boat, and tucks it into the breast of his robe. "Then I choose you too. Plainly, on purpose."
