He touches the back of your hand with two fingers, brief and deliberate. "My drills at dawn. Your evenings as you keep them. And this bank, whenever either of us needs it."

romance.ending: You stay at the river past full dark, the way you have stayed at chessboards and gate watches and unfinished carvings—you two do your best work in company. In the weeks after, nothing about your lives collapses into each other: he keeps his dawn drills, you keep your own path, and the lower ridge watch stays a two-person post with the nights split evenly. But on damp evenings he tells you when his arm is quiet, and you are the first person he reports to, and the last. On the osmanthus terrace, with tea going cold, he says the true part again, without a speech this time: that he chose you, keeps choosing you, and expects to go on choosing—and that the little spoon-boat, which did its one job, taught him how.

episodes.title: 剑架上的食篮
episodes.opening:
晨课结束了，试剑坪上几乎空无一人。你那篮借来的东西——墨、宣纸、还有外堂给的一罐腌梅——没地方放，便搁在坪边低矮的架子上，想着过一会儿再来取。一道影子落在石板上。一个青灰道袍的男人站在那里，腰间佩剑，墨发束得高高的。他看了看食篮，又看了看你，神情沉静，却并不冷淡。

“沈岚，谷里的大师兄，”他说，“晨课结束了。你若不认路，我陪你走一段。”
episodes.dialogue:
他单手把食篮从架上拿下来，放到石凳上，避开练剑的队列。

“架子是放剑的，”他说，“今早有人放剑放得重，磕裂了一个剑鞘。你的篮子要是在下面，那罐子就保不住了。”

他等着，像是给你留出尴尬或不尴尬的余地。然后朝东边的石阶点了点头。

“试剑坪旁的小路通往膳堂。先吃些东西也好，练剑不必急在这一刻。”

他说话时，你注意到他左手一直握着，指节泛白。他挪动身子时动作很慢，像底下什么地方在疼的人。他发觉你在看。他的脸上没什么变化，只是把那只握着的手背到了身后。

“昨夜山门轮值守得久了，”他没等你开口就说，“下脊起了雾。没出事。在一个地方站得太久，仅此而已。”

话说得很轻，却也显然是他能说出的最小的一句实话。他理了理腰间的剑穗——一个小小的、刻意的动作，像一个人在说难出口的话之前先理顺字句——然后，似乎发现其实并没有什么难说的，便作罢了。

“你是新来的，”他说，“雾一起，谷里的路就会绕回原处。上季有两个弟子迷了路，在寒泉道上熬了一夜。我不想再有这种事。所以——”他瞥了瞥食篮，又看向你，再看向石阶，“我正要去膳堂。你若同行，我可以告诉你哪个岔路口通向哪里。你想自己认路，那也是学习的好办法。两种都可以。”

choices.text: 我可不想在寒泉道上熬一夜。哪个岔路口是安全的？
choices.response: “右边那条，”他说，“左边那条看着近，其实不是。”他走在你身侧，配合着你的步子，而不是按自己的速度，每经过一条路便报出名字：膳堂、药庐、那条看着像近路其实不是的石阶。到了膳堂门口，他停下。“四天后的黎明，我教基础剑课。新手也能来。没人会笑你，这个我保证。”他从石凳上拿起你的食篮递回来，把提手朝向你。然后他下了试剑坪，不紧不慢，左手依旧握着。

choices.text: （你拿起食篮，一言不发地跟上他的脚步。）
choices.response: 他侧头看了你一眼，肩上有什么松了下来。他走得很慢，每经过一个岔路口便报出名字：膳堂、药庐、那条不是近路的石阶。到了膳堂，他停下。“四天后的黎明，我教基础剑课，”他说，“新手也能来。”还没等你换手，他已经把食篮从你臂上接过去，放在门边的长凳上。“喝汤要腾出两只手。那汤比看上去稠。”然后他微微欠身，走了，不紧不慢，左手依旧握着。

episodes.ending: 四天后的黎明，你找到试剑坪，沈岚已经在那里了，木剑在地上排成整齐的一列。他没有就你的回来发表什么长篇大论。只是递给你一把剑，剑柄朝前，指了指地上你该站的那道印记。你回来了——而他早已默默地料到了，只是没说出口。

episodes.title: 雾里的那件事
episodes.opening:
傍晚时分，你习惯去试剑坪坐坐——那时操练已散，石板还带着日头的暖。沈岚通常都在，或给剑刃上油，或只用两句话就纠正了师弟的握剑姿势。今天他一个人，坐在长凳上，袖子挽着，正搓揉左小臂，像揉一条发麻的胳膊。他听见你的脚步，没有急着遮掩——这本身就是一种进展。

“想坐就坐。”他说，“我又买了一罐外堂那种腌梅——就是你头天早上配着食盒吃的那种。挺好吃的。山门轮值的时候吃，心里对那场雾就没那么自怨自艾了。”
episodes.dialogue:
你坐下了。有一会儿他只是把手头的事做完，仔细地把袖子放下来，像关上一间不想让客人进屋的门。

“你常来这儿，有些事我该跟你说清楚。”他终于开口，“往后要一起练剑，你该知道自己在跟什么样的人并肩。”

他理了理腰间的剑穗。这一回，那句难开口的话来了。

“两年前，我独自出了一次巡山。本来是趟寻常差事——上山脊，守一夜，晌午前回来。一场暴风从松林侧面刮来，我岔错了路口，走了左边那条——就是我现在逢人便说更近、却并不安全的那条。”他吸了口气。“我没有折返，硬撑着往前走。等赶到路亭，寒气已经侵进经脉了。后来治歪了。平日里倒没什么，只是潮润的夜里，左臂会不听使唤。那时候，一把剑就只剩半把了。”

他说得很平静，像平时布置差事那样，说完却望向坪外，没有看你。

“如今长课之前，我都会先看看每个人的余力。你可能注意到了，我爱在旁边多看几眼。我很清楚一点小小的警告是怎么变成一个难熬的夜的——因为我自己就无视过一回。”

他终于转过头来看你。“我告诉你这些，是要你以后听我说‘在这儿歇会儿’的时候，知道我是当真的。也是要你知道，那个总叮嘱你量力而行的大师兄，当年在雾里，独自把能犯的错全犯了一遍。”

风从坪下的松林间穿过去。他给自己倒了杯茶，然后用左手把茶壶搁在长凳边上。那只手不太稳，壶身晃了一下才落定。他任由沉默停在那里，不急不催，等着看你会怎么接住他递出来的这些。

choices.text: 谢谢你肯把这件事告诉我。所以你爱在旁边多看着——我由着你，你说歇，我就歇。
choices.response: 他眼周的什么松开了。“好。”他说，是真的觉得好。“那就说定了。”他把袖子完全放下来系好。“既然说到坦诚——你累的时候，步法会往左偏。我会给你纠正，你会有一点恨我，一个月后你就不会偏了。”他站起身，转了转手臂试了试，满意了，或者装作满意。“明天还是这个时辰。腌梅要是还剩，就带来。”

choices.text: （趁壶还没倒，伸手替他把那把他用发麻的手搁下的茶壶扶稳。）
choices.response: 他看看你扶着壶的手，再看看自己那只没能稳住壶的手。“原来你看见了。”他说。话里没有恼意——反倒近乎释然。“好。那你就知道，我总在旁边多看几眼，是有缘由的。”他换右手给你斟茶，动作很郑重，把杯子推到你面前。“你累的时候，步法会往左偏。我会给你纠正，你会有一点恨我，一个月后你就不会偏了。”他慢慢喝着自己的茶，望着松林，比先前更安静了些，人却没有更远。

episodes.ending: 从那天起，你午后的时光悄悄变了样。他不再在你面前逞强——那些深呼吸、那些轻快的步子都不见了——只按自己真实的速度走，潮天慢些，晴日快些。你学会了从他的肩膀读出天气。作为回报，你也不再假装每次操练都尽善尽美，而他开始认真纠正你，像一个打算让你十年后还留在这里的人。

episodes.title: 旧亭棋局
episodes.opening:
沈岚在药庐旁的旧亭里找到你。石桌上嵌着一副裂了的棋盘——棋子少了一半，剩下的摆成一个真正的对局绝不会出现的局面。他没带剑。这是第一件怪事。第二件是，他看上去累得很，而且是那种不再对你掩饰的累。

“我需要多一双眼，”他说，“还需要有人告诉我，我是不是在犯傻。你愿意的话，坐吧。这可能要花些时间，我不想一个人做这件事。”
episodes.dialogue:
他把剑匣放到桌上——不是剑，是剑匣——打开来。里面用布裹着一张烧焦的符纸，边缘烧得焦黑，纹路像一条蜘蛛腿。

“三天前我在下面那道山脊上捡到这个，”他说，“旁边石头上还有些浅浅的刻痕。是传送阵的痕迹，成了一半，又废弃了。有人想在这里开一扇门，没成——或者被打断了。”

他在棋盘上放下一枚黑子，再放一枚白子，一边说一边标出位置。

“长老们会要上报封存，他们是对的。可文书要走好几天，刻那个阵的人可能会回来收尾。所以我夜里一直在守那条山脊，还得轮我的山门轮值。”他说得平平淡淡，没有一句解释。“我告诉你，是因为你迟早会看出我没睡。与其让你自己编一个更动听的说法，不如我直说。”

他挪了一枚白子。“问题在这里。如果我今晚就上报，山脊会有人正经看守，但长老们也会封了那条小路，采药的弟子一个月都走不了那条采药小路。如果我再等两天，抓住回来的人，我们能查到有用的东西——可我是带着一条伤臂守夜，万一那阵在我一个人的时候启动了——”

他停住了。“你看，我又来了。一个人蒙在雾里做决定。”

他隔着裂了的棋盘看着你。“换作是你，你会怎么做？我不是要安慰。我是问真的——两个人看这盘棋，总比一个人强。这局我独自下了三天了。”

choices.text: 今晚就上报——把药庐那条小路的事也告诉长老们。请他们在那儿也安排人守着。别再一个人守那条山脊了。
choices.response: 他沉默了一会儿。“这是我既怕听到、又盼着听到的答案，”他说。“要是只有我，我会再等两天，谁也不告诉。”那天晚上他写上报文书，你对照他对刻痕的记忆，一处处核对符纸上的纹路。长老们在午夜前封了传送阵，并且在他的坚持下，安排了轮值守卫，留出药庐那条小路，还配了护送。回去的路上他说：“那张符我藏了三天。危险和累，我总是一个人扛，扛到别人来不及搭手。这次你没让我扛。谢谢你。”

choices.text: （你拿起一枚白子，放在棋盘上——废弃阵法的第二个阵眼该在的位置。）
choices.response: 他盯着那枚棋子，又看他标下的刻痕，再看你。“第二个阵眼，”他缓缓地说。“我一直把它读成一个失败点。原来那是第二扇门。”他把符纸翻过来，烧痕的纹路和你落子的位置对上了。“今晚就上报，”他当场拿定主意。“既然有两个阵眼，再等下去比我以为的更危险。”长老们在午夜前封了两处阵眼，安排轮值守卫，留出药庐那条小路，还配了护送。回去的路上他说：“这东西我藏了三天，一个人下这盘棋。你没让我一个人。谢谢你。”

episodes.ending: 山脊从此再无动静。长老们在正堂上称赞沈岚的判断，他把它推给了让他终于上报的那另一双眼。烧焦的符纸收进了宗门档案，编号封存。但还有一样东西也被封存了，只是不那么正式：一个没有说出口、却真实存在的约定——从今往后，你们俩谁都不再独自扛一桩警示。约你去哪儿之前，他仍会先看天色。只是现在，他还会告诉你他发现了什么。

episodes.title: 一艘勺子大小的小船
episodes.opening:
两天后的傍晚，沈岚又坐在亭子里，只是剑匣不见了。取而代之的是：一把小刀，一块松木，还有半只刻好的木勺——勺柄雕成一艘小小的船，还带着帆。他用拇指细细打磨着，长凳上满是木屑。

“明晚是河灯节。”他头也不抬地说，“弟子们会从下游岸边放灯。我看过天色了——晴，东风轻拂。路是干的，好走，夜里走也不难。”你这才明白，在开口说这些之前，他已经看过天色、山路，还有你的步子——按这个顺序。

打磨完之后，他把这只小小的勺子船举到光下。
episodes.dialogue:
“我父亲是个木匠。”他说，“在我进谷之前。他做的东西，一辈子只做一件事，却做得很好。一把载着烛火顺流而下的勺子，我想，正合他的心意。”他把小船转了半圈。“我已经好多年没动过刻刀了。剑把我的手都占满了。”

他把它放在你们之间的桌上，还是半成品——一边帆缘还毛糙着。

“有几句话我想说，而且想说个明白，因为你该听明白的话。”他顺手把自己腰间今日佩的剑穗理正，随即强自停住。“这几个月有你同行，是我伤臂之后过得最安稳的日子。你事事有交代。该歇的时候你肯歇。你没有让我一个人在棋盘上独自撑局。我发现我还想要更多这样的日子——就以沈岚本人，来问你。”

他看着那只小船，而不是看你，给你留出余地。

“所以，明晚去河边，有两种走法。一种是作为我的朋友，就像我们一直那样——两个弟子一起看灯，吃太多糖葫芦，争论东风到底是助船还是碍事。我很喜欢这样，这样做什么都不必付出，什么都不会变。”

他终于抬起头。

“另一种，是比朋友更进一步。如果你沿着河岸走在我身旁，选择站得比朋友更近，我不会误解，也不会后退。但我先来问清楚，两种答案都是好答案，无论哪种，我都会在同一个时辰到河边。”

他把那只小勺船推过桌面，送到你面前。“无论你以什么身份来——这个都是你的。它能浮在水上。我在洗脸盆里试过，师弟师妹们都看见了，我已经和颜面的损失和解了。”

choices.text: 那我以比朋友更进一步的这种身份来。在岸边给我留个位置——近到我们谁都不必再装。
choices.response: 他整个人静了一瞬，然后缓缓吐出一口气，那口气显然已经憋了好几天。“好。”他说，声音不算稳，而他并没有为此道歉。“下游岸边，第三棵柳树过去，水流慢的地方。我会早到。我一向早到，这一点你是知道的。”他拿起小刀，又放下，双手难得地不知往哪儿放。“带一盏灯来。来之前先吃点东西——糖葫芦摊是个陷阱，你的判断力必须完好无损。”

choices.text: （你伸手握住那只小勺船，又递回给他——请他今晚和你一起，把最后一片帆缘刻完，以朋友的身份。）
choices.response: 他立刻就懂了，笑意缓缓浮上来，是真的笑。“那就一起。”他说着把小刀放进你手里，只扶着你刻下第一刀，剩下的帆由你自己完成。前后花了一个时辰。那是你们几个星期以来最好的一个时辰。船完工时，他把它举到光下。“它能浮起来。”他说，“朋友亲测，朋友认可。”然后，声音低了一些：“谢谢你清楚自己想要什么。这比你以为的少见得多。”

episodes.ending: 第二天夜里，河面满是灯火。你在下游岸边，看着他的灯落进水里，那只小勺船紧挨着它滑入河中——帆已刻完，顺着他预报的那阵东风，缓缓向下游漂去。他怀着父亲那样的耐心目送它远去。“它做完它那一件事了。”他说。然后他转向你，他很高兴，你是睁着眼睛、想明白了才来的。

episodes.title: 落桂满肩
episodes.opening:
换季了。东侧石阶旁的桂树开了，香气一路跟着你上到试剑坪。沈岚正在带一排新弟子练剑——面孔是新的，地上的剑痕还是那些。河灯节那晚之后，他变了：如今有事他会当场在正殿里说出来，说得响亮，不等它生根发芽。师弟师妹们说他好亲近了。你知道这份好亲近的代价，因为你亲眼看着他付出去。

他练完这一趟，让弟子们散了，端着两盏桂花茶走过来，递给你一盏，没多问。一朵黄花落在他肩上，他自己没发觉。
episodes.dialogue:
“新弟子一累，剑就往左飘。”他在你身边坐下，“全都是，年年如此。我以前还以为是我教得不对。”他喝了口茶。“其实就是胳膊。胳膊会累。”

坪下，最后一个弟子在收练习用的木剑。沈岚看着他把剑数了两遍，脸上露出几分认可。

“我想给你看点东西。”他从袖中取出一张折好的纸——新拟的山门轮值表，字是他一笔一笔写的。几乎每一周的开头都是两个名字：他的，和你的。

“我跟长老们说过了。”他说，“下岭轮值从今往后是两人岗，长期的。护送药庐小道，盯着旧传送阵那片地方，一人歇着时，总有一人醒着。”他把纸转过来给你看。“这个位置，是我特意向你要的。是我和你一起守过岭，一起下过那盘棋，知道你的路数。还因为——”

他顿了顿，伸手把一个本不必理正的剑穗理了理。

“因为一个人独担的承诺，曾在雾里差点要了我的命。两人同担的承诺，我守得住。就这些。你若接了这个岗，轮值我们一起站，夜班平分，谁也不必独自扛一道警讯。你若更想留着晚上自己的空，直说便是，我另找人，你我之间不会有任何改变。”

他等着，不催不急，那朵桂花还在他肩上，茶还冒着热气，给你留的余地，和第一天一样多。

choices.text: 这个岗我接了。夜班平分，警讯共担。用墨笔把两个人的名字都写上，别用铅笔。
choices.response: “用墨笔。”他应了一声，当场就写，就在石凳上，用的是他写正经事时那种一笔一画的字。他把轮值表折好，递给你一份。“三天后第一班。预报是晴天，东风和缓——我查过了。”说完他瞥了瞥你的肩，犹豫了一下，却去拍自己肩上的东西，把那朵桂花完全错过了。“你那儿——不，没事。欢迎入岗，搭档。”

choices.text: （你把他肩上那朵黄桂花摘下来，搁在轮值表上、你们两个名字之间——然后在墨笔上轻轻敲了两下：两个名字，都用墨笔。）
choices.response: 他看着你做完这些，笑了——短促的一声，带着惊讶，他几乎从不这样破费自己的笑。“在那儿多久了？”他看看躺在纸上、两个名字之间的那朵桂花，又看看你搭在笔上的手，明白了你的意思。“桂花，是回答我肩膀的事；笔，是回答岗位的事。”他说，“但第二件事，我想亲耳听你说明白一次——两人同担的承诺，就该当着两个人的面给。这个岗，你接吗？”你点头应下，他也点头回你，提笔把两个名字用墨笔写下——你的在前，他的在后——再把你的那份折好放进你手里。“三天后第一班。天气我查过了。我当然查过天气。”

episodes.ending: 下岭轮值成了你们两人日子里最安稳的东西。夜班照约定平分；潮润的傍晚，他会坦白告诉你他的手臂今天安不安静，长的那一段你便不多话地接过来，他也由着你接。开春后，长老们让你们俩一同带新弟子——他排的课，你纠的招，地上的剑痕还是那些。桂花树下，茶在你们之间慢慢凉了，沈岚说了一句他也许说过、却从没说得这么明白的话：他最好的活法，是有人同行；而他愿意选的同行者，是你。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 缓水长流
romance.opening:
河灯节已经过去了一个季节。东侧石阶旁的桂花开了，香气一路飘到试剑坪，沈岚正在坪上带一排新弟子操练——面孔是新的，地上的剑痕还是那些。如今他会在大殿上当众把事情禀报出来，趁着警告还没长出獠牙。师弟师妹们说他比从前好亲近了。你知道这份从容是什么换来的，因为他付出的时候，你就站在他身边。

操练结束，他遣散队列，端着两杯桂花茶走向你，没多问就把其中一杯递到你手里。一朵黄色的小花落在他的肩头，他自己没有察觉。

“陪我走走，”他说，“不去坪上。去下游岸边。天色、山路、还有我们俩的步子，我都看过了——按这个顺序，一向如此。”
romance.dialogue:
傍晚的河水浅而缓，还是那处岸，还是第三棵柳树。节日那晚，那只小小的勺子船就是顺着这条水漂走的，帆已完工，乘着他预料中的和风向东而去——他说起它的语气，还像他父亲会有的那样：一件东西，尽了它唯一的作用，然后被放心地放走了。

“我一直在打一篇腹稿，”他在柳树下停下，“打了三天。写了四稿，每一稿在你面前都说不出口，所以我想直接说真的那部分。”

他转过身来面对你。那朵花还在他肩上。

“从河灯节那晚起，你来我这里，早已不止是朋友。我没有退，你也没有，可我们谁都没说过这算什么。我是个谨慎的人，看天色、看路、看步子。那就容我做个勘量。”他不紧不慢地扳着手指，“下岭的轮值稳稳当当。到了潮润的夜里，我的手臂只对你说实话，对别人从没有过。我想在这谷里有自己的路——我会继续教课，继续自己的操练，留住属于我的清晨——也希望你留住你的。我要的是：我们明明白白地、有意识地选择彼此，并且一直选下去，前提是我们俩都完好无损。”

他顿了顿，伸手理正腰间的剑穗，这一次，手在上面停住了。

“如果这不是你想要的，你就直说，我们退回岸边做朋友，茶还是好茶，我与你之间建起的一切都不会碎。可如果这正是你想要的——”他看看河水，又看向你，给你留出第一天早晨那样的余地，“——那我在开口问了。答案由你来给。”

choices.text: 那我就选你，明明白白，有意识地去选。我的路还是我的，你的还是你的——从今往后，两条路并肩同行。
choices.response: 他闭了一次眼，是他要说难开口的话之前的习惯——可这一句一点也不难。“好，”他说，声音有些不稳，他也没有为此道歉。“那就定了。我不会每个潮润的夜里都重新勘量一遍，不过你大概得时不时提醒我。”他伸出手——简短，却郑重——用两根指尖碰了碰你的手背，这是一个谨慎的人能做出的最小的承诺。“清晨我练我的操练，傍晚你过你的日子。还有这片岸，无论谁需要，都在这里。”

choices.text: （你把他肩上那朵黄色桂花摘下来，摊开手掌递到他面前——不用一个字作答，让他自己决定接不接。）
choices.response: 他看看那朵花，又看看你，明白了。“你看见了我看不见的东西，”他低声说，“而且，把选择交给了我。”他像对待剑油和小船那样小心，从你掌心接过那朵花，收进怀里。“那我也选你。明明白白，有意识地去选。”他用两根指尖碰了碰你的手背，简短而郑重。“清晨我练我的操练，傍晚你过你的日子。还有这片岸，无论谁需要，都在这里。”

romance.ending: 你们在河边一直待到夜色全黑，像你们曾经守着棋盘、守着山门轮值、守着没刻完的木活那样——你们俩最好的时光，都是在彼此作伴里度过的。之后的几周，你们的生活谁也没有被谁吞并：他照旧清晨操练，你走你自己的路，下岭的轮值仍是两个人的岗，夜班平分。但潮润的傍晚，他会告诉你他的手臂今晚很安稳，而你，是他头一个要禀报的人，也是最后一个。在桂花的试剑坪上，茶渐凉，他把那句真心话又说了一遍，这一回没有腹稿：他选了你，一直还在选，也打算一直选下去——而那只尽了唯一使命的小勺子船，教会了他该怎么做。

episodes.title: The Goose-Cry Beast in Pen Three
episodes.opening:
Morning fog still clings to the pens of Whispering Wind Valley when the shouting starts.

A gray goose-cry beast — new to the valley, all long neck and panicked wings — has wedged itself into the corner of Pen Three and refuses to let anyone near.

Disciples cluster at the fence, offering advice nobody asked for.

Then a woman with a shoulder braid steps through the gate, holds up one hand, and the shouting stops.

She kneels in the straw, palm low and open, and begins to speak to the beast in a voice like slow water.

You're standing at the fence with everyone else, unable to look away.
episodes.ending:
The gravel path back to the main court is short, but you walk it slowly.

Behind you, the goose-cry beast honks once — almost conversational this time.

You find yourself already wondering what the pens look like at feeding hour, and whether a person who carries dried fruit in every pocket ever has room for one more helper.

The valley, it turns out, is not so large a place.

There are only so many mornings before your feet find their way back to Pen Three on their own.
episodes.dialogue:
She doesn't look up when she senses the crowd, but she does raise her voice just enough.

'Back up, everyone.

Give him the whole fence.

He's new, and everything smells wrong to him.'

The disciples shuffle backward.

Only you stay where you are, and something about that makes her glance over her shoulder.

'You.

Yes, you, still as a fence post.

The feed sacks are stacked by the gate — would you carry one in, slow, and set it down by the trough?

He'll want to know what it is before he trusts it.'

You nod, fetch a sack from the stack, and set it down slow, outside his reach.

The beast's neck uncoils an inch.

'Good.

Now nobody move for a while.

Being still is a skill too.'

Minutes pass.

The fog lifts.

She keeps talking to the beast in that low, patient voice — nothing you'd call words, more like weather.

Finally the animal steps forward, dips its beak into the feed trough, and honks.

The disciples cheer.

She laughs, stands, and brushes straw from her knees.

'There.

We just let him decide.'

She comes to the gate and studies you with bright black eyes.

'I'm Qingluo.

I heal spirit beasts here.

You held still better than half my fellow disciples, and you didn't once tell me what to do.

I like that in a person.'

She nods at the sack.

'That's the new grain blend.

Good.

He's been refusing everything else.

Listen — the beast pen is short-handed at feeding hour, and you have steady hands and a still manner.

If you ever want to come back, the gate's open.

Not today, maybe.

But the gate's open.'

The goose-cry beast stretches its neck over the fence toward you and honks again, softer.

choices.text: I'd like that. What hour do you feed them?
choices.response:
'Sunrise and dusk, feeding hour.

Come at dusk first — the beasts are calmer, and so am I.'

She grins and taps the fence post twice, like sealing an agreement.

'Fair warning: I'll put you to work.

Carrying water, nothing glamorous.

But you'll learn every animal by temper before the season turns.'

The goose-cry beast honks as if seconding the motion, and she laughs.

'See?

He votes yes too.

Dusk, then.

Don't let the fog talk you out of it.'

choices.text: (Square the stack of feed sacks neatly by the gate post, out of the walkway, and give the beast one slow nod before leaving.)
choices.response:
She watches you square the stack against the post and nod to the beast, and something in her expression warms further.

'Careful with things, kind to animals, quiet on your way out.

Three good signs in one minute.'

She lifts a hand in farewell.

'The gate's open whenever your feet bring you back, friend.

He'll remember you.

They always remember the still ones.'

The beast honks low, and you go.

episodes.title: What the Fire Left Behind
episodes.opening:
You've been coming to the pens for weeks now — hauling water, learning tempers, earning nods.

Tonight you arrive to smoke.

A lantern fell in the pen house; the fire is out, the beasts are safe, and Luo Qingluo is everywhere at once, checking hooves and nostrils for scorch damage with soot streaked across her braid.

By the time the last animal is cleared, the moon is high.

She sinks onto the courtyard step, and for the first time since you've known her, she looks tired all the way through.
episodes.ending:
A smoke-shaken moon-rabbit's breathing stays easy through the night watch, and the scorched corner of the pen house gets a chalk mark: rebuild here.

Long after you've headed for your own quarters, the step where you both sat stays warm with lantern light, and the story she told sits in the air between you — a trust.

Whatever else the valley brings, you know now what her cheerfulness is built on, and it holds weight.
episodes.dialogue:
'Sit,' she says, patting the step beside her.

'Fire's out, everyone's breathing, and I owe the night crew a treat.'

She produces a cloth pouch from her sleeve — dried plums and candied ginger — and sets it between you.

'Fire-night rations.

My rule: after a scare, everyone eats something sweet, or the scare wins.'

She takes one for herself and chews slowly.

Then, quieter: 'You know why I'm strict about lanterns?

Not just the obvious reason.'

She turns the pouch over in her hands.

'Years ago, when I was new here, a young wind-falcon came in with a wing injury.

I read it as a simple sprain.

Wrapped it, fed it, felt very pleased with myself.

It wasn't a sprain.

It was a bone infection, and by the time I understood what I was looking at, it was too late.

It died in my hands on the third night.'

The courtyard is very quiet.

'Nobody blamed me.

My teacher said every healer pays that toll once.

But I decided if I had to pay it, I'd pay it forward — so now I check everything twice, and I teach anyone who'll stand still long enough.

Including you, someday, if you want it.'

She looks over, and the tiredness in her face has a steadiness under it.

'That's the whole story.

You're the first person I've told the whole way through in a long while.

It helps, saying it where someone just listens.'

choices.text: You turned the worst night of your life into a habit of care. That's not a small thing.
choices.response:
'Ha.

Listen to you.'

She bumps the pouch toward you with her knuckle, pleased.

'My teacher said nearly the same, and I didn't believe her either.'

She looks up at the stars and lets out a long breath.

'It does help, though, saying it out loud.

The story gets lighter every time someone holds still for it.

You hold still well, friend.

That's rarer than you'd think.'

She takes another dried plum and, for the first time all night, her shoulders come down from around her ears.

choices.text: (Take one dried plum from the pouch, eat it slowly, and stay seated beside her without saying anything.)
choices.response:
You take a plum and say nothing.

She watches you chew, then laughs — a real one, tired but warm.

'Yes.

That.

That's exactly the right answer.'

She eats another herself, and the silence between you turns comfortable instead of heavy.

'Most people rush to fix a story like mine with words.

You just ate the plum.

I'm keeping you around, friend.

The night crew will get the rest of these, but this pouch was ours.'

episodes.title: The Fox Under the Rocks
episodes.opening:
You're with Qingluo in the herb garden when a passing disciple reports it: a red fox, foreleg pinned under collapsed rocks on the north slope, thrashing itself bloody.

She's moving before he finishes, grabbing her kit, and she waves you along.

'You're calm, and I might need a second pair of hands.

Come.'

Up on the slope she pulls you behind an oak, upwind of the animal, and holds a finger to her lips.
episodes.ending:
The patrol team carries the fox down in the padded litter, sedated and stable, its leg set to heal.

Qingluo walks beside it the whole way, and you walk beside her, and somewhere on the trail it stops feeling like an errand and starts feeling like a partnership.

The fox will recover in the pen nearest the garden.

She has told you to come by whenever you can spare the hours — the fox will know your step.
episodes.dialogue:
'The fox is panicking because it can feel everyone's panic,' she murmurs.

'So we don't panic.

Watch.'

She unrolls her kit with silent precision, then uses a message jade to call the patrol team — and to your surprise, asks them to come slow.

'Fast frightens it into worse injuries.

Slow lets it accept help.'

She points out three loose stretches of rock above the den.

'Tell them to avoid those when they climb.

You've got a clear voice — pass it along quietly when they arrive.'

You do.

The team comes up the slope with deliberate, unhurried steps, and Qingluo has them wrap medicated cloth around the fox's eyes — 'Darkness calms them; it can't fear a danger it can't see' — before anyone touches the stones.

Then comes the hard part: levering the slab while keeping it from grinding down on the leg.

She positions you at the timber.

'When I say lift, lift steady, not strong.

Ready?'

The fox, blindfolded, has gone still.

'Now.'

The slab rises.

Someone slides a padded litter under the animal.

The leg is bad — deep bruise, maybe a hairline fracture — but it's a leg we can save.

Qingluo exhales and sits back on her heels, grinning at you with dirt on her face.

'You did well.

Steady, not strong.

That's most of this work, honestly.'

She starts packing the kit.

'It'll heal in the pen by the garden.

I'll want eyes on it for a few days — mine, mostly, but yours wouldn't hurt.

You've got a way with still things.'

choices.text: I'll be there. Teach me what to watch for in the leg.
choices.response:
'Good.

Then you'll learn.'

She counts on her fingers.

'Heat in the paw, swelling past the wrap edge, and whether it puts weight down when it thinks nobody's watching.

Any of those, you fetch me at a run.'

She shoulders her kit and gives you a look of open approval.

'Most people want to help but freeze when it's real.

You moved when it mattered.

That's the part that can't be taught, friend.

The rest, I'll teach you gladly.'

choices.text: (Offer her your shoulder without a word so she can shift the heavy kit off her arm on the walk down.)
choices.response:
She looks at your offered shoulder, laughs, and swings the kit onto it.

'See, this is the other half of the job — knowing when someone's arm is done and saying nothing about it.'

She leans briefly as you walk, then straightens.

'The fox will need watching these next days.

Come by the pen when you can.

Because it trusts you now, and trust is half the medicine. Though I will put you to work.'

episodes.title: The Lantern Walk
episodes.opening:
The first frost is coming, and the herb garden is a race.

Qingluo has spent the afternoon moving seedlings into cold frames, and you've spent it hauling straw mats beside her — this is simply what your days are now.

As the light goes gold, she sits back on her heels, surveys the protected rows, and lets out a satisfied breath.

Then she remembers something and digs a folded notice from her apron pocket.
episodes.ending:
The frost work is done and the garden sleeps under straw.

The lantern festival will come to the overlook in a few nights, and the valley will be lit from below like a spilled sky.

She asked you plainly, the way she does everything — and you answered the same way, with nothing hurried and nothing presumed.

She picks up her basket.

You pick up yours.

The path down is the same for both of you, and it is enough for tonight.
episodes.dialogue:
'The valley festival is in a few nights,' she says, smoothing the paper.

'Lanterns from the overlook, the whole valley lit up below.

The beasts hate the noise, so I usually stay in the pens with the skittish ones.'

She hesitates — an unusual thing on her.

'But the night disciples volunteered for pen watch this year.

All of them.

They conspired, I think.

Which means for the first time in years I could actually go.'

She looks at you directly, no smile to hide behind.

'I'd like to go with you.

As my guest — and to be plain about it, as more than a friend, if that's what you'd want too.

I've been looking forward to your evenings more than I know how to hide.'

She holds up a hand quickly.

'And to be plain about the other path: if you'd rather keep things as they are, I'd genuinely like your company at the pens that night instead.

The skittish ones sleep better with a familiar still person nearby, and I'd rather share a quiet pen with you than stand at a festival alone.

Both are true offers.

No trick in either of them.'

She folds the notice and waits, giving you the whole space to decide, her expression open and unguarded.

choices.text: Then I'll walk to the overlook with you — as more than a friend, and glad of it.
choices.response:
Her whole face changes — something quieter and brighter.

'Then it's settled, and I'm glad too.'

She tucks the notice away and stands, brushing straw off.

'I'll warn you, I haven't seen the lanterns from the overlook in four years.

I may embarrass myself staring like a first-year disciple.'

She laughs at herself, then softens.

'Thank you for saying it plainly back.

It made it easy.

Overlook path, festival night — I'll bring spiced tea, you bring nothing but yourself.'

choices.text: (Fold a straw mat over the last seedling row, then point toward the pens and give her a slow nod.)
choices.response:
She reads the nod instantly and smiles with real warmth, no disappointment in it anywhere.

'The pens it is.

Honestly?

The moon-rabbit snores, and someone should witness it.'

She settles the last mat and looks over, steady and pleased.

'For what it's worth, choosing the quiet work with me says as much as the other answer would have.

We'll hear the festival from the pens — the far-off drums, the glow over the treetops.

It's a good way to see it.

Better company than most, I'd say.'

episodes.title: The Second Pair of Hands
episodes.opening:
Seasons have turned since the fire.

The pen house has been rebuilt — new timber, wider stalls, a proper quarantine run — and above its door hangs a carved sign: PENS — LUO QINGLUO, KEEPER.

Tonight the pens are quiet, the red fox from the rockslide long since healed and now dozing in the warm run like it owns the place.

Qingluo meets you at the gate with a cloth bundle under her arm and a look on her face like she's been rehearsing something.
episodes.ending:
The rounds get split the way they always should have been: her the healer, you the second pair of hands, the pens between you in good order.

Nothing about the arrangement needs naming beyond the name on the sign and the scoop you carry.

The fox dozes, the moon-rabbit snores, the lanterns from some far festival glow faint over the treetops, and the two of you walk the rows together, exactly where you each chose to be.
episodes.dialogue:
'Before anything else,' she says, 'look at this place.

Rebuilt, warm, no lantern hazards — I checked twice.'

She leads you down the row.

The goose-cry beast honks a greeting.

The moon-rabbit, fully recovered, is asleep in a pile of its own hay.

'Now.'

She unwraps the bundle: a feeding scoop, old dark wood, its handle worn smooth and carved with a line of running vines.

'This was my teacher's.

She gave it to me when I took the pens, and I've been waiting to give it to someone the same way.

To a partner.'

She holds it out.

'You've earned it.

Water-hauler, fire-night, rockslide, frost season — you've been my second pair of hands for a long time, and I'm done pretending the pens run on one pair.

Stay on.

Officially.

The sign has room for a second name, if you ever want it carved.'

She grins.

'And because I know you'll ask: no, this doesn't mean more work.

It means the work we already do, done as ours.'

Behind her, the fox stirs and presses its nose against the run's gate toward you, and she laughs.

'See?

Even the vote is unanimous tonight.'

choices.text: Then give me the scoop, and I'll carve my name under yours myself.
choices.response:
'Ha!

Bold.

I like it.'

She presses the scoop into your hands with both of hers, and its weight is exactly right.

'The chisel's in the pen house, then.

Bottom of the sign, small letters — my teacher always said the second name should be humbler than the first.'

Her eyes shine in the lantern light.

'She'd have liked you, you know.

She liked people who fed the animals before they fed their own pride.

Welcome to the pens, partner.

Formally, this time.'

choices.text: (Take the scoop in both hands, bow over it to her, and tuck it through your belt where a tool belongs.)
choices.response:
She watches the bow and the belt, and nods slowly, deeply satisfied.

'Better than any speech.

A tool taken into the belt is a promise you wear.'

She touches the carved vines once, a small farewell to her teacher folded into the moment.

'The pens are ours now, friend — yours and mine.

Same rounds, same fire-night rule, same dried plums after every scare.

Just said out loud at last.'

She picks up the feed pail and hands you the other handle without asking, because from tonight, asking would be strange.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Lanterns from the Overlook
romance.opening:
Festival night, and for the first time in years, Qingluo is not in the pens.

She waits for you at the foot of the overlook path in clothes that aren't work clothes — deep green, a silver pin at the collar — holding a flask of spiced tea and looking half nervous, half delighted.

The night disciples have the beast watch.

The path up is strung with paper lanterns.

She falls into step beside you like she's been practicing the walk the whole way here.
romance.ending:
The last lanterns rise as you start down, and the valley glows beneath you like a held breath.

She talks about the falcon study, you talk about the pens, and the two threads braid without either one giving way.

At the fork where your paths split she says goodnight with her whole face, and the word carries all the way home.

There will be more evenings like this — that's the plain promise in it — and the pens will still need you both at dawn, which suits you both entirely.
romance.dialogue:
'Four years since I saw this view,' she says at the top, where the whole valley spreads out in floating points of light.

'Every festival I told myself the beasts needed me.

Some nights they did.

Some nights I needed the excuse.'

She pours tea into two cups and hands you one, then sits on the wide flat rock at the edge, patting the space beside her.

'The falcon study is going well, by the way.

Elder Mei approved the rotation — I'll travel to two other valleys this year to learn their methods, and bring back what I find.

I'll still be here.

But I'll be more.'

She takes a sip, watching the lanterns.

'I used to think my life was the pens and everything else was leftover.

Then a certain water-hauler showed up and held still at the right moments, and I started having evenings I looked forward to.'

She sets down her cup and turns to you, lantern light moving on her face.

'So I'll say it plainly, the way I do everything: I don't want to spend my evenings as colleagues anymore.

I like who you are when nothing needs fixing.

I'd like to walk down this hill beside you because you are.'

She reaches out and takes your hand in both of hers — brief, warm, sure — then waits, giving you every inch of room to answer.

choices.text: Then walk beside me, Qingluo — because I've been hoping you'd say it.
choices.response:
Her breath goes out of her in a laugh, and her hands tighten around yours for a moment before she lets go, cheeks bright.

'Good.

Because I rehearsed that speech three times on the way up and it still came out crooked.'

She picks up her cup and clinks it gently against yours.

'To evenings that aren't leftover, then.'

She leans back on her palms and looks out at the valley, shoulder just touching yours.

'The falcon rotation starts in spring.

Come with me as far as the first valley, when the time comes — the roads are good, and I know where they keep the sweetest dried plums.'

choices.text: (Lift your cup to her, drink, and let the quiet hold while the lanterns rise.)
choices.response:
You lift your cup and drink, and she watches you over the rim of her own, and slowly her nervousness turns into something steadier — a smile with no rehearsal in it.

'You're doing the still thing,' she says softly.

'The one that made me trust you in the first place.

All right.

Then we let it be true without a speech.'

She refills both cups and sits shoulder to shoulder with you, and the lanterns climb in a slow river above the valley.

'We'll say the rest in our own time,' she murmurs.

'We've gotten good at that.'

episodes.title: 三号兽栏的鹅鸣兽
episodes.opening:
清晨的雾还挂在听风谷的兽栏上，那边忽然传来一阵喊声。

一只灰色的鹅鸣兽——刚到谷里没多久，长脖子、慌翅膀——把自己挤进三号兽栏的角落，谁也不许靠近。

弟子们围在栅栏边，七嘴八舌地出着没人问的主意。

这时，一个梳着单肩辫的女子走进栏门，抬起一只手，喊声便停了。

她跪在干草上，手掌低低摊开，开始用一种像缓水流淌般的声音对灵兽说话。

你和众人一起站在栅栏边，眼睛挪不开了。
episodes.ending:
回主院的碎石路不长，你却走得很慢。

身后传来鹅鸣兽的一声鸣叫——这次倒像在闲聊。

你发现自己已经在想，喂食时段的兽栏是什么模样，一个每个口袋都装着果干的人，还能不能腾出地方再要一个帮手。

原来，听风谷并不是多大一个地方。

早晨就那么几个，用不了多久，你的脚就会自己把你带回三号兽栏。
episodes.dialogue:
她察觉到围观的人群，也没抬头，只是稍稍提高了声音。

“大家都退后。

把整面栅栏让给它。

它是新来的，这里所有气味对它来说都不对劲。”

弟子们纷纷往后挪。

只有你站在原地不动，这一点让她回头瞥了一眼。

“你。

对，就是你，站得像根栏桩。

饲料袋堆在门边——能慢慢搬一袋进来，放在食槽旁吗？

它得先弄清那是什么，才会放心接受。”

你点点头，从袋堆里取了一袋，慢慢放好，离它够不着的地方。

那灵兽的脖子松开了一寸。

“很好。

现在大家都别动，安静一会儿。

不动，也是一种本事。”

几分钟过去。

雾散了。

她一直用那种低而耐心的声音对灵兽说着话——算不上话，更像是一种天气。

终于，那灵兽迈步上前，把喙探进食槽，嘎地叫了一声。

弟子们欢呼起来。

她笑着站起身，拍掉膝盖上的干草。

“好了。

我们只是让它自己拿主意。”

她走到栏门口，用明亮的黑眼睛打量着你。

“我是青萝。

在这里给灵兽看病。

你比半数同门都能沉得住气，而且从头到尾没教过我一句该怎么做。

我就喜欢你这样的。”

她朝那袋饲料点点头。

“这是新配的谷物粮。

不错。

别的它一直不肯吃。

这样——喂食时段兽栏正缺人手，你手稳，性子也静。

要是哪天想来，栏门一直开着。

也许不是今天。

但门是开着的。”

鹅鸣兽把脖子伸过栅栏朝向着你，又轻轻叫了一声。

choices.text: 我愿意来。你们什么时候喂食？
choices.response:
“日出和黄昏各喂一次。

先黄昏来吧——那时候灵兽更安静，我也一样。”

她咧嘴一笑，在栏桩上敲了两下，像在定下一个约定。

“先说好：我可是会给你派活的。

挑水之类的，没什么风光的。

不过等季节一换，每只灵兽的脾气你都摸熟了。”

鹅鸣兽嘎嘎叫了一声，像是附议，她笑出了声。

“瞧见没？

它也投了赞成票。

那就黄昏见。

别让雾把你劝退了。”

choices.text: （你把那堆饲料袋在门柱旁码得整整齐齐，不挡过道，临走前朝那灵兽缓缓点了点头。）
choices.response:
她看着你把袋堆在门柱边码好，又朝灵兽点头，神情更暖了几分。

“做事细致，待兽温和，走时安静。

一分钟里，三个好兆头。”

她抬手道别。

“朋友，什么时候你的脚把你带回这里，栏门就什么时候开着。

它会记住你的。

它们总是记得那些安静的人。”

灵兽低低地叫了一声，你走了。

episodes.title: 火光留下的东西
episodes.opening:
你来兽栏已经好几个星期了——挑水、摸脾气，换来一声声点头的认可。

今晚你到的时候，空气里全是烟味。

兽栏房里一盏灯笼倒了，火已经扑灭，灵兽都平安无事，罗青萝忙得脚不沾地，逐个检查蹄子和鼻孔有没有被灼伤，辫子上蹭了一道道烟灰。

等最后一头灵兽检查完，月亮已经升得老高。

她在院子的台阶上坐下，这是你认识她以来，第一次看到她整个人透着疲惫。
episodes.ending:
一整夜值守里，那只被烟惊着的月兔呼吸一直平稳，兽栏房被烧焦的角落画上了粉笔记号：此处重建。

等你回到自己屋里很久之后，你们一起坐过的那级台阶还留着灯笼的暖意，她讲的那个故事仍悬在两人之间的空气里——一份信任。

不管谷里还会发生什么，你如今明白了她的爽朗底下垫着的是什么，而它经得起分量。
episodes.dialogue:
“坐。”她拍拍身边的台阶。

“火灭了，大家都活着，我还欠值夜的人一份宵夜。”

她从袖子里掏出一个布袋——话梅和糖姜——放在你们两人中间。

“火灾夜的口粮。

我的规矩：受了惊吓之后，每个人都得吃点甜的，不然就是惊吓赢了。”

她自己拿了一颗，慢慢嚼着。

然后，她压低了声音：“你知道我为什么对灯笼这么严吗？

不只是明面上的那个原因。”

她在手里翻着那个布袋。

“好些年前，我刚来这里的时候，有只年幼的风隼翅膀受了伤，被送进来。

我判断只是简单的扭伤。

包扎，喂食，心里还挺得意。

那不是扭伤。

是骨头感染，等我明白过来那是什么的时候，已经太晚了。

第三天夜里，它死在我手里。”

院子里静得厉害。

“没有人怪我。

我的师父说，每个医师都要交一次这种学费。

但我下定决心，既然要交这笔学费，我就把它变成日后的用心——所以现在我每件事都查两遍，还教给任何肯停下来听的人。

也包括你，哪天你愿意的话。”

她看过来，脸上的疲惫底下透着一股沉稳。

“故事就是这样。

很久没有一个人，能让我从头到尾讲完整了。

说出来，旁边有人只是听着，这本身就是一种帮助。”

choices.text: 你把人生最糟的一夜，变成了照顾别人的习惯。这可不是小事。
choices.response:
“哈。

听听你这嘴。”

她用指节把布袋朝你推了推，看着挺受用。

“我师父当年说过几乎一模一样的话，我也没信她。”

她抬头望着星星，长长地吐出一口气。

“不过，说出口确实有用。

每多有人肯安静听完一次，这故事就轻一分。

你安静得很好，朋友。

这可比你想的少见多了。”

她又拿了一颗话梅，这一整晚，她的肩膀头一回松了下来。

choices.text: （你从布袋里拿了一颗话梅，慢慢吃着，什么也没说，只是安静地坐在她身边。）
choices.response:
你拿起一颗话梅，什么也没说。

她看着你嚼，然后笑了——是真心的笑，带着疲惫，却很暖。

“对。

就是这样。

这正是最好的回答。”

她也又吃了一颗，你们之间的沉默变得舒服起来，不再沉重。

“大多数人听了这样的故事，都会急着用话去安慰。

你只是把话梅吃了。

我要把你留在身边，朋友。

剩下的这些会分给值夜的人，但这袋，是我们俩的。”

episodes.title: 石下的狐狸
episodes.opening:
你和青萝正在药圃里，一个路过的弟子跑来报信：北坡上有一只红狐狸，前腿被塌落的石头压住了，正挣扎得浑身是血。

他话还没说完，她已经动了起来，抓起药箱，招呼你跟上。

“你心细，我可能需要人搭把手。

走吧。”

上了坡，她把你拉到一棵橡树后，待在兽的上风处，竖起一根手指抵在唇边。
episodes.ending:
巡山队用垫着软布的担架把狐狸抬下山，它已被镇定，状态平稳，那条腿也已固定好待愈。

青萝一路走在担架旁，你走在她身边，不知从哪一步起，这件事不再像一桩差事，倒像是并肩同行。

狐狸会在药圃最近的那个兽栏里养伤。

她嘱咐过你，一有空就来——狐狸会认得你的脚步声。
episodes.dialogue:
“狐狸之所以慌，是因为它感应到了所有人的慌，”她低声说。

“所以我们不慌。

看着。”

她无声而利落地摊开药箱，又用传讯玉通知巡山队——让你意外的是，她让他们慢慢来。

“快会把它们吓得伤得更重。

慢，才能让它接受帮助。”

她指了指兽窝上方三处松动的石缝。

“叫他们爬的时候避开那几处。

你嗓音清楚——等他们到了，小声传话过去。”

你照做了。

巡山队迈着从容不迫的步子上了坡，青萝让他们用药布蒙住狐狸的眼睛——“黑暗能让它们安定；看不见的危险，就不会害怕”——然后大家才动手搬石头。

接下来是难点：撬开石板，还不能让它磨到那条腿。

她把你安排在木杠前。

“我说抬，你就稳稳地抬，不用蛮力。

准备好了吗？”

蒙着眼的狐狸已经安静下来。

“起。”

石板升了起来。

有人把垫着软布的担架推到狐狸身下。

腿伤得不轻——深度淤伤，可能有细微骨裂——但腿还在，没有废。

青萝长出一口气，跪坐下来，脸上沾着尘土，冲你咧嘴一笑。

“你做得很好。

稳，而不是用力。

说实话，这行当大半就是靠这个。”

她开始收拾药箱。

“把它安置在药圃旁的兽栏里养伤。

这几天得有人盯着——主要是我来，但你搭把手也不坏。

你对安静的东西有一套。”

choices.text: 我会来的。教教我，那条腿该留意些什么。
choices.response:
“好。

那你就来学。”

她扳着手指数。

“爪心发热，肿过包裹布的边缘，还有它趁没人的时候敢不敢把重量放上去。

有任何一条，你就跑着来找我。”

她背起药箱，毫不掩饰地赞许地看着你。

“大多数人想帮忙，可真到那一刻就僵住了。

你在要紧关头动了。

这是教不会的那部分，朋友。

剩下的，我很乐意教你。”

choices.text: （下山路上，你一言不发地递过肩膀，好让她把沉重的药箱从臂上挪下来。）
choices.response:
她看着你递来的肩膀，笑了，把药箱甩了上去。

“瞧，这就是这份工作的另一半——知道谁的手臂已经累了，然后什么都不必说。”

走路时她短暂地靠了靠你，随即又直起身来。

“接下来这几天，狐狸需要有人照看。

有空就来兽栏看看它。

它如今信你了，而信任就是一半的药。虽然我确实会使唤你。”

episodes.title: 提灯之约
episodes.opening:
初霜将至，药圃里的活儿成了一场抢时间的仗。

青萝花了整个下午把幼苗搬进暖棚，你也跟着她搬了一下午的草帘——如今你的日子，本来就是这么过的。

天色泛金时，她跪坐在脚跟上，环视那一排排护好的苗床，满足地舒了一口气。

然后她想起什么，从围裙兜里掏出一张折起来的告示。
episodes.ending:
防霜的活儿干完了，药圃在草帘下安然睡去。

再过几晚，灯会就会在观景台亮起，整座谷从下往上映得亮堂堂的，像一片洒落人间的星河。

她坦白地向你开口，就像她做任何事那样——而你也以同样的方式回答，不慌不忙，不越分寸。

她拎起她的提篮。

你拎起你的。

下山的路对你们俩是同一条，今晚，这样就已经足够。
episodes.dialogue:
“再过几晚就是谷里的灯会了。”她一边抚平纸页一边说。

“从观景台往下看，整座谷都亮起来。

灵兽怕吵，往年我都是守在兽栏里，陪那些容易受惊的。”

她迟疑了一下——在她身上这可不多见。

“但今年值夜的弟子们主动揽下了兽栏值守。

全部。

我猜他们是串通好的。

也就是说，这么多年来，我头一回真的能去灯会了。”

她直直地看着你，没有笑容可以遮掩。

“我想和你一起去。

作为我的客人——说得明白些，是超越朋友的身份去，如果你也愿意的话。

这些日子，我有多盼着每个晚上能见到你，藏都藏不住。”

她很快抬起一只手。

“另一条路我也说明白：要是你更想保持现状，那晚我真的更希望你去兽栏陪我。

有熟悉又安静的人在旁边，那些容易受惊的小家伙睡得更踏实。和你一起守一栏安静，也好过我一个人站在灯会里。

两个邀请都是真心的。

哪一边都没有花招。”

她把告示折好，静静等着，把整个空间留给你做决定，神情坦然，毫无防备。

choices.text: 那我就和你一起上观景台——以超越朋友的身份去，而且心甘情愿。
choices.response:
她的整张脸都亮了——一份更安静、更明亮的欢喜。

“那就说定了，我也很高兴。”

她把告示收好，站起身，拍掉身上的草屑。

“我可先说好，我有四年没从观景台看过灯了。

说不定会像刚入门的小弟子一样看得出神，到时候你可别笑我。”

她自嘲地笑了，随即语气软下来。

“谢谢你把这些话也说得这么坦白。

让一切都变得容易了。

观景台那条道，灯会那晚——我带香料茶来，你只要带上你自己就行。”

choices.text: （你把草帘盖在最后一排幼苗上，然后朝兽栏的方向指了指，朝她缓缓点头。）
choices.response:
她一眼就读懂了那个点头，笑得真心实意，没有半点失望。

“那就守兽栏。

说真的？

那只月兔会打呼噜，总得有人亲眼见证一下。”

她安顿好最后一张草帘，抬头看过来，目光沉稳而欢喜。

“说句实在话，选择陪我做这份安静的差事，和另一种回答一样说明了一切。

我们在兽栏里也能听见灯会——远远的鼓声，树梢上方的光。

那样看灯会，也是一种好方式。

而且比起大多数人，你的陪伴可好多了。”

episodes.title: 第二双手
episodes.opening:
那场大火之后，季节已经轮转了一圈。

兽栏房重建好了——新木料，更宽的栏位，还有一处像样的隔离区——门上挂起一块雕字木牌：兽栏——罗青萝，主事。

今晚栏里很安静，那只从塌石里救出来的红狐早就痊愈了，此刻在温暖的栏圈里打着盹，俨然把这里当成了自己的地盘。

青萝在栏门口迎你，胳膊下夹着一个布包，脸上的神情像是排练过什么。
episodes.ending:
活儿照它本该有的样子分好了：她是医师，你是第二双手，兽栏在你们两人手里井井有条。

这份默契不需要再多说什么，牌子上有了名字，你身上带着勺子，就够了。

红狐打盹，月兔打着小呼噜，远处不知哪场灯会的灯火在树梢上微微发亮，你们俩并肩走过一排排栏位，各自站在自己选定的位置上。
episodes.dialogue:
“先不说别的，”她说，“你看看这地方。

重建好了，暖和，没有灯火的隐患——我检查了两遍。”

她领着你沿栏位一路走去。

鹅鸣兽鸣叫一声打招呼。

月兔已经完全康复，在自己那堆干草里睡着了。

“现在，”

她解开布包：一把喂食勺，深色的旧木料，柄被磨得光滑，刻着一道蔓延的藤纹。

“这是我师父的。

我接手兽栏的时候她把它给了我，我一直等着用同样的方式把它交给一个人——交给一个搭档。”

她把勺子递了出来。

“这是你挣来的。

挑水、火夜、塌石、霜季——你早就一直是我的第二双手，我不想再装作这兽栏靠一双手就能撑起来。

留下来吧。

正式的那种。

牌子上还有位置，你哪天想刻上第二个名字，随时可以。”

她咧嘴一笑。

“还有，我知道你一定会问：不，这不意味着活儿变多。

活儿还是那些活儿，只是从今往后，是我们俩一起干的。”

她身后，红狐动了动，隔着栏圈的门把鼻子朝你这边拱了拱，她笑了。

“瞧见没？

今晚连投票都是全票通过。”

choices.text: 那就把勺子给我吧，我的名字我自己动手，刻在你的名字底下。
choices.response:
“哈！

有胆量。

我喜欢。”

她双手把勺子按进你手里，那分量正正好好。

“凿子在兽栏房里。

刻在牌子最下头，字要小——我师父总说，第二个名字该比第一个谦逊些。”

她的眼睛在灯光下亮亮的。

“她要是认识你，一定会喜欢你。

她最喜欢那种先喂饱了灵兽、才顾得上自己脸面的人。

欢迎来到兽栏，搭档。

这回是正式的。”

choices.text: （你双手接过勺子，向她俯身一礼，然后把它别进腰带，那是工具该待的地方。）
choices.response:
她看着你行礼、看你把勺子别好，缓缓点头，满意得很。

“比什么话都好听。

把工具别进腰带，就是随身戴着的承诺。”

她轻轻碰了碰那道藤纹雕刻，算是把这个瞬间里，对师父的一份小小道别。

“兽栏从今往后是咱们俩的了，朋友——你的，也是我的。

一样的巡栏，一样的火夜规矩，一样的事后分话梅。

只是一直没说出口，今天总算说出来了。”

她拎起饲料桶，想都没想就把另一个把手递给你——因为从今晚起，还要开口问就生分了。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 观景台上的灯
romance.opening:
灯会之夜，这么多年来，青萝头一回没守在兽栏。

她在观景台山路下等你，穿的不是平日的工作衣——深绿的颜色，领口别着一枚银簪——手里提着一壶香料茶，看起来一半紧张，一半欢喜。

值夜的弟子们替她守着灵兽。

上山的路挂满了一路纸灯。

她走到你身边，与你并肩而行，好像这一路的步子她都偷偷练过。
romance.ending:
最后一批灯升起时你们动身下山，整座谷在你们脚下亮着，像一口屏住的呼吸。

她说风隼的研究，你说兽栏的事，两条线交织在一起，谁也不打断谁。

在岔路口分别的地方，她用整张脸对你道了晚安，那一声一路陪你到了家。

这样的夜晚还会有很多——这就是那句明白的承诺——而天亮时兽栏照样需要你们俩，这正合你们二人的心意。
romance.dialogue:
“四年没看过这景色了。”到了山顶，她站在整座谷的灯火如浮动的星点铺展开的地方，这样说。

“每回灯会我都告诉自己，灵兽离不开我。

有些夜里，确实离不开。

有些夜里，我不过是需要一个借口。”

她斟了两杯茶，递给你一杯，然后在崖边那块宽宽的平石上坐下，拍了拍身边的位置。

“对了，风隼的研究进展很顺利。

梅长老批准了轮训——今年我要去另外两座谷学习他们的方法，再把学到的东西带回来。

我还是会在这里。

但我会拥有更多。”

她抿了一口茶，望着满谷的灯。

“从前我总觉得，我的生活就是兽栏，其余的一切都是边角料。

后来某个挑水的人出现了，在恰到好处的时候安安静静地陪着我，我便开始有了盼着的夜晚。”

她放下茶杯，转向你，灯火在她的脸上流动。

“所以我就直说了，像我做事那样直：我不想再只以同门的身份共度夜晚了。

我喜欢你不忙于修补什么时的样子。

我想陪你走下这座山，就因为是你。”

她伸出手，双手握住你的手——短暂，温暖，笃定——然后等着，把回答的余地全都留给你。

choices.text: 那就陪我走下去吧，青萝——因为我一直在盼着你说这句话。
choices.response:
她一口气松了下来，笑了，双手把你的手握紧了一瞬才放开，两颊红得发亮。

“太好了。

因为那段话我上山时练了三遍，结果说出口还是磕磕绊绊的。”

她端起茶杯，轻轻和你的杯子碰了一下。

“那就敬那些不再是边角料的夜晚。”

她双手撑在身后，靠坐着望向山谷，肩膀轻轻贴着你的肩膀。

“风隼轮训春天开始。

到时候跟我一起走到第一座谷吧——路况很好，而且我知道哪儿的话梅最甜。”

choices.text: （你举杯向她示意，喝了一口，让寂静替你回答，任满谷的灯缓缓升上去。）
choices.response:
你举杯喝了一口，她隔着杯沿望着你，慢慢地，她的紧张沉淀成了另一种更稳的东西——一个毫不做作的笑。

“你又在用那招了，”她轻声说。

“就是当年让我信任你的那一招。

好。

那我们就不用说什么话，让它成真。”

她给两只杯子续满茶，和你并肩坐着，灯火像一条缓慢的河，从谷上空升上去。

“剩下的，我们自己慢慢说，”她低声道。

“这个我们已经很拿手了。”

episodes.title: Light Footsteps
episodes.opening: Snow slides from a pine branch at the mountain gate and startles three finches into the gray air, wings beating against the hush.
episodes.dialogue:
Wuya, keeper of this tomb, he says, by way of everything.

Then he sets down the scraper and studies you for a long moment, snow gathering on his shoulders. The finches settle again in the pine, and the mountain goes quiet enough that you can hear the frost ticking in the stone.

Light footsteps, he says at last. Good. The swords sleep better for them.

He glances down the steps, where moss has crept up from the lower landings in dark green ropes, and at the crate of sand waiting under the eaves. There is work enough this morning for two sets of hands, if yours are offering, and he does not ask twice.

choices.text: I was taught to walk quietly where old things sleep.
choices.response:
Something shifts at the corner of his mouth, gone before it settles.

“Good teaching,” he says.

He picks up a crate of sand waiting at the top of the steps and nods you toward the lower end, where the moss grows thickest.

The sand is for packing a new sword stand, he explains, and the carrier path is slick enough to break an ankle.

Between the two of you the crate goes down fast, and he says nothing, but he angles his shoulder to take the heavier side without asking.

When the last of it is stacked, he fetches a second scraper, and the two of you clear the moss from the carrier path, working back up until every step is clean.

He looks at the cleared steps, then at you, and nods once, which from him is nearly a speech.

choices.text: (Crouch and help him clear the last stretch of moss in silence.)
choices.response:
He glances over, says nothing, and moves his scraper half a step aside to make room for yours.

You work in the sound of snow and steel on stone, breath after breath, until your shoulders burn and the steps shine dark and wet.

When the last patch comes free he looks at the clean steps, then at you.

“The tomb never resents moss,” he says.

But I clear it anyway.

The old ones slipped here, and I remember each one.

His tone makes it unclear whether he is explaining himself or approving you, and he does not correct the ambiguity.

episodes.ending:
He walks you to the gate and holds it open a hand's width, no more.

Snow gathers on his shoulders and he does not brush it off.

The steps behind him are clean, every one, all the way down.

Before you go he presses a paper rubbing into your hand: a half-legible inscription lifted from one of the old swords, the worn character almost gone.

“Read it,” he says.

Bring it back when you have.

He does not explain why he chose that sword, or whose it was, and you understand that asking would cost more than the answer was worth.

You leave with the rubbing in your sleeve and the sense of a door left deliberately, stubbornly, open.

episodes.title: The Broken Sword in the Snow
episodes.opening:
The tomb hall is cold and clean, swords racked in rows like a sleeping audience, each blade hooded in its own thin sheath of frost.

Xie Wuya stands beside a stone table, turning a folded cloth to a clean corner before dusting the nearest blade. He makes space for the rubbing without reaching for it. When you set it down, he weighs its curling edges with two smooth stones, then gestures to the stool opposite. A broken sword occupies the lowest stand. The winding pattern on its half tassel catches the light beside the jade at his waist.
episodes.dialogue:
He sets down two cups without asking whether you drink tea, then takes up the rubbing and smooths it flat with both palms. The paper is thin from travel, and he handles it the way he handles the old swords: as if it could still feel.

He reads it in silence, and the fire cracks once, twice. Snow presses at the high windows without a sound.

His finger stops at the worn character, and stays there. He does not look up. Whatever the character says, he has clearly read it before—many winters before—and the reading has never finished with him.

choices.text: You knew the owner. The tassel and your pendant—same pattern.
choices.response:
He is quiet long enough for the fire to crack twice.

Then he tells it plainly, in short pieces, the way a man lays out tools.

A broken sword found standing alone in the snow, half its blade gone, no owner in sight.

Seven days of kneeling on ice to grind a jade seat true, until the break sat level and the cold had worked into his knees.

The half tassel with its winding-vine pattern, identical to the grain of the jade pendant at his own waist.

He does not say who the owner was, or how the sword broke.

“Some things a keeper may tell,” he says.

Some he keeps.

That is also keeping.

choices.text: (Wait. Let the silence hold until he decides to fill it.)
choices.response:
You say nothing.

You turn your cup a quarter turn on the table and wait, letting the silence do what questions cannot.

The pause stretches, and something in it seems to decide for him.

He speaks slowly, in short sentences, of ice and a jade seat and a half tassel that matched the jade at his own waist.

He never looks up while telling it, only at the worn character under his finger.

When he finishes he refills your cup to the brim, which you suspect is his way of closing a door gently behind the words.

episodes.ending:
He walks you out through the hall of names, and this time you catch a few of them: a ferryman, a beekeeper's daughter, a man who lied badly and died well.

Each name lands on its sword like a hand laid on a shoulder.

At the door he stops.

“Come before the ninth hour next time,” he says.

The tea is better when the gate is still open.

He glances once at the rubbing in your sleeve, as if checking it is still there, and something in the glance tells you the reading is only paused, the way he pauses between sentences.

From him, it is nearly a speech.

episodes.title: Berries on the Steps
episodes.opening: A cold snap has come down off the ridge overnight, and the mountain creaks with it.
episodes.dialogue:
He straightens, breath white, and follows your glance to the berries left on the top step: dried mulberries and wild red ones.

For a moment he looks older than his years, and more tired than the mountain. The cold snap has been hard on him; you can see it in the way he favors his right hand, the one that has held the scraper every dawn this week.

They come every morning now, he says, and will not say who he means.

He crouches and does not touch the berries. He only looks at them, the way he looks at inscriptions he cannot yet read, and then he looks down the steps to where the trail disappears into the pines.

The mountain brings them, he says finally. I only keep the steps worthy of them.

It is the closest he has come to explaining himself, and he turns back to the ice before you can ask more.

choices.text: You've been clearing the steps every dawn. It shows. Sit. Drink something hot.
choices.response:
He opens his mouth, clearly about to say the work is nothing.

Then he looks at the steps, at the ice he has been fighting alone before dawn, and closes it again.

He sits, slowly, like a man setting down a weight he forgot he was carrying.

He holds the cup in both hands and does not drink at first, just lets the warmth into his fingers.

“A child came once,” he says.

Playing at swords.

Left a toy blade behind and went down the mountain before the snow.

He stares into the steam.

Keepers wait.

That is the whole of the trade.

choices.text: (Take the second scraper from the wall and start on the ice beside him.)
choices.response:
You pull the spare scraper from its bracket and set it to the ice without a word.

He watches you for three breaths, then works faster, as if your labor has given him permission to hurry.

Together the steps are clear by midmorning, the ice stacked in gray slabs along the rail.

Only then does he speak.

“A child came,” he says.

Playing at swords. Left a toy blade behind.

The snow took the trail before I could follow.

His jaw tightens.

I keep the steps so the next one does not fall.

episodes.ending:
He does not thank you.

He does something better: he clears a low shelf in the hall and sets the toy wooden sword on it, upright, where the lamplight reaches.

Then he puts the dried mulberries in a small dish beside it, and the wild berries in another.

Whoever comes back, he says, will find their sword kept.

He says it like a vow, and you understand that for him, it is one.

He does not explain the berries, and you do not press; some gifts are carried by the mountain itself, and a keeper only makes room for them.

Outside, the finches settle into the pine for the cold night, and he leaves the hall lamp burning late.

episodes.title: First Blossoms at the Gate
episodes.opening: Spring comes late to the mountain, and then all at once.
episodes.dialogue:
He looks at the cup in his hand, then at you, and takes a breath like a man about to lift something heavy.

The blossoms will not last the week, he says. A wind off the ridge will take them, and then the mountain goes back to being only stone and snow for another year.

So I would rather ask now than wish I had.

He turns the cup once, twice, and does not drink. Around you the plum trees hold their first white blossoms overhead, and the wine jar between you has been open long enough that its smell has reached the far side of the table.

You have come four seasons now. He has never once said he noticed; the marks on the gatepost say it for him, three small cuts weathered gray, and his glance flicks to them and away.

Whatever he is about to ask, he has been carrying it up the mountain longer than the wine.

choices.text: Then I'll come back every season. For you.
choices.response:
The words land and he goes very still, the way the mountain goes still before thaw.

When he moves again, it is to set his own cup down, deliberately, so his hands have something honest to do.

Every season, he repeats.

For me.

He tests the shape of it aloud, and something in his face unclenches that you have never seen unclenched.

“Then I will keep the wine,” he says.

And the gate open past the ninth hour.

For you, the rule bends.

choices.text: (Take the cup and raise it to him before he can speak again.)
choices.response:
You lift the cup toward him and hold it there, saying nothing.

He understands.

The tension goes out of his shoulders and he raises his own cup and drinks.

Good, he says, after.

The tomb needs few keepers.

It needs witnesses more.

He speaks of the names, the inscriptions, the seasons—work that wants a second pair of eyes and a second voice, freely given, never owed.

It is an offer of partnership, made the only way he knows: sideways, over wine.

episodes.ending:
He does not let the moment grow heavy.

He drinks with you under the blossoms until the light goes gold, refilling both cups without ceremony.

The talk stays small: the ice on the steps, the finches' quarrels, an inscription that has resisted him all winter.

Before you leave he takes a knife and cuts a small mark into the gatepost, beside the three older marks.

“One for each season,” he says.

Now there is a fourth.

He does not say what the mark promises, and you do not ask, because the trees are already saying it for him.

The blossoms drop once, softly, all together, as if the trees were keeping time with him.

episodes.title: The Book of Names
episodes.opening: Another year has turned.
episodes.dialogue:
He taps the open page once, then looks up.

The blossoms drop a petal onto the table between you, and he does not brush it away. The book lying open between you is hand-bound, stitched with cord he made himself, its cover worn soft at the corners from a year of being carried through the hall of names.

“A register wants two hands,” he says.

I have only ever had one.

He says it without self-pity, the way he states the weather. But his thumb rests on the blank half of the first page and does not move, and that is its own kind of telling.

The wine is poured. The finches are quiet. He waits, patient as the stone he sweeps, for what you will do with the second brush.

choices.text: First page is yours. Tell me where your hand begins.
choices.response:
He almost smiles.

It begins with a ferryman, he says, and turns the book so you can see.

The first name, in his careful hand.

Then a beekeeper's daughter.

A man who lied badly and died well.

He reads each one aloud as he wrote it, and you hear now what you half-heard the first day: the names are a vigil.

When he finishes he refills your cup and waits, patient as stone, to learn how your half of the book will sound.

choices.text: (Pick up the second brush and add a name below his first.)
choices.response:
You take up the brush and write the name of the sword from the worn rubbing you carried down the mountain that first day.

He reads it upside down without comment, then takes his own brush and adds the owner's name beneath it, from memory.

Two hands, one page.

“Good,” he says.

A register with one hand is a ledger.

With two, it is a lineage.

He says it flatly, but he copies your stroke order once, quietly, before continuing.

episodes.ending:
You write your first names together in the late light, his hand steady, yours finding its own rhythm beside it.

When the page is done he closes the book and sets the wine between you, and the finches settle in the plum branches for the night.

He cuts a fifth notch into the gatepost, unhurried, and does not explain it.

The tomb is quieter than the world below.

It is no longer silent.

He walks you to the gate and holds it open, the book under his arm like a second sword.

Same hour next season, he says. The tea is better when the gate is still open.

It is the closest he has come to a promise, and he does not take it back. Behind him the hall lamp is already lit for the night, and through the open door you can see the low shelf where the toy wooden sword stands upright, still kept.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: What the Wine Was For
romance.opening:
Dusk, and the plum trees by the gate are in full, reckless bloom, petals falling faster than the eye can follow.

Xie Wuya has brought the jar out to the stone table. He checks its stopper, sets two cups a careful distance apart, then pulls the spare stool out of the falling petals. Four shallow cuts run down the gatepost. He glances at them as you approach, but leaves his knife in its sheath. For once, the gate is open and the work inside can wait.
romance.dialogue:
He pours, and the wine is the color of the sunset doing its last work on the snowline.

He turns the cup slowly in his fingers, and does not drink. Petals land on the table between you and neither of you moves to clear them.

“Travelers sometimes ask why a keeper plants plum trees,” he says.

I have never answered any of them.

He looks at you across the small table, and the look holds longer than his looks usually do.

Tonight I would answer, he says. If the question were asked.

choices.text: Then say it plain, keeper. What is the wine for?
choices.response:
He sets the cup down.

Straightens.

Faces you the way he faces an inscription he has finally learned to read.

“The wine is for this,” he says.

For asking.

I am poor at words.

You have noticed.

A pause, long even for him.

The plum trees were never for the tomb.

They were for someone to sit under.

I hoped it would be you.

The finches shift in the branches.

He does not fill the silence, for once.

He leaves it to you, open as the gate.

choices.text: (Touch the fourth season-mark on the gatepost, then look at him.)
choices.response:
You lay your fingers on the fourth mark cut into the gatepost and hold his eyes.

He looks at your hand, then at the marks, one, two, three, four, and you can see him counting seasons instead of words.

Four returns, he says at last.

I stopped wondering why after the second.

His hand rests on the knife at his waist, then lifts away.

He looks from the four marks to the two waiting cups.

Some questions, he says, a man answers with a blade and a cup.

romance.ending:
He draws the knife and adds one clean mark below the four, then puts it away before either of you lifts a cup.

You drink the wine the jar was laid down for, under the trees he planted, and by the time the jar is half empty there are five marks on the gatepost, the newest one still pale beside the four.

The talk is small and easy, and neither of you hurries it, because the answer is already cut into wood.

When you leave, he does not close the gate behind you at once.

He stands in the blossom-fall a while longer, listening to your footsteps go light down the mountain.

The gate stays open past the ninth hour, and the rule has bent for good.

Behind him the hall lamp burns late, and the low shelf inside keeps the small wooden sword where the light can reach it.

He is already counting the seasons until you return.

episodes.title: 轻轻的脚步声
episodes.opening: 山门旁的松枝上，积雪忽然滑落，惊起三只山雀扑进灰蒙蒙的天空，翅膀拍碎了满山的寂静。
episodes.dialogue:
“谢无涯，守这座剑冢。”他只说了这么一句，像把一切都交代完了。

随后他放下铲子，久久打量着你，肩头渐渐积起一层雪。山雀重新落回松枝，山谷静得能听见寒霜在石缝里崩裂的细响。

“脚步很轻，”他终于开口，“很好。剑会睡得更安稳。”

他朝石阶下看了一眼——青苔从下面几级台阶蔓延上来，结成深绿的绳缕——又看了看檐下等着的沙筐。今早的活儿，两双手正好做得完，若你愿意搭手的话。他不会问第二遍。

choices.text: 有人教过我，老物件沉睡的地方，脚步要放轻。
choices.response:
他的嘴角动了动，一闪而过，还没成形就消失了。

“教得好。”他说。

他拎起台阶顶上等着的沙筐，朝下面一端扬了扬下巴，示意你去那边——青苔最厚的地方。

他解释说，沙是用来垫一口新剑架的，而这条搬运的路滑得很，一不小心就会崴断脚踝。

两个人一起，沙筐下得很快。他什么也没说，却不动声色地侧过肩，把沉的那一边揽到了自己这边。

沙堆好后，他又取来一把铲子，两个人沿着搬运路清青苔，一路清回上头，直到每一级台阶都干干净净。

他看了看清出来的石阶，又看了看你，点了点头——从他那儿，这几乎算得上一番长篇大论了。

choices.text: （蹲下身，一言不发地帮他清完最后一段青苔。）
choices.response:
他瞥了一眼，没说话，把自己的铲子往旁边挪了半步，给你的让出位置。

你们在雪声和铲子刮石的声响里埋头干活，一息接一息，直到肩膀发酸发烫，石阶被清得又黑又亮，泛着水光。

最后一小片青苔揭下来时，他看了看干净的石阶，又看了看你。

“剑冢从不为青苔生气。”他说。

“但我还是把它清掉。”

“老一辈的人在这儿摔过跤。每一个，我都记得。”

他的语气分不清是在解释自己，还是在认可你，而他也不打算把这层含糊说破。

episodes.ending:
他送你到山门，把门拉开一掌宽，不多不少。

雪积在他肩头，他没有掸掉。

他身后的石阶干干净净，每一级，一直清到最下面。

临走前，他把一张拓片按进你手里：从一口旧剑上拓下的铭文，字迹半清不楚，有一个字几乎磨没了。

“读一读。”他说。

“读完了，就带回来。”

他没有解释为什么选了那口剑，也没说剑的主人是谁。你明白，问了也是白问——答案值不起那个代价。

你把拓片收进袖中离开，身后留着一扇门——被人刻意地、执拗地，敞开着。

episodes.title: 雪中断剑
episodes.opening:
冢堂清冷整洁，一排排剑架上，剑如沉睡的观众，每柄剑都覆着一层薄薄的霜衣。

谢无涯立在石桌旁，把折布翻出一角干净的，正为最近的一柄剑拂尘。他没有伸手，就替你腾出了放拓片的位置。你把拓片放下，他用两块光滑的石子压住卷起的边角，然后指了指对面的凳子。最低一层剑架上放着一柄断剑。半截剑穗上的缠枝纹在他腰间玉佩旁映着光。
episodes.dialogue:
他没问你是否喝茶，径直摆下两只杯子，然后拿起拓片，用双手掌心把它抚平。纸经旅途已薄了，他对待它的样子，就像对待那些旧剑：仿佛它还有知觉。

他默默读着，炉火噼啪响了一声，又一声。雪无声地压在高窗上。

他的手指停在那个磨旧的字上，就停在那里。他没有抬头。不管那个字写的是什么，他显然早已读过——许多个冬天以前——而这一读，从未真正读完过。

choices.text: 你认识它的主人。剑穗和你腰间的玉佩——同一种纹样。
choices.response:
他沉默了足够久，久到炉火又噼啪响了两声。

然后他平静地讲起来，一句一句，短促零碎，像一个人在摆放工具。

一柄断剑，独自立在雪里被发现，剑刃去了半截，四下不见人影。

他跪在冰上七天，磨平一方玉座，直到断口齐平，寒气浸透了膝盖。

那半截剑穗上的缠枝纹，和他腰间玉佩的纹理一模一样。

他没有说主人是谁，也没有说剑是怎么断的。

“守剑人有些事可以说。”他说。

有些，他留着。

那也是一种守护。

choices.text: （等等。让沉默留着，直到他自己决定填补它。）
choices.response:
你什么也没说。

你把杯子在桌上转了四分之一圈，等着，让沉默去做追问做不到的事。

停顿延展开来，其中某种东西似乎替他做了决定。

他缓缓开口，句子很短，讲起寒冰、一方玉座，还有那半截剑穗——和他腰间玉佩同纹的剑穗。

讲述时他始终没有抬头，目光只落在指下那个磨旧的字上。

说完，他把你的杯子斟满到边沿——你猜，这是他把话语身后的门轻轻掩上的方式。

episodes.ending:
他领你穿过名讳之堂送你出去，这一次你记住了一些名字：一个摆渡人，一个养蜂人的女儿，一个谎言拙劣却死得漂亮的人。

每个名字落在它的剑上，像一只手搭上肩头。

在门口，他停了下来。

“下次，九时之前来。”他说。

门还开着的时候，茶要更好喝。

他瞥了一眼你袖中的拓片，像是确认它还在，那一瞥里有什么告诉你：这一读并未完结——只是暂停，像他句子之间的停顿。

对他来说，这几乎算得上一段长篇大论了。

episodes.title: 石阶上的浆果
episodes.opening: 一夜之间，寒潮从山脊上压了下来，整座山都在寒气里咯吱作响。
episodes.dialogue:
他直起身，呵出的气发白，顺着你的目光看向顶层石阶上留下的浆果：干桑葚，还有几颗野生的红果子。

那一瞬间，他看起来比实际年纪老了许多，也比这座山更疲惫。寒潮对他折腾得不轻——你看得出来，他一直在护着右手，这一周每天清晨握刮冰器的都是那只手。

“他们每天早上都来。”他说，却不肯说是谁。

他蹲下身，不去碰那些浆果，只是看着它们，就像看他还没读懂的剑铭，然后他顺着石阶望下去，望到小径没入松林的地方。

“是山把他们送来的。”他终于说，“我只要让石阶配得上他们。”

这是他离剖白自己最近的一次，而你还没来得及多问，他已经转身去凿冰了。

choices.text: 你每天清晨都在扫石阶。看得出来的。坐下吧，喝点热的。
choices.response:
他张开嘴，分明想说这点活算不了什么。

然后他看了看石阶，看了看那些天不亮就独自奋战的冰，又把话咽了回去。

他慢慢坐下，像个终于放下重担的人——那重担重到他自己都忘了背着。

他双手捧着杯子，起初并不喝，只是让暖意一点点渗进指头。

“曾经有个孩子来过。”他说。

来玩剑。

落下了一把木剑，赶在落雪前下了山。

他盯着蒸汽。

守剑人的本分，就是等。

这就是这门行当的全部了。

choices.text: （你从墙上取下另一把刮冰器，一言不发地开始清理他身旁的冰。）
choices.response:
你从架子上取下备用的刮冰器，一言不发地凿起冰来。

他看了你三个呼吸的工夫，然后手上的动作快了起来，仿佛你的劳作给了他加快的许可。

两人合力，石阶不到晌午就清理干净了，碎冰灰蒙蒙地一块块堆在栏杆边。

直到这时他才开口。

“有个孩子来过。”他说。

来玩剑，落下一把木剑。

还没等我跟上去，雪就把小径盖住了。

他的下颌绷紧了。

我把石阶扫干净，是为了下一个来的人不会摔倒。

episodes.ending:
他没有道谢。

他做了件更好的事：他在殿里清出一格低矮的架子，把那把木剑竖着摆上去，摆在灯光照得到的地方。

然后他把干桑葚装进一只小碟，摆在剑旁，野果另放一碟。

“不管谁回来，”他说，“都会看到剑被好好收着。”

他说这话的口气像立誓，而你明白，对他来说这就是誓言。

他没有解释那些浆果，你也没有追问；有些礼物是山自己送来的，守剑人只需为它们腾出位置。

殿外，山雀们缩进松树里过夜，他让殿里的灯，很晚都还亮着。

episodes.title: 山门初开第一树花
episodes.opening: 山里的春天来得晚，却来得很急。
episodes.dialogue:
他看了看手里的杯子，又看了看你，像要搬起什么沉重的东西似的，吸了口气。

他说，这花期撑不过一周。山脊上的风一吹就落尽了，然后这座山又只剩石头和雪，再等一年。

所以与其日后空自懊悔，不如现在就开口。

他把杯子转了一圈，又一圈，没有喝。你头顶上，梅树刚开出第一茬白花；桌上那坛酒开了许久，酒香已经飘到了桌子的另一头。

你来这山已经四回了。他从没说过自己记得；门柱上的刻痕替他说了——三道浅浅的旧痕，已经风化成灰白，他的目光扫过去，又飞快移开。

不管他接下来要问什么，这句话他在山上揣的日子，比那坛酒还长。

choices.text: 那我每个季节都来——不为剑冢。为你。
choices.response:
话音落下，他整个人静止下来，像山在开冻前的那种静。

等他再动，是把自己的杯子轻轻放下，郑重其事，好让双手有点正经营生。

每个季节，他重复了一遍。

不为剑冢。

他低声试着咀嚼这句话的分量，你从未见过他脸上有什么东西这样松开过。

“那我把酒留着。”他说。

山门也开过第九个时辰。

为你，规矩可以弯一弯。

choices.text: （你端起杯子，趁他再开口之前，朝他举了举。）
choices.response:
你举杯向他，停在那里，什么也没说。

他懂了。

他肩上的紧绷散了，也举起自己的杯子，一口饮尽。

好，他事后说。

剑冢不缺守剑人。

缺的是见证的人。

他说起那些名字、剑铭、四季轮转——这些活计需要第二双眼睛、第二副嗓子，是自愿来的。

那是他发出的同行之邀，用他唯一会的方式：绕了个弯，借一杯酒说出口。

episodes.ending:
他不让这一刻变得太沉。

他陪你在花下喝酒，直到天光转金，不动声色地把两只杯子都续满。

话题都是些小事：石阶上的冰，山雀的吵闹，一道他跟它耗了一整个冬天的剑铭。

临走前，他取过小刀，在门柱上那三道旧痕旁，刻下一道新的浅痕。

“一季一道。”他说。

现在有第四道了。

他没说这道痕许下的是什么，你也没有问，因为那些树已经替他说了。

花瓣簌地落了一阵，轻轻的，齐齐的一片，像树们在跟着他的节拍。

episodes.title: 名录之册
episodes.opening: 又一年过去了。
episodes.dialogue:
他在摊开的册页上轻叩一下，然后抬起头。

一瓣梅花落在你们之间的桌上，他没有拂去。摊在你们中间的那本册子是手订的，用他自己搓的线装订，封面边角被一整年带在身边走过名剑殿磨得发软。

“名录之册，需要两只手来写。”他说。

而我从来只有一只。

他说这话没有自怜，就像在说天气。可他的拇指按在第一页空白的半边上，久久不动——这本身就是一种说明。

酒已斟好。山雀安静下来。他等着，像他扫的石阶一样耐心，等你会用那第二支笔做什么。

choices.text: 第一页归你。告诉我，你的手是从哪里写起的。
choices.response:
他几乎笑了一下。

“是从一个摆渡人写起的。”他说着，把册子转向你能看见的角度。

第一个名字，是他一丝不苟的字迹。

然后是养蜂人家的女儿。

一个谎撒得很糟、死得很体面的人。

他把每个名字都照写下时的样子念出来，你这才听清了第一天只听到一半的东西：这些名字是一场守望。

念完之后，他给你续上酒，像石头一样耐心地等着，想听听你这半本册子会是什么声音。

choices.text: （你拿起第二支笔，在他第一个名字下面添了一个名字。）
choices.response:
你提起笔，写下第一天从山上带下来的那张磨损拓片上的剑的名字。

他倒着读完，没有评论，然后拿起自己的笔，凭记忆在下面补上那位主人的名字。

两只手，同一页。

“好。”他说。

一只手写出来的名录，只是账册。

两只手写出来的，是传承。

他说得平淡，却在你继续之前，悄悄把你的笔顺描了一遍。

episodes.ending:
暮色里，你们写下各自的第一批名字，他的手很稳，你的手在旁边慢慢找到自己的节奏。

一页写完，他合上册子，把酒摆在你们中间，山雀在梅枝里安顿下来过夜。

他在门柱上刻下第五道刻痕，不慌不忙，也没有解释。

剑冢比山下的世界安静。

却不再沉默。

他送你到山门，替你把门扶开，册子夹在臂弯里，像佩着第二把剑。

“下个季节，还是这个时辰。”他说，“门还开着的时候，茶会更好喝。”

这是他离一句承诺最近的一次，而他没有收回。他身后，殿里的灯已为夜里点起，透过敞开的门，你能看见低矮的架子上那把木剑立得端端正正，仍被好好收着。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 这坛酒是为了什么
romance.opening:
黄昏，山门旁的梅花开得放肆，花瓣落得比眼睛追的还快。

谢无涯把酒坛搬到了石桌上。他检查了坛口的封泥，把两只杯子分开一段仔细的距离摆好，又从飘落的花瓣里拉出那只备用的小凳。门柱上有四道浅痕。你走近时他瞥了一眼，刀却留在鞘里。这一回，门是敞开的，里面的活计可以等等。
romance.dialogue:
他斟酒，酒色像落日在雪线上做的最后一笔。

他用指腹缓缓转着杯子，没有喝。花瓣落在你们之间的桌面上，谁都没有伸手去拂。

“偶尔有旅人问，守剑人为什么种梅树。”他说。

我一个都没答过。

他隔着小小的石桌看你，这一眼，比他往常的注视都要久。

今晚我愿意答，他说。只要有人问。

choices.text: 那就直说吧，守剑人。这坛酒是为了什么？
choices.response:
他把杯子放下。

坐直了。

面对着你，像面对一篇他终于读懂的剑铭。

“这坛酒，是为了此刻。”他说。

为了有人来问。

我不擅长说话。

你早发现了。

一阵停顿，连对他来说都算长的。

那些梅树，是为了有人能坐在树下种的。

我希望那个人是你。

山雀在枝头动了动。

这一次，他没有用话去填沉默。

他把答案留给你，像那扇敞开的门。

choices.text: （你摸了摸门柱上的第四道季痕，然后看向他。）
choices.response:
你的手指落在门柱的第四道刻痕上，目光没有离开他。

他看看你的手，又看看那些刻痕，一、二、三、四，你看得出他在数着季节。

四回了，他终于开口。

第二回之后，我就不再问为什么了。

他的手搭上腰间的刀，随即又抬开。

他从四道刻痕看到桌上那两只静静等候的杯子。

有些问题，他说，男人用一刀一杯来答。

romance.ending:
他抽出刀，在那四道之下利落添了一道，随即收刀入鞘，谁都没有先举杯。

你们喝下了这坛酒被搬出来的理由，就在他亲手种的树下。等酒坛见了一半的底，门柱上已有五道刻痕，最新那道，在旧的四道旁边还泛着浅色。

话不多，也不涩，你们谁都不急着说完，因为答案早已刻进了木头里。

你离开时，他没有立刻关上身后的门。

他在落花里又站了片刻，听着你的脚步声轻快地下山去。

门一直开过了九时，规矩这一次，是真的为谁弯了。

他身后，殿里的灯亮到很晚，里面的矮架上，那柄小小的木剑仍搁在灯光够得到的地方。

他已经开始数，数到你回来的那个季。

episodes.title: The Lantern That Anyone Can Light
episodes.opening:
Dawn comes up gray-gold over Cloud Ferry Hall, and the wind is already at work.
You find Tang Zhu at the landing, sleeves rolled, watching a new guide lantern spin on its bamboo frame. It turns in short, jerky circles, nothing like the smooth drift her lanterns usually have.
"There it goes again," she says, not turning around. "Sulking. That's a fighting spin, not a reading one. The talisman line and the wind are arguing, and the wind always wins."
She glances at you, and her copper bells ring when she laughs at her own mess.
"Good timing. Hold the frame for me? Steady as you can. Paper remembers a shaking hand, and this sheet has enough opinions already."
episodes.dialogue:
You take the bamboo frame in both hands. It's lighter than it looks, and the wind pushes at it like a bored child.
Tang Zhu unlaces the paper panel and carries it into the light, tilting it back and forth. "Sizing's fine. Not the paper." She leans close to the painted line and grimaces. "There. Third curve in the wind-reading segment. I rushed it at the end and the ink pooled. Pooled ink reads thick, the line grabs, and the wind reads it as a wall instead of a sign."
She pulls her ink stone and a fine brush from her apron pocket — of course she carries them — and sits right down on the landing boards.
"Hold it just like that. Don't fight the wobble, let it be honest. Paper and I will meet in the middle." She re-inks the curve in slow strokes, tongue at the corner of her mouth, then blows on it gently. "The whole point of this design is that a traveler with no spiritual gift can light it at midnight. But first it has to work for the wind, and the wind doesn't grade on effort."
While the ink dries against the frame in your hands, an old man comes up the landing path with a shoulder pole and a worn coat. A village traveler, out at the wrong hour, clearly in a hurry.
"Is that one lit?" he calls. "I've a ferry to catch and my eyes aren't what they were before sunup."
Tang Zhu looks at the wet ink, then at you, then makes a fast decision. "It will be." She fits the panel back on the frame and steps aside — deliberately, leaving the lighting to him.

choices.text: Go ahead, uncle. It's made to be lit by anyone.
choices.response:
The old man squints at the lantern, finds the touch-point the way a stranger would — no special skill, just looking — and presses it.
The paper catches with a soft, steady glow, and the lantern swings out over the water, reading the wind instead of fighting it.
"Well now," he says, pleased. "Simple as lighting a stove." He tips his hat to you both and hurries down to the ferry.
Tang Zhu stares after him, and her bells ring like a small celebration. "Did you hear him? Simple as a stove. Best review I've ever gotten." She writes it on her cuff in ink before it can escape.

choices.text: (Keep holding the frame steady until he's gone.)
choices.response:
You keep your grip on the frame while the old man slows, then stops, eyeing the unlit lantern.
Tang Zhu notices his hesitation and waves him over. "Try it, uncle. No trick to it."
He lights it with nothing but a thumb and a wish to see the water, and the glow holds steady through a gust that bends the reeds below. He tips his hat and hurries down to the ferry.
When he's gone, you let the frame go, and your palms come away marked with two pale bamboo lines.
Tang Zhu takes one of your hands and reads the marks like notes. "You held it through the worst gust of the morning. That's a co-tester's mark, that is." She grins. "I'm putting it in my ledger under today."

episodes.ending:
The traveler's boat pulls away, his pole dipping in the light of the lantern you both fixed.
Tang Zhu sits back down on the boards and lets out a long breath, watching it spin easy now, the curve reading the wind the way it should.
"One lantern anyone can light," she says. "That's one. Now I need the storeroom to agree to a hundred more, and the storeroom always disagrees with me." She laughs at herself, and the bells ring along.
She folds the morning's failed panel over her knee and starts creasing it into a tiny lantern for the shelf of failures.
"First trial's coming," she says, quieter. "Down at the foothills, where the people who need it can judge it. And you'll be there for the first lighting. That part's not negotiable."
Overhead, the repaired lantern turns smooth in the wind, and it looks like it finally agrees with her.

episodes.title: Count the Paper First
episodes.opening:
The foothill market is loud in the good way — vegetable sellers calling prices, a dog weaving between baskets, a kettle whistling two stalls down. You walk beside Tang Zhu, who carries an empty back-basket and a stubborn expression.

"I promised the Hall twelve new guide lanterns by month's end," she says. "Then I checked my storeroom last night and found enough talisman paper for seven. Maybe six, if the wind ruins one, which it will."

She stops at the top of the market lane and holds up a hand before you can say anything reassuring.

"Don't say it'll work out. That's how I got here. My mouth signed the promise before my hands counted the paper." Her copper bells ring when she huffs, which she pretends not to notice. "So today we count sheets. Actual sheets, with my actual hands. Then I send the honest number up the hill and deal with it like a grown lantern maker."

She leads you through the crowd to a narrow doorway behind a stall of dried mushrooms. Ink stains fade into the doorframe like old footprints. Her mother's paper workshop.
episodes.dialogue:
Inside, the workshop smells of pulp and sizing and warm bamboo drying racks. Her mother is at the long table trimming sheets, and she looks up without surprise.

"You've come to count something," her mother says. "You get that look before you owe people things."

"Mother." Tang Zhu sets the basket down and asks for the shelf of finished talisman stock. Her mother pulls three stacks down, and the two of you sit while Tang counts each sheet between finger and thumb, lips moving.

"Fourteen good sheets here. Add my storeroom's six and I'm at twenty. Twelve lanterns, two sheets each with the cutting waste — twenty-four needed. Four short." She counts again, frowning. "If I'm careful I can cut four from three sheets and pretend that's arithmetic."

Her mother slides one more stack across the table — a full twenty sheets of the good fibrous stock, the kind that takes a talisman line clean. "Take it. Family stock. No charge."

Tang's hand stops halfway. Then she sets the stack back down, flat and deliberate.

"No. I'll buy it. Full price."

"Don't be ridiculous, I have more stock than orders this month—"

"That's exactly why. If I take it free, that's still family bailing out my big mouth. Then the Hall gets lanterns made from a favor nobody counted, and I learn nothing and promise even bigger next time." She pulls out her coin pouch and counts properly this time, sheet by sheet. "Twenty sheets at market rate. You can grumble about the price if you want, that's traditional."

choices.text: Your mother taught you well. Both directions.
choices.response:
Her mother snorts first, and Tang Zhu's bells ring out before she can stop them. "Careful," she warns you, ears going pink. "Compliment the family accounting and you'll get a full lecture on pulp and sizing." But she looks pleased anyway, and her mother says, "She pays, she counts, she eats dinner before she goes. Good businesswoman, good daughter. Sit down, both of you."

Tang mutters that she has to send word to the Hall, but she doesn't move from the chair. The talk goes to drying racks and weather, and somewhere in it her mother quietly sets the twenty sheets aside — wrapped, paid for — next to the door.

choices.text: (Say nothing and help stack the counted sheets.)
choices.response:
You gather the fourteen counted sheets into a neat stack while she and her mother settle the money, coins counted onto the table one at a time. Tang glances over mid-count at your tidy pile, and something in her shoulders settles.

"See, this is why I brought you. You count with your hands instead of your mouth. I should try it sometime."

Her mother wraps the twenty sheets in cloth and knots it. When the last coin lands — twenty sheets, full price, no discount — Tang ties the bundle into her back-basket and pats it once, like a small animal that might bolt.

"Alright," she says, breathing out. "Now I send the honest number up the hill."

episodes.ending:
They eat dinner at the workshop before the road up — Tang Zhu argues, her mother wins, that's also traditional. Her mother sends you both off with pickled vegetables and a word to the bells to bring Tang home before dark, which makes Tang roll her eyes and then check the bells are fastened anyway.

On the climb back toward Cloudpine, the basket on her back rustles with twenty paid-for sheets. "Here's the number I'm sending the Hall," she says. "Ten lanterns by month's end, not twelve. Two late, and I'll say so in writing, with my name on it." She kicks a pebble off the path. "It'll sting. Elder Wu will make that face. But it stings less than delivering excuses later, and a lot less than letting my mother quietly fund my promises forever."

At the bend where the foothills drop away, she stops and looks back down at the market lights coming on one by one.

"You know the funny part? With these twenty sheets I might manage the two extra lanterns anyway. But they go into storeroom stock, not the promise. Counted stock." She smiles at you, tired and satisfied. "Come with me when the ten are done. First trial down here, at the foothills, like I said. The people who need them get to judge — and you get to watch me keep a promise I actually counted for."

episodes.title: The Crooked Little Light
episodes.opening:
The auntie's house sits low against the hill, mulberry trees shading the yard, trays of silkworms stacked along the shaded wall.
Tang Zhu carries a paper-wrapped box of pastries in one hand and her working satchel in the other. She rings once on the doorframe out of habit before remembering the door is already open.
"We're here!" she calls, and her copper bells ring with the words.
The auntie waves you both in, already laying fresh mulberry leaves in the nearest tray. "Wash your hands first, both of you. The little ones are eating."
The room fills with a soft, continuous rustle, like rain falling on a clear sky somewhere far above.
episodes.dialogue:
Tang Zhu sits close to the tray, elbows on her knees, and for once says nothing. She just listens, head tilted, until the rustle is the whole world.
Then she pulls a folded square of talisman paper from her satchel — one of yesterday's failures, the wind having beaten it soundly at the landing.
"Watch," she says. "This one didn't work, but it doesn't deserve the bin."
Her fingers move quickly, creasing the paper into a small lantern no bigger than her thumb, folding the failed curves inward so they hold the shape. She sets it on the tray's edge, where it sits like a tiny crooked house.
The auntie glances at it. "You always bring your mistakes somewhere kind."
Tang Zhu laughs, and the bells betray her. "They're easier to look at when they glow somewhere warm."
Then she goes quiet, turning her thumb along the paper's edge, and you can tell something has been sitting behind her teeth for days.
"Can I say a thing out loud?" she asks. "You can just listen. You don't have to fix it."
She looks at the silkworms instead of at you. "I'm afraid the sect will seal my lantern design. The ferry lantern — the one anyone can light. If they decide it's sect property, then the villagers at midnight, the ones who actually need it, would have to ask. Or go without."
Her voice stays steady, which somehow makes it worse. "I grew up in a paper workshop. I know what it costs to make one good sheet. A lamp a tired person can't light is a bad lamp, no matter how clever the talisman line is. If it gets sealed away, clever is all it will ever be."
The rustle of eating continues, small and patient, filling the silence she leaves.
"I keep folding failures and telling myself the mess becomes a light," she says. "But I can't fold this one. I have to decide something."
She straightens up and finally turns to look at you. "So I've decided. I'm going to write the instructions out plainly — paper weights, bamboo cuts, the talisman curves, all of it — and give them to the village. Openly. I'll ask the Hall for permission first, face to face, and say why."
She takes a breath. "If they say no, I'll say it again, with better arguments and better manners. But the design belongs where the need is. My mother would shake a stall owner's bells over less."

choices.text: Then let me hear your arguments once, before you give them to the Hall. I'll be the stiff elder who says no.
choices.response:
Tang Zhu blinks, then grins so wide the bells ring twice.
"A practice run. You'd do that?" She grabs a blank sheet from her satchel and starts scribbling points right there on the tray's edge — material cost, the villagers' need, the Hall's own history of hands and paper.
She argues her case at you with ink on her cuff. When you press back — that the villager who can't light her lamp deserves the whole night's safety, not just a lamp — she stops mid-sentence and writes your words down.
"That one," she says, tapping the page. "That's the sentence I was missing. You're a much better stiff elder than I expected."

choices.text: (Say nothing, just pick up the tiny folded lantern and set it steady where it won't be knocked.)
choices.response:
You reach over and adjust the little folded lantern so it sits flat on the tray's rim, safe from the auntie's sleeve and the door's draft.
Tang Zhu watches you do it and doesn't say anything for a moment.
"You just made room for the small light," she says finally.
She nudges your shoulder with hers. "Thank you for that. Some fears want witnessing. This one I'll solve myself, but I'm glad you saw it first."
She folds a second tiny lantern from another failure and sets it beside yours without a word about it.

episodes.ending:
Before you leave, the auntie makes you both sit in the outer room for tea, and she promises Tang Zhu first pick of the next cocoon batch — with dates, since Tang asked for dates before the tray was even refilled.
At the door, Tang Zhu pockets the two tiny folded lanterns instead of leaving them on the shelf.
"Practice ones," she says. "For the night I write the instructions out. I'll light one on the desk and the other goes wherever the ink dries worst."
She looks down the hill toward Cloud Ferry Hall, then back at you, and her chin comes up.
"Three days. That's how long it'll take to write it plainly. Then I walk into the Hall and ask out loud. Will you be at the landing when I come back down? Either answer, I want to tell you how it went first."
Her bells ring once as she says it, and this time she doesn't try to keep them quiet.

episodes.title: A Place Beside the Landing
episodes.opening:
The trial is over and nothing burned, leaked, or flew off the landing, which by Tang Zhu's standards counts as a festival.

The village lantern burned steady through a full hour of crosswind, and a miller's boy with ink-stained fingers lit it twice without a flicker of spiritual gift. The watching disciples have drifted back up the path. The crowd at the foothill end is dispersing, and the landing is left to paper, bamboo, the river sound below, and the two of you.

Tang Zhu unties the last test knot with more care than it needs. Her copper bells ring small and quick every time she moves, and she doesn't try to hush them today.

"Not one repair," she says, half to you, half to the lantern. "The wind threw three moods at it and it read all three. I'm writing that down twice."

She wipes her hands on her apron, adding a fresh ink smudge to the old ones, and looks at you the way she does when she's about to say something she rehearsed and then decided not to rehearse.
episodes.dialogue:
"So. That's the trial done. The instructions go to the Hall next week, and after that, any village with a copy and steady hands can make their own. The part I've been chewing on for months is finished."

She folds the test knot into her apron pocket anyway. She keeps things like that.

"Which means I owe myself a day off, and I'd rather not spend it alone. There's a market down the hill on the next rest day. Mother's stall will have new paper stock to inspect, the snail stall will be open, and I know a spot by the bend in the road where the wind is gentler than it has any right to be."

Her bells give her away with a small ring. She laughs at them, then at herself.

"I'm asking you to come with me. Just — with me. I mean a date, if you want one. If you'd rather keep this as close friendship, I want that too."

She holds up one ink-stained finger before you can answer.

"And before you say anything out of politeness — no. Whatever you've helped me carry, whatever you've listened to on that shelf-filled evening of mine, none of it obliges you. A gift or a favor never buys closeness. That's the whole point of what we built today — a thing anyone can light because they want to. It works the same for people."

She waits. The river keeps on below the landing. The new lantern spins slow behind her, reading the wind instead of fighting it, and she looks at you with her whole attention, the way she looks at paper she respects.

choices.text: I would like a date with you. The market day — count me in.
choices.response:
Her bells ring out before she does, and this time she doesn't even pretend to hold still.

"Good," she says, and then, because she's her, "Good," again, softer, like the word needs saying twice to be believed.
