choices.response: 他安静了片刻，随后轻声笑了——是事情落在心坎上时才会有的那种浅笑。“这话像是一个已经学会把句子说完整的人说的。”他在长凳上转过身，正对着你。“那我们就把它保持简单吧。不要誓言，不要仪式——一晚一晚地来。如果你愿意，明晚有一支我一直排练的曲子，我想让你从头到尾完整地听一遍，中途不加任何打断。我只为你一个人演奏。”

choices.text: （握住他的手，告诉他你也想继续和他约会。）
choices.response: 他低头看着你覆在他手上的手，然后抬眼看你，没有抽回。“这样回答已经够清楚了。”他的声音温暖而平稳。你替他斟茶时，他扶着杯子，让茶水稳稳注满。“那明晚的事也说定了——有一支曲子，我想让你完完整整地听一遍。之后，还有之后的一晚。一次一晚，每一晚都由我们自己选择。”他把那碟南瓜递给你。“趁热吃。我们还有一整晚。”

romance.ending:
茶棚外的街道渐渐安静下来，摊贩们收拾完了东西。杯中的茶从滚烫变得温热，你们俩都不曾介意。

宋闻弦向后靠了靠，望着灯火点点的街道。“你知道吗，从前我总以为，开口去求什么——求一段独奏，求署名，求一个属于自己的位置——是天底下最难的事。到现在也不算容易。可是坦率地问一个人是否还愿意留在这里，并且完完整整地听清那个回答……原来这才是比较容易的那种开口。是你让这件事变得容易了。”

他朝你微微偏过头。“那么，明天见。排练结束后的回廊，或者光线好的话就在院子里。我会带上笛子，把曲子从第一个音符演奏到最后一个。你只需要听着——就像你一直以来的那样。”

茶棚主人开始叠凳子准备打烊，他提起了笛盒。沿着灯影通明的街道送你回去的路上，他低声哼起了几个小节——你猜想，那就是他明天要为你演奏的那支曲子。他察觉到自己哼出了声，笑了，却毫不窘迫。

到了各自归家的路口，他伸出手。你握住了，宋闻弦笑起来。“明天见。又一次约会。”他等你松开手才往家走。你回头时，他也正好回头。

episodes.title: The Page Beside It
episodes.opening:
The archive is warm with late-afternoon light when you arrive. Clara Gu has set two pages side by side on the long table, each weighted at the corner with a smooth stone. She gestures you over without looking up.

"Good timing," she says. "I need a second pair of eyes, and daylight is leaving."

The left page is the original daily chronicle from two weeks ago. The right is the revision filed in its place. Same date, same events, one difference she wants to be sure of.

"Read the third line of each," she says. "Slowly. Tell me what you see."

The sun has moved past the window's high ledge, and the light now falls short of the table by a hand's width. She wants to hold the pages up, and she cannot hold them steady and read at the same time.
episodes.dialogue:
"The third line," she says again, patient, as if reminding a copyist student. "Go on."

You lift the original into the light with both hands while she steadies the revision flat beneath it. In the original, the attendant on night watch is recorded as having *asked to leave her post*. In the revision, the words have become *was permitted to leave her post*.

Clara is quiet a moment. Then she sets down her brush.

"Do you see what that does?" she says. "The first says she chose. The second says she was allowed. Someone tidied her decision away. In a few years no one will know she spoke up at all."

She folds her hands on the table and looks at both pages the way she looks at everything that crosses her desk, as if letting the matter finish before she judges it.

"I am not going to take either page," she says. "And I am not going to name her in anything. She still works here. Her choice is hers."

Instead, she pulls a plain working sheet toward her and begins a marginal note, dated, signed, referencing both pages by their filing numbers. Nothing stolen. Nothing exposed. Only the trace of a change, so it can be found by anyone who looks.

"Hold the original a little higher," she says. "The last character is faded. I want to copy it exactly, not as I assume it."

You lift the page into the last of the sun. She leans in, brush poised, and writes the character stroke by stroke. When she finishes, she sits back and breathes out, the way she does when a lamp is finally put out for the night.

"That's all," she says softly. "It's small. But small things hold."

choices.text: If it's small, why does it feel heavy?
choices.response:
Clara looks up, and her quiet bright eyes settle on you.

"Because it was her word," she says. "One word, and a person's choice becomes someone else's permission. I've seen a single changed word decide a servant's future. Maybe I feel it more than I should."

She presses the marginal note flat beneath the stone and leaves it in the open, where anyone working the desk will pass it.

"Thank you for asking, though," she adds. "It helps to know someone else sees the weight too."

choices.text: (Say nothing and keep holding the page steady in the light)
choices.response:
You lower the page slowly, keeping it level until she reaches for it. Clara takes it gently and returns it to its place beside the revision, corners aligned.

"You didn't ask what I plan to do about it," she says. "Most people would."

She smooths the marginal note once with her fingertips.

"I'm glad you didn't. This one is mine to carry. But you held the light for me, and that was exactly the help I needed."

episodes.ending:
By the time the marginal note is filed, the sun has gone past the window entirely, and Clara lights the desk lamp herself.

She pours two cups of plain tea, still warm from the pot at her elbow, and sets one on your side of the table. On the shelf, the original and the revision sit where they have always sat, side by side, nothing between them but the trace that anyone can now follow.

"The discrepancy is recorded," she says. "No names. No danger to her. If someone looks, they'll find it. If no one looks, at least the archive holds it honestly."

She pulls her leisure book toward her, and you notice a flowered note tucked between its pages, a thin branch drawn on it. Her fingers rest on the page a moment longer than needed.

"There's more to organize before the spring banquet," she says. "The records of past gatherings. It's slow work, and it goes better with company. Will you come by the window again, some afternoon?"

She asks it plainly, without pressing, the way she leaves everyone a way out. The lamp is steady, the tea is warm, and the question stays open between you.

episodes.title: One Arrow in the Pot
episodes.opening:
It is a rare day off, and the garden outside Everpeace Palace is loud with other people's holidays. Clara has set the pitch-pot on the grass a fair distance from the path, with two bundles of arrows between you.

"I should warn you," she says, tucking a loose sleeve back. "My record is one arrow in, and that was a lucky day. You may end up teaching me instead."

She hands you the first arrow anyway, with the seriousness of someone presenting an official document.

The sun is warm on the bricks, and ducks drift past the garden pool behind you.
episodes.dialogue:
Clara goes first, to show you how it is done. She squares her shoulders, squints, and throws.

The arrow lands three steps to the left with a clink on the bricks. She laughs, head tipping back, and her white-jade hairpin slips loose and drops into the grass.

"Oh no," she says, kneeling to search for it. "Now you have seen the historian defeated in a public garden. Please keep this out of the chronicle."

You help her look, and find the pin near the pot itself. It gleams in the sun, plain and well-worn. She takes it back with both hands, an oddly careful gesture for such a small thing.

"It was a gift," she says, straightening it in her hair. "When I finished my copyist years. I have worn it every day since, and yet it still escapes me when I laugh too hard."

She hands you an arrow and watches your throw with genuine attention, missing nothing, saying nothing yet.

When both of you have missed several times in a row, she sits back on her heels and looks at the pot instead of at you.

"Can I tell you something plain?" she says. "At work, I pride myself on being careful. But sometimes caution becomes silence. I see a word in a record that should not be there, and I wait. I tell myself the time is not right, that I must not draw attention. And so the wrong word stays a little longer."

She picks up an arrow, turns it over, and sets it down again.

"It is safer to be quiet. I know that. But a record that stays wrong because of my caution is still wrong, and I am the one who kept it so."

choices.text: Then pick one. One correction, done properly, through the record itself.
choices.response:
Clara is quiet for a moment, then nods, the way she confirms a document against its original.

"One," she agrees. "Through the proper channels, filed where it can be traced, corrected beside the original and never over it. Nothing done in the dark."

She names it aloud, plainly, without names attached: a small gathering record from last season, one altered word that quietly changed who made a choice. She has checked it three times and filed nothing.

"I will write the correction tomorrow morning, when the light is steady, and sign my own name to it." She picks up an arrow and, to her visible surprise, lands it in the pot. "There. One arrow in. Perhaps the day is telling me something."

choices.text: (Say nothing. Pick up an arrow and hand it to her, and keep listening.)
choices.response:
You hand her an arrow instead of an answer. She takes it, and something in her shoulders loosens.

"Thank you," she says. "For not rushing to fix me. Most people have advice ready before I finish the sentence."

She throws, misses by less than before, and sits with that for a while. The ducks pass the pool again; the leaf at the ripple's edge keeps turning after they stop.

"I already know which correction I want to make," she says at last. "One record, one word, filed properly beside the original. Through the archive channels, my own name at the bottom, nothing hidden."

She glances at you. "I did not need anyone to tell me to be brave. I needed someone to sit here while I decided it myself. That, you did."

episodes.ending:
The afternoon runs down the way good ones do, with no particular end. You take turns throwing until the arrows are scattered in honest disarray around the pot.

Clara gathers them up, counting aloud, and reports the final tally: one arrow in, hers, and it should be recorded for posterity.

She walks back with you as far as the path splits, the hairpin holding firm this time.

"Tomorrow I make the correction," she says. "If it goes well, I will tell you how it went. If it goes badly, I will tell you that too, because you listened without telling me what to do, and that is rarer than one arrow in."

She bows slightly, in the small way of a day off rather than a duty, and heads toward the archive.

episodes.title: The Flowered Note
episodes.opening:
The archive is quiet after the evening rounds. Lamps are lit but low, and the last of the day's light still reaches the window where Clara's stool sits.

She is at her desk when you arrive, a letter open before her and her leisure book beside it. Her white-jade hairpin catches the lamplight as she looks up.

"You came at a good hour," she says. "I received something today, and I would rather not sit with it alone."

She does not turn the letter toward you. Instead she slides it aside, gently, the way she moves a page she has decided to keep to herself.

"Sit, if you like. The tea is still warm, and I have one small task to finish before the lamps are dimmed."
episodes.dialogue:
She takes a pressed osmanthus petal from a small envelope and lays it between the pages of her leisure book, right beside the folded letter she has tucked there.

"The letter is from the older servant who went home last year," she says. "You remember me telling you about the packing, the two jars of plums. She writes now and then."

She straightens the petal with one fingertip, careful not to crack it.

"I won't read her words to you. She wrote them to me, about her garden and her knees in the cold, and those are hers to give or not give. But I will tell you what it did to me. It made me miss her. And it made me think about how I write about people while they are still here."

She rises, crosses to the shelf where the gathering records sit, and brings down a slim volume from a past spring banquet.

"One entry here was revised after the fact. A servant's choice at that gathering was tidied into something more convenient. The original shows what she actually chose to do. The morning after our game, I filed the correction I promised you. It was accepted. The original and the revision have sat side by side since then."

She sets the volume open on the desk and takes out a fresh slip of paper.

"Tonight I want to add an index slip. The correction is already there, but a reader has to know where to look. One line pointing to both versions will help someone find the truth without changing either page."

She dips her brush and pauses, glancing at you with a small, wry look.

"I practiced what to say to you on the walk back from the letter box. I am still not sure I said it well. But you are here, and the tea is warm, so I will count the evening a success either way."

choices.text: You said it well. And she'd be glad her letter led to this.
choices.response:
Clara's shoulders ease, and she gives you a look that is half gratitude, half laughter at herself.

"You always know when to say the small true thing," she says. "Very well. Then I will stop rehearsing and simply write."

She sets brush to paper and writes the index slip in her careful copyist's hand. She blots it, dates it, and files it in the catalog so any reader can find the original, the revision, and her earlier correction.

"There," she says softly. "I did the hard part that morning. I am glad I followed it through tonight."

She pours you a fresh cup of tea as if to mark the small occasion, and holds hers up a little, like a toast she doesn't quite name.

choices.text: (Sit quietly and let her finish before she judges it.)
choices.response:
You settle onto the stool and say nothing. Clara notices, and something in her posture loosens.

"Thank you," she says. "You have learned my habit. Let the matter finish before judging it."

She works in silence, the brush moving steadily. Once she stops, rereads a line, and changes a single word to a plainer one. Then she blots the note, dates it, and files the index slip in the catalog, pointing to the correction she made weeks ago.

She sits back and exhales, hands resting on her knees the way they do when a weight has settled.

"Done," she says. "She will never know, and she should not have to. That is the kind of record I can live with."

The lamp flickers, and she reaches for the teapot, moving it to your side of the desk before it can be in anyone's way. Then she pauses, studying you across the lamplight.

"I am glad it was you sitting there tonight," she says, simply, and says nothing more about it.

episodes.ending:
The archive grows quieter as the lamps are dimmed one by one. Clara returns the gathering record to its shelf, the new index slip filed where a reader can find her earlier correction.

She keeps her leisure book open a moment longer, the pressed petal resting beside the folded letter, then closes it and ties the cord.

"Tomorrow the spring banquet preparations begin in earnest," she says, pulling her outer robe straight. "But tonight the chronicle is true, and a friend's letter is safe in a book, and the tea got drunk while it was warm. That is a good account of an evening."

At the door she pauses, one hand on the frame, and looks back at you a moment longer than the goodbye requires.

"I would like to look through the records of past gatherings with you before the banquet, if the days allow. Come find me by the window when the light is steady."

episodes.title: A Choice Not Filed
episodes.opening:
The afternoon light reaches one stool by the archive window, and Clara has set two cups of plain tea on it, still warm.
She is out of her usual posture today. Her scrolls are stacked and finished, the ceremonial records back in their places, and she has tucked her leisure book under her arm as if she means to show you something in it.
"I checked the ink and the edges of every page that came in this morning," she says, "and there was nothing that needed me. So I thought this hour could be ours."
Outside, the paper pinwheel on the sill turns steadily toward the breeze, one way only.
She sits down, adjusts her white-jade hairpin, and looks at you with those quiet bright eyes.
episodes.dialogue:
"I have been counting something lately," Clara says, wrapping both hands around her cup. "Hours. The ones I spend with you."
She smiles a little at her own phrasing. "A historian should be precise, so let me be precise. The work still matters to me. But when I finish archiving early now, my first thought is whether you might come by. That is new, and I did not want to leave it unsaid."
She turns the cup slowly in her hands. "Nothing said by this window goes into an official record. Whatever you answer, it stays between us, the way pressed petals stay inside a leisure book."
The breeze lifts one corner of a page on the sill and lets it settle.
"I would like to ask you for a date, away from the archive," she says. "If friendship is where you want us to stay, I value that too. You owe me neither answer. I only wanted to ask plainly."

choices.text: Then let it begin here—will you take an afternoon with me, away from the archive, as a date?
choices.response:
Clara's eyes widen slightly, then soften. "A date," she repeats, as if checking the word's weight before filing it somewhere safe.
She sits up straight, hands on her knees, letting the matter finish before she judges it. "Yes," she says. "I would like that very much."
"Not during working hours," she adds, warmth and laughter in it. "And not near any ledger, or you will find me checking the edges of the teahouse menu. There is a bench by the garden pool where the sun slants just right in the late afternoon, and the ducks make good company. Next day off?"
She reaches over and touches the rim of your cup with one finger, a small toast. "This one does not go in the chronicle either. But I will remember it exactly."

choices.text: (Tell her you want to stay close friends, then set your cup down beside hers.)
choices.response:
You tell her you want to stay close friends. Clara nods without pressing. She shifts on the stool so the sun falls on both of you, and drinks her tea while it is still warm.
"You know," she says after a while, "when the older servant left for home, what I missed was afternoons like this one. Two people, a window, nothing that needs solving."
She rests her shoulder lightly against yours, careful and unhurried. "I hear you. Close friendship, kept outside the records, is a real answer and a good one."
The pinwheel on the sill turns its one faithful direction. She opens her leisure book to the page with the pressed petal and shows it to you without comment.
"Come back when you finish archiving tomorrow," she says. "The light will be here, and so will I."

episodes.ending:
Whichever way the hour went, it stays by the window, out of every ledger.
Clara walks you to the archive door and stops in the doorway, half in the lamplight, half in the last of the sun.
"Whatever we called this today," she says, "it was an original. I keep those beside me now."
She touches her white-jade hairpin once, a small habitual blessing, and smiles.
"The records of past gatherings still need organizing before the spring banquet," she says. "But the hour after that is ours to decide when it comes."
The pinwheel turns behind her, steady toward the breeze, and the afternoon ends gently, promising nothing except that it happened.

episodes.title: The Leisure Book
episodes.opening:
The archive is closed for the half-day before the spring banquet, and Clara has carried a small table out to the corridor by the sunny window. On it sit the pitch-pot, a lidded ceramic pot of plain tea, two cups, and her leisure book with its flowered notes sticking out at odd angles.
She has tied her sleeves back with a plain cord and set her white-jade hairpin more firmly than usual. She checked the wind twice before choosing this spot; the paper pinwheel on the windowsill turns steadily toward the garden.
"I checked the records twice this morning," she says, pouring the first cup, "so the chronicle can manage without me until the lamps go out. Sit. The stool by the window is yours. It has your name on it by now, informally."
The sun reaches the stool exactly as promised. Somewhere below, the two ducks cross the garden pool, and a leaf spins long after their ripples should have stopped.
episodes.dialogue:
She throws first and misses by a full step, the arrow clinking on the bricks the way she once told you it did. She does not sigh, only marks the distance with a pebble and hands you the second arrow.
"One in between the two of us would make a fine afternoon," she says. "I am not ambitious about arrows."
Her next throw catches the rim, wobbles, and drops in. She laughs, and the hairpin slips; this time she catches it and lays it flat on the table beside the tea, as if setting down official duty along with it.
"I looked at the banquet records this week. Past gatherings, names, toasts, who sat where." She turns her cup slowly. "Your name is not in them, and it will not be. I keep that part of my life off the page on purpose. The missed arrows and the tea and this book belong to the afternoon, not the chronicle."
She opens the leisure book to a pressed osmanthus petal, then to the flowered note where someone once drew three leaves for shade, and lets you look without hurrying you past either page.
"There is one thing I would like to ask," she says, and for a moment she does the thing with her hands on her knees, sitting up straight, letting the question finish before either of you judges it. "Another day like this one, when the work allows. No occasion, no errand, nothing to record. Only if you would want that too. I am not assuming the answer."

choices.text: I'd like that. Mark it on no calendar, and I'll still come.
choices.response: She smiles, and it is the small real one. "No calendar," she agrees. "When the sun reaches that stool and the pot is on the table, you will know it is the day." She refills your cup before her own, and spends her next throw explaining, badly and happily, why the rim counts as nearly a victory for both of you.

choices.text: (Pick up the arrow she missed and set it gently in the pot.)
choices.response: She watches the arrow settle and says nothing for a moment, then laughs outright. "That counts for the household, not for either of us. We will call it a draw." She reaches over and turns the pinwheel so it faces the breeze properly, then pours the second cup and slides the leisure book to the middle of the table, where you can both reach it.

episodes.ending:
The afternoon ends the way the good records do, with nothing forced. When the sun slants past the window, she gathers the arrows, rinses the cups with clean water from a basin by the garden wall, and puts the hairpin back where it belongs.
At the corridor's turn she stops. "Thank you for the afternoon. It is not in the chronicle and it will not be, and that is exactly why it was good." She holds up the leisure book briefly, like a small salute. "I will be at my desk tomorrow if you want the dull version of me. But I will keep this stool by the window ready, just in case."
She goes back toward the archive with her steps unhurried, and the leaf by the garden pool keeps turning long after the ducks have gone. Whatever the next ordinary day looks like, there is a place set aside for you in it.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: A Day We Chose
romance.opening:
The archive lamps are out early today. Clara Gu waits for you by the corridor outside, not at her desk, which is how you know this is not an errand. Her white-jade hairpin sits where it always does, and she carries no scrolls.

She has set a small table under the eaves where the afternoon sun reaches: two cups, a plain teapot, and the pitch-pot with its bundle of arrows. The leisure book lies closed beside her elbow, a flowered note marking her place.

"I asked for the whole afternoon," she says. "Not a quarter hour between duties. The whole thing."

She straightens the cups, then looks at you the way she does when a document needs an honest reading.

"Tea, a game, and time to talk outside the archive," she says. "And before we leave, I want to ask you something plainly."
romance.dialogue:
She sits with her hands resting on her knees, back straight, and lets the question stand without hurrying past it.

"Nothing here goes beside the originals," she adds. "This is ours, and only ours, and it can stay small."

She pours, and steam rises between you. She takes out a pressed osmanthus petal and sets one on the table, turning it so the light catches it.

"I checked the ink on this one," she says, deadpan. "Edges and corrections first. Old habits."

She sets the pitch-pot between you. "We take turns. No keeping score, or keeping score only badly. My first arrow ever missed by three steps and clinked on the bricks, so your worst throw today will still be respectable company."

Her first arrow lands near the mouth of the pot and hops out. She laughs, and the hairpin slips half a finger's width before she pushes it back.

"You saw nothing," she says, and hands you the next arrow.

When the last arrow is thrown, she sets it down and looks at you directly.

"Do you still want to date me? I would rather hear your own answer than assume kindness means yes."

choices.text: Yes. I still want this. I want days like today with you.
choices.response:
Clara is quiet for a moment, then nods once, as if recording it somewhere no one else will ever read.

"Then it is settled. We both said it out loud."

She fills your cup again before her own, a courtesy she usually reserves for people she is fond of.

"I will tell you something I have never put in any chronicle. I am better at tracing other people's choices than at making my own. But this one I made a while ago. I am only glad it matches yours."

choices.text: (Take her hand and say, "Yes. I still want to date you.")
choices.response:
You take her hand and say it plainly. She does not pull away. She listens to the whole answer before she speaks.

"All right," she says softly. "Thank you for saying it. Yes from me too."

She turns her hand in yours so your fingers lace, then slides the teapot to your side of the table, the way the older servant once moved it for her.

"Then drink before it cools. And when you miss the pot, and you will, I promise to laugh kindly. That is my promise for this afternoon."

romance.ending:
The sun slants past the eaves before either of you notices. The arrows are gathered, the teapot is empty, and Clara's leisure book has moved from her elbow to the table, opened once when she wanted to show you a line and closed again when the line was not as good as the company.

She stands, brushing her dress straight, and does not put the pitch-pot away.

"Leave it here," she says. "No one will move it. And if it stays, then a next time is easier to arrange."

She looks toward the garden pool, where two ducks have just gone by and a leaf is still turning at the edge of their ripples.

"I will not presume to set the day," she says. "You choose a morning, or I choose an evening, or we argue cheerfully about it by the window. Any of those suits me. What matters is that neither of us is waiting on the other to speak first."

She touches the white-jade hairpin once, a habit when she is pleased.

"Thank you for today," she says. "I want to keep dating you, one day at a time." She holds out her hand. You take it, and the two of you walk toward the garden gate together, already talking about where to meet next.

episodes.title: 旁边的这一页
episodes.opening:
你到档案馆时，午后的光还亮着。顾清和已在长桌上把两页纸并排摆开，各压了一角镇石。她朝你招了招手，没有抬头。

“来得正好，”她说，“我需要第二双眼睛，日光快没了。”

左边那页是两周前的起居日志原件，右边是归在原位的修订本。同一天，同一件事，只有一处差异她想确认。

“读读每页的第三行，”她说，“慢慢读，告诉我你看到什么。”

太阳已经移过窗沿，光离桌面还差一手宽。她想把纸举起来看，可纸要举稳，字就没法同时读清。
episodes.dialogue:
“第三行，”她耐心地又说了一遍，像在提醒抄书的学生，“接着读。”

你双手把原件举向光，她把修订本在下面抚平。原件里，那位值夜的宫女是“请求离岗”；修订本里，字句成了“被准许离岗”。

顾清和沉默片刻，放下了笔。

“你看清这一改意味着什么了吗？”她说，“前者是她自己选的，后者是她被允许。有人把她的决定抹平了。再过几年，就没人知道她开口说过话。”

她没有提高声音。她把双手交叠放在桌上，像看每一份经过她案头的东西那样看着两页纸，先让事情说完，再作评判。

“我不打算拿走任何一页，”她说，“也不会在任何地方写出她的名字。她还在这里当差，她的选择属于她自己。”

她拉过一张素白的工作笺，开始写一条边注，注明日期、签名，并按归档编号同时引用两页。这条差异记录，留在原件与修订本并排保存的档案里。没有偷取，没有揭发，只有一处改动的痕迹，任何查阅的人都能找到。

“把原件再举高一点，”她说，“最后一个字淡了。我想照原样抄，而不是照我猜的样子。”

你把纸页举进最后一缕阳光里。她凑近，提笔悬腕，一笔一画地写下那个字。写完，她靠回椅背，长出一口气。

“就是这样了，”她轻声说，“事情很小。可小东西才留得住。”

choices.text: 既然很小，为什么感觉这么沉？
choices.response:
顾清和抬起头，安静明亮的眼睛落在你身上。

“因为那是她亲口说的话，”她说，“一个字，一个人的选择就变成了别人的许可。我见过一个被改掉的字决定一个宫人的将来，所以在这件事上，我大概比应有的程度更在意。”

她把边注压平在镇石下，留在明处，案前当值的人经过都能看见。

“不过，谢谢你问出口，”过了一会儿她又说，“知道也有别人看见这份重量，心里会好受些。”

choices.text: （什么也不说，继续把纸页稳稳举在光下）
choices.response:
你把纸页举着，一动不动。顾清和在沉默里工作，一笔一笔临摹那些淡去的笔画，屋里只有毛笔的声音。

写完时，她抬头看了你一眼，微微一笑。

“你没有问接下来打算怎么办，”她说，“大多数人都会问。”

她轻轻从你手中接过纸页，放回修订本旁原来的位置，四角对齐。

“我很高兴你没问。这件事该由我自己来扛。但你为我举住了光，那正是我最需要的帮助。”

episodes.ending:
边注归档完毕时，阳光已经离开窗户，顾清和亲手点亮了案头的灯。

她倒了两杯素茶，茶还带着手边壶里的余温，把一杯放在你那侧桌上。架上，原件与修订本仍照旧并排放着，两者之间除了如今任何人都能追查的痕迹，别无他物。

“差异已经记录在案了，”她说，“不写名字，不给她添麻烦。有人查，就会查到。没人查，至少档案馆诚实地留住了它。”

她把自己的闲书拉过来，你注意到书页间夹着一张印花笺，上面画着一根细细的枝条。她的手指在那页上多停了一会儿，没有说话。

“春宴之前还有不少要整理的，”她说，“历次宴会的记录。这活儿慢，有人陪着做会顺当些。哪个下午，你还愿意再来这扇窗边吗？”

她问得直白，不带催促，像她给每个人都留的那条退路一样。灯光稳稳的，茶是温的，那个问题就这样坦然地留在你们之间。

episodes.title: 一箭入壶
episodes.opening:
难得的休沐日，长宁宫外的园子里满是旁人过节的喧闹。顾清和把投壶摆在路边草地上一段不近不远的距离外，你们两人之间放着两束箭。

“我得先提醒你，”她一边拢起宽袖一边说，“我的最好纪录是中了一支，而且那天纯属运气好。说不定最后变成你教我。”

话虽如此，她还是把第一支箭递给了你，郑重得像在呈递一份公文。

阳光暖暖地照在砖地上，鸭子在你身后的园池里缓缓游过。
episodes.dialogue:
顾清和先投，示范给你看。她端端正正站好，眯起眼，掷了出去。

箭落在左边三步开外，砖地上发出一声轻响。她笑了起来，头向后一仰，那支白玉簪松脱了，落进草丛里。

“哎呀，”她跪下来找簪子，“这下你见识到史官在众目睽睽的园子里落败了。请千万别把这段写进起居注。”

你帮她一起找，最后在投壶边上发现了那支簪子。它在阳光下泛着光，素净而温润。她双手接过，对这样一件小东西来说，那动作意外地珍重。

“这是件礼物，”她把簪子重新插好，“是我誊抄差事期满的时候收的。从那以后我天天戴着，可它总在我笑得太厉害的时候溜走。”

她递给你一支箭，专注地看你投掷，不放过任何细节，却什么也没说。

等到你们两个连续失手了好几次，她跪坐着往后一靠，望着投壶而不是望向你。

“我能跟你直说一件事吗？”她说，“在宫里当差，我一向以谨慎自许。可有时候，谨慎变成了沉默。我在记录里看到一个不该有的字，然后我等。我告诉自己时机未到，不能引人注目。于是那个错的字就多留了些日子。”

她拾起一支箭，翻过来看了看，又放下。

“沉默更安全，我知道。可一份因为我的谨慎而一直错下去的记录，依然是错的，而让它一直错下去的人，是我。”

choices.text: 那就挑一件。就一处订正，规规矩矩地做，走记录本身的流程。
choices.response:
顾清和沉默了片刻，然后缓缓点头，像是在拿文书与原件核对。

“一处，”她应道，“走正当的渠道，存档在可查的地方，订正放在原件旁边，绝不覆盖原文。不在暗地里做任何事。”

她坦白地说了出来，不点名道姓：上一季的一份小型宴集记录，有一个被改动过的字，悄悄改变了当初是谁做的选择。她核对了三遍，却一直没有呈报。

“明天早上，趁光线稳当的时候，我会把订正写出来，签上我自己的名字。”她拾起一支箭，出手投去，连她自己都露出了惊讶的神色——箭落进了壶里。“看，中了一支。也许今天在提醒我什么。”

choices.text: （什么也不说。拾起一支箭递给她，继续听。）
choices.response:
你没有回答，只是递给她一支箭。她接过去，肩头有什么东西松了下来。

“谢谢你，”她说，“谢谢你没有急着替我解决。大多数人还没等我把话说完，建议就已经备好了。”

她投出一箭，比之前偏差得小了些，然后安静地坐了一会儿。鸭子又游过池子；涟漪边缘的那片叶子，在鸭子停下之后还在转。

“其实我已经知道想订正哪一处了，”她终于说，“一份记录，一个字，规规矩矩地放在原件旁边呈报。我会走档案的正式渠道，落自己的名字，什么都不隐瞒。”

她看了你一眼。“我不需要有人叫我要勇敢。我需要有人在我下决心的时候坐在这里。这件事，你做到了。”

episodes.ending:
午后像所有好日子一样，不知不觉就过去了，没有一个确切的收尾。你们轮流投掷，直到箭支在壶四周散落成一片坦率的凌乱。

顾清和把箭收拢起来，一面数一面向你报出最终战果：中了一箭，是她中的，理应载入史册，流传后世。

她送你回去，一直走到岔路口，这一次簪子稳稳地没有松动。

“明天我就去做那处订正，”她说，“顺利的话，我会告诉你结果如何。不顺利的话，我也会告诉你，因为你听我说完，却没有指点我该怎么做——这比中一箭还要难得。”

她微微欠身行礼，是休沐日的那种小礼，而非当差时的规矩，然后朝档案库的方向走去。

episodes.title: 花笺
episodes.opening:
晚间巡查过后，书阁里一片安静。灯已点上，但光线很低，一天里最后的天光仍落在顾清和那张凳子旁的窗前。

你到时，她正坐在书案前，面前摊着一封拆开的信，闲书放在信旁。她抬起头，白玉簪在灯下一闪。

“你来得正巧，”她说。“我今天收到了一样东西，不想一个人搁在心里。”

她没有把信转向你，而是轻轻把它推到一边，像挪开一页决定留给自己看的纸。

“愿意的话就坐吧。茶还温着，熄灯之前，我还有一件小事要办完。”
episodes.dialogue:
她从一个小信封里取出一枚压平的桂花瓣，夹进闲书里，正好挨着书中那封折好的信。

“信是去年告老还乡的那位老仆写来的，”她说。“你记得我说过收拾行李的事，还有那两罐腌梅。她时不时来信。”

她用指尖把花瓣抚平，小心不让它裂开。

“她信里写的话，我不会念给你听。那些话是她写给我的——写她的家、她的园子、她天冷时犯疼的膝盖。说不说由她。但我会告诉你，这封信在我心里起了什么。”

她双手交叠放在案上，目光落在信的边缘。

“它让我想念她了。这是最简单的一部分。它也让我想到，我是如何在人们还在世时为他们落笔的，而绕开一个人的真实选择去写，又是多么容易。”

她起身走到放宴集记录的书架前，取下一册从前某次春宴之前的薄卷。

“这里有一条记载是事后被改过的。那次宴集上，一位仆人的选择被修饰成了更省事的样子。原件记着她实际做了什么。那次投壶之后的第二天，我照答应你的，补上了勘注。书阁收下了，原件和修订本也并排存放，谁都可以查证。”

她把卷册摊开放在案上，抽出一张新纸。

“今夜我要再补一张索引签。勘注已经在卷里，可后来的人得先知道去哪儿找。索引上只写原件、修订本和勘注的位置，不改动任何一页。”

她蘸了墨，停了停，带着一点自嘲的神色瞥了你一眼。

“取信回来的路上，我一直在练习要怎么对你说这件事。到现在也不确定说好了没有。不过你在这里，茶也温着，那这个晚上怎么都算成了。”

choices.text: 你说得很好。而且她要是知道这封信引出了这件事，也会高兴的。
choices.response:
顾清和的肩膀松了下来，看你的目光里，一半是感激，一半是笑她自己。

“你总知道什么时候该说出那句小小的真话，”她说。“好，那我不再在心里演练，直接写了。”

她提笔落纸，用她誊抄工整的笔迹写下索引签。写完，吸干墨迹，注上日期，归进目录，后来的人就能找到原件、修订本和她先前写的勘注。

“好了，”她轻声说。“难的那一步，我那天已经走了。今晚又往前走了一步。”

她给你斟了一杯新茶，像为这件小事作个纪念，又举起自己那杯，朝你微微一举——像一记她没说出口的祝辞。

choices.text: （安静地坐着，让事情过去之后她再去评判。）
choices.response:
你在凳子上坐下，什么也没说。顾清和注意到了，她的姿态松快了些。

“谢谢你，”她说。“你学会了我的习惯——让事情先过去，再去评判它。”

她安静地写了一会儿，笔稳稳地移动。有一次她停下，重读一行，把一个字换成了更平实的说法。然后她吸干墨迹，注上日期，把索引签归进目录，指向几周前那条勘注。

她靠回椅背，呼出一口气，双手在膝上放了一会儿，像一块石头终于落了地。

“成了，”她说。“她永远不会知道，她也不必知道。这才是我能安心的那种记录。”

灯花闪了闪，她伸手拿起茶壶，挪到你那一侧的案上。然后她隔着灯光端详了你片刻。

“今夜坐在这里的是你，我很高兴。”她说得简简单单，没有再多说一个字。

episodes.ending:
灯一盏一盏地暗下去，书阁越发安静了。顾清和把宴集记录放回架上，新索引签也归了档，以后的人能从那里找到她先前写的勘注。

她把闲书多摊开了一会儿，压平的花瓣就放在那封折好的信旁边，然后合上书，系好系带。

“明天春宴的筹备就要正式开始了，”她说着，把外袍抻平。“但今夜，实录是真的，友人的信安安稳稳地藏在一本书里，茶也趁温喝完了。这个晚上，账目清清楚楚。”

在门口，她停了停，一只手扶着门框，回头看了你片刻，比一句道别所需的要长。

“如果日子允许，我想在春宴之前，和你一起翻一翻历次宴集的记录。等光线稳了，到窗边来找我。”

episodes.title: 未入档的选择
episodes.opening:
午后的阳光照到档案库窗边那张凳子上。顾清和已经在上面摆好两杯素茶，还温着。
她今天坐得不像往常。卷宗已经堆叠完毕，礼制记录也归回了原处，臂弯里还夹着那本闲书，像是要拿给你看什么。
“今早送来的每一页，我都查过墨迹和纸边了，”她说，“没有一处需要我。所以我想，这一个时辰，可以属于我们。”
窗外，窗台上的纸风车迎着微风，稳稳地朝一个方向转着。
她在你身边坐下，扶正白玉发簪，用那双安静明亮的眼睛看着你。
episodes.dialogue:
“最近我在数一样东西，”顾清和双手捧着茶杯说，“是时辰。是和你一起度过的那些。”
她对自己这话微微一笑。“史官应该精确，那我就说得精确些。工作对我依然重要，起居注也重要。可如今我一早归档完毕，头一个念头却是你会不会过来。这是新的感受，我不想让它一直没说出口。”
她慢慢转着手里的杯子。“这扇窗边说的话，都不会进正式记录。无论你怎么回答，它都只留在我们之间，像压好的花瓣留在闲书里那样。”
微风掀起窗台上一页纸的边角，又让它落下。
“我想约你到档案库外面见一面，作为一次约会。”她说得很直白，“如果你想让我们保持亲近的朋友，我也珍惜。无论怎么回答，你都不欠我什么。我只是想问清楚。”

choices.text: 那就从这里开始吧——你愿意找个下午，离开档案库，和我赴一次约会吗？
choices.response:
顾清和的眼睛微微睁大，随即柔和下来。“约会，”她把这个词重复了一遍，像是在掂它的分量，然后才妥帖地收进心里。
她坐直身子，双手放在膝上——这是她让事情先说完再作判断时的习惯。“好，”她坦然地说，“我非常愿意。”
“但不能在工作时间，”她补充道，语气里有暖意，还有一点笑意，“也别靠近任何账册，不然你会发现我在检查茶馆菜单的边缘。园子池塘边有一条长凳，傍晚阳光斜照得恰到好处，鸭子也是好伴。下个休沐日怎么样？”
她伸过手来，用指尖碰了碰你杯沿，算是一场小小的碰杯。“这一次也不写进起居注。但我会记得分毫不差。”

choices.text: （告诉她你想保持亲近的友谊，再把茶杯放在她的茶杯旁。）
choices.response:
你告诉她，你想继续做亲近的朋友。顾清和点点头，没有追问。她在凳子上挪了挪，让阳光照到你们两个人身上，趁茶还温着慢慢喝。
“你知道吗，”过了一会儿她说，“当年那位年长的仆妇回乡去了，我怀念的是这样的午后。两个人，一扇窗，没有什么需要解决的事。”
她的肩轻轻靠上你的肩，小心而不急促。“我听见了。留在记录之外的亲近友谊，也是一个真实而好的回答。”
窗台上的风车朝着它唯一忠实的方向转着。她翻开闲书，找到夹着压花的那一页，什么也没说地递给你看。
“明天你归档完就过来吧，”她说。“阳光会在这里，我也会。”

episodes.ending:
无论这一个时辰如何度过，它都留在窗边，不入任何册页。
顾清和送你到档案库门口，在门框边停下，一半在灯火里，一半在最后的日光中。
“不管今天我们怎么称呼它，”她说，“它都不是对任何东西的修订。它是一份原件。我如今会把原件留在身边。”
她轻轻碰了一下白玉发簪，是个小小的、习惯性的祈愿，然后笑了。
“春宴之前，往昔聚会的记录还得整理，”她说，“可在那之后的下一个时辰——”她把话留着不说满，像一扇为你不关上的门，“——到时候由我们决定。”
风车在她身后转着，稳稳地迎着微风。午后就这样温和地结束了，只许诺它曾经发生。

episodes.title: 闲书
episodes.opening:
春宴前半日，档案馆闭馆，顾清和把一张小桌搬到向阳窗边的廊下。桌上摆着投壶——一只画着环纹的陶壶——一壶带盖的清茶、两只杯子，还有她的闲书，花笺从书页间歪歪斜斜地探出来。
她用一根素绳束起袖口，把白玉簪比平日插得更牢。你注意到她选这个位置之前看了两回风向；窗台上的纸风车稳稳地朝着花园的方向转。
“今早我把卷宗核了两遍，”她一边倒第一杯茶一边说，“所以在熄灯之前，起居注离了我也无妨。坐吧，窗边那张凳子是你的。它如今算是记着你的名字了，非正式的那种。”
阳光如期落在那张凳子上。楼下某处，两只鸭子游过园中水池，一片叶子在水纹早该停了之后还在打转。
episodes.dialogue:
她先投，差了整整一步，箭在砖上叮当一声——正像她从前告诉过你的那样。她没有叹气，只拿一颗小石子标出落点，把第二支箭递给你。
“咱们俩合起来能进一枝，就算不错的下午了，”她说，“我对箭没有野心。”
下一轮她的箭擦着壶口晃了晃，落了进去。她笑出声，发簪又滑了下来；这回她接住它，平放在茶壶旁边，像把公务也一并放下了。
“你知道吗，这星期我翻了宴会的记录。历次聚会的名字、祝酒、座次。”她慢慢转着杯子。“里面没有你的名字，以后也不会有。我是有意把生活里这一部分留在纸外的。这里发生的事——投偏的箭、这盏茶、这本书——属于这个下午，不属于起居注。”
她翻开闲书，先是一瓣压平的桂花，再翻到一张花笺，上面有人曾为遮荫画了三片叶子。她让你慢慢看，两页都不催你。
“有一件事想问你，”她说。那一瞬她双手按在膝上，坐得笔直，让问题先说完，再由你们二人各自去掂量。“改日再过这样一个下午，等差事容得下的时候。不为任何场合，不为任何差遣，也没有什么要记档的。只在你自己也愿意的前提下。我不预设答案。”

choices.text: 我愿意。不用写在任何历书上，我也会来。
choices.response: 她笑了，是那种小小的、真切的笑。“不写在历书上，”她应道，“等阳光照到那张凳子，壶摆上了桌，你就知道是那一天了。”她先给你续了茶，才轮到自己，然后一边投下一箭，一边笨拙又快乐地解释，为什么那支擦过壶口的箭，对你们俩来说也算得上一场差一点成功的小胜仗。

choices.text: （把她投偏的那支箭拾起来，轻轻放进壶里。）
choices.response: 她看着那支箭落定，沉默了片刻，随即笑出声来。“这一枝算这个院子的，不算你我的。咱们就算平局。”她伸手把纸风车摆正，让它正对着风，然后倒上第二杯茶，把闲书往桌子中间挪了挪，挪到你们两个都够得着的地方。

episodes.ending:
这个下午的收尾像好的记录一样，没有半分勉强。日头斜过窗子后，她收起箭，用园墙边水盆里的清水洗净杯子，把发簪戴回原处。
廊子的转角处她停了下来。“谢谢你陪我过了这个下午。它不在起居注里，以后也不会在，而它好就好在这里。”她略略举起那本闲书，像行了个小小的礼。“明天我在案前，若你想见那个无趣的我。但这张窗边的凳子我会一直留着，以防万一。”
她朝档案馆走去，步子不急不缓，园中水池边那片叶子在水纹里转着，鸭子早已游远了。下一个寻常日子会是什么样子尚不可知，但那里似乎已为你留出了一个位置。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 我们自选的一日
romance.opening:
今天档案馆的灯早早熄了。顾清和在廊下等你，不在书案前——仅此一点你就知道，这不是什么差事。白玉簪照旧簪在原处，手里没有带任何卷宗。

她在午后阳光照到的屋檐下摆了一张小桌：两只杯子，一把素茶壶，还有投壶和一捆箭。闲书合着放在她手肘旁，夹着一枚压花书签。

“我告了整整一个下午的假，”她说。“不是当值之间的一刻钟，是完完整整的一个下午。”

她摆正茶杯，然后像面对一份需要诚实解读的文书那样，直直地看着你。

“今天我想和你待满整个下午。喝茶，投壶，在档案库之外好好说话。离开之前，我还有一个问题想直接问你。”
romance.dialogue:
她双手搭在膝上，坐得笔直，让这个问题先立在那里，不急着翻过去。

“这里的一切都不会放到原件旁边，”她补充道。“它是我们俩的，只属于我们，也可以一直这样小小的。”

她斟茶，蒸汽在你们之间升起。她取出一枚压好的桂花瓣摆在桌上，转了转，让光线落在花瓣上。

“这一片我验过墨了，”她面无表情地说。“先看边缘和涂改，老习惯。”

她把投壶放到你们中间。“我们轮着来。不计分，或者说，只马马虎虎地计。我这辈子第一支箭偏了三步，当的一声磕在砖上，所以你今天掷得再差，也算得上好同伴。”

她的第一支箭落在壶口附近，又蹦了出去。她笑起来，玉簪滑下了半指，她随即推了回去。

“你什么也没看见，”她说着，把下一支箭递给你。

最后一支箭投完，她放下箭，直直地看着你。“现在我想问：你还愿意和我继续约会吗？我想听你亲口回答，不想只凭你的神情猜。”

choices.text: 是的。我仍然想要。我想和你一起度过像今天这样的日子。
choices.response:
顾清和静了片刻，然后点了一下头，仿佛把这句话记在了某个永远不会被旁人读到的地方。

“那就这样定了。因为我们两人都亲口说了出来。”

她先替你续上茶，才轮到自己——这是她只对亲近之人才有的小小礼数。

“告诉你一件我从没写进任何起居注的事。我擅长追索别人的抉择，却不太擅长做自己的。但这一件，我早已做好了。我只是庆幸，它恰好与你的相同。”

choices.text: （握住她的手，说：“是的，我还想和你继续约会。”）
choices.response:
你握住她的手，把话说得很清楚。她没有抽回手，先把你的回答听完了。

“好，”她轻声说。“谢谢你说出来。我也愿意。”

她在你掌中翻过手，十指相扣，然后把茶壶推到你那一侧，像在说：先喝茶，别急着把话说完。

“那么趁热喝吧。等你失手没投进壶里的时候——你一定会失手的——我保证善意地笑。这是我今天下午的约定。”

romance.ending:
日光斜过屋檐，你们谁都没有察觉。箭已收拢，茶壶已空，顾清和的闲书也从手肘旁挪到了桌上——她曾打开一次，想给你看一行字，又发觉那行字不及眼前的人，便重新合上了。

她站起身，抚平裙摆，却没有把投壶收走。

“就留在这儿吧，”她说。“没人会动它。它留在这里，下一次就更好安排了。”

她望向园中池畔，两只鸭子刚游过，一片叶子还在它们荡开的涟漪边缘打着转。

“我不敢擅自定下日子，”她说。“你挑一个上午，或者我挑一个傍晚，或者我们就在窗边高高兴兴地争一争。哪一样都合我意。要紧的是，我们谁都不必等着对方先开口。”

她轻轻碰了一下白玉簪，那是她高兴时的习惯。

“谢谢你今天陪我，”她说，“我想继续和你约会。下一次也这样，好吗？”她朝你伸出手。你握住她的手，一起往园门走，边走边商量下回在哪儿见。

episodes.title: The Cracked Pane
episodes.opening:
The lantern market smells of oil and sugar, and Kian stops at a stall where a glass lamp sits apart from the others.
One pane is cracked, a hairline running like a dry riverbed.
He turns it in the lamplight and does not haggle.
"It still gives light," he says, more to himself than to anyone.
Then he notices you watching, and he turns a beat late, the way he still does when someone calls him Qi'an.
"Ah.
Forgive me.
Kian," he adds, tapping his own chest.
"The court name is theirs.
This one is mine.
" He holds the cracked lamp up between you.
"The merchant will sell it cheap because of the flaw.
But a lamp is judged at night, not in daylight, and at night you would never know.
"
episodes.dialogue:
He buys it.
He counts out the coins the way his father taught him, checking the tally twice before the seller's palm closes, and he catches himself doing it and laughs.
"Old habit.
My father kept the caravan accounts.
I once promised a man double the wool we had, and my father made me count the bales myself until the number lived in my hands.
" He wraps the lamp in cloth with surprising care.
"Where I live, there was a rose that opened first after every rain.
My mother tends the garden.
She wrote to me that this year it bloomed before all the others, and she could not say why.
I think about that flower more than I should.
" He glances at you sideways.
"You stood there a while, so I decided you were listening before you asked.
" The crowd flows past, and he steps with it, keeping the lamp cradled against his ribs.

choices.text: "A flaw you can name is a fact about the lamp you can work with."
choices.response:
He stops walking and looks at you properly.
"That is exactly what the repairman said.
A traveler fixed my barbat once, cracked soundboard and all, and he would not take payment until I said his name back to him.
I still remember it.
You give a thing a name and it stops being broken.
" He lifts the wrapped lamp a little.
"So this one has a story now, and it is partly yours.
"

choices.text: Say nothing. Walk beside him to the edge of the market.
choices.response:
The silence is not uncomfortable, and he does not fill it with court politeness.
At the lantern market's edge he pauses under the last row of hanging lights.
"You listen the way my mother does.
She never interrupts the garden.
She just stands there until it shows her what it needs.
" He says it plainly, then seems surprised at himself.
"That was a private thing to say to someone I met over a cracked lamp.
But there it is.
"

episodes.ending:
At the mouth of the lane he offers you the lamp to hold, just for a moment.
It is warm from his hands and lighter than it looks.
"Cracked pane," he says, "and it held.
" He takes it back before you can protest, nods once, and walks toward the Hall of the Four Directions, the lamp swinging gently at his side.
Behind him the market keeps burning its hundred unbroken lanterns, and somehow the flawed one is the one you will remember.

episodes.title: Two Names for One Star
episodes.opening:
The observatory terrace is cold after dark, and Kian is there alone with Xie Dengwei's star charts spread on a stone table, weighted at the corners with small brass weights.
When he hears your footsteps he calmly lifts one chart and tilts it toward you.
"Come settle a quarrel for me.
Astronomer Xie gave me a name for that star there, the bright one low in the east.
I gave him mine.
He insists they are different stars because the names are different.
" He smiles.
"I insist they are the same star, because the light is the same light.
" The wind moves his hair across his jaw and he pushes it back, still looking at the sky rather than at you.
episodes.dialogue:
"In my tongue we call it the Shepherd's Lantern," he says, pointing.
"He calls it something I mispronounce beautifully.
I have been practicing.
Listen.
" He tries the Chinese name twice, gets it wrong twice in two different ways, and laughs at himself without a trace of embarrassment.
"Third time.
" He gets it right, barely, and looks pleased as a boy.
"You see.
Two names, one star.
My cousin Dara would have said that proves names are worthless.
He once tried to trade a brass button for a horse, so I no longer trust his judgments.
" He rolls the chart closed but does not leave.
"My mother writes that the first rose opened after the rain again this year.
She marks the day on the wall of the garden house.
Years of days, in her own hand.
I think names work the same way.
Said often enough, in the right place, they stay.
" He glances at you.
"Tell me what your people call it.
I will keep both.
"

choices.text: Tell him the name you grew up hearing for that star.
choices.response:
He repeats it carefully, syllable by syllable, until it sits right in his mouth.
"Now I have three names for one star.
I am rich and slightly confused.
" He writes it in the margin of Xie Dengwei's chart, in his own borrowed characters, the strokes crooked but legible.
"The astronomer will scold me for defacing his chart.
It is worth it.
"

choices.text: Shake your head. You never learned the star's name.
choices.response:
He considers this with real seriousness.
"Then you know it the way my mother knows her roses.
No name, only the habit of looking.
" He wraps the chart in its cloth.
"That is not a lesser way.
I catalog things because I am far from home and it comforts me.
You look at things because they are there.
One of us is probably wiser, and it is late enough that I will not say which.
"

episodes.ending:
He walks you down the terrace steps, charts under his arm, and at the bottom he stops.
"The light is the same light," he says again, quieter now, as if closing an argument he has been having with himself all evening.
"Whatever we call it.
" Then he heads for the Hall of the Four Directions, and above the wall the Shepherd's Lantern, under whichever name, keeps its low and steady burn.

episodes.title: Read the Tally
episodes.opening:
The evening before the regent's audience, Kian comes to the guest hall carrying a ledger and a face that is trying very hard to be calm.
He sits across from you, opens the ledger to a page dense with figures, and slides it over.
"My father taught me to check a tally before offering a promise.
Tomorrow I offer one to Regent Xiao.
Tonight I cannot see this page straight.
I have read it so many times the numbers have started to move.
" His hands rest flat on the table, and you notice they are not quite steady.
"Would you read it?
Fresh eyes.
Tell me what the caravan carries and what it asks, in your own words, and I will know if it says what I think it says.
"
episodes.dialogue:
While you read, he does not watch you.
He watches the lamp on the table instead, the small glass one with the cracked pane, and he tells you things the ledger will not show.
"The inspection schedule at the Southern Gate took a year.
Yue Changning meets the caravans at dawn, every dawn, and now the checks are written down instead of decided by mood.
That line there, the one about food and shelter during verification, that took the longest.
A traveler stranded at a gate with empty hands is a man with no dinner.
" You finish reading and he finally looks up.
"Well?
Say it plainly.
Flatter me tomorrow, not tonight.
" When you give it back to him in your own words, he closes his eyes for a moment, then nods slowly.
"Yes.
That is what it says.
Thank you.
" He taps the ledger twice.
"A promise only matters after I know who must keep it.
Tomorrow I learn if it is them.
Or me.
"

choices.text: "You already know who keeps it. You do. You've done it at that gate every dawn for a year."
choices.response:
He is quiet for a long moment.
"That is a kind reading, and I want it to be true.
" He straightens the ledger's corners.
"But a permit is not kept by one man.
It is kept by clerks I have never met, in winters when I am not there.
That is what I must make true tomorrow.
Still.
" He puts a hand briefly over his own chest.
"Still.
Thank you.
I will carry that sentence into the hall.
"

choices.text: Say nothing. Refill his cup and let him sit with the numbers.
choices.response:
He accepts the cup and drinks without looking at it.
The lamp flame moves in the draft, and the cracked pane throws a thin doubled line of light across the table.
"You are good at this," he says at last.
"The sitting.
My mother does it too.
She sits with the garden before she touches it.
" He draws the ledger back toward himself, and this time when he reads it, his hands are steady.

episodes.ending:
He leaves late, ledger under his arm and the lamp lit, its crack a thin bright seam in the dark corridor.
At the door he turns.
"If I come back tomorrow having lost the negotiation, I will come back with a narrower request and I will ask you to read that one too.
And if I win, you are reading it anyway, because I will be too busy being pleased with myself to be trustworthy.
" The corridor takes his footsteps, and the small light wobbles away down the hall.

episodes.title: The Garden After the Audience
episodes.opening:
The regent heard the petition.
The regent did not end it.
Kian walks the guest hall garden with his kaftan collar undone for the first time since he arrived, and the evening air moves against his throat like something unfamiliar.
He finds you near the stone bench under the old plum tree and does not stand on ceremony.
"You heard.
Narrower than I wanted.
Seasonal permits only, with the shelter clause kept and the winter clause dropped.
" He sits down heavily beside you.
"A year ago that would have felt like losing.
Now I know what a narrow request can grow into.
The schedule at the Southern Gate started narrower than this.
" He looks at the dark water of the pond, then at you, and the court quickness drains out of his voice.
"But that is not what I came to say.
"
episodes.dialogue:
He turns so that he faces you fully, and there is nothing performed in it.
"Five years ago I corrected a tally and won a season.
Since then there is a schedule, and a shelter clause, and Yue Changning at the gate at dawn.
And there is this garden, where I have been practicing names and losing arguments about stars.
" He breathes out.
"What we are, you and I, I have been careful not to name, because naming a thing too early is how you break it.
My father checked a tally before he promised.
So.
I am checking now, and the count is yours to make.
" He holds your eyes.
"I am asking you to choose, plainly, with no debt to my petition and no weight from it.
The caravans were never yours to bargain with, and neither is this.
Friend is a true answer.
I would like to be your partner.
If you want that too, say so; if you want friendship, say that.
Whichever you say, the permits stand, the schedule stands, and I stand in this garden either way.
" The wind moves through the plum tree and neither of you looks up.

choices.text: "I want us to be a couple."
choices.response:
He laughs once, softly, and lays his hand palm-up on the bench between you.
"A couple.
I would like that very much.
" He waits for you to decide whether to take his hand.
"I write to my mother whenever a caravan travels west.
May I tell her about us in the next letter?
There is no hurry to decide that tonight.
" The pond has gone dark.
For once he lets a question wait without preparing the answer.

choices.text: "Friend. A true answer, and one I mean."
choices.response:
He nods, and the nod is steady.
"Friends.
I am glad we can say it plainly.
" He settles back against the bench, leaving room between you.
"Dara will be insufferable when I tell him I have a friend who out-argues an astronomer.
He can be insufferable.
The button and the horse, and he still talks about it.
" He points out a frog on the pond wall, watching it try to climb a wet stone.
You stay to see whether it makes it.

episodes.ending:
You sit in the garden until the lanterns along the wall burn low, and whichever answer was given, it holds.
The petition stands on its own terms, seasonal and narrow and real.
Kian walks you as far as the guest hall steps, says goodnight in his own tongue, and translates it before you ask: the road behind you, the road ahead.
In the morning the Southern Gate opens at dawn, and the schedule holds.

episodes.title: The Clear Schedule
episodes.opening:
The morning is the fifth spring since the first banquet, and the Southern Gate opens with a sound like a held breath let go.
Yue Changning stands at the checkpoint with the new inspection schedule in hand, and Kian stands beside her with the caravan manifests, and for once neither of them is checking anything.
The schedule is one page.
It fits in a traveler's pocket.
It says what is inspected, when, and where a stranded traveler eats and sleeps while the papers are read.
Kian slides it toward you across the gatehouse table.
"Read it," he says.
"You read the first tally.
It is only right you read the last page.
"
episodes.dialogue:
"Yue Changning wrote half of this," he says, while the first caravan of the season passes through the gate behind you, bells and dust and thin Camels complaining.
"I argued for the rest.
We fought over one line for a week.
The one about verification, about no one waiting outside the wall.
" He looks at her, and she looks back with the flat patience of a person who has stood at this gate at dawn a thousand times, and he grins.
"She won.
The line is better her way.
" He turns back to you.
"You know what my father would say.
He would say, count it.
So I counted.
Five springs.
One seasonal agreement grown into a standing schedule.
Dara came with this caravan, and he tried to trade a brass button for a mule at the last stop, so some things do not change either.
" He sets the schedule down and smooths it flat with both palms.
"My mother's rose opened first after the rain again.
She says it is the roots.
I used to think that was a saying about roses.
It is not a saying about roses.
"

choices.text: "Five years, and the whole thing fits on one page. That's the real victory."
choices.response:
He laughs.
"The regent's clerks wanted forty pages and three seals.
I told them a traveler at dusk cannot read forty pages by torchlight, and Yue Changning told them a page must fit a coat pocket, and between the two of us they surrendered.
" He rolls a copy and presses it into your hands.
"Keep this one.
The first tally and the last page.
A matched set.
"

choices.text: Say nothing. Watch the caravan pass through the open gate.
choices.response:
He watches with you, and for a while neither of you speaks, and the gate does its work.
Dust settles on his kaftan and he does not brush it off.
"The first year I stood here," he says finally, "I thought the work was the petition.
It was never the petition.
It was this, over and over, at dawn, until it was boring.
Boring is the victory.
Nobody writes ballads about boring.
" He sounds very content about it.

episodes.ending:
The last animal of the caravan clears the gate, and Yue Changning closes the schedule book with a snap that sounds like approval.
Kian walks you back along the wall toward the Hall of the Four Directions, and in the small garden he stops by the bench under the plum tree.
"The cycle can begin again with the next caravan," he says.
"The hall will still have me.
The schedule will hold without me.
That is the difference between a favor and a thing that is built.
" He looks at the garden, the gate, the road.
"My mother would tell you the roots are the whole of it.
She is right, as usual.
"

speak.text: ♡ I want to be a couple

romance.title: The Repaired Lamp
romance.opening:
The regent's hall is full and formal, and Kian is calm in a way he was not the first time he stood here.
The petition is five years settled now, the schedule working at the Southern Gate without argument.
He carries the glass lamp with the cracked pane, repaired since, the seam a thin bright line of new glass.
He waits beside you while the audience is called.
"You chose in a garden," he says quietly, so only you can hear.
"It is only right you stand here when it is named.
" The regent nods, and Kian steps forward, and he does not reach for your hand in front of the court.
He reaches for your eyes, and holds them.
romance.dialogue:
"Regent Xiao," he says, clear and quick, "I ask permission to light this lamp in your hall.
" He does not explain the crack.
He explains the repair.
"A traveler fixed my barbat once and would not take payment until I remembered his name.
This lamp was broken when I bought it, and it has given light every night since I had it mended.
My mother writes that her first rose opens before all the others after rain, and she says it is the roots.
" He turns the lamp so the court can see the bright seam.
"Five years ago I came here to ask for a season.
I stayed, and the season became a schedule, and the schedule became a road that does not strand anyone.
And I did not do it alone.
" He looks at you again.
"This person read my first tally when my eyes were too tired to see it straight.
This person chose me in a garden, plainly, when I asked.
I am not in the habit of naming what is mine before I am sure.
I am sure.
The lamp, the road, and this.
All three are kept things, and keeping is the whole of it.
" He lights the wick and the flame stands steady, and the cracked pane throws its thin doubled line of light across the polished floor, unmistakable, whole.

choices.text: Step forward beside him. "What he keeps, I keep. Ask him about the tally sometime."
choices.response:
The court murmurs and Kian laughs, one short unguarded sound he will pretend later never happened.
"The tally," he says, recovering, "is a story for a smaller room.
But the keeping, that part was said exactly right.
" Under the table, out of every protocol's sight, his hand finds yours and stays.

choices.text: Stay where you are, and meet his eyes until he smiles.
choices.response:
He understands at once that the silence is the answer, and his whole face changes.
"You see how it is," he tells the regent.
"I do the talking.
The rest of it happens without me.
" The regent's mouth twitches at one corner, which from Regent Xiao is a standing ovation, and the lamp burns on between you, its bright seam unhidden.

romance.ending:
After the hall empties, the two of you carry the lamp back through the dusk to the Hall of the Four Directions, past the small garden where the answer was given.
Kian sets it on the windowsill of his rooms, where the light can reach the courtyard.
"My mother will want every detail," he says, already composing the letter in his head, "the lamp, the regent's twitch, your one sentence in the great hall.
She will say the rose knew.
She always says the rose knew.
" Outside, the gate road runs west toward her garden, and the schedule at the Southern Gate holds at every dawn, and on the sill the lamp with its bright seam burns without flickering, a kept thing among kept things.

episodes.title: 灯罩上的裂纹
episodes.opening:
启安把那盏小玻璃灯摆在窗台上，指腹顺着灯罩上一道细裂摸了一遍，又一遍。
傍晚的光从裂纹里漏进来，在他袖口画了条亮线。
「你来得正好。
」他回头，笑的时候露出一点无奈，「我在想，这盏灯还能不能用。
它跟着我从家乡走过来，路上磕的。
裂纹不长，可是擦灯的时候，手总能碰到它。
」他挪了挪灯座，让光偏开一点，「烧油脂的时候不烫手，就是心里不太舒服。
你说，是留着它，还是让它歇了？
」
episodes.dialogue:
他没等你答，先把灯罩取下来，对着天光看了看那道裂痕。
「其实我出门前就知道它裂了。
」启安把灯罩托在掌心，「那晚在戈壁边上歇脚，风把驮架掀了半边，我第一件事不是捡散落的货，是先找这盏灯。
找到的时候它就多了这道口子。
」他把灯罩轻轻放回窗台，声音慢下来，「带它出来，是因为家里院子也有一盏一样的。
我母亲每晚点着，说灯亮着，回家的人就不会走错门。
我带了一盏出来，算是替她守路。
」他忽然笑了，抬手把一缕垂下来的卷发别到耳后，「你看，我数账从不出错，偏偏带一件易碎的东西走一千里。
」窗外的更鼓敲了一声，他偏头听了听，「四方馆的人喊我名字，我还是反应慢半拍。
启安。
多叫几次就顺了吧。
你叫我的时候，我自己都得愣一下，才想起来是在叫我。
」他拿起一小瓶玫瑰水，往自己手背抹了点，递到你鼻子底下，「闻闻？
我母亲园子里就是这个味道。
她信里说，有一株玫瑰今年开得特别晚，别人都谢了它才开。
我猜它是在等我回去。
」他说这话的时候，眼睛弯着，语气却认真，像在核对一笔很重要的账。
他抬起头，「你晚上出门办事吗？
要是路过灯市，替我看一眼，有没有和这个差不多大小的灯罩。
裂纹可以留着，但我想让里面的光稳一点。
」

choices.text: 「裂纹不用遮，灯还亮着就值。」
choices.response:
启安愣了一下，随即笑出声，抬手朝你做了个请的手势。
「这句话我得记下来，将来写在给达拉的信里。
我那个小表弟，小时候想拿一颗铜扣换一匹马，人人都笑他，就我父亲没笑，只让他先把铜扣擦亮再说。
你这句话，和擦亮铜扣是一个道理。
」他把灯罩扶正，往炉边挪了挪，「那就留着裂。
今晚我点它。
」他伸手拨了拨灯芯，光透过裂纹在墙上折出一小道亮痕。
「是我该谢谢你。
我在这儿说话还总怕说错，你这么一说，我忽然不怕了。
」

choices.text: 不说话，只是伸手指了指那道裂纹的位置。
choices.response:
启安顺着你指的地方看过去，看了好一会儿。
屋里静下来，只有更鼓的余音。
「我父亲以前教我，对数之前先安静。
」他终于开口，声音放得很低，「他说账本会自己说话，你要是不吵，就听得见错在哪儿。
」他伸出手指，隔着一寸的距离虚描那道裂纹，像在纸上描一个数字。
「你看，它从底部往上走，到一半就停了。
没穿顶。
它撑住了。
」他直起身，长出一口气，肩膀松了下来。
「好，留着。
不换灯罩了。
」他从腰带上解下一小块软布，把灯座细细擦了一遍，动作慢，稳。
「坐一会儿吧，我给你倒茶。
灯点起来，比白天好看。
」

episodes.ending:
灯终于点上了。
裂纹里的光比别处细，斜斜地落在窗纸上，像一笔没写完的字。
启安盘腿坐在灯旁，慢条斯理地给巴尔巴特琴上松香，一边上一边小声哼着什么。
哼到一半他停下来，问你要不要听一支家乡的曲子，说完不等回答，先拨了一个音。
琴声很低，像是怕吵着灯。
那一晚他没再提请愿，也没提账本，只提了一次母亲，说晚开的那株玫瑰，等他回去的时候大概已经谢了，但明年还会开。
临走时他把灯往窗台内侧推了推。
「放在这儿，明天早上你从园子里过，抬头就看得见。
」他说这话时正对着灯，你只看见他侧脸的笑。
裂纹还在，但再没有人提要不要换掉它。

episodes.title: 一颗星的两个名字
episodes.opening:
观星台的石阶还带着白天的余温。
启安仰着头，一只手搭在栏杆上，另一只手在半空划了一道弧线，停在一颗亮星上。
「在那边。
」他压低声音，像怕惊动什么，「我们叫它苏赫拉，意思是玫瑰。
你们的星图上叫它什么来着，我总记不住那个音。
」他偏过头看你，眼睛里有星光，「一颗星，两个名字，指的是同一样东西。
我每次想起这个，就特别高兴。
你呢？
」
episodes.dialogue:
他把从家乡带回来的星图在石台上铺开，四角压上随身带的玉扣和一小袋藏红花，免得被夜风吹走。
「你看这儿，」他的指尖顺着星图上一组连线走，「我们那儿的牧人，看这颗星定了三百年的路。
商队夜行，它偏一分，我们就知道走岔了。
」启安抬起头，卷发被夜风掀起一角。
「我父亲第一次带队走夜路，就是靠它。
他跟我说过，星星认名字，你叫得对了，它就一直在原来的地方等你。
」他忽然低头笑了一下，是自己汉话说岔了的那种笑，「不对，我这句话说得绕了。
意思是，名字各叫各的，路是一条路。
」他把星图往你那边推了推，「上次谢灯微同我对星名，她指给我看你们这里的说法，我当时就想，回去要画进我这张图里。
所以你看，图的边上留了空。
」星图边缘果然留了一行空白，墨迹还没沾上去。
「你帮我写吧。
用你们的字，写它的名字。
写完这颗星就有两个名字了，一个在你们的夜里，一个在我的夜里，可它还是那颗星。
」他说这话时语速慢了下来，逐字掂量着，像在请愿殿上措辞那样认真，又比那时松弛得多。
夜风把烛台的火苗压低了一线，他伸手拢了拢，然后从怀里摸出一个小瓷瓶。
「玫瑰水，路上剩下的最后一点了。
擦在手腕上，夜里不招虫。
」他顿了顿，补充道，「也是我母亲园子里的方子。
好东西我都带一小份，不多的。
」他把瓷瓶搁在星图一角，挨着藏红花，然后重新抬眼找那颗星。
「你看，它升上来了。
比我家乡看见的位置高。
第一次在这儿看见它的时候，我一个人在四方馆的园子里站了半个时辰。
」

choices.text: 一边写下一个名字，一边把家乡的叫法也跟着念了一遍。
choices.response:
启安听着你念出「苏赫拉」的音，眼睛慢慢睁大了一点，随即笑得肩膀都抖了。
「对，就是这个音！
你念得比谢灯微还准。
」他俯身看你落笔，每写完一个字就跟着轻声读一遍，读到一半忽然安静下来。
「我到这里以后，学着写你们的字，一笔一笔都拆开记。
今天有人往我这边写，还是第一次。
」他没有再说下去，只是等墨迹干透，才小心地把星图卷起来，用那根系琴匣的皮绳捆好。
「这张图回乡之后挂在我房间里。
以后我母亲看到边上那行字，会问是谁写的。
我就说，是一个夜里陪我看星星的人。
」他把「陪」字说得又轻又稳。

choices.text: 把星图推回去，请他自己用汉字写下那颗星的名字。
choices.response:
启安愣了一瞬，随即明白了，耳根在星光下微微发亮。
「让我写？
」他拿起笔，蘸墨的手停在半空，「我写过请愿的折子，写过账目，没在你们的星图上写过字。
写错可就留在这儿了。
」你不接笔，他只好深吸一口气，一笔一笔写下去。
写到第三个字的时候手抖了一下，那个字歪了一点，他盯着看了半天，没刮掉。
「就让它歪着。
」他放下笔，指着那个字，「歪的那一笔是我的，其余的是你们的。
以后看见它，我就想起今晚是谁把笔塞回我手里的。
」他把瓷瓶往你那边推了半寸，「玫瑰水归你了。
理由我想好了：今晚你教会我的，比一瓶水多。
」

episodes.ending:
下观星台的时候，夜已经深了。
启安把星图卷得紧紧的，抱在怀里像抱着一件比琴还金贵的东西。
石阶上他走在你外侧，一手虚扶着，嘴里还在小声对那颗星，先用他的名字念一遍，再用刚学来的名字念一遍，念第二遍的时候明显慢，字咬得很用力。
走到园子口，他停下来。
「我来得匆忙，路上丢了些东西，也捡了些东西。
」他想了想，换了个说法，「不对，应该是换了一些。
丢了的那颗铜扣，是达拉的，我一直记着。
捡的，是今晚这个写法。
」他朝你拱了拱手，姿势学得一本正经，袖口的宝石扣在灯下闪了一下。
「明天我还要去南门找岳长宁，对查验的时刻。
你要是得起早，就别陪我了。
要是不起早，我在南门那边等你，商队进城的时候，是他一天里最忙也最好看的时候，我说的好看是指马蹄和尘土，你别误会。
」说完他自己先笑了，转身往四方馆走，走了几步又回头补了一句，「星图我收好了，压在琴匣底下，丢不了。
」

episodes.title: 请愿前夜对账
episodes.opening:
客厅的烛台点了两支，账册在桌上摊开，纸角被石镇纸压得平平整整。
启安的袖子挽到小臂，一手拿笔，一手数着算筹，数到一半抬起头。
「你来得好。
」他往旁边挪了挪凳子，给你空出半张桌，「明天我在殿上递请愿，为商队要过关的文书和查验的安排。
今晚这一遍，我想找人陪我对。
以前在家，父亲对数的时候，桌上永远坐两个人。
他念，我核。
」他把算筹往你那边推了推，「今晚你念，我核，行吗？
」
episodes.dialogue:
账册从第一页翻起，是出发前记的那本，边角磨得起了毛。
「这本是从家乡带来的，路上翻了一千里。
」启安的指尖停在其中一行，「这儿，出发前查出一处错数。
三十七驮记成了七十三驮，差点多报了一倍的货。
那天晚上我和父亲在灯底下翻了两个时辰才找出来。
他没骂我，只说了一句，承诺之前先对数。
这句话我带到现在。
」你每念一个数，他就用算筹在桌上点一下，点得又轻又匀。
对到中途，他忽然停下来，按住你正要念的下一行。
「等一下。
这个数，乳香，二十担。
沈阙登记的时候我记的是二十担，可路上我们折耗了半担，抵了住店的费用。
明天的请愿里我要不要提这半担？
」他自问自答地皱起眉，又自己摇头，「要提。
隐瞒的事一多，往后每一条都可信不起来。
父亲要是坐在这儿，他也会说提。
」烛花爆了一声，他伸手剪了剪，火光稳下来，他的眉头也松了些。
他难得说得这么直，手仍然搭在账册上：「我怕的是殿上有人问我，商队凭什么信你。
我就想说，因为每一个数我都陪着走过夜路。
可这话在殿上说，未免太软。
」他抬眼看你，那点不安在眼睛里没藏住，「你们这儿的人，听软话吗？
」不等回答，他又低头核完了最后一行，合上账册，掌心在封皮上按了按，像按住一颗不太安分的心。
「对了。
还有一个数没进账册。
」他放慢了速度，「五年，如果这一季的许可再批下来，商队能来五年。
我数的时候手会抖，你信不信。
」他把手伸平给你看，指尖很稳，然后自己先笑了，「看，不抖。
那是刚才在路上偷偷抖过的。
」

choices.text: 「软话也是话，说真的就行。」
choices.response:
启安慢慢靠回椅背，把这句话在心里过了一遍。
「说真的就行。
」他重复了一遍，然后忽然坐直，「那我就这么写进腹稿里。
明天有人问，我就答：商队信我，因为每个数我都核过，连折耗的半担乳香我也带来了。
」他抓起笔，蘸墨，把这句添在草稿的末尾，写完自己读了一遍，耳根有点红。
「殿上说这种话，怕是要被人笑。
可是笑我的人，也拿不出更真的话来。
」他把笔搁下，郑重地朝你拱手，这一回拱得很标准，不像上次那种学的样子。
「父亲的对数，配上你这句话，明天应该够用了。
」

choices.text: 不说劝的话，只把那半担乳香的折耗数目清清楚楚补写在页边。
choices.response:
启安看着你落笔，看那行小字端端正正落在页边，看了很久没说话。
烛火跳了一下，他伸手把账册转了个方向，让那行字正对自己。
「你什么都没劝我。
」他的声音有点哑，清了清嗓子才接着说，「可是我看见这行字，就知道该怎么办了。
半担是半担，写在这儿，它就不怕问。
」他把页边那行字用指腹轻轻抚平，仿佛怕墨没干透。
「从前是父亲坐在我对面，现在是这一行字坐在我对面。
都是一样的。
」他合上账册，用皮绳捆好，捆得比平时紧。
「今晚我不改一个字了。
你写的，我核的，齐了。
」

episodes.ending:
账册捆好之后，屋里那股紧绷的劲儿忽然散了。
启安起身活动肩膀，走两步，又折回来，从柜子底层摸出一小袋藏红花，掂了掂。
「明早泡水，喝了上殿。
家乡的规矩，大事之前喝这个，说是稳心，其实是给我自己一个仪式。
」他把袋子放在你手边，示意留着分。
「明天你要是不上殿，就在四方馆等我。
散了朝我头一个回来，进门第一句话，先说数，再说别的。
要是成了，我请你去灯市，看那个我一直说好却没带你去过的摊子。
要是没成，也去，账算清了，就再来一遍。
」他说这话的时候已经在收拾算筹了，一根一根归位，码得整整齐齐，像在收一副棋。
烛台吹灭之前，他又看了一眼那页页边的补注，然后很轻地把账册放进琴匣最底层，压在琴的下面。
「这样，琴走到哪儿，它跟到哪儿。
」

episodes.title: 园中的那道选择题
episodes.opening:
四方馆的小园里，玫瑰开到最盛的时候。
启安蹲在花畦边，小心翼翼把一根被雨压弯的枝条扶起来，用麻绳绑在支架上，绑完才在石凳上坐下。
「修枝我母亲教过我，绑要绑松，给它留出长粗的余地。
」他拍了拍手上的土，忽然安静下来，看着那株花，「许可已经批下来了。
今天叫你来，是为一件事，我想了很久，得由你来选，我不能替你选。
」
episodes.dialogue:
他坐得很直，两只手放在膝上，是他在殿上候召时那种坐法，只是眼睛比那时软。
「你陪我从灯罩的裂纹走到今天。
对过账，认过星星，前天在马球场边你还笑话我骑马的样子。
这些日子，对我比通行许可还重要。
」他停下来，把最后一句想清楚了才说，「所以今天我不绕弯。
你要是愿意，我想同你做恋人。
你要是不愿意，我想同你做朋友，像现在这样，一天都不缺。
两条路我都想清楚了，无论你走哪一条，我都走得动。
这是我先开的口，难的这道题给你，不公平，可是替你选更不公平。
」说完他呼出一口气，从袖中取出两样东西并排搁在石凳上：一颗擦得发亮的铜扣，一小盏迷你的玻璃灯，巴掌大，是那盏裂纹灯照着样子新做的。
「铜扣是达拉的，我替他收着，看见它就想起商队的故事。
玻璃灯是新点亮的一次。
」他把两样东西的间隔摆得一样远，「我不解释哪个是什么意思，不然就成了出题考你。
你伸手拿哪一样，或者两样都不拿，只坐一会儿，我都算数。
」他起身，走到花畦那头，背对着你修剪另一根枝条，剪刀声很轻很匀。
他没有走远，也没有回头，肩背绷着，是他自己说的那种「上殿前偷偷抖过」的绷法。
玫瑰的香气漫过来，暮色一寸一寸压低，园子里只剩剪刀声和远处更夫的第一声梆子。

choices.text: 「我想和你成为恋人。」
choices.response:
启安放下剪刀，走回石凳前，在你身旁坐下。
「恋人。
」他又念了一遍，笑意慢慢漫上来，「我很愿意。
」他把那盏小玻璃灯挪到两人中间，伸出手，掌心朝上，停在那里等你。
「要牵手吗？
不想也没关系，我们先在这里坐一会儿。
」他看着灯里稳稳的火光，过了一阵才说：「下一封家书，我想告诉母亲。
不过写什么、什么时候写，都先和你商量。
」

choices.text: 「做朋友吧。我想和你一直这样相处。」
choices.response:
启安点点头，把石凳上的铜扣收回袖袋。
「好，朋友。
谢谢你说得清楚。
」他坐稳了，给你留出位置。
「达拉问起来，我就说，我在这里有个能和我争星星名字的朋友。
他一定要问谁争赢了。
」池边的青蛙跳了两回，还没爬上湿石头；他指给你看，自己先笑了。
你们看着它终于挪上去，才起身往馆门口走。

episodes.ending:
无论石凳上留下的是哪一样，或者什么都没留下，暮色里那株被绑好的玫瑰枝都稳稳立在架上。
启安送你到四方馆门口，馆里的灯笼一盏一盏亮起来，他在灯下站定，郑重其事地拱手，袖口的宝石扣闪了一下。
「今晚的事，我明天不讲给沈阙听，他登记东西登记得太快了，嘴也一样。
」他笑，往后退了半步，「你回去路上小心。
商队下个月进城，岳长宁的查验时刻我排好了，到时候我在南门，你从人群里一眼就能认出我，穿靛蓝袍子，背琴，手里提灯。
这几样，五年了都没变过。
」他转身上台阶，走到一半又停住，背对着你站了一息，没有回头，只是抬起一只手挥了挥，袖摆扫过灯笼的光。
那晚小园的灯亮到很晚，修枝的剪刀收在窗台上，麻绳头垂下来，被夜风轻轻吹着。

episodes.title: 查验时刻交到你手上
episodes.opening:
清晨的南门，尘土还没起来，岳长宁已经在门下核第一支商队的文书。
启安站在城门边的阴凉里，怀里抱着一份誊抄工整的册子，见你来了，抬手招了招。
「来得早，好。
」他把册子拍了拍，「五年了，今天是最后一件事，比第一件还重要。
我跟岳长宁约了此刻，把这份查验时刻交出去。
你来，是因为它一半是你的。
」
episodes.dialogue:
册子翻开，里面是工整的汉字和几个旁注的波斯小字。
「第二年我们定的这个时刻，商队几时进城、几时核验、几时领歇处的牌子，一条一条，都是你陪我对出来的。
第三年大雨那年，提前来的商队能有地方住，靠的就是它排得够细。
」启安一页页翻过去，指腹在某页的页边停住，那里有你当年补写的折耗小字。
「看，这行。
半担乳香。
我一直留着它，提醒自己账要经得起问。
」他合上册子，理了理系绳，往岳长宁那边走了两步，又停下，回头。
「你先别急着高兴。
我交出去之后，就不再常驻了。
新商队下个月到，有一位年轻的使节带队，我要带他赴宴，让他在殿上自己开口。
这是我在这里学的最重要的一课：好请愿能教会人自己说。
」他声音放缓，眼睛在晨光里眯起来，「母亲信里说，那株晚开的玫瑰去年结了籽，她收着，等我回去种。
我走之前问你最后一件事，不对，不问了。
」他自己摇头笑了，转身朝岳长宁走去，脚步很稳。
交接很简短。
岳长宁翻开册子，一条条核过，在末页按了印，抬头说了一句查验的时刻排得细，比官办的好用。
启安道了谢，弯腰把册子双手奉上，直起身时朝你的方向抬了抬下巴，意思分明：这一半的印，是你陪出来的。
商队的头一匹马踏进城门，蹄声撞在门洞里，尘土缓缓扬起来，五年就这样落了地。

choices.text: 「下支商队进城时，我还来看查验。」
choices.response:
启安眼睛一亮，转身大步走回来，靛蓝的袍角扫起一点尘土。
「好，一言为定。
」他站定，忽然意识到什么，压低了声音，「虽然是我先开的头，但是这一句是你说的，我照单全收。
」他从袖中摸出一小块干玫瑰花瓣夹的纸片，递过来，「波斯星名的写法，我抄了一份最常用的。
下支商队里有几个走新路线的牧人，他们认星的法子和我们又不一样，到时候你听我讲，讲完咱们再往册子上添一条。
」他抬头看了看城楼上刚升起的日头，「岳长宁收了册子，往后就是官办的规矩了。
我们私下再对账，对的是新路、新星、新玫瑰。
这个账，对一辈子也行。
」

choices.text: 不说话，只站在原地，一直看到册子在岳长宁手里落定。
choices.response:
启安交完册子走回来，发现你还站在那儿，一动不动地望着城门。
他没有出声，就顺着你的目光一起看。
商队鱼贯而入，驮架上乳香的木箱摞得整整齐齐，沈阙在门边候着登记。
看了很久，启安才低声开口：「五年前我进这道门的时候，手里只有一盏灯和一把琴，名字还是官员临时给的。
」他顿了顿，「现在册子交出去了，反而觉得手轻。
轻得有点不习惯。
」他侧过头看你的侧脸，像在核对什么，「你也不说话。
好。
这种时候不说话，比说话难。
」蹄声、尘土、守卒的号令在门洞里来回滚，两个人在阴凉里站到商队过完，谁也没有先动。
「走吧，」启安终于说，往城内抬了抬下巴，「头一炉茶我去讨，讨来分你。
以后商队每次进城，这炉茶都这么分。
」

episodes.ending:
册子留在了岳长宁手里，南门的查验照旧一队一队过，时刻牌挂得和第二年一样准。
启安在四方馆又住了些时日，教那位年轻使节在殿上如何自己开口，一遍一遍陪他把话理顺。
使节第一次开口那天，启安坐在殿外廊下，手里摩挲着一颗铜扣，听见里面传来年轻人的声音，笑了。
启程前夜，他把小玻璃灯的灯罩取下来擦了一遍，那道裂纹还在，他用指腹描过，像老朋友打招呼。
达拉的铜扣缝进了行囊内衬。
给母亲的信里写了一切，从灯罩到星图边上的那行字，最后一句是：玫瑰籽请留好，我回去亲手种。
新一季的商队入城那天，南门的时刻牌准时挂出，牌角有一行小字，是誊抄时添上去的：某年某月，与友人共核。
启安走在商队前头，回头朝城门上望了一眼，灯笼下面站没站着人，他没看清，但他挥了挥手。
琴声混进驼铃里，出了城，一路向西。

speak.text: ♡ 我想和你成为恋人

romance.title: 同一次见面，一盏修好的灯
romance.opening:
清晨的南门还蒙着薄薄的雾。
启安把册子抱在臂弯里，另一只手提着那盏玻璃灯，灯罩上的裂纹被金胶描过，像一道细细的金线。
你走近时，他先把灯举高了一点。
「看，修好了。
今天它要同册子一起，见岳长宁。
」
romance.dialogue:
他把灯放在城门边的石栏上，退半步，让晨光从裂纹里穿过去。
「金胶是我母亲家乡的补瓷法子，她补过一只碗，摔成三瓣，补完比原先结实。
我托人带了胶来，补了一个月，每道缝都要等它干透。
」他俯身把灯芯拨正，火苗立起来，透过金线在石栏上投下一小片碎亮。
「你陪我从它裂的第一天走到今天。
对账那晚你说软话也是话，观星台上你把名字写进我的图里，园子里你拿起了这盏灯。
五个年头，一笔一笔，全在这盏灯上了。
」他直起身，把册子夹稳，掌心在封皮上按了按。
「今天两件事一起办。
册子交给岳长宁，是给商队的。
灯点亮着带过来，是给我们俩的。
母亲信里说玫瑰籽收着等我，我打算这次回去种下，种好了给你捎一枝来，干的花，路上不会谢。
」他深吸一口气，难得有点紧张，抬手把一缕卷发别到耳后，「还有一件事我盘算了整夜。
五年许可批下来的时候，我在灯底下哭了，没让人看见。
今天当着你的面我说出来：这五年，是我这辈子最好的一段路。
往后商队一年一季地来，我就一年一季地回，两头跑，但是两头都有灯。
」岳长宁那边已经在核文书了，朝这边扬了扬下巴。
启安抱起册子，又拎起灯，灯还亮着，白天的光里那点火苗细得几乎看不见，可裂纹里的金线被它照得清清楚楚。
「走吧，」他说，声音稳了，「同一次见面，把两样都交出去。
」

choices.text: 「灯我来提，册子你来交，两样一样都不落下。」
choices.response:
启安把灯柄递过来，手在半空停了一瞬，看着你接稳了才松开。
「好。
你提灯，我交册。
」他伸手替你拢了拢被晨风吹起的衣角，动作很轻，「你提着它走过这道门洞，我就当是把这五年也一起提过来了。
」交接办得干脆。
岳长宁一条条核过，按印，说时刻排得细。
启安弯腰双手奉上，直起身时回头看了一眼你手里的灯，火苗在雾里晃了一下，立住了。
回来的路上他一直看着灯，走到近前才说：「回去我把灯座做成双头的。
一支灯芯照我的星图，一支照你写的字。
」

choices.text: 不接灯，只替他把被风吹歪的灯罩扶正，然后朝岳长宁那边点点头，示意他快去。
choices.response:
启安低头看着你扶正灯罩的手，看了很久，什么也没说。
然后他笑着摇了摇头，抱紧册子朝城门下走去。
脚步声在门洞里滚了一圈，交接，按印，道谢，他回来得比想象中快。
你还守着灯。
「你连灯都没让我提。
」他在石栏边站定，声音里有点哑的笑意，「可你替我扶正了灯罩。
这个更好。
五年里你就是这样，扶正我要走的路。
」他伸手覆上你扶过灯罩的那只手，握了一下，松开。
「册子交了，灯还亮着。
今天办成的两件事，一件有印，一件有光。
」

romance.ending:
册子留在了岳长宁手里，按了印，从此南门的查验时刻成了官办的规矩，牌角那行与友人共核的小字也一并誊了进去。
灯被提回四方馆，在窗台上亮了一整个白天。
启程那天，使节在殿上自己开了口，启安在廊下听完，掌心里握着一颗铜扣，笑得比谁都久。
行囊里，星图边上那行字被金胶护了角，琴匣底下压着五年的账册抄本，铜扣缝在内衬最稳的地方。
启安在城门口回头，你在城门上。
他没有喊话，只是把玻璃灯高高举起，裂纹里的金线在晨光里亮了一下，像一次挥手。
信是半个月后到的：玫瑰籽种下了，就种在补过瓷的那只碗旁边；灯座改成了双头，一支照星图，一支照信。
信的末尾写着：商队秋后再来，南门的时刻牌，还认得我们。

episodes.title: The Blank Page
episodes.opening:
The city sounds distant outside the rented meeting room.

Nadia Haddad turns a blank page toward you, sets her black pen across it, and introduces herself without hurry: brand strategy, independent, one table and one moodboard with nothing pinned to it yet.

A crooked potted plant leans against the windowsill, taller than the lamp beside it.

She has the posture of someone who has never once needed to fill a silence to win an argument.
episodes.ending:
She writes Thursday on a card and slides it across the table, pen on top so it does not drift.

Whatever you decide, the plant stays where it is, and the blank page stays where it is, waiting without urgency.

Outside, the afternoon has gone on being ordinary.

Inside, one sentence stands a little steadier than it did an hour ago, and someone has offered to sit with it again next week.
episodes.dialogue:
Nadia: Before anything else — how do you want to be seen in this room?

By whoever this pitch is for.

We start there, or we start nowhere useful.

(She waits, two full seconds, unhurried.)

Good.

Now say the version you'd say if no one were grading you.

The rough one.

I'll keep it between us and the plant.

(She listens, then taps the blank page once.)

There.

That's the spine.

Everything else is scaffolding we can take down and rebuild.

What I do is help you say what must be said with poise — which mostly means finding out you already know the sentence, and it's just standing crooked.

(She glances at the plant.)

Don't judge its posture.

It grew toward the light I gave it, which wasn't much.

I left the agency last spring.

I packed my own boxes, which felt appropriate.

A friend offered to drive, and I kept saying there was nothing left to carry until there was only one box, and the plant stuck out the top, and I said it would crush the leaves if I set anything on it.

So I didn't.

I settled the plant’s box in the back seat, then sat in the passenger seat myself.

(A pause, two seconds.)

I told her I was a little afraid only after she'd parked.

It seemed safer to admit once we'd arrived.

That's my whole method, if you want it.

Write what you actually believe first, in a drawer.

Then write the persuasive version.

If the persuasive version ever contradicts the drawer, you've gone hoarse for nothing.

I learned that the expensive way — rehearsing a pitch until my voice gave out, saying things I didn't believe, perfectly.

(She uncaps the pen.)

Now.

Your sentence.

Say it badly first.

Bad first drafts are honest; polished first drafts are usually borrowed.

choices.text: Okay. Rough version — here it goes.
choices.response:
You say it badly, and it lands better than any rehearsed version would have.

Nadia writes it down word for word, including the stumble.

'That's the one.

We'll dress it later, but the bones are yours.'

She reads it back once, taps the page, and asks a single question about who needs to hear it.

The plant leans in the window light, and the room feels less like an audition and more like a workshop.

choices.text: (Reach over and straighten the crooked plant a quarter turn toward the light.)
choices.response:
Nadia watches you turn the pot and says nothing for a moment.

'It'll lean back,' she warns.

'It always does.

It's stubborn about its own direction.'

Then she smiles, briefly and genuinely, and pulls the page back toward herself.

'Fine.

You handle the plant, I'll handle the sentence.

Say it badly now — badly is allowed here.'

episodes.title: The Dog and the Omitted Part
episodes.opening:
Saturday, a fenced grass field near the river.

Nadia is holding a leash, and the leash is holding a brown dog with strong opinions about fetch.

The friend who owns the dog has gone to park the car, which is how Nadia has ended up here alone, sleeves rolled, burgundy suit jacket folded over the fence rail.

The dog has already explained, twice, that it loves this game and will never tire of it.

Ever.
episodes.ending:
When the friend finally jogs over, Nadia hands the leash back with both hands, like returning something borrowed and intact.

The dog immediately drags its owner toward one last squirrel-shaped rumor.

Nadia picks up her jacket, shakes the grass off, and looks at you.

'Same time next month,' she says.

'I'll bring the ball.

I know my weaknesses now.'

The field keeps its noise; the afternoon keeps its shape.
episodes.dialogue:
She emphasized — twice — that this dog especially loves fetch.

(The dog hits the end of the leash like a furry wrecking ball and rebounds.)

I now understand there was a part she omitted.

The part where loving fetch is a full-time position with no benefits.

(The dog returns the ball.

Nadia rolls it along the grass.

The dog returns.

She rolls it back along the ground.

It returns.

She looks at you with perfect dignity.)

I'm aware of how this looks.

I'm aware the dog is winning.

(Another two-second pause while the dog waits, trembling with readiness.)

You came.

Good.

I wasn't sure a Saturday request would survive the week.

Most people agree to things on Thursdays and renegotiate on Saturdays.

(She rolls it again, a shorter distance this time.)

Since we have a captive audience — the dog, I mean — I wanted you to hear it from me.

The agency job.

I've been telling it as a tidy story: left to work with small businesses, help quiet people say no clearly, very noble, very intentional.

It's true, but it's the persuasive version.

The drawer version is that I got very good at presenting things, and one morning I couldn't remember which of my sentences I actually believed.

So I packed a box, settled the plant in the back seat and rode in the passenger seat, and started over.

(The dog drops the ball directly on her shoe.)

Thank you.

Your feedback is noted.

(She picks it up.)

Your turn to roll it along the ground.

I want to see your form.

And then I want to hear how the sentence from our first session has been behaving in the wild — whether it stood steadier or whether you let someone talk you back into the crooked version.

choices.text: Honestly? The sentence wobbled once, but I said it anyway.
choices.response:
Nadia listens without interrupting, which is a skill she clearly practices.

'It wobbled and you said it anyway.

That's the whole job, actually.

Wobbling is load-bearing.'

She rolls the ball along the grass within the leash’s reach, and the dog bounds after it, returning it to her shoe.

'Next time it will wobble less.

Because you got used to the weight.'

choices.text: (Take the ball and roll it firmly along the grass, farther than necessary but within the leash’s reach, and watch the dog go.)
choices.response:
The roll is magnificent — stopping just inside the leash’s reach, where the dog scoops up the ball after two enthusiastic bounds and brings it back.

Nadia watches its whole path across the grass with one hand in her pocket and the other holding the leash.

'Overcompensating,' she diagnoses.

'I respect it.

Also, the fence thanks you; that was nearly a jailbreak.'

She picks a blade of grass off her sleeve.

'You didn't answer my question about the sentence, which is also an answer.

We'll circle back when the dog is tired.

Dogs tire.

Sentences don't, unfortunately.'

episodes.title: Black Sesame, Two Bowls
episodes.opening:
A small dessert shop with fogged windows and six tables.

Nadia has claimed the corner one and is standing two bowls of black sesame paste on the table when you arrive.

Her phone is propped against the napkin holder, mid-video-call, and on the screen a woman with Nadia's eyebrows is saying something emphatic in Arabic.

Nadia looks up, entirely unembarrassed.

'You're early.

Good.

My mother insists on meeting people before the sesame gets cold.'
episodes.ending:
The call lasts until both bowls are empty, which takes a while, because nobody is in a hurry.

Her mother extracts a promise about the green scarf, and Nadia extracts a promise about the stewed potatoes, and you are included in both without ceremony.

Outside, the rain has thinned.

Nadia holds her umbrella over the space between you — not quite shared, not quite separate — and says the shop was a good choice.

The walk to the corner is short.

Neither of you rushes it.
episodes.dialogue:
Nadia: Mama, this is the person I told you about.

The one with the sentence.

(Her mother leans into frame — at first only half her forehead is visible, then all of her, scrutinizing.)

Yes, they look reliable.

Yes, in person.

No, I'm not telling you what the sentence was; it's not mine to tell.

(Her mother laughs and says something that makes Nadia close her eyes briefly.)

She says anyone who eats sesame paste slowly has a patient character.

She's judging you favorably based on dessert.

This is her most reliable method.

(Her mother disappears briefly and returns with her own bowl — the same black sesame, a continent away.)

We've started doing this.

She eats, I eat, we pretend it's the same table.

It started a few weeks ago when I suddenly wanted her stewed potatoes — the ones I remembered but couldn't quite get right.

I called while cooking, and she answered with half her face in frame until we adjusted the camera to her stove.

Two pots, one call. She told me to add a small sip of water.

I asked, 'Whose small sip?' She laughed and showed me her cup. Later she reminded me of the butter at the end, and I added it to my plate.

(Nadia stirs her bowl.)

I tell you this because you'll notice something eventually anyway: I show very little.

I trained it out of myself — presentations, composure, all of it — and now the volume knob sticks.

My mother has never once accepted this.

She reads me through a phone screen across a time difference, and she's never wrong.

(Her mother calls out a question.)

She wants to know if you eat properly.

This is the background check.

Answer carefully.

choices.text: Tell your mother I'm eating very well today. Honestly.
choices.response:
Her mother beams and delivers a verdict in Arabic.

Nadia translates with reluctance: 'She says we should both have another small bite, and that you may come for potatoes if you are ever in her city, and that I should stop hiding my face when I'm pleased.'

She takes another spoonful, slowly, defiantly.

'She's wrong about the last part.

Obviously.'

Her mother, audibly, disagrees.

choices.text: (Lift your bowl slightly toward the phone screen, a small toast.)
choices.response:
Her mother laughs so warmly that two nearby tables look over.

'She says you have good manners and I should keep you,' Nadia reports, ears slightly pink.

'I would like the record to show I said nothing of the kind.'

Her mother says something else, longer.

'Now she's reminding me about the potato recipe.

Out loud.

To me.

Including the butter she helped me add last time.'

Nadia stares at the screen, then at her bowl, and takes another bite without commentary.

episodes.title: The Unfinished Sky
episodes.opening:
Nadia's building has a rooftop she has apparently been saving.

She leads you up the stairwell with two glasses of lemonade balanced on a small tray, past a corkboard she has mounted near the door: a grid of blank cards, each one a pale rectangle of sky photographed from this exact spot, none of them finished.

The evening is warm.

The city hums below like it's minding its own business for once.
episodes.ending:
The evening ends the way it had to: at the rail, watching the first star make its unreliable appearance while the sky goes from peach to slate.

The corkboard keeps its unfinished grid.

The pen stays on the table.

Nadia refills the lemonade without being asked, and the conversation moves at the pace of people who have decided there will be more evenings like this one.

The city hums.

Nobody has to prove anything.
episodes.dialogue:
Nadia: The board is my one dishonest habit.

I photograph the sky, print the card, and then I can never finish it — I keep waiting for the version that's worth pinning.

My mother calls it perfectionism.

I call it a two-second pause that never ends.

(She sets down the tray on the rooftop table, with the black pen and a jug of lemonade beside the two glasses.)

I asked you here for a reason, and I'd rather say it plainly than arrange it to look accidental.

I like how my weeks have become.

You're in them.

I want to say the next part without a strategy deck, so — (two full seconds) — there are two shapes this can take, and both of them are good, and I will not be wounded by either.

The first: more than this.

Closeness, deliberately, the kind you choose out loud rather than drift into.

I'm bad at showing it, but I'm very good at meaning it.

The second: friendship, kept and honored, a real thing I have too few of, and I'd rather have it honestly than half of something else.

(She folds her hands.)

This is the one pitch I won't rehearse.

Whatever you want, say it or don't, and we'll build from there.

The lemonade is good either way.

I checked.

choices.text: I want the first shape. Partners — more than this, chosen out loud.
choices.response:
Nadia exhales, one controlled breath, the composure cracking just enough to show the person maintaining it.

'Good,' she says.

'Then it's said, and it's real, and neither of us has to guess.'

She pours the lemonade, hands you a glass, and touches her own glass to yours with a small, definite click.

'I'll still be bad at showing it.

You'll have to read the pauses.

There are only two seconds in each; you've had practice.'

choices.text: (Without speaking, use the black pen to write friends on a sky card and slide it toward her, choosing friendship, kept and honored.)
choices.response:
Nadia nods before you've even finished writing, steady and unflinching.

'Then that's what it is, and I'm glad of it.

Truly — you should see my calendar; friendship slots are scarce.'

She pours two glasses and hands you one.

'For the record, this is the answer I'd have respected either way.

I mean it.

Now drink, and tell me which blank sky we're finishing first, because you're an accomplice now.'

episodes.title: The First Slice
episodes.opening:
A small paper crown sits on Nadia's head at an angle that suggests someone else put it there and she lost the argument.

Her apartment is warm and orderly except for the crooked plant, which has leaned further into its own opinion.
