She pulls a battered guidebook from under the counter and shows you the page, the pencil faded, a pressed leaf tucked there that was definitely not in any official collection.

Lena: I still do that.

Write down the color instead of the thing.

It is easier and it is worse.

She sips her tea.

Lena: Anyway.

You heard it from a girl at a garden who got shown up by a leaf.

Your turn to be embarrassed for me.

Do you have a version of that?

A thing you stared straight at and missed?

choices.text: I probably have a few. Tell me the rest of the butterfly one first.
choices.response:
There is no rest, she says, delighted.

That is the whole thing.

A sleeve borrowed a butterfly, a kid waited with us, I got a pencil note.

But she tells it again anyway, slower, adding the part about the greenhouse glass being warm and the smell of wet dirt on the walkways.

She says the girl's mother asked her to wait in place, and the three of them watched together without touching the butterfly. That shared patience is the detail she keeps returning to.

Then she points her shears at you like a small gavel and says you are on the hook for your version next visit.

She clearly intends there to be a next visit.

choices.text: (Lift the edge of the penciled guidebook page gently, let it settle, and set the book back open on the counter where she can reach it.)
choices.response:
She watches you handle the book like it might bruise, and something in her shoulders comes down an inch.

“You get it,” she says.

Most people would flip to the end to see what else is in there.

She leaves the book exactly where you put it, open, and pours you more tea without being asked.

For the record, she says, the pressed leaf is a weed.

It grew through a crack by the garden gate and I took it anyway.

Some things you keep because of the day they came with.

She says it lightly, but she says it looking at the page, not at you.

episodes.title: What the Season Sends
episodes.opening:
You find her at the dawn market, of all places, kneeling in a canvas apron among buckets while vendors shout prices over each other.

It is apricot season at the stalls, and Lena is supposed to be buying for the week.

The trouble is visible from ten feet away: she has overshot, badly, chasing a shade.

Her crate is stacked with apricot-toned stems she has no orders for, and the vendor is giving her a look that is patient the way a landlord is patient.

The morning is cold, and her breath shows, and she is smiling anyway.
episodes.ending:
By afternoon the cafe display holds a low apricot arrangement that makes two regulars stop mid-sip, and the last stems stand in the window jar with the crooked ones, waiting to mean something.

Lena pencils the tally, folds the pad shut, and calls it a lesson she keeps re-enrolling in.

The season sent what it sent.

She arranged the truth she had, and it turns out the truth was generous this once.

Nobody went home crying in the bad way.
episodes.dialogue:
Lena: Do not say it.

I know.

She holds up an apricot stem like evidence against herself.

Lena: The shade was perfect.

Perfect, and forty stems too much of it.

The wedding order was last month, there is no wedding, there is just me and my inability to walk past a color having a good day.

The vendor clears his throat.

Lena: Yes, yes, I am paying for all of it, Rafi, you vulture.

She counts bills out, laughing, then sits back on her heels in the cold and looks at the crate like it is a small disaster with nice manners.

Lena: Here is the actual problem.

I cannot sell these fresh by myself.

The shop is one room and my afternoon cafe run takes maybe fifteen stems.

The rest wilt by Thursday and Thursday does not care that they were beautiful on Tuesday.

She stands, dusts her knees, and hefts the crate with a grunt.

Lena: I could take them to the cafe, obviously.

But the cafe display is one vase.

One.

And there is a shelter two blocks over that never says no to flowers, but I have never once walked in there because, and I quote, I would not know what to do with my hands.

Which is a lie.

I always know what to do with my hands.

I just do not know what to do with showing up somewhere I have no arrangement for.

She looks at you sideways, half joking, half not.

Lena: You are uninvolved and therefore wise.

Walk with me.

Tell me which of my two dumb options is less dumb, or invent a third one, or just carry the other end of this crate while I figure out how to want less than perfect.

choices.text: The shelter. You'll figure out your hands once someone takes a stem from them.
choices.response:
She stares at you for a second, then barks a laugh that startles Rafi two stalls down.

Fine.

Fine!

She splits the crate between you and marches the two blocks like she is going to return a defective toaster.

Inside, a woman with tired eyes takes a stem, then a handful, then starts directing Lena where the big common-room vase lives.

Twenty minutes later Lena's hands are doing exactly what hands do, and she walks out quieter than she went in.

Thursday, she says on the corner.

I am going back Thursday.

I did not even arrange anything.

They just took them.

choices.text: (Take the other end of the crate and start walking toward the shelter without a word.)
choices.response:
You just lift your end and go, and after a beat of betrayed blinking, she follows.

She mutters the whole way about people who answer questions with their feet, but she does not slow down.

At the shelter she hangs back by the door while the staff descend on the crate, and you watch her watch a teenager put one apricot stem in a paper cup of water on a windowsill.

Lena's hands are finally still.

Okay, she says on the walk back.

That is the third option.

It was my option and I walked past it every week.

She does not thank you out loud.

She buys you a coffee the size of a fire hydrant instead.

episodes.title: The Forgotten Tune
episodes.opening:
Evening, and the shop is down to lamplight and the last wrapping of the day.

Lena hums something under her breath while she works, eight bars, then stops, frowns, and hums it again exactly the same way, which means it is stuck and she knows it.

The window jar now holds three crooked stems, a small parliament of failures.

A flyer for a record shop across town sits folded on the counter, corner chewed, older than the day's paper.

She catches you hearing the hum and gives up the pretense immediately.
episodes.ending:
Saturday stays penciled on the flyer, a small appointment with an unnamed song.

Lena finishes the bouquet, sets it in the cooler, and turns the shop sign with the ease of someone whose evening went better than expected.

Whatever Saturday turns out to be, the tune has stopped being a thing she hums alone in lamplight, and that much is already settled.
episodes.dialogue:
Lena: Okay, you heard that, so now you are involved.

She puts down the shears.

Lena: There is a song.

I heard it coming out of the dawn market, some van idling by the flower stalls, eight bars and then the driver found his parking spot and his taste in music.

I have been humming it for two weeks.

Two weeks.

My hands know it better than my head does, which is how everything worth knowing works, apparently.

She unfolds the flyer and smooths it flat.

Lena: There is a record shop across town where the owner lets you play things before you buy, and he claims he can name any tune from a hum.

Any tune.

He has a beard that suggests he has had time to practice.

I keep almost going on my day off and then I keep arranging things instead, because a Wednesday bouquet does not judge you if you hum at it.

She turns the flyer toward you and taps it once.

Lena: Come with me Saturday.

If the beard fails, we fail together, and failure is much funnier as a duo.

If he names it, I owe the song a home and I will play it in this shop until the crooked stems file a complaint.

She is suddenly very interested in a spare leaf, trimming it with great focus.

Lena: No pressure.

Well.

Some pressure.

The good kind.

The kind that means I would rather do this with you than without you, which I am saying out loud because apparently that is a thing I do now.

So.

Saturday?

choices.text: Saturday, and let's make it a date afterward. Just the two of us, as partners.
choices.response:
The shears stop.

Lena looks up, and for once the florist who arranges everything does not arrange a clever reply first.

A date, she repeats.

Just us.

A slow, bright smile arrives like something finally in season.

Yes.

Okay.

Yes.

She writes Saturday on the flyer in pencil, then adds a time, then crosses out the time and writes a better one.

“I will close early,” she says.

The flowers will survive.

I will hum at them all week and they will just have to cope.

She hums the eight bars once more, and this time it sounds like a beginning instead of a snag.

choices.text: (Without speaking, write friends and Saturday on the flyer, add a small doodle of a crooked stem, and slide it back.)
choices.response:
Lena looks at the doodle, then at you, and laughs until she has to put a hand on the counter.

A crooked stem.

For our crooked quest.

She pencils Saturday in properly and pins the flyer to the corkboard by the cooler, right at eye level, which is where she puts things she means.

“Saturday,” she says.

Two friends versus one bearded oracle.

The odds are terrible and I cannot wait.

She resumes wrapping, humming, and the hum has a swing in it now, like the eight bars finally know where they are going.

episodes.title: The First Red Tomato
episodes.opening:
Seasons have moved through the shop since the record shop day: the window jar now holds a whole row of crooked stems, a standing exhibit of beautiful failures, and the calendar by the cooler has a small circled note on the first Saturday of the month that has been there for a while now.

Lena meets you at the door carrying a clay pot like a trophy.

In it, a tomato plant, and on it, one tomato that has finally gone properly red.

The tune, for the record, turned out to be called something nobody can believe, and it plays in this shop most mornings now.
episodes.ending:
The tomato is split down the middle on a cutting board, still warm from the sill, and it tastes exactly like the effort of two people who kept showing up.

The pot goes back on the windowsill to ripen the next one.

The calendar's first Saturday is circled through the coming month, and the one after that has a smaller circle, like a habit practicing being permanent.

The shop hums.

It hums better than those old eight bars.
episodes.dialogue:
Lena: Behold.

She sets the pot on the counter with ceremony.

Lena: The first red tomato of the sill empire.

It grew crooked, obviously, toward the glass, because everything I keep does that.

But it ripened, which is more than I can say for my record-keeping.

She wipes her hands on the apron, and there is something almost formal under the grin.

Lena: Can I say a thing without turning it into a whole moment?

The first-Saturday thing.

You come, we do the cafe displays, we have lunch, I talk you into one flower you did not plan on.

It has been, what, every month for a while now.

And I realized I stopped putting it in pencil.

Look.

She turns the calendar.

The circle is in pen.

Lena: I just want it said out loud once, by me, in daylight: this is a standing thing.

First Saturday.

Ours.

We both have other things, and that is exactly why it counts.

She picks the tomato, twists it free, and holds it up between two fingers like a small sun.

Lena: First picking goes to you.

That is the rule I just invented.

And the rule after that is you bring the bread next time, because I have the tomatoes and the coffee and no self-control around bakeries, so the division of labor is clear.

She halves the tomato with a paring knife right there on the counter, juices running, utterly unbothered by beauty standards for once.

Lena: Well?

Do we have a deal, first Saturdays, in pen?

choices.text: First Saturdays, in pen. And I'm bringing the good bread.
choices.response:
In pen, she repeats, and writes nothing, because it is already written, and you both look at the calendar like a signed thing.

The good bread, she says, gravely.

Then the deal is sacred.

She salts your half of the tomato without asking, the way you do for someone whose tastes you have memorized.

She talks about the sill empire's expansion plans, a pepper maybe, a scandal.

The shop hums around the two of you, and the row of crooked stems in the window stands at attention like it approves of the paperwork.

choices.text: (Take the halved tomato, eat it, and tap the calendar's pen circle once.)
choices.response:
No speech needed.

You eat your half, it is absurdly good, and you tap the pen circle once, which is a whole sentence.

Lena nods back, equally wordless, and that is the treaty signed.

She leans on the counter and looks at the sill empire with satisfaction.

A year ago I could not walk into a shelter with an armful of flowers,” she says.

Now I have a standing appointment and a tomato with a friend.

She grins.

That came out wrong and I am keeping it.

First Saturday.

Bring the bread.

The shop hums on, and neither of you corrects the calendar.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: What the Season Sends, Returned
romance.opening:
Evening again, lamplight, the tune playing low from the little speaker by the cooler, the one the bearded oracle finally named after three hums and one argument.

The window jar holds a full row of crooked stems now, and the tomato plant on the sill is on its second fruit.

Lena has been strange all visit, in a specific way: bright, and repeatedly almost saying something, and trimming the same spare leaf three times.

Since your first date after the record shop, the first Saturday of each month has become an evening for the two of you, circled in pen on her calendar.

Finally she reaches under the counter and comes up with a small paper envelope, worn soft at the corners, and sets it between you.
romance.ending:
The crooked stems stand in their window jar, and Lena keeps the remaining bookmarks with the care she always has.

The tune plays through and starts over, which it is allowed to do now.

Lena has her shop and her mornings and her crooked parliament; you have your days, and the first-Saturday circle in pen, and this exact evening together, given room to keep its own shape.

The season sent what it sent.

It was enough, and then some.
romance.dialogue:
Lena: Okay.

I have shown exactly two people this and one of them was a mail carrier by accident.

She opens the envelope.

Inside: bookmarks.

Dozens, pressed flat, flowers you recognize from the seasons you have been coming here, each one laminated in careful little sleeves.

Lena: The first bouquet I ever made that nobody bought.

Every unsold stem after that, too.

I could not throw them out, so I pressed them, and then I had a drawer full of pressed years and no idea what they were for.

She picks one up, turns it in the lamplight.

Lena: The secret is I never knew what the keeping was for.

I just kept.

And then somewhere along the way the shop got a regular who noticed the crooked stem by the window, and helped carry a crate to the shelter two blocks over, and listened to my butterfly story, and suddenly the drawer made sense.

Now I can offer one to somebody who has been here while the drawer began to mean something. Keeping it myself is allowed too.

She slides the envelope toward you, then holds up one finger.

Lena: Not a forever contract.

You can take a bookmark or leave it with me; I keep the shop, we both keep our own lives, which I like, and I am not giving up my mornings at the market for anyone, do not ask.

But this part I am saying plainly, because you taught me things arrive when they arrive and it is stupid to arrange them to death: I would keep choosing this.

You, this, the crooked everything.

If you would keep choosing it too.

She trims one spare leaf, hands steady, eyes not on the leaf for once.

Lena: So.

Do you still choose us, whether the bookmark travels or stays?

choices.text: I choose it. Every crooked stem of it.
choices.response:
Lena exhales like she has been holding a breath since the dawn market two years ago.

Okay, she says, and then laughs at herself for saying okay.

She takes one bookmark out of the envelope, the very first pressed stem, and tucks it into your hand, folding your fingers over it with both of hers, brief and warm and then gone.

That one is yours.

“The rest stay in the drawer,” she says.

A girl does not give away her whole spring at once.

Then, because she is still Lena, she adds a stray crooked stem of sweet pea to the window jar, adjusts its angle a millimeter, and steps back to look.

“There,” she says.

Arranged.

choices.text: (Close the envelope gently, press it back toward her, and tap the window jar where the crooked stems stand.)
choices.response:
You close the envelope and slide it home to her, and tap the jar of crooked stems instead.

Her face does something complicated and then settles into a warm smile as she understands you want the keepsakes to stay hers.

Right, she says softly.

They are mine.

The keeping was mine all along.

She pulls out the very first pressed bookmark, the original, and tucks it into the battered guidebook, on the page where the word blue is penciled, which makes her laugh at her own symbolism and pretend she did not plan it.

She taps the jar back.

“Deal,” she says.

Still us, first Saturdays, and the whole crooked parliament stays home. I can keep these and keep choosing you.

episodes.title: 先选一枝
episodes.opening:
雨点在玻璃上敲出轻柔的节奏，小店弥漫着剪下的花茎和湿润绿意的气息。

莉娜·哈特系着沾满花粉的围裙，放下剪刀，从桶里挑出最漂亮的一枝花毛茛。

她隔着柜台递过来，像是在交给你一个小小的事实。

她身后，一桶桶色彩排成行列，窗边的玻璃罐里独自斜倚着一根浅色的歪茎，没有包装，也没卖出去。
episodes.ending:
那根歪茎最后被放进了窗边的罐子里，就在花毛茛旁边，看起来刚刚好。

莉娜用铅笔把集市的时间写在一小片包装纸上，像递一份小小的条约一样推过柜台。

雨一停，她已经回到剪刀前，哼着歌，店里闻起来像一小片田野搬进了屋。

那扇门总有一种在你身后显得很近的感觉。
episodes.dialogue:
莉娜：莉娜·哈特，独立花艺师。

今天你不必把一切都弄得井井有条。

先挑一种颜色，剩下的我来搭配。

亮色还是柔和色？

你看起来像是在两者之间犹豫，而这正是个好的起点。

大多数人抓最扎眼的那束，到周二就后悔了。

一枝就好。

今天一种颜色就够了。

那么，选哪个？

亮色，还是柔和色？

顺便说一句，哪个答案都对。

我核实过。

她把花毛茛放下，在米色围裙上擦了擦手，朝窗边的罐子点点头。

莉娜：那一枝长歪了。

在货车上追着光，一路横着长。

没人买歪的，所以它们就住在我窗边，直到我想明白它们是为什么而生的。

她笑了，有点不好意思。

莉娜：有一次，我为了给一场婚礼追到最正的杏色，错过了送花的时间。

新娘哭了，可不是高兴的那种哭。

种植商还是给我留了一束，出于同情还是敬意，我没问过是哪个。

就是那时我明白了，季节送来什么就是什么。

你搭配的是你手上的真实。

她一边说，一边剪掉一根茎上多余的叶子，小小的咔嚓声给她的句子打着标点。

莉娜：我每天下午都会给街那头的咖啡馆换花。

他们在收银台边摆了个小花瓶，熟客们假装没注意，然后又不停地注意。

你要是哪天四点左右路过，看看那个柜台。

那就是我的一天被陌生人看见的地方。

总之。

回到你身上。

亮色还是柔和色？

别说两个都要。

人人都说两个都要。

两个都要是配色方案。

choices.text: 柔和色。今天想要点不冲着我嚷嚷的东西。
choices.response:
莉娜眉开眼笑，像你通过了一场小小的私人考试。

柔和色，她重复了一遍，抽出一枝灰粉色的花毛茛，还有一茎灰绿色、毛茸茸的东西。

她修剪、转身、再修剪，什么都没解说，又什么都解说了。

好了，她说。

它就安安静静地待在那儿，值得一看。

她用素纸包好，不系丝带，放进你手里。

这次算我请客，她说，因为你在我还没劝你之前就选好了。

这比你想象的少见得多。

choices.text: （越过那些亮色的桶，伸手碰了碰窗罐里那根歪茎。）
choices.response:
你的手指越过一切，先停在了那根歪茎上。

莉娜安静下来，然后从心底深处笑出声。

好，她说。

好。

就它了。

她端起罐子，像举行一个小小的仪式一样放在你们之间的柜台上。

歪的就歪的。

它一辈子横着长，现在还站着呢，所以。

她剪掉一片多余的叶子，丢进堆肥，然后在包装纸上写了点什么。

不收钱，她说。

它一直在等一个眼神不好、直觉很好的人。

episodes.title: 她写下的那抹蓝
episodes.opening:
下午稍晚的花店是另一副模样：水桶补满，剪刀擦净，当天的送往咖啡馆的花束套着纸套在工作台上等着。

莉娜用牙咬着一根花茎朝你挥手，像一朵玫瑰叼在一副理智得多的嘴唇之间。

你第一次来时那根歪茎还立在窗边的罐子里，她又在旁边添了一根歪的，看来这已经成了传统。

后屋的电炉上水壶冒着汽，她倒了两杯茶，根本没问你要不要。
episodes.ending:
导览册仍摊开在柜台上，她包完最后几束送往咖啡馆的花，那个“蓝”字还留在原处，记着当年蝴蝶飞走、女孩把那抹颜色记下的那一刻。

莉娜倒完最后一点茶，说四点的陈列不会自己摆好，却丝毫没有催促的意思。

水壶咔哒一声关了。

花店守着它的小时光，就像她握着一根花茎：轻轻的，不要求它此刻成为别的什么。
episodes.dialogue:
莉娜：你快成常客了，这很危险，因为我会开始跟你说些心里话。

她坐在柜台后的木箱上，一边说话一边包花，双手自顾自地动着。

莉娜：好吧，说一件事。

一个故事，然后我们继续假装我是专业人士。

有一年春天，我去植物园看蝴蝶。

所有人都站在那儿盼着蝴蝶落到自己身上，对吧？

非常正常的人类行为。

我当时盯着一片叶子，一心盼着有蝴蝶落上去，然后我发现那片叶子自己的背面就有翅膀。

一只蝴蝶，收拢着，在休息。

我盯着答案看了十分钟，却还在乞求另一个答案。

后来真有一只飞过来，落在我浅色的袖子上。

我放下了那只差点抬起来的手，一动不动。

旁边一个小女孩悄悄跟她妈妈说，那朵花开在人身上了。

我告诉她，那天我一定是选对了衣服。

她也想有蝴蝶落到自己身上，她妈妈让她就在原地等着。

我们三个人看着那对翅膀在我手腕附近开合。谁都没有伸手去碰。

等它飞到另一片叶子上时，小女孩做了那种孩子不想让某件事结束时的小撇嘴。

我给女孩指了指蝴蝶新的落脚处，等她看清了才走开。

她笑了，转了转花束，系上绳结。

莉娜：我把翅膀的那种蓝写进了导览册的空白页。

蓝，还有环绕着它的细细的深色边。

好像那样就能把它留住似的。

她从柜台下抽出一本破旧的导览册给你看那一页，铅笔字已经褪色，里面夹着一片压制叶片，那绝对不属于任何正式收藏。

莉娜：我现在还这么做。

写下颜色，而不是那个东西。

这样更容易，也更糟。

她抿了口茶。

莉娜：总之。

这些话是在花园里被一片叶子抢了风头的女孩说的。

该轮到你替我尴尬了。

你有没有类似的经历？

有没有什么东西你直直盯着却错过了？

choices.text: 我大概也有几件。先跟我说完蝴蝶那件事吧。
choices.response:
没有后续了，她开心地说。

就这些，整件事。

一只袖子借走了一只蝴蝶，一个孩子陪我们一起等，我得了一条铅笔笔记。

但她还是又讲了一遍，更慢，补上了温室玻璃是温热的、走道上湿泥土气味这些细节。

她说女孩的妈妈让她在原地等，三个人就那样一起看着，谁都没碰那只蝴蝶。那份共同的耐心，是她反复提起的细节。

然后她把剪刀像小法槌一样指着你，说你下次来得交你的版本。

她显然是打算有下次的。

choices.text: （轻轻掀起写了铅笔字的那页导览册的边角，让它自己落回去，再把书摊开放回柜台上她够得着的地方。）
choices.response:
她看着你捧着那本书，像捧着一件会碰伤的东西，她肩上有什么松了一寸。

你懂的，她说。

大多数人会直接翻到最后，看看里面还夹了什么。

她让书就停在你放的地方，摊开着，又没等你开口就给你续了茶。

顺便说一句，她说，那片压制叶片是棵杂草。

它从花园大门边的裂缝里长出来，我还是把它摘走了。

有些东西你留着，是因为它带来的那一天。

她说得很轻，但说这话时她看着的是那一页，不是你。

episodes.title: 季节送来的东西
episodes.opening:
你偏偏是在清晨的市场找到她的，她跪在水桶之间，系着帆布围裙，摊主们此起彼伏地喊着价钱。

摊位上正流行当季的杏色花材，莉娜本该只是采购这一周的用量。

麻烦在十步开外就看得见：她为了追一种色调，超买得厉害。

她的木箱里堆满了杏色花茎，而这些花茎没有对应的订单，摊主看她的眼神耐心得像房东一样。

清晨很冷，她呼出的气凝成白雾，可她还是在笑。
episodes.ending:
到了下午，咖啡馆的陈列台上摆着一组低矮的杏色花艺，让两位常客喝到一半停了下来，最后那些花茎和歪歪扭扭的花一起立在窗边的玻璃罐里，等着某天有意义。

莉娜用铅笔记完账，合上本子，说这是她一直在反复重修的一课。

季节送来了什么，就是什么。

她用手头拥有的真实摆了花，而这一次，真实竟然相当慷慨。

没有人因为难过而哭着回家。
episodes.dialogue:
莉娜：别说出来。

我知道。

她举起一根杏色花茎，像呈上对自己不利的证据。

莉娜：那个色调太完美了。

完美，而且多买了四十根。

婚礼订单是上个月的，婚礼早没了，现在只剩下我，和我那见到一种颜色状态正好就挪不动步的毛病。

摊主清了清嗓子。

莉娜：是是是，我全都会付钱的，拉菲，你这吸血鬼。

她数着钞票递过去，笑着，然后在寒冷里坐回脚跟，看着木箱，像在看一场举止还算体面的小灾难。

莉娜：真正的问题在这儿。

我一个人没法趁新鲜把这些卖掉。

店里就一间屋，我下午送咖啡馆的那趟顶多用掉十五根。

剩下的到周四就蔫了，而周四才不管它们周二有多美。

她站起来，拍掉膝盖上的灰，哼了一声提起木箱。

莉娜：我当然可以把它们带去咖啡馆。

可咖啡馆的陈列只有一个花瓶。

一个。

而且两个街区外有个收容所，对花从来不说不要，但我一次都没走进去过，因为——引用我自己的话——我不知道手该往哪儿放。

这是谎话。

我永远知道手该往哪儿放。

我只是不知道，到了一个我没准备任何花艺的地方，该怎么出现。

她斜眼看你，半开玩笑，半不是。

莉娜：你是局外人，所以有智慧。

陪我走一段。

告诉我我这两个蠢选项哪个没那么蠢，或者发明第三个，或者就帮我抬木箱另一头，让我慢慢想明白，怎么才能想要得比完美少一点。

choices.text: 去收容所。等有人从你手里接过一根花，你就知道手该放哪儿了。
choices.response:
她盯着你看了几秒，然后爆出一声大笑，把两个摊位外的拉菲都吓了一跳。

好吧。

好吧！

她把木箱的分量分给你们两人，然后大步走了两个街区，像要去退一台坏掉的烤面包机。

在里面，一位眼神疲惫的女士接过一根花，然后是一把，接着开始指挥莉娜，说大活动室的花瓶放在哪儿。

二十分钟后，莉娜的手正做着双手天生会做的事，她走出去时，比进来时安静多了。

周四，她在街角说。

我周四还会再来。

我甚至什么都没摆。

他们就这么收下了。

choices.text: （一言不发地抬起木箱另一头，朝收容所走去。）
choices.response:
你只是抬起你那一头就走，她眨着被背叛似的眼睛愣了一拍，跟了上来。

一路上她都在嘀咕，说有些人居然用脚回答问题，但她没有放慢脚步。

到了收容所，工作人员一拥而上围住木箱，她退到门边，你看着她看着一个少年把一根杏色花茎插进窗台上一只装了水的纸杯里。

莉娜的手终于安静了下来。

好吧，她在回去的路上说。

这就是第三个选项。

那本来就是我自己的选项，而我每个星期都从它旁边走了过去。

她没有当面道谢。

她给你买了一杯消防栓那么大的咖啡。

episodes.title: 被遗忘的旋律
episodes.opening:
傍晚，店里只剩下灯光和今天最后一束要包的花。

莉娜一边干活一边低声哼着什么，八个小节，然后停下，皱皱眉，又一模一样地哼了一遍——这说明旋律卡在她脑子里了，而她自己清楚。

窗边的罐子里现在插着三根歪歪扭扭的花茎，一个小小的失败者议会。

一张城里那家唱片店的传单折着放在柜台上，边角被咬过，比今天的报纸还要旧。

她发现你听到了那哼声，立刻放弃了假装没这回事。
episodes.ending:
周六仍然用铅笔写在传单上，像和一个没有名字的旋律的小小约定。

莉娜包好花束放进冷藏柜，翻过店门口的牌子，动作从容得像一个晚上过得比预期更好的人。

不管周六最后会怎样，那段旋律已经不再只是她在灯光下独自哼的东西了，这一点早已尘埃落定。
episodes.dialogue:
莉娜：好吧，你听到了，所以现在你也有份了。

她放下剪刀。

莉娜：有一首歌。

我是在早市那边听到的，一辆面包车在花摊旁边怠速着，八个小节，然后司机找到了停车位，也找到了他的音乐品味。

我已经哼了它两个星期。

两个星期。

我的手比我的脑子更记得它，而显然，一切值得记住的东西都是这样运作的。

她展开传单，把它抚平。

莉娜：城那头有家唱片店，老板允许你先试听再买，他还声称光凭哼几句就能说出任何歌名。

任何歌。

他那把胡子说明他有大把时间练过。

我每次休息日都差点去了，结果每次都改成摆弄花，因为对着周三的花束哼歌，它不会评判你。

她把传单转向你，在上面敲了一下。

莉娜：周六陪我一起去吧。

如果那把胡子失败了，我们就一起失败，而两个人一起失败要有趣得多。

如果他说出了歌名，我就欠这首歌一个家，我会在这家店里一直放它，直到那些歪花茎提出抗议。

她突然对一片多余叶子产生了浓厚兴趣，极其专注地修剪起来。

莉娜：没有压力。

嗯。

有一点压力。

好的那种。

那种意味着我宁愿和你一起去做、也不愿一个人去的那种，我把它说出口，是因为显然我现在会做这种事了。

所以。

周六，行吗？

choices.text: 周六去，之后我们再把它变成一次约会。就我们两个人，作为恋人。
choices.response:
剪刀停住了。

莉娜抬起头，这一次，那个凡事都要先安排妥当的花匠没有先安排出一句机灵的回话。

一次约会，她重复道。

就我们俩。

一个缓慢而明亮的笑容浮现出来，像某种终于到了季节的东西。

好。

好。

好。

她用铅笔在传单上写下周六，又添了一个时间，然后划掉那个时间，写了一个更好的。

我会提前打烊，她说。

花会撑住的。

我会对它们哼一整周的歌，它们只能自己想办法适应。

她又哼了一遍那八个小节，这一次听起来像是一个开始。

choices.text: （不说话，在传单上写下“朋友”和“周六”，画上一根歪歪扭扭的花茎的小涂鸦，再推回去。）
choices.response:
莉娜看看那个涂鸦，再看看你，笑得不得不扶住柜台。

一根歪花茎。

献给我们这场歪歪扭扭的追寻。

她认认真真地用铅笔写下周六，把传单钉在冷藏柜旁的软木板上，正对着视线的高度——那是她放真正当真的东西的地方。

周六，她说。

两个朋友对阵一位留着胡子的神谕者。

胜算糟糕透顶，而我等不及了。

她继续包花，哼着歌，那哼声里现在有了节奏的摆动，仿佛那八个小节终于知道自己要去哪里了。

episodes.title: 第一颗红番茄
episodes.opening:
自唱片店那天以来，季节已在店里流转了几轮：窗台罐子里如今插着一整排歪歪扭扭的花茎，像一场“美丽的失败”常设展，冷藏柜旁的日历上，每月第一个周六的位置画着一个小小的圈，已经挂在那里好一阵子了。

莉娜在门口迎接你，手里捧着一个陶盆，像捧着奖杯。

盆里是一株番茄，枝上挂着一颗终于真正变红的番茄。

顺便说一句，那首曲子后来查出来叫一个谁都不敢相信的名字，如今店里大多数早晨都放着它。
episodes.ending:
番茄在砧板上被切成两半，还带着窗台的余温，尝起来正是两个人一次次如约而至所付出的那份心意的味道。

陶盆放回窗台，等着下一颗成熟。

日历上接下来这个月的第一个周六被圈了起来，再下一个月则画着一个小一点的圈，像一个习惯正在练习成为永久。

店里嗡嗡作响。

比那八小节更好。
episodes.dialogue:
莉娜：请看。

她郑重其事地把陶盆放在柜台上。

莉娜：窗台帝国的第一颗红番茄。

它长歪了，显然，朝着玻璃的方向，因为我养的每样东西都这样。

但它成熟了，这可比我的记录本事强多了。

她在围裙上擦了擦手，笑容底下带着几分近乎正式的东西。

莉娜：我能说件事，但不把它弄成什么大场面吗？

就是第一个周六这件事。

你来，我们摆咖啡馆的花艺，一起吃午饭，我说服你买一枝你原本没打算买的花。

已经……差不多每个月都这样，有一阵子了吧。

然后我发现，我不再用铅笔写它了。

你看。

她把日历转过来。

那个圈是用钢笔画的。

莉娜：我只是想亲口、在大白天里说一次：这是一项固定的事。

第一个周六。

属于我们的。

咱们俩都有别的事，这才是它算数的原因。

她摘下番茄，拧下来，用两根手指举着，像举着一颗小太阳。

莉娜：初摘归你。

这是我刚发明的规矩。

之后的规矩是，下次你带面包来，因为我有番茄有咖啡，就是一进面包店就毫无自制力，所以分工很明确。

她当场用小刀在柜台上把番茄切成两半，汁水流淌，头一回完全不在乎什么美观标准。

莉娜：怎么样？

我们说定了，第一个周六，用钢笔写？

choices.text: 第一个周六，用钢笔写。而且我带的是好面包。
choices.response:
用钢笔写，她重复了一遍，却什么也没写，因为早就写好了，你们俩一起看着日历，像看一份签了字的文件。

好面包，她郑重地说。

那这约定就是神圣的了。

她没问就往你那半块番茄上撒了盐，那是她早已记住你口味的自然动作。

她聊起窗台帝国的扩张计划，也许种个辣椒，那可就是一桩丑闻了。

店里在你们俩周围嗡嗡作响，窗台上那排歪歪扭扭的花茎挺立着，像是在为这份文书表示赞许。

choices.text: （拿起那半块番茄吃掉，然后轻敲一下日历上的钢笔圈。）
choices.response:
不需要说话。

你吃掉你那半，好吃得离谱，然后轻敲了一下那个钢笔圈，这本身就是一整句话。

莉娜点头回应，同样一言不发，条约就此签订。

她靠在柜台上，满意地望着窗台帝国。

一年前，我抱着一捧花连收容所都不敢进，她说。

现在我有一个固定约会，还有一颗番茄和一位朋友。

她咧嘴一笑。

这话说得不对劲，但我就留着它了。

第一个周六。

带面包来。

店里继续嗡嗡作响，你们谁也没去改日历。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 季节送来的，如数奉还
romance.opening:
又是傍晚，灯光，小音箱里低声播放的曲调——音箱放在冷藏柜旁，播的正是那首让胡子神谕者哼了三次、吵了一架才终于报出名字的曲子。

窗边的罐子里如今立着满满一排歪歪扭扭的花茎，窗台上的番茄植株结出了第二颗果子。

从你这次到店起，莉娜就一直很反常，以一种很具体的方式：神采奕奕，好几次话到嘴边又咽回去，还把同一片多余的叶子修了三次。

自从唱片店之后你们的第一次约会起，每个月的第一个周六就成了属于你们两人的夜晚，用钢笔在她的日历上圈了出来。

终于，她伸手到柜台下面，拿出一个小纸信封，边角已被磨得发软，放在你们两人之间。
romance.ending:
歪歪扭扭的花茎立在窗边的罐子里，莉娜照她一贯的细心收好剩下的书签。

那首曲子放完一遍又从头开始，如今它是被允许这么做的。

莉娜有她的店、她的清晨和她的歪歪扭扭议会；你有你的日子、日历上钢笔圈出的第一个周六，以及这个确切的、被留出空间保持自己形状的共处夜晚。

季节送来了它送来的东西。

那已经足够了，甚至还有富余。
romance.dialogue:
莉娜：好吧。

这件事我只给两个人看过，其中一个还是邮递员，纯属意外。

她打开信封。

里面是书签。

几十枚，压得平平整整，都是你这些季节里来店里时认得的花，每一枚都细心地封在小袋子里。

莉娜：那是我做出的第一束没人买的花。

之后每一支没卖出去的花茎也是。

我舍不得扔，就把它们压平了，然后我就有了一抽屉压平的岁月，却完全不知道它们是干什么用的。

她拿起一枚，在灯光下翻转着看。

莉娜：秘密就是，我从来不知道留着这些是为了什么。

我只是留着。

然后不知从什么时候起，店里来了位常客，注意到了窗边那支歪花茎，帮我把一箱花搬到两个街区外的收容所，听我讲蝴蝶的故事，忽然间，那个抽屉就有了意义。

现在我可以把其中一枚送给一个在抽屉渐渐有了意义的这段日子里一直在这里的人。当然，自己也留一些也是被允许的。

她把信封朝你推过来，然后竖起一根手指。

莉娜：这不是一份永久契约。

你可以拿走一枚书签，也可以把它留给我；我守着我的店，我们各自过各自的生活——这一点我很喜欢，而且我不会为任何人放弃我在市集的清晨，别问。

但这一部分我要明明白白地说出来，因为你教会了我，东西该来的时候自然会来，把它们安排到死是很蠢的：我会一直选择这个。

选择你，选择这一切，选择所有歪歪扭扭的东西。

如果你也愿意一直选择它的话。

她修掉一片多余的叶子，手很稳，眼睛却头一回没落在叶子上。

莉娜：那么。

无论书签是随你走还是留下来，你还选择我们吗？

choices.text: 我选择它。连每一支歪歪扭扭的花茎一起。
choices.response:
莉娜长长地呼出一口气，像是两年前那个清晨市集起就一直憋着一口气。

好吧，她说，然后为自己说了好吧而笑出声。

她从信封里取出一枚书签，正是最早压下的那支花茎，把它塞进你手心，用她的双手把你的手指合拢上去，短暂而温暖，随即收回。

这一枚是你的。

其余的都留在抽屉里，她说。

一个姑娘不会把自己的整个春天一次送光。

然后，因为她终究还是莉娜，她往窗边的罐子里又添了一支歪歪扭扭的香豌豆，把角度调了一毫米，退后一步端详。

好了，她说。

插好了。

choices.text: （轻轻合上信封，把它推回她那边，再敲一敲立着歪花茎的窗边罐子。）
choices.response:
你合上信封，把它推回她手里，转而敲了敲那罐歪歪扭扭的花茎。

她的表情先是复杂了一下，随即舒展开一个温暖的微笑，因为她明白了你想让这些纪念物留在她那里。

对，她轻声说。

它们是我的。

这份珍藏从头到尾都是我的。

她抽出最早的那枚压花书签，原版的那一枚，夹进那本破旧的导览册里，夹在用铅笔写着蓝色两个字的那一页，这让她为自己的象征手法笑出声，又装作不是故意安排的。

她回敲了一下罐子。

成交，她说。

还是我们，还是第一个周六，整个歪歪扭扭议会都留在家里。我可以留着这些，也继续选择你。

episodes.title: The Smiley Cup
episodes.opening:
Northstar Creative, seven days before launch.

The pitch meeting has just ended, and the office smells of burnt coffee and marker fumes.

Evan Gu stands by the whiteboard in his charcoal suit, badge pushed aside, sleeves already rolled.

On the table between you sits a ceramic cup someone has drawn a lopsided smiley face on in marker.

Evan sets his black portfolio down, uncaps a dry-erase marker, and studies the board like it might argue back.

You barely know him—two weeks of emails and one introductions meeting.

He glances at the cup, then at you.
episodes.dialogue:
Evan here.

That cup has been circulating this floor for three years.

Whoever draws the smiley passes it on when they survive a bad meeting.

Congratulations—it's yours now.

I'd say it's an honor, but mostly it means you sat through Marla's budget slides without hiding under the table.

He wipes his hands on a napkin and sits down across from you, leaving one chair's width of space.

Before we scatter, I want to flag something.

Client revisions came in an hour early, and two of them contradict the timeline we pitched.

I'm not going to pretend that's fine.

I'm also not going to stand here and assign blame to whoever estimated the build phase.

My old lead used to say every problem needs an owner, but no mistake is solved by finding a scapegoat.

So.

Options.

One: I take both revisions tonight and you get them back cleaned up tomorrow.

Two: we split them, thirty minutes each, and we both leave by eight.

Three: we push back on the client and spend political capital we may need later.

He taps the marker against the table, once.

His voice is even, but you notice the crease pressed into his suit jacket's hem, sharp as a fold from a garment bag someone never removed.

He catches you looking and, for the first time, smiles slightly.

Bought it with my own savings, first proper suit.

Wore it to a negotiation I wasn't even leading.

Learned that day that the clothes don't carry the meeting.

He slides the smiley cup an inch toward you.

So—before you decide anything about revisions.

How's your day actually been?

You look like you could use ten minutes of honesty.

choices.text: My day's been long, honestly—and I'll take option two. We split the revisions and both leave by eight.
choices.response:
Evan nods, and something in his shoulders loosens half an inch.

Good.

Option two it is.

He takes a sticky note, writes the two revision numbers, and tears it in half, sliding one piece across the table to you.

He picks up his portfolio, then pauses.

And thank you for saying the honest part first.

People around here are learning to skip it.

Don't.

His tone is quiet, and he waits until you pocket the note before standing.

choices.text: (Slide the smiley cup back toward him and start clearing the table without a word.)
choices.response:
Evan watches you stack the napkins and right the fallen markers, and he huffs a small laugh.

All right—you've made the table very tidy, and told me exactly nothing about the revisions.

He caps his marker and sets it down, hands open on the table.

I'm not going to guess at silence and write a plan you never agreed to.

So, plainly: option two, the split, thirty minutes each, both out by eight?

He turns the smiley cup slowly on the table, once around.

Or—we try something else entirely. Option one, I take both revisions and you go home on time.

Or three, we push back on the client together tomorrow morning.

Whichever it is, it's yours to name, not mine to assume.

Pick one—or don't, and I'll put all three on a sticky note and leave the choice with you overnight.

He waits, marker untouched, leaving the decision entirely on your side of the table.

episodes.ending:
The revisions got sorted fairly, and by eight the office is quiet.

Evan walks you as far as the elevator, portfolio under his arm, the smiley cup washed and drying on the rack behind him.

“Same time tomorrow,” he says.

And if the client pushes back, we push back together.

The elevator doors close on him rolling his sleeves down, the crease in his jacket finally smoothed out.

episodes.title: The Gray-Headed Cat
episodes.opening:
Four days to launch.

The revisions from the other night settled fairly, and since then you and Evan trade the last hour of every day, comparing notes at the long table while the floor empties.

Tonight the schedule board is a thicket of arrows, and Evan has done his habit—wiped everything but three critical items.

He drops into the chair opposite you with a takeaway container, notices a strand of light-colored fur on his trouser leg, and stops mid-sentence.

He picks it off, holds it up to the light, and his expression does something you haven't seen before.

It softens.
episodes.dialogue:
Ah.

Evidence.

He folds the fur into a napkin with unnecessary care.

You've probably wondered why I leave at strange hours some nights.

There's a cat in my old building—a gray-headed thing, half-feral, limps on the left front paw.

I used to live there, and the neighbors fed it, but nobody sat with it when it was sick.

So I'd go over, sit on the edge of the sofa across from wherever it was hiding, and just watch it.

See if anything looked wrong.

He turns the takeaway container in his hands without opening it.

First few times, its eyes would narrow at me like I owed it money.

Eventually it let me stroke its back, two slow passes, no more.

Then I'd leave quietly and close the door soft.

He laughs at himself, short and unembarrassed.

I'm telling you this because yesterday the vet called.

The limp is arthritis, manageable, and the building manager has agreed to let a volunteer check on it weekly.

I put my name down.

Which means Tuesdays I leave at six, sharp, and the launch plan needs to survive without me for one hour a week.

He looks up, direct.

I'm not telling you this to make the schedule my problem to hide.

I'm telling you because you'll see me leave and I'd rather you know it's a cat with a gray head and not me dodging work.

He finally opens the container.

Also, I now own one pair of trousers permanently coated in fine fur, and I've decided that's a fair trade.

Your turn.

Anything on your desk that isn't actually about the launch?

choices.text: Tuesday at six is yours, no questions. The cat's checkup matters more than one hour of arrows on a board.
choices.response:
Evan blinks, then nods slowly, as if filing the sentence somewhere important.

Thank you.

He means it; you can hear it.

Most people would've asked what the backup plan was.

He writes TUES 6PM on the board in the corner, small, untouchable, outside the three critical items.

The backup plan is that I work faster the other four days, he says, and for once he doesn't sound like he's bracing for an argument.

choices.text: (Step up to the board and start laying out tomorrow's arrows so his hour fits.)
choices.response:
Evan watches you quietly rearrange the schedule so a gap opens at six on Tuesdays, and he doesn't interrupt.

When you're done he studies the board and exhales.

You just did in ninety seconds what I spent an hour not asking anyone to do.

He taps the gap with his marker, leaving it there, then sits back.

The cat gets his Tuesday.

The launch gets the rest of you both, and neither one has to be a secret.

episodes.ending:
The board keeps its small Tuesday slot through every revision that follows.

Evan leaves on time that Tuesday and every Tuesday after, and comes back with fur on his sleeves and, once, a photo of the gray-headed cat eating from a proper bowl.

Nobody on the team asks why anymore.

It's simply part of the plan, the way good plans make room.

episodes.title: The Blundered Game
episodes.opening:
Launch day minus two.

Evan called it an early finish—an hour at the park near the office, his treat, because the team hit every checkpoint.

He's brought a folding chess set from his bag, and you play on a stone table under a gingko tree while office workers stream past.

Evan is winning, comfortably, until he doesn't.

He moves his rook, stares at the board, and his face goes still.

You've watched him all week: under pressure he's been pulling tasks back onto his own desk, staying later than anyone, his tone clipping shorter.

Now he's made an obvious, unforced blunder, and he knows it.
episodes.dialogue:
Well.

That's the worst move I've made all month.

He doesn't take it back; house rules, apparently.

He leans back on the stone bench and looks at the gingko leaves instead of the board.

I've been running on fumes, and it shows.

This week I took back three tasks that were already assigned—yours included, briefly, and I did it without asking.

That was wrong, and I'm sorry.

My tone Tuesday was more commanding than the situation deserved.

He rolls his sleeves up, the old pre-difficult-conversation habit, though there's no one here to brace against but you.

Can I tell you something that isn't about work?

There's a photo I keep on my desk.

One year I went home for my father's birthday and brought flowers.

He loved standing in the bright spot by the window when pictures were taken.

I found a tall glass pitcher, put the flowers in it, and he carried it around the room trying positions until the light hit right.

Then he said I'd photographed the flowers too little, and he took one himself—and made it his profile picture.

It still is.

He turns a chess pawn over in his fingers.

The pitcher sits on his shelf back home, and when I visit, we argue about where the flowers should stand, every time, like it's a tradition neither of us will drop.

I bought one for my own place, and it's on my shelf now—empty so far, but today I'm fixing that.

I'm telling you because I've been so busy owning everything that I forgot the point of finishing things is having somewhere to put them down.

He sets the pawn back on the board, beside the blundered rook, and leaves both where they are.

Your move.

And after—do me a favor.

If I start hoarding tasks again, say it to my face.

I'd rather hear it from you than discover it in a resignation letter.

choices.text: Deal—but only if you also let yourself lose at chess occasionally. Your move was bad, and the game goes on.
choices.response:
Evan laughs, a real one, from somewhere lower than politeness.

Fair.

The blunder stays on the board as a monument to my exhaustion.

He studies your position properly for the first time all game, and you watch him actually think instead of perform.

When you eventually take his rook, he nods like you've done him a service.

“There,” he says.

Now we're even, and I feel more like a person.

Next week, if I catch myself hoarding, I'll show you the board first.

choices.text: (Reach over and move one of his scattered pieces back into a defensible line, saying nothing.)
choices.response:
Evan watches your hand rearrange his position into something survivable, and for a long moment he says nothing at all.

Then, quietly: You know, that's the first time this week anyone has fixed something of mine without making a speech about it.

He squares the pieces on his side, all of them, including the blundered rook.

I'll take the reminder.

Loud tasks, quiet fixes—that's the ratio I've been getting backwards.

He studies the board you've saved, then taps the edge of the table.

Tell you what—let's count this one as a practice board, no result recorded, and start a proper game from the opening.

You teach, I learn, and this time I offer you the first move.

episodes.ending:
You play on, and it runs close—the light shifts while you both lean over the squares.

Evan loses on purpose only a little.

On the walk back he stops at a corner stall and buys a small bunch of white flowers, saying the pitcher on his shelf has been empty long enough and today it gets its first bunch.

At the office door he pauses.

“In two days we finish this launch,” he says.

Tonight, the flowers get their light.

It sounds like a man putting something down on purpose, and leaving it there.

episodes.title: Mushroom Buns
episodes.opening:
Launch day.

It went well—no fires, no scapegoats, the smiley cup passed to someone new.

That evening, Evan appears at your desk with a canvas bag and the particular posture of a man about to make a request.

Before a hard conversation he rolls his sleeves and pushes his badge aside; tonight his badge is already in his pocket, sleeves down, off the clock entirely.

The bag smells, unmistakably, of mushrooms and dough.

The office around you is emptying for the weekend.
episodes.dialogue:
So.

Confession.

I made too many mushroom buns.

My father's recipe—I've been making it since before I could legally be trusted with a steamer, and my hands apparently still think I'm cooking for a family of eight.

There are thirty.

And an update while we're counting: the Tuesdays turned into something more.

This morning I asked the building manager if I could adopt the gray-headed cat instead of just visiting, and he said yes—so starting this weekend, the cat moves in with me.

Voluntarily, on both sides—I'd like to think.

Which means I'm about to be one person and one resident cat, and the cat has opinions but no appetite for mushrooms.

He sets the bag on the desk, not quite handing it over.

The steamer basket that fits them is at my place, and buns reheat badly in an office microwave.

So here's the invitation, plainly: come to my apartment tonight.

I'll steam them properly, there's tea, and the balcony has two chairs and a decent view of nothing in particular.

No agenda, no schedule talk.

He holds up a hand before you can answer.

And to be clear about the terms, because I don't want ambiguity doing my talking for me: this is a door, not a test.

If you come as a friend, we eat buns and complain about fonts, and that's a good night and I'll be glad of it.

If you'd rather it be more than that—then say so, and we'll see where it goes, slowly, with you allowed to change your mind at any steamer basket along the way.

Either way, the buns exist and they are excellent, and I will not take no personally.

He stands there, hands loose at his sides, the canvas bag between you like a small steaming question mark.

The elevator dings somewhere down the hall.

Whatever you say next, he'll hear all of it.

choices.text: Then let's be more than friends, Evan. I'd like to see where this goes—slowly, starting with those buns.
choices.response:
Evan's breath goes out of him in a way you've never seen at any launch meeting—relief, plainly worn.

Okay, he says, and then, more steadily, Okay.

Good.

He picks up the bag and doesn't try to take your arm or your hand; he just walks beside you to the elevator, close enough that your shoulders almost brush.

At his door he pauses.

House rule: nobody steams alone.

You'll learn the recipe, and I'll probably get the folding wrong on purpose so you have something to correct.

choices.text: (Pick up the canvas bag and nod toward the elevator—coming as a friend, and glad of it.)
choices.response:
Evan reads the nod exactly right, and his smile is warm without any question hiding in it.

Friend it is.

He falls into step beside you.

For the record, he says as the elevator doors open, friends who make room for a cat's Tuesday and help me slow down when I'm hoarding are rarer than good launches.

I'm keeping you.

At his place he hands you the tea tin like it's an official duty, and the evening runs long and easy, full of steamer noise and complaints about fonts.

episodes.ending:
The buns were excellent and there are still too many of them.

Evan sends you home with a stacked box and a promise that the recipe has a second lesson in it.

The balcony's two chairs stay where they are, side by side, and on the sill between them sits a small pot of soil the two of you planted together after dinner—a bulb, he said, that blooms when it's good and ready.

episodes.title: What the Bulb Was Waiting For
episodes.opening:
Months have passed since launch night.

The friendship settled into its own weather: Tuesday check-ins, a standing monthly dinner where the mushroom bun count remains, stubbornly, too high, and messages that begin with board screenshots and end with photos of a gray-headed cat asleep on a radiator.

Tonight you're on Evan's balcony, the two chairs side by side, the city doing its low evening hum.

And on the sill, the pot you both planted that first night has done something.

A bloom has opened—deep, unapologetic red, absurd against the concrete.

Evan is standing very still in front of it, tea going cold in his hand.
episodes.dialogue:
“It waited,” he says.

Months of nothing, and I watered it on faith and your reminders, and now this.

He crouches to look at it properly, sleeves rolled, badge long forgotten somewhere indoors.

My pitcher is on the shelf behind us, by the way—the one I first filled with flowers after that chess afternoon.

Fresh flowers in it every week since spring.

I keep the light on it in the evenings.

He settles into the chair beside you, and there's an ease in how he does it that took a long time to build.

Can I put something on the table?

Not a schedule item.

A commitment.

I've been offered a lead role on the next big account.

Bigger team, bigger messes, same me.

I said I'd decide by Friday.

He turns the teacup in his hands.

The old me would have said yes in the meeting and spent a year hoarding every task until I broke.

The me you helped slow down over a chessboard wants to say yes and build it differently—owners for everything, room in the plan, Tuesdays that stay sacred.

He looks over at you.

I'm telling you first because you're part of how that me exists.

So here's what I'm proposing, plainly: whatever I build next, you get the unvarnished version of it—the wins and the hoarding relapses—and in return I'll keep showing up the same way for yours.

Friends who tell each other the truth before it becomes a resignation letter.

He raises his cold tea slightly toward the red bloom.

To the bulb that took its time.

And to whatever we're building.

He waits, not demanding anything, just present, the way he was on the edge of a sofa watching a limping cat decide whether to trust him.

choices.text: Take the role, and hold me to the same standard. Truth first, Tuesdays sacred, and I'll water your plants when you travel.
choices.response:
Evan's grin is immediate and unguarded.

Deal.

He actually extends his hand, and the handshake is firm and brief and entirely a friend's.

Then he laughs at himself.

A handshake over plant care.

My father would have photographed it from six angles and made it his profile picture.

He pours fresh tea for both of you, hot this time, and the conversation runs past dark—team names, the cat's Tuesday, the bun count that will never shrink.

The red bloom stays open on the sill between you the whole time, unbothered by how long the light stays on.

choices.text: (Refill his cup from the hot teapot before your own, and tap the rim of his cup with yours.)
choices.response:
Evan watches you serve him first, and something in his face settles, like a plan arriving at its right number.

He taps his cup back against yours, a small clear ring in the evening air.

“Understood,” he says.

No speech needed.

He drinks, then leans back and looks at the bloom.

Friday, I accept the role.

And I'm putting your name in my notes app under the heading 'people who slow me down'—it's a short list and I intend to keep it that way.

The tea goes cold a second time and neither of you minds.

Below, the city hums; above, the bulb that took its time holds its red open against the dark.

episodes.ending:
Evan takes the role on Friday, and the first thing on his new board is a corner note: TUES 6PM.

The monthly dinner survives every deadline since, bun count unchanged.

The red bloom eventually fades, and Evan presses it in his notebook between two meeting agendas, which he claims is symbolism and you claim is clutter.

The pot stays on the sill, and next spring there are two bulbs in it.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Room in the Plan
romance.opening:
Months have passed since the night of the mushroom buns.

The relationship grew the way Evan builds anything now: deliberately, with room left in the plan.

There are Tuesday dinners, a shared shorthand for bad meetings, and a gray-headed cat—now a permanent resident of the apartment—who has accepted you as the second-slowest pass on its back.

Tonight is Evan's balcony, the two chairs side by side, the city humming below.

On the sill, the pot you planted together that first night has opened—a deep red bloom, months in the waiting.

Evan stands before it with two cups of tea, sleeves rolled, and for once he doesn't rush to speak.
romance.dialogue:
“I had a whole structure for tonight,” he admits.

Two options, consequences listed.

Very professional.

He hands you a cup and sits, close enough that the armrests touch.

Then I looked at this flower and threw the deck away.

So here's the plain version.

I'm glad it was you at that whiteboard with the smiley cup.

I'm glad you helped me slow down over a chessboard when I was hoarding myself into the ground.

I'm glad the cat likes you, because the cat has terrible taste in people and excellent taste in patience.

He sets his cup on the sill beside the pot.

My father had this tall glass pitcher.

He carried it around the room on his birthday, hunting for the light, and the photo he took of the flowers in it is still his profile picture.

I used to think the lesson was about finding the right position.

It's not.

It's that some things only look right when you stop arranging and just stand in the light with them.

He turns to face you fully, and his voice loses its last bit of boardroom polish.

I'm not asking for a merger.

We both keep our own work, our own friends, my Tuesdays with the cat, your life I still only know in installments and want to keep learning.

I'm asking whether you want to keep choosing this—slowly, on purpose, with either of us free to say it's harder on any given week.

He waits.

No badge to push aside, no board to wipe clean.

Just a man in rolled sleeves, a red bloom between you, and the whole evening ahead.

Whatever you say, he'll hear all of it, and the tea will still be warm.

choices.text: Then I choose it, Evan—slowly, on purpose. Starting with the fact that you talk too much when you're nervous, and I like it.
choices.response:
Evan laughs, and the nervousness in it is honest and unhidden.

Guilty.

I'll work on the talking.

He won't, and you both know it.

He reaches over and, briefly, rests his hand over yours on the armrest—one warm, deliberate touch, gone again before it asks for anything more.

There, he says softly.

Logged.

First entry in the new plan, and I left room in it for everything after.

He picks up his tea, and his eyes are bright.

Stay for the second pot.

The cat comes out around nine, and I want you here when it decides to sit on your side of the balcony.

It's been planning that for weeks.

I've seen it scouting.

choices.text: (Lift your cup and touch its rim gently against his, holding his eyes over the steam.)
choices.response:
The small clear ring of porcelain is answer enough.

Evan exhales, long and slow, like a man setting down something he's carried across a finish line.

“Okay,” he says.

Good.

He turns his chair a few degrees so the two of you face the bloom together, shoulders just touching.

For the record, he murmurs, that was the correct option.

There were only two, and you found a third.

He drinks his tea while the light on the flowers goes soft.

The cat appears at nine, and settles on the sill below the pot, gray head tucked, unbothered by how long the evening runs.

romance.ending:
A second pot of tea happens, and then a third, and the city hums through all of them.

Evan's calendar keeps its Tuesdays, your life keeps its own installments, and the plan—his word, always—has room in it for both.

The red bloom lasts another week; when it fades, Evan photographs it from several angles, says his father would approve, and makes it his profile picture.

The pot stays on the sill.

Next spring, there are two bulbs in it.

episodes.title: 笑脸杯
episodes.opening:
北辰创意，距离上线还有七天。

提案会刚散场，办公室里还飘着煮糊的咖啡味和马克笔的气味。

顾言穿着深色西装站在白板旁，工牌推到一边，袖子已经卷起来了。

你们之间的桌上放着一只陶瓷杯，不知是谁用马克笔在上面画了个歪歪扭扭的笑脸。

顾言放下黑色文件夹，拔开白板笔的笔帽，盯着白板打量，像它在跟他对峙似的。

你跟他几乎不熟——两周的邮件往来，加一次见面认识。

他瞥了一眼那只杯子，又看了看你。
episodes.dialogue:
顾言。

这只杯子在这层楼传了三年了。

谁扛过一场糟糕的会，就把笑脸画上，再传给下一个人。

恭喜——现在归你了。

我倒不敢说这是什么荣耀，不过它多半说明，你听完玛拉的预算幻灯片没钻到桌子底下去。

他在纸巾上擦了擦手，在你对面坐下，中间留出一把椅子的距离。

散会之前，有件事想跟你打个招呼。

客户的修改意见提前一小时到了，其中两条跟我们提案里排的进度是冲突的。

我不会装作这没问题。

但我也不会站在这儿，去追究当初是谁估的工期。

我以前的上司常说：问题要有明确的负责人，但失误不能靠找替罪羊解决。

所以。

给你几个选项。

一：今晚两条修改都归我，明天你拿到的就是整理好的版本。

二：我们分了它俩，一人半小时，八点前各自下班。

三：我们顶回去，跟客户硬碰，花掉那笔以后可能要用的政治资本。

他用马克笔在桌上轻轻敲了一下。

他的声音很平稳，但你注意到他西装下摆压出的一道折痕，利落得像是衣服从买来那天起就一直挂在防尘袋里，从没人取出来过。

他发现你在看，第一次微微笑了。

自己攒钱买的第一套像样的西装。

穿去了一场根本轮不到我主导的谈判。

那天我才明白，撑场面的从来不是衣服。

他把笑脸杯朝你那边推了一寸。

所以——在决定怎么处理修改意见之前。

你今天过得到底怎么样？

你看起来像是需要十分钟说点真心话。

choices.text: 说实话，今天挺漫长的——而且我选方案二。修改意见我们分了，八点前各自下班。
choices.response:
顾言点点头，肩上有什么东西松了半寸。

好。

就方案二。

他拿起一张便利贴，写下两个修改条目的编号，撕成两半，把其中一半推到桌子那头给你。

他拿起文件夹，又停了一下。

谢谢你先说了实话。

这地方的人，正学着把实话省略掉。

别学。

他的语气很轻，没有一点命令的意思，一直等你把那半张便利贴收进口袋才站起来。

choices.text: （你把笑脸杯往他那边推回去，一句话不说，动手收拾桌子。）
choices.response:
顾言看着你把纸巾摞好，把滚落的马克笔一支支立起来，轻轻笑出了声。

行——桌子是被你收拾得非常整洁了，可关于修改意见，你什么也没告诉我。

他扣上笔帽放下，双手摊在桌面上。

我不会去猜沉默的意思，更不会替你写一份你根本没同意过的计划。

所以，直说吧：方案二，一人半小时，八点前一起走？

他慢慢转着桌上的笑脸杯，转了一整圈。

或者——我们干脆换个路子。方案一，两条修改都归我，你按时回家。

再或者方案三，明天一早，我们一起去顶客户。

选哪个，由你说了算，不由我替你猜。

一句话的事——你要是不说，我就把这三个选项全写在便利贴上，留给你考虑一晚上。

他等着，手始终没碰那支笔，把决定权完整地留在你那半边桌上。

episodes.ending:
修改意见分配得公平妥当，到了八点，办公室安静下来。

顾言夹着文件夹，送你到电梯口，那只笑脸杯已经洗净，在后面的架子上沥干。

“明天同一个时间。”他说。

客户要是再找麻烦，我们一起顶回去。

电梯门合上时，他正把卷起的袖口放下来，西装上那道折痕，总算被抚平了。

episodes.title: 灰头猫
episodes.opening:
距离上线还有四天。

前几天那轮修改总算落定了，从那以后，你和顾言每天交换最后一个小时，在大桌边对笔记，办公室渐渐空下来。

今晚排期板上箭头密密麻麻，顾言又做了他那个习惯动作——擦掉一切，只留下三件最要紧的事。

他拿着外卖盒，在你对面坐下，忽然注意到裤腿上粘着一根浅色的毛，话说到一半停住了。

他把那根毛捏下来，举到灯下看，脸上露出一种你从没见过的神情。

软下来了。
episodes.dialogue:
啊。

证据。

他把那根毛仔细地折进纸巾里，那份小心实在没必要。

你可能一直纳闷，为什么有些晚上我走得出奇地早。

我以前住的那栋楼里有只猫——灰脑袋，半野的，左前腿有点跛。

我在那儿住过，邻居们喂它，可它病的时候没人陪它坐坐。

所以我就过去，在它藏身的地方对面沙发边坐下，就那么看着它。

看有没有哪里不对劲。

他手里转着外卖盒，没打开。

头几次，它眯着眼睛看我，好像我欠它钱似的。

后来它肯让我摸摸背了，慢慢地来回两下，仅此而已。

然后我就悄悄离开，轻轻带上门。

他自嘲地笑了，笑得短促，也不觉得难为情。

跟你说这个，是因为昨天兽医打来电话。

跛腿是关节炎，能控制，物业也同意让志愿者每周去看它一次。

我报名了。

也就是说，每周二我六点准时走，上线计划得学会每周没有我一个小时。

他抬起头，目光很直接。

我告诉你这些，是不想让排期变成我一个人藏着的难题。

我说这些，是因为你会看见我离开，我宁可你知道那是为了只灰脑袋的猫，而不是我在躲活儿。

他终于打开外卖盒。

另外，我现在有一条裤子永远沾满细毛，我觉得这买卖不亏。

该你了。

你桌上有没有什么事，其实跟上线没关系？

choices.text: 周二六点归你，我一个问题都不问。猫的复查比板上一小时的箭头重要。
choices.response:
顾言眨了眨眼，缓缓点头，像把这句话收进了什么重要的地方。

谢谢。

他是认真的，你听得出来。

大多数人会先追问备用方案是什么。

他在白板角落写下“周二 18:00”，小小的，碰不得，在三件要事之外。

备用方案就是我其余四天干快一点，他说，这一次，听不出那种准备迎接争吵的语气。

choices.text: （你起身走到白板前，重新排布明天的箭头，给他的那一小时腾出位置。）
choices.response:
顾言安静地看着你调整排期，把周二六点空出来，他没有打断。

你弄完，他端详着白板，呼出一口气。

你九十秒就做到了我花一个钟头都没好意思开口让人做的事。

他用马克笔点了点那个空档，把它留在那里，然后坐回去。

猫得到了他的周二。

上线的其余部分归我们两个，而且哪一样都不用再当秘密。

episodes.ending:
那之后的每一轮修改，白板上都留着那一小块周二的位置。

那个周二顾言准时离开，之后每个周二都是，回来时袖口沾着猫毛，有一次还带回一张照片——灰头猫正从一个正经的猫碗里吃东西。

团队里再没人问为什么了。

它就是计划的一部分，好计划总会留出余地。

episodes.title: 走错的那步棋
episodes.opening:
距上线还有两天。

顾言提议提前收工——去公司附近的公园待一个小时，他请客，因为团队把每个节点都按时完成了。

他从包里拿出一套折叠棋盘，你们在银杏树下的石桌上对弈，下班的上班族从旁边陆续走过。

顾言一路领先，赢得从容，直到他不再从容。

他走了车，盯着棋盘，脸色一下子僵住了。

这一周你一直在观察他：压力一大，他就把任务往自己手里揽，比谁都走得晚，说话也越来越短促。

现在他走了一步明显又毫无外力逼迫的昏招，而他自己清楚。
episodes.dialogue:
唉。

这是我这个月走得最烂的一步。

他没有悔棋——看来这是规矩。

他靠回石凳上，目光落在银杏叶上，不看棋盘。

我最近全靠硬撑，也撑出破绽了。

这周我收回三个已经分派出去的任务——其中也包括你的，虽然只是短暂的，而且我事先都没问。

那是我的错，对不起。

周二我的语气也太命令了，那件事根本用不着那样说。

他卷起袖口，还是那个谈棘手问题前的老习惯，尽管这里只有你一个人可对。

能跟你说点工作以外的事吗？

我桌上放着一张照片。

有一年我回老家给父亲过生日，带了花。

他拍照时总爱站在窗边那块亮地方。

我找来一只高玻璃壶，把花插进去，他捧着它在屋里转来转去，换了好几个位置，直到光打对了才罢休。

然后他说我把花拍得太少了，自己拍了一张——还设成了头像。

到现在也还是那张。

他手指间捻着一枚棋子。

那只玻璃壶还摆在他老家的架子上，每次我回去，我们都要争一遍花该插在哪儿，回回如此，像成了我们俩谁也不肯放下的传统。

我给自己的住处也买了一只，现在就在我的架子上——还空着，不过今天我打算改变这一点。

我跟你讲这些，是因为我最近忙着把所有事都攥在手里，忘了把事情做完的意义，本来就在于有地方可以放下来。

他把那枚兵放回棋盘，挨着那枚走错的车，两颗棋子都没再动。

该你了。

还有——帮我个忙。

要是我又开始往自己手里揽任务，当面跟我说。

我宁愿从你这儿听见，也不想从一封辞职信里发现。

choices.text: 行——但你也得偶尔认输才行。你刚才那步就是臭棋，棋还得接着下。
choices.response:
顾言笑了，是真心那种笑，从比客套更深的地方冒出来。

公平。

这步昏招就留在棋盘上，当作我疲惫的纪念碑。

整盘棋他头一回认真琢磨你的布局，你看着他真的在思考，而不是在演。

等你终于吃掉他的车，他点点头，像你帮了他一个忙。

“就是这样。”他说。

这下扯平了，我也觉得自己更像个人了。

下周要是我又发现自己开始揽活，我先给你看棋盘。

choices.text: （你伸过手，把他散乱的一颗棋子挪回一条守得住的线上，什么也没说。）
choices.response:
顾言看着你的手把他的局面整理成还能下下去的样子，好一阵子，他一个字都没说。

然后，他轻声说：你知道吗，这一周里，这是第一次有人帮我修正了什么，却没就此发表一通长篇大论。

他把他那边的棋子一一摆正，包括那枚走错的车。

这个提醒我收下了。

高声喊的是任务，悄悄修的是漏洞——这个比例我一直弄反了。

他端详着你救回来的这盘棋，然后敲了敲桌沿。

这样吧——这盘就当练习局，不计胜负，我们重新从开局下一盘正儿八经的。

你教，我学，这回先手让给你。

episodes.ending:
你们接着下，局面咬得很紧——你们俩都俯身盯着棋盘，光线悄悄变了。

顾言只是稍微放了一点水。

回去的路上，他在街角的小摊前停下，买了一小束白花，说他架子上的玻璃壶空了太久，今天该迎来第一束花了。

在公司门口，他停了一下。

“再过两天，这次上线就收尾了。”他说。

今晚，先让花晒晒光。

听起来像一个人在刻意放下什么东西，而且决定就让它待在那儿。

episodes.title: 蘑菇包子
episodes.opening:
上线日。

一切顺利——没起火，没找替罪羊，笑脸杯传给了新的主人。

傍晚，顾言出现在你的工位前，拎着一个帆布袋，站姿透着一股有事相求的味道。

要谈棘手问题之前，他会卷起袖口、把工牌推到一边；今晚他的工牌已经收进口袋，袖子也放下来了，完全不在线上。

袋子里飘出一股明明白白的蘑菇和面团味。

办公室里的人正陆续下班，准备过周末。
episodes.dialogue:
是这样的。

坦白一件事。

蘑菇包子做多了。

我爸的配方——从还没到能合法碰蒸锅的年纪我就开始做了，看来我的手到现在还以为自己在给八口人做饭。

一共三十个。

数包子的时候顺便报个更新：周二的那些相遇，变成了更进一步的东西。

今天早上，我问了物业管理员，能不能不再是探望、而是正式收养那只灰头猫——他答应了。所以从这个周末起，猫就搬来跟我住。

双方都是自愿的——我愿意这么想。

也就是说，我即将变成一个人加一只常住猫，而那只猫很有主见，但坚决不吃蘑菇。

他把袋子放在桌上，没有真的递过来。

装它们的蒸笼在我家，包子在办公室微波炉里加热会很难吃。

所以，把邀请明明白白说出来：今晚来我家吧。

我会好好把包子蒸上，有茶，阳台上摆着两把椅子，还有一片不怎么样的、但挺好看看的风景。

不谈工作，不排日程。

你还没来得及回答，他先抬起了手。

把条件说清楚，因为我不想让含糊替我说话：这是一扇门。

如果你以朋友身份来，我们就吃包子、吐槽字体，那也是个很好的夜晚，我会很高兴。

如果你想要的不止于此——那就直说，我们慢慢看它会走到哪儿，你随时可以在任何一个蒸笼前改变主意。

无论如何，包子是真实存在的，而且非常好吃，被拒绝我也不会往心里去。

他站在那儿，双手自然垂在身侧，帆布袋放在你们中间，像个冒着热气的小问号。

走廊尽头的电梯叮了一声。

不管你接下来说什么，他都会认真听完。

choices.text: 那我们就做不止朋友的关系吧，顾言。我想看看这条路会走到哪儿——慢慢来，从这些包子开始。
choices.response:
顾言长长地呼出一口气，那种样子，你在任何一次上线会上都没见过——如释重负，明明白白写在脸上。

好，他说，然后更稳一些地又说了一遍，好。

太好了。

他拎起袋子，没有伸手来挽你的胳膊或牵你的手，只是走在你身边，一路陪你到电梯，近得你们的肩膀几乎要碰到。

到他家门口，他停了一下。

家规：不许一个人蒸包子。

配方你学着，而我大概会故意把褶子捏错，好给你留点纠正我的余地。

choices.text: （拎起那个帆布袋，朝电梯的方向点头示意——以朋友身份赴约，而且欣然如此。）
choices.response:
顾言把这个点头读得分毫不差，笑意温暖，里面没有藏任何问号。

那就当朋友。

他与你并肩而行。

说句实在话，电梯门打开时他说，愿意给一只猫留出周二、又肯在我什么都往自己身上揽时拉我一把的朋友，比成功的上线还要稀有。

你这个朋友，我留定了。

到了他家，他把茶叶罐郑重其事地交到你手里，像在完成一项正式交接。这一晚过得又长又轻松，满是蒸锅的声响和对字体的吐槽。

episodes.ending:
包子非常好吃，但还是多得吃不完。

顾言让你带走一摞打包盒，还许诺说，这套配方的第二课还在后头。

阳台上的两把椅子依然并排摆在那儿，中间的窗台上多了一小盆你们晚饭后一起种下的土——他说，那是一颗球茎，等它养足了劲，自然就开花了。

episodes.title: 那颗种球一直在等的
episodes.opening:
上线那晚已经过去好几个月了。

你们的友情有了自己的节奏：每周二互通近况，每月一次雷打不动的晚饭——蘑菇包子的数量依然固执地总是点太多——还有那些消息，开头是白板截图，结尾是一只灰头猫趴在暖气片上睡觉的照片。

今晚你在顾言家的阳台上，两把椅子并排摆着，城市在脚下低低地嗡鸣。

窗台上，你们第一晚一起种下的那盆花，有了动静。

一朵花开了——很深、毫不掩饰的红，衬着水泥墙显得近乎荒唐。

顾言一动不动地站在它面前，手里的茶已经凉了。
episodes.dialogue:
“它一直在等。”他说。

几个月毫无动静，我全凭信念浇水，再加上你提醒，现在它开成这样。

他蹲下去仔细看它，袖口卷着，工牌早就忘在屋里什么地方了。

对了，我的玻璃壶在我们身后那个架子上——就是那天下午下完棋、我第一次往里插花的那只。

从春天起，每周都换新鲜的花。

晚上我总留着灯照着它。

他在你旁边的椅子上坐下，那份自如，是花了很长时间才攒出来的。

我能把一件事摆到桌面上吗？

不是排期表上的事。

是一份承诺。

有人请我去做下一个大项目的负责人。

团队更大，乱摊子更大，人还是我。

我说周五之前给答复。

他转着手里的茶杯。

以前的我会在会上当场答应，然后用一年时间把所有活儿都攥在手里，直到把自己压垮。

而那个被你在棋盘边慢慢磨慢了的我，想答应下来，但换个做法——每件事都有负责人，方案里留足缓冲，周二雷打不动。

他看向你。

我先告诉你，是因为那个我能存在，有你一份。

所以我把话说明白：我接下来不管做什么，你都拿到不加修饰的版本——成绩也好，故态复萌的揽活儿也好——作为交换，你的事我也会同样在场。

做那种在事情变成辞职信之前、就彼此说真话的朋友。

他朝那朵红花微微举了举已经凉掉的茶。

敬这颗不慌不忙的种球。

也敬我们正在一起搭的一切。

他等着，不催你，也不要求什么，只是在场——就像当年坐在沙发边上，看那只一瘸一拐的猫决定要不要信任他时那样。

choices.text: 接下这个职位，然后照样拿标准要求我。真话优先，周二雷打不动，你出差的时候我帮你浇花。
choices.response:
顾言立刻笑了，毫不设防的那种。

成交。

他真的伸出手来，握手干脆利落，完完全全是个朋友的握法。

然后他自己先笑了。

为浇个花握手。

我爸要是看见，得从六个角度拍下来设成头像。

他给两人都倒了新茶，这次是热的，话题一直聊到天黑之后——团队起名，猫的周二，还有永远瘦不下去的包子数量。

那朵红花一直开在你们中间的窗台上，毫不在意灯亮了多久。

choices.text: （你先给自己续茶之前，用热茶壶先给他续上，再用杯沿轻轻碰了碰他的杯子。）
choices.response:
顾言看着你先给他倒茶，脸上的什么东西落定了，像一个方案终于对上了该对的数字。

他回碰了一下你的杯子，一声清脆的小响，落在晚风里。

“明白了。”他说。

不用多说什么。

他喝了一口，然后靠回椅背，看着那朵花。

周五，我接。

然后我会在手机备忘录里记下你的名字，标题叫“能让我慢下来的人”——这个名单很短，我也打算让它一直这么短。

茶第二次凉掉了，你们谁都没在意。

楼下城市低鸣；楼上，那颗不慌不忙的种球在黑暗里红得坦荡。

episodes.ending:
周五，顾言接下了那个职位，新白板上的第一样东西是个角落便条：周二晚六点。

那顿每月一次的晚饭扛过了之后所有截止日期，包子数量始终未变。

红花最后谢了，顾言把它夹进笔记本里，压在两份会议议程之间——他管这叫有象征意义，你管这叫乱堆东西。

花盆还在窗台上，明年春天，里面会有两颗种球。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 给方案留点余地
romance.opening:
蘑菇包子那晚之后，几个月过去了。

这段感情，像如今的顾言做任何事那样慢慢生长：有节奏，有章法，方案里总留着余地。

有每周二的晚饭，有关于糟糕会议的专属暗号，还有那只灰头猫——如今已是公寓的常住居民——它也认了你，让你成为摸它后背时第二慢的那一个。

今晚在顾言的阳台上，两把椅子并排放着，城市的低鸣在脚下流动。

窗台上，你们第一晚一起种下的那盆花开了——一朵深红色的花，等了几个月。

顾言端着两杯茶站在它面前，袖子卷着，这一次，他难得地不急着开口。
romance.dialogue:
“今晚我本来准备了一整套结构，”他坦白。

两个选项，后果一条条列好。

非常职业。

他递给你一杯茶，坐下，近到扶手挨着扶手。

然后我看了看这朵花，把那套方案整个扔了。

所以，来说最直白的版本。

我很高兴，当时站在白板前抱着笑脸杯的人是你。

我很高兴，在我把自己越攒越累的时候，是你陪我下棋，教我慢下来。

我很高兴猫喜欢你，因为这只猫看人的眼光烂透了，挑耐心的眼光却好得不得了。

他把茶杯放在窗台上，挨着花盆。

我父亲有一只很高的玻璃壶。

每年生日，他都捧着它在屋里走来走去，找光线。他拍下的那张壶里鲜花照，到现在还是他的头像。

我以前以为，这故事讲的是要找对位置。

其实不是。

它是说，有些东西只有当你不再摆弄它，只是陪它一起站在光里，才真正好看。

他整个人转向你，声音里最后一点会议室的客套也褪掉了。

我不是在谈什么合并。

我们各自留着自己的工作、自己的朋友，我留着我的周二和猫，你的生活我还只是分期了解着，并且想一直这样慢慢懂下去。

我想问的是，你愿不愿意继续做这个选择——慢慢地，有意识地，而且任何一周，我们俩任何一个人都可以说：这周有点难。

他等着。

没有要推到一边的工牌，没有要擦干净的白板。

只有一个卷着袖口的男人，你们之间一朵红色的花，和一整个还长着的夜晚。

无论你说什么，他都会听完，而茶，还是会温的。

choices.text: 那我选它，顾言——慢慢地，有意识地。从这条开始：你紧张的时候话特别多，而我挺喜欢的。
choices.response:
顾言笑了，笑里那点紧张，坦坦荡荡，一点没藏。

认罪。

我会改改话多的毛病。

他不会改的，你们俩都知道。

他伸过手来，短短一瞬，把手覆在你搭在扶手上的那只手上——一个温暖而郑重的触碰，还没索取更多，就收了回去。

好了，他轻声说。

记下了。

新方案的第一条，后面的一切，我都留了余地。

他端起茶，眼睛亮亮的。

留下来喝第二壶吧。

猫九点左右出来，我想让你在这儿，看它决定坐到你那半边阳台。

它策划这事好几周了。

我亲眼看见它踩过点。

choices.text: （你端起茶杯，轻轻碰了碰他的杯沿，隔着热气与他对视。）
choices.response:
瓷器那一声轻脆的碰撞，已经是回答了。

顾言长长地、缓缓地呼出一口气，像一个终于把重负放下来的人。

“好，”他说。

太好了。

他把自己的椅子转了几度，让你们俩一起面向那朵花，肩膀若即若离地挨着。

郑重声明，他低声说，刚才那是正确选项。

明明只有两个选项，你却找到了第三个。

他喝着茶，花上的光线渐渐变得柔和。

九点整，猫出现了，蜷在花盆底下的窗台上，灰色的脑袋埋起来，全然不在乎这个夜晚要多长有多长。

romance.ending:
第二壶茶泡上了，然后是第三壶，城市的低鸣陪着它们一路淌过去。

顾言的日历留着每周二，你的生活留着它自己的分期，而那份方案——他的口头禅，永远是——给两边的日子都留了余地。

那朵红色的花又开了一周；凋谢的时候，顾言从好几个角度给它拍了照，说他父亲一定会赞成，然后把它设成了自己的头像。

花盆还留在窗台上。

第二年春天，盆里冒出了两个种球。

episodes.title: What We Know, What We Assume
episodes.opening: Northstar Creative, seven days before launch. The pitch meeting has just broken up and the conference room smells like burnt coffee. Amara Okafor stands at the whiteboard alone, taping printed quotes beside three columns of marker: what we know, what we assume, what we still need to ask. One card curls loose and slides to the floor. She's in a cobalt blouse, twists pinned back, a slim folder under one arm, and she looks up as you come in for the pen someone left behind.
episodes.dialogue:
Amara Okafor here, cultural strategy.

I just came up for air from five regions' worth of material.

How's your day going?

Don't worry, I'm not going to recruit you into anything.

Yet.

The last campaign shipped on a beautiful assumption.

Somebody decided one market's answers would travel cleanly to another, and it turned out people had been saying yes to be polite the whole time.

Sixty interviews, one wrong reading, and a launch that had to be walked back.

So now the interviewees' own words sit right next to the whiteboard, where nobody can paraphrase them into agreement.

I keep hearing the pitch team say the regional options are 'extra flavor.' Flavor gets cut when budgets tighten.

Choice doesn't.

That's the gap I'm trying to close before Friday.

Anyway.

You caught me mid-lecture, and the material will still be here tomorrow.

If you'd rather talk about something else, I'd rather hear that.

Actually — one thing first.

Do you know why I keep the three columns separate?

Most people merge them by lunch.

choices.text: Because once an assumption gets written next to a fact, everyone stops checking which is which.
choices.response: Amara points the marker at you like a conductor's baton. 'Exactly. That's the whole disease in one sentence.' She writes nothing down, but she looks at you a second longer than she needs to, filing something. 'The quotes stay in their own lane, then. Come argue with my columns sometime — I trust people who check.'

choices.text: (Pick up the fallen quote card and hold it out to her without a word.)
choices.response: She takes the card, reads the quote on it, and smiles at the timing. 'This one is literally a woman saying nobody asked her what she wanted. You just handed her back her own sentence.' She tapes it up carefully, corners flush. 'Quiet and useful. I'll remember that combination.'

episodes.ending: She caps the marker and steps back to look at the wall — five regions, three columns, and a border of real voices holding the assumptions in place. 'Friday's review, room's open to anyone who reads,' she says, gathering her folder. It's a door left unlatched. She wishes you a good evening by name, and the whiteboard glows under the office lights long after she's gone.

episodes.title: The Second Pencil Line
episodes.opening: Two days into launch week and you've started reading the quote wall on your way past it. Tonight the office has emptied except for one desk lamp near the window, where Amara sits with a battered paperback and a stack of transcripts. A fat stack — she's re-checking the assumption column line by line. She looks up, not startled, as if she'd half expected company, and moves her bag off the second chair without being asked.
episodes.dialogue:
You again.

Good.

You're the only person this week who reads the wall instead of nodding at it.

Sit, if you want.

I'm hiding from my own inbox.

Can I show you something that isn't work?

I found this book in a secondhand shop years ago — a novel with the margins full of someone's notes.

Pencil, tiny handwriting, arguments with the author on every page.

It opens with everyone warning the heroine about a certain man, and the first note says, flatly: Don't trust him.

A hundred pages later, same pencil, different verdict: Okay, trust him once.

The stall owner who sold it to me told me to watch for one more thing — she changes her mind again before the end, and I've never been sure whether she was right to.

And here's the part I love.

Later that first week, when I reached that turn, instead of scribbling a rebuttal or crossing anything out, I took a pencil and wrote one very small line: I want to wait a bit longer.

That's it.

No erasing, no crossing out.

The old notes and the new small line sit together on the same page.

I think about that more than I should.

Especially this week, when everyone wants one verdict from five regions and I keep wanting to write, in very small letters, it depends.

Anyway — that's my evening.

What's yours?

choices.text: Have you ever written a small line like that outside the book?
choices.response: Amara laughs, low, surprised at herself. 'Nobody's ever asked me that. My first one outside the book was in a strategy memo, actually — next to a line about what users in a market I'd never visited would obviously want. I wrote: ask them, not me. Took me three more years to actually live by it.' She taps the paperback's cover. 'The book taught me the size. Small enough that you're not shouting anyone down.'

choices.text: (Lean in and read the visible margin notes without touching the page.)
choices.response: She turns the book a few degrees toward the lamp and lets you read in silence. The pencil notes crowd the edges — questions, grumbles, one small triumphant underline. 'You didn't grab it,' she says after a moment. 'You let it stay theirs. That's the whole skill I interview for, and you just did it to a stranger's twenty-year-old handwriting.'

episodes.ending: She closes the book on her finger and leaves it there, keeping her place the old-fashioned way. The transcripts sit untouched for a while, and neither of you treats that as wasted time. 'The wall will survive one evening,' she says finally, and means it — a new habit for her. When you both finally stand to leave, she tucks the paperback into her folder next to the launch documents, the same shelf for both, and walks you as far as the stairwell before turning back for her coat.

episodes.title: Two Tickets, Folded Together
episodes.opening: Launch week's worst review just ended — the client's old brief surfaced, the one asking for regional choices to be stripped out. Amara verified it's likely outdated, but 'likely' isn't a launch answer, and she's been carrying the verification alone. So when she says she needs air, you end up at the small amusement park outside the city, shutters half down, colored slides packed close together. She takes the window seat at a snack counter and watches the rides like they're data.
episodes.dialogue:
I came out here once before a big deadline, just to watch people choose things.

Which slide, which seat, whether to hold the rail.

Nobody's polite in a queue for a slide.

You get the truest answers in the world.

Look at those three lanes — same ride, everyone picks differently, and no one thinks the others picked wrong.

That's all I'm asking the campaign to allow.

But here's my problem, said out loud for the first time: that outdated brief.

I found it, I'm the one verifying it, and I've decided that means I have to do every part of it myself.

Which is nonsense, because Friday doesn't care who's tired.

I've been rewriting my own column all week — what I know, what I assume, what I still need to ask.

Turns out 'I must fix this alone' is in the assume column, written in permanent marker.

Terrible penmanship, that column of mine.

Oh — hold on.

Wind's picking up.

Your folder page.

Got it — here.

It nearly made the balloon seller's day; he's been watching us like we're a show.

He's holding two tickets folded together, by the way.

Been holding them a while.

I think they're for the little train, and I think he's waiting for someone to ask.

Shall we embarrass ourselves?

choices.text: Then let me take one part of the brief — I'll chase the dated signature and you draft the response.
choices.response: Amara goes still, then exhales like something unclenched. 'You'd do that? To split the work properly.' She pulls a napkin over and divides it with a borrowed pen: your name, her name, an actual boundary line. 'There. It's in writing. If I try to take it back Friday, show me the napkin.'

choices.text: (Take the caught folder page back from her, pull a napkin over, write 'signature check' on your half, and slide it and the pen toward her.)
choices.response: She looks at the pen, then at you, and something in her shoulders drops an inch. 'You're letting me say it first. That's — yes. All right.' She writes two names on the napkin and pushes half across the table. 'You take the signature hunt, I'll draft. I always assume nobody wants the boring half. Assume column again.'

episodes.ending: The napkin division of labor survives the ride home on the late train, folded into her folder next to the paperback and the launch notes. The balloon seller never does give away his two folded tickets, but he waves as you leave. Back at the office the next morning, you find the dated signature in the archived brief and send the page to Amara. She checks its version against the current approval and attaches both to her response; the client still has to confirm which governs Friday. With that request sent, the assumption column on the whiteboard has one item crossed out in pencil, not marker — I must fix this alone — with a small new line beside it in different handwriting. Amara points at it when you arrive and says nothing at all, which from her is a thank-you.

episodes.title: The Bird on the Ledge
episodes.opening: Launch eve. The campaign shipped with all five regional options intact — the outdated brief formally retired that afternoon — and the office is a strange, weightless place of cold pizza and open windows. Amara finds you at the window ledge, where a round, absurdly fat bird has claimed the railing outside, feathers puffed against the evening. She sets down two paper cups, hands you one, and watches the bird with open delight.
episodes.dialogue:
Look at him.

He's flown through five regions' worth of weather to sit on our railing and judge us.

He's not wrong.

We did it, by the way — all five choices shipped.

The napkin is framed on my desk now; don't ask.

So.

Before everyone scatters back to their own projects, before this turns into one of those things we meant to do — there's a public viewing night at the observatory this Saturday.

The plaza one, with the volunteers and the big telescope.

I went years ago, before I moved here for this job.

A volunteer steadied the tube for me and asked if I could see it, and I didn't move my eye for the longest time, because for a second I genuinely believed I could touch that dent in the moon.

Then I went to the back of the queue and queued all over again, like a person with sense.

I've never gone back since.

Always a deadline.

There's never not a deadline.

So — Saturday.

I'd like company.

The kind where we stand in a queue and look up and don't talk about markets once.

What do you say?

choices.text: Saturday, with you. I'd like it to be a date.
choices.response: Amara sets her cup down slowly, and her smile arrives before her words do. 'A date. All right. I was hoping one of us would say it plainly — I've been drafting versions in my head all week, which is very me.' She glances at the bird. 'He approves. He's been giving me that look for twenty minutes. Saturday, then. I'll bring the paperback — the one with the stranger's margin notes. If the queue's long, we can reread them together and argue about whether she was right to change her mind.'

choices.text: (Raise the paper cup toward her in a small toast, and let the smile answer for you.)
choices.response: Amara clinks her cup against yours, understanding without a word being spent. 'Friends it is — and I mean that as a real category, not a consolation one.' She leans on the railing beside you. 'Good. Then Saturday I get to be entirely myself, no subtext to manage. You'll queue with me twice, like sensible people, and we'll argue about whether that bird could survive out there. He's clearly thriving on ambition alone.'

episodes.ending: Saturday arrives clear and cool. The observatory plaza is crowded with families and students; the volunteer with the steady hands is there, and the queue moves slowly, exactly as promised. Amara queues twice that night, back of the line both times, and never once checks her phone. The telescope's long shadow lies across the stones, and the moon is more than a smudge above the rooftops.

episodes.title: Spice Biscuits and the Long Queue
episodes.opening: Two years later, a new launch, a new city office that already feels familiar. Amara arrives at your desk with a tin of spice biscuits she baked herself — slightly lopsided, aggressively cinnamon — and sets it down without ceremony. She opens the tin and tries to line the biscuits up along its rim; one leaning tower collapses against her thumb, and she breaks the fallen biscuit and sets half on a clean napkin beside you. Then she turns the calendar so you can see Saturday's public viewing time and puts her pen down. On the wall behind you, the quote-and-columns method now has its own laminated card. On her desk, the framed napkin. On Saturday's calendar, an observatory viewing night, third annual.
episodes.dialogue:
Biscuits.

Don't analyze them, eat them.

I've been baking the recipe my aunt sent — I asked her how she measures the spice and she said until it smells like home, which is useless and perfect, and I thought of our wall.

We've trained half the company, you know.

New hires get shown the three columns before they get shown the coffee machine.

And I've stopped trying to fix everything myself — mostly.

I still draft the whole plan at two in the morning sometimes, but now I leave the boring half on your desk with a napkin note, and you never once made me feel foolish for needing that.

So.

Saturday.

Third year running.

Same plaza, same queue, same rule: no market talk until the moon comes up.

I've decided this is what we are now — the two people who check the assume column, in campaigns and in ourselves.

Standing commitment, renewable annually, no paperwork.

Agreed?

Two rules I've adopted since I stopped fixing everything myself, for the record: 'This part needs a different system.' And: 'If this year's evening doesn't work, we find another one.'

The queue is a habit, not attendance I get to demand.

choices.text: Agreed — and this year I'm queuing twice with you, and I'm bringing the questions.
choices.response: Amara grins and steals one of her own biscuits back. 'Bringing the questions. That's the best job on the wall and you know it.' She taps the tin. 'My aunt says the recipe survives because everyone who gets it changes one thing and writes it down. I changed the cinnamon. You're changing the questions. Same page, both notes staying.'

choices.text: (Take a biscuit, eat it slowly, and nod once — the agreement sealed without a speech.)
choices.response: She watches you chew with the seriousness of a defense hearing. 'Well? Verdict?' Whatever your face does, it makes her laugh and push the tin closer. 'Good. She'd approve. She always said you can hear an honest yes better than you can hear a polite one. You've never once been polite at me when it mattered. That's why the napkin's framed and not filed.'

episodes.ending: Saturday, the plaza is as crowded as ever and the volunteer with the steady hands recognizes Amara now, waving her toward the telescope. You queue at the back anyway, by choice. Somewhere in the second queue she hands you the last biscuit from the tin without looking away from the sky. The commitment needs no ceremony: every launch, the wall goes up; every year, the long queue. The telescope's shadow crosses the stones between you, and neither of you stands anywhere but in it.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Dent in the Moon
romance.opening: Third annual viewing night for you and Amara. The observatory plaza is crowded; she's already claimed a place in the queue, holding the tin of spice biscuits she baked that morning, margin notes paperback in her coat pocket. The moon hangs above the rooftops, a small bright dent in a dark sky, and she's watching it instead of her phone. That, from her, is a whole speech.
romance.dialogue:
You made it.

I saved you a place — don't tell the queue police.

Biscuit?

This batch finally smells like my aunt's kitchen.

Three viewing seasons, and look at us.

The wall method has outlived two campaigns and one reorganization.

I travel more now — three regions just this season — and I come back instead of just forwarding slides, which my old self would call inefficient and my current self calls the entire point.

And you're still the person who reads the wall.

I've been thinking about what I want to say tonight, and I keep deleting it, so here's the unedited version.

I don't want the annual renewal anymore.

I want the standing version — the one where choosing each other isn't a calendar event.

Not because either of us needs completing.

I like my life and you like yours; I want to keep both and add this.

Also, full disclosure: I still take on too much, I will absolutely draft a two a.m. plan about us at some point, and you have my permission to napkin me.

So.

Standing version?

choices.text: Standing version — and I'll bring the questions, every year, starting with this one.
choices.response: Amara laughs, and it comes out brighter than the plaza noise around you. 'Starting with this one. That's a yes with structure. I've never been so happy to be outmaneuvered.' She presses the biscuit tin into your hands. 'Then it's official by our standards — witnessed by a queue, a moon, and one extremely fat bird who better still be alive out there. My aunt's rule: everyone who gets the recipe changes one thing and writes it down. Consider us both written.'

choices.text: (Take her hand briefly, turn it over, and place the first biscuit of the tin in her palm.)
choices.response: She looks at the biscuit, then at you, and her voice goes soft and certain. 'Answer by recipe. All right.' She eats it slowly, watching the moon the whole time. 'Yes. Standing version. You didn't need words — you never have. But I'm writing it in the margin anyway, very small, next to the old notes, so both versions stay on the page. That's how I keep things. Nothing erased.'

romance.ending: The volunteer with the steady hands waves you both forward. Amara bends to the eyepiece and doesn't move for the longest time — the same stillness as years ago, believing for a breath that she could touch the dent in the moon. Then she steps back and offers you the telescope, and goes to the back of the queue to wait for a second turn, unhurried, certain the evening is long. The telescope's shadow lies across the stones between the line and the stars, and you both stand in it, together, with your own lives waiting patiently at home.

episodes.title: 我们知道的，和我们假设的
episodes.opening: 北辰创意，上线前七天。提案会刚散场，会议室里还飘着一股咖啡烧糊的味道。阿玛拉·奥卡福独自站在白板前，把打印出来的引语一张张贴在三栏马克笔字旁边：我们知道的、我们假设的、还需要去问的。一张卡片卷了边，滑落到地上。她穿着钴蓝衬衫，小辫向后盘起，腋下夹着一个薄文件夹。你进来捡之前有人落下的笔时，她抬起了头。
episodes.dialogue:
阿玛拉·奥卡福，做文化策略的。

我刚从五个地区的材料里抬起头，眼睛都花了。

你今天过得怎么样？

别担心，我不会拉你去做什么的。

暂时不会。

上一场活动，就是败给了一个很漂亮的假设。

有人认定一个市场的答案可以原封不动地搬到另一个市场，结果发现大家从头到尾说‘好’只是为了客气。

六十场访谈，一个读错的答案，一次被迫撤回的上线。

所以现在，受访者的原话就贴在白板旁边，谁也没法把它们转述成自己想听的意思。

我总听提案组说，地区选项是‘附加风味’。预算一紧，风味第一个被砍掉。

但选择不会。

这就是我想在周五之前补上的缺口。

好了。

你撞上我讲课了，材料明天还会在这儿。

你要是想聊点别的，我更想听那个。

不过——先问一件事。
