When the baskets returned, we each took our own bowl and let the steam settle. She offered the vegetable ones, but I put the first mushroom dumpling into the bowl she held out. Half a day's work; she should taste my share first.

She asked whether the filling was good or the wrapping. Both, I said. We both laughed. We divided the rest, and I carried my food box back here. Still smelled it at the door.

She looks from the shield to the bin.

The day wasn't a commission. We each did our part, and we both got dinner. I can remember that without turning every offered hand into more work.

There is one thing that is not working and not resting, if you are inclined.

The scrap bin.

I sorted nothing before I sat down, and tomorrow morning I will need the right pieces fast.

I tap.

You hand me what rings true.

That is all.

No fire, no hammer, no craft.

Just an ear and an arm.

She looks at you over the blanket's edge.

It is a small thing.

But small things done on a rest day, for no pay — my teacher had an opinion about those.

He approved.

Loudly.

choices.text: Give me the bin. And move over — that stool fits two, and you're visibly cold.
choices.response:
Bruna stares.

Then, slowly, she scoots sideways on the stool, blanket half-offered, gruff as a locked door.

I am not visibly cold.

I am... thermally economical.

Hmph.

She drags the scrap bin over with her foot.

Fine.

You sit, you sort, you keep half the blanket if you must — it is a wide blanket, I did not choose it for company.

She taps a piece of copper, listens, and hands you nothing for the first three tries.

Then her eyes crinkle.

A watchwoman's shield, and a warm stool.

Tomorrow is already better arranged than my last six years.

choices.text: (Kneel by the scrap bin, pick up the first piece, and hold it out toward her tap.)
choices.response:
You kneel and offer the first piece of scrap.

Bruna taps it, listens, shakes her head.

Next.

She works through the bin with you in an easy rhythm — tap, listen, keep or toss — and the pile of true-ringing copper grows at her elbow.

See, she says midway, this is the trick of it.

I tap.

You hand.

Neither of us does the other's job.

That is most of what a workshop is.

She sets down a finished handful and looks at the blanket, then at you, and wordlessly drops one corner of it over your shoulder without stopping the rhythm.

Do not mention this to anyone.

Hmph.

episodes.ending:
Before you leave, you finish the last few pieces together: she taps, you offer the next, and she points each accepted piece toward tomorrow's row. By late afternoon the scrap bin is sorted, the shield plates are laid out in tomorrow's order, and the banked forge glows like a sleeping animal.

Bruna walks you to the door, blanket still around her shoulders, and stops under the chalk sign.

Six days to the deadline, one day spent, and I am not sorry, she says.

The shield will ring true.

So will I, tomorrow.

She raps the doorframe twice.

Come back when the watchwoman collects it.

I want someone there who knows what today cost — and who knows it was worth it.

episodes.title: A Rest Day Beyond the Workshop
episodes.opening:
Spring is deciding whether to arrive.

At the workshop, the watchwoman's folding shield is gone — collected, Bruna reports, with a handshake and a jar of honey.

On the bench lies a folded paper: a hand-drawn map of the hill above the valley, where wild plum trees grow.

Bruna's thumb rests on the X at the top.

She has clearly redrawn it twice.

She slides it across the bench toward you and stands very straight, like someone presenting a finished piece.
episodes.dialogue:
The watchwoman told me where this hill is.

Wild plums, she said, and a spring that stays warm even in frost.

I have never seen it.

I have taken rest days at my friends' houses, as you know. But I have never planned a whole day on that hill for the pleasure of the walk. The workshop day with you sorting scrap made me want company without a commission between us.

She taps the map.

So.

Here is the offer, and I will say it plainly, because roundabout is for other people.

On my next rest day, I am walking up that hill.

I am bringing bread, the good blanket, and nothing that rings.

I want you to come with me.

Not as a customer.

Not as an extra pair of hands.

Just as you.

She folds her arms, chin up, but her thumb is tapping her own arm — the tell of someone listening hard for a ring.

And there is a second thing under the first thing, so listen.

Somewhere on that walk there is a fork, and I do not know which way we take it.

One way, we are the kind of friends who climb hills and share blankets and that is a complete and good thing, and I will be glad of it my whole life.

The other way, we are — more.

She does not look away.

I am a third-grade artificer and I cannot forge an answer to that.

It has to be chosen clearly by both of us, in words or in a gesture we understand, and I am choosing to ask.

Whatever you say on that hill, the walk itself stays.

The bread stays.

The friendship stays.

I do not make things that break when the fire changes.

She pushes the map fully across the bench.

So.

Three days from now, at the baker's door, sunrise.

You can tell me your answer now, or you can tell me on the hill.

Both are allowed.

Hmph.

I have rehearsed this speech four times.

It has never once come out the same.

That is how you know it is honest.

choices.text: I want to become partners, Bruna. Let's take that walk as our first one together that way.
choices.response:
Bruna goes very still.

Then the stillness breaks into something bright and slightly stunned.

The more, she repeats.

Out loud.

Witnessed by a map and a bench.

Hmph.

Her thumb stops tapping.

Good.

Then I will say my half now so the hill does not have to carry it: I want the more.

I have wanted it since the day you stopped at my stall and cared what that crooked sign was trying to say.

She picks up the map and holds it like a finished commission.

Sunrise, three days.

I will bring the bread and the blanket.

You bring the walking.

And Bruna Ember — she taps her chest, where the failed piece glows — does not make things that break when the fire changes.

Neither, I think, do you.

choices.text: (Fold the map carefully, point to the path for friends, and place it back in her open hand.)
choices.response:
You fold the map along its creases, point to the path for friends, and return it to her open palm.

Bruna looks down at the route you indicated, and understanding arrives on her face like heat reaching the far side of the room.

The hill, then, she says quietly.

The hill and the bread and the blanket, and us becoming close friends. That is the friendship that stays.

She nods, once, firmly, and there is no disappointment in it — only a door closing gently that she is glad existed.

That is a good answer.

Do not let anyone tell you a complete thing is a lesser thing.

She tucks the map into her apron.

Sunrise, three days.

Bring your appetite and your ear.

The plums do not care which we are.

They will bloom for friends same as for anything.

episodes.ending:
Three days later, at sunrise, you and Bruna leave the baker's door with a paper map, a wrapped loaf, and a rolled gray blanket.

The hill above the valley is misted gold; somewhere on its flank, wild plums are deciding to bloom.

You walk up together — the two of you, who chose, plainly and on purpose, the shape your fire would take.

episodes.title: First Spring, Every Spring
episodes.opening:
A year has turned.

The Hearth Workshop's back plot — once bare packed dirt — now holds six plum shoots in a careful row, each staked with a strip of copper stamped with a date.

Bruna is on her knees in the soil, apron swapped for a work coat, silver hair tied back with a strip of leather.

The gray blanket hangs over the workshop's outside chair like a flag.

She hears your step on the gravel and does not turn around, but her shoulders lift.
episodes.dialogue:
You are late.

The first fresh leaf on this row opened this morning and you missed it by four hours.

Hmph.

She pats the dirt beside her and you kneel in the hollow she left.

Look at it.

Small enough to miss beside the older leaves, and it opened after the last frost anyway.

She taps the copper stake.

Planted last spring. That is the date on the stake, not the date of today's new leaf.

We planted six, and six took.

I checked the arithmetic all winter.

Here is what I decided while the shoots slept, and I decided it properly, the way I decide a forge weld — slowly, and with the whole fire.

She sits back on her heels and faces you.

This is ours now.

Not mine that you visit.

Ours.

Every first day of spring, we plant.

On the seventh days when we both want company, whoever arrives first can put the kettle on. The step is my responsibility; helping is an offer, not the price of your stool. We can both decline a visit and still be friends.

You have a hook inside that door now — third one from the left, the one I put at your shoulder height.

Your stool is worn to the shape of you.

She pulls a small cloth bundle from her coat and unwraps it: a seventh copper stake, stamped blank.

This one stays unstamped until next spring.

If we are still doing this — and we are, I have already checked with myself twice — we stamp it together with the new date, and the row becomes a calendar of us.

She holds it out flat on her palm.

My teacher said a workshop is just a promise with a roof on it.

This plot is ours.

The stool is yours.

The hook is yours.

The seventh day is ours.

Say you are in, and say it every spring, because promises like this are maintained.

Like a good fire.

Like us.

choices.text: I'm in. Keep it blank for now, and next spring we'll choose a new date together.
choices.response:
Bruna nods once, the way she nods at metal that rings true.

Then she offers the blank stake and you take it, copper warm from her palm.

“Every spring,” she says.

Out loud.

Witnessed by six shoots and a blanket.

She grins — quick, crooked, entirely hers.

Now dig.

The seventh hole goes at the end of the row, and I dug six already, so the arithmetic says it is your turn.

She works beside you in the warm dirt, shoulder near yours, and hums something that might be a bellows-count.

Push, count, hold.

It rings true.

choices.text: (Take the blank stake, make a seventh hole at the end of the row, and set the stake firmly into it.)
choices.response:
You take the stake, loosen the soil at the end of the row to make a seventh hole, and set it in place.

Bruna watches the whole thing without a word, then clears her throat roughly.

“Aye,” she says.

That is an answer too.

She pulls the leather tie from her hair, shakes it loose, reties it, buys herself a moment.

My teacher would have liked you.

He liked people who answer with their hands.

She looks down the row — six stamped stakes and one blank, waiting for its date.

Next spring we stamp it together.

And the spring after.

She picks up the kettle.

Come inside.

The step is swept, the fire is banked, and the stool knows your shape.

First spring, every spring.

Hmph.

I will hold you to it, and you will hold me.

That is how a promise keeps warm.

episodes.ending:
Before going inside, you make sure the blank stake stands upright in the new hole, firming the soil around its base. It marks room for next spring rather than a sapling planted today.

Inside, the workshop glows.

The primer with Master Odo's name sits spine-out on its shelf; the hook at your shoulder height holds your coat; your stool is worn to the shape of you.

Bruna pours two cups and sets them on the bench between you, steam rising.

Through the open door, the plum row stands in the evening light — six stamped, and the seventh blank in the ground, waiting for next spring's date.

A promise with a roof on it, maintained every spring, by you and Bruna, two friends who show up.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Shape the Fire Took
romance.opening:
A year has turned.

The Hearth Workshop's back plot — once bare packed dirt — now holds six plum shoots in a careful row, each staked with a strip of copper stamped with a date.

Bruna is on her knees in the soil, work coat over her shoulders, silver hair tied back with a strip of leather.

The gray blanket hangs over the outside chair.

She hears your step on the gravel and does not turn, but her whole posture changes — the way a banked fire leans toward an opened door.
romance.dialogue:
You are late.

The first fresh leaf on this row opened this morning and you missed it by four hours.

Hmph.

She pats the dirt beside her and you kneel in the hollow she left.

Six planted, six took.

I checked the arithmetic all winter, and while the shoots slept, I did my own forging.

Quietly.

Properly.

The way I do a weld — slow, and with the whole fire.

Beside the row she has laid a seventh young plum, a marked place for its planting hole, and a copper stake stamped with today's date. This spring's addition waits until you have both chosen where it belongs.

She reaches to the chain at her neck and lifts the brightest charm on her chest: the folded gold piece, its crack a seam of light.

I told you once this was a failed piece.

My journeyman exam.

Too much fire, uncontrolled, cracked the mold.

Master Odo folded the crack into a seam and hung it on me, and I have worn it every day since, because it was the first thing that told the truth about me.

She works the chain over her head.

The clasp is worn.

I could fix it in an hour at the bench.

I have not fixed it in a year.

Do you know why?

Because I was waiting to find out what it was for.

She holds it out flat on her strong palm, gold seam catching the light.

I know now.

It is not for the exam.

It is not for him.

It is for the person I want beside me on every rest day from here to the last one — not because I need mending, and not because you do.

Because cracked things, tended, become patterns.

And you are my pattern.

She looks at you straight, thumb steady at last.

I am not asking you to move in, or to stay when you should go.

You have your own life; keep it.

I want it beside mine, the way two fires keep one room warm without becoming one fire.

Take the charm, or do not.

Tell me in words, or answer with a clear gesture, whichever way. We are already partners; I am asking how we want to keep choosing that, not asking you to start again.

I have rehearsed nothing this time.

That is how you know it is true.

choices.text: Then it's mine to wear and yours to have given — I choose you, Bruna. Every rest day.
choices.response:
Bruna exhales like a bellows finally allowed to rest.

She lifts the chain and — carefully, asking with a pause long enough to refuse — fastens it at your collar, her warm hands brief at your neck and then gone.

There, she says, rough-voiced.

Failed piece, reforged.

Cracked is not ruined.

She sits back and looks at you wearing it, and laughs — short, bright, bellows-fed.

Hmph.

Master Odo would say the fire found its shape.

She taps the ground between you.

Now dig.

The seventh hole does not dig itself, and my partner in all things does not get to just wear the jewelry.

You and Bruna work side by side in the warm dirt, leaving each other room, until the light goes gold.

choices.text: (Touch her offered palm briefly, then release it and point from the charm to her heart and from yourself to the waiting plum.)
choices.response:
You touch her offered palm for one brief moment, then release it. You point from the charm to her heart, and from yourself to the waiting plum.

Bruna is silent a long moment.

Ah, she says softly.

You are telling me it belongs where it has always lived.

With me.

And that you are staying anyway.

She closes her own fingers around the charm and holds it against her coat for a moment — a forge at rest. Then she slips its chain back over her head.

“That is a true answer,” she says.

The charm keeps its own history.

And I keep you.

Hmph.

She picks up the trowel and passes it over.

Seventh hole.

Partner.

Dig.

You and Bruna plant the last shoot together as the evening turns gold around you.

romance.ending:
Before leaving the plot, you check the seventh young plum together, firm its soil, and set its dated copper stake beside it at the end of the row.

Inside, the workshop glows: Master Odo's primer on its shelf, the hook at your shoulder height, your stool worn to the shape of you.

Bruna pours two cups and touches hers to yours with a small forge-bright clink.

Two fires, one room, she says.

Your life stays yours.

Mine stays mine.

And this — she gestures at the plot, the bench, the space between you — we tend together, every first spring, every seventh day.

The plums will bloom whether we watch or not.

We intend to watch.

Hmph.

For a very long time.

episodes.title: 挂着诚实招牌的摊位
episodes.opening:
秋日的手工艺集市弥漫着刨木屑和烤栗子的香气。

沿着摊位走到一半，有一处比别处更暖：一座小铁砧，一排挂饰，还有一位穿皮围裙的精悍女子，银发向后拢起，铜色的皮肤被炉火映成橙色。

角落里歪挂着一块木牌：布鲁娜，锻造工匠——每第七日歇业。

她用一个指节敲了敲一只开裂的灯罩，像别人听钟声那样侧耳倾听。

布鲁娜，锻造工匠。

别站那么远。

炉火不咬人，除非你坚持把自己当成废料。

她用有力的双手把灯罩翻过来。

裂了不等于毁了。

只要你肯，它想成为一个暖身挂饰。

你捧着它的样子，说明它对某个人依然重要。

哼。

很好。

由仍然在乎的人送回来的破损之物——那是我最喜欢的客人，因为他们稀少。

她把灯罩放在铁砧上，朝你推来一枚未完成的挂饰，火星在它身后升起。
episodes.dialogue:
感受一下。

是暖的，对吧？

不是烫。

暖比烫更难。

谁都能做出会烧的东西。

做出能让你保暖的东西，那才是手艺。

她的目光扫向那块歪斜的招牌，脸上掠过一丝疲惫。

你要是不想理会那块招牌，就不理吧。

反正别人都这样。
我写下它，是在一个冬天——我接了四百件委托，一周忘了吃饭。

我的手抖得厉害，把一面折叠盾砸在了自己脚上。

那块招牌维持的时长和我的耐心差不多，也就是说，不长。

她哼了一声。

别那样看我。

我很好。

我一直很好。

不好的是日程表。

现在。

我可以在集市结束前开始修你的灯罩，但这里的铁砧是借的，炉火也浅。

真正的活儿在炉火工坊做。

三天后过来，我会把它作为新的东西放回你手里。

面包店过去第三扇门，带铜合页的那扇。

我们说定了，还是你想站在那儿假装读招牌？

她又看了一眼招牌，这一次疲惫让位于一丝小小的、私藏的愉悦。

我确实在那天休息。有时我甚至离开工坊。一位老友添了孩子，我带着自己买的面包过去。洗了手，换下工作围裙。那房子听起来像一支商队把全部家当倒进了门厅。

我告诉那位父亲，他的客人可以等。那个小家伙显然更有话要说。

她摊开一只宽大而空着的手。

他问我想不想抱孩子。我老实说，我更愿意坐着看。然后那只小手伸了过来，我便递上一根干净的手指。他像夹钳一样攥住。我坐得比在自己工作台前任何时候都直。

等孩子打了个哈欠松开手，我慢慢收回手指。朋友去安顿他；我等着。切好的面包在变凉，但它终究还是面包。他回来后我们一起吃了。

他担心一顿饭吃到一半被叫走。我把篮子里剩下的推近了些。够重新暖起来，我说。不用跟婴儿赛跑。

出门时我小声说，他的孩子抓握力真不小。哼。原来一个休息日可以不产出任何东西，却盛住一些东西。我正在学着分辨这两者。

她回到灯罩前。

三天。这一件会得到稳定的手，而不是我拥有的每一个小时。

choices.text: 那块招牌是整条街上最诚实的东西。有必要的话，就让它继续歪着吧。
choices.response:
布鲁娜眨了眨眼，随即笑出声——短促的、像风箱鼓风般的笑。

诚实。

哼。

我的老师常说，铁炉不管你愿不愿意都会说出真相。

看来我挂了一块同样会说话的招牌。

她满意地敲了两下铁砧。

那么，三天后。

来取你的挂饰，如果你碰巧撞见我在休息日干活，我允许你什么都不说，只是露出失望的表情。

我听说那招对我非常有效。

choices.text: （坐到客人的凳子上，一言不发地看她双手干活。）
choices.response:
你坐上了凳子。

布鲁娜瞥了一眼，点点头，继续她的敲击——先倾听每一件裂开的器物，再决定它想成为什么。

很好，过了一会儿她说。

大多数人喋喋不休。

金属喜欢安静，我也一样。

她一言不发地干了整整一分钟，然后压低声音补了一句：这张凳子没怎么被用过。

客人都站着。

他们只想快点做完交易。

你坐下的样子，像是打算留下来陪炉火。

三天。

工坊，面包店过去第三扇门。

我会记得你来过。

episodes.ending:
三天后，还没等你敲门，那扇铜合页的门就开了。

布鲁娜递出一枚小小的挂饰——灯罩被重新锻过，那道裂纹如今成了一条明亮的折叠铜缝，像地图上的一条河，贯穿正中。

它还会响，她说。

听。

它比从前响得更暖了。

裂了不等于毁了；这个纹样开始有了名字。

她看着你在手中翻看它，而在她身后，你注意到工坊里那块歇业招牌比集市上的那块直了一些。

只是一点点。

以后常来，她说。

我工作台旁有张凳子，现在是你的了。

我决定了。

episodes.title: 扉页上的名字
episodes.opening:
集市的书摊是一片潮湿书脊和泛黄地图的杂乱之地。

布鲁娜在午休时来到这里，围裙还系在身上，用厨师般的细心翻着书页。

她在一本薄薄的、被水渍浸过的书前停下：一本关于风箱操作的入门书，封面上盖着几十年前炉火工坊的印记。

她的拇指停在那印记上，一动不动。

注意到你时，她并没有把书藏起来。

反而把它举了起来。

看这个。

她敲了敲那印记。

我在学会认字之前，先学会了认火。

这本入门书——那时候每个学徒都发一本。

学徒的第一年是在风箱前度过的。

不是铁砧。

是风箱。

推，数，停。

推，数，停。

我的手臂疼得厉害，眼泪掉进煤里，煤却毫不在意。

她翻到扉页，那里用工整的字迹写着一位旧主人的名字，下面还留着题献的空白。

奥多师傅。

我的老师。

隔着整个屋子，他都能听出一块金属里的谎言。

她安静了片刻，然后轻哼一声。

我要告诉你一件我不会写在招牌上的事。

看到这个了吗？

她摸了摸胸前最亮的那枚护符——一小片折叠的金属，稳定地发着金光。

那是一件失败的作品。

我的出师考试。

我本该锻造一块能保温一整夜的暖石。
episodes.dialogue:
我的那块保温了六天，还把模具撑裂了。

考官判了它不及格。

他们说，火候过头了。

失控。

奥多师傅拿起那件碎掉的东西，把裂缝折成一道接缝，挂在我身上。

他说，姑娘，你身上有座熔炉。

它需要一个形状。

她笑了，短促而温暖。

从那以后，我一直在试着给它一个形状。

大多数时候，我修的是别人坏掉的东西，因为那比整理我自己的日程容易。

哼。

别把这话传出去。

她把入门书夹在腋下，在摊上放下两枚铜币。

我买下它了。

不是为了读——每一页我都记得。

是为了在扉页上写一个名字。

奥多师傅从来没有得到过一块像样的纪念牌。

一本写着他的名字的书，放在他教书的工坊里，那就是一块纪念牌。

她斜眼看了看你。

你看起来是个稳当的人。

明天来工坊，帮我握着笔。

第一次落笔，两只手总比一只手好。

写到重要的字母时，我的手还是会抖。

她的手指沿着合上的书边划过。

书里的名字总能让我措手不及。不只是他。有一次我在集市上看到一本诗集，印着一位老朋友的名字。我们聊了那么多年菜价和天气，而她一直在写诗。

我向摊主确认了一下，买下了那本薄薄的书。把本来要买的盐都忘了。夹着书径直去了她家门口。

她问我是在哪儿找到的，一脸窘迫。就在摊上，我说。你的名字印得清清楚楚；你又不是把它埋到地底下去了。

我的朋友刚收到印好的书，还没来得及送人。我让她别送我免费副本。这本是我自己买的。她可以在这本上题字送给布鲁娜，只要别把我写得像挂在墙上的展品。

等墨迹干的时候，她给我读了一首诗，写的是夜里听见邻居在砍东西。她一直猜是砍菜，直到第二天早上才知道是砍柴。我大笑起来，又翻回那一页重读了一遍。

在她家门口，她指着我空空的购物袋。那时我才想起盐这回事。我拍了拍额头，抱紧书，又回集市去了。

布鲁娜对自己轻哼一声，然后敲了敲入门书。

那本书还是我的，题字也在。这一本则属于工坊的书架。两个不同的名字，两种不同的纪念。明天，我们给这一本一个应有的位置。

choices.text: 那我会来的，我们要把他的名字写得漂漂亮亮，让整个工坊都记住它。
choices.response:
布鲁娜的笑容来得又快又歪。

大话。

我会记着让你兑现的。

她掂了掂那本入门书。

那就明天吧，早上的排队结束之后。

还有，听着——如果你画歪了一道墨线，我现在就告诉你，奥多师傅自己的字迹才叫糟糕。

他一半的笔记看起来就像蜘蛛掉进了灰堆。

你写什么都会是一种进步。

她在书摊边缘停了停。

我已经很久没有开口谈起他了。

说出来感觉很好。

哼。

明天见。

choices.text: （把手轻轻搭在入门书旁的摊架上，让这个动作替你说话。）
choices.response:
你把手放在旧书旁边的摊架上。

布鲁娜看了看你的手，又看了看你的脸，她肩上的什么松了下来。

嗯。

这就够了。

她用出人意料的轻柔把入门书包进布里。

每次我提起他，人们都会说抱歉。

你没有。

很好。

抱歉是留给葬礼的。

这不是葬礼。

这是一个名字得到它的书。

她侧身绕过一个木箱。

明天还是来一趟吧。

那支笔很沉，而我的手更擅长抡锤子。

你会看着这件事被妥当地完成，而你也会亲眼见过它。

这对我来说很珍贵。

episodes.ending:
第二天下午，阳光洒在工坊的工作台上。

布鲁娜用一只前臂把入门书压平；那支笔比看上去更沉，墨水在听话之前晕开了一次。

两人一起，在扉页旧主人名字的下方，用工整的字母写下了一行题献：纪念奥多师傅，炉火工坊。

她读了两遍，像敲金属那样敲了敲书页，点了点头。

声音是正的，她说。

她把入门书放上铁砧上方的书架，书脊朝外，正好在火光能照到的地方。

现在，工坊记得他了。

而在我忘记的那些日子里，它替我记得。

episodes.title: 真正休了的休息日
episodes.opening:
铜铰链门上，休息告示下面多了一行新写的粉笔字：休息日。

除非工坊着火，否则别敲门。

里面，锻炉压得很低。

布鲁娜裹着一条厚厚的灰毯子，坐在顾客凳上——你的凳子——工作台上摆着一面组装到一半的折叠盾，盾板像一朵倔强的花一样扇形展开。

她抬起头，被抓了个正着，也懒得装出别的样子。

哼。

你看见告示了。

她把毯子裹得更紧，毫不羞愧，还带点挑衅。

是的。

这就是我。

在我的休息日。

裹在毯子里。

那笔委托是给山谷上游一位夜巡女卫做的折叠盾。

六天后交货。

我的手想干活，所以我告诉它们：行，咱们就只看看它。

看不是干活。

她瞪着那面盾，盾毫不在意。

既然你站在那儿摆着那副表情，那就给你一本诚实的账。

我落后了。

不算严重。

但换作从前的布鲁娜，天一亮就会生起锻炉，干到手指发烫，提前完工，再接两笔委托把空档填满。
episodes.dialogue:
正是那条路，害我裹进了毯子里。

她敲了敲最近的一块盾板。

声音依然清亮。

好板子。

代价，她说，是这个：盾要等到明天。

今天我休息，那位女卫拿到的会是一双沉稳的手做出来的盾，而不是一双疲惫的手。

她永远看不出区别。

我看得出来。

这就是没人会为之鼓掌的部分。

她挪了挪身子，毯子滑了下来；你看得出她其实不够暖，而她绝不会承认。

这让我想起在一位老朋友家桌边的一个秋天。我们包了蒸饺。她摆出素馅和蘑菇馅两种；我两样都闻了闻，没装模作样地犹豫，直接拿了蘑菇馅。

我们面对面坐着。风一动，晾晒的衣影就不时掠过桌面。我在自己蒸笼里的每个饺子之间都留了一点空隙。朋友问我，是不是打算一个人吃掉整笼蘑菇馅的。

你要是再包得慢一点，我告诉她，我可能真会。

她把脸埋进毯子边上笑。

她把自己的蒸笼挪到我旁边，两笼一起端进了厨房。我收好面粉和多余的饺子皮，然后等着她回来，和她一起擦桌子。不是所有事都需要我一个人收尾。

蒸笼端回来时，我们各自端起自己的碗，让热气慢慢散去。她把素馅的推过来，我却把第一个蘑菇饺子放进她伸过来的碗里。半天的活儿；她该先尝尝我那份。

她问，是馅好还是包得好。都好，我说。我们俩都笑了。剩下的我们分了，我提着自己的食盒回到这里。到门口还闻得到那股香味。

她的目光从盾移到废料箱。

那一天不是什么委托。我们各做了自己那份，然后两个人都吃上了晚饭。我可以记住这一点，而不必把每一双伸过来的手都变成更多活儿。

有一件事，既不算干活也不算休息，如果你愿意的话。

废料箱。

我坐下之前什么都没分拣，明天一早我就得很快找到合适的料。

我来敲。

你把声音对的那块递给我。

就这样。

不用生火，不用锤子，不用手艺。

只要一只耳朵和一条胳膊。

她从毯子边上看着你。

这是件小事。

但在休息日做的小事，不图报酬——我师父对这种事有个说法。

他赞成。

声音很大地赞成。

choices.text: 把废料箱给我。再挪一挪——那张凳子坐得下两个人，而你明显冷了。
choices.response:
布鲁娜瞪着你。

然后，慢慢地，她在凳子上往旁边挪了挪，把毯子分出一半，语气硬得像一扇上了锁的门。

我没有明显冷。

我只是……在节省热量。

哼。

她用脚把废料箱拖了过来。

行。

你坐下，你分拣，实在要分毯子你就分一半——毯子很宽，我当初选它可不是为了有人作伴。

她敲一块铜料，侧耳听，前三次什么都没递给你。

然后她的眼角弯了起来。

一面女卫的盾，一张暖和的凳子。

明天已经比我过去六年安排得都好了。

choices.text: （在废料箱旁蹲下，拿起第一块料，朝她敲击的地方递过去。）
choices.response:
你蹲下身，递上第一块废料。

布鲁娜敲了敲，听了听，摇摇头。

下一块。

她和你一起，用一种轻松的节奏把整箱料过了一遍——敲、听、留或扔——她手肘边那堆声音清亮的铜料越堆越高。

瞧见没，她干到一半时说，诀窍就在这儿。

我敲。

你递。

谁也不替谁干那份活。

一间工坊，大半就是这么回事。

她放下手里挑好的一把料，看了看毯子，又看了看你，然后一言不发地把毯子的一角搭到你肩上，节奏一刻没停。

不许对任何人提起这件事。

哼。

episodes.ending:
你离开之前，你们一起做完了最后几块：她敲，你递下一块，她把每块选中的料指向明天要摆的那一排。到傍晚，废料箱分拣完毕，盾板按明天的顺序摆好，压低的锻炉像一头睡着的野兽一样发着光。

布鲁娜送你到门口，毯子还披在肩上，在粉笔告示下面停住。

离交货还有六天，用掉了一天，而我不后悔，她说。

这面盾会发出清亮的声音。

明天，我也会。

她在门框上敲了两下。

等那位女卫来取盾的时候，你再过来。

我想有个人在场——一个知道今天付出了什么代价、也知道这代价值得的人。

episodes.title: 工坊之外的休息日
episodes.opening:
春天还在犹豫要不要来。

工坊里，女守卫的那面折叠盾不见了——布鲁娜汇报说，是靠一次握手和一罐蜂蜜收走的。

工作台上放着一张折好的纸：一张手绘的地图，画的是山谷上方那座山，山上有野李树。

布鲁娜的拇指停在山顶的X上。

她显然已经重画过两次。

她把地图推过工作台递给你，站得笔直，像在展示一件完工的作品。
episodes.dialogue:
女守卫告诉了我那座山的位置。

她说，有野李子，还有一眼即使在霜冻天也温热的泉水。

我从没见过那里。

你知道的，我在朋友家度过休息日。但我从没为了一次纯粹的散步之乐，在那座山上规划过一整天。那天和你一起在工坊分拣废料，让我想要一段没有委托横在我们之间的陪伴。

她敲了敲地图。

所以。

这是我的提议，我会直说，因为拐弯抹角是留给别人的。

下一个休息日，我要走上那座山。

我会带上面包、那条好毯子，以及任何会响的东西都不带。

我想让你和我一起去。

不是作为顾客。

不是作为多出来的一双手。

只是作为你。

她双臂抱在胸前，下巴微抬，但她的拇指在敲着自己的手臂——这是有人在竖起耳朵等一声铃响的破绽。

而且在这件事底下还藏着另一件事，所以听好。

那条路上有一个岔口，我不知道我们会走哪一边。

走一边，我们就是那种一起爬山、共享毯子的朋友，而那是一件完整而美好的事，我会为此高兴一辈子。

走另一边，我们是——更多。

她没有移开视线。

我是个三级机关师，可我锻造不出这个问题的答案。

它必须由我们两个人清清楚楚地选择，用言语，或用一个我们都懂的手势，而我选择开口来问。

无论你在那座山上说什么，这次散步本身都会留下。

面包会留下。

友谊会留下。

我不做火一变就碎的东西。

她把地图整个推过工作台。

所以。

三天后，面包房门口，日出时分。

你可以现在告诉我答案，也可以到山上再说。

两种都行。

哼。

这段话我排练了四遍。

没有一次说得一模一样。

这就是你知道它真诚的方式。

choices.text: 我想和你成为伴侣，布鲁娜。就让那次散步成为我们以这种方式同行的第一次吧。
choices.response:
布鲁娜僵住了。

然后那份僵滞碎裂成某种明亮而略带怔忡的东西。

更多，她重复道。

出了声。

有一张地图和一张工作台作证。

哼。

她的拇指停止了敲击。

好。

那我现在就把我的那一半说出来，免得让那座山来背负：我想要更多。

从那天你在我摊位前停下、在意那块歪斜招牌想说什么的时候起，我就想要了。

她拿起地图，像捧着一件完工的委托那样握着它。

日出，三天后。

我带面包和毯子。

你带走路这件事。

而布鲁娜——她敲了敲胸口，那件失败的作品在那里发着光——不做火一变就碎的东西。

我想，你也不会。

choices.text: （小心地把地图折好，指向通往朋友的那条路，再放回她摊开的手心里。）
choices.response:
你沿着折痕把地图折好，指向通往朋友的那条路，再把它放回她摊开的手掌。

布鲁娜低头看着你指的那条路线，理解像热气漫到房间另一头那样浮上她的脸。

那就上山，她轻声说。

山、面包和毯子，还有我们成为亲密的朋友。这就是会留下的那份友谊。

她坚定地点了一次头，里面没有失望——只有一扇她庆幸存在过的门被轻轻合上。

这是个好答案。

别让任何人告诉你，完整的东西就是次一等的东西。

她把地图塞进围裙里。

日出，三天后。

带上你的胃口和你的耳朵。

李子树不在乎我们是什么。

它们会为朋友绽放，和为任何事物一样。

episodes.ending:
三天后，日出时分，两个身影离开面包房门口，带着一张纸质地图、一条包好的面包和一卷灰色毯子。

山谷上方的那座山笼罩在金色的薄雾里；在山坡某处，野李树正决定绽放。

你们一起向上走去——两个人清清楚楚、心甘情愿地选择了你们的火将呈现的形状。

episodes.title: 第一个春天，每一个春天
episodes.opening:
一年过去了。

炉火工坊的后院——曾经是光秃秃的夯土——如今整齐地立着一排六株李树苗，每株都插着一条刻有日期的铜牌。

布鲁娜跪在泥土里，围裙换成了工作外套，银发用一条皮绳束在脑后。

那条灰毯子像一面旗子，搭在工坊外的椅子上。

她听见你踩在碎石上的脚步声，没有回头，但肩膀微微一抬。
episodes.dialogue:
你来晚了。

这一排的第一片新叶今天早上展开了，你晚了四个小时。

哼。

她拍了拍身旁的泥土，你跪进她留下的那个凹坑里。

看它。

小得几乎会被老叶盖过，可它还是在最后一场霜冻之后照样展开了。

她敲了敲铜牌。

去年春天种下的。牌上刻的是种植的日期，不是今天新叶的日期。

我们种了六株，六株都活了。

整个冬天我都在反复核对这笔账。

树苗沉睡的时候，我认真想清楚了一件事，而且是用我决定一次锻焊的方式想清楚的——慢慢地，用整炉的火。

她坐回脚跟上，面对着你。

从现在起，这是我们的了。

不是你偶尔来探望的我的地方。

是我们的。

每年春天的第一天，我们一起种树。

在我们俩都想要人陪的那些第七天，谁先到谁就把水壶坐上。台阶是我的责任；帮忙是一种心意，不是你坐凳子的代价。我们都可以拒绝一次来访，也依然是朋友。

那扇门里现在有一个属于你的挂钩——从左数第三个，我按你肩膀的高度装的。

你的凳子已经磨出了你的形状。

她从外套里掏出一个小布包，打开：第七根铜牌，上面没有刻字。

这根先空着，不刻字，留到明年春天。

如果我们还在坚持这件事——我们会的，我已经跟自己确认过两次了——我们就一起把新的日期刻上去，这一排就会变成一部属于我们的历书。

她把它平摊在掌心递过来。

我的师父说过，工坊不过是一个加了屋顶的承诺。

这块地是我们的。

凳子是你的。

挂钩是你的。

第七天是我们的。

说一句你加入，而且每年春天都要说一遍，因为这样的承诺不是一次锻成的东西。

它们需要养护。

像一炉好火。

像我们。

choices.text: 我加入。先空着吧，明年春天我们一起选一个新的日期。
choices.response:
布鲁娜点了一下头，就像她对一件敲起来声音纯正的金属点头那样。

然后她递出那根空白的铜牌，你接了过来，铜牌还带着她掌心的温度。

每年春天，她说。

大声说出来。

有六株树苗和一条毯子作证。

她咧嘴一笑——迅速、歪斜，完全是她的样子。

现在挖吧。

第七个坑在这排的尽头，前六个我已经挖好了，所以按账算，轮到你了。

她在温热的泥土里在你身旁干活，肩膀靠近你的肩膀，哼着一段也许是风箱节拍的调子。

推，数，稳住。

声音纯正。

choices.text: （接过空白的铜牌，在这排尽头挖出第七个坑，把铜牌稳稳地插进去。）
choices.response:
你接过铜牌，把这一排尽头的土松开，挖出第七个坑，把它插进去。

布鲁娜一言不发地看着整个过程，然后粗声清了清嗓子。

好，她说。

这也算一个回答。

她把束发的皮绳扯下来，甩散头发，重新扎好，给自己争取了一点时间。

我师父会喜欢你的。

他喜欢用手回答问题的人。

她望向这一排——六根刻了字的铜牌，和一根空白的，等着它的日期。

明年春天我们一起刻。

再下一个春天也是。

她提起水壶。

进来吧。

台阶扫过了，火封好了，凳子记得你的形状。

第一个春天，每一个春天。

哼。

我会拿这话盯着你，你也会盯着我。

承诺就是这样保温的。

episodes.ending:
进屋之前，你确认那根空白的铜牌在新坑里立得笔直，把底部的土又压实了些。它标记的是明年春天的位置，而不是今天种下的一株树苗。

屋里，工坊亮堂堂的。

那本写有奥多师父名字的入门书书脊朝外立在书架上；按你肩膀高度装的挂钩挂着你的外套；你的凳子磨出了你的形状。

布鲁娜倒了两杯，放在你们之间的工作台上，热气升腾。

透过敞开的门，李树那一排立在暮色里——六根刻了字，第七根空着插在土里，等着明年春天的日期。

一个加了屋顶的承诺，每年春天养护一次，由两个说到做到的朋友。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 火焰最终成形的样子
romance.opening:
一年过去了。

炉火工坊的后圃——曾经是光秃秃的夯土——如今整齐地立着六株李树苗，每株都插着一条刻有日期的铜牌。

布鲁娜跪在泥土里，工作外套披在肩上，银发用一条皮绳束在脑后。

那条灰毯子搭在外面的椅子上。

她听见你踩在碎石上的脚步声，没有回头，但整个姿态都变了——像一炉压好的火苗朝敞开的门倾过去。
romance.dialogue:
你来晚了。

这一排的第一片新叶今天早上展开，你晚了四个小时。

哼。

她拍了拍身旁的泥土，你跪进她留下的那个小坑里。

种下六株，成活六株。

整个冬天我都在核对这笔账，趁树苗沉睡的时候，我也做了自己的锻造。

安安静静地。

规规矩矩地。

就像我做一道焊缝那样——慢慢来，用整炉的火。

在那排树苗旁边，她放好了第七株小李树，标出了种植穴的位置，还有一块刻着今天日期的铜牌。今年春天的这一株，要等你们两人一起选定它该属于哪里。

她伸手到颈间的链子，把胸前最亮的那枚坠子提起来：那件折叠的金器，裂缝是一道透光的接缝。

我跟你说过，这是一件失败的作品。

我的出师考试。

火候太猛，失控，模具裂了。

奥多师傅把裂缝折成一道接缝，挂在我身上，从那天起我每天都戴着它，因为它是第一件说出我真相的东西。

她把链子从头上取下来。

搭扣已经磨损了。

我可以在工作台上一小时就修好它。

可我一年都没修。

你知道为什么吗？

因为我在等，等弄明白它究竟是为什么而存在的。

她把它平摊在有力的掌心上，金色的接缝映着光。

我现在知道了。

它不是为了那场考试。

也不是为了他。

它是为了那个我希望从今天起直到最后一个休息日都陪在我身边的人——不是因为我需要修补，也不是因为你需要。

因为有了裂痕的东西，只要被好好照料，就会变成纹样。

而你，就是我的纹样。

她直直地看着你，拇指终于稳住了。

我不是要你搬来同住，也不是要你在该走的时候留下。

你有你自己的生活；留着它。

我要的是它挨着我的生活，就像两炉火让同一间屋子暖着，却不必烧成一炉。

收下这枚坠子，或者不收。

用言语告诉我，或者用一个明确的动作回答，都行。我们早已是伴侣了；我问的是我们想怎样继续这样选择，不是要你从头再来。

这一次，我什么都没有预演。

这就是你知道它是真的的方式。

choices.text: 那它就归我戴，也归你赠出——我选择你，布鲁娜。每一个休息日。
choices.response:
布鲁娜像一具终于获准歇息的风箱那样长长吐出一口气。

她提起链子，然后——小心翼翼，用一段足够让你拒绝的停顿先征询——把它扣在你的衣领上，温热的手在你颈边一触即离。

好了，她哑着嗓子说。

失败之作，重新锻成。

有裂痕不等于毁了。

她坐回去，看着戴着它的你，笑了——短促、明亮，像被风箱吹旺的火。

哼。

奥多师傅会说，这炉火终于找到了自己的形状。

她敲了敲两人之间的地面。

现在，挖。

第七个坑不会自己挖好，而我事事同行的伴侣，可不能只负责戴首饰。

你们在温热的泥土里并肩劳作，给彼此留着余地，直到天色转成金色。

choices.text: （短暂地碰了碰她摊开的掌心，然后松开，指一指坠子再指她的心口，又指自己再指那株等待的李树。）
choices.response:
你短暂地碰了碰她摊开的掌心，然后松开。你指了指坠子，再指她的心口，又指了指自己，再指那株等待的李树。

布鲁娜沉默了许久。

啊，她轻声说。

你是在告诉我，它属于它一直待着的地方。

在我这里。

而你无论如何都会留下。

她用自己的手指合拢坠子，把它贴在外套上按了片刻——像一炉歇息的火。然后她把链子重新套回头上。

这是一个真实的回答，她说。

坠子留着它自己的历史。

而我留下你。

哼。

她拿起小铲，递了过来。

第七个坑。

伴侣。

挖。

你们在暮色转成金色时，一起种下了最后一株树苗。

romance.ending:
离开苗圃之前，你们一起查看第七株小李树，把土压实，把那块刻着日期的铜牌插在整排的末端。

屋里，工坊亮着：奥多师傅的入门书立在架上，那个钩子挂在你齐肩的高度，你的凳子已经磨出了你的形状。

布鲁娜倒了两杯，用她的杯子轻轻碰了碰你的，发出一小声炉火般清脆的响。

两炉火，一间屋，她说。

你的生活还是你的。

我的还是我的。

而这个——她指了指苗圃、工作台、你们之间的那片空间——我们一起照料，每一个初春，每一个第七天。

李树开不开花，不在于我们看不看。

但我们打算看着。

哼。

看很久很久。

choices.response:
Lyra laughs, delighted, and plants the heel of her hand on the table.

There.

A slow beat, then.

She plays the phrase again at half speed, and it comes out wistful, almost like a lullaby.

The cook leans out of the kitchen to listen.

She finishes, bows her head to the imaginary crowd, and grins at you.

One vote for melancholy.

I am outvoted by the moon and one honest stranger.

The second half goes gentle tonight.
choices.text: Play it slow, and let the room decide what it feels like.

choices.response:
She watches your fingers settle, and something in her face goes soft and focused.

Ah.

You would rather knock than talk.

Good.

She plays the phrase once more, then falls quiet and taps the answer back on the lute body, trading little rhythms with you across the room while the tap-tap of the cook's ladle keeps honest time.

When your knock matches hers, she beams.

There it is.

Joyful, then, and slightly stubborn.

I will write it exactly that way.
choices.text: (Set your cup down and tap the rhythm back on the table.)

episodes.dialogue:
You knock twice on the tabletop in answer, and she tilts her head, curls sliding off one shoulder, grinning like you have handed her a gift.

Oh, a customer with opinions.

Excellent.

Listen again.

She plays the half-phrase once more, slower this time, letting the last string ring.

Three ways to take it.

I can sing it bright, like a festival with too much wine.

I can sing it slow, like someone missing a harbor.

Or I can sing it the way the knock came to me, which is honestly a little rude, wouldn't you say?

She plucks the phrase again, playful, watching your face rather than the strings.

The troupe pays me in soup and a bed upstairs, so the soup is safe either way.

But the song is better when somebody in the room has skin in it.

She leans back, lute balanced on her knee.

So.

Second verse, your ruling.

And before you answer, know that I have been wrong before.

I once sang a traveler's hometown name wrong, right in the middle of the chorus, and he left without his dinner.

Since then I ask first and sing second.

She turns a tuning peg, waits, and lets the open note hang in the lamplight.

Your call.

I will follow it wherever it goes, and I will not sulk if you choose wrong.

There is no wrong.

There is only what the room wants to hear, and tonight the room is you.
episodes.ending:
She plays the second half to match your choice, and the tavern goes quiet enough to hear the fire.

Afterward she carries her lute to your table and sits down with the supper the cook sends over, eating and talking about the phrase you settled between you, turning it over like a coin she has not spent yet.

Before the lamps burn low she hums it once more, complete now, and points at you when the last note lands.

That one has your fingerprints on it.

It stays in my book with your name beside it, or as close as I can get without asking a stranger for their name.
episodes.opening:
The Lantern Step is half full, which is the honest kind of full.

You have a table near the wall and a cup you have not touched, because the evening's entertainment has stopped mid-song.

A young woman with a moon-white shawl sits on the stage with a slender lute, holding one last note open instead of finishing it.

When the murmur dies, she looks directly at your corner.

You.

Yes, you, the quiet one by the wall.

I have half a tune and no ruling on the rest.
episodes.title: Three Ways to Order a Song

choices.response:
She laughs, but she answers plainly.

Ombra, the jujube hills east of the pass.

We winter there some years, when the roads allow it.

My mother still writes to ask whether I am keeping the good teapot safe for festival nights, and I still burn the rice if I am the one watching it.

She turns the cake over in her hands.

I have not written them since the spring.

I will tonight.

You are a menace, you know that?

One question, and my whole road bends homeward for a page.
choices.text: Where would you go, if the road ever bent that way?

choices.response:
She glances up, finds you simply there, and keeps going, quieter now.

Sorry.

You did not need the whole ledger.

She smiles a little.

But you listen like the wall in a confessional, and that is rarer than talent.

She finishes the cake and dusts her hands.

Most people clap at me.

You just stay.

It is a strange kindness, staying, and I have learned not to waste it.
choices.text: (Stay exactly where you are and let the silence be a place to talk.)

episodes.dialogue:
She breaks the cake in half and sets the bigger piece in front of you without asking.

Careful, this is contraband.

My friend Oves in the troupe buys these every single town, and tonight he bought two, which means either generosity or he is sulking about the set list again.

She takes a bite, chews, and her eyes go somewhere farther off than the tavern wall.

You know what is funny about a jujube cake?

It tastes like a specific street.

Not a city, a street.

There was a woman two doors from our old lodging who made them, and she would chase us off the step if we sang before paying.

She looks down at the cake in her hand, very seriously, and says, thank you, to it.

Then she laughs at herself.

Ignore that.

Habit.

When you grow up moving, food does the remembering for you.

She turns the cake over.

We joined the Moonstring troupe when I was seventeen, my lute and I and one bag that lied about its weight.

My mother cried at the gate, then made us take the good teapot, which weighs more than the bag.

It is in the wagon right now.

She smiles, but her thumb keeps moving over the cake's paper wrapping.

I have sung in forty towns and I could not tell you which one my mother thinks I am in tonight.

Probably the last one she got a letter from.

That is the trouble with this trade, wouldn't you say?

You give songs to everyone and forget to send one home.

She looks up suddenly, catching herself.

Listen to me.

You came for cake and I am handing you my whole childhood like it is part of the set list.
episodes.ending:
The tavern empties around you in ones and twos.

Oves calls down from the stairs that dawn comes whether they sleep or not, and Lyra waves him off without breaking the conversation.

When the lamps are trimmed she wraps the remaining half of the cake carefully and does not put it away, keeping it on the table between you until the very last minute, as if some things should stay in the room where they were said.

At the door she turns back once.

Same table tomorrow, if the town permits.
episodes.opening:
Three nights on, the Lantern Step knows your order and Lyra knows your table.

Tonight she arrives with a paper-wrapped jujube cake and drops into the chair across from you like it was reserved.

She is off duty, shawl loose, no lute, which somehow makes her harder to ignore.

The troupe leaves in three mornings.

She sets the cake down between you and pats it once, like a small animal that might bolt.
episodes.title: The Cake That Remembers

choices.response:
She plays the alternate ending through once, then laughs at herself.

There.

It is out of my hands and into the room.

You realize what you have done.

I can never retire that ending now.

Someone in this town will ask for it, and I will have to admit the ferryman's version finally got let in because a stranger in the corner told me the room could hold both endings.

She plays it again, softer, committing it to memory.

Thank you.

Truly.

A song that can end two ways is worth two songs.
choices.text: Sing it the way you heard it. The room can hold both endings.

choices.response:
She catches you not leaving, and something steadies in her.

Right.

You are still here, so the song is not over.

She plays the alternate ending slowly, working it out note by note while you listen, and when she lands it, she exhales like someone setting down a heavy bag.

There it is.

Kept.

She looks at you across the empty room.

You did not say a word and I still felt like someone was holding the other end.

That is a rare talent.

Do not lose it.
choices.text: (Stay in your chair, and keep listening without filling the silence.)

episodes.dialogue:
She sets the lute across her knees and plays the little road song from the top, the one she learned three towns back.

It goes well until the last verse, where she stops, frowns, and shakes her head.

No. That is not how the ferryman sang it.

She tries the ending again and it comes out the tavern version, polished, safe.

She stops again.

Two endings.

That is the trouble with learning songs on the road.

The first version installs itself, and the second one knocks politely forever and never gets let in.

She looks at the lute like it has betrayed her.

I heard the original on the ferry, from a man with a voice like gravel in a bucket.

His ending went down, not up.

The whole room here hums along with the up one, so I sing the up one.

And every time I do, I can hear the gravel man clearing his throat in the back of my skull, deeply unimpressed.

She glances at the door, then at you.

The troupe moves on the day after tomorrow.

If I do not settle this ending tonight, it rides in my head unsettled for another hundred miles, and that is how songs die, quietly, from indecision.

She squares her shoulders and puts the lute steady on her knee.

So here is the cost, and I am telling you before I pay it.

If I sing the down ending in public, half this room will think I made a mistake.

My reputation is soup and a bed, and mistakes are bad for soup.

She takes a breath.

But you are the room right now.

Practically the whole room.

One customer and a dying fire.
episodes.ending:
She plays the song through once more, start to finish, and lets the ending land where it landed.

Then she closes the lesson like closing a book.

Good.

That one is settled, and I am glad I heard the other ending before it walked off the ferry for good.

She lifts the lute case onto her shoulder, pauses at the foot of the stairs, and hums the first two notes of the road song back at the room, a receipt for the evening.

The troupe leaves the day after tomorrow.

She does not say what happens after that, but she says goodnight like someone who intends to find out.
episodes.opening:
The following night, the troupe has a night off, which means the Lantern Step has a different singer and Lyra has a table.

She has claimed the corner across from you with a cup of something warm, lute case propped against the wall like a sleeping dog.

The fire is low.

She is humming, stops, frowns at her own hum, and starts again.

Apparently this has been going on internally for some time, and you are about to hear the external version.
episodes.title: The Ferryman's Ending

choices.response:
She goes still, and then her whole face does the thing it does before a high note.

You are sure?

Because I do not ask twice, and I never ask at all, so this is me, asking.

She sits beside you on the bench, close but not leaning, and plays the wordless song at last, unhurried, letting the river keep the tempo.

When it ends she does not fill the silence.

So that is what I sound like when I am not performing.

I would like to find out what else that sounds like.

With you.

Slowly.

No schedule.
choices.text: Then sing me the wordless one. And let this be a courtship, not a concert.

choices.response:
She nods slowly, and there is no disappointment in it, only a kind of relief, like a note resolved correctly.

A friend at the river.

She stays beside you and plays the wordless song anyway, quietly, the way you would give someone a key to a room they may use whenever they like.

When it ends she says, you are the only person who has heard it sober, and leaves it there.

The sun crawls.

The sketch grows a second figure.

It looks right.
choices.text: (Stay on the bench beside her, and let the friendship be the whole answer.)

episodes.dialogue:
She is already seated when you arrive, shawl over her shoulders, a charcoal stick behind one ear and a folded paper on her knees.

Look at me.

Portrait artist.

She holds up the sketch, which is mostly river and one ambitious swan.

I am charging the swan nothing, since it sat for free.

She pats the bench beside her, leaving a respectful gap.

Sit, or stand, or pace, whichever your legs have planned.

The troupe leaves tomorrow, and I have been walking past this river for a week pretending I was not going to miss it.

She flips to a fresh page.

So.

Before I go, one invitation, and I want you to hear the whole of it before you answer.

She tucks the charcoal behind her other ear.

There is a song I have never performed in public.

No words.

It is not for sale and it is not for the stage.

It is the only thing in my book I have never let a room vote on.

She looks at the river, not at you.

I have sung it exactly twice, both times alone, both times to a moon that was frankly indifferent.

And lately I keep thinking, if I leave this town without singing it to one person who is not a moon, it goes back in the book for another year.

She turns to face you at last.

So here is the choice, and I mean it as a real one.

I can sing it for you here, this afternoon, and whatever it is between us, it can simply be this, a friend at the river, and I will be glad of that for the rest of the road.

Or, if you want more than that, we start there, with that song, and see what it grows into.

No promises asked, none given.

She smiles, a little nervous for the first time you have seen.

The swan is watching.

No pressure.
episodes.ending:
The sun crosses the far roofline before either of you moves.

The sketch ends up with a second figure in it, small, by the water.

Lyra packs the charcoal, shoulders the lute, and walks back toward the Lantern Step with you, talking about the swan's terrible work ethic.

At the corner where your ways split for the evening, she stops, taps the folded sketch against her palm, and says, tomorrow, then, whatever tomorrow is.

And it sounds like a plan.
episodes.opening:
She found you at breakfast and slid a folded paper next to your cup: a lopsided sketch of the riverfront, with an X and the words here, when the sun is low.

The troupe leaves tomorrow.

You find her at the X in the late gold light, the river moving slow past the pilings, and she waves the sketch like a flag of a very small country.
episodes.title: The Riverfront Sketch

choices.response:
She grins and lays her hand flat on the book between you.

Then it is a contract.

Every town, one letter, no excuses about bad roads or bad ink.

And when the troupe circles back this way, this table, this wall, first night.

She stands and slings the lute bag.

I have sung for kings' cousins and one very committed goat.

None of them ever asked me for the boring parts.

Keep being the person who asks.

The road is easier with somewhere to aim the letters.
choices.text: Then let's make it a standing thing. Every town, one letter, and this table when you pass through.

choices.response:
She waits, and when you simply take the book without a word, she laughs and lets you.

Right.

Actions.

I forget who I am dealing with.

She watches you copy the address in your own hand, and her voice goes softer than the morning.

You know, most people collect my songs.

You collect my logistics.

It is somehow the greater honor.

She takes the book back, checks your handwriting, and nods once, satisfied.

There.

Now I owe the post office and you.

I keep my debts.
choices.text: (Take the songbook and write the address in it yourself, without a word.)

episodes.dialogue:
She looks up and does not pretend to be surprised.

You found me.

Good.

I was forty percent sure the letter would just sit on this table forever, growing mysterious.

She scoots over and makes room on the bench.

Sit.

The troupe loads at midday, so we have the whole morning, and I have spent mine doing this.

She shows you the page.

Under the song, in her round handwriting, it says: For the corner table, the Lantern Step, where the second half got decided.

She closes the book on your finger gently.

I finished the wordless one, by the way.

It has words now.

Three of them.

I am not telling you which.

A bard keeps some things in reserve, wouldn't you say?

She looks out at the street, where the wagon is being loaded.

We winter in the jujube hills this year.

Oves already asked if the cakes travel well, which tells you everything about Oves.

And I wrote my mother from three towns back, an actual letter, four pages, and I told her about a stranger at a tavern who knocked a rhythm on a table and changed the ending of a song.

She said the stranger sounds patient.

Mothers are terrifying.

She turns back to you, and her voice settles into something less performance-shaped.

Here is the thing I have been turning over.

Songs are easy to give away.

They weigh nothing.

But a friendship across a road, that takes actual work, the boring kind, letters and dates and remembering which towns flood in spring.

She taps the table.

So I am asking for the boring kind.

Promise me logistics.
episodes.ending:
The wagon lurches forward at midday with the good teapot aboard and Oves guarding a box of jujube cakes like treasure.

Lyra rides on the tailboard, not waving, because you agreed that waving is for strangers.

Instead she knocks three notes on the lute body, the rhythm from the first night, and the whole street can hear it.

The letters begin that winter, and every one of them ends the same way: this table, first night, when the road comes back.
episodes.opening:
Months later, and the road has brought the Moonstring troupe back through this town twice.

This morning it leaves for the winter circuit, and Lyra has claimed the corner table before dawn, a candle, her songbook, and two cups of something steaming.

When you come in she pushes the second cup across without looking up from the page, where she is writing something in careful, un-bardlike handwriting.
episodes.title: Morning Before the Road

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

choices.response:
She laughs, bright and unsteady at once.

The third word was going to stay hidden until the pass.

You are impossible.

Her smile settles, and she gives you the answer plainly.

The last word is you.

The three are: I love you.

She leaves a breath of quiet after it, long enough for the words to belong to the morning rather than a performance.

She takes your hand, presses it once, and lets go, keeping her promise about slowness.

Then I will spend the whole climb composing the verse.

Fair warning: it will be honest, and honesty is the one thing I cannot make catchy.

She steps up onto the wagon.

Write to me.

Sing back, even badly.

Especially badly.
choices.text: Then tell me the third word before you go, and I'll keep it until the pass.

choices.response:
You do not ask, and she understands immediately.

Ah.

You would rather it arrive than be announced.

She nods slowly, pleased.

Then it stays in the song, and the song stays in the book, and the book comes back this way when the thaw does.

She knocks the three notes once more, softer.

Keep the table.

Keep the wall.

I will keep the third word.

That is a fair division of the road between us.
choices.text: (Say nothing, and knock the three-note rhythm back on the table.)

romance.dialogue:
She looks up, and this time she does look surprised, pleased-surprised, the way she looks when a room sings back a verse she did not teach them.

You came.

I gave the letter a fifty-fifty chance and the road a seventy-thirty, and here you are beating both odds.

Sit.

She moves her boots off the bench.

Careful with the teapot, it is the good one and my mother asks about it more than she asks about me.

She pours, and steam fogs between you.

The troupe leaves within the hour.

Winter circuit, the jujube hills, then the river towns when the ice breaks.

I will be gone most of a season.

She says it plainly, no drama, watching your face while she says it.

So.

Before the wagon, the report.

The wordless song has words now.

Three.

It has been performed exactly four times, all of them for an audience of one, and every time it was better than the last, which I attribute to the audience.

She turns her cup slowly on its saucer.

And I have been honest with myself, which is a new and uncomfortable hobby.

What I want is not a promise.

Promises made at wagon-wheels are bad luck and worse architecture.

What I want is this: that when the thaw brings the troupe back up the river road, the first thing I do off the wagon is walk here, and the first thing I find is you, at this wall, pretending you did not count the days.

She smiles, and for once there is no performance in it at all.

In exchange, I will write.

Real letters, not songbooks.

And the third word stays mine until I am standing close enough to sing it at a civilized volume.

She glances at the street, where Oves is already arguing with a wagon wheel.

That is my whole offer.

Slow, seasonal, and entirely without guarantees.

Wouldn't you say it is enough?
romance.ending:
The wagon rolls with the good teapot wrapped in her spare shawl and Oves asleep on the cakes.

Lyra rides the tailboard and does not wave, because waving is for strangers and the two of you settled that long ago.

Instead she sings the three-word song, quiet enough that only the road hears it, and the last note stays open the way it always has.

The letters come through the winter, one a month, each signed with three small notes instead of a name.

The thaw brings the troupe back up the river road, and the first thing off the wagon is her.
romance.opening:
The letter came a week ago: one line, a drawing of the corner table, and the words before the wagon.

Now it is a cold bright morning and the troupe's wagon stands loaded in the square outside the Lantern Step.

Lyra is inside at the corner table with the good teapot, two cups, and her songbook closed and squared in front of her like a decision already made.
romance.title: Before the Wagon

choices.response:
莱拉笑出了声，一脸高兴，一只手撑在桌上。

好。

那就是慢板。

她把那半句再弹一遍，速度放了一半，弹出来满是怅惘，几乎像一首摇篮曲。

厨子从厨房探出头来听。

一曲终了，她朝想象中的听众低头一礼，又冲你咧嘴一笑。

忧郁一票。

我被月亮和一位诚实的陌生人打败了。

今晚的后半段就温柔着唱。
choices.text: 弹慢一点，让这屋里的人自己决定听出什么。

choices.response:
她看着你的手指落定，脸上的神情忽然柔和下来，专注起来。

啊。

比起说话，你更喜欢敲。

好。

她把那半句再弹一遍，然后安静下来，在琴身上敲出应答，隔着整间屋子跟你一来一回地打节奏，厨子的大勺在厨房里一下一下，稳稳地打着拍子。

当你的敲击和她的对上时，她眉开眼笑。

就是它了。

那就是欢快，还带点倔。

我就照这样写下来。
choices.text: （你把酒杯放下，照着那个节奏在桌上敲了回去。）

episodes.dialogue:
你在桌面上敲了两下作为回应，她歪了歪头，卷发滑下一侧肩膀，笑得像你刚送了她一份礼物。

哦，来了位有主见的客人。

太好了。

再听一遍。

她把那半句又弹了一次，这次更慢，任凭最后一根弦嗡嗡地荡着。

这半句有三种唱法。

我可以唱得亮堂，像酒喝多了的节庆。

我可以唱得慢，像有人在想念一座港湾。

或者，照刚才那两下敲桌子的劲儿来唱——说实话，那可是有点没礼貌，你说呢？

她又拨了一下那半句，带着点顽皮，眼睛盯着你的脸，不看琴弦。

旅团付我的是一碗汤和楼上的一张床，所以汤是稳的，怎么唱都不亏。

但要是屋里有人真心押了注，这歌才唱得有味道。

她向后一靠，鲁特琴稳稳架在膝上。

所以。

第二段，你说了算。

不过在你开口之前，先告诉你，我错过。

有一次我在副歌正中间，把一位旅人的家乡唱错了名，他连晚饭都没吃就走了。

从那以后，我先问清楚，再开口唱。

她拧了一下弦轴，等着，让那个空音悬在灯光里。

你定。

它往哪儿走我就跟到哪儿，就算你选错了我也不会摆脸色。

本来就没有选错这回事。

只有这屋子想听什么——而今晚，这屋子就是你。
episodes.ending:
她照你的选择弹完了后半段，整间酒馆安静得能听见炉火的噼啪声。

唱完之后，她抱着琴走到你的桌边坐下，接过厨子送来的晚饭，一边吃一边跟你聊你们一起定下的那半句，翻来覆去地琢磨，像在把玩一枚还舍不得花出去的硬币。

灯油将尽之前，她把这曲子完整地哼了一遍，最后一个音落下时，她指了指你。

这曲子上有你的指纹。

它会留在我的谱子里，旁边写着你的名字——或者，至少写到我不必开口向陌生人讨名字的程度。
episodes.opening:
灯笼阶酒馆坐了一半的人，是那种实在的半满。

你靠墙坐了一张桌子，手边的酒一口没动，因为今晚的演出正唱到一半，停住了。

一个披着月白披肩的年轻女人坐在台上，怀里抱着细颈鲁特琴，最后一个音悬着不落。

等窃窃私语平息下来，她径直望向你那个角落。

就是你。

对，就是你，靠墙那位安静的朋友。

我手上有个半截的调子，剩下怎么收，还没个说法。
episodes.title: 一首歌的三种点法

choices.response:
她笑了，但答得很认真。

奥姆布拉，山口东边的枣树丘陵。

路好走的那几年，我们会在那儿过冬。

我娘至今还写信来问，好茶壶留着没有，节日夜里得用；而我只要负责看火，米饭准糊。

她把枣糕在手里翻了个面。

开春之后，我就没给他们写过信了。

今晚就写。

你真是个祸害，知道吗？

就一个问题，我整条路就往家的方向弯了一页。
choices.text: 如果哪天路弯向那个方向，你会回哪儿去？

choices.response:
她抬眼一瞧，发现你就这么安静地待着，便继续说了下去，声音放轻了。

抱歉。

你没必要听我一笔一笔翻旧账。

她微微一笑。

可你听人说话的样子，像告解室里的那面墙——这可比有天分稀罕多了。

她吃完枣糕，拍掉手上的碎屑。

大多数人对着我做的事就是鼓掌。

你只是留下来。

留下来，是一种很奇怪的温柔。我学会了不浪费它。
choices.text: （你留在原地没动，让这份沉默变成一个可以说话的地方。）

episodes.dialogue:
她把枣糕掰成两半，不打招呼就把大的那半推到你面前。

小心点，这可是违禁品。

旅团里我朋友奥维斯，每到一个镇子都要买这玩意儿。今晚他买了两块——要么是发了善心，要么是又对曲目单生闷气了。

她咬了一口，慢慢嚼着，眼神飘到比酒馆墙壁更远的地方。

你知道枣糕最好笑的是什么吗？

它尝起来是一条具体的街的味道。

不是一座城，是一条街。

我们以前住处隔壁两门，有位大婶会做这个。我们唱歌不给钱的话，她能把我们从台阶上轰走。

她低头看着手里的枣糕，无比郑重地对它说了声：谢谢你。

然后她自己笑了。

当我没说。

老习惯了。

从小四处漂泊的人，记忆都交给食物来保管。

她把枣糕翻了个面。

我十七岁那年加入了月弦旅团，带上我的琴和一个死不承认自己有多重的行李袋。

我娘在门口哭了一场，回头非让我们带上那把好茶壶——比行李袋还沉。

它现在就在货车上。

她笑着，拇指却一直在枣糕的油纸上蹭来蹭去。

我在四十个镇子唱过歌，可我根本说不出我娘以为我今晚在哪儿。

八成还停留在她收到上一封信的地方。

干这行就是这么回事，你说呢？

你把歌送给所有人，却忘了寄一首回家。

她忽然抬起头，像是惊醒了自己。

听听我说的这些。

你是来吃糕的，我却把整个童年都端给你，好像它是曲目单上的一项。
episodes.ending:
酒馆里的客人三三两两地散了。

楼梯上传来奥维斯的喊声，说天亮不等任何人；莱拉朝他摆摆手，没让话头断掉。

熄灯之前，她把剩下的半块枣糕仔细包好，没有收起来，就一直搁在你俩之间的桌上，直到最后一刻——仿佛有些话，就该留在说出口的那个房间里。

走到门口，她回头看了你一眼。

明天，还是这张桌子——只要这座镇子允许。
episodes.opening:
三天过去，灯笼阶酒馆已经记得你点的东西，莱拉也记得你的位置。

今晚她抱来一块用油纸包着的枣糕，一屁股坐进你对面的椅子，仿佛那位置早就留好了。

她下了工，披肩松松地搭着，没带琴——反倒让人更没法忽视她。

旅团三天后一早就出发。

她把枣糕放在你俩中间，轻轻拍了拍，像拍一只随时会跑掉的小动物。
episodes.title: 会记路的枣糕

choices.response:
她把那个新结尾完整弹了一遍，然后自嘲地笑了。

好了。

这下它不归我了，归这屋子了。

你可想清楚自己干了什么。

这个结尾我再也收不回去了。

以后这镇上总会有人点它，那我就得承认——摆渡人的版本终于进了门，只因为角落里一个陌生人说，这屋子装得下两个结尾。

她又弹了一遍，更轻，把音符一个个记进心里。

谢谢你。

真的。

一首能有两种结尾的歌，抵得上两首歌。
choices.text: 照你听到的那样唱。这屋子装得下两个结尾。

choices.response:
她发现你没有走，心里有什么东西稳了下来。

对。

你还在这儿，说明这首歌还没完。

她慢慢地弹那个新结尾，一个音一个音地琢磨，你静静听着。等她终于落定最后一个音，她长长呼出一口气，像放下了很沉的行李。

就是它了。

留住了。

她隔着空荡荡的店堂看着你。

你一句话没说，我却觉得有人牵着绳子的另一头。

这可是很少见的天赋。

别丢了。
choices.text: （你留在椅子上，不打断沉默，继续听。）

episodes.dialogue:
她把鲁特琴横在膝上，从头弹起那首小路上的歌，三个镇子以前学来的那首。

弹得挺顺，直到最后一段，她停住，皱起眉，摇了摇头。

不对。摆渡人不是这么唱的。

她又试了一遍结尾，出来的却是酒馆里的版本，圆润、保险。

她又停了下来。

两个结尾。

这就是在路上学歌的麻烦。

第一个版本自己安了家，第二个版本永远在门外有礼貌地敲门，永远进不来。

她看着琴，像看一个背叛了她的东西。

我是在渡船上听到的原版，唱歌的是个嗓音像桶里砂砾的男人。

他的结尾是往下走的，不是往上。

可这店里的人都跟着往上那个调子哼，所以我也就唱往上那个。

每次唱的时候，我脑后那个砂砾嗓都会清清嗓子，一脸嫌弃。

她朝门口瞥了一眼，又看向你。

旅团后天就走。

今晚要是不把这个结尾定下来，它就得在我脑子里悬着再晃一百里，歌就是这么死的——不动声色，死于犹豫不决。

她挺直肩膀，把琴稳稳架在膝上。

那好，代价是有的，我在付之前先跟你说清楚。

我要是当众唱往下那个结尾，这店里一半的人都会以为我唱错了。

我的名声就是一份汤和一张床，而唱错对汤没好处。

她吸了口气。

可现在你就是这间屋子。

几乎算得上整间屋子。

一位客人，一炉快灭的火。
episodes.ending:
她把整首歌又从头到尾弹了一遍，让结尾落在哪里就停在哪里。

然后她像合上一本书那样，收了这堂课。

好了。

这一首算定了。幸好另一个结尾下了渡船一去不回之前，我听见了它。

她把琴匣背上肩头，在楼梯口顿了顿，朝店里回哼了小路歌的头两个音，算是给今晚打的一张收条。

旅团后天就走。

之后的事她没有说，可她道晚安的样子，像是打算去弄清楚。
episodes.opening:
第二天晚上，旅团休演，灯笼阶酒馆换了别的歌手，莱拉也就有了自己的桌子。

她占了你对面的角落，捧着一杯热饮，琴匣靠在墙边，像一条睡着的狗。

炉火烧得很低。

她哼着什么，停了，对那声哼皱皱眉，又重新开始。

看样子这事在她心里已经憋了一阵子，而你现在要听到外放的版本了。
episodes.title: 摆渡人的结尾

choices.response:
她怔住了，然后整张脸露出她要唱高音前才有的那种神情。

你想好了？

因为我从不问第二遍——其实我从来就不问。所以这一次，是我，在问。

她在你身边的长凳上坐下，靠得很近，却没倚过来，终于弹起那首无词歌，不慌不忙，让河水来定节拍。

一曲终了，她没有急着用话去填那份安静。

这就是我不表演时的声音。

我想知道，它还能是什么样。

和你一起。

慢慢地。

不赶日程。
choices.text: 那就把那首无词歌唱给我听吧。让今天是一场求爱，不是一场演出。

choices.response:
她缓缓点头，里面没有失望，只有一种如释重负，像一个音终于落对了。

河边的一个朋友。

她还是留在你身边，把那首无词歌轻轻弹了，就像把一把钥匙交给某人——那间屋子，你想什么时候来住都行。

一曲终了，她说，你是唯一一个清醒时听过它的人。然后就到此为止。

太阳慢慢挪着。

速写上多了第二个人影。

看起来刚刚好。
choices.text: （你在她身边的长凳上坐下，让这份友情本身成为全部的回答。）

episodes.dialogue:
你到的时候，她已经坐下了，披肩搭在肩上，耳后别着一根炭条，膝上摊着折好的纸。

看看我。

肖像画家。

她举起那张速写——大半是河，外加一只野心勃勃的天鹅。

天鹅我不收钱，反正它是免费坐的模特。

她拍了拍身边的凳子，留出一段很有分寸的空隙。

坐，站着，来回踱步，随你的腿怎么安排。

旅团明天就走，可这一周我天天路过这条河，假装自己不会想念它。

她翻到新的一页。

所以。

我走之前，有一个邀请。我想让你听完整了再回答。

她把炭条别到另一只耳朵后面。

有一首歌，我从没在公开场合唱过。

没有词。

它不出售，也不上台。

它是我歌本里唯一一首，从没让一个屋子的人投票表决过的。

她望着河，没看你。

我只唱过两次，两次都是独自一人，唱给一轮——说实话相当无动于衷的月亮。

最近我总在想，如果我就这么离开这个镇子，从没把它唱给一个不是月亮的人听，那它就只能在歌本里再躺上一年。

她终于转过身来面对你。

所以，选择在这里，我说真的，这是个真实的选择。

我可以就在这里、就这个下午，唱给你听。不管我们之间是什么，它就止于此——河边的一个朋友。往后的路上，我会为此高兴。

或者，如果你想要更多，那我们就从这里开始，从这首歌开始，看它能长成什么样子。

不要你许诺，我也不许诺。

她笑了——你头一次见她有点紧张。

天鹅在看呢。

别有压力。
episodes.ending:
直到太阳越过远处的屋脊，你们俩谁都没动。

最后那张速写上多了第二个人影，小小的，在水边。

莱拉收起炭条，背起鲁特琴，和你一起往灯笼阶酒馆走，一路数落着那只天鹅糟糕的敬业精神。

走到傍晚你们要分道的那条街角，她停下来，用折好的速写拍了拍手心，说：那就明天见——不管明天是什么。

那听起来像一个计划。
episodes.opening:
吃早饭时，她找到你，把一张折好的纸塞到你的杯子旁：一张歪歪扭扭的河畔速写，上面画了个叉，旁边写着：太阳低垂时，到这里来。

旅团明天就出发了。

金色的夕照里，你照着那个叉找到了她。河水缓缓流过木桩，她把速写举起来挥了挥，像挥一面很小很小的国家的国旗。
episodes.title: 河畔速写

choices.response:
她咧嘴一笑，把手平放在你们中间的歌本上。

那就成了契约。

每个镇子一封信，不许拿路难走、墨不好当借口。

旅团再绕回这边的时候，这张桌子，这面墙，第一晚。

她站起身，背起琴袋。

我给王公的亲戚唱过歌，还给一只特别执着的山羊唱过。

他们谁也没跟我要过无聊的部分。

继续做那个会开口要的人吧。

路上有地方可以寄信，走起来就轻多了。
choices.text: 那就把它定成规矩。每个镇子一封信，你路过这里，就回这张桌子。

choices.response:
她等着，见你不声不响地拿走歌本，笑了一声，随你去了。

行啊。

用行动说话。

我都忘了自己在跟什么人打交道了。

她看着你一笔一画抄下地址，声音比这个清晨还轻。

你知道吗，大多数人收集的是我的歌。

你收集的是我的安排。

这不知怎么反而是更大的荣幸。

她收回歌本，端详了一下你的字迹，满意地点了点头。

好了。

现在我欠邮局和你了。

我的债，都是要还的。
choices.text: （你一言不发，拿过歌本，亲手把地址写了进去。）

episodes.dialogue:
她抬起头，没有假装惊讶。

你找到我了。

很好。

我本来四成把握，那封信会永远躺在这张桌上，越躺越神秘。

她往边上挪了挪，在长凳上腾出位置。

坐。

旅团中午才装车，整个上午都是我们的，而我已经用它干了这么件事。

她把那页纸递给你看。

歌的下面，用她圆圆的字迹写着：致灯笼阶酒馆的角落桌，歌的后半段在这里定了稿。

她轻轻合上歌本，压住你的手指。

对了，那首无词歌我写完了。

现在它有词了。

三个字。

我不告诉你是哪三个。

吟游诗人总得留一手，你说呢？

她望向窗外，街上的货车正在装货。

今年冬天我们去枣丘过冬。

奥维斯已经问过枣糕经不经得起颠簸，这话把奥维斯这个人说得明明白白。

三个镇子之前，我给我母亲写了信，一封真正的信，写了四页。我告诉她，有个陌生人在旅店里敲着桌面打节奏，改写了一首歌的结尾。

她说，这个陌生人听起来很有耐心。

母亲们真可怕。

她转回身来看着你，声音落了下来，不再是表演的腔调。

有件事我一直在琢磨。

歌是最容易送出去的东西。

它们没有重量。

可隔着一条路的友情，那是要下真功夫的，是那种无聊的功夫：写信、定日子、记住哪些镇子一到春天就发水。

她敲了敲桌面。

所以我想求的，就是这种无聊的功夫。

不是许诺什么感情。

是许诺安排。
episodes.ending:
中午，货车启程了，车上载着那把好茶壶，奥维斯守着一箱枣糕，守得像守宝物。

莱拉坐在车尾板上，没有挥手，因为你们说好了，挥手是给陌生人的。

她只是在琴身上敲了三个音，第一晚的那个节奏，整条街都听得见。

那个冬天，信开始一封封寄出，每一封的结尾都一样：这张桌子，第一晚，等路绕回来。
episodes.opening:
几个月过去，这条路的月弦旅团已经两次路过这座小镇。

今天早上，旅团要出发去冬季巡演，天还没亮，莱拉就占了角落那张桌子：一支蜡烛、她的歌本，还有两杯冒着热气的东西。

你进来时，她头也没抬，把第二杯推了过去。她正低头在纸上写着什么，字迹工整，一点也不像吟游诗人的手笔。
episodes.title: 启程前的清晨

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

choices.response:
她笑出了声，又明亮，又有一丝不稳。

第三个字本来是要藏到山口才说的。

真拿你没办法。

她的笑容落定，然后坦坦白白地给了你答案。

最后一个字，是你。

三个字连起来是：我爱你。

说完她留了一口气的安静，久到让这三个字归清晨所有。

她握住你的手，轻轻一按，便松开了，守住了她说的慢慢来。

那这一路上山，我就把那段词谱出来。

先提醒你：它会很诚实，而诚实是我唯一唱不讨巧的东西。

她登上车。

给我写信。

要回歌给我，哪怕唱得难听。

尤其要难听。
choices.text: 那就趁你还没走，把第三个字告诉我，我替你守到山口。

choices.response:
你没有问，她立刻就懂了。

啊。

你宁愿让它自己抵达，也不想听它被宣布。

她缓缓点头，很受用。

那它就留在歌里，歌留在本子里，本子在化冻的时候随我一起回到这条路来。

她又轻轻敲了一遍那三个音符。

桌子留给你。

墙留给你。

第三个字留给我。

这条路，我们就这么公平地分了。
choices.text: （你什么也没说，只在桌上敲出那三个音符的节奏，敲了回去。）

romance.dialogue:
她抬起头，这一次是真的露出惊讶来，又惊又喜——就像满屋子的人齐声唱出她没教过的那一段时，她脸上那种神情。

你真的来了。

我给这封信五五开的胜算，给这条路七三开，结果你把两个赔率都赢了。

坐。

她把脚从长凳上挪开。

小心那把茶壶，它是把好壶，我娘问起它的次数比问起我还多。

她倒茶，热气在你们之间袅袅散开。

旅团一小时内就要出发。

先走冬季路线，去枣丘，等开河化了冰，再沿河去各个镇子。

我会有大半个季度不在。

她说得平平静静，不带一点戏剧腔，眼睛却一直看着你的脸。

所以。

车行之前，交个底。

那首无词歌，如今有词了。

三个字。

它总共被唱过四次，每一次的听众都只有一个人，而且一次比一次唱得好——这功劳我记在听众头上。

她慢慢转着茶碟上的杯子。

我也对自己坦诚了一回，这可是个新鲜又难受的习惯。

我要的不是承诺。

在车轮边许下的诺言，既不吉利，也盖不起房子。

我要的是这个：等开春化冻、旅团沿河路回来，我下车做的第一件事，就是走到这里；而我见到的第一个人，是你坐在这堵墙边，假装自己没数过日子。

她笑了，这一次笑容里没有半点表演。

作为交换，我会写信。

真正的信，不是歌本。

而第三个字，仍归我保管，直到我站得足够近，能用一个文明的音量把它唱出来为止。

她瞥了一眼街上，奥维斯已经在跟一只车轮吵架了。

这就是我的全部条件。

慢慢来，跟着季节走，不作任何保证。

你说呢，这样够不够？
romance.ending:
车启动了，那把好茶壶用她的备用披肩裹着，奥维斯在货堆上睡着了。

莱拉坐在车尾板上，没有挥手——挥手是给陌生人预备的，而你们俩早就不是了。

她只是唱起那首三个字的歌，轻得只有这条路听得见，最后一个音像往常一样，久久不落。

信整个冬天陆续寄来，一月一封，每封落款处不写名字，只画三个小小的音符。

开春化冻，旅团沿着河路回来了，第一个从车上下来的，是她。
romance.opening:
信是一个星期前送到的：只有一行字，一幅角落那桌子的画，还有四个字——车行之前。

此刻是清晨，天冷而亮，旅团的车已装好行李，停在灯笼阶酒馆外的广场上。

莱拉坐在店里角落那张桌旁，备着那把好茶壶和两只杯子，歌本合着，端端正正摆在面前，像一个早就做好的决定。
romance.title: 车行之前

episodes.title: The Bootlace at the Shoe Shop
episodes.opening:
Late afternoon at the edge of the star-lit forest, near the old shoe shop.

A child sits on the step, one boot off, laces knotted around a torn-out briar sprig, and a crowd of neighbors has gathered to watch a mage work.

She stands with a floating astrolabe and a chart weighted down by four river stones, indigo robes dusted with road grit.

A silver ornament catches the last light.

She looks up as you approach, and does not seem surprised that you, a stranger, have wandered into a small local crisis.
episodes.dialogue:
Meilin Starfall, third-rank observer mage of the Star-script Academy — I log the gate tides and calibrate translocation coordinates.

Though today's work is humbler.

This boy's bootlace caught a briar two streets back, and the knot has since been declared unsolvable by three adults and one very confident dog.

I offered a minor unbinding charm.

He asked if the charm would eat the boot.

I said no.

He said he would rather wait for you, because you looked like someone who unties things properly.

So here we both are, outvoted by a child.

The chart is for afterward — I'm calibrating a coordinate above the forest, and I thought I'd do it where there were witnesses.

A mage kneeling in a ditch alone tends to alarm people.

A mage kneeling in a ditch next to a shoe shop is merely eccentric.

Would you take the lace?

I'll hold the boot steady.

I can shift small objects, but a knot is a problem of patience, not weight, and patience is your department this afternoon.

choices.text: Hold it firm. This knot wants to be talked out, not pulled.
choices.response:
She steadies the boot without comment and watches your fingers work.

'Interesting,' she says.

'You address the knot directly.

Most people address the lace.'

When the briar finally slides free, the boy cheers, and she notes something in her three-column notebook.

'Under known: the knot is gone.

Under inferred: you are useful.

Under safe to defer: everything else.'

choices.text: (Sit on the step beside the boy and hold the boot steady yourself, saying nothing.)
choices.response:
You take the boot from her hands and brace it between your knees.

She raises an eyebrow, then crouches to your level and picks the briar loose with two fingers and a small shimmer.

'A division of labor,' she says, approving.

'I do the magic, you do the dignity of the situation.'

The boy puts his boot back on, problem forgotten.

episodes.ending:
The boy runs off to tell everyone the mage was beaten by a bootlace.

Meilin straightens her chart, then hesitates.

'The bookshop owner asked me to deliver a corrected report today, and I did, and I find I have no further errands,' she says.

'I'll be calibrating above this forest for some weeks.

If you pass the gate at dusk, I can show you which star helps find north.

One star.

There is no need to memorize the whole chart at once.'

She gathers her stones and waits, unhurried, for whatever you decide.

episodes.title: The Sour Sweet Test
episodes.opening:
The dusk meetings at the gate became a habit without anyone announcing it.

Today Meilin has an errand in town and asks, plainly, if you'd like to walk along.

The candy shop on the market street smells of burnt sugar and lemon peel.

She stands before the jars like a scholar before an unfamiliar text, shawl tucked over one arm, and the shopkeeper is already reaching for a paper bag.

A stone bridge waits on the way back, and the evening is in no hurry.
episodes.dialogue:
The shopkeeper says this is the sourest candy he stocks.

Preserved green fruit, salted plum heart, a sugar shell that fights back.

I told him I like that.

He nodded and asked if I wanted two bags.

I said one is enough, because I have company now, and company should be consulted.

Do you want to try one, or would the milk candy suit you better?

The milk candy is in that jar — gentler, no arguments.

I buy it for long observation nights.

It doesn't fight back, which on the fourth hour of a gate tide is the correct personality for a sweet.

Take whichever.

This is not a test.

I have administered tests professionally and they look nothing like a candy counter.

While you choose — there is something I should tell you, since we keep meeting and you keep not asking why a third-tier observation mage delivers paper reports to a bookshop.

Years ago I signed an incident report that blamed an apprentice for a calibration error.

My error, not hers.

I corrected it.

Signed the correction, carried it to every office that had read the first one.

It cost me a season's standing and gained me a very cold winter of paperwork.

I am not telling you to confess anything.

I am telling you so you know the chart I read from has been rewritten in my own hand, once, at cost.

That is the person holding the candy bag.

choices.text: Then I'll take the fighting one. Tell me if I regret it.
choices.response:
She pays for both bags without argument.

On the bridge she watches you bite through the sugar shell and wince.

'The sourness peaks, then turns,' she says, folding the paper bag closed against the river wind.

'The apprentice in my report sent me a plum from her family's tree the following spring.

I kept the note.

Some corrections come back sweet if you wait out the peak.'

choices.text: (Shake your head at the sour jar and tap the milk candy jar twice instead.)
choices.response:
She laughs — a short, real sound.

'The fourth-hour choice.

Sensible.'

She buys one of each anyway.

On the bridge she hands you a milk candy unwrapped, keeps the sour one for herself, and eats it without flinching.

'The report I told you about — I read it aloud before I signed the correction.

Saying it plainly made it true.

You do that for people just by listening.'

episodes.ending:
You cross the stone bridge with the bags folded shut against the wind.

Below, the river carries the last light.

Meilin asks, without looking away from the water, whether tomorrow's tide reading interests you or bores you — both answers are permitted, she says, and both come with a seat on the observation bench.

The candy is nearly gone by the time the town lamps come on, and neither of you mentions leaving early.

episodes.title: The Ferry and the Gate Tide
episodes.opening:
Rest day.

Meilin takes the small ferry across the river to the market, and you go with her.

The crossing is crowded: an old woman with a vegetable basket, a fisherman dozing against the rail, a straw hat abandoned on a neighboring bench.

Meilin's astrolabe spins slow circles above her palm, and she keeps glancing at it instead of the water.

Something in the tide is off.

She has not said so yet, but her notebook is already open.
episodes.dialogue:
The astrolabe says the gate tide is rising faster than my last calibration assumed.

Not dangerous yet.

But my coordinates above the forest will drift by nightfall, and a drifted coordinate on a major portal is how teams arrive in the wrong province.

Major portals need a full team — I can't hold one alone, and I won't pretend otherwise.

What I can do today is re-anchor my reference points from the far shore, where the sightline is clean.

That takes two hours of standing very still in a market crowd, logging stars in daylight, which looks absurd and feels worse.

Last rest day on this ferry, an old woman boarded with her basket, and a straw hat vanished off that bench — she was sure the fisherman took it.

It had simply blown.

I said mages also wait their turn for the ferry, and she laughed at me.

I think of it whenever the tide makes me impatient.

So: two hours of stillness, then the market.

There's a fruit stall I like — I've had two places picked out in my head since we boarded.

If you'd rather spend the day as a day, and not as an assistant to a woman standing rigid among cabbages, say so now.

The errand is mine.

The market can be ours.

choices.text: Then log your stars. I'll hold your notebook and tell you when you drift.
choices.response:
She hands over the notebook wordlessly and stands among the cabbages, astrolabe humming.

Twice you call her name when her attention slips toward the tide.

Twice she resets.

'Assisted calibration, one observer, one anchor,' she writes afterward.

'Unorthodox.

Effective.'

The tide is logged before dark — not solved, but measured, and she calls that a real victory.

choices.text: (Sit on the ferry rail and simply stay where she can see you, saying nothing.)
choices.response:
You don't volunteer; you just remain in her sightline the whole crossing — and when she steps off onto the far shore to work, you find a bench at the market's edge, squarely in her view, and keep it through both hours.

She works faster, she admits later, because she stopped checking whether you'd left.

'Some support is a fixed point,' she says over fruit at the stall, tired and pleased.

'The tide still rises.

But I know its speed now, and I know where you sit.'

episodes.ending:
The tide is measured, not tamed — she says plainly it will need a full team within the season, and that she has already sent the request.

At the fruit stall she pays for green plums and hands you the first one.

'For the record,' she says, 'I did today's work better because you were there.

That is not a spell.

It is just true, and I log true things.'

The ferry carries you home under the first real stars, her chart finally quiet on her knee.

episodes.title: Model Naming Day
episodes.opening:
The gate observation bench, evening.

Meilin has built something new: a small brass and glass model of the forest sky, star-marked and slowly turning on a pin, sized to sit on two open hands.

Weeks of tides and teamwork went into the recalibration, and tonight the gate is steady.

She sets the model on the bench between you and takes out her three-column notebook, but for once she does not open it.
episodes.dialogue:
This is the corrected sky.

Every star above this forest, re-anchored, the drift removed — my team's work and mine, finished this week.

It needs one more thing before I present it to the Academy, and that thing is a name.

Not for a star.

Stars have names.

For the model itself — the instrument.

Academy instruments carry the name of whoever first reads them aloud.

I could name it myself, but I have decided I don't want to, and I am allowed to decide that.

So I am asking you, here, on the bench, with the gate steady and the evening long.

And because you know me by now, you also know there is a second question under the first, and I will not make you guess it.

I have come to want you in my evenings in a way that has outgrown the word colleague.

If you feel the same, say so tonight, while you name the model, and we will walk forward from there as more than friends — slowly, and with everything still revisable, because that is how I do my best work.

If you don't, name the model anyway, and we will be friends of the kind people write about in old letters and mean it.

Either answer is a good one.

Neither one is a reading I will pretend came from the chart.

The chart is silent on this.

The asking is mine.

choices.text: Call it Meilin's Answer — and my answer is yes.
choices.response:
She goes very still, then laughs once, unguarded.

'Meilin's Answer,' she repeats, as if testing the calibration.

'The Academy will hate the sentiment and approve the precision.'

She writes the name in the known column, and your yes beside it — not in the inferred column, she notes, in the known one.

The model turns between you all evening, and she sits closer than she has ever sat, her shoulder a warm, deliberate inch from yours.

choices.text: (Slide the notebook toward her and write the name 'Northward' in the known column yourself.)
choices.response:
She reads the word upside down and her whole face softens.

'Northward.

The star that helps find north — you remembered.'

She signs beneath it, co-namer, and closes the notebook gently.

'Then we are the kind of friends old letters are about,' she says, no sorrow in it, only certainty.

She splits the last of the milk candy with you, and the model turns on the bench between the two of you, who chose each other plainly.

episodes.ending:
The model turns on the bench between you, named, the gate steady behind it.

It was decided explicitly, by the two of you, with the chart silent and the evening willing.

Meilin packs the instrument last, wrapping it in her star-map shawl like something that matters, and says the walk back is long enough for one more constellation — whichever one you want, at whatever pace you want, for as long as you both keep choosing these evenings.

episodes.title: The Hand-Drawn Sky
episodes.opening:
A season has turned since the naming night.

The gate needed its full team; the team came; the coordinates held.

Northward sits in the Academy's hall now with two names on its plate, and Meilin has a new habit: she teaches.

Tonight the observation bench holds two cups — one filled and one waiting — a freshly drawn chart, her ink pen, and an open ink pad, because she is making you a gift that no instrument can produce — a sky drawn by hand, wrong in places, honest in all of them.
episodes.dialogue:
Don't judge the ink smudge.

Instruments are precise; friends are present, and I was present when a moth attacked my pen.

This chart is yours — every constellation above the forest as I'd draw it for one particular student, which is a different document than the one I'd draw for the Academy.

Sloppier.

Kinder.

It marks the north star first, because you learned that one from me on a bootlace afternoon, and I have decided that is where your sky begins.

Now — the commitment, since we are both people who say things plainly.

I have requested a permanent posting here.

Observation mage of this forest, resident, with a teaching bench and a standing budget for milk candy.

It was approved this morning.

And I want your promise in return, not of romance and not of duty — a standing appointment.

First clear night of each week, this bench, this chart, your questions.

If a night must be missed, it is named and rescheduled, never quietly skipped.

That is the whole treaty.

I have watched people treat my readings as fate they must obey, and I have watched friendships dissolve from politeness, and I want neither.

I want a scheduled, revisable, signed-in-ink friendship with the one person who helped a stranger with a bootlace and never once asked me to be less precise.

Sign here, or amend the terms.

Amendments are encouraged.

I am told good treaties have them.

choices.text: I'll sign — but I'm adding a clause: you teach me to draw one star myself.
choices.response:
You write the new clause in the margin and sign the line beneath it.

She reads the amendment twice and her eyes shine.

'Accepted.

Clause two: one star, drawn by the student, filed in the known column.'

She guides your hand's position with a pointed finger only, no touching, and you draw the north star crooked beside hers.

'Crooked and correct,' she declares, turning the chart to admire your addition.

'The best kind of star.

The best kind of clause.'

choices.text: (Press your thumb to her ink pad, then leave its print on the signature line and look at her until she laughs.)
choices.response:
She laughs exactly as predicted.

'A thumbprint.

Unorthodox, binding, very you.'

She writes 'sealed by thumbprint, witnessed by mage' beneath it and blows on the ink.

'The treaty stands.

First clear night, this bench.'

Then she adds, quieter, 'I have signed reports that changed my life with less ceremony than this.

This one is better.'

episodes.ending:
Meilin stamps her seal beside your mark and sets the chart on the bench to dry.

The chart lies there, signed and sealed between the two of you, and the treaty with it: a standing night each week, missed nights named and rescheduled, a resident mage and you, with your own ink.

Meilin pours the second cup, which has been waiting the whole conversation, and points out the north star as if for the first time — taking her time, exactly as promised, with all the seasons ahead still revisable.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Known Column
romance.opening:
A season has turned since the naming night.

The gate team came and went; the coordinates held; Meilin's Answer stands in the Academy hall with its name spoken aloud by its co-namer.

Tonight Meilin waits at the gate not with instruments but with a folded paper and a paper bag of milk candy, and for the first time since you've known her, her astrolabe hangs still at her hip.

She has something to say and has evidently rehearsed saying it.
romance.dialogue:
I rehearsed this on the walk over.

It did not help.

So: plainly.

The Academy has offered me a senior posting in the capital — better instruments, better tides, a title.

I have asked for a resident posting here instead, and it was approved this morning.

I chose this forest.

I chose it partly for the gate, and partly, mostly, for the evenings at this bench, which have become the fixed point I calibrate everything else against.

You should know that my chart has no column for what we are.

I checked.

There is known, inferred, and safe to defer, and what I feel about you has been promoted out of all three — it is no longer inferred, it is not deferrable, and 'known' was too small a word for it.

I am not asking you to follow me anywhere.

I am asking whether we agree to keep choosing each other, night by night, with full permission to revise — because the best work I have ever done, magical or otherwise, started with a correction I signed in my own hand, and I would rather build us the same way.

Slowly.

Honestly.

Revisable.

If yes, take this — it is a fresh page from my corrected report, separate from my first chart.

The first chart still holds a scorched library-tower loan record with your name on it. I have kept it private. If you want to see it, I will show you; if not, it stays folded.

This page is for a choice we make now.

It is not blank tonight.

choices.text: Then write us in the known column — and I'll sign beside it.
choices.response:
She unfolds the new report page under the gate light: and on it, in her careful hand, a single new column heading — chosen.

She writes both names beneath it and turns the pen toward you.

When you sign, she exhales like someone releasing a held calibration.

'Logged,' she says, unsteady and radiant.

'Known.

Chosen.

Revisable.

Everything I believe in, in one column.'

choices.text: (Fold the page closed gently in her hands and press your palm over it, holding it there.)
choices.response:
She stills under the gate light, then covers your hand with her own — one brief, deliberate touch, the first and only.

'Yes,' she says, understanding without the word.

'That is also an answer.

Perhaps the truer one.'

She keeps the page folded against her heart.

'Then we proceed as we always have — plainly, slowly, one clear night at a time.

I have never been so pleased to leave a variable unsolved.'

romance.ending:
The gate hums steady behind you, and Meilin walks the forest path home beside you, the corrected page kept close against her and the milk candy bag open between you.

She is resident mage of this forest; you are the fixed point she chose.

There will be tides and teams and seasons, and every clear night a bench, and the chart between you stays open — written in her hand, chosen by you both, revisable for as long as you both keep choosing it.

episodes.title: 鞋铺门口的鞋带结
episodes.opening:
傍晚时分，星光森林边缘，老鞋铺旁。

一个孩子坐在台阶上，一只靴子脱了下来，鞋带缠着一根扯下来的荆棘枝打了结，一群邻居围拢过来，看一位法师干活。

她站在那里，身旁悬浮着一具星盘，一张图表用四块河石压着，靛蓝色的长袍上沾满旅途的尘土。

一件银饰映着最后的天光。

你走近时她抬起头，对你这个陌生人闯入这场小小的本地危机似乎毫不意外。
episodes.dialogue:
梅琳·星落，星文学院三阶观测法师——我负责记录门潮汐并校准传送坐标。

不过今天做的是件更不起眼的小事。

这孩子的鞋带在两条街外缠上了一根荆棘，这个结随后被三位大人和一只非常自信的狗判定为无解。

我提出用一个小型解缚咒。

他问那咒语会不会把靴子吃掉。

我说不会。

他说他宁愿等你，因为你看起来像个会把结解得规规矩矩的人。

于是我们俩都在这儿了，被一个孩子否决了。

这张图表是之后要用的——我在校准森林上方的一个坐标，想着不妨在有见证人的地方做。

一个法师独自跪在水沟里，容易让人惊慌。

一个法师跪在水沟里，旁边还有家鞋铺，那顶多算有点怪。

你愿意接手这根鞋带吗？

我来扶稳靴子。

我能移动小物件，但解结靠的是耐心，不是力气，而今天下午，耐心归你管。

choices.text: 扶稳了。这个结得靠劝，不能硬拽。
choices.response:
她一言不发地扶稳靴子，看着你的手指动作。

“有意思，”她说。

“你是在跟结本身说话。

大多数人只顾着跟鞋带较劲。”

荆棘终于滑脱时，男孩欢呼起来，她在她的三栏笔记本上记了一笔。

“已知栏：结没了。

推断栏：你很有用。

可暂缓栏：其余一切。”

choices.text: （在男孩身边坐下，自己扶稳靴子，一言不发。）
choices.response:
你从她手里接过靴子，夹在两膝之间固定住。

她挑了挑眉，随即蹲到你身边，用两根手指和一点微光把荆棘挑了出来。

“分工合作，”她赞许地说。

“我负责魔法，你负责维护场面的体面。”

男孩穿回靴子，问题早被抛到脑后。

episodes.ending:
男孩跑去告诉所有人，法师被一根鞋带打败了。

梅琳把图表理直，然后迟疑了一下。

“书店老板让我今天送一份修订过的报告，我送到了，然后发现自己再没有别的差事了，”她说。

“接下来几周，我都会在这片森林上空做校准。

如果你黄昏时路过那道门，我可以指给你看哪颗星能帮你找到北方。

就一颗星。

不必一口气把整张图表都背下来。”

她收起河石，不慌不忙地等着，看你怎么决定。

episodes.title: 酸与甜的考验
episodes.opening:
城门口的黄昏会面，不知不觉成了习惯。

今天梅琳要进城办件差事，便直截了当地问你，愿不愿意同行。

集市街上的糖果铺里飘着焦糖和柠檬皮的气味。

她站在糖罐前，像学者面对一部陌生的典籍，披肩搭在一条手臂上，店主已经伸手去拿纸袋了。

回去的路上有一座石桥等着，而黄昏并不着急。
episodes.dialogue:
店主说，这是他店里最酸的一种糖。

腌制的青果，盐渍的梅子心，还有一层会还手的糖壳。

我告诉他我喜欢这种。

他点点头，问我要不要两袋。
