The caravan has stopped two nights at the coastal town, and tonight is yours. Valeria found you after supper and said only, "Come on, the light's going, and I want the good seat."
Now you sit beside her on the stone embankment where the whole sea opens past the last row of rooftops. The wind has cooled since sunset, and the small boats are coming back in, one by one.
She has her sketchbook out, but she isn't drawing the harbor. Her pencil moves in small strokes near the bottom of the page, something with a straight edge and a little curve of light beneath it.
"Not the boats tonight," she says, catching your look. "Something else. Give me a minute and you'll see it."
A gull settles on a bollard nearby, decides you two are boring, and leaves. The masts knock softly against each other in the harbor. Valeria keeps drawing.
episodes.dialogue:
She turns the page toward you at last. It's a door. A plain door, drawn from memory, with a lamp hanging beside it and a warm yellow glow shaded under it, spilling onto the step.
"Some door I passed on a survey," she says. "I never learned whose. I just liked that somebody left the lamp burning before dark, for whoever came home."
She holds the page steady against the wind. "I keep it so I can see a lit doorway even out in the mist."
A small boat slides behind a larger ship, mast gone, and she lifts her chin without seeming to notice she's doing it, waiting for it to reappear. It does. She smiles and looks back at you.
"You know what's strange? Lately, when I draw, I keep adding things below the door." She tilts the page. Small flowers, a little crooked, by the step. "I caught myself thinking I might want a place like that someday. A door of my own. Flowers by it."
She says it lightly, the way she says most things, but she doesn't turn it into a joke this time.
"Don't look at me like I'm quitting the road," she adds, laughing a little. "I still like it. I like the forks and the inns and the beans with radish. But a scout is allowed to know which door she'd walk toward, I think."
She closes the sketchbook partway, keeping the door lamp visible in the gap, and looks out at the water. "Your turn. What does yours look like? Your idea of home. I'm not guessing, and I'm not filling in the blank for you."
She waits, patient as she is at a fork, three breaths and then as many more as you need.

choices.text: A lit window somewhere, and someone who keeps my pace.
choices.response: Valeria is quiet for a moment, then nods slowly, like you've marked a fork she can read. "A lit window and someone who keeps my pace," she repeats. "That's a good route. Not the fastest one, but the one you'd actually take." She taps the sketchbook against her knee. "For what it's worth, that's the kind of door I drew. The lamp's lit because somebody's expected. Not because the house is showing off." She glances at you sideways, and something warm and unguarded passes over her face before she grins. "If you ever find that window, save me a seat near it. I'll bring the radish."

choices.text: (Say nothing yet; just lean a little closer and look at the sketch again.)
choices.response: You don't answer right away. You lean in and look at the door lamp again, the crooked flowers, the small pool of yellow light on the step. Valeria notices and doesn't rush you. "Take your time," she says. "I asked because I wanted to know, not because I need it tonight." She rests the open sketchbook on her knee between you, angled so you can both see it. The boats keep coming in. After a while she says, softly, "Whenever you're ready. Or not tonight at all. The door isn't going anywhere, and neither, tonight, am I."

episodes.ending:
The last small boat comes in while the sky is still holding a little color, and Valeria marks it with a satisfied nod, like a route checked off. She closes the sketchbook and tucks it into her cloak.
"Inn before it gets cold," she says, standing and brushing off her cloak. "The innkeeper will have the beans on, and I intend to add radish to mine and defend that choice if anyone laughs."
She pauses at the top of the embankment and looks back once at the harbor, the lamps coming on along the waterfront one by one. "See? Doors everywhere, once you start looking."
Walking back through the last row of rooftops, she matches your pace without being asked. At the inn door she holds it open, warm light falling out onto the stones, and says, "One more story tonight before I go up. I never hurry that part." Inside, the table is warm, and tomorrow the road is still there, waiting, with a way back.

episodes.title: A Way Back
episodes.opening:
The harvest festival in the river town smells of roasted chestnuts and spilled cider. Lanterns hang between the stalls, and past the well a fiddler is tuning up, drawing one long note that makes a few dancers shuffle their feet early.

You find Valeria by the sidelines, where she said she would be. She has a small plate of grapes in one hand, and her new soft-soled boots are pointed toward the lantern light instead of the road. Her shortbow leans against a barrel behind her, within reach even here. Old habits.

She sees you and lifts the plate a little, offering. "Good timing. I was two grapes away from walking into the circle by myself and getting the steps wrong in front of everyone." Her grin is easy, but she shifts over on the low wall to make room, which is her way of saying sit, stay.

The fiddler starts a quick tune. The circle forms without either of you, turning and trading partners, and Valeria watches it the way she watches a fork in the road, counting the turns. Then she sets the plate down between you and doesn't reach for it again.

"Before we get swept up," she says, "I want to say a thing plainly. I'm out of practice at it, so give me a breath."
episodes.dialogue:
She waits three breaths. You count them with her, because you know the habit now.

"The next survey is a long one. Northeast forks, the ruined tower with the collapsed stair. Ten days, maybe twelve." She turns the plate a half-turn without looking at it. "When I come back, I'll find you at the inn, and we'll eat beans, and it'll be good. It's always good. But it's always after the work. Every time we've had, it's come after something. A path I marked, or a caravan that made it through."

She finally looks at you. Her voice stays light out of habit, but she doesn't let a joke land this time. "I want time with you that isn't a reward for surviving something. That's the plain version. I've been circling it for a month like a fork I haven't checked yet."

The dancers shout at a turn gone wrong and laugh it off. A lantern swings overhead and her face goes warm gold, then shadow, then gold again.

"So here are the paths," she says, holding up two fingers like she's laying out a map. "One. After this survey comes back safe, you and I try a proper day together. Not a festival, not a rest stop between legs of a caravan. Whatever that looks like, I'd like to find out." She folds one finger down. "Two. We keep exactly what we have. Close friends, by choice. That is not the lesser path, and I want to be clear about that. I've walked beside you on real roads. That doesn't change either way."

She lowers her hand to her knee. "Neither answer changes which routes I scout or whether I watch your pace on a climb. You're my companion on the road no matter what. This is only about the evenings." A small breath, almost a laugh. "I've offered options to caravan masters with less nerves than this. Say whichever one is true. I'll wait three more breaths if you need them. I've got grapes and nowhere to be until the tune ends."

choices.text: A date. After the survey. I'll be at the inn when you come back.
choices.response:
Valeria's shoulders drop half an inch, like she's set down a pack she'd forgotten she was carrying. "All right," she says, and then again, softer, like the word needs a second try to stick. "All right. A date."

She picks up the plate, takes a grape, and eats it with ceremony, which is how you know she's covering something. "Northeast forks first. I'll mark the way back on every one of them, so I can stop worrying on the road and start looking forward instead. That's a first, mind you. Usually I look forward on accident."

The fiddler tightens the tempo and the circle speeds up. Valeria stands, wipes her hands on her cloak, and holds one out to you. "The survey's ten days. This dance is three minutes. Let's not waste the ratio." Her hand is steady. So is her smile, mostly, except at the edges.

choices.text: (Shake your head and say, "Friends. Keep what we have.")
choices.response:
Valeria nods before you even finish, quick and sure, the way she confirms a route is safe. "Friends. Done." No pause, no wounded look. The matter is settled like a fork marked.

"I'm glad you said it straight," she adds, sitting back down beside you. "Half the trouble on the road is people guessing instead of saying." She nudges the plate toward you. "And for the record, you don't owe me a softened version. Friends by choice is a route I'd pick anyway."

The tune changes to something quicker. She stands and offers her hand for the dance exactly as she would have either way. "Come on. Fill out the set with me. And when I'm back from the northeast forks, you're telling me a story I haven't heard. That's the toll for making me wait three breaths."

episodes.ending:
However you answered, the circle takes you both. The turns change fast enough that Valeria ends up at the front sooner than she expects, and she glances back once to confirm the next move, then raises her hand on the beat. Near the musicians she tosses her chin at the fiddler, and he grins and tightens the tempo for her, same as some festival years ago.

Afterward, you both wind up at the low wall again, breathing hard, the plate of grapes long since emptied by strangers. Valeria ties her cloak looser and looks toward the road out of town, the one she'll take northeast in two days. "I'll leave buttons at every fork," she says. "Three by the roots, like always. So when you're ready to come toward me, the way's already marked."

The lanterns burn lower. She stays for one more story from the cider stall keeper before going up, because she never hurries that last part.

The survey comes next. After it, whichever path you chose together is waiting, already walked partway by her.

episodes.title: One More Story
episodes.opening:
The last fork of the survey is marked by late afternoon, and the mist thins as you and Valeria walk back toward the inn.
She checks the three silver buttons she left there that morning, nods once, and brushes a wet leaf off the root beside them.
"Still true," she says. "Way back confirmed. Twice in one day. That's a good day."
Her boots are muddy to the ankle and her shortbow hangs loose on her back, unused. The whole route kept its promises.
When the inn's lamplight shows through the last row of trees, she slows to match your pace instead of going ahead, the way she always does.
episodes.dialogue:
Inside, the innkeeper looks up from the long table and doesn't ask what you want. "Beans are on. You'll want the radish, Valeria."
"You know me too well," Valeria says, pulling out a chair for you first.
She adds the pickled radish to her own bowl last, then pushes the jar toward you in case you want some.
The side hall is half full. A guest near the stove is telling a story about a cart axle that snapped on a perfectly good road, and Valeria leans her chin on her hand to listen.
"We finished early," she says to you between bites. "No strange rustles worth three breaths. One goose, though. Near the second tower. Probably the same goose."
She laughs quietly at that. "I marked the home fork for the whole caravan this time. Three buttons at the last fork, chalk on the tower stone. Even the newcomers can read it."
She looks at her bowl for a moment.
"I used to think marking a way home was the smaller part of the work. The bold part was the survey, the mist, the towers. But this is the job. Everyone walks back in. That's the whole score."
When the guest's story winds down, she stays seated instead of heading upstairs and nods at you.
"One more story," she says. "I never hurry this part. Sit back down, or stay standing if your legs prefer it. Either way, we're not done at this table yet."
The guest starts a new one, about a ferryman who charged by rumor instead of by distance, and Valeria snorts into her beans.

choices.text: You've earned that easy evening. The whole caravan walked home because of you.
choices.response:
Valeria points her spoon at you, but her eyes are warm.
"Careful. Say things like that and I'll start believing the road likes me back."
She nudges the radish jar closer to you, the way she does when she's pleased and doesn't want to make a speech about it.
"The buttons did the work. I just put them where they'd be found," she says. "But thank you. Truly. I'll take that over a medal."
Then she settles back to catch the end of the ferryman story, keeping her chair beside yours.

choices.text: (Stay in your chair and listen to the story beside her without saying anything.)
choices.response:
You stay where you are, and Valeria notices. She doesn't comment on it, but her shoulders come down an inch.
She tips her bowl toward you in a small toast, beans and all.
"This," she says quietly, under the guest's voice, "is the good part. The road gives you forks. The inn gives you this."
The ferryman story gets to its ridiculous ending and she laughs with everyone else, easy and unguarded.
When the laughter dies, she glances at you. "Same table next survey? I'll set out the extra bowl myself."

episodes.ending:
The stories run out not because anyone decided, but because the stove burns low and the innkeeper starts stacking bowls with pointed patience.
Valeria carries hers to the kitchen, wipes your spot on the long table, and stands at the foot of the stairs with her pack on one shoulder.
"Tomorrow the caravan takes the safe line," she says. "Buttons at every fork, chalk on the tower. Everyone walks home. That's the ending I like."
She smiles at you, plain and sure.
"And this," she adds, tapping the stair rail once, "the road and the table both. Some people think you have to pick the grand one. I don't. A friend who keeps my pace and stays for one more story — that's the whole prize."
She takes the first step up, then pauses.
"Goodnight. See you at the fork before dawn. Three buttons — you know the way."

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Slow Dance
romance.opening:
The survey is finished. The last fork is marked, the ruined tower checked, and the Moon Gate wagons are safely on the better line. By the time you and Valeria walk up to the inn, the lamps are already lit along the road.

Inside, the long table smells of stewed beans. Valeria orders two bowls and asks the innkeeper, without needing to say it twice, for pickled radish added at the end. She carries one bowl to you and sets it down.

"Full circle," she says. "Survey done, bowl warm, and you still here. I count that as the route paying out."

In the side hall, someone has dragged the tables back for a small circle dance. The fiddler is tuning, quick enough that half the room looks up. Valeria eats her beans slowly, watching the dancers with a sideways glance she does not bother to hide.
romance.dialogue:
She sets her spoon down when the bowl is empty and turns her chair toward you.

"So. Before the music gets ahead of me." Her voice stays light, but she says the next part plainly. "We agreed we'd ask each other things straight. So here's mine. After this survey, after everything, do you still want to date me? Not as a waypoint between my routes. As a thing we keep."

She waits. She has a scout's patience and she uses all of it on you.

"You should know what you're saying yes to," she adds. "I'll still be gone sometimes. Forks, towers, misty mornings. I won't promise to stop scouting, and I won't pretend I want to. But I'll always leave you the way back. Buttons at the forks, a letter at the inn, and my boots pointed home. That's the shape of it."

The fiddle starts up behind her. She doesn't turn around.

choices.text: Yes. I still want to date you. Distant roads and all.
choices.response:
"Good," she says, and the word comes out faster than she meant it, which makes her laugh at herself. "Good. Then you already know the terms."

She stands, wipes her hands on her cloak, and holds one out to you. On the floor, the circle is still loose enough to join. She takes your hand without fuss, fits the simple steps, and when the lead comes to her she glances back to confirm the next turn with you before raising her hand.

She does not toss her chin at the fiddler to quicken the tempo. She keeps it exactly where it is.

choices.text: (Take her hand and say, "Yes. I still want to date you.")
choices.response:
She looks at your hand around hers, then up at you, and something in her shoulders lets go.

"I'm glad you said it," she says quietly. "I wanted to ask, not guess."

She closes her fingers around yours, stands, and walks you toward the circle. She doesn't announce it to the room. She just steps in at the edge, sets the pace, and keeps checking that your feet are under you as much as the path ahead.

romance.ending:
The tune winds down and neither of you moves to the next one. Valeria steers you to the low wall by the window instead, and you sit with the last of the tea.

"One evening isn't enough to get sloppy at this," she says. "So let's call it one date, properly planned. Next time I'm in town after a survey. Nothing ambitious. Warm bowl, lamplight, maybe I finally show you the embankment where the sea unfolds after the rooftops."

She taps the table once, sealing it.

"I'll mark the forks for everyone on the road, and send word to the inn before I return. When I'm back, I'd like another evening with you, if you're free." She glances at the dancers, then back at you, and her smile is the unhurried one. "Same time next survey. Don't let anyone rearrange the chairs before we get back."

episodes.title: 三枚银纽扣
episodes.opening:
进暮林一个小时后，雾气低垂的岔路口到了。小路绕着一丛老树根分成两股，瓦莱莉娅先蹲下来，双脚稳稳踩开，拂开最大那条树根底下的湿叶。三枚小小的银纽扣排成一列，半埋在土里。
“喏。”她的指尖在纽扣上方的空气里点了点，没有碰到。“树根旁三枚，左岔路的退路，今天早上做的记号。哪天一条路没有退路了，那才值得担心。”
她站起身，从腰间袋子里摸出一枚纽扣递给你，还带着贴着她胯侧焐出的温度。“拿着。不是纪念品，是工具。我们要是走散了，你就去找它的兄弟们。”
商队的货车还落在弯道后面，看不见。右岔路向上爬，通向一座废塔，塔影在灰天下歪斜地立着；左岔路往下低走，沿着一条听得见却看不见的水流。
就在这时，右岔路的灌木丛里传来一阵窸窣。瓦莱莉娅抬起的手停在半空。她没有去摸弓，只是盯着灌木，数着。
一息。两息。三息。
“是鹿，”她轻声说，“穿过去了，没停留。不过你看见我怎么做的了吗？我没猜。我等了。”
episodes.dialogue:
她转向你，有那么一会儿，脸上惯常的轻松被放了下来，像到营地卸下的行囊。
“我直说了，到了这一步，开玩笑是会害死人的。右岔路快，但又窄又高，废塔挡住弯道的视线。要是上面有东西等着，我们就丢了退路。左岔路长、也湿，但它有两个出口，水声还能盖住我们离开大路的动静。”
她等着，看的是你的脸，不是树丛。“我不是要你信任我。我是问，你自己看出来了吗？你跟我走过足够多的岔路口了。”
当你看向左岔路，她缓缓点头。“好。我要的就是这个——不是附和，是眼睛。”
她朝来路竖起两根手指，商队的手势：左岔路、走远路。身后某处，一辆货车吱呀一声，消息传了回去。
然后她就在岔路口一块平整的石头上坐下，掏出一条苹果干。“我们在这儿等他们。说实话，这是暮林里最好的位置——背靠树根，两条路都看得见。”
她嚼了一会儿，短促又轻声地笑自己。
“你知道好笑的是什么吗？我刚才把话说得那么轻巧。一句大概是鹿，已经走了好像没什么大不了。”她用手指翻着那条苹果干。“可那三息里，我的心一直跳得飞快。每次都是。我只是学会了不让它爬到脸上——一个害怕的斥候，会带出一支害怕的商队。但跟你在一起，我宁愿让你知道那是真的。”
她看向你。“还有，你不是我在押送的货物。这句话我要说出口。你是跟我一起读岔路的人。两双眼睛，比一个好斥候加一个站在她身后的人，值钱得多。”

choices.text: 那下一个岔路口，我跟你一起数那三息。
choices.response:
瓦莱莉娅的眉毛扬了起来，然后她笑了——不是打趣的那种，是更小、更真的一种。
“数出声？你知道吧，两个人数，比一个人数要慢。”她拍了拍身边那块平整的石头。“可这也意味着，那三息里，谁都不是一个人。成交。下个岔路口，你起头，我收尾。还有，要是我们对听到的声音有分歧，不管怎样都走更安全的路。这是规矩。”

choices.text: （在她身旁的石头上坐下，分吃那条苹果干。）
choices.response:
你坐下来。她不用你开口，就把苹果干掰成两半，把大的那半递给你。
“同伴的份。”她说，“斥候的特权，是挑石头。”
她靠回树根上，肩膀几乎碰到你的，看着雾气在左岔路间流动。“这是斥候训练里不会教的部分——等待。你以为等待不算什么，可做得对的话，等待就是全部的工作。”

episodes.ending:
第一辆货车绕过弯道时，你们还坐着。车夫喊话说，左岔路看着像绕远的路。
“它就是绕远。”瓦莱莉娅站起身，掸了掸披风，回喊道，“但它也是回家的路。”
你还没来得及把银纽扣还她，她已把它按回你的掌心。“留着。你会比我先用上——我自己每一枚在哪儿，我都知道。”
商队驶入左岔路，车轮在湿石上沙沙作响。瓦莱莉娅走在前面，跟着货车的速度，而不是她自己的。走到一半，她回头看了你一眼，本只是想确认你的脚下，却发现你早已跟了上来。
“两双眼睛。”她说，多半是说给自己听的，然后又面向前方。前方，道路弯向水边，雾气之后的某处，会有一家亮着灯的旅店、一碗热食，和上楼之前再听的一个故事。

episodes.title: 入夜后的旅店
episodes.opening:
旅店里飘着柴火和灯油的气味，炉火旁的长桌还留着白天的余温。桌上放着一张废纸和一截炭条。瓦莱莉娅·诺克斯坐在你对面，面前一碗炖豆子，她把最后一点腌萝卜撕成小块，最后才拌进去——完全按她喜欢的顺序。
“顺序很重要。”她用勺子在碗沿敲了两下。“萝卜要最后放，不然就煮软了，忘了自己是什么。”
今晚大堂半满。一支商队挤在火边烘斗篷，一个行李被泥浆硬结的独行旅人坐得不远，听得见这边的谈话。从瓦莱莉娅进门起，他就一直在看她——看她怎么跟老板说笑，看她肩膀那副轻松的姿态。
你认得那种眼神。那是认定了她的从容意味着外面的路一定不值一提的人的眼神。
episodes.dialogue:
旅人放下杯子。“你就是今天走过东边岔路的那位斥候？我的队伍明天走那条路。你一路笑着讲一只鹅就过来了。”
“鹅是真的，”瓦莱莉娅说，“脚印特别大，叶子上都是湿的。我判断是有小型野兽经过，正盘算几个选项，那家伙就从树后面摇摇摆摆走出来了。”
“原来如此。斥候对着鹅傻笑，还管这叫工作。”他耸耸肩，说不上刻薄，只是笃定。“还好路都不难走。”
瓦莱莉娅放下勺子。她没有提高嗓门，也没有停止微笑，但你见过这种沉静——就在某个岔路口，她等了三次呼吸的时间，才开口给选项。
“危险是真的，”她平静地说，“所以我才在事后说笑，不是在事中。那条岔路上每个出口我都查过了。明天你的队伍要是走错了线，树根旁的三颗银纽扣标出了退路。读纽扣本该只有同伴学过——不过今晚我可以免费讲给你听。”她重新拿起勺子。“要豆子吗？萝卜要最后放。”

choices.text: 今天有动静响起来的时候，她等了三次呼吸的时间。我亲眼看见的。这就是这份工作。
choices.response:
旅人看看你，又看看瓦莱莉娅，那份笃定松动了些。“三次呼吸。”他低声重复了一遍。
瓦莱莉娅用勺子指了指你，一脸得意。“看吧？有证人。我的名声又能多撑一天了。”但在桌子底下，她的靴尖轻轻碰了一下你的脚——无声的道谢。

choices.text: （把那张废纸和炭条推到她面前）
choices.response:
瓦莱莉娅低头看了看纸，又抬起头，笑容变了形状——少了些打趣，多了些认真。“哦？”她说，“有人会看场合嘛。”
她把纸在桌面上铺平，旅人不自觉地凑了过来。一个斥候要动笔画的东西，他忽然很想看。

episodes.ending:
瓦莱莉娅把纸转向你们两人，开始画——还不是画路。“先画退路。”她说，“一条只奖励莽撞的路线，画得差。”她勾出岔路，然后是沿着长苔石头延伸的撤退线，再在树根处点了三个小圈。“纽扣放这儿。你见到自然就认得了。”
旅人把椅子拉近，问他的队伍该走哪条线。她一板一眼地告诉了他。等他早早回房去仔细收拾行李后，她把草图推到你面前。“你来添一笔，加在任何你会想要第二个出口的地方。别人的眼睛，总能看见被我抹平的东西。”
后来炉火烧得低了，她端着碗送去厨房，回来又坐下——上楼之前再听一个故事，从不匆忙。她轻敲你们一起画的那张草图。“明天车队出发前，我们先把这条路走一遍。你，我，还有那条退路。”

episodes.title: 门边的灯
episodes.opening:
商队在滨海小镇已经停了两个晚上，今晚是属于你们的时间。晚饭后，瓦莱莉娅·诺克斯找到你，只说了一句：“走吧，天快黑了，我要占个好位置。”
现在你们并肩坐在石砌堤岸上，越过最后一排屋顶，整片大海在眼前铺开。日落之后风凉了下来，正如补网人当初说的那样，小船一艘接一艘地往回港里去。
她掏出速写本，画的却不是港口。铅笔在页面下方细细移动，画的是一个边缘笔直、底下带着一小弯光晕的东西。
“今晚不画船，”她察觉到你的目光，“画点别的。等一分钟，你就明白了。”
一只海鸥落在附近的系船柱上，觉得你们两个太无趣，很快飞走了。港里桅杆轻轻碰响。瓦莱莉娅继续画着。
episodes.dialogue:
她终于把本子转向你。那是一扇门。一扇凭记忆画下的朴素门，门边挂着一盏灯，灯下晕出一小片暖黄，落在台阶上。
“很久以前画的，”她说，“某次勘路时路过的一扇门，到今天也没弄清是谁家的。我只是喜欢那种感觉——有人赶在天黑前把灯点上，等着回家的人。”
她顶着风把画页扶稳。“我留着它，这样在雾里赶路时，也能记得一扇亮着灯的门是什么样子。”
一艘小船滑到一艘大船后面，桅杆不见了。她不自觉地抬起下巴等着它重新出现，连自己都没察觉。它出现了。她笑了笑，回头看你。
“你知道奇怪的地方在哪吗？最近画画的时候，我总在门下面添东西。”她把画页倾斜过来。台阶旁有几朵小小的花，画得有点歪。“我发现自己会想，说不定哪天，我也想要这么一个地方。一扇自己的门，门边有花。”
她说得很轻，像说大多数事那样，但这次她没有把它变成玩笑，就让这句话坦坦荡荡地留在你们之间。
“别用那种眼神看我，好像我要退出这条路似的，”她笑着补了一句，“我还喜欢这条路。喜欢岔路口、旅店，还有加腌萝卜的炖豆子。不过我想，斥候也有权知道自己愿意朝哪扇门走去。就是这样而已。”
她把速写本合上一半，让那盏门灯还留在缝隙里，然后望向水面。“该你了。你的那扇门是什么样子？你心目中的家。我不猜，也不替你填空。我想听你亲口说出来。”
她等着，像她在岔路口那样耐心——先等三口呼吸，然后你需要多久，她就等多久。

choices.text: 某处一扇亮着灯的窗，还有一个愿意跟上我脚步的人。
choices.response: 瓦莱莉娅安静了片刻，缓缓点头，像你刚标出一条她能读懂的岔路。“一扇亮着灯的窗，一个跟上我脚步的人，”她重复道，“好路线。不是最快的，但是你真正会走的那条。”她用速写本轻敲膝盖。“不瞒你说，我画的就是那种门。灯亮着，是因为有人在等，不是为了给房子撑场面。”她斜眼看了你一下，那一眼里有某种温暖而不设防的东西，随后咧嘴一笑。“哪天你真找到那扇窗，给我留个旁边的座位。萝卜我带。”

choices.text: （先什么都不说，只是稍稍靠近一点，再看一眼那幅速写。）
choices.response: 你没有立刻回答。你凑近了些，再看那盏门灯，那些歪歪扭扭的花，还有落在台阶上的那一小片黄光。瓦莱莉娅注意到了，却没有催你。“慢慢来，”她说，“我问是因为想知道，不是今晚非知道不可。”她把摊开的速写本搁在膝上，放在你们两人之间，斜着让你们都看得见。船一艘接一艘地进港。过了一会儿，她轻声说：“等你准备好了再说。今晚不说也行。那扇门哪儿也不会去，今晚，我也是。”

episodes.ending:
最后一艘小船进港时，天边还留着一抹颜色。瓦莱莉娅满意地点了点头，像核对完一条路线。她合上速写本，收进短披风里。
“趁天没冷透，回旅店吧，”她站起身，拍了拍披风，“店主该把豆子炖上了，我打算往自己那份里加萝卜，谁笑话我就跟谁理论到底。”
她在堤岸顶端停了一下，回头望了一眼港口，滨水的灯一盏接一盏地亮了起来。“看吧？一旦开始留意，到处都是门。”
穿过最后一排屋顶往回走时，不用谁开口，她就配合着你的脚步。到了旅店门口，她替你拉开门，暖光洒在石阶上。“今晚在上楼之前，再听一个故事。这一环我从来不赶。”屋里，桌子是暖的，而明天，路还在那里等着，带着一条回得去的路。

episodes.title: 一条回来的路
episodes.opening:
河畔小镇的丰收祭飘着烤栗子和苹果酒的气味。灯笼挂在摊位之间，水井那头，一位拉小提琴的乐手正在调音，拉出一个长长的音符，惹得几个舞者笑着提前踏起了步子。

你在场边找到了瓦莱莉娅·诺克斯，正是她说会等的地方。她一手端着一小盘葡萄，新软底靴的靴尖朝着灯笼的光，而不是朝着大路。短弓靠在身后的木桶上，就算在这里也伸手可及。老习惯。

她看见你，把盘子微微抬了抬。“来得正好。再差两颗葡萄，我就要自己走进舞圈，当着所有人的面跳错步子了。”她笑得轻松，却在矮墙上挪了挪，给你腾出位置——这是她在说：坐下，留下。

乐手奏起一支轻快的曲子。舞圈在你们两人之外自动成形，旋转着、交换着舞伴。瓦莱莉娅看着它，就像她看路上的岔口一样，数着每一次转身。然后她把盘子放在你们中间，不再伸手去拿。

“趁我们还没被卷进去，”她说，“我想把一件事说清楚。我很久没练习把话说直了，所以容我喘口气。”
episodes.dialogue:
她等了三口呼吸。你陪她一起数，因为你已经熟悉这个习惯了。

“下一次勘测路途很长。东北边的岔路群，还有那座楼梯塌了的废塔。十天，也许十二天。”她看也不看地把盘子转了半圈。“等我回来，我会在客栈找你，我们一起吃炖豆子，那会很好。一直都很好。但总是在活儿干完之后。我们拥有的每一次，都是某件事之后才来的。我标好了一条路，或者我完好无损地回来了，或者商队顺利通过了。”

她终于看向你。出于习惯，她的声音依然轻快，但这一次她没让玩笑落地。“我想要一段和你在一起的时间，不是作为从什么险境里活下来的奖赏。这就是直白的说法。这一个月我一直在绕着它打转，像绕着一个还没查探过的岔口。”

舞者们在一个转错的节拍上喊了一声，又笑着混了过去。一盏灯笼在头顶摇晃，她的脸被照成温暖的金色，又暗下去，又亮起来。

“所以，路是这样的，”她竖起两根手指，像在摊开一张地图。“一。等这次勘测平安回来，你和我试着过正经的一天。不是节日，不是商队两段路程之间的歇脚。好好过一天。怎么过才让你开心，我想听听。”她弯下一根手指。“二。我们保持现在的一切。亲近的朋友，彼此选择，不重新谈判。这不是次一等的路，这一点我要说清楚。我曾在真正的路上与你并肩走过。无论选哪个，这一点都不会变。”

她把手放回膝上。“无论哪个答案，都不会改变我勘测哪些路线，也不会改变我是否在攀爬时留意你的速度。无论如何，你都是路上的同伴。这只关乎那些夜晚。”她轻轻吐了口气，几乎像笑。“我给商队主报选项的时候，都没这么紧张。说哪个是真的就说哪个。需要的话，我可以再等三口呼吸。我有葡萄，曲子结束之前哪儿也不用去。”

choices.text: 一次约会。勘测之后。你回来时，我会在客栈等你。
choices.response:
瓦莱莉娅的肩膀垂下了半寸，像卸下了一副她自己都忘了背着的行囊。“好，”她说，然后又轻声重复了一遍，仿佛这个词需要再试一次才能站稳。“好。一次约会。”

她重新拿起盘子，捏起一颗葡萄，郑重其事地吃了下去——你由此知道她在掩饰什么。“先去东北边的岔路。我会在每一个岔口都标好回来的路，这样在路上我就能不再担心，而是开始期待。这可是头一遭，提醒你。平时我都是碰巧才期待起来的。”

乐手加快了节奏，舞圈转得更快了。瓦莱莉娅站起身，在披风上擦了擦手，向你伸出一只手。“勘测是十天。这支舞是三分钟。别浪费这支舞。”她的手很稳。她的微笑也是，除了边缘处微微发颤。

choices.text: （摇摇头，说：“做朋友。保持现在这样。”）
choices.response:
你话还没说完，瓦莱莉娅就点了头，干脆而笃定，就像她确认一条路线安全时那样。“朋友。就这么定了。”没有停顿，没有受伤的神情，事情像一条标好的岔路一样尘埃落定。

“我很高兴你说得这么直白，”她在你身边重新坐下。“路上一半的麻烦，都出在人们靠猜而不靠说。”她把盘子朝你推了推。“而且说清楚，你不欠我一个委婉的版本。彼此选择的朋友，本来也是我自己会选的路。”

曲子换成了更轻快的一段。她站起身，向你伸出手邀舞，像是无论你选哪条路，她都会这样做。“来吧。陪我跳完这一轮。等我从东北边的岔路回来，你要给我讲一个我没听过的故事。这是你让我等了三口呼吸的过路费。”

episodes.ending:
乐手换了支快曲子。瓦莱莉娅拉着你走进舞圈。转身越来越快，瓦莱莉娅不知不觉就转到了舞圈前排，她回头看了你一眼确认下一步，然后合着节拍抬起了手。靠近乐手的地方，她朝拉琴的乐手扬了扬下巴，他咧嘴一笑，为她加快了节奏，和多年前某个丰收祭上一样。

之后，你们两人又回到了矮墙边，喘着粗气，那盘葡萄早已被陌生人吃光了。瓦莱莉娅把披风系得松了些，望向出镇的那条路，两天后她就要从那里往东北去。“我会在每一个岔口留下纽扣，”她说。“树根旁三颗，一如既往。所以等你准备好朝我走来的时候，路已经标好了。”

灯笼的光渐渐暗下去。她在上楼之前，又留下来听卖苹果酒的摊主讲了一个故事，因为最后这一段她从不赶时间。

接下来是勘测。勘测之后，你们一起选的那条路正在等着，已经被她先走过了一段。

episodes.title: 再讲一个故事
episodes.opening:
勘测的最后一个岔路口在傍晚前标记完毕，暮色林边缘的雾气渐渐散去，你和瓦莱莉娅·诺克斯一同往旅店走。
她查看了早上留在树根旁的三颗银扣，点点头，拂掉上面的一片湿叶。
“依然有效，”她说，“归路确认无误。一天之内确认两次，连对我来说，这也算好日子了。”
她的靴子沾满没过脚踝的泥，短弓松松挂在背后，一次都没用过。整条路线守住了承诺。
旅店的灯光透过最后一排树影显现出来时，她放慢脚步，与你的步子合在了一起，而不是像往常那样先走一步。
episodes.dialogue:
店内，店主从长桌边抬起头，不用你开口。“豆子炖好了。你要加腌萝卜的，瓦莱莉娅。”
“你太了解我了。”瓦莱莉娅说着，先为你拉开一把椅子。
她最后才往自己碗里加腌萝卜，然后把罐子推到你面前，万一你也想加。
侧厅坐了一半的客人。炉火旁有人正讲一个故事：一条好好的路上，车轴断了。瓦莱莉娅手托着下巴听。
“我们收工早，”她一边吃一边对你说，“没有值得等三口气的怪声。不过第二座塔附近有一只鹅。多半还是那只。”
她低声笑了。“这次我为整支商队都标好了返程岔口。最后一个岔路口放了三颗银扣，塔石上画了粉笔线，连新人都能看懂。”
她看着自己的碗，片刻后才再开口。
“我以前总觉得，标归路是这行里次要的部分。了不起的是勘测，是雾，是塔。可说实话呢？这才是这份工作。每个人都平安走回来。这才是全部。”
那位客人的故事收了尾，她没有上楼，仍坐着，朝你点点头。
“再讲一个故事。这个环节我从来不赶。坐下吧，腿要是愿意，站着也行。反正这张桌子旁的事还没完呢。”
客人开了个新头，讲一个船夫不按路程收费，而是按传闻收费，瓦莱莉娅差点把豆子喷出来。

choices.text: 这个轻松的夜晚是你挣来的。整支商队都因为你才平安回了家。
choices.response:
瓦莱莉娅用勺子指了指你，眼神却是暖的。
“小心点。再说这种话，我可要开始相信这条路也在喜欢我了。”
她把腌萝卜罐子又往你那边推了推，像她高兴却不想发表感言时的样子。
“起作用的是银扣。我只不过是放在了找得到的地方。”她说，“不过，谢谢你。真心的。这可比什么奖章都让我受用。”
然后她靠回椅背，去听船夫故事的结尾，椅子一直挨着你。

choices.text: （留在椅子上，什么都不说，陪在她身边听故事。）
choices.response:
你留在原地，瓦莱莉娅注意到了。她没有说破，但肩膀放松了一寸。
她朝你微微举了举碗，算是小小的致意，连豆子一起。
“这个，”她在客人的声音下轻声说，“就是最好的部分。路给你岔口，旅店给你这个。”
船夫故事讲到那个荒唐的结局，她和所有人一起笑起来，轻松得毫无防备。
笑声落下时，她瞥了你一眼。“下次勘测还是这张桌子？那只多出来的碗，我亲自摆。”

episodes.ending:
故事不是谁决定停的，而是炉火烧得低了，店主带着明显的不耐开始收拾碗碟。
瓦莱莉娅把自己的碗端进厨房，擦净长桌上你的位置，然后背着单肩行囊站在楼梯口。
“明天商队走安全的线路，”她说，“每个岔口都有银扣，塔上有粉笔线。每个人都走回家。这是我最喜欢的结局。”
她朝你笑了笑，平淡而笃定。
“还有这个。”她轻轻敲了一下楼梯扶手，“路，和这张桌子。有人觉得你必须选更宏大的那个。我不这么想。一个跟得上我脚步、愿意留下再听一个故事的人——那就是全部的奖赏。”
她迈上第一级台阶，又停了一下。
“晚安。天亮前的岔路口见。三颗银扣——你认得路。”

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 慢舞
romance.opening:
勘查结束了。最后一个岔路口做了标记，废塔也查过了，月门商队的货车稳稳走上了更好的路线。等你和瓦莱莉娅·诺克斯走回客栈时，路边的灯已经一盏盏亮了。

屋里，长桌上飘着炖豆子的香气。瓦莱莉娅要了两碗，跟老板说最后加腌萝卜，一遍就说明白了。她端起一碗放到你面前。

“这一趟真顺利。”她说，“勘查做完了，饭还是热的。能和你一起回来，就值了。”

侧厅里，有人把桌子拖到墙边，腾出一块地方跳圆舞。拉小提琴的乐手正在调音，一个音拉出来，半屋子的人都抬了头。瓦莱莉娅慢慢吃着豆子，用毫不掩饰的余光看着舞池。
romance.dialogue:
碗一空，她就放下勺子，把椅子转向你。

“那么。趁音乐还没追上我。”她的声音还是轻松的，但下面那句说得很直。“我们说好了有事直问。所以这是我的问题：这次勘查之后，经历了这一切，你还想和我交往吗？不是只在我两次出任务的空档里见一面。是想认真维持下去的那种。”

她等着。她有斥候的耐心，这会儿全用在你身上。

“你应该清楚自己在答应什么。”她补了一句，“我有时还是会离开。岔路、塔楼、起雾的清晨。我不会答应不再做斥候，也不会假装我不想。但我会一直给你留下回来的路。岔路口的银扣子，客栈里的信，还有我朝着家的方向走的靴子。大概就是这些。”

身后的小提琴响了起来。她没有回头。

choices.text: 想。我还是想和你交往。哪怕隔着遥远的路。
choices.response:
“好。”这个字脱口而出的速度连她自己都没料到，她笑了一声。“好。那条款你已经知道了。”

她站起身，在斗篷上擦了擦手，朝你伸出一只手。舞池里的圆圈还松散得足以加入。她不客套地牵起你的手，踩上简单的舞步。轮到她领舞时，她先回头和你确认了下一步的转向，才抬起手。

她没有朝琴师扬下巴让他加快节奏，只是让曲子照原来的样子奏下去。

choices.text: （握住她的手，说：“想。我还是想和你交往。”）
choices.response:
她低头看着你握住她的那只手，然后抬眼看你，肩上有什么东西松了下来。

“很高兴你说出来了。”她轻声说，“我想问出口，而不是靠猜。”

她的手指收拢，握紧你的手，站起身，领你走向舞池。她没有向全屋人宣布什么。只是从边缘迈进去，定下节奏，一边留意前方的路，一边不时确认你的脚下站稳没有。

romance.ending:
曲子渐渐收尾，你们俩谁也没动身去跳下一支。瓦莱莉娅把你引到窗边的矮墙旁坐下，两人端着剩下的茶。

“我不太会跳舞，今晚只学会了这几步。”她说，“所以我们把它算作一次正经安排好的约会吧。下次我勘查完回镇的时候。不用特意安排什么大事。一碗热饭，一盏灯，也许我终于带你去看那道石堤——屋顶尽头，整片海在那里展开。”

她在桌上轻轻敲了一下，把约定敲定。

“我会给路上的每个人做好岔路标记，回来之前先给客栈捎信。等我回来，如果你有空，我想再和你过一个晚上。”她瞥了一眼舞池里的人，又回头看你，笑容是从容不迫的那种。“下次勘查回来，同一个时间。到时候还坐这两个位置。”

episodes.title: The Second Exit
episodes.opening:
The forest edge smells of wet stone this morning. You stand with Seren Vale at the marked boundary of the ruins while the survey team checks packs and murmurs about the light.

Seren walks the perimeter slowly, one gloved finger tracing the boundary stones. You have watched this routine twice now: blade checked, exits counted, the way back walked end to end before anyone steps forward.

"Three exits," Seren says, stopping beside you. "The main gate, the collapsed arch on the east wall, and the low passage north. The arch is narrow, so it's the second option, not the first."

The team leader calls that they're ready. Seren nods, then pauses and looks at you the way one colleague looks at another.

"You've read the field notes I lent you. If I signal with two fingers, move to the nearest exit without waiting for me. Not because you matter less. Because you matter the same — and waiting for me is how people get trapped."
episodes.dialogue:
Inside, the ruins are cooler than the forest. Seren takes point, reading the walls in short glances rather than long stares, and the team moves between the marked stones in a loose line.

The trouble starts at the second chamber. A support rune on the far wall flickers — once, twice — then gives a thin, wrong hum. Seren's hand goes up. Everyone stops.

"Minor rune, failing early," Seren says quietly. "The ceiling above it is loose rubble. It will hold for minutes, not hours."

You watch the old habit surface: the straightening of the shoulders, the half-step forward that says I will handle this alone. Then Seren catches it too, and stops mid-step.

The blade comes down flat against the thigh, the way a person sets down a cup before an honest conversation.

"I need help," Seren says. The words come out level, not easy. "This is normally a one-person anchor job, but the rune sits above loose stone. If I cast and hold alone, my hands are full if it fails fast. I need someone bracing the rubble line while I work, and two people watching the arch."

The team leader points at you. You are nearest, and Seren neither argues you out of the position nor shifts you somewhere safer.

"Brace here." Seren indicates a handhold beside you. "You'll feel it before you hear it. If it shifts, call it, and we both go for the arch. Same signal. Same exit."

Seren kneels at the rune, palms flat, and begins the slow work of easing the failing lines apart. The hum climbs. Dust sifts from the rubble above your hands — a fine gray rain.

"Holding," Seren says, voice tight with concentration. "Talk to me. Any movement?"

You watch the stone seam above your knuckles. It holds. The hum drops, drops again, and finally settles into something steady and ordinary.

Seren sits back on both heels, breathes once, and looks at the wall rather than the team. Then, quietly: "That's the first time I've asked. It went better than every time I didn't."

choices.text: You counted us in. That's why it worked.
choices.response:
Seren looks at you a moment, then gives a small nod, as if confirming a suspicion.

"I did. Three exits, two braced hands, one plan." Seren sheathes the blade properly now. "I used to think the count was for my sake. It's for everyone's. Yours included."

The team leader signals the all-clear. Seren rises, offers no grand thanks — just walks the chamber again with you, at the same pace, not behind.

choices.text: (Stand by the braced line a moment longer, checking the stone yourself before saying anything.)
choices.response:
Seren notices your hand still resting near the seam and waits, patient, while you check it a second time.

"Steady," Seren agrees. "And you didn't move when the dust came. That's not nothing."

There's no ceremony in it. Seren simply stands, brushes stone grit from one glove, and gestures toward the north passage — walking beside you as before, with the small difference that you both know what your hands did in that room.

episodes.ending:
The team finishes the survey an hour later and comes back out through the main gate, exactly as planned. Nobody uses the arch. Nobody uses the north passage. Seren seems to find this the best possible outcome.

At the boundary stones, the team leader reports the findings. Seren signs the log, then adds a line in the margin — you catch a phrase about a braced rubble line holding under a failing rune. The report will credit the team. Seren will make sure it does.

While the others pack up, Seren walks the exits one more time, on principle. Then Seren comes back and stands beside you at the edge of the trees, where the light is returning to something normal.

"The academy teaches us to hold alone," Seren says. "It took me a long time to learn that holding alone is one option, not the definition of the job."

Seren glances at the ruins, then back at you.

"There's a used bookshop in a small town, run by an old friend of mine. The hero in one of his books crosses three mountains before lunch and never once eats. Next time you're free — no mission, no runes — I'd like to show you that."

It's an invitation, plainly offered, with room to say no. Seren checks the sky, counts something behind the eyes out of old habit, and waits.

episodes.title: The Quiet Bookshop
episodes.opening:
The bell over the door rings when Seren holds it open for you. The bookshop smells of dust and old glue, and afternoon light falls in long stripes across the shelves. The man behind the counter looks up, recognizes the silver-blond hair, and raises an eyebrow at the two of you together. Seren returns the look and says only, 'We were in the area.' You suspect that is not entirely true; the area is a half-day's walk from the forest edge.

Seren runs a gloved finger along a shelf of used adventure novels and pulls one out with a worn spine. 'This one,' Seren says, showing you the cover of a hero mid-leap over a chasm. 'I've read it twice. He crosses three mountains before lunch and never once eats.' The friend behind the counter snorts and adds that the hero never sleeps either, which Seren concedes with a small nod, as though confirming a tactical report.

There are two chairs by the window, and the friend pushes a third toward you without being asked. Seren sits, sets the blade against the wall where it can't knock anything over, and for a moment just watches the street. 'No mission today,' Seren says, mostly to the window. 'The academy was informed I would be unreachable. It took some persuading.'
episodes.dialogue:
Seren opens the book to a page near the middle and reads aloud, deadpan, in the flat tone of an official report: the hero, having crossed the mountains, declines a hot meal because 'hunger is for those who stop.' The friend laughs first, then you, and Seren's mouth twitches in a way that counts as laughing, for Seren.

'He never eats,' Seren says, closing the book on one finger. 'And by the last chapter he faints from exhaustion, and a village herbalist saves him. The book treats it as a twist.' The friend points out that Seren once skipped a meal during a survey and was found eating bread behind a ruin wall at dusk. Seren considers this. 'That was strategy,' Seren says, with dignity, and the friend says it looked like hunger.

The friend disappears into the back and returns with a paper bag from the bakery two doors down, still warm. Seren takes one and eats it slowly, properly, sitting down the whole time, and says, 'See. This is the chapter he never wrote.' You are offered the bag first, before Seren takes a second.

After a while the friend goes to help a customer at the far shelves, and the window chair grows quiet. Seren turns the book over in both hands and speaks without preamble, the way Seren does when a thought has been carried a while.

'I have been thinking about what I said at the ruins. About asking for help.' The blade rests against the wall, out of reach, which you notice Seren did on purpose. 'Rescue is easy to ask for. It has a shape. Someone is in danger, you call, they come. It has rules.'

Seren looks at the street, where a woman is arguing gently with a dog about a stick. 'This is harder. Sitting in a chair on a free afternoon, next to someone, asking for nothing and offering nothing but the sitting. I am trained for sieges. I am not trained for this.' A pause. 'I nearly did not come. I drafted three reasons to be busy.'

Seren sets the book down and looks at you directly. 'So. Thank you for being the part that was easy. The showing up. The rest, I am practicing.'

choices.text: 'For the record, you're doing fine at the sitting part.'
choices.response: Seren blinks once, then nods slowly, as if filing the assessment where serious reports go. 'Then I will log today as a successful exercise.' The corner of Seren's mouth does the thing that counts as a smile. 'Though I warn you, practice implies repetition. The friend has two chairs. He will notice if they stay empty.' From behind the shelves, the friend calls out that the chairs are always there, and Seren says, quietly, 'You see. Even the shop agrees.'

choices.text: (Take a pastry from the bag and hand Seren the second one without a word.)
choices.response: Seren accepts it with both hands, which is more ceremony than a pastry requires, and eats it in small, unhurried bites. 'He never eats,' Seren says at last, nodding at the closed book. 'We are better than the hero. That is a low bar, and I am content with it.' The quiet that follows is not awkward, and Seren stays in it with you, watching the dog win the argument about the stick.

episodes.ending:
The light goes gold before anyone suggests leaving. The friend refuses payment for the book — 'shelf copy, personal, not for sale' — but Seren leaves coins under the paper bag anyway, and the friend pretends not to see, which is how they have settled this argument for years.

Outside, Seren pauses on the step and looks back at the window, the two chairs, the shelves. 'I used to think rest was what happened between missions,' Seren says. 'It is apparently a thing you have to choose. Repeatedly. Like a vow, but kinder.'

Seren adjusts the cloak, checks the road both ways out of habit, then doesn't check again. 'The bakery is two doors down and the stall with the second pastry is on the way back,' Seren says. 'If you are in no hurry, the afternoon has room in it. And next time —' a small breath, the sound of someone choosing — 'next time I will ask for the chair sooner.'

episodes.title: On the Lakeshore
episodes.opening:
The lake outside the small town is flat today, the kind of flat that makes the far shore look close. Seren walks the stony edge with you, cloak unclasped and folded over one arm. The academy's summons is a day away yet.

"This is the shore I mentioned," Seren says. "Where my first stone skipped twice and I counted it as progress."

There is a dry rock partway down the bank, worn smooth by other visitors. Seren sits on it first, then nods at the space beside you, leaving the choice to you. The water laps in small unhurried sounds. Behind the tree line, a bird repeats itself.

Seren picks up a flat stone and weighs it in one hand. "Fair warning. My reputation does not survive contact with this lake."
episodes.dialogue:
The first throw skips twice and sinks. Seren watches the ripples close over it.

"Twice," Seren says. "Consistent with the historical record."

The second throw skips three times. Seren turns to you. "Progress. You're a witness now. That matters at the academy."

A third stone goes sideways and plops straight down. Seren exhales through the nose, almost a laugh, and sits back down. For a while there is just the water and the birds.

"I've been thinking about the perimeter," Seren says eventually. "When the rune failed and I asked for help instead of handling it alone. My hands still didn't like it. They wanted to be the only one standing in front."

Seren turns a stone over in one palm, not throwing it.

"Here's the thing I don't say often. If someone matters to me, my first instinct is to put myself between them and everything. And that sounds noble, but it isn't always. Sometimes it just takes their choice away."

The stone is set down deliberately on the rock between you.

"What I want is protection as a choice. Both people standing, both people deciding. It's slower. It risks more. But I've seen the other version — where the spellblade runs dry and the party nearly pays for one person's answer."

Seren looks at you, steady and unhurried.

"You don't have to answer any of that. You can just sit. This shore is good for sitting. It's most of what it's for, honestly."

choices.text: Then I'll take the choice. I stay because I want to, not because you stand in front of me.
choices.response:
Seren is quiet for a moment, and the shoulders ease, the way a lowered blade changes a room.

"Good," Seren says. "That's the answer I hoped for, and the one I won't take for granted."

Seren picks up two stones, hands you the thinner one, and settles back on the rock. "Your throw first. I'd like to see if the shore is kinder to you than it is to me."

choices.text: (Sit down beside Seren and say nothing, watching the water.)
choices.response:
You sit, and Seren doesn't fill the silence, which is its own kind of company. The lake keeps its small sounds going.

A while later, Seren passes you a flat stone without a word — an invitation with no deadline attached.

"Thank you for staying," Seren says at last. "Not everyone knows sitting counts."

The stone rests warm in your hand. Neither of you throws it for a long time.

episodes.ending:
The sun leans west and the water turns pewter. Seren stands, brushes off the cloak, and returns the last flat stones to the shore with small, ceremonial care.

"Three skips remains my record," Seren says. "I'd like to keep it that way for at least another season."

The walk back toward town is unhurried. At the fork where the road splits toward the bookshop and the inn, Seren pauses.

"Tomorrow I report to the academy. After that, I don't know what they'll send. But this shore keeps." Seren meets your eyes once. "And so do I. When there's a next time, it'll be because we both chose it."

Seren lifts a hand in a small farewell and takes the bookshop road. Behind you, faintly, you hear one last stone skipping across the water.

episodes.title: A Choice Kept Free
episodes.opening:
The escort ends the way the good ones do: slowly, and before dinner.
The survey team packs its gear by the ruin gate while Seren walks the perimeter one last time, counting the exits out of habit even though nothing went wrong. The rune held. The dragon-shadow kept to the far tower. You carried your own weight the whole way, and Seren noticed without saying so.
By the time the wagons roll off, the sun is low and gold on the forest edge. Seren pulls off one glove and flexes the hand, then looks at you the way he looks at a field before stepping into it.
"Walk with me a little?" he asks. "The road back is quiet, and I'd rather not end the day with an order."
You fall in beside him. The path runs past the perimeter markers toward the small town, and for a while the only sound is boots on packed dirt and a bird somewhere insisting on its evening.
episodes.dialogue:
Halfway to the marker post, Seren stops. He lowers his blade hand first — an old habit, unnecessary out here, but he does it anyway — and turns to face you.
"I've been drafting this conversation for two weeks," he says. "In letters I didn't send. It kept coming out wrong, so I'll say it plainly."
He breathes once, the way he does before something that matters.
"I like the time we spend. More than escort duty asks of it. And I want to know what you'd like it to be — a date, outside any academy obligation, or a close friendship, chosen and kept. Either is a good answer. Neither is a test."
He keeps his hands still and his eyes on yours.
"I'm not asking you to decide quickly, and I'm not asking you to decide for my sake. Whatever you choose, I'll still count the exits, still walk you to the road, still be the same person beside you. The only thing that changes is the name we give it."
A pause. The bird has given up its argument.
"One more thing, so there's no misunderstanding," he adds. "I won't abandon my work to prove anything, and I won't ever point at a sacrifice and call it affection. If we go forward, we go forward in ordinary days. Soup, pastries, a slow game, a road kept open. That's the whole of what I can honestly offer — and I think it's a great deal."
He waits. Not anxiously. The way he waits for a team member to make their own call at a fork in a ruin.

choices.text: Then let's call it a date. Outside all of it — no duties, no obligations.
choices.response:
Seren's shoulders settle a fraction, and something quiet crosses his face that is very close to a smile arriving early.
"A date," he repeats, as if fitting the word into his kit alongside the blade and the rations. "All right. Then it should be somewhere with no exits to count. The lakeshore, perhaps — though I'll warn you my skipping record there is a matter of public embarrassment."
He glances down the road toward town.
"I'll bring the pastries. You pick the day. Whenever it sits right with you — I have no wish to schedule this like a mission briefing."

choices.text: (Say nothing yet — just walk on beside him, shoulder close, and let the quiet answer.)
choices.response:
Seren falls back into step with you without needing the words filled. After a few paces he nods, mostly to himself.
"Friendship, then, until told otherwise," he says. "Chosen, not default. That distinction matters to me."
He takes the longer fork, the one that adds ten minutes to town.
"I walk this way when I have nowhere to be. If you'd like company on ordinary days — market walks, a slow board game, a bench — you have only to say which day. I'll be there with the pastries and no agenda."

episodes.ending:
Seren walks you as far as the last perimeter marker, where the forest edge opens toward town.
"Same road next time," he says. "Nothing about today changes my work, or yours. But it does change my mornings a little — I'll be looking forward to a day I didn't receive by summons."
He stops there, deliberate about not walking you all the way to your door, as if a good ending should leave the next beginning to you.
"Set the next meeting however it suits you," he says. "A market morning. An evening at the lake. Or nothing for a while, and that's fine too. I'll keep the second chair by the door either way."
He turns back toward his cabin, unhurried, and the last you see of him is the cloak's stitched moons catching the last of the light.
Whatever the two of you are now, it started on an ordinary road, with both of you free to choose it again tomorrow.

episodes.title: The Unrushed Game
episodes.opening:
The market walk was ordinary in the best way. Seren bought a paper bag of pastries at the stall he has visited twice before — two pieces, no argument with himself this time — and you walked beside him through the small town while he counted nothing at all.

Now the bookshop is half-lit, the friend gone home early and the key left under the usual brick. The counter is cleared except for a grid board set up from the back shelf, its stones sorted into two small dishes.

"He trusts me with the key," Seren says, hanging his cloak on the hook he installed for him. "Which I suspect is also a test of whether I dust."

He sets the pastry bag between the two chairs, one piece for each, and sits down across from you with the unhurried air of someone who has nowhere else the whole evening.
episodes.dialogue:
"We play slowly," he says, placing the first stone. "That's the whole rule. If either of us rushes, the other is allowed to point at the pastry bag as remedy."

The game takes shape between you. He is careful with his placements, and when you make a good move he pauses over the board and nods once, filing it away.

"I meant to say something," he says, after a few quiet turns. He lowers his hand to the table, the way he lowers his blade before words that matter. "On the road back from the escort, I asked what we might be. You stayed beside me on the long road, and I understood that as friendship. I chose it too. I choose it again now."

"Friendship. I chose it, the way I pick a road that has good footing and a view I like."

He turns a stone over in his fingers before placing it. "I've spent years learning to ask for help instead of taking danger alone. You were there when I first managed it. That's not a small thing to build on."

"The next visit is optional," he adds. "Not because I'm retreating. A vow you can't revoke is a cage, and I don't intend to cage this. Come when coming is what you want. I'll be doing the same."

He sets his stone down and nudges the pastry bag an inch toward you. "Eat. The hero in the three-mountains book would be proud, and he's proud of very little."

choices.text: Then I choose it too. The whole thing.
choices.response:
Seren's expression doesn't change much, but his shoulders settle, the way they do when an exit check comes back clean.

"Good," he says simply. "Then we're agreed, and neither of us had to be rescued into it."

He turns the next stone over in his fingers, and there is a lightness in how he sets it down. "Your move," he says. "And no rushing. We have the whole evening, and now we know we have the rest besides."

choices.text: (Open the pastry bag and set his share in front of him.)
choices.response:
Seren looks at the pastry, then at you, and something in his eyes is warmer than the lamp.

"That's answer enough," he says. "Slower and better than any I could have made."

He breaks his piece in half and sets one half by your hand — a small, deliberate thing, done without a word about it. The board waits while you both eat, in no hurry at all.

episodes.ending:
The game ends with the board nearly full and no clear winner, which Seren declares the correct outcome for an evening like this.

He dusts the shelves before leaving, on principle, and writes a short note to the bookshop friend about which book he borrowed. The key goes back under the brick.

Outside, the market street is quiet and the forest edge is a walk away. He pauses at the corner and looks down the road toward his cabin.

"I'll leave the second chair where it is," he says. "It's earned its keep."

Then he lifts a hand, unhurried, and turns toward home — the road back open, the next visit yours to make whenever it suits you. That is the whole of it, and by any measure he trusts, it is a good day.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Walk Without Armor
romance.opening:
The lakeshore outside the small town is quiet in the late afternoon. The water lies flat, and the stones along the bank are the same gray ones from the first skipping morning.

Seren is already there, sitting on the dry rock with a cloth-wrapped basket beside him. His cloak is folded under him instead of worn, and his blade is nowhere in sight. It is the first time you have met him with neither.

He looks up when your steps reach him, and the surprise on his face is brief before it settles into something warmer. "You found the spot. I worried I described it badly."

"The birds got here before you did," he adds, nodding toward the shallows. "But they don't mind company. Sit wherever you like. The rock is wide enough for two if you don't mind the cold."

The air smells like water and dry grass. The road back to town is a short walk behind the tree line. He notices you glance that way and nods, as if to say yes, that's still open.
romance.dialogue:
Seren waits until you are settled, then turns so he is facing you properly. He takes one slow breath, the kind you have seen him take before saying something that matters.

"I want to ask you something plainly, so you can answer it plainly," he says. "Last time, when I asked about a date, you chose to try this with me. I have been looking forward to today since then. But looking forward to something is not the same as it still being true."

He sets his hands in his lap. No armor, no blade, nothing for the words to hide behind. "Do you still want to date me? Not out of politeness, not because I made the trip. Just what you actually want."

The water laps quietly while he waits. He does not fill the silence or soften the question into something easier. His eyes stay on you, patient, the way he waits on a survey line before anyone steps forward.

"If the answer changed, that's an honest answer too," he says. "We would still have a basket of food and an afternoon, and neither would be wasted. But if it hasn't changed, I would very much like to hear it."

choices.text: Yes. I still want to date you.
choices.response:
Seren's shoulders lower, and a small, unguarded smile crosses his face. "Good," he says. "Then mine is unchanged too."

He lifts the basket onto the shared rock between you and unwraps it: bread, a mild onion soup in a sealed pot, and two pastries wrapped separately. "One for each of us. I bought them on the same trip, on purpose."

The soup is simple and warm. He eats slowly, unhurried, and tells you about a book he nearly bought for its terrible cover alone — a hero who crosses a mountain range without once stopping for lunch.

When the meal is done he wipes his hands and looks out at the water. "Same time next week? The stall with the second pastries is in town on market days. I could walk it with you first, then we come back here." He waits for your yes or your counter-suggestion, as if either would make him equally glad.

choices.text: (Reach over and rest your hand over his, then say yes.)
choices.response:
He looks down at your hand over his, then up at you. "Yes?" he asks, making sure the word matches the gesture.

When you say it aloud, he turns his hand palm-up under yours and holds it loosely, as though learning the weight of it. "Then mine is the same. I still want this."

He keeps your hand a moment longer, then opens the basket with his free one. "The soup survived the walk. That is my whole contribution, so you may judge me on it."

You eat together on the cold rock, his shoulder close to yours, and the afternoon passes at the pace of the water. Before the light goes gold he says, quietly, "Next week there's a market in town. Walk it with me first, and we can end here again." He waits for your answer rather than assuming it, and when you agree, he nods once, satisfied, and starts planning which stall to visit first.

romance.ending:
The sun goes low over the water and the birds settle in the shallows. Neither of you is in a hurry to leave, so neither of you does.

When the light finally begins to fade, Seren packs the empty pot and wraps the cloth with the same care he gives his blade. He walks you as far as the tree line, then stops at the edge of it.

"Next week, then," he says. "Market first, then here. And if one of us cannot come, we say so and choose another day. No oaths required." He smiles at that, small and sure.

He watches until you are on the road, and you hear him pick up his cloak and basket behind you, unhurried, taking his own way home at his own pace. The path back to town is easy to find in the last light, and ahead of it there is a day already chosen, waiting for both of you.

episodes.title: 第二个出口
episodes.opening:
清晨的森林边缘带着湿石头的气息。你和塞伦站在遗迹的标记边界外，勘测队正在检查行囊，低声议论着光线。

塞伦沿周界缓缓走了一圈，一根戴着手套的手指描过界石。这套流程你已经见过两次：检查刀刃，数清出口，在任何人踏入之前把退路从头到尾走一遍。

“一共三个出口，”塞伦在你身旁停下。“正门、东墙那座坍塌的拱门，还有北面的低矮通道。拱门很窄，所以它是第二选择，不是第一。”

队长喊话说大家准备好了。塞伦点点头，随即停了停，用看待同僚而非乘客的目光看向你。

“你读过我借你的现场笔记。如果我伸出两根手指，就立刻前往最近的出口，不必等我。不是因为你不如我重要。而是因为你同样重要——等人，正是人们被困的原因。”
episodes.dialogue:
遗迹里比森林更凉爽。塞伦走在最前面，用短促的瞥视而非长久的凝视读着墙壁，队伍在标记石之间松散地排成一线。

麻烦始于第二个石室。远处墙上的一枚支撑符文闪烁了一下——又一下——随即发出一声细而异常的嗡鸣。塞伦抬手。所有人停下。

“小型符文，提前失效了，”塞伦低声说。“它上方的天花板是松散的碎石。撑得住几分钟，撑不住几小时。”

你看着那股旧习惯浮现出来：肩膀挺直，半步向前，那姿态分明在说这件事我一个人来。你见过这样的情形。你也看见塞伦同样意识到了这一点的瞬间。

塞伦在半步之间停住。刀身放平，贴在大腿上，像一个人在进行坦诚对话之前先放下茶杯。

“我需要帮助，”塞伦说，语气平稳，却并不轻松。“这本是一个人就能完成的锚定作业，但符文悬在松石上方。如果我独自施法并维持，它一旦突然失效，我的双手根本腾不出来。我需要有人撑住碎石线，我才能作业，另外两人盯着拱门。”

队长指向你。你离得最近，而塞伦既没有劝你离开这个位置，也没有把你调去更安全的地方。

“在这里撑住。”塞伦指着你身旁的一处把手。“你会先感觉到，然后才听到动静。如果石头动了，就叫出来，我们一起奔向拱门。同一个信号，同一个出口。”

塞伦在符文前单膝跪下，双掌平贴，开始缓缓分开那些失效的符文线路。嗡鸣攀升。碎石从你双手上方的石堆中筛落，像一场细灰色的雨。

“撑住了，”塞伦说，声音因专注而绷紧。“跟我说说话。有动静吗？”

你盯着指节上方的石缝。它撑住了。嗡鸣声降下来，又降下来，最终归于某种平稳而寻常的声音。

塞伦双膝跪坐向后靠，呼吸了一次，目光落在墙上，而非看向队伍。然后轻声说：“这是我第一次开口求助。结果比我每一次不开口的时候都要好。”

choices.text: 你把我们所有人都算进了计划里。所以才会顺利。
choices.response:
塞伦看了你片刻，随后轻轻点头，像确认了一个猜测。

“是的。三个出口，两双撑住的手，一个计划。”塞伦这才把刀稳稳收回鞘中。“我从前以为计数是为了我自己。其实它是为了所有人。包括你在内。”

队长发出解除警报的信号。塞伦起身，没有说任何盛大的感谢——只是与你并肩、以同样的步速，重新走了一遍这个石室，而不是走在你身后。

choices.text: （在撑住的石缝旁再多站一会儿，先亲自检查一遍石头，再开口。）
choices.response:
塞伦注意到你的手仍搭在石缝附近，便耐心等待，让你做了第二次检查。

“很稳，”塞伦认同道。“灰尘落下来的时候，你没有挪动。这不是小事。”

没有任何仪式感。塞伦只是站起身，掸去手套膝盖处的石屑，朝北面通道做了个手势——依旧与你并肩而行，只是有一点点不同：你们两人都知道，在那间石室里，你的双手做了什么。

episodes.ending:
一小时后，勘测队完成任务，按计划从正门走出。没有人用到拱门，也没有人用到北通道。塞伦似乎觉得这就是最好的结果。

界石旁，队长汇报了勘测发现。塞伦在记录上签名，然后在页边添了一行——你瞥见一句关于碎石线在符文失效时撑住了的话。这份报告会归功于整个队伍。塞伦会确保这一点。

趁着其他人收拾行装，塞伦出于原则又把几个出口各走了一遍。然后折返回来，站在树影边缘你的身旁，那里的光线正恢复成寻常的样子。

“学院教我们独自支撑，”塞伦说。“我花了很久才明白，独自支撑只是众多选项之一，不是这份工作的定义。”

塞伦朝遗迹望了一眼，然后又看回你。

“有家旧书店，开在一座小镇上，是我的一位老朋友经营的。他店里有一本书，主角翻过三座山才到午饭时间，却从没吃过一口饭。下次你有空的时候——没有任务，也不碰符文——我想带你去看看。”

这是一份邀请，坦然发出，并留有拒绝的余地。塞伦看了看天色，出于旧习惯在心里数了数什么，然后等待你的回答。

episodes.title: 安静的书店
episodes.opening:
塞伦为你推开门，门上的铃铛轻轻响了一声。书店里是灰尘和旧胶水的气味，午后的光在微倾的书架间投下长长的条纹，书架塞得太满，显得有些吃力。柜台后的男人抬起头，认出了那头银白的头发，又看见你们两人站在一起，挑了挑眉。塞伦神色平静地迎上那道目光，只说了一句：“我们正好路过。”你怀疑这话并不完全属实——这里离森林边缘要走半天的路。

塞伦戴着手套的手指沿一排二手冒险小说的书脊滑过，抽出一本磨损得很厉害的。“这本，”塞伦把封面转向你，封面上那位英雄正跃过一道深谷。“我读过两遍。他午饭前翻过三座山，却没吃过一口饭。”柜台后的朋友嗤笑一声，补了一句那位英雄也从不睡觉。塞伦微微点头，像在确认一份战术报告。

窗边有两把椅子。朋友不用任何人开口，便把第三把椅子推到你面前。塞伦坐下，把剑靠在不会碰倒任何东西的墙上，有那么一会儿，只是看着街道。“今天没有任务，”塞伦说，多半是对着窗户说的。“我已经告知学院今天联系不上。费了些口舌才说服他们。”
episodes.dialogue:
塞伦翻到书中靠中间的一页，用官方报告般平板的语气面无表情地朗读：那位英雄翻过群山之后，拒绝了一顿热饭，理由是“饥饿属于会停下来的人”。朋友先笑了，接着是你，而塞伦的嘴角动了一下——对塞伦而言，这就算笑了。

“他从不吃东西，”塞伦用一根手指夹着合起书说。“到最后一章，他因为体力不支晕倒，是一位村里的草药师救了他。书里把这当成一个转折。”朋友指出，塞伦有一次勘测期间也跳过了一顿饭，黄昏时被人发现躲在遗迹墙后啃面包。塞伦认真地想了想。“那是战术，”塞伦有尊严地说。朋友说那看起来就是饿的。

朋友消失到后屋，回来时手里提着一个纸袋，是两扇门外那家面包房的，还温热着。朴素的点心，甜得不算过分。塞伦拿了一块，坐得端端正正，慢慢吃完，然后说：“看，这就是他从来没写过的那一章。”在拿第二块之前，纸袋是先递给你的。

过了一会儿，朋友去远处的书架帮一位顾客，窗边渐渐安静下来。塞伦双手捧着那本书翻来覆去，然后开门见山地说起话来——这是塞伦把一个念头揣了很久之后的样子。

“我一直在想我在遗迹那边说的话。关于求助的事。”剑靠在墙上，放在伸手够不到的地方——你注意到这是故意的。“求救是容易开口的。它有形状。有人遇险，你呼叫，有人赶来。它有规则。”

塞伦望向窗外，一个妇人正和一条狗温和地争论一根棍子的归属。“这更难。一个空闲的下午，坐在椅子上，坐在某人身边，不求什么，也不给什么，只是坐着。我受过围城战的训练。没受过这个。”停顿了一下。“我差点没来。我起草了三个今天很忙的理由。”

塞伦把书放下，直视着你，蓝灰色的目光很稳。“所以，谢谢你承担了容易的那部分。出现在这里。剩下的，我在练习。”

choices.text: 你很会陪人安静地坐着。
choices.response: 塞伦眨了一下眼，然后缓缓点头，仿佛把这份评估归档到重要报告那一栏里。“那我就把今天记录为一次成功的演练。”塞伦的嘴角做出那个算作微笑的动作。“不过我要提醒你，练习意味着重复。朋友有两把椅子。如果它们一直空着，他会注意到的。”书架后面，朋友喊话说那两把椅子永远都在。塞伦轻声说：“你看。连这家店都同意了。”

choices.text: （从纸袋里拿一块点心，一言不发地把第二块递给塞伦。）
choices.response: 塞伦用双手接过，郑重程度超出了一块点心所需的礼数，然后一小口一小口、不慌不忙地吃着。“他从不吃东西，”塞伦终于开口，朝那本合上的书点了点头。“我们比那位英雄强。这个门槛很低，而我对它很满意。”随后的安静并不尴尬。那是无需填补的安静，塞伦陪你一起待在里面，看着那条狗赢得了关于棍子的争论。

episodes.ending:
在任何人提议离开之前，光线已经变成金色。朋友拒绝为这本书收钱——“架上那本是店主自己的，不卖”——但塞伦还是在纸袋下面留了几枚硬币，朋友则假装没看见。多年来他们就是这样解决这场争论的。

门外，塞伦在台阶上停了停，回头望向那扇窗、那两把椅子，还有像老兵一样倾斜着的书架。“我以前以为，休息就是任务之间发生的事，”塞伦说。“原来它是一件你必须主动选择的事。一次又一次。像誓言，但更温和。”

塞伦整了整披风，出于习惯朝路的两个方向各看了一眼，然后没有再看第二眼。“面包房就在两扇门外，那个能让人买第二份点心的摊位在回去的路上，”塞伦说。“如果你不赶时间，这个下午还有余地。而且下一次——”一次小小的呼吸，一个人做出选择的声音，“下一次我会更早开口要那把椅子。”

episodes.title: 湖畔
episodes.opening:
今天小镇外的湖面十分平静，平静得连对岸都显得近在眼前。塞伦与你沿着布满石子的湖边走着，斗篷解开了搭扣，叠起来搭在一条手臂上。学院的征召还有一天才到。

“这就是我提过的那片湖岸，”塞伦说，“我第一次扔石头弹跳了两次，就把它算作进步的地方。”

岸边下方有块干燥的岩石，被来客磨得光滑。塞伦先在上面坐下，然后朝旁边的位置点点头，把选择留给你。湖水以细小而从容的声音拍打着。树线后面，一只鸟在重复着自己的叫声。

塞伦捡起一块扁平的石头，在手里掂了掂。“先提醒你一句。我的名声在这座湖面前不堪一击。”
episodes.dialogue:
第一块石头弹跳了两次，然后沉了下去。塞伦看着涟漪将它合拢，脸上毫无表情。

“两次，”塞伦说，“与历史记录一致。”

第二块弹跳了三次。塞伦转向你，带着一丝极细微的停顿宣布：“进步。你现在是见证人了。这在学院里可是要紧的。”

第三块斜着飞出去，直直地扑通落水。塞伦从鼻子里呼出一口气，几乎算得上一声轻笑，重新坐回岩石上。有一阵子，只剩下水声和鸟鸣。

“我一直在想遗迹外围的事，”塞伦终于开口，声音低了一些，“符文失效的时候，我选择了求助，而不是独自处理。可我的手至今还是不喜欢那样。它们想成为唯一站在前面的人。”

塞伦在掌心里翻转着一块石头，没有扔出去。

“有件事我不常说。如果有人对我重要，我的第一反应是把自己挡在那个人和一切之间。这听起来高尚，但并非总是如此。有时候，这只是在剥夺对方的选择。”

那块石头又翻转了一次，然后被刻意放下，搁在你们之间的岩石上。

“我想要的是，保护成为一种选择。两个人都站着，两个人都参与决定。这样更慢，也要冒更大的险。但我经历过另一种版本——法力耗尽，整个队伍几乎为一个人的答案付出代价。”

塞伦望向湖面，然后看向你，蓝灰色的眼睛沉着而从容。

“你不必回答这些。你只要坐着就好。这片湖岸很适合坐着。说实话，坐着就是它最大的用途。”

choices.text: 那我就接受这个选择。我留下来，是因为我愿意，不是因为你挡在我前面。
choices.response:
塞伦沉默了片刻，肩头的姿态松了下来，就像出鞘的剑归了鞘。

“好，”塞伦说，“这正是我盼望的答案，也是我不会视为理所当然的答案。”

塞伦捡起两块石头，把较薄的那块递给你，然后在你身边坐好。“你先扔。我想看看这片湖岸对你是不是比对我仁慈一些。”

choices.text: （在塞伦身边坐下，什么也不说，望着水面。）
choices.response:
你坐下了，塞伦没有用话语填满沉默。湖面持续着它细碎的声音。

过了一会儿，塞伦一言不发地递给你一块扁平的石头，一份没有期限的邀请。

“谢谢你留下来，”塞伦最后简单地说，“不是所有人都知道，坐着也算数。”

石头留在你手里，被岩石焐得温热。很久，你们谁都没有把它扔出去。

episodes.ending:
太阳西斜，湖水泛出锡灰色。塞伦站起身，掸了掸斗篷，带着一种小小的、近乎仪式般的郑重，把最后几块扁平的石头放回岸边。

“三次弹跳依旧是我的纪录，”塞伦说，“我想让它至少再保持一个季节。”

回小镇的路走得从容。在三岔路口——一条路通往书店，一条通往旅店——塞伦停下脚步。

“明天我要向学院述职。之后，我不知道他们会派我去做什么。但这片湖岸会一直在。”塞伦与你对视了一眼，目光沉稳。“我也一样。如果还有下一次，那会是因为我们两个人都做出了选择。”

塞伦抬起手，小小地挥了挥作别，踏上了通往书店的路。而你隐约听见，身后有一块石头最后一次掠过湖面的声音。

episodes.title: 保留自由的选择
episodes.opening:
护送任务结束得像所有顺利的任务一样：不慌不忙，赶在晚饭之前。
勘测队正在遗迹门口收拾装备，塞伦最后一次巡视周边，出于习惯数着出口，尽管什么意外都没发生。符文撑住了。龙影也守在远处的塔楼。这一路上你都自食其力，塞伦注意到了，只是没有说出口。
等马车启程时，太阳已经低垂，金色的光洒在森林边缘。塞伦摘下一只手套，活动了一下手指，然后用他踏入一片区域前打量地形的目光看向你。
“陪我走一段？”他问。“回程的路很安静，我不想用命令来结束这一天。”
你走到他身边。小路经过周边的标记桩，通往小镇，有那么一会儿，唯一的声响是靴子踩在压实泥土上的声音，还有某处一只鸟执拗地唱着傍晚的歌。
episodes.dialogue:
走到标记桩的一半，塞伦停了下来。他先垂下握剑的手——一个旧习惯，在这里并无必要，但他还是做了——然后转身面对你。
“这场对话我打了两周的草稿，”他说。“写在没寄出的信里。怎么写都不对劲，所以我就直说了。”
他深吸一口气，像他面对要紧事之前那样。
“我喜欢我们共处的时光，超出了护送职责所要求的程度。我想知道你希望它是什么——一次约会，在学院义务之外的约会，或者是一段亲密的友谊，由你选择并珍视。两者都是好答案，都不是考验。”
他的双手安静地垂着，目光落在你眼中。
“我不是要你急着决定，也不是要你为了我而决定。无论你选什么，我依然会数出口，依然会送你到路口，依然是你身边同一个人。唯一改变的，只是我们给它的名字。”
一阵停顿。那只鸟放弃了它的争执。
“还有一件事，以免产生误会，”他补充道。“我不会为了证明什么而抛下我的工作，我也绝不会指着一场牺牲称之为爱意。如果我们继续走下去，那也是在平凡的日子里走下去。一碗汤、几块点心、一局慢棋、一条保持畅通的路。这就是我能诚实给出的全部——而我认为，这已经很多了。”
他等待着。不是焦灼地等，而是像他在遗迹岔路口等待队员自己做决定那样等。

choices.text: 那就叫它约会吧。在这一切之外——没有职责，没有义务。
choices.response:
塞伦的肩膀微微放松下来，一种安静的神色掠过他的脸，几乎像是一个提前到来的微笑。
“约会，”他重复了一遍，像是在把这个词收进行囊，与剑和干粮放在一起。“好。那地点应该选一个不需要数出口的地方。也许去湖边——不过我得提醒你，我在那里打水漂的战绩已经是公开的笑柄了。”
他朝小镇方向的道路望了一眼。
“点心我来带。日子你来定。你觉得合适的时候就行——我不想把这件事安排得像任务简报。”

choices.text: （先什么都不说——只是走在他身边，肩膀靠近，让沉默来回答。）
choices.response:
塞伦重新跟上你的步伐，不需要用言语去填补什么。走了几步之后，他点了点头，更多是对自己点的。
“那么，就是友谊了，直到另有说明，”他说。“是选择的，不是默认的。这个区别对我来说很重要。”
他选择了较长的那条岔路，多走十分钟才到镇上的那条。
“我没有去处的时候就走这条路。如果你愿意在平凡的日子里有人作伴——逛集市、下一局慢棋、坐一条长椅——你只需说哪一天。我会带着点心赴约，不带别的目的。”

episodes.ending:
塞伦送你走到林边最后一根路标。往前就是回镇的路。
“下次还是走这条路吧，”他说，“不用等护送任务，我也想见你。”
他停在路标旁，没有替你决定下一次见面的日子。“镇上有集市，湖边也不错。哪天方便，我们再说。”
他朝你挥了挥手，转身往小屋走。暮光落在他斗篷上绣着的月亮上。走出几步，他又回头，看见你还站在那里，便笑了一下。

episodes.title: 不急不缓的一局
episodes.opening:
集市之行平常得恰到好处。塞伦在光顾过两次的摊子上买了一纸袋点心——这一次买两块，不再和自己讨价还价——然后你陪他穿过小镇，他什么都没有去数。

如今书店里只有半明半暗的灯光，店主朋友提早回家了，钥匙照例留在那块砖下面。柜台收拾干净了，只摆着一副从后面书架取出的棋盘，棋子分装在两只小碟里。

“他把钥匙交给我，”塞伦说着，把斗篷挂在店主特意为他钉的挂钩上，“我怀疑这同时也是在考验我擦不擦灰。”

他把点心袋放在两把椅子之间，一人一份，然后在你对面坐下，带着一整晚都无处可去的从容神色。
episodes.dialogue:
“我们下慢一点，”他落子时说，“这是全部的规则。谁要是急了，另一个人就有权指着点心袋当作补救。”

棋局在你们之间渐渐成形。他落子谨慎，当你走出好棋，他会在棋盘上停顿片刻，点一下头，像是要把这一步记在心里。

“我有话想说，”几个安静的回合之后，他说。他把手放到桌上，就像在说出要紧的话之前先放下剑那样。“护送回来那天，我问我们之间该怎么称呼。你没有急着开口，只陪我走了那条长路。我明白了，我们愿意继续做朋友。现在，我还愿意再选一次。”

“友情。这是个完完整整的选择，就像我挑一条落脚稳当、风景也合心意的路。”

他把一枚棋子在指间翻过一面，然后才落下去。“这些年我一直在学着开口求助，而不是独自面对危险。我第一次做到的时候，你就在场。这份基础，并不算小。”

“下一次见面是可有可无的，”他补充道，“不是因为我在退缩。而是不能收回的誓言只是一座体面的牢笼，我不打算这样困住它。想来就来，不想来也没关系。我也一样。”

他放下棋子，把点心袋朝你那边推了一寸。“吃吧。三座山那本书里的主角会为此骄傲的——而他能骄傲的东西可不多。”

choices.text: 那我也选它。选这份完完整整的友情。
choices.response:
塞伦的神色没有太大变化，但他的肩膀松了下来，就像确认过退路无恙时的那种放松。

“好，”他简单地说。“那我们说定了，而且谁都不是被谁救进这份约定里的。”

他把下一枚棋子在指间翻过一面，落下去时带着一点轻快。“该你了。不许急——我们有一整个晚上，而且现在知道，往后还有的是。”

choices.text: （打开点心袋，把他那份摆在他面前。）
choices.response:
塞伦看看点心，再看看你，他眼里的东西比灯光还要暖。

“这就足够作答了，”他说。“比我所能给出的任何回答都更慢，也更好。”

他把自己那份掰成两半，将一半放到你手边——一个小小的、刻意的动作，一个字也没提。棋盘在一旁静静等着，一点也不着急。

episodes.ending:
棋局结束时棋盘几乎摆满，却没有分出明显的胜负，塞伦宣布，对于这样一个夜晚，这正是最恰当的结局。

离开之前，他出于原则把书架掸了灰，还写了一张短笺给书店的朋友，说明自己借了哪本书。钥匙放回砖下。

外面，集市街一片安静，森林边缘只有一段路远。他在街角停下，顺着路望向他的小屋。

“那第二把椅子我就留在原处了，”他说。“它已经证明了自己的用处。”

然后他抬起手，从容地挥了挥，转身回家——归途畅通，下一次见面，由你在合适的时候自己决定。就是这样，而以他信任的任何一种标准来衡量，这都是很好的一天。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 不穿铠甲的散步
romance.opening:
傍晚时分，小镇外的湖畔十分安静。水面平得能映出天色，岸边那些灰色的石头，正是你记得的第一个打水漂的清晨所见的那一批。

你到达时，塞伦已经坐在那块干燥的岩石上，身旁放着一个用布包着的篮子。他的斗篷没有披在身上，而是叠好垫在身下，他的剑也不见踪影。这是你第一次见到他两样都不带。

当你的脚步声传到他那里时，他抬起头，脸上的惊讶一闪而过，随即化为某种更温暖的神情。“你找到这个地方了。我还担心是我描述得不好。”

“鸟儿比你先到，”他朝浅滩那边点了点头。“不过它们不介意有伴。随便坐吧，这块岩石够宽，坐得下两个人，只要你不嫌它凉。”

空气中弥漫着水和干草的气味。树线后面，回镇的路只有短短一段。他注意到你朝那边看了一眼，点了点头，仿佛在说：是的，那条路一直都在。
romance.dialogue:
塞伦等你坐定，才转过身来，正面朝向你。他缓缓吸了一口气——你见过他在说出要紧的话之前的那种呼吸。

“我想坦白地问你一件事，好让你也能坦白地回答，”他说。“护送结束后，在回程的路上，我问你愿不愿意和我约会，你答应了。从那时起，我就一直期待着今天。但期待一件事，并不等于它依然成立。”

他把双手放在膝上。没有铠甲，没有剑，没有任何可以让这些话语躲藏的东西。“所以现在轮到你选了。你还想和我交往吗？不是出于礼貌，也不是因为我跑了这一趟。只说你真正想要的是什么。”

湖水静静拍打着岸，而他安静地等待。他没有用话语填补沉默，也没有把问题软化为更轻松的版本。他的目光一直停留在你身上，耐心地，就像在勘察线上等待任何人迈出第一步时那样。

“如果答案变了，那也是一个诚实的答案，”他说。“我们依然有满满一篮食物和一个下午，哪一样都不会浪费。但如果它没有变，我会非常想听你亲口说出来。”

choices.text: 是的。我还想和你交往。
choices.response:
塞伦的肩膀放松下来，脸上浮现出一个不加掩饰的微笑。“好，”他说。“那么我的心意也没有变。”

他把篮子提到你们之间那块共享的岩石上，解开布包：面包、一罐密封的温和洋葱汤，还有两块分别包好的点心。“一人一块。我是特意在同一趟买齐的。”

汤简单而温暖。他吃得慢条斯理，还讲起一本书——他差点只因封面画得太糟就把它买下来，封面上那位英雄翻过一整条山脉，却没停下来吃过一顿午饭。“到最后他就晕倒了，”他说，“是草药师救的他。书里把这写成转折。我看是报应。”

吃完后，他擦了擦手，望向水面。“下周同一时间？那家会让人忍不住买第二块点心的摊位，集市日会在镇上。我可以先陪你逛，然后我们再回到这里。”他等着你答应，或者提出别的安排，仿佛任何一种回答都会让他同样高兴。

choices.text: （伸出手，覆在他的手上，然后说出“是的”。）
choices.response:
他低头看了看覆在他手上的那只手，然后抬眼望向你。“这是答应了吗？”他问道，想确认这句话和这个动作说的是同一件事。

当你大声说出来时，他在你的手心下翻转手掌，手心朝上，轻轻握住，像是在体会它的重量。“那么我的心意也一样。我依然想要这份关系。”

他又多握了片刻，然后空出的那只手打开篮子。“汤撑过了这一路。这是我全部的贡献，所以你可以就此评判我。”

你们在那块冰凉的岩石上一起用餐，他的肩膀挨着你的肩膀，整个下午以流水的速度缓缓过去。光线转成金色之前，他轻声说：“下周镇上有集市。先陪我走走，然后我们再回到这里结束这一天。”他等着你的回答，而不是擅自假定。当你答应后，他满足地点了一下头，开始盘算先去逛哪个摊位。

romance.ending:
太阳低低地沉向水面，鸟儿们在浅滩安顿下来。你们俩都不急着离开，所以谁也没有动。

当光线终于开始暗淡时，塞伦收拾好空罐子，用他对待剑一般的小心把布包好。他送你到树线那里，然后在边缘停下脚步。

“那么，下周见，”他说。“先逛集市，再来这里。如果我们中有人来不了，就说出来，另选一天。不需要什么誓言。”说到这里他笑了，笑意虽小，却很笃定。

他一直望着你走上那条路，你听见身后他拿起斗篷和篮子的声音，不慌不忙，以自己的节奏走自己的路。回镇的小路在暮色中不难辨认，而路的前方，是一个已经选定的日子，正等着你们两个人。

episodes.title: Three Knocks and an Umbrella
episodes.opening:
The corner shop sells umbrellas, batteries, and news you didn't ask for.

Rain has pinned everyone under the awning, including a stranger with silver hair and a translucent coat that beads water like a windshield.

A small light glows near their ear.

They are holding a folded umbrella upside down, studying it the way a jeweler studies a forged ring.

When the door chimes for another customer, they turn toward the sound and record something on a slim slate.

Then they notice you noticing, and straighten with visible effort, like someone remembering a body has posture.
episodes.ending:
The rain thins to a drizzle.

You end up sharing the dry strip of awning, one closed umbrella standing between you like a chaperone.

Sora-7 writes one last line on the slate and angles it so you can read it: ITEM ACQUIRED.

LESSON PENDING.

They look at the wet street, then at you, and seem to be waiting for the shape of an answer.

Whatever you say next, they will record it carefully, and the corner will be a slightly different place tomorrow.
episodes.dialogue:
Sora-7: Good evening.

I knocked three times according to your etiquette.

Is that too forward?

I have since learned that knocking is for doors, and this is a shop.

Corrections have been made.

I am Sora-7, interstellar archivist, currently... locally based.

My transport made an unscheduled stop in your atmosphere and has not made a scheduled departure since.

This umbrella is for the rain.

The rain appears to be winning an argument with me.

I have been standing here for eleven minutes, and in that time I have observed that humans carry these closed, then open them at the threshold, then close them again indoors, wet.

Is the wetness part of the ritual?

I ask because the clerk answered my first three questions with a smile and my fourth with a phone call to someone he described as his manager, which I believe is either a rank or a threat.

You have been watching me for four of those eleven minutes.

That is not an accusation.

I archive what I see.

You watch with what I would call a kind expression, though my taxonomy of human expressions is only forty percent complete and self-graded.

May I ask a practical question?

When a stranger holds a door for you here, what is owed?

I have received three conflicting reports.

One says nothing.

One says thanks.

One says a small nod, but only if the door was heavy.

The variance is troubling at scale.

If I cannot calibrate a door, I worry what I will do with a farewell.

I am told your species considers farewells very important, and I have a machine at my campsite that agrees with them more than I would like.

So: the door question.

You seem like a reliable primary source.

I will record your answer verbatim, and I will not embellish it, even if it would make a better story.

That is my one professional vow.

Record truth, not myth.

Mostly I made the vow because myths are harder to alphabetize.

choices.text: A simple thanks is always safe. Nobody audits it.
choices.response:
Sora-7 writes it down, then underlines it twice.

A simple thanks.

Always safe.

No audit.

They look up, genuinely relieved, as if a small cosmic weight has been reclassified as a small local one.

Then they say, That is efficient.

My species admires efficiency.

We would have added a form.

They ask your name for the citation line, and when you give it, they repeat it once, carefully, like setting down glassware.

The recorder by their ear pulses softly.

Filed, they say.

You are now my first verified source on Earth.

Please do not retire.

choices.text: (Silently take the umbrella from their hands, flip it right side up, and hand it back.)
choices.response:
Sora-7 watches the rotation with the stillness of someone observing a solar eclipse.

Ah, they say.

Orientation.

The canopy faces the sky.

That is... yes.

That explains the clerk's face.

They take it back with both hands and bow slightly, an angle you suspect is calibrated rather than casual.

They turn the umbrella over twice more, confirming the lesson, then record the event in full: an unnamed human performed a silent correction, and the correction was accepted.

They tell you this is the best kind of entry.

One action, zero ambiguity.

Their records are full of arguments; this one is just a fact.

episodes.title: The Bird That Wore a Box
episodes.opening:
The park is the kind with a broken fountain and a bench that faces the good tree.

Sora-7 is already there when you arrive, sitting exactly in the middle, hands flat on their knees, a thermos beside them labeled in three alphabets.

They stand when they see you, sit, then stand again, visibly negotiating etiquette.

Their slate is propped against the thermos, cycling through photographs: starfields, a cargo bay, and one image that is unmistakably a bird standing on a luggage cart with a foam packing box on its head.

They pat the bench beside them.

Not the middle.

They have learned about edges.
episodes.ending:
The fountain gurgles its half-hearted gurgle.

Sora-7 closes the archive with the reluctance of someone ending a good chapter, then opens a new file and titles it aloud: Local Sources, Volume One.

Your name goes at the top.

They explain, with complete seriousness, that a verified source who also laughs is statistically priceless, and that they intend to protect this dataset.

Then they ask what you do on this planet when the weather is good and there is no work, because they have observed kites in the park and have a hypothesis about strings.

It is, you realize, an invitation.

You have until next weekend to prepare an answer.
episodes.dialogue:
Sora-7: You came.

I prepared two greetings.

The one for an empty bench was shorter.

Before anything else: an update.

My return chart is sixty percent complete.

The rest is what my instructor called the hard part.

I call it sitting very still.

Now, a confession.

I have been reviewing my trainee files, back when I worked the route archive station, and I found a record I have never shown anyone.

I did not know it was shareable.

May I show you?

I will narrate.

This is the cargo deck of a transport I served on, my second posting.

Trainees washed the travel photographs by hand then, and we pinned the good ones above the sorting desk.

These are mine.

This one is a nebula, standard.

This one is a dockworker asleep on a crate, also standard.

And this one—this is the reason I kept the file.

Do you see the bird?

A long-legged bird, species unverified, that boarded at a fueling stop and refused all eviction notices.

It took up residence on the luggage cart.

We named it Crew.

Then one day a foam packing crate fell from a shelf, and—there.

Do you see.

The box landed on its head.

Perfectly.

Like a helmet.

And the bird did not remove it.

It walked the deck for two full shifts wearing that box, bumping gently into things, and the entire crew did not work.

We laughed until the senior archivist fined us for noise.

I laughed so hard I had to sit on the floor, which trainees are not supposed to do, so I sat on the floor in a way that looked like inventory.

Here is my question, and I have carried it for a long time: someone should have taken the box off.

It was the obvious kind act.

I was closest, and I did not.

I only laughed.

So I want to know—later, when the record blurs, who took it off the bird?

And the answer, when I finally pulled the maintenance log, was: no one.

The bird itself shook it off, here, this frame, mid-stride, box tumbling, entirely unassisted.

It never needed us at all.

We needed it.

That whole shift, the deck was behind schedule and everyone was happy, and it was because of a bird in a box that rescued itself.

I filed it under HUMOR at the time.

I now think it belongs under something larger.

I am still looking for the word in your language.

Some words, I have decided, deserve to be found rather than assigned.

choices.text: Maybe the word is gift. It gave you the laughing, and asked nothing back.
choices.response:
Sora-7 goes very still, then writes the word down in their alphabet and in yours.

Gift, they repeat.

An exchange where one side does not know it is trading.

They look at the bird photo for a long moment.

Then the file is misfiled on purpose, they say.

I will move it to a new category and name the category after this conversation.

They tell you, formally, that you have now contributed to the interstellar route archive, and that the contribution will carry your citation.

Then, off duty, they admit the truth: they have read many human records about laughter, and this is the first time they have heard one described from the inside.

They would like more of those.

Inside descriptions.

From you specifically.

choices.text: (Quietly tap the photo of the bird, box mid-fall, frozen mid-stride.)
choices.response:
Sora-7 follows your finger to the frame and enlarges it.

The bird, one leg lifted, the box tipping, caught at the exact instant before freedom.

You did not say anything, they observe.

You only pointed.

That is also an answer.

They study it again and something in their posture settles.

I was not the one who helped, they say slowly, but I was the one who kept the record.

Perhaps that is my version of the act.

Someone must remember the bird was magnificent.

They save the enlarged frame as a new file header, then, unexpectedly, they laugh—a short, careful sound, clearly practiced from recordings but real.

They note the date.

First unsupervised laugh: witnessed.

episodes.title: The Kite at Wave Height
episodes.opening:
The park has set up folding tables for kite painting, and a volunteer with a laminated clipboard is already regretting the glitter.

Sora-7 sits among the children with perfect posture, sleeves rolled to the elbow, a half-painted paper kite before them and seven brushes arranged in a precise row.

A name tag on their coat reads SORA in careful handwriting.

When they spot you they light up in the restrained way of someone who has practiced lighting up.

They pat the empty chair beside them.

On the table, a small sign reads: PAINT YOUR JOURNEY.

Sora-7 has clearly taken this literally.
episodes.ending:
The volunteer calls it a day, and the sky begins to sort itself into evening.

Sora-7 carries the kite under one arm like a colleague.

At the park gate they stop and look back once at the empty sky, then log something on their slate.

They tell you the file for today is already complete, which is unusual—usually they are still adding footnotes for weeks.

Then they ask, in the careful voice they use for real questions, whether the park does this again next season, and whether some things on this planet are rhythms.

You get the feeling that whatever you answer will end up in an archive light-years from here, filed under the name of someone who sat down next to a stranger with a paintbrush.
episodes.dialogue:
Sora-7: You came.

I calculated you might not, so I prepared two greetings, one for each outcome.

The other one was shorter.

Before anything else: an update.

My return chart is at sixty percent completion.

The remaining forty percent is what my instructor used to call the hard part and what I call the part where I sit very still.

Now, today's assignment.

The sign says paint your journey, and I have decided to comply literally.

This is a transport vessel—the kind I served on for my second posting.

From a distance, a ship is a dot.

Up close, it is corridors and noise and a dockworker asleep on a crate.

So I am painting it from what I am calling wave height: the altitude where you can still see the whole ship and still see the people in it.

Two yellow windows so far.

And at the rail, a hand.

I painted it huge, and the children have been asking why.

Here is my reasoning.

From the ground, a real hand would be too small to see.

A hand this size says: someone is aboard, and they are glad of it.

Somewhere far off, someone may look up and wave back at a painted hand on a paper kite.

That is not accuracy.

That is reach.

The volunteer says my silver is the most optimistic color on the table.

I have decided to accept this as a professional review.

Now, one problem remains, and it requires a second archivist.

The hull line has to run unbroken from bow to tail ribbon, and my hands are archive hands—they hesitate at anything important.

Will you hold the paper steady while I paint it?

If it wobbles, the record shows a dent, and I would rather the dent be a shared one.

That is the whole plan for today.

A ship, a hand, two windows, and a line drawn by four hands instead of two.

After that, we fly it, and we find out whether the sky agrees with the design.

choices.text: The big hand is a good idea. Somewhere far off, someone will wave back.
choices.response:
Sora-7 holds the kite at arm's length and studies the oversized hand.

You think it will be seen, they say.

That is the purpose, then.

Not accuracy.

Reach.

They add a second stroke of silver to make the hand brighter, then sign the corner of the kite in their own alphabet and, underneath, in careful printed letters, yours.

Co-credited.

The volunteer, passing with her clipboard, squints at the design and says it is the most optimistic ship she has seen all day.

Sora-7 thanks her with a small nod—heavy door protocol, applied to compliments—and tells you quietly that the entry for today will need two names, and that this is the first file in their career with that feature.

choices.text: (Silently dip a brush and paint a small passenger in one of the two yellow windows.)
choices.response:
Sora-7 watches the small passenger appear in one of the two yellow windows and does not move for a moment.

A passenger, they say.

You have added a passenger.

They lean in and inspect your brushwork with archival gravity, then take their own brush and add a tiny railing outside that window, so the passenger has somewhere to stand.

The little girl at the next table leans over and announces that the ship has someone in it now.

Correct, Sora-7 tells her solemnly.

It did not before.

They record the amendment on their slate—vessel modified by local collaborator, structural and emotional—and when they look up, they are doing the practiced lighting-up again, but badly, which means sincerely.

episodes.title: The Postcard Machine
episodes.opening:
The boardwalk at dusk smells like fried batter and salt.
