He holds up the jacket to show you the inside — and there, pinned into the existing inner pocket, is a spare electrical fuse, fat and slightly scorched at one end.

'This one blew three weeks ago.

I keep it as a reminder.'

He threads the needle again, squinting.

'Here's the story, since you're stuck here anyway.

I was on with a guy who works nights at the container docks.

Good caller.

Regular.

He's telling me about their warehouse — half the lights just died over there, whole dock in the dark — and mid-sentence, my whole signal drops.

Dead air.

You know what dead air on pirate radio feels like?

Like the ocean swallowed you.'

He ties off a stitch, bites the thread.

'Because it was me.

The tap — the line I run this whole station on — sparked in the junction box at the exact same second his warehouse went down.

Same grid.

Same overloaded night.

I took his story and made it my blackout.'

He laughs, but there's a flat note under it.

'Phone rang again almost before I'd gotten the board back up.

Same guy.

He called back in the dark, from the dock, just to finish his story.

He didn't even care that I'd vanished.

He just wanted someone to hear the ending.'

Diego sets the jacket down and finally looks at you.

'When I hung up, I realized both my pant legs were soaked through.

I'd been standing in a puddle the whole time fixing the line and never noticed.

So the next day I started a second inner pocket.'

He pats the fresh stitching.

'For the new fuse.

When this one blows.

Call it a memorial.

The station carries a lot of bills, and most of them aren't money.'

The song ends.

He flips the mic live, tells his listeners the rain sounds better with company, and slides a fresh voicemail tape into the deck — the box of them behind you is nearly full now, years of strangers' voices on cassette.

'One day I'll sit down and listen to all of them straight through,' he says.

'One day when the line holds.'

choices.text: Then get a legal line before the next fuse blows — the listeners would rather lose a night than lose you.
choices.response:
Diego is quiet for a moment, which for Diego is a geological event.

'I know,' he says finally.

'I've known for three years.

But going dark to fix it means nights when nobody's on this frequency.

And the people who are only awake at 3 a.m. — they don't reschedule their loneliness.'

He picks the needle back up, working the stitch slower now.

'I'll think about it.

That's not nothing.

Coming from me, thinking about it is practically a signed contract.'

He doesn't promise, and you both hear the shape of what he didn't say.

choices.text: (You pick up the second needle from his kit and hold the jacket seam taut for him.)
choices.response:
He blinks at you, then huffs a laugh and keeps stitching.

'Okay.

Assistant seamstress of the resistance.

Don't let this go on your résumé.'

The two of you finish the pocket together in silence broken only by rain and the low hum of the board.

When it's done, he slides the scorched fuse into the old pocket and holds the jacket up like a finished flag.

'Two pockets.

One for what blew, one for what will.

That's the whole station in a jacket, honestly.'

He says it lightly, but he wears the jacket the rest of the night like it matters.

episodes.ending:
The rain eases near dawn and the last caller signs off.

Diego walks you down as far as the first landing, jacket on now, both pockets loaded, and stands there a beat longer than usual.

'Same stairs tomorrow,' he says.

'Bring nothing.

You're the only thing on the schedule I never want to cross off.'

Below, the noodle stall's lantern flickers on for the morning shift, and the tower hums above you both, holding, for now.

episodes.title: Six A.M. Supply Ship
episodes.opening:
Diego calls you at an hour he never calls anyone: not 3 a.m., but 2 a.m., voice low and urgent and trying to sound casual about it.

'Are you busy?

Don't answer that.

Come up.

Bring your walking shoes.'

When you reach the control room he's got a record sleeve in his hands — plain kraft paper, no label except one song title handwritten in careful ink.

'A listener sent this,' he says.

'The pharmacy-night-shift one.

She writes me letters about all the people who come in at night who can't sleep and can't get help.

And in her first letter, she requested one song.

This song.

And now she's sent me the record itself.

Only problem—' he turns it over, helpless — 'I don't own anything that plays records.'
episodes.dialogue:
He lays the sleeve on the mixing board like it's evidence.

'Look at this.

Handwritten.

Just the song name — the exact one from her first letter.

She remembered her own request from a year ago.

No, seriously, who does that?

Who keeps track of what they asked a stranger on the radio to play?'

He paces the small room, stepping over colored wires.

'I can't play it.

I can't frame it and hang it up, that's not what she sent it for.

She sent it so the song would go out over the city, at night, for everyone awake who can't sleep — the people she stands across a counter from and can't fix.'

He stops pacing.

'And here's the part where it gets complicated.

The supply ship that carries turntables — actual equipment, the only reliable channel for it — lifts off at six a.m. from the east docks.

The pawnshop two districts over has one turntable left, the owner told me on the phone, and he lives above the shop, and it's already two-thirty, and the rain from last week turned half those streets into a river again.'

He looks at you, and for once he isn't performing the dilemma, he's actually in it.

'I could wait for the next ship.

It's a month out.

Or I could go now, in the dark, through the flooded streets, wake up a pawnshop owner, and make the six a.m. boat.

If I miss it, the record waits a month.

If the tower line sparks while I'm gone, the station goes dark with nobody at the board.'

He grabs his jacket — the one with two pockets now — and holds it without putting it on.

'I'm going.

I already know I'm going.

The question is whether I'm going alone and whether the board sits empty.'

He glances at the deck, the live light, the sleeping city.

'I've never left the board with someone else sitting at it.

That's not a small thing for me.

But you're not nobody, and the song can't wait a month.

She wrote that letter a year ago.

She's waited long enough.'

choices.text: I'll hold the board — play the tapes, keep the light on. Go get the turntable.
choices.response:
Diego stares at you for three full seconds, then moves — jacket on, portable recorder grabbed, a scribbled page of board instructions pressed into your hands.

'Fader up for tapes, nothing else, if it sparks, kill the red switch and do NOT be a hero.'

At the door he turns back.

'You know what this means?

At 3 a.m. tonight, someone's still listening — and for the first time, someone's still broadcasting.'

He's gone down the stairs two at a time, and the tower is yours, humming, alive, the needles breathing under your hand.

choices.text: (You pull on your own jacket and point at the door — you're coming with him.)
choices.response:
Diego's whole face changes.

'Both of us?

Then the board goes dark for two hours and I don't care — no, I do care, but less.'

He kills the transmitter properly, leaves a note taped to the deck for any listener who somehow climbs two hundred stairs, and holds the door.

The flooded streets are slow going, streetlights doubled in the water, and he talks the whole way — about the letters, the pharmacy counter, the song — and when the pawnshop's deadbolt finally gives at 3:40 a.m., the owner blinking at him dripping and you beside him holding a record sleeve, Diego laughs like the whole night was worth it.

episodes.ending:
The turntable reaches the east docks before six, and the crate goes out on the supply ship with the handwritten sleeve riding on top.

Two days later a turntable arrives at the tower, and at 3 a.m. sharp the needle drops — the crackle mixing with rain-washed neon light through the porthole.

Diego lets the whole song play without saying a word, which is the longest silence of his career.

Afterward he only says: 'That was for the night shift.

She knows who she is.'

He never mentions the flooded streets again — but the record lives at the tower now, sleeve worn soft at the corners from being handled.

episodes.title: The Fever Broadcast
episodes.opening:
The broadcast goes strange tonight — Diego's voice, still warm, keeps losing its footing mid-sentence, words sliding a half-beat late.

When the last caller hangs up at 4 a.m., he mutes the mic and puts his head down on the mixing board like it's a pillow he's been promised for years.

His forehead, when he lifts it, is unmistakably flushed.

'I'm fine,' he says, in a voice that is not fine.

'Totally fine.

The tower's fine.

Everyone's fine.'

He coughs.

The tower hums around you both, indifferent.
episodes.dialogue:
He tries to stand and thinks better of it, sitting back down on the stool with a thud.

'Okay.

Slight fever.

Slight.

It's the rain season, everyone's got it.

Aunt Dolores sent up soup yesterday, I'm basically cured already.'

He gestures at the mic without realizing it, the way he always does, as if the listeners could see him.

'Here's the actual situation, because you'd figure it out in five minutes anyway.

I've got a fever, and I do not stop shows.

Ever.

Three years, never missed a night.

Because the whole point — the entire point — is that nobody at 3 a.m. turns the dial and finds silence.'

He rubs his face.

'But I can barely string a sentence together, and you heard me up there.

I was cooking the words.

So I've been sitting here for an hour doing math I don't like.'

He turns the stool to face you, and his voice drops out of radio cadence into something plainer.

'Option one.

You sit at the board and play the tapes.

The voicemail tapes — the whole box, three years of them.

I've never aired them straight, it's always been me talking around them.

But they're real, they're the realest thing I own, and the station would still be a heartbeat even if it's not my heartbeat.'

He coughs again, grinning through it.

'Option two — and this is the one I keep almost not saying.

I go down the stairs, right now, tonight, and I stay at Aunt Dolores's stall until this fever breaks.

Days, maybe.

Which means the tower goes dark.

First entire night dark in three years — not the two hours I once lost to a pawnshop run, a whole night, nights, with nobody at the board.

And I keep a spare fuse in my jacket because I know exactly how this station dies, and I know exactly what it costs to keep it alive, and I have never once let myself find out what happens if I just... put it down for a week.'

He looks at you, fever-bright and honest.

'I'm not asking you to decide for me.

I'm asking which of us I'm more afraid of disappointing.

No, seriously — that's the whole math.

So tell me what you see from out there.

The listeners.

The stairs.

You.'

choices.text: Play the tapes with me tonight — then take the week. And Diego... I don't want to be just the listener who climbs the stairs. Be mine.
choices.response:
Something in Diego's face unclenches.

'You think they'd wait?'

he asks, and you tell him, and he believes you, or believes you enough.

That night you sit shoulder to shoulder at the board while he narrates the tapes in a wrecked, happy voice — Dolores's storm rant, the dock caller's unfinished story, a hundred strangers saying someone's still listening.

At dawn he stands at the top of the stairs, fever and all, and says: 'One week.

If the antenna's still standing when I come back, I'll know it can survive without me.

That might be the best thing this station ever does for me.'

Then, softer, off the fader: 'And — yes.

To the other thing you said.

Ask me again when I'm not radioactive with fever, but yes.'

He goes down slowly, and the tower hums behind you, unowned and alive.

choices.text: (You pull the stool closer, take the spare fuse from his jacket pocket, and set it on the board between you — you're staying through the fever with him.)
choices.response:
Diego looks at the fuse, then at you, and laughs until he coughs.

'You're going to nurse the pirate radio guy through a fever in a water tower.

That's going in the tapes.

That's going in the LEGEND.'

He lets you steer him to the cot in the back room and, for the first time in three years, the broadcast goes to tape and silence and the hum of the tower — and nobody dies of it.

He sleeps in actual stretches.

When the fever breaks two days later, he finds you asleep in the chair by the board and doesn't wake you, just sits there listening to the tapes quietly, wearing his jacket with both pockets full.

episodes.ending:
A week later the tower is standing, the show is his again, and something has shifted in the way he says 'we' when he talks about the station.

He stands at the board with the fever fully gone and tells his listeners, on air, that the station learned it has more than one heartbeat.

Then, off-air, quieter, he asks if you're free this weekend — not for a broadcast, not for a shift.

Just for something.

He won't say what.

He's smiling, which means it matters.

episodes.title: Sorting the Tapes
episodes.opening:
The weekend thing turns out to be this: the entire control room floor covered in cassette tapes.

Hundreds of them, in wobbly stacks, sorted into rough piles that Diego keeps rearranging and then un-rearranging.

He's wearing the bomber jacket even though it's warm in the tower, both pockets bulging, and there's a pot of Aunt Dolores's soup keeping warm on a hotplate by the board.

'Okay,' he says, cracking his knuckles.

'Three years of voicemails.

We're listening to all of them, we're labeling them, and we're building the archive.

This is my weekend.

This is my Super Bowl.'
episodes.dialogue:
He slots the first tape and a stranger's voice fills the room — someone crying gently at 3 a.m. three years ago, and then laughing, because Diego said something dumb and kind and it worked.

Diego beams like he's hearing it for the first time.

'That's the whole station in ninety seconds,' he says.

'That's why it has to be real.

You can steal the signal.

You can steal the power, technically I would know —' he pats his jacket pocket — 'but you can't fake that.

That person was alone and then, for ninety seconds, was not.'

The two of you work through the afternoon.

He tells the story behind every third tape — the dock caller who finished his story in the dark, the pharmacy letter-writer whose record still sits by the turntable, sleeve worn soft.

Somewhere around tape two hundred, he goes quiet, holding one cassette and looking at it.

'This is the storm night,' he says.

'Dolores's slot.

The one that spun empty through the whole rain.'

He loads it anyway, and the tape hisses — an hour of storm sound and silence — except at the very end, faint, there's a knock and Dolores's voice, recorded from the flooded alley: an apology, a laugh, a promise to call next storm.

Diego sits back.

'She made it onto the empty tape.

She was there the whole time at the end of it.'

He writes the label slowly, in careful ink: DOLORES — STORM NIGHT — SHE CAME BACK.

Then he looks up at you across the floor of tapes, and his voice goes off-radio, plain and certain.

'I want to say something and I want you to hear all of it.

This station used to be mine.

Then you climbed the stairs, and you sat with me through a fever, and you helped get that record on the air — and somewhere in there it stopped being mine and started being ours.

Not on paper.

There's no paper.

But I'm telling you it's true.'

He holds up the felt pen.

'So.

Co-archivist.

There's a chair at this board with your name on it if you want it painted on.

Not a job — I don't pay, there IS no pay.

Just this: as long as the antenna's standing, this is yours too.

No, seriously.

I mean it exactly like that.'

choices.text: Paint the chair. But we split the archive work — you listen, I label, and neither of us does a storm night alone again.
choices.response:
Diego laughs so hard he has to put the pen down.

'Deal.

Split shifts.

Nobody wades through floodwater solo ever again — that clause goes in the invisible contract.'

He paints the chair that afternoon, DIEGO AND — and stops, and hands YOU the pen for the second half, because he says it has to be your handwriting.

The finished chair sits at the board with both names on it, slightly crooked, slightly perfect.

That night's show, he introduces the co-archivist on air, and the switchboard lights up with three years of listeners who somehow already knew.

choices.text: (You take the felt pen and add your name under his on the tape box lid, then slide Dolores's storm tape into the first slot of the new archive shelf.)
choices.response:
Diego watches you write and doesn't say anything for a long moment, which for him is a geological event.

Then, quietly: 'Yeah.

That's exactly right.

First tape in the archive is hers.'

The two of you build the shelf together through the evening, slot by slot, soup going cold and getting reheated twice.

By dawn the archive stands finished against the wire-tangled wall, and the storm tape sits in slot one, labeled, found.

Diego stands back with his hands in his jacket pockets and says the tower finally feels like it has a floor under it.

episodes.ending:
The archive stands full against the tower wall, Dolores's storm tape in its place. The chair at the board is yours.

The show goes on at 3 a.m., some nights his voice, some nights yours, some nights both, and the listeners can't always tell who's who — which Diego says is the best review the station ever got.

When the next storm comes, Dolores calls in, on time, on slot seven, and both of you are there to answer.

As long as the antenna's standing, it's yours too.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Slot Seven, Filled
romance.opening:
The weekend thing turns out to be this: the entire control room floor covered in cassette tapes.

Hundreds of them, in wobbly stacks, sorted into rough piles Diego keeps rearranging and un-rearranging.

He's wearing the bomber jacket despite the warmth, both pockets bulging, Dolores's soup keeping warm on a hotplate by the board.

But tonight he's distracted — checking the clock more than the tapes — because tonight, for the first time in three years, slot seven is going to be filled on purpose.

Dolores promised to call in at 3 a.m. sharp, storm or no storm.
romance.dialogue:
At 2:58 he's already hovering by the phone line, adjusting things that don't need adjusting.

'She never makes appointments,' he tells you.

'Thirty years at that stall, and in the three years this station's existed, every storm night she just — calls.

Tonight I asked her at the stall and she said yes like it was obvious.

No, seriously, she said, of course, mijo, I've been calling you for years, it's about time you invited me properly.'

The clock turns.

The phone rings.

He answers on air, and Dolores's voice fills the tower — loud, warm, teasing him about his fever, about the soup, about the girl from the pharmacy letters who apparently also listens.

The whole city gets to hear Diego Salazar get fussed over by a noodle-stall aunt for ten unbroken minutes, and he lets it happen, laughing, gesturing at the mic, eyes shiny.

When she hangs up, he sits down slowly on the stool.

'Three years ago,' he says, and it's not for the audience anymore, or not only, 'a stranger called this station and said three words: someone's still listening.

That's why any of this exists.

That's why the fuse in my pocket, the tapes, the flood, all of it.

And somewhere in the last few months, that stopped being a story I tell on air and started being a thing that's true every single night, because you're on the other end of it.'

He turns the stool to face you, and his voice drops out of radio cadence entirely — plain, a little unsteady, entirely his.

'I've been trying to figure out how to say this without a script.

There's no script for it.

So here it is, no seriously, here it is:

I want you to be the person the stairs lead to.

Both directions.

I want the 3 a.m. calls and the 3 p.m. soup and the flooded streets and the boring ones too.

I want to know if you want that — and if the answer's no, the chair at this board is still yours and always was, and I will never make it strange.

But if it's yes—' he laughs, nervous, real — 'then slot seven isn't empty anymore.

It's got you in it.'

choices.text: Yes. Both directions. I'll take the stairs and the slot — put me on the tape, Diego, I want it on the record.
choices.response:
Diego's whole face does something unguarded and bright, and he reaches over — one brief, warm press of his hand over yours on the board, there and gone, like a signature.

'On the record,' he repeats, and then, because he is who he is, he actually does it: flips to the tape deck, records himself saying it — the date, the tower, the two names — and files it in the archive with a label in careful ink.

On air, he tells the listeners the station has news but he's keeping it, just this once, for himself.

The switchboard lights up anyway.

They always know.

choices.text: (You pick up the felt pen and write your name and his on the storm tape's blank label, then hand it back to him.)
choices.response:
Diego takes the tape, reads both names, and understands completely.

'Slot seven,' he says, hoarse.

'You just filled it yourself.'

He slots the tape into seven, where it will live, and presses his hand briefly over yours on the board — one warm moment, then back, both of you grinning like fools at a mixing board at 3:20 in the morning.

Dolores calls back ten minutes later because she heard the pause in his voice on air, and he tells her everything, and the whole city gets to hear him happy.

romance.ending:
Slot seven stays filled.

The archive grows, and the show goes on at 3 a.m. — some nights his voice, some nights yours, some nights both, trading sentences like a duet.

Diego still keeps a spare fuse in his jacket, still says yes to every caller, still fears the night the antenna comes down.

But now the fear has an answer, and it lives two hundred stairs away and also right beside him.

As long as the antenna's standing, he's here — and so are you, and the signal might be stolen, but nothing else about it is.

episodes.title: 第七格
episodes.opening:
凌晨两点五十一分，热线电话响了，迭戈照例第二声就接起——一边喘气一边直播，戴着单边耳机，塔下的城市嗡嗡作响。

在电波里，他是一张没有脸的声音。

但今晚播音室的门没锁——你凭着一个传闻和一条借来的频率爬上塔来，还没决定要不要敲门，他已经在朝你招手了。

控制室里有股暖烘烘的灰尘和旧磁带的味道。

他身后的架子上，七个贴了标签的格子一字排开，第七格里躺着一盘完全没有标签的磁带。
episodes.dialogue:
迭戈把话筒静音了一秒，咧嘴笑着，好像你带给他的是件礼物。

“你居然真的一步步爬上来了。

没人这么干。

大家都是打电话、写信、听着我的节目入睡——可没人会在凌晨三点爬两百级生锈的梯子。”

他朝整个房间比划了一圈，电线、调音台，蓝紫色的光从舷窗透进来。

“欢迎来到我的帝国。

其实就一座水塔。

说真的——这就是帝国的全部了。”

他转回调音台前，推了推一个推子，目光落在第七格上。

笑容淡了一点，没消失，只是低了些。

“那格空了一阵子了。

是多洛雷斯阿姨的格子。

她在这座塔脚下摆了个面摊——三十年，同一个角落。

每个暴风雨夜，雷打不动，她都会打进来，骂我净放些伤心的歌。

上次那场大雨，第七格就那么空转了一整个风暴，没有人打来。”

他没拿起那盘磁带，只是轻轻敲了敲。

“有位听众来信说，她那天早上没出摊。

于是我带着便携录音机，蹚过积水去看她。

她没事——第一件事居然是跟我道歉。

为耽误节目道歉。

你敢信吗？

她站在被淹的小巷里，跟电台主持人道歉。”

他笑了，但比平时轻了些。

“我反正把她那段数落全录下来了。

就在那盘带上。

我总想给它贴个标签，又一直没贴。

空着的格子不用擦掉，对吧？

就留着那个位置，等那个人回来。”

直播的指示灯闪烁起来。

他把话筒切回直播，告诉听众有位朋友一路爬了上来，然后，避开推子，轻描淡写地——其实一点也不轻——问了那个问题：“那么——我该怎么称呼你？

这个台上的每个人都有名字。

只不过我的一般有一半是编的。”

choices.text: 听众怎么叫我就怎么叫吧——我能爬上来，说明我首先是个听众。
choices.response:
迭戈仰头大笑，是那种真心的笑，然后凑近话筒宣布：水塔迎来了史上第一位爬楼梯上来的听众，就在凌晨三点的直播里。

热线立刻亮了，一堆人打进来求证这事是不是真的。

他任由大家猜了整整一分钟，笑得很开心，然后拉过一把椅子放在你旁边，近到能看清调音台上指针的呼吸。

“首先是个听众。”他重复了一遍，像在把这句话收进什么安全的地方。

“这是这个台上最好的头衔。

打进电话的人来来去去。

听的人才留下来。”

choices.text: （你轻轻敲了敲第七格里那盘没贴标签的磁带，看着他。）
choices.response:
他看看磁带，又看看你的手，再看看你，肩膀松下来了一点。

“是啊。”他轻声说。

“就是那盘。”

他切回直播，告诉听众今晚来了一位还不需要名字的客人——那种会注意到空位的人。

扬声器里，打进电话的人低声表示赞同。

他把一把椅子拉到自己身边，接下来的一个小时里，他不住地瞟向第七格，好像它身边终于有人坐着了。

episodes.ending:
凌晨四点，节目渐渐收尾，迭戈送你到塔门口，夹克搭在肩上，嘴还在说个不停——说那些打进电话的人，那些信，还有明天肯定会重新出摊的面摊，因为多洛雷斯总会重新开张。

在楼梯口，他停下来，说出他对每个人都会说的那句话，这次比平时更认真：只要天线还立着，他就在。

然后他又即兴补了一句：楼梯随时都开着。

你们都知道，你还会再爬一次的。

episodes.title: 夹克里的保险丝
episodes.opening:
你最近常爬这座水塔，迭戈已经不再在电台里播报你上线了——他只是把话筒偏开，无声地朝你比个口型：随便坐。

今晚雨下得绵密，打进电话的听众也少。歌与歌的间隙，他在做一件奇怪的事：缝衣服。

一根针，一卷线，一条橄榄绿飞行员夹克摊在他膝盖上，正专注地缝一个新内袋，那架势像在拆什么危险品。

调音台嗡嗡低鸣。

雨点敲着舷窗。

他嘴里咬着线，还在说话。
episodes.dialogue:
“别笑，”他头也不抬地说。

“这可是精细活儿。”

他把夹克举起来给你看内侧——原有的那个内袋里，别着一根备用保险丝，胖乎乎的，一端还有点烧焦的痕迹。

“这根是三周前烧的。

我留着当提醒。”

他又穿起针线，眯着眼。

“既然你反正被这场雨困在这儿了，那就听我讲个故事。

那晚我正在跟一个在集装箱码头值夜班的哥们儿连线。

很好的听众。

老熟人了。

他正跟我说他们仓库的事——那边一半的灯突然熄了，整个码头一片漆黑——话说到一半，我的信号整个掉了。

死寂一片。

你知道海盗电台的直播里出现死寂是什么感觉吗？

像被大海整个吞掉。”

他打了个结，咬断线头。

“因为出事的是我。

我这整个电台的盗接线——就在他仓库断电的同一秒，在接线盒里冒了火花。

同一张电网。

同一个超负荷的夜晚。

我把他的事故，播成了我自己的停电。”

他笑了，但笑声底下有点发闷。

“我刚把调音台抢救回来，电话就又响了。

还是那个哥们儿。

他在黑灯瞎火的码头，打电话回来，就为了把故事讲完。

他根本不在乎我刚人间蒸发。

他只是想有个人听完那个结尾。”

迭戈放下夹克，终于看向你。

“挂电话的时候我才发现，两条裤腿全湿透了。

我一直站在一滩水里修线，全程没发觉。

所以第二天，我开始缝第二个内袋。”

他拍了拍刚缝好的针脚。

“装下一根保险丝。

等这根烧断的时候用。

就当是个纪念。

这台电台背着很多账，大多数不是钱。”

一首歌唱完了。

他把话筒推上直播，告诉听众们雨声有人陪着听会更动听，然后把一盒新的留言磁带塞进机器——你身后那箱已经快满了，好几年的陌生声音都录在磁带上。

“总有一天，我要坐下来，把它们从头听到尾，”他说。

“等哪天线路稳住了再说。”

choices.text: 那就趁下一根保险丝烧断之前去弄条合法线路——听众们宁愿少听一晚，也不愿你出事。
choices.response:
迭戈沉默了一会儿——对迭戈来说，这可是地质纪元级别的大事。

“我知道，”他终于开口。

“三年前我就知道了。

可停播去修线，就意味着有些夜晚这个频率上空无一人。

而那些只有凌晨三点才醒着的人——他们的孤独可不会改期。”

他重新拿起针，这回针脚走得慢了些。

“我会考虑的。

这可不是随口说说。

从我嘴里说出来的‘考虑一下’，差不多等于签了合同。”

他没许下承诺，而你们俩都听清了他没说出口的那部分。

choices.text: （你从他的针线包里拿起另一根针，替他把夹克的接缝绷紧。）
choices.response:
他冲你眨了眨眼，随即轻笑一声，继续缝。

“行啊。

抵抗组织的助理裁缝。

可别把这写进简历。”

你们俩一起把内袋缝完，整个过程安安静静，只有雨声和调音台低低的嗡鸣。

缝好后，他把烧焦的保险丝塞进旧口袋，像举起一面完工的旗帜那样举起夹克。

“两个口袋。

一个装烧掉的，一个装将要烧的。

说实话，这一件夹克，装下了整个电台。”

他说得轻描淡写，可那一晚剩下的时间，他都穿着这件夹克，好像它真的很重要。

episodes.ending:
快天亮时雨势渐歇，最后一位听众下了线。

迭戈送你下楼，一直走到第一处平台，夹克已经穿在身上，两个口袋都装着保险丝。他在那儿站了片刻，比平时久一点。

“明天还是这些楼梯，”他说。

“什么都不用带。

你是我日程表上唯一一件永远不想划掉的事。”

楼下，面摊的灯笼为早班亮了起来，一明一灭；水塔在你们头顶低鸣着，撑着，至少此刻还撑着。

episodes.title: 清晨六点的补给船
episodes.opening:
迭戈打来电话的时间，是他从不打给任何人的时间：不是凌晨三点，而是凌晨两点。声音压得又低又急，却又竭力装出随口一提的样子。

“有空吗？

算了，别回答。

上来一趟。

穿上好走路的鞋。”

你到控制室时，他手里拿着一张唱片封套——素牛皮纸，没有任何标签，只有一个用工整墨迹手写的歌名。

“一位听众寄来的。”他说。

“就是在药房上夜班的那个。

她写信跟我讲，深夜里有多少人睡不着、也求助无门地走进药房。

她的第一封信里，就点了一首歌。

就是这首歌。

现在她干脆把唱片本体寄来了。

唯一的问题是——”他把唱片翻过来，一脸无奈，“我手上没有任何能放唱片的东西。”
episodes.dialogue:
他把封套放在调音台上，像摆放一件证物。

“你看看这个。

手写的。

只有歌名——和她第一封信里点的那首一模一样。

一年前自己点过的歌，她还记得。

说真的，谁会这样啊？

谁会一直记着自己请一个电台里的陌生人放过的歌？”

他在小小的房间里踱步，跨过缠成一团团的彩色电线。

“我没法播它。

也没法把它裱起来挂着——那不是她寄来的用意。

她寄来，是要这首歌在夜里传遍整座城市，传给每个睡不着还醒着的人——传给她隔着柜台面对、却帮不了的那些人。”

他停下脚步。

“接下来才是麻烦的地方。

运送唱机的那班补给船——正经设备，唯一的可靠渠道——清晨六点从东码头起飞。

隔两个街区那家当铺还剩最后一台唱机，老板在电话里跟我说的，他就住在铺子楼上。现在已经两点半了，上礼拜那场雨又把那边半数的街道泡成了河。”

他看向你，这一次他不是在表演两难，他是真的陷在里面。

“我可以等下一班船。

那要一个月以后。

或者我现在就出发，摸黑蹚过被淹的街道，把当铺老板从床上叫起来，赶清晨六点的船。

要是错过了，唱片就得等一个月。

要是我不在的时候水塔线路打了火花，电台就会黑掉，调音台前一个人都没有。”

他一把抓起夹克——如今有两个口袋的那件——攥在手里，却没穿上。

“我要去。

我已经决定要去了。

问题只在于，我是一个人去，还是调音台就这么空着。”

他扫了一眼机器、直播灯、和沉睡的城市。

“我从来没在调音台前坐着别人的时候离开过。

对我来说，这不是小事。

可你不是外人，而且这首歌等不了一个月。

那封信是一年前写的。

她等得够久了。”

choices.text: 调音台交给我——放磁带，看好灯。你去把唱机弄回来。
choices.response:
迭戈盯着你足足三秒，然后动了起来——套上夹克，抓起便携录音机，把一页写满操作说明的纸塞进你手里。

“推子负责磁带，别的都别碰，要是冒火花，立刻关掉那个红色开关，千万别逞英雄。”

到了门口他又回头。

“你知道这意味着什么吗？

今晚凌晨三点，还有人在听——而第一次，还有人在播。”

他两步一跨地冲下楼梯，水塔归你了，嗡嗡作响，活着的，指针在你手底下轻轻呼吸。

choices.text: （你披上自己的外套，朝门口一指——你要跟他一起去。）
choices.response:
迭戈整张脸都变了。

“我们俩都去？

那调音台就黑两个小时，我不在乎——不对，我在乎，但没那么在乎了。”

他把发射器规规矩矩地关掉，在机器上贴了张字条，以防哪个听众真的一路爬上两百级楼梯，然后替你撑住门。

被淹的街道走得慢，路灯在水里拖出双重的倒影，他一路都在讲话——讲那些信，讲药房的柜台，讲那首歌——凌晨三点四十分，当铺的死锁终于打开，老板睡眼惺忪地看着浑身湿淋淋的他，和站在他身边捧着唱片封套的你，迭戈笑了，好像这一整夜都值了。

episodes.ending:
唱机赶在六点前送到了东码头，木箱随补给船发出，手写封套就搁在最上面。

两天后，一台唱机运抵水塔。凌晨三点整，唱针落下——唱片的沙沙声混着被雨水洗过的霓虹光，一起从舷窗涌进来。

迭戈一句话没说，让整首歌完完整整地放完。那是他主持生涯里最长的一次沉默。

放完之后他只说了一句：“这首歌，献给夜班的人。

她知道自己是谁。”

他再没提过那条被淹的街道——但那张唱片从此住在水塔里，封套的四个角都被人摩挲得发软了。

episodes.title: 发烧的直播
episodes.opening:
今晚的播音有点不对劲——迭戈的声音依然温暖，却总在句子里失足，每个词都慢半拍才落下来。

凌晨四点，最后一位听众挂断电话后，他关掉话筒，把头埋进调音台，像趴在一个欠了他多年的枕头上。

他抬起头，额头明显泛红。

“我没事，”他用一副明明有事的嗓音说。

“完全没事。

水塔没事。

所有人都没事。”

他咳了一声。

水塔在你们周围嗡嗡作响，漠不关心。
episodes.dialogue:
他试着站起来，又觉得不妥，一屁股跌回凳子上。

“好吧。

有点发烧。

一点点。

雨季嘛，人人都这样。

多洛雷斯婶婶昨天送了汤上来，我基本已经好了。”

他像往常一样，不自觉地冲着话筒比手势，好像听众能看见他。

“跟你说实话吧，反正五分钟之内你也会看出来。

我发烧了，但我不停播。

从来不停。

三年，一晚都没缺过。

因为这一行的全部意义——全部意义——就是凌晨三点没有人拧开旋钮，只听到一片死寂。”

他抹了把脸。

“可我现在连一句完整的话都说不利索，你在上面也听到了。

我刚才播得词不达意。

所以我已经在这儿坐了一个钟头，算一笔我不想算的账。”

他把凳子转过来面向你，声音从电台腔降下来，变得很平常。

“方案一。

你来调音台放磁带。

留言磁带——整箱，三年的量。

我从来没原样播过它们，一直都是我在它们旁边绕着说话。

可它们是真的，是我拥有的最真的东西，就算那心跳不是我的心跳，电台也还是一颗在跳的心。”

他又咳了一声，咳着咳着笑了。

“方案二——也是我差点一直不肯说出口的那个。

我现在、今晚就下楼，去多洛雷斯婶婶的摊子上待着，直到烧退。

几天，也许。

也就是说，水塔要停播了。

三年来第一个整夜的黑屏——不是上次跑去当铺弄丢的那两小时，是一整夜，甚至好几夜，调音台前没有人。

我夹克里常备一根保险丝，因为我太清楚这电台会怎么死，也太清楚让它活着要付出什么代价，而我从来没让自己知道，如果我就这样……放下它一个星期，会发生什么。”

他看向你，眼睛烧得发亮，却很坦诚。

“我不是要你替我拿主意。

我是在算，我们俩之间，我更怕让哪一个人失望。

说真的——全部的账就是这一笔。

所以告诉我，站在外面看，你看到了什么。

听众。

楼梯。

还有你。”

choices.text: 今晚陪我一起放磁带——然后你去休一周。还有迭戈……我不想只做那个爬楼梯上来的听众。做我的人吧。
choices.response:
迭戈脸上有什么东西松开了。

“你觉得他们等得到吗？”

他问。你告诉他，他信了，或者至少信得够了。

那一晚，你们肩并肩坐在调音台前，他用一副沙哑却开心的嗓子给磁带做解说——多洛雷斯的暴风雨牢骚，东码头来电者没讲完的故事，一百个陌生人说“还有人在听”。

天亮时，他顶着烧站在楼梯口，说：“一周。

等我回来，天线要是还立着，我就知道它离开我也能活。

这也许是这座电台为我做过的最好的事。”

然后，声音放轻，避开了推子：“还有——嗯，好。

你刚才说的那件事。

等我烧退了、不那么‘带毒’的时候再问我一遍，但答案是好。”

他慢慢走下楼梯，身后水塔嗡嗡作响，无人值守，却依然活着。

choices.text: （你把凳子拉近，从他夹克口袋里掏出那根备用保险丝，放在你们之间的调音台上——你打算陪他一起熬过这场烧。）
choices.response:
迭戈看看保险丝，再看看你，笑到咳起来。

“你要在水塔里照顾一个海盗电台主播退烧。

这事得录进磁带里。

得录进传说里。”

他任由你把他扶到里屋的折叠床上。三年来第一次，播音交给了磁带、寂静和水塔的嗡鸣——而没有人因此死掉。

他睡了几段真正完整的觉。

两天后烧退了，他发现你趴在调音台旁的椅子上睡着了，没有叫醒你，只是坐在那儿安静地听磁带，身上穿着他的夹克，两个口袋都是满的。

episodes.ending:
一周后，水塔还立着，节目重新回到他手里，而他说到“我们”这个词的方式，有些东西悄悄变了。

他站在调音台前，烧已经完全退了，在电波里告诉听众：这座电台学会了，自己不止一颗心跳。

然后下了节目，他更轻声地问你，这周末有没有空——不是播音，也不是值班。

只是有点事。

他不肯说什么事。

他在笑，那就说明这事很重要。

episodes.title: 整理磁带
episodes.opening:
周末要做的事原来是这样的：整个控制室的地板上铺满了磁带。

几百盒，歪歪扭扭地摞成堆，迭戈把它们粗粗分了几类，然后翻来覆去地重新归类又打乱。

明明塔里挺暖和，他还是穿着那件飞行员夹克，两个口袋都鼓鼓的，调音台旁的电炉上温着一锅多洛雷斯姨妈做的汤。

“好，”他活动着指关节说。

“三年的听众留言。

咱们全部听一遍，全部贴标签，把档案库建起来。

这就是我的周末。

这就是我的超级碗。”
episodes.dialogue:
他把第一盒磁带塞进机器，一个陌生人的声音充满整个房间——三年前的凌晨三点，有人在轻轻哭，然后又笑了，因为迭戈说了句又蠢又温柔的话，管用了。

迭戈笑得一脸灿烂，好像第一次听到似的。

“这就是整个电台的九十秒缩影，”他说。

“所以陪伴必须是真的。

信号可以偷。

电也可以偷——这个我懂行——”他拍了拍夹克口袋，“但这个东西装不出来。

那个人当时是一个人，然后有九十秒，不再是了。”

你们俩就这么干了一下午。

每隔三盒磁带，他就讲一个背后的故事——那个在黑暗里把故事讲完的码头来电者，那个写信的药房顾客，他寄来的唱片至今还摆在唱机旁，封套都磨软了。

大概听到第二百盒的时候，他安静下来，捏着一盒磁带盯着看。

“这是风暴夜那盘，”他说。

“多洛雷斯的时段。

整个下雨的夜里，它一直在空转。”

他还是把它放了进去，磁带沙沙作响——整整一个小时的暴风雨声和沉默——只在最末尾，很轻很轻地，有一声敲门，还有多洛雷斯的声音，从被淹的小巷里录下来的：一句道歉，一声笑，一个下次风暴一定打来的承诺。

迭戈靠回椅背上。

“她录进了这盘空白带上。

她其实一直都在，就在它的结尾。”

他慢慢地、一笔一画地用墨水笔写下标签：多洛雷斯——风暴夜——她回来了。

然后他隔着满地磁带抬头看你，声音离开了电台腔，平实而笃定。

“我想说件事，我要你完完整整地听完。

这个电台以前是我的。

后来你爬上了楼梯，你陪我熬过一场发烧，你帮那张唱片上了节目——不知不觉间，它不再只是我的，成了我们的。

没有写在纸上。

根本也没有纸。

但我告诉你，这是真的。”

他举起那支马克笔。

“所以。

联合档案员。

调音台边有把椅子，你想的话，可以把你的名字刷上去。

不是什么职位——我不发工资，本来就没有工资。

只有这么一条：只要天线还立着，这里也是你的。

说真的。

我就是这个意思，一个字都不多。”

choices.text: 把名字刷上去吧。但档案活儿得咱俩分——你负责听，我负责贴标签，还有，谁也不许再一个人熬风暴夜。
choices.response:
迭戈笑得直不起腰，笔都拿不稳了。

“成交。

轮班制。

谁也不许再单枪匹马蹚洪水——这条写进那份隐形合同里。”

那天下午他把椅子刷上名字，刷到“迭戈和——”就停了手，把笔塞给你，让你写后半截，他说那必须是你的笔迹。

刷好的椅子摆在调音台边，两个名字都在上面，有点歪，也有点完美。

当晚的节目里，他向听众介绍了新上任的联合档案员，导播台的三年老听众纷纷打来电话——他们好像早就知道了。

choices.text: （你接过马克笔，在磁带箱盖上他的名字底下添上自己的名字，然后把多洛雷斯的风暴磁带插进新档案架的第一格。）
choices.response:
迭戈看着你写，好一阵子没说话——对他来说这简直是地质纪元级的事件。

然后他轻声说：“嗯。

就该这样。

档案库的第一盘磁带，是她的。”

你们俩一起搭架子，搭了一整晚，一格一格地装，汤凉了热、热了又凉。

到天亮时，档案架靠着缠满电线的墙立好了，风暴磁带放在第一格，贴好了标签，找到了归属。

迭戈双手插在夹克口袋里退后一步，说这水塔总算让人觉得脚下有底了。

episodes.ending:
档案架靠在水塔墙边，装得满满当当，多洛雷斯的风暴磁带就放在属于它的位置。调音台边那把椅子是你的了。

凌晨三点的节目继续播着，有些夜里是他的声音，有些夜里是你的，有些夜里是你们俩的，听众常常分不清是谁——迭戈说，这是电台开播以来得到的最高评价。

下一次风暴来的时候，多洛雷斯准时打来电话，第七格时段，你们俩都在，一起接起来。

只要天线还立着，这里也是你的。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

romance.title: 第七格，填上了
romance.opening:
周末要做的事原来是这样的：整个控制室的地板上铺满了磁带。

几百盒，摇摇欲坠地摞成几摞，粗粗分了堆，迭戈一会儿重新理一遍，一会儿又打乱。

天挺热他还是穿着那件飞行员夹克，两个口袋鼓鼓囊囊，多洛雷斯的汤放在调音台边的小电炉上温着。

但今晚他有点心不在焉——看表比看磁带还勤——因为今晚，三年来头一次，第七格要被人正式地填上了。

多洛雷斯答应凌晨三点整准时打进来，管它来不来台风。
romance.dialogue:
两点五十八分，他已经守在电话线旁边转悠，拨弄一些根本不用拨弄的东西。

“她从来不定约的。”他跟你说。

“那个摊子摆了三十年，这电台开播三年，每个台风夜她就是——自己打过来。

今晚我在摊子上开口邀请，她答应得好像天经地义。

说真的，她说：当然啊，小家伙，我都给你打了好几年电话了，你早该正经请我上节目了。”

表针转过去。

电话响了。

他在直播里接起，多洛雷斯的声音灌满整座水塔——响亮、热络，打趣他发过烧，打趣那碗汤，还打趣药房来信里的那个姑娘，原来她也在听。

全城听众围观迭戈·萨拉查被一个面摊大婶连续十分钟嘘寒问暖，他就这么由着它发生，笑着，对着话筒比手势，眼睛亮晶晶的。

她挂了电话，他慢慢在凳子上坐下。

“三年前，”他开口，这话不再是对听众说的了，或者不只是，“一个陌生人打进电台，说了一句话：还有人在听。

这一切才存在。

我口袋里的保险丝、那些磁带、那场水灾，全都是因为那句话。

而这几个月里的某一天，它不再只是我在电波里讲的故事，而是变成了每一个夜晚都真实发生的事——因为你就在那一头。”

他把凳子转过来面向你，声音完全脱掉了电台腔——平平实实，有点不稳，全然是他自己。

“我一直在琢磨，怎么不带稿子把这句话说出来。

这种事没有稿子。

所以就这样吧，说真的，就这样：

我想让这些楼梯通向的人就是你。

两个方向都是。

凌晨三点的电话，下午三点的汤，被淹的街道，还有那些无聊透顶的普通日子，我都想要。

我想知道你是不是也想要——如果答案是不，调音台边这把椅子还是你的，一直都是，我绝不会让气氛变尴尬。

可如果是——”他笑了，紧张，但真实，“那第七格就不再空着了。

里面装的是你。”

choices.text: 我愿意。两个方向都要。楼梯我来爬，格子也归我——迭戈，把我录进磁带里，我要白纸黑字记下来。
choices.response:
迭戈整张脸一下子亮起来，毫无防备，他伸过手来——在你放在调音台上的手背上轻轻一按，温热的，落下去又收回来，像签了个名。

“记下来。”他重复了一遍，然后，因为他是迭戈，他真做了：转到磁带机前，录下自己念的这段话——日期、水塔、两个人的名字——然后存进档案，标签上工工整整写着字。

直播里他告诉听众，电台有个消息，但这一次，他要自己留着，不播。

导播台的灯还是全亮了。

他们总是知道。

choices.text: （你拿起那支软头笔，在台风磁带的空白标签上写下你的名字和他的名字，然后把磁带递回给他。）
choices.response:
迭戈接过磁带，看着两个名字，全都懂了。

“第七格。”他哑着嗓子说。

“你刚刚自己把它填上了。”

他把磁带放进第七格，让它从此住在那儿，然后在调音台上轻轻按了一下你的手背——一个温热的瞬间，随后收回，凌晨三点二十分，你们俩对着调音台傻笑着。

十分钟后多洛雷斯打了回来，因为她在电波里听出了他声音里的停顿，他把一切都告诉了她，于是全城都听见了他有多高兴。

romance.ending:
第七格一直是满的。

档案越攒越多，凌晨三点的节目照常开播——有些夜晚是他的声音，有些是你的，有些是两个人的，一句接一句，像对唱。

迭戈的夹克里还是备着保险丝，对每个来电还是照单全收，还是怕天线被拆的那一夜。

但现在这份恐惧有了答案，答案住在两百级楼梯之外，也就在他身边。

只要天线还立着，他就在——你也在，信号或许是偷来的，可除此之外的一切，没有一样是假的。

choices.response: He nods once, as if you confirmed something he had already half-counted on. The simulator hum steadies under his hand. He opens the maintenance channel, sends the request in plain language, and leans back. For a while neither of you talks, and he does not fill the silence with procedure. That, you will learn later, is rare.
choices.text: Just say it plainly, however it comes out. I'll wait for it.

choices.response: You slide the untouched cup toward him, then fold your hands and let the quiet sit there. He watches it arrive, and something in his shoulders lowers a degree. Then he opens the channel and sends the request himself, unpolished. When he turns back, he pours the second cup without asking, and slides it across the table.
choices.text: (Slide the untouched cup of tea toward him.)

episodes.dialogue:
He sets the beacon down and takes his hands off the table, which you will learn is what he does before saying something that might land badly.

'Ravi Sen. Ship’s envoy. Communications are muted. There are no delegations now, just you and me.'

He looks toward the simulator. Its hum drops into a faint rattle, then steadies.

'That's been happening all evening. Maintenance needs a request before they'll inspect it. I've drafted three versions. None says what I mean.'

He turns the small console toward you. The public maintenance form has a blank description box; the diplomatic messages remain closed.

'I don't know what's loose. I know the sound changes when the deck shifts to low gravity. That's enough to report. Instead I've written a paragraph about service continuity.'

He deletes the paragraph. The box waits.

'Eleven years of finding words both sides can accept. You get good at smoothing a sentence before anyone hears it. Then you sit with a rattling machine and can't ask for someone to look at it.'

He pushes the breakfast tray clear of the console and sets an untouched cup between you.

'I was going to ask you how to word the request. That would be making you do my job for me.'

He looks at you instead.

'What I'd actually like is company while I say one thing badly and send it anyway. Tea is here, if you want it. No work required.'
episodes.ending: He walks you as far as the deck hatch, then stops, as if the doorway were the edge of his jurisdiction. The corridor lights are still on night cycle. He says he will leave the simulator log unlocked on the off chance you come back, and that the tea is better at ground-time breakfast, whenever that lands for you. The hatch closes. The station hums on around you, and somewhere behind it, a man is rehearsing a sentence he did not need to rehearse.
episodes.opening: The diplomatic deck is dark except for the beacon, a slow amber pulse that has been asking for attention all shift. Ravi Sen sits with his jacket still buttoned at midnight, station time, a breakfast tray at his elbow because his body keeps a ground time zone the windows refuse to honor. The gravity simulator behind him hums, steadying the deck. He kills the beacon with two fingers, and the amber dies. Just you, the hum, and a man whose whole job is choosing words for other people.
episodes.title: Ground Time

choices.response: He takes the question as plainly as you asked it, and something eases. He says it is because you are the one person he does not rehearse for. He says the worst part was not fear of punishment. It was sitting with the families’ grief and knowing he had chosen it, and that no one would ever thank him. Then he asks whether you have eaten, because his breakfast has gone cold and the question is easier.
choices.text: Why tell me this one, out of everything you carry?

choices.response: You do not reach for the story or fill the gap after it. You sit with it, the way you sat with the tea. He watches you not flinch, and his sentences, already short, get shorter. He says he has never said that aloud at this hour to anyone. Then he checks the time, says breakfast is technically still open on his clock, and opens the breakfast menu so you can choose something if you want it.
choices.text: (Turn your chair to face the window, leaving the silence unbroken.)

episodes.dialogue:
He turns the cup a quarter turn, then sets it down.

'There's something I haven't said aloud here. You can tell me to leave it for another breakfast.'

He waits, and then takes his hands off the table.

'Once I manually delayed three battle reports. They were supposed to go straight through. I held them.'

He looks at the window before continuing.

'I won't give you unpublished coordinates or names. Those aren't mine to share. The part that is mine is the decision. I read the reports, saw that the next message would send people onward, and asked for a check before forwarding them. Procedure said immediate. I chose delay.'

He does not offer the choice as a rule anyone else should follow.

'I still don't know what every minute cost. There were losses. There were families who never received the people they expected back. I can't turn what I did into a clean sentence where everyone gets home.'

His breakfast has gone cold. He notices and leaves it alone.

'I am sure of the facts. The part I am not sure of is whether telling you changes anything, or only costs me something. Most of what I carry, I can file. This one I carry by hand.'

He looks back at you.

'You stayed while I sent that request without asking for a translated word. That seemed like a place where this could land without my making it sound better first.'
episodes.ending: He orders another tray, and it arrives and he eats at his own pace, ground time, while the station runs its morning around him. Before you part he says, plainly, that he would like to keep this — the hour, the table, the talking that needs no drafting. Not as an appointment. As a thing that happens. You say the next one is on your clock, whichever clock that turns out to be, and he almost smiles at that.
episodes.opening: Ground-time breakfast, again, except this time you are both at the small table by the gravity simulator, and the tray in front of him is real instead of ceremonial. He has stopped wearing the full jacket. The beacon is off; you checked. He eats the way he talks, unhurried, and between bites he asks after nothing official. Eleven years of wording other people's sentences, and here he is eating eggs at what his body insists is morning while the planet burns orange past the glass.
episodes.title: Hand-Carried

choices.response: He stops walking. He says he has spent eleven years making sure other people's sentences arrive intact, and he had not noticed he was doing it to you. Then, plainly: I will stop checking my work around you. That is the whole promise. It is small and he means it, and he does not dress it up as more than it is. He resumes walking, half a step closer than before.
choices.text: You don't have to draft yourself for me. Say it however it lands.

choices.response: You say nothing and simply keep pace, matching his steps on the deck. He notices. Halfway down the garden ring he exhales, and his sentences shorten on their own, the register setting itself down without being asked. By the time you reach the bay he is talking the way he talked over that first untouched tea. He says, quietly, that you are easier to be around than an empty room, and he does not take it back.
choices.text: (Keep walking beside him, unhurried.)

episodes.dialogue:
He watches you fall into step, then nods slowly.

Here is what I meant by asking you to walk: I am not asking you to fix this.

I am asking for company while I think.

That is a different thing, and I do not want to pretend the second is unnecessary because I am used to refusing the first.

He is quiet a moment.

The hearing is in six hours.

Whatever happens, the ambassador will want a version of events that is smoother than the truth.

I will give the ambassador the smooth version, because that is the job.

But you will get the true one, later, at ground time, at our table.

He almost smiles.

I am sure of half of this — that I want to tell you.

The timing I cannot promise.

That is the honest shape of it.
episodes.ending: The hearing ends the way these things end: deferred, not resolved, the ambassador's caution intact and the cargo lane open for another round. Ravi finds you afterward in the garden ring, jacket wrinkled for the first time you have seen, and gives you the true version before he gives anyone the smooth one. Nothing is cured. The deadlock will take months. But he sits down across from you without rehearsing, and that is its own kind of progress.
episodes.opening: The deadlock has eaten nine days. A trade envoy from the rim delegation will not meet face to face, and every translated proposal dies in transit. Ravi looks wrung out even in his good jacket. Tonight he asks you to walk the outer garden ring with him while he thinks aloud, and what he thinks aloud is that he may have to sit across from the envoy and say nothing at all for an hour — just watch the planet turn — and trust that silence translates itself. His hands are not steady. He does not pretend they are.
episodes.title: Silence, Translated

choices.response: He sets his cup down and takes his hands off the table. Let me say back what I heard, he says, and his voice is not the working voice: you are asking to be partners, and I want that too. He is quiet for three full seconds, the longest silence you have seen him allow. Then, plainly, no drafting: I have wanted to say that first for weeks. I kept translating it into safer sentences. I am sure of this. All of it. He lifts his cup to yours, and he glances toward the glass where tomorrow's comet will pass.
choices.text: I don't want to be only your visitor. I want to be your partner — the person you don't have to translate yourself for.

choices.response: You raise your cup and settle into your usual place across the table, keeping the familiar distance between friends. He meets your quiet toast and nods, relief moving through him as you make yourself comfortable without a speech. Then he says the thing he has been circling: that what you two have is rare, that he does not want to risk renaming it, and that he is glad you made room for that friendship so he can name it without hiding behind procedure. He raises his cup. To the table.
choices.text: (Raise your cup to his, then settle back into your usual place across the table without a word.)

episodes.dialogue:
He does not open the folder yet.

Before anything else: I want to say something without a preamble, and I may be bad at it.

He takes his hands off the table.

I have spent eleven years being the space between two sentences.

With you, I am not between anything.

I am just on my side of the table.

That is the whole speech.

He slides the folder across anyway.

The comet passes tomorrow, 04:40 station time.

The garden ring will have the best view on this side of the orbit.

I have reserved the east bench.

No agenda, no delegation, no one else.

He hesitates, then finishes it.

I am asking you to be there.

What we are to each other — that part is yours to say, not mine to assume.

I would rather hear the true answer than a comfortable one.
episodes.ending: At 04:40 the following morning, you meet on the reserved east bench, each carrying a cup of tea. You stay until the comet's tail thins and the planet's dawn line catches it, and somewhere in there the folder gets closed and forgotten. The morning finds you both still there, two cups drained, the reserved sign long since flipped face-down. He walks you back through the garden ring at a ground-time stroll, talking about nothing that needs translating, and the station's morning opens around you both.
episodes.opening: He finds you at the simulator table with a folder he does not open and two cups of tea, one of which he sets in front of you without a word about it. There is a comet coming through the system — unimportant officially, he says, which is why nobody has claimed the garden ring's east bench at 04:40 station time. He has already reserved it. He sits down across from you, and for the first time since you have known him, he opens his mouth, closes it, and starts over.
episodes.title: The East Bench

choices.response: He replays it, then laughs — actually laughs, a sound you have heard maybe twice in all this time. Correct on both counts, he says. The route is fixed; the timing I cannot promise. He pulls the second chair out with his foot and sits. Then, plainly: I used to eat alone at an hour nobody shared. Now I check the clock and think, you will be up. That is not a small thing. That is the whole thing. He opens the folder. It is blank. He admits he brought it out of habit and closes it again.
choices.text: Let me say back what I heard: you're keeping the hour, and you're keeping me in it.

choices.response: You sit down across from him without a word and start eating, the way you have over many breakfasts, and he understands the answer before you could have phrased it. He watches you for a moment, then pushes the folder aside. You know, he says, eleven years of training and the most useful thing I ever learned at this table was when to leave a sentence unsaid. He eats. The planet turns. Neither of you translates anything.
choices.text: (Sit down, pick up a fork, and start eating without a word.)

episodes.dialogue:
He replays your greeting, nods.

Let me say back what I heard: you kept the hour, and you noticed the drawer.

Correct on both counts.

He takes his hands off the table.

The drawer is the rotation.

I filed a standing request — same shift block, every cycle, this station.

They almost never grant one.

They granted it.

I think the hearing last season helped; the ambassador cited my patience in the record, which was generous, since mostly I was just tired.

He turns his cup a quarter turn.

I am sure of half of this — I am staying.

The timing of the next posting I cannot promise, but the table is in the request itself, so the table survives any posting.

He looks at you plainly.

I also wrote one more line into it.

Standing guest access to this deck, your name in the log.

Not staff.

A guest.

The distinction matters to me.

You were never the help, and I did not want a form to imply otherwise.
episodes.ending: You eat the whole breakfast at ground time, the way the first one should have gone, and when the station's morning cycle catches up he walks you to the hatch and does not stop at the edge of his jurisdiction this time — the guest log cleared you through it weeks ago. He says the same thing he says every cycle now: next breakfast is on whichever clock wakes first. Given the drawer, given the standing line in the rotation file, that is not a guess anymore. It is a schedule neither of you minds keeping.
episodes.opening: Two seasons have settled over the station, and the simulator table has become a place with a reputation: if you want Ravi Sen off the record, that is where he is. Tonight the deck is dark, the beacon cold, and he is already there when you arrive — jacket off, two trays, and a drawer beside his seat that used to hold briefing folders and now holds tea. He has stopped standing when officials enter the deck. He stands for you. The planet burns orange past the glass, right on time.
episodes.title: The Standing Line

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

choices.response: He lets out a breath he has clearly been holding since before you sat down. Let me say back what I heard, he says, and then abandons the procedure halfway through. No. You asked for the whole sentence. I will give you that. He takes his hands off the table. Then, unedited: I love you. I have for a while, and I kept translating it into smaller sentences because I was afraid the plain one would only reach the diplomat. He looks at you, and none of the working voice is left. It reached you. That is all I wanted.
choices.text: Say the plain one. The one you stopped translating.

choices.response: You cross the small deck and sit down beside him instead of across, close enough that your shoulders almost touch, and you stay there, saying nothing. He looks at the space between you, then at you, and understands. The ordinary version, he says quietly. Is that your yes? You nod, close beside him. Then mine is yes too. I love you. That is the sentence I meant to say. He does not reach for you. He does not need to. The bench holds you both, and the planet turns, and nothing about it needs translating.
choices.text: (Sit down beside him instead of across, close, and say nothing.)

romance.dialogue:
He looks from the two breakfast trays to you and shakes his head, smiling at the ordinary arrangement.

“This,” he says.

This is what I wanted.

He takes his hands off the table.

Then, plainly, with nothing smoothed: I am not asking you to orbit me.

I have watched enough things circle each other up here without ever meeting.

I am asking for the ordinary version.

Breakfasts that are not scheduled around postings.

A life where you are not the one person I talk to without rehearsing, because rehearsing has stopped being necessary even when you are not in the room.

He is quiet.

I am sure of all of this.

For once, the timing too.

He slides the print across the table, face up now.

It is the east-bench reservation, printed with both our names.

I made it after we chose what we wanted at the simulator table.

I would like this to be a habit we both keep choosing.

That is the whole request.

There is no annex.
romance.ending: You stay on the east bench until the planet's dawn line crosses the glass, talking about the small future — which clock you will keep, whose drawer holds the tea, where the print should hang. The choice is made; the small arrangements can wait. The east-bench reservation already has both your names in it, and his sentences have stopped arriving pre-drafted. When you finally rise, he holds out his hand. You take it for a moment, then let go. Then you walk the garden ring together at ground-time pace, unhurried, while the station's morning opens around the two of you, who no longer need an interpreter.
romance.opening: A year of ground-time breakfasts, a survived deadlock, and one comet later, the east bench has your name in its reservation log — his handwriting, no title attached. Tonight he is there early with two trays and, for the first time, no folder at all. Just a small printed slip face-down beside the tea. The beacon on the deck behind you is dark. The planet turns. He waits until you reach him, and then he does something you have never seen him do: he lets a silence run long on purpose, and is comfortable in it.
romance.title: No Annex

choices.response: 他点了点头，仿佛你证实了他早已半数指望的事情。模拟器的嗡鸣在他手下渐渐平稳。他打开维护频道，用最直白的语言发出申请，然后靠回椅背。有一阵子你们谁都没说话，他也没有用流程术语去填补沉默。你以后会知道，这很罕见。
choices.text: 直说就好，想到什么说什么。我等着。

choices.response: 你把那杯没动过的茶推到他面前，然后双手交叠，让安静留在那里。他看着你的动作，肩上的什么东西松了一分。接着他打开频道，亲自把申请发了出去，不加修饰。等他转回来时，他没问一声就倒上第二杯茶，推过桌面。
choices.text: （把那杯没动过的茶推向他。）

episodes.dialogue:
他把信标放下，双手离开桌面——你以后会知道，这是他在说可能不中听的话之前的习惯。

“拉维·森。飞船特使。通讯已静音。现在没有代表团，只有你和我。”

他朝模拟器望去。它的嗡鸣降成一阵轻微的咔啦声，随后又平稳下来。

“整个晚上都是这样。维护部门要先收到申请才会来检查。我起草了三个版本。没有一个说出了我的意思。”

他把小控制台转向你。公开的维护表单上有一个空白的描述框；外交信道依然关闭。

“我不知道是什么松了。我只知道甲板切换到低重力时声音会变。这足够上报了。可我却写了一段关于服务连续性的话。”

他删掉了那段话。空白框等着。

“十一年来，我都在寻找双方都能接受的措辞。你会在任何人听到之前就把句子磨得圆滑。然后你坐在一台咔啦作响的机器旁，却请不动人来看一眼。”

他把早餐托盘从控制台旁推开，在你们之间放上一杯没动过的茶。

“我本来想请教你该怎么措辞这份申请。那等于让你替我做我的工作。”

他转而看着你。

“我真正想要的，是有人陪着我把一件事说得笨拙，然后照样发出去。茶在这儿，想喝就喝。不需要做任何事。”
episodes.ending: 他送你到甲板舱门处才停下，仿佛门框就是他权限的边缘。走廊的灯仍处于夜间模式。他说他会把模拟器日志保持解锁状态，万一你回来呢；还说地面时间早餐时的茶更好喝，至于那对你是什么时候，随你。舱门合上。空间站继续在你周围嗡鸣，而在嗡鸣深处的某处，有个人正在排练一句他本不必排练的话。
episodes.opening: 外交甲板一片昏暗，只有信标亮着，一道缓慢的琥珀色脉冲，整个班次都在请求关注。空间站时间的午夜，拉维·森仍扣着外套的纽扣坐着，手肘边放着一份早餐托盘，因为他的身体守着地面时区，而舷窗拒绝承认它的存在。他身后的重力模拟器嗡鸣着，稳住整块甲板。他用两根手指关掉信标，琥珀色熄灭。只剩下你、嗡鸣声，和一个以替别人斟酌措辞为全部工作的男人。
episodes.title: 地面时间

choices.response: 他听着你用自己的平实话语把问题送回给他，某种东西松动了。他说最难熬的不是怕受罚，而是坐在那些家属的悲痛旁边，明知这是他自己选择的，而且永远不会有人感谢他。然后他问你吃过东西没有，因为他的早餐已经凉了，而这个问题要容易一些。
choices.text: 你背负的一切里，为什么偏偏把这件事告诉我？

choices.response: 你没有伸手去接那个故事，也没有填补它之后的空白。你陪着它待着，就像你陪着那杯茶一样。他看着你没有退缩，他本就简短的句子变得更短了。他说他从未在这个钟点对任何人把那句话说出口。然后他看了看时间，说按他的钟来算早餐在技术上还没结束，便打开早餐菜单，让你想的话可以点些东西。
choices.text: （把椅子转向舷窗，让沉默保持完整。）

episodes.dialogue:
他把杯子转了四分之一圈，然后放下。

“有件事我在这里从没说出口过。你可以让我留到下一次早餐再说。”

他等着，见你留下，便把手从桌上移开。

“有一次，我手动延迟了三份战报。它们本该直接传送出去。我扣下了它们。”

他看向舷窗，然后继续。

“我不会给你未公开的坐标或名字。那些不归我分享。归我的部分是那个决定。我读了报告，看到下一条消息会让人继续前进，于是要求在转发之前先核查一遍。规程要求立即执行。我选择了延迟。”

他没有把这个选择说成别人也该遵循的规则。

“我至今不知道每一分钟付出了什么代价。有伤亡。有家属永远没有等到他们期盼归来的人。我没办法把我做的事变成一句干净的话，让每个人都平安回家。”

他的早餐已经凉了。他注意到了，却没有去动它。

“事实我很确定。我不确定的是，告诉你这件事会不会改变什么，还是只会让我付出代价。我背负的大部分东西，都可以归档。这一件，我是用手捧着的。”

他重新看向你。

“我发出那个请求的时候，你留了下来，没有要求翻译一个字。那看起来像是一个地方，可以让这件事落地，而不必先让我把它修饰得更好听。”
episodes.ending: 他又点了一份托盘，送来之后他按自己的节奏吃着，按地面时间，而空间站的清晨在他周围运转。分别之前，他直白地说，他想留住这个——这个钟点，这张桌子，这种不需要起草的交谈。不是作为约定。而是作为一件自然发生的事。你说下一次按你的钟来算，不管那最终是哪一种钟，他听了几乎笑了一下。
episodes.opening: 又是地面时间的早餐，只是这一次你们都坐在重力模拟器旁的小桌边，他面前的托盘是真正的食物，而不是仪式性的。他已经不再穿那件全套制服外套了。信标是关着的；你确认过。他吃东西像他说话一样，不慌不忙，两口之间问的都是些无关公务的事。十一年来他都在替别人措辞造句，而此刻他正在吃鸡蛋，按他身体坚持认定的清晨，舷窗外那颗行星燃烧着橙色。
episodes.title: 手捧的重量

choices.response: 他停下脚步。他说，这十一年来他一直在确保别人的话完好无损地送达，却没察觉自己也在对你这样做。然后他直白地说：我会在你面前停止检查自己的措辞。这就是全部的承诺。很小，但他是认真的，而且他没有把它粉饰得比实际更大。他继续往前走，比之前近了半步。
choices.text: 你不必在我面前先打草稿。想怎么说就怎么说。

choices.response: 你什么也没说，只是在甲板上跟上他的步伐，与他步调一致。他注意到了。走到花园环道一半时，他呼出一口气，他的句子自然而然地变短了，那种正式的语调没等任何人开口就自己放了下来。等你们走到海湾时，他说话的样子已经和第一次那杯没人动过的茶时一样了。他轻声说，和你在一起比待在一间空房间里更自在，而且他没有收回这句话。
choices.text: （在他身旁不紧不慢地继续走着。）

episodes.dialogue:
他看着你跟上他的脚步，然后缓缓点头。

我请你散步，想说的是：我不是要你来解决这件事。

我只是想在我思考的时候有人陪着。

这是两回事，我不想因为我习惯于拒绝前者，就假装后者并不重要。

他沉默了片刻。

听证会在六小时之后。

无论结果如何，大使都会想要一个比真相更圆滑的说法。

我会给大使那个圆滑的版本，因为这是我的职责。

但你会听到真实的版本，晚些时候，在地面时间，在我们的桌旁。

他几乎要笑了。

这件事我有一半是确定的——我想告诉你。

时机我无法承诺。

这就是它诚实的样子。
episodes.ending: 听证会以这类事情惯常的方式收场：被搁置，而非解决，大使的谨慎原封不动，货运航道留给下一轮再谈。事后，拉维在花园环道找到了你，他的外套第一次出现了皱褶，他先给了你真实的版本，然后才把圆滑的版本给别人。什么都没有痊愈。僵局还要持续几个月。但他没有预先排练，就坐到了你对面——这本身就是一种进展。
episodes.opening: 僵局已经持续了九天。边缘代表团的一位贸易特使拒绝面对面会谈，每一份翻译好的提案都死在了传递途中。拉维即使穿着他那件体面的外套，看起来也被榨干了。今晚，他请你陪他绕外圈花园环道散步，边走边把想法说出来——他说出来的想法是，他也许得坐在特使对面，整整一个小时什么都不说——只是看着脚下的星球转动——然后相信沉默会自己完成翻译。他的手不稳。他也不假装它稳。
episodes.title: 被翻译的沉默

choices.response: 他放下茶杯，双手离开桌面。让我把我听到的复述一遍，他说，声音不再是那种工作时的腔调：你在请求成为我的伴侣，而我也想这样。他安静了整整三秒，是你见过他允许自己沉默最久的一次。然后，直白地，不再打草稿：这几个星期我一直想说这句话。我总把它翻译成更安全的句子。这件事我很确定。全部都是。他举杯与你相碰，目光扫向玻璃外，明天的彗星将从那里掠过。
choices.text: 我不想只做你的访客。我想成为你的伴侣——那个你不必再为他翻译自己的人。

choices.response: 你举起茶杯，在桌对面你惯常的位置坐下，保持着朋友之间熟悉的距离。他回应了你无声的举杯，点点头，见你不必发表宣言便安然自处，他松了口气。然后他说出了那个他一直绕来绕去的话：你们之间的东西很珍贵，他不想冒险给它改名，而且他很高兴你为这份友谊留出了空间，让他可以不必躲在程序背后就说出它的名字。他举起茶杯。敬这张桌子。
choices.text: （举杯与他的相碰，然后一言不发地回到桌对面你惯常的位置。）

episodes.dialogue:
他还没有打开文件夹。

在说别的之前：我想说一件事，不加任何铺垫，而且我可能说不好。

他把双手从桌面上移开。

十一年里，我一直是两句话之间的空隙。

和你在一起，我不在任何东西之间。

我只是坐在桌子的我这一边。

这就是全部的发言。

他还是把文件夹推了过来。

彗星明天经过，站时04:40。

花园环将是这条轨道这一侧视野最好的地方。

我已经订下了东侧长椅。

没有议程，没有代表团，没有其他人。

他犹豫了一下，然后说完。

我在请你到场。

我们彼此是什么——那部分由你来说，而不是由我来假定。

我宁愿听到真实的答案，也不愿听到一个让我舒服的答案。
episodes.ending: 第二天清晨04:40，你们在预订的东侧长椅上碰面，各自端着一杯茶。你们一直待到彗尾变淡、行星的晨昏线追上它，而在这中间的某个时刻，文件夹被合上、被遗忘。清晨发现你们俩都还在那里，两只杯子已经见底，预订牌早已翻面朝下。他以地面时间的散步速度陪你穿过花园环往回走，聊着些不需要翻译的闲话，空间站的清晨在你们两人周围展开。
episodes.opening: 他在模拟桌旁找到你，手里拿着一个没有打开的文件夹和两杯茶，其中一杯被他不声不响地放在你面前。一颗彗星正在穿越这个星系——官方说法是不重要，他说，所以站时04:40没有人认领花园环的东侧长椅。他已经预订好了。他在你对面坐下，而自你认识他以来第一次，他张开嘴，又合上，重新开始。
episodes.title: 东侧长椅

choices.response: 他重放了一遍你的话，然后笑了——是真的笑出声来，这声音你在这段日子里大概只听过两次。他说，两点都说对了。航线是固定的；时间我可不敢保证。他用脚把第二把椅子拉开，坐下。然后，坦白地说：我以前总在一个没人共享的钟点独自吃饭。现在我会看看表，心想，你该起来了。这不是小事。这就是全部的事。他打开文件夹。里面是空的。他承认自己是出于习惯才把它带出来，然后把它合上放着。
choices.text: 让我复述一下我听到的：你在守着那个钟点，而且把我守在了里面。

choices.response: 你一言不发地在他对面坐下，开始吃饭，就像过去许多顿早餐那样，他还没等你开口就已经明白了答案。他看了你一会儿，然后把文件夹推到一边。你知道吗，他说，受了十一年训练，我在这张桌上学到的最有用的一课，是什么时候该把一句话咽下去不说。他吃饭。星球转动。你们俩谁也没有翻译任何东西。
choices.text: （坐下，拿起叉子，一言不发地开始吃饭。）

episodes.dialogue:
他重放了一遍你的问候，点了点头。

让我复述一下我听到的：你守住了那个钟点，而且你注意到了那个抽屉。

两点都说对了。

他把双手从桌上拿开。

抽屉就是轮换。

我提交了一份长期申请——同一个班次时段，每个周期，这个空间站。

这种申请他们几乎从不批准。

他们批准了。

我想是上一季的那次听证会帮了忙；大使在记录里引用了我的耐心，这算是客气了，因为其实我多半只是累了。

他把杯子转了四分之一圈。

这件事我有一半是确定的——我要留下来。

下一次派驻的时间我无法保证，但这张桌子就写在申请本身里，所以无论派到哪里，这张桌子都还在。

他坦率地看着你。

我还在里面多写了一行。

本甲板的长期访客权限，日志里写着你的名字。

不是工作人员。

是客人。

这个区别对我很重要。

你从来都不是什么帮手，我不想让一张表格暗示别的意思。
episodes.ending: 你们在地面时间吃完了整顿早餐，就像第一顿本该有的样子，当空间站的晨间周期追上来时，他送你到舱门口，这一次没有停在权限的边界上——访客日志几周前就放你通过了。他说着如今每个周期都会说的那句话：下一顿早餐，归先醒来的那个时钟管。有了那个抽屉，有了轮换申请里那行长期条款，这已经不再是猜测了。那是一份你们俩都不介意遵守的日程。
episodes.opening: 两个季节在空间站上沉淀下来，模拟器桌已经成了一个有名有姓的地方：如果你想让拉维·森脱离记录说话，那就是他在的地方。今晚甲板一片昏暗，信标冷着，你到达时他已经在了——外套脱了，两个餐盘，座位旁有个抽屉，从前放简报文件夹，现在放茶。官员们走进甲板时，他已经不再起身了。他为你起身。玻璃外，那颗星球准时地燃着橙色。
episodes.title: 长期条款

speak.text: ♡ 你想和他成为恋人

choices.response: 他长长呼出一口气——显然从你坐下之前就一直屏着。让我复述一下我听到的，他说，然后半途放弃了这套流程。不。你要的是那句完整的话，我就给你。他把双手从桌上移开。然后，不加修饰地说：我爱你。已经有一阵子了，我一直把它翻译成更小的句子，因为我怕那句直白的话只会传到外交官那里。他看着你，工作用的声音一点不剩。它传到了你这里。这就是我想要的全部。
choices.text: 说出那句直白的。那句你不再翻译的。

choices.response: 你走过小小的甲板，不是坐到他对面，而是坐到他身边，近到肩膀几乎相触，然后你就待在那里，什么也不说。他看着你们之间的距离，再看看你，明白了。普通版本，他轻声说。这就是你的“是”吗？你点头，紧挨着他。那么我的也是“是”。我爱你。这就是我一直想说的那句话。他没有伸手，也不需要。
choices.text: （不是坐到他对面，而是坐到他身边，靠近，什么也不说。）

romance.dialogue:
他从两份早餐托盘看向你，摇了摇头，对这个普通的安排微笑。

这个，他说。

这就是我想要的。

他把双手从桌上移开。

然后，直白地，不加任何修饰：我不是要你绕着我转。

我在这里看过太多东西彼此环绕却从未相遇。

我要的是普通版本。

早餐不再围绕调令安排。

一种生活，在其中你不再是我唯一一个不用打腹稿就能说话的人，因为打腹稿已经没有必要，哪怕你不在房间里。

他安静下来。

这一切我都很确定。

这一次，连时机也是。

他把那张打印件推过桌面，正面朝上。

那是东长椅的预约，印着我们两个人的名字。

是我们在模拟台前选好各自想要的东西之后，我去订的。

我希望这成为我们俩都愿意一直保持的习惯。

这就是全部的请求。

没有附件。
romance.ending: 你们在东长椅上待到行星的晨线掠过玻璃，谈论着小小的未来——保留哪一只时钟，茶叶放在谁的抽屉，那张打印件该挂在哪里。选择已经做出；小小的安排可以慢慢来。东长椅的预约里已经写下了你们两个人的名字，而他的句子不再提前打好草稿。当你们终于起身，他伸出手。你握了片刻，然后松开。然后你们以地面时间的步调一起走过花园环道，不慌不忙，空间站的清晨在两个不再需要翻译的人身边展开。
romance.opening: 一年的地面时间早餐，一场挺过来的僵局，还有一颗彗星之后，东长椅的预约记录里有了你的名字——他的笔迹，没有附头衔。今晚他早早到了，带着两份托盘，而且第一次，完全没有文件夹。只有一张小小的打印纸条，正面朝下放在茶旁边。你身后甲板上的信标是暗的。行星在转动。他等你走到他身边，然后做了一件你从未见他做过的事：他故意让一段沉默持续很久，并且在其中安然自得。
romance.title: 没有附件

episodes.title: The Iron Cat
episodes.opening:
Rain drums the tin roof under the overpass.

The shop is one warm yellow lamp against the blue-violet neon bleeding in from the street: shelves of drone parts, a scarred workbench, and Hayato Abe crouched at it, turning over a drone with a cracked wing, tapping the casing with a fingertip as if asking where it hurts.

He looks up when the door rattles.

Oil smudges near his temple; a prosthetic left forearm glows faint gold along the seam as he moves.

“Hayato Abe.

I fix things.

Don’t tell me what’s broken yet — the thing itself will say, and I can hear it.

Set it down and sit a while?”
episodes.dialogue:
“Set it there.”

You set the little cast-iron cat on the bench.

Its tail is a wind-up key, and somewhere inside it there used to be a music movement.

He doesn’t pick it up right away.

He winds the tail two slow turns and listens — really listens, eyes shut — to the dry grind of a cylinder that won’t turn.

“Gummed.

And one tooth on the comb’s snapped.

That’s the flat note you’ve been hearing.”

He hums a few off-key notes along with what the tune should sound like, then opens a battered notebook with a column of names and writes something under one of them.

The door bangs and an older woman comes in out of the rain, shaking her umbrella.

She holds out her right hand without a word.

Her repaired left-hand prosthesis, matte gray, waits on the counter.

“Mrs. Otsuka.

Done since Tuesday.”

He sets it in her palm.

She fits it to her wrist, then flexes it, frowns, flexes again.

“It’s… smoother?”

“Loosened the damping half a step.

You were slowing down on cold mornings.

Figured it shouldn’t fight you.”

She laughs, thanks him twice, and goes.

He writes one line under her name in the notebook and doesn’t add another word.

“Your cat needs a comb tooth I don’t stock.

It comes Thursday.

Leave it with me, or come back and sit while I chase the rust out of the cylinder.

Either way.”

He’s already turned back to the cracked-wing drone, lamp yellow on his rolled sleeves.

choices.text: You changed her wrist’s damping before she said a word about it. How did you know?
choices.response:
He half-smiles without looking up.

“Listen first, fix second.

She’s been coming three years.

Her wrist clicks on cold days — you can hear it when she signs the slip.

Machines tell you what’s wrong.

People mostly do too, if you quit rushing to answer them.”

He taps the notebook.

“That’s the job book.

Names, parts, dates.

The quirks list stays in my head.

Every regular’s machine, every regular.

Nothing I was told.

Everything I heard.”

Then he goes back to the drone, and the silence he leaves behind feels like an invitation rather than a door closing.

choices.text: (Wind the iron cat’s tail two more turns and hold it to your ear, the way he did.)
choices.response:
He watches you listen instead of talking.

The grind comes first, then — underneath it — a thinner, sadder sound.

“Hear that?

Cylinder’s salvageable.

Most people wind it once and hand it over.

You listened twice.”

He makes a small mark in the notebook and turns it so you can see: a fresh line, and it isn’t under Mrs. Otsuka’s name.

“Thursday, then.

The stool’s free.

Rain’s got hours left in it, and I’ve got a drone with a cracked wing that talks too much.”

episodes.ending:
He nods at the shelf where the iron cat sits open, cylinder soaking in a jar.

“Thursday.

Comb tooth comes with the morning delivery, and you’ll hear the tune with its missing note restored.”

The rain keeps its rhythm on the tin roof.

He goes back to the cracked-wing drone, humming half a note off key, and the yellow lamp holds the shop steady behind you all the way out into the neon.

episodes.title: The Seventh Street Lamp
episodes.opening:
Since that first Thursday you’ve come by often enough that Hayato stopped saying “sit a while” and just leaves the stool clear.

The iron cat plays its tune again, three notes still a hair flat, and he refuses to tune them.

“It’s allowed one flaw.

Makes it honest.”

Tonight the rain’s back, and on the bench lies a dented courier drone that keeps doing something strange: every route he plots, it flies a wide, stubborn arc around the old streetlight on Seventh Street.

He’s had it open for an hour, probing, saying nothing.

Tonight, unprompted, he says something.
episodes.dialogue:
“This one’s not broken.”

He turns the drone over and angles a cracked screen toward you: a maintenance log, lines of timestamps.

“Six months back.

Impact under the Seventh Street lamp: a billboard, a broken wing.

I repaired that wing.

Wiring’s fine; no sensor fault in the log.”

He closes the panel.

“It still detours.

Not a sensor fault.

I checked twice.”

His thumb runs along the drone’s scuffed shell.

“Its owner brought it back because the detour wastes power.

Same customer, same drone I repaired half a year ago.

It learned to avoid that lamp after the billboard strike.

My master taught me to listen before changing anything.

The man who ran this corner before me.”

He taps the casing gently, the way he does, as if asking where it hurts.

“Things remember a fall.

I could wipe the log, recalibrate, force it straight.

It’d obey.

But it isn’t wrong, exactly.

It’s just avoiding the place it got hurt.”

He huffs, almost a laugh, no humor in it.

“I walk around that lamp too.

Every time.

Haven’t stood under it in years.”

It’s the most he’s ever said about himself, and he says it to the drone, not to you.

He recalibrates the wing sensor without clearing its flight record, then shows you the test log: the same detour, lower power use.

“Owner still wants it straight.

I call this steadier.”

He sets it on the shelf, label side out, ready for collection, and leaves it there while he waits for your answer.

choices.text: Wipe the log. Let it fly straight — its owner would prefer that.
choices.response:
Hayato’s hand stops at the shelf.

A long minute.

“They asked.

I heard them.”

But he doesn’t wipe it.

“I kept the record.

Recalibrated the wing sensor so the detour uses less power.

It remembers a fall.

That isn’t a fault to erase.”

He re-shelves it, label out.

“The owner can see the test log at collection.

Same route, steadier flight.

That is the repair I can stand behind.”

He has answered plainly rather than promising a straight line, which is rare enough that you both let his words sit there without touching the machine.

choices.text: (Touch the drone’s scuffed shell once, lightly, and step back from the bench.)
choices.response:
He watches your hand, then the drone, then you.

“Yeah,” he says, like you’d agreed on something out loud.

He opens the notebook and, under the customer’s job record, beside the drone’s number, writes one line: avoids the light, not broken.

He squares it on the shelf himself.

“Some things you don’t fix.

You keep them company till they’re ready.”

Then, quieter, almost to the machine: “Same as people.”

He picks up the next job without ceremony, but the drone stays where he can see it from the bench, and so does the line he wrote about it.

episodes.ending:
“Thursday, if you feel like coming by,” he says.

“The stool will be clear.

Or another day; the customer can collect this without either of us making it a ceremony.”

He glances up to leave room for an answer, then goes back to his work.

The rain eases to a drizzle.

He hums two off-key notes along with the shelf’s charging hum and starts on a fan that won’t spin.

The repaired drone stays label-side out, its log intact, while he explains why he is keeping the fan’s old housing.

episodes.title: What Holds
episodes.opening:
The notice went up on the corner post this week, laminated and official: structural inspection of the overpass corner stalls; unlicensed sites to be cleared.

Hayato pinned it inside the shop, next to the door, where he’d see it every time he walked out.

He hasn’t said anything about it.

Tonight a storm is coming in hard, and the rolling shutter jams halfway — the latch at the bottom rail has sheared clean off, leaving the shop open to the rain and whatever the wind decides to carry in.

He stands in the gap, collar up, looking at the broken latch like it might explain itself.
episodes.dialogue:
“Need a second pair of hands.

Not skilled ones.

Steady ones.”

He hands you the latch plate and a screwdriver — a newer one from his apron, not the old one pinned at the bench corner.

You hold the plate against the shutter’s bottom rail while the first gusts hit the tin roof.

“Hold it there.

Don’t fight the wind.

Wait between gusts — it’ll give you a gap.”

It does.

He drives the bolts, checks the throw, runs the shutter down.

It seats with a heavy, satisfying clack.

“Good.

That holds.”

While he coils the cord, you ask about the old screwdriver — the one pinned at the corner of the workbench, handle worn smooth, position unmoved for as long as the shop has stood.

He takes a few seconds longer than he needs to answer.

“Master’s.

First thing he ever handed me.

It doesn’t get used.

It stays.”

He says it the way he tightens a bolt: once, exactly, done.

In the back of the shop, past the shelves, something sits under a canvas cover — boxy and unopened, with clean space around it and a canvas cover nobody lifts.

You’ve noticed it before.

In all the years this corner has run, nobody has asked him why it’s there.

“Inspection’s in two weeks.

If the corner doesn’t pass, they clear it.

I could fold the shop now, quietly, before it gets taken.

Or I file the permit papers and stand for it.”

He looks at the pinned notice, then at the latch he just fixed.

“I’m not a man who promises.

But I don’t fold.”

choices.text: File the papers. This corner was his, and now it’s yours — stand for it.
choices.response:
“Yours.”

He repeats the word like he’s checking its weight.

Then a short nod.

“Permit office opens at eight.

I’ll be first in line.”

He takes the notice down, unfolds it flat, and starts reading it properly, line by line, the way he listens to a machine.

“Two weeks.

Electrical, structural, fire clearance.

All fixable.”

He glances at you.

“You held a latch steady in a storm.

That’s most of the skill set for standing for something.

Come Thursday — I’ll want a witness who knows the difference between fixed and patched.”

choices.text: (Set the sheared-off latch piece on the bench beside the old screwdriver, and nod at the notice.)
choices.response:
He looks at the sheared metal next to the old screwdriver — the broken thing and the kept thing, side by side — and something settles in his face.

“Right,” he says.

He takes the notice down, smooths it on the bench, and finds a pen.

The application goes under the lamp, half filled out before the storm really lands.

“I was going to file it either way,” he says.

“But I write slower when nobody’s watching.

Stay and watch.

It goes faster.”

And it does — you hold the paper against the curl of the wind, and he writes like a man who has decided.

episodes.ending:
Rain hammers the tin roof; the shutter holds.

He finishes the permit application under the yellow lamp, leaving the witness line blank.

“Thursday, if you want to stand with me,” he says.

“No signature needed tonight.”

The canvas-covered shape in the back stays covered, patient as ever.

Two weeks to an inspection, and for the first time all week, Hayato hums along with the wind instead of fighting it.

episodes.title: The Unfinished Drone
episodes.opening:
The inspection passed.

The notice came down from beside the door and Hayato filed it in a drawer without ceremony, which for him is a parade.

Tonight the repair queue is empty — a rare, ringing quiet under the overpass, just rain and the lamp.

He wipes the bench twice, which he only does when he’s stalling.

Then he walks to the back, takes a breath you can see, and lifts the canvas off the boxy shape you have never once asked about.
episodes.dialogue:
“You never asked.

Most people never notice what stays covered.”

Under the canvas is a drone — old frame, hand-soldered joints, a wing assembly half-built and frozen mid-thought.

A thin layer of dust lies on its body; the edges around it are clean.

He has always wiped around it, never the machine itself.

“Master’s first.

His whole life he never finished it.

He’d start, stop, start again.

When he died, it was exactly this: half a wing, no cover, no answer.”

He sets it on the bench between you, dead center, under the best light.

“This shop is his craft, kept going.

That’s not a secret I tell people.

It’s the only one I have.”

He turns the half-built wing over in his hands, careful as if it were a wound.

“I’ve had every part to finish it for three years.

Every part.

I keep finding reasons it isn’t the right night.

Here’s the truth of it — the day it flies, I’m out of excuses.

No more ‘almost done.’

He’s finished being almost here.

It would just be gone, all the way.”

He looks at you then, straight on, which he almost never does.

“I can’t do the last of it alone.

I’ve tried.

So — help me finish it.

Sit at this bench with me, nights, until it flies.

I’m better with machines than words.

About the only thing I’ve got to brag about.

So I’ll say the rest plain: I don’t want the stool empty.

And I don’t want it empty just for the drone.”

The rain fills the silence he leaves.

His hands are still on the wing.

He doesn’t take his eyes off you.

choices.text: Then say it plainer. I’ll be here for the drone — and for you. If that’s what you’re asking.
choices.response:
For a moment he doesn’t move at all.

Then he exhales, long, like a valve releasing.

“Yeah,” he says.

“That’s what I’m asking.”

He reaches over and turns the lamp a shade brighter, and the corner of his mouth goes up and stays there.

“Fair warning.

I don’t say much.

What I do is show up and fix things.

If that’s enough —” he sets the wing down between you, closer to your side of the bench — “then it starts tonight.”

He slides the second stool around so you’re both facing the work, and for the first time in three years he picks up the soldering iron for that drone without hesitating.

choices.text: (Pull the second stool to the bench and start sorting the parts tray by size, smallest first.)
choices.response:
He watches you sort — washers, shims, the tiny screws smallest first — and something in his shoulders lets go.

“Good hands.

Patient ones.

That’s what this bench needs.”

He pulls his stool around so you’re both facing the drone and slides the tray to the middle, shared.

“Partner at the bench, then.

Not staff, not customer.

A friend who chooses to work beside me.”

He picks up the soldering iron, hesitates one breath over the half-built wing — and doesn’t put it down.

“Nights, until it flies.

You and me and his last stubborn project.”

It isn’t everything he didn’t say.

But it’s said, and it’s true.

episodes.ending:
The lamp burns late.

The half-wing takes its first new joint in three years, and the second stool stays at the bench, not across from it.

Outside, the rain lets up around midnight and neither of you notices.

The shop’s only secret isn’t a secret anymore, and under the yellow light it stops being a weight and starts being a project.

episodes.title: Quiet Static
episodes.opening:
Spring again, or near it — the overpass drips instead of pours, and the neon reads softer through the mist.

It’s a first-Sunday morning, which has come to mean one thing under this overpass: the free-repair bench is open.

A folding table, a hand-lettered sign, a line of neighbors with toasters, fans, and one memorable waffle iron.

Hayato works the bench; you keep the list, matching names to pending jobs in his battered notebook.

Since the night you pulled up that second stool, the master’s drone has come apart and gone back together more times than either of you can count.

Tonight, after the line is gone, is the night it flies.
episodes.dialogue:
“Last one’s done.

Waffle iron’s got years left.

Tell Mrs. Otsuka her hand’s ready Thursday — I loosened the elbow this time.”

You close the notebook.

The street empties.

He doesn’t move toward the shutters.

He stands at the back bench, where the drone sits assembled for the first time — whole wing, closed cover, hand-soldered seams holding.

“It’s ready.

Been ready a week.

I kept finding one more wire to re-dress.”

He turns it over once, gently, the old habit, as if asking where it hurts.

Nothing hurts.

“You know what I was afraid of.

That the day it flew, I’d be out of excuses.

That he’d be gone all the way, no ‘almost done’ left to hide behind.”

He sets it on the empty stretch of pavement past the lamp.

“So here’s what I figured out, late, like I figure everything out.

Finishing it doesn’t end him.

It’s the opposite.

Everything he taught me is in my hands right now.

It flies because of that.

He’s not almost here.

He’s here.”

He opens the throttle.

The drone lifts — wobbles, catches, rises clean past the lamp’s yellow circle into the blue-violet dark, and hums a steady circle over the corner.

Hayato hums along with it, off-key, not caring who hears.

“Steady flight.

First time in its life.”

He lands it soft.

His eyes are wet and he doesn’t hide it, doesn’t explain it either.

He just cleans his hands on the apron, slow, done.

“First Sunday, next month, this table’s out again.

You keep the list, I keep the bench.

That’s not a favor between us.

That’s the arrangement.

Permanent.

I don’t say things twice, so — that was it.”

He looks at the drone, then at you, and nods once, the way he does when a repair is finished and true.

choices.text: Permanent, then. First Sundays — your bench, my list. It’s a deal, partner.
choices.response:
“Deal.”

He says it flat and means it completely.

“Waffle iron lady’s already told six people.

We’ll need a bigger table.”

He chalks the next date on the shutter frame where the notice used to hang — the spot where bad news lived, now holding a plan.

“You run the list your way.

I run the bench mine.

We don’t interfere.”

A beat.

“Mostly.”

He picks up the drone and carries it inside like something that finally gets to rest, and sets it — not in the back under canvas — on the front shelf, facing the door.

choices.text: (Open the battered notebook to a fresh page, write “First Sundays,” then hand it to him.)
choices.response:
He takes the notebook, reads the page, and huffs — the closest thing he has to a laugh.

“Making it official in my own book.

Sneaky.”

He signs under your line, date and all, then tears nothing out and crosses nothing out.

“Witnessed.

Binding.

That’s how it works in this shop.”

He chalks the next First Sunday on the shutter frame where the notice used to hang.

“Bigger table next month.

And the drone goes on the front shelf — facing the door.

Things that are finished get to be seen.”

episodes.ending:
Before locking up, Hayato makes sure the master’s drone is settled on the front shelf, facing the door.

The lamp goes off, and the neon takes the corner back, blue-violet and calm.

The drone sits where customers will see it, and the notebook goes back in your bag, ready for the next First Sunday.

Under the overpass, the free bench has a schedule, the shop has two people it can count on, and Hayato locks the shutter with the easy clack of a thing that will open again next month.

Some repairs end.

This one became a habit instead — the better outcome, and the one he chose on purpose.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: Straight Line
romance.opening:
The free-repair bench is packed away, the last neighbor gone home with a working kettle.

Weeks of nights at the second stool have done their work: the master’s drone sits whole on the back bench, wing closed, seams holding, finished down to the last hand-soldered joint.

Hayato has run out of small wires to re-dress and he knows it.

The rain has thinned to mist.

The lamp is yellow, the neon beyond it blue-violet, and he stands in front of the drone the way he stands in front of machines that are about to tell him something.
romance.dialogue:
“Tonight.

No more excuses — I’ve used them all.”

He turns it over once, gently, the old habit, as if asking where it hurts.

Nothing hurts.

“You know what I was afraid of.

The day it flies, I’m out of ‘almost done.’

He’s finished being almost here.”

He carries it past the lamp to the open pavement.

“But I figured something out, late, the way I figure everything.

Finishing it doesn’t end him.

Everything he taught me is in my hands right now.

It flies because of that.

He’s not almost here.

He’s here.”

Throttle open.

The drone lifts, wobbles, catches, and rises clean past the lamp into the dark, humming a steady circle over the corner.

Hayato hums with it, off-key, loud enough that you hear him smiling before you see it.

“Steady flight.

First time in its life.”

He lands it soft.

His eyes are wet.

He doesn’t hide it and doesn’t explain it.

He just looks at you, straight on, the way he almost never does.

“Three years I kept this shop so I’d have somewhere to stand still.

Then you sat down at that stool, and the shop started moving again.

So — plain, since words aren’t my craft: the drone’s finished.

We aren’t.
