She finishes her tea slowly, reluctant to end the hour, and when she stands she takes both cups to the bin without being asked, because that's who she is on a shoreline.

Friday, she says at the top of the seawall.

Bring a coat you don't love.

It's going to get splashed.

episodes.ending:
Friday's crossing is black water and stars, and when the bloom ignites under the hull — blue light tracing every wave — nobody on the boat says a thing.

Leilani leans over the rail with her hand pressed over her heart, watching the glowing wake, and for a long time she doesn't say a word, which from her says everything.

When she finally speaks, her voice is unsteady and she doesn't try to hide it.

“Logged,” she says.

Witnessed.

Better than the photographs.

The bloom trails the boat for miles, and she stays at the rail until the glow fades, and you stay beside her, and neither of you needs to explain why.

episodes.title: The Page She Never Showed
episodes.opening:
Seasons turn, and the rhythm holds: the monthly reef check, the debris runs, the standing argument about whether parrotfish or wrasse have more personality.

You have your own signal now, the one she taught you, and you use it across the station deck when the radio's too loud.

Tonight she's on the observation deck at sunset with the old logbook closed on her knees.

She pats the bench beside her, and when you sit, she keeps her hand on the cover a moment, deciding something.

The first stars are out over Tideglass Harbor, and she watches them instead of you while she gathers her words.
episodes.dialogue:
There's a page in here I've never shown anyone.

Not the childhood one — a different one.

The last page.

Years ago, on a night dive, I saw something glow that I couldn't identify.

Not a jellyfish, not an anglerfish, nothing in any key I own.

I sketched it before it faded.

I've never published it, never mentioned it, because a sketch without a specimen or a photograph is just a story, and I didn't want to be the person who tells stories.

But I've kept looking.

Every survey, every night crossing, I've kept one eye open for it.

And lately I've been thinking — maybe the reason I haven't found it is that I've been looking alone.

choices.text: Show me. And when we find it together, we'll document it properly — your name on the record.
choices.response:
She opens the page and turns it toward you: a careful pencil sketch, soft-edged, hard to believe it's just graphite.

She watches your face while you look, and whatever she finds there makes her nod once, decision made.

Together, then, she says — her sighting, your eyes, both names on the record if it ever earns one.

She starts planning out loud the way she does: which nights, which currents, what conditions it would take.

Then she stops and laughs at herself, and says the planning can wait until tomorrow.

Tonight is just for having shown someone at last.

She leaves the logbook open on her knees, sketch up, like she's finally letting it out in public.

choices.text: (Stay seated beside her, shoulder to the rail, and wait — no reaching, no hurry.)
choices.response:
She takes her time, and you let her.

When she's ready she opens the last page herself and holds it where you can see: the sketch, soft-edged and strange, hard to believe it's just pencil.

Then she goes quiet, and you go quiet with her, and the two of you sit shoulder to shoulder with the secret finally out.

She says, eventually, that she'll keep looking for it — and that it's better company now, the search, knowing someone else knows.

You nod to say you'll keep an eye out too.

She smiles and says that changes things more than you'd think.

episodes.ending:
She writes something new under the sketch — a date, and two sets of initials, yours beside hers — and labels it in her small square hand: co-witnessed, search ongoing.

Not a publication, she says, tapping the page.

A promise between documenters.

She closes the logbook and holds it a moment before stowing it in the dry bag where it lives.

Then she stands, stretches, and looks out at the dark harbor, already talking about the next survey and which nights the currents might favor.

The first stars are fully out now.

She says the search just got twice as likely, and heads for the stairs, calling back that you're welcome to come along.

speak.text: ♡ You want to be a couple

romance.title: The Last Page
romance.opening:
Since the night of the bloom, things have grown at their own pace — her rule, honored by both of you: separate houses, separate work, and a standing sunset walk on the days the tide turns.

Tonight is one of those days.

She's at the dock when you arrive, returning a spiral shell to the rocks with the same care she gave it the first afternoon you ever watched her, the old logbook under her arm, the bay calm.

She greets you with her shoulder bumping yours, easy and warm, and for a while you walk the waterline together as the sun goes down.

Then she stops at the rail, and her hand finds yours, and she goes quiet in the way that means something is being decided.
romance.dialogue:
I want to show you the last page of this.

Not the childhood entry — you've seen that.

The final page.

Years ago I saw something glow out there that I've never been able to name, and I sketched it before it faded, and I've never shown a living soul.

I've been looking for it ever since, on every survey, every night crossing.

I used to think showing anyone would take away from it.

But the bloom night taught me different — some things get bigger when you witness them with someone.

So here it is.

The last secret I have, and the one I've been saving for the person I'd want standing next to me when we finally find it.

choices.text: Show me. All of it — I'm in.
choices.response:
She opens the last page and shows you the sketch, and her eyes stay on your face while you look.

It's soft-edged and strange, hard to believe it's just graphite, and she narrates the sighting in her plain short way — the depth, the cold, the thirty seconds it burned before it was gone.

Then she closes her hand over yours on the rail and says the search is a shared one now, both names in the log when it's found.

She laughs at herself, a little teary, and blames the wind off the water.

The tide comes in under the dock, slow and steady, and she leans her head against your shoulder and watches the bay like she's daring it to glow again.

choices.text: (Step closer and simply nod.)
choices.response:
She waits, giving you room to answer or not, the tide coming in under the dock.

Your nod is answer enough.

She opens the logbook to the last page and holds it between you — the sketch, soft-edged, hard to believe it's just pencil — and watches your face while you take it in.

When you look up she's close, her forehead nearly touching yours, and she says quietly that she's shown you the last of her secrets, and it didn't take away from anything.

It made it yours too.

The last of the daylight fades, and she stays there at the rail, her hand warm around yours, in no hurry to be anywhere else in the world.

romance.ending:
By the time you both move, it's fully dark, and the first stars are out over the bay.

She talks on the walk back like a news report nobody asked for — the wrasse tucking in, the parrotfish she swears holds a grudge, the eelgrass moving with the tide — and you wouldn't trade it.

At the top of the dock she stops, holds the logbook up for a second facing the water, like a little salute to the sketch's home turf.

Then she closes it, tucks it under her arm, and laces her fingers through yours for the walk home.

She says the search starts in earnest this season — two sets of eyes, one logbook, and a whole season of good nights to pick from.

episodes.title: 转向的潮水
episodes.opening:
潮水刚转向，风停了，潮镜港的海湾很平静。

莱拉妮·凯奥哈蹲在码头边缘，潜水服卷到腰间，深色的手指捻着一只螺旋贝壳翻看，然后把它放回原处——两块长满藤壶的礁石之间的缝隙里，分毫不差。

她注意到你在看，却不慌不忙。

灯塔的白色光束扫过水面，她身后某处，研究站的无线电从敞开的窗户里响着。

她在腿上擦了擦手，站起来，先笑了再开口。
episodes.dialogue:
我叫莱拉妮。

我研究海洋生物——珊瑚礁调查、鱼类计数，所有这些，都在山上的那间研究站。

潮水刚转向，所以接下来一段时间海面会很温和。

这是我们今天能遇到的最好的一个小时。

想陪我走到浅滩去吗？

先说好：我会经常停下来。

下面有一只海蛞蝓，我整整一周都想弄清它的种类，如果它出来了，我可不会从它旁边走过去。

还有，路上看到垃圾，我们就捡起来。

这是除潜水之外我唯一的一条规矩。

choices.text: 你带路吧。我还从没和一个真正了解这片海湾的人一起看过它。
choices.response:
她笑得很干脆，把网兜往肩上一甩。

然后她沿着水线往前走，边走边讲解——哪种鱼占哪片地盘，海流怎么从防波堤的缺口过去，为什么鳗草比看上去重要。

她不断回头看你在不在身边，悄悄放慢脚步配合你。

到了浅滩，她蹲下，招手让你也蹲下，指着那只海蛞蝓——小小的，橙色衬着石头，颜色张扬得离谱。

她没有碰它。

她只是看着，也让你看，两个人都不说话，但一点不别扭。

choices.text: （蹲下来，仔细看她刚放回礁石的那只贝壳。）
choices.response:
她没等你，自己蹲到你身边，膝盖压在湿石头上，近到不用伸手就能指给你看。

那是一只螺旋贝壳，完好无损，大多数人会把它揣进口袋的那种。

你用眼神问她为什么要放回去。

她把贝壳转向光亮，让你看清里面还有一只小寄居蟹住着。

她说，这壳是它的家。带回家它就只是个摆设，留在这儿才有人住。

她把贝壳放回原来的缝隙，调整了一下，满意地坐回去。

然后她带着新的兴趣看向你，再次邀请你去浅滩走走，这次走得更慢。

episodes.ending:
回去的路上，她在一张缠在鳗草里的塑料袋前停下，一言不发地扯出来，塞进腰间的网兜。

网兜已经很沉了——瓶盖、钓线、一团缠结的绳索。

她一边干活一边闲聊，说起周四要做的珊瑚礁调查，还说有第二双眼睛帮忙，计数会顺利得多。

回到码头时天已经傍晚了，她朝研究站的船扬了扬下巴，已经在盘算明天的事。

她说，每次潜水都有新惊喜，今天这个惊喜是碰上了好的同伴。

她拎起网兜，用两根手指朝你敬了个礼，哼着不成调的曲子往山上走去。

episodes.title: 航海日志记得的事
episodes.opening:
星期四，调查船停在码头晃着，莱拉妮还没打招呼就把写字板塞到你手里。

样带线已经画好，物种清单用她小小的方方正正的字打印出来，潮汐表夹在栏杆上。

她先照例把约好的信号复习了一遍——好、停、结束潜水——让你挨个演示，直到她满意为止。

装备都收好之后，她忽然安静下来，和她平时不太一样。

她从防水袋里掏出一本破旧的航海日志，翻过多年的记录，停在靠前的一页。

那页上的字迹更圆润。

更稚嫩。
episodes.dialogue:
能跟你说件事吗？

这是我写的第一篇记录。

那时候我还小，海比我大得多，我照样怕它——又怕又爱，两种感觉同时有。

我写下来，说总有一天我要叫得出这片海湾里每条鱼的名字。

所有人都说，长大后这心思就淡了。

可它没淡。

越长大我反而越投入。

这一页我从不给人看。

总觉得那像把自己最里面的东西摊给别人看。

可你每次出海都在，没人叫你捡垃圾你也捡，学那些信号学得像它们真的很重要。

所以。

给你看了。

choices.text: 这可能是我听说过的所有航海日志里最勇敢的一篇记录。
choices.response:
她低下头，既高兴又有点不好意思，在那一页上轻敲了两下。

又怕又爱，她说——不管做什么事，这样都不赖，对吧？

她念出其中一行，那稚嫩的字迹里列着三种鱼，如今她已经能凭求偶花纹认出它们。她笑说这份清单从那以后长了多少。

整个海湾，她说。

还没做完呢。

然后她轻轻合上日志，重新挺起肩膀开始干活。

第一条样带线在等着，好潮汐不会一直有。

但你都感觉到了，你们之间有什么东西不一样了，而且干活的时候也一直都在。

choices.text: （伸出手，手掌平放在日志封面上，什么也不说。）
choices.response:
她看看你的手，再看看你，明显松了一口气。

不用说话，她轻声说。

这比你想象的少见得多。

干活时，她把日志摊开在你们中间的长凳上，时不时瞟一眼，确认它还在那儿。

调查进行得很顺——你的计数干净得她检查了两遍然后笑了，说也许该把写字板永久交给你。

回程时她没把日志收起来。

她把它放在膝盖上，拇指一直搭在那页旧记录上。

有些事不用说出口，她在码头说。

你刚刚做到了。

episodes.ending:
回到码头，她翻开一本崭新的日志，用她小小的方方正正的字在第一页顶端写下日期。

旧的那本被小心地放进防水袋。她就是舍不得。

她告诉你下个月的礁盘调查需要两条船，她已经把你的名字写进了名单——又马上补充说你可以拒绝，但她希望你别。

然后她扛起装备朝工作站走去，在坡道顶上停了一下，回头看了看平静的海湾。

episodes.title: 航道里的渔网
episodes.opening:
刚过正午，无线电里传来呼叫：北部航道外发现一只被幽灵渔网缠住的海豚，是一支渔船队报告的。

莱拉妮在通讯还没结束时就已经动了起来——摊开海图，检查刀具，把面镜摆在工作台上，发动机已经打着。

北上的一路大家都很专注，谁也不说话。前方涌浪里那道灰色的背鳍浮出水面的样子不对——被拖得下沉、倾斜。

她用平稳低沉的声音指挥全场，分配位置，就算时间紧，也让每个人把手势信号再复述一遍。

然后她最后转向你，眼神比以前任何一次都严肃。
episodes.dialogue:
下水之前，听我说。

那是单丝渔网，在尾柄上缠了两圈——一个错误的动作，它就会收紧。

我先下，我来剪，你负责观察。

如果你发出我们约好的结束潜水信号，我就上浮，不许争辩，不许等着我看还能不能再剪一刀。

我是认真的。

我当过那个多剪了一刀才肯上来的人，是队友把我拖出来的，我不再对别人做这种事了。

也盯着海豚，但更要盯着我。

说好了？

choices.text: 那我从头到尾守在观察位，我盯的是你，不只是海豚。
choices.response:
她看起来有一瞬间想争辩几句，但最后只是小小地点了一下头，点得很认真。

在水里她动作利落，刀贴着网边割，每次她抬头，你的信号已经打出去了。

海豚两次猛地挣动，渔网绷紧；两次你都打出平掌停止的手势，她就停住、等一等、换口气，再接着剪。

最后一股网线断开，海豚游了出去，船员们在船上欢呼起来。

她浮上来把面镜推到额头上，咧嘴笑着，第一件事就是看向你，打出你们练过的水面平安手势。

平安。

你把信号打回去，她在航道中间笑出了声。

choices.text: （接过船缆，在船舷边把绳子盘好备用，整个潜水过程中目光不离她的面镜。）
choices.response:
她瞥见那盘备好的缆绳，隔着面镜都能看出她放松了一点。

很好，她打出手势，翻身入水。

这次潜水她很紧张，但动作精准——她的刀在缠绕处作业，海豚有气无力地慢慢挣扎，渔网被拉得吱嘎响。

你把缆绳备好，眼睛一直没离开她；她的脚蹼挂上一个松脱的网圈时，你已经探身去抓绳子，结果她赶在你抛绳之前自己挣脱了。

最后一刀落下，海豚有力地蹬水游走，船上炸开了欢呼。

她自己爬上扶梯，摆手谢绝搀扶，浑身湿透却很得意，经过时在你肩上用力一握。

这就是我说的搭档，她说。

绳子备好了，眼睛也没离开过。

episodes.ending:
返程途中，她给自己前臂包扎得歪歪扭扭，你从她手里拿过急救包，趁她还没来得及争辩就把绷带重新缠得整整齐齐。

她任由你来，这本身就是一种信号，然后坐在船尾，绷带缠得妥妥帖帖，在上面屈伸着手指。

航道在你们身后，那道废弃的渔网还沉在渔船队报告的位置，等按计划去回收。

她在航海日志里把坐标划了两道横线，并给清除队标出了渔网的位置。

今晚那只海豚会跃出海面，她说，它不会知道我们是谁，这样最好。

她看看海豚消失的方向，又看看手臂上的绷带，自嘲地笑了——又一次被抓个正着，原来她才是那个需要被人照看的人。

episodes.title: 夜幕之后的邀请
episodes.opening:
接下来是一个月琐碎的工作：清理漂浮垃圾、填写数据表，还有她在码头上安安静静的陪伴。

然后某个傍晚，她端着两杯姜茶在防波堤上找到你，天开始变凉了，港口的灯也陆续亮了。

她挨着你坐下，递给你一杯，有一阵子你们就那么看着水面，谁也没说话。

她看起来有事想说，转着手里的杯子，转了一会儿才开口。

不管那是什么，她已经揣在心里好几天了。
episodes.dialogue:
夜航定在周五出发，黎明前回来。

大陆架外缘正在形成一场藻华——卫星过境显示的叶绿素数值，是我在这里从未见过的。

等它达到峰值，海水会发光。

生物发光，真正的蓝色火焰，每一道浪痕都是一团光。

我读过关于它的资料，看过其他观测站的照片，但我从未亲眼见过，从小小年纪把它写进观测日志起，我就一直想看。

这是一段又长又冷的航程，而且藻华不保证会按模型预测的时间达到峰值。
但我不想和一船研究人员一起去看。

我想和你一起看——以朋友的身份，或者以更亲近的关系，看你想选哪一种。

跟我来吗？

choices.text: 我跟你去。不只是为了藻华——我想和你不只是朋友。
choices.response:
她长长吐出一口气，然后笑自己居然这么紧张。“不只是朋友，”她轻声重复了一遍，“好。我也一直这么想。”

她承认，航行计划她其实已经起草过两次，又删掉两次，怕你更想睡觉。

现在她从外套里掏出折好的海图，在你们之间的石面上摊开，用一根手指描出航线，说着航向、燃油，还有她要打包的防寒装备。

事情就这么定下来了，顺理成章。

她轻轻用杯子碰了碰你的——敬藻华，她说，也敬我们。

choices.text: （举起你的姜茶，轻轻用杯子碰一下她的，然后注视她的眼睛。）
choices.response:
她立刻读懂了，整张脸都亮了。

这是答应了，她说，你确认了。她端着杯子靠回去，双手捧着，望着黑漆漆的海面。

她细数着这段航程——寒冷、耗时、时间可能对不上的风险——然后停下来说，今晚这些都不重要。

今晚就是防波堤上的茶，和跟对的人一起定计划。

她慢慢喝完茶，舍不得结束这个夜晚，起身时不用人开口就把两个杯子拿去垃圾桶，她在海边一向是这样。

周五，她在防波堤顶上说。

带一件你不那么心疼的外套。

会被浪打湿的。

episodes.ending:
周五的航程是漆黑的海水和满天星辰，当藻华在船底亮起来——每一道浪都被照成蓝色——船上安静了下来。

莱拉妮俯身在栏杆上，一只手按在心口，看着发亮的尾迹，好一阵子一句话也没说，对她来说，这已经是最高评价了。

当她终于开口，声音有点不稳，她也不打算掩饰。

记录在案，她说。

亲眼见证。

比照片好多了。

藻华追着船绵延数英里，她一直待在栏杆边直到光暗下去，你留在她身旁，你们谁都不需要解释为什么。

episodes.title: 她从未示人的那一页
episodes.opening:
季节流转，节奏依旧：每月的珊瑚礁巡查、垃圾清理行动，还有那场关于鹦嘴鱼和隆头鱼谁更有个性的长期争论。

如今你有了自己的信号——她教你的那一个——当电台太吵时，你就在站台的甲板上用它。

今晚，她坐在观景台上，膝盖上放着一本合上的旧航海日志，天快黑了。

她拍了拍身旁的长椅，等你坐下后，她的手在封面上停了片刻，像是在下决心。

她望着港口上空刚出来的几颗星星，没看你，慢慢斟酌着措辞。
episodes.dialogue:
这里面有一页，我从未给任何人看过。

不是童年那页——是另一页。

最后一页。

多年前，在一次夜潜中，我看到了一种发光的东西，我无法辨认。

不是水母，不是鮟鱇鱼，我手头所有的检索图鉴里都没有。

在它消失之前，我把它画了下来。

我从未发表过，从未提起过，因为没有标本或照片佐证的素描只是一个故事，而我不想成为那种只会讲故事的人。

但我一直在寻找。

每一次调查，每一次夜间巡航，我都留一只眼睛留意着它。

最近我一直在想——也许我一直没找到它的原因，是我一直在独自寻找。

choices.text: 给我看看。等我们一起找到它，就正式记录在案——署上你的名字。
choices.response:
她翻开那一页，转向你：一幅很细致的铅笔素描，画得挺柔和。

她观察着你的表情，而她在你脸上看到的一切让她点了点头，下定了决心。

那就一起找吧，她说——她的目击，你的眼睛，如果它真能载入记录，就署上我们两个人的名字。

她开始像往常一样大声规划：哪些夜晚、哪些洋流、需要什么样的光线。

然后她停下来，笑自己太心急，说规划可以留到明天。

今晚，只是终于把秘密展示给了一个人的夜晚。

她让日志摊开在膝上，素描朝着天空。

choices.text: （在她身旁坐着，肩膀靠着栏杆，静静等待——不催促，不伸手。）
choices.response:
她不急，你也由着她，身后的港湾在暮色里慢慢暗下去。

等她准备好了，她亲自翻开最后一页，举到你能看见的地方：那幅素描，边缘画得很柔和。

然后她安静下来，你也陪她安静，两个人肩并肩坐着，把这个秘密终于说了出来。

最后她说，她会继续寻找它——而且现在这份寻找有了更好的陪伴，因为知道还有另一个人知道。

你点点头，表示你也会留一只眼睛留意着。

episodes.ending:
她在素描下方写下新的内容——一个日期，两组姓名首字母，你的挨着她的——并用她那小小的方正字迹标注：共同见证，搜寻继续。

这不是发表，她敲了敲那一页说。

这是记录者之间的约定。

她合上日志，捧了片刻，然后把它放回那个防水袋里——它一直放的地方。

然后她站起身，伸了个懒腰，望向黑下来的港湾，已经开始谈论下一次调查，以及哪些夜晚洋流可能有利。

天上的星星已经出来了。

她说，搜寻的可能性一下子翻了一倍，然后朝楼梯走去，把门给你留着，万一你想跟上来。

speak.text: ♡ 你想和她成为恋人

romance.title: 潮水带来的一切
romance.opening:
自那夜海水发光之后，一切都慢慢来——这是她的规矩，你们两人都遵守：各自的家，各自的工作，以及每逢潮水转向的日子，一场雷打不动的日落散步。

今晚正是这样的日子。

你到达时，她正在码头上，把一枚螺旋贝壳放回礁石间，那份小心和你们初见那个下午一模一样。她腋下夹着那本旧观测日志，海湾很平静，天正渐渐暗下来。

她用肩膀轻轻撞了撞你的肩膀，算是打招呼，轻松而温暖。有一阵子，你们沿着水线并肩走着。

然后她在栏杆边停下，她的手找到你的手，她安静下来——那种安静，意味着有什么事正在被决定。
romance.dialogue:
我想给你看这本日志的最后一页。

不是童年那篇——你已经看过了。

是最后一页。

多年前，我在那片海上看到过一团我至今叫不出名字的光，我在它熄灭之前把它画了下来，从没给任何活人看过。

从那以后，我一直在找它——每一次调查，每一次夜航。

我以前总觉得，给任何人看都会让它变小。

但海水发光的那夜让我改了主意——有些东西，两个人一起看到，反而记得更牢。

所以，就是它了。

我最后一个秘密，也是我一直为那个人留着的秘密——那个我想在终于找到它时并肩的人。

choices.text: 我愿意。真正的分享，我加入。

然后她在栏杆上把手覆上你的手，说从现在起，这场寻找是两个人共同的了——找到它的那天，日志上会写着两个名字。

她笑自己有点眼眶发热，怪罪起海面上吹来的风。

潮水在码头下慢慢涨上来。她把头靠在你的肩上，望着海湾。

当你抬起头，她已近在咫尺，额头几乎贴着你的额头。她轻声说，她把最后一个秘密给你看了，而它没有变小。

它也变成了你的。

天色越来越暗。她握着你的手，站在原地，不急着去任何地方。

romance.ending:
等你们两人动身时，天已经全黑了，海湾上空亮起了第一批星星。

回去的路上她一直说着话，像一份没人要求的新闻播报——隆头鱼钻进礁缝过夜，那条她发誓记仇的鹦嘴鱼，随潮水起落的海草——而你一点也不想换掉这些。

然后她合上日志，夹回腋下，十指与你相扣，一起走回家的路。

她说，这场寻找从这个季节正式开始——两双眼睛，一本日志，还有大把的时间。

episodes.dialogue:
He doesn't startle at the sound of you.

He finishes a note in a small waterproof logbook, then turns with an unhurried smile.

'You picked a good time.

Building's empty, lights are down, and the jellyfish are about to rise.

They rise on their own schedule, not ours.'

He gestures you closer to the glass, keeping a careful arm's length of professional space.

'Third shelf, second bell.

She's been sluggish all week.

Watch her tonight and you can tell me if I'm right about when she moves.'

He crouches, checks a thermometer with a practiced eye, and murmurs something to the water too low to catch.

Then, over his shoulder: 'Visitors aren't usually back here after closing.

How did you get in?'

You explain — a wrong turn down the service corridor, a door propped for a delivery.

He nods slowly.

He stands, wipes his hands on his apron, and studies you with frank, gentle curiosity.

'I have two more hours of rounds.

Tanks don't care that it's late.

You can walk with me or sit and watch the jellyfish.

Either way, I'll tell you what I see, if you want to hear it.'

The jellyfish rise at 1:14, eleven minutes after his prediction, and he takes the loss with a quiet laugh and a corrected entry in his logbook.

By the time the rounds end, the sky over the service exit is starting to lighten.

He walks you to the door and hesitates there, key ring in hand.

'I'm here most nights.

If you ever take another wrong turn, the jellyfish rise around one.'

He says it plainly, like a fact, and lets you decide what to do with it.
episodes.opening:
The Night Tide City Aquarium after closing is quiet — hallway lights dimmed, just the hum of the filtration system.

You took a wrong turn past the service wing and now stand before the deep-sea tank, where a man in a dark work apron crouches with a clipboard, murmuring to the water.

A moon jelly drifts past his shoulder.

He glances up, unsurprised, and offers a small nod.
episodes.title: The Hour After Closing

episodes.dialogue:
He leads you to the ray tank, picks up a bucket of feed and a checklist, and doesn't ask how you got in anymore.

'You're becoming part of the routine.

The fish have noticed.

The checkered turtle does her lap ten minutes earlier when she hears your footsteps.'

He hands you nothing — not yet — but lets you stand inside the rail this time, past the visitor line.

Visitors stand there.

You're standing here.'

He says it lightly, like it's just a fact.

As he works through the checklist he talks, low, about what he's seen with his own eyes: an octopus that unscrews jar lids out of boredom, a lagoon ray that sulks when the filtration hum changes pitch.

'People think the night shift is lonely.

It isn't.

It's quiet, and quiet is different.'

He pauses at a valve, checks it twice against his list, and his voice drops further.

'There's a question people ask me, eventually.

Why a man my age spends his nights talking to fish.'

He leaves a long pause there.

The checkered turtle surfaces at the far end and slaps the water once, and he smiles.

You can ask it or not.

I'll answer either way.'
episodes.ending:
Afterward he walks you out through the kelp wing.

'Same time tomorrow,' he says at the door, then corrects himself.

'Or whenever.

The fish don't keep a schedule.

But I'd notice if the footsteps stopped.'

He doesn't say more than that.

He never does.

Still, it doesn't feel like a brush-off.
episodes.opening:
Two weeks later, your wrong turns are just visits.

The night guard waves you through now without looking up from his crossword.

You find Mateo in the kelp wing, sleeves rolled, organizing a wall of valves and brushes in an order that looks like chaos until you realize every handle faces the same way.

He hears you before he sees you.

'Evening,' he says to the tank, then turns with that calm smile.

'The turtle's been asking about you.

In her way.'
episodes.title: The Question People Ask

On the workbench lies a maintenance log thick as a brick, open to a page dense with his small even handwriting.

'Filter three,' he says finally, without turning.

'Its readings dip every night around three.

Just for a few minutes.

The sensors say nothing's wrong.

But the young ray — the spotted one, tank seven — she keeps rubbing herself against the intake screen at exactly that hour.

Same spot, every night.'

He turns, and he looks tired.

'I've been staying past my shift to watch her.

Last night I stayed until five.

The data and the fish disagree, and I've decided to trust the fish.'

He spreads the log open wider — weeks of his own off-hours, timestamps, sketches of the ray's position against the screen.

'I filed a request for a manual inspection of that filter.

It might take the city weeks to approve it.

Budget, paperwork.

Meanwhile she keeps scraping herself.'

He rubs the back of his neck.

'I can adjust the flow by hand each night.

It's an hour of extra work, and it's a patch, not a fix.

But it's something I can do tonight, with my own hands, while the paperwork takes forever.'

He picks up the flow valve key and weighs it in his palm, looking at you.

'You didn't have to come tonight.

The fish and I both noticed that you did.'
episodes.ending:
The hand adjustment takes just under an hour, and he narrates it the whole way — pressure here, resistance there, the ray circling to watch from a respectful distance.

When it's done, the readings hold steady through the three o'clock hour for the first time in weeks.

The inspection request is still in the city's queue; the patch is still a patch.

But the ray stops scraping the screen that night, and Mateo writes the time in the log like it matters, because to him it does.
episodes.opening:
The message came at noon, six words: 'Filter three.

Tonight, if you can.'

Now you push into the pump room past midnight and find it cold and loud, pipes sweating along the walls.

Mateo stands at the workbench with a flashlight between his teeth, cross-referencing two printouts that clearly disagree.

When he sees you, he takes the flashlight out of his mouth and looks, for one unguarded second, relieved.

'You came.

Good.

I could use eyes that aren't mine.'
episodes.title: What the Fish Knows

Mateo goes very still, the way he does when something matters.

'I don't — say things well,' he says.

'So I'll say this once, plainly.

I don't want you as a visitor anymore.

I want the mornings too.

The bad ones, the gray ones, the ones where nothing goes right.'

When he finishes, he doesn't look away; he just watches you and slowly smiles, and you smile back.
choices.text: Then I choose the dawn. With you.

'Good.

It has the best view of the pool, and it's held every friend I've ever made here.'

He stays beside you, a careful hand's width away, and the two of you watch the anemones open in the dark.

'Dawn comes on its own either way.

I'm glad you're here tonight.'

episodes.dialogue:
He's at the touch tank when you arrive, sleeves wet to the elbow, letting a hermit crab walk across his palm.

'Good timing,' he says.

'Two things tonight, and I've been rehearsing one of them for a week, which for me is practically a speech.'

He sets the crab down gently and dries his hands.

'First thing.

The city approved the inspection for filter three.

A real fix, real parts.

I put your name in the report — you were the witness the night we confirmed it, and the inspector wanted to know who'd stood there and seen it.

The inspector asked if you were staff.

I said no.'

He pauses.

'I said you were the person who watches the water with me.

She seemed to understand.'

He leads you out of the pump wing, down the dim corridor, to the small tide pool exhibit near the exit — the one with the bench in front of it, where the building's last window shows the harbor.

He sits, and pats the bench beside him, and doesn't fill the silence with fish facts for once.

'Second thing.

My days off are Tuesdays.

I've spent three years of Tuesdays sleeping until noon and reading marine reports nobody assigned me.

Last Tuesday I caught myself wishing it were a night so I'd have a reason to be here.

That's when I knew I had to say something.'

He turns to you, and the calm smile is there, but nervous underneath it.

'There's a place up the coast where the tide goes out before dawn and the sand is full of things that only exist for an hour.

Starfish, glass shrimp, the light coming up over the water.

I've always gone alone.

I'd like to show you.

But you should know what you're choosing between — that's a dawn, and it's early, and it's mine to share.

Or this bench is here, and the nights are here, and friendship doesn't need a sunrise to be real.

I'd be glad with either.

Truly.'
episodes.ending:
The tide pool anemones close around two, and Mateo walks you out the same as always, holding the door with his shoulder.

'The report comes out Friday,' he says at the threshold.

'Filter three, fixed properly.

Your name's in it.'

He looks at the harbor, then back at you.

'I'm not going to forget any of this.

None of it.'
episodes.opening:
Three weeks.

The ray in tank seven swims easy now, and Mateo has started leaving a second stool inside the rail — not offered, just there, every night.

Tonight there's an envelope tucked under it with the aquarium's seal.

He's waiting by the touch tank, and something in his posture is different: shoulders straight, hands still, like a man who's finally worked up the nerve to say something.
episodes.title: The Bench and the Dawn

He's different in small ways.

And he talks more, still low, still leaving gaps, but filling them faster when you're there.

'The ray's fully grown,' he tells you, walking the rounds.

'She runs the tank now.

The new juveniles get out of her way.'

He stops at the deep-sea tank, the first one, where it started.

'I got a letter last month.

A university, of all places.

They read the filter three report — the one with your name in it — and they want me to consult on a coastal monitoring project.

Part-time.

Days, mostly.'

He laughs, short and disbelieving.

Daylight.

I told them I'd think about it.'

He leans on the rail.

A year ago I knew the exact hour the jellyfish would rise and I couldn't have told you what I wanted for myself.

He takes a thermos from his bag, pours two cups, and hands you one.

The university letter stays pinned to the pump room corkboard, and he takes the consultancy — one daylight day a week, he reports, squinting like a mole, but grinning about it.

The tours continue on the first Friday of each month. Beside the sign-up sheet, Mateo leaves you an invitation: 'Bench division. Come as a guest whenever you like.'

episodes.opening:

You find him at the deep-sea tank, the first one, where the jellyfish rise around one.

He hears your footsteps and doesn't turn.

'Punctual,' he says.

'The fish will be pleased.

So will I.'
episodes.title: The Bench, One Year On

Better.

The jellyfish begin to rise behind the glass, right on his schedule, and he watches them for a moment before going on.

He sets the closed sea glass box on the bench between you, then lifts it and holds it out. You take it — and take his hand with it, deliberately, your fingers closing over his in plain answer.

'I'm saying yes,' you tell him.

'To being closer.

To mornings, sometimes.

To ours — the grammar isn't that hard.'

Mateo looks at your joined hands, taking in every detail, then laughs — low, unguarded, real.

'Ours,' he repeats, testing the word.

You tuck the closed box safely into your pocket. He walks you out through the kelp wing, and at the door he doesn't let go until you do.

'Same time tomorrow,' he says.

The fish have their schedule.

We're working on ours — together.'

The touch tank is drained for its annual cleaning, and Mateo has commandeered the bench by the harbor window instead — two cups, a thermos, and a small flat box he keeps not-quite-looking at.

When your footsteps come down the corridor he exhales, long, like he's been holding it since Tuesday.

'Sit,' he says.

'The tank's empty, the night's quiet, and I've finally found the words.

Most of them.

The important ones, at least.'
romance.title: The Grammar of Ours
